en: [1] Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, in the section on the Determination of Time (*Kālanirṇaya*).
The First Chapter: An Exposition on the Specific Applications of the Year, the Solstice, and the Particular Months for Specific Ritual Acts.
May Gaṇapati grant you auspiciousness, when he is well-pleased.
Even Brahmā falters in his power to influence even the most trivial action; yet,
when that good fortune has arisen— made easily attainable by prostrating at his feet— even the sovereign splendor of Indra enters the lap of a pauper without restraint.
May that Goddess of Speech herself, who eternally sits upon the lion-throne of the tongue of Puṇyahiraṇyagarbha, bestow upon you abundant blessings— she,
by the moonlight of whose stainless, tender toe-nails the ocean of poetry surges forth.
The nectar-ocean of the Word-Brahman sports unrestrainedly within the minds of the wise.
Homage to that Śiva, the very nature of the creation, dissolution, and protection of the universe; to him whose lotus feet sever the flood of afflictions for those who bow before them;
and to him who assumes vast bodies for his manifold, spontaneous, and unrestrained divine play.
Even for the sake of establishing the true state of reality, which is not found by reciting the words of the three Vedas.
[2] O charming one, this new praise of you, Kṛṣṇa, is truly heart-stirring;
you know how I have quickly displayed my cleverness in acting (*bharate*).
For that beloved alone understands whatever you do, O Aśubharate.
Thus addressed, Madhuvana, his face turned toward the answer, protected you by embracing his beloved. || 4 ||
May those rays of the Lord, the Sun— the Master of Day— which dispel the distress of those in calamity, sever for you the misfortunes of setting out upon the path to the city of Death (Kṛtānta);
for by them, through compassion, it is as if the entire world is being fashioned anew as if out of gold.
The circle of the quarters of the sky appears as if fashioned from the passion of scattered colored powders. || 5 ||

King Siṃhaśakti, known as Saṅghaṇa, the lord of the earth and the ornament of monarchs, who possesses eyes like the rājīva lotus, reigns victorious in the world; he has appeared in the lineage of the full and cool-rayed moon.
His son was Jaitrapāla, whose splendor was like that of Indra over the circle of the earth.
From this [lineage] was born King Kṛṣṇa, a vessel for glories that cause wonder. || 6 ||
There exists a king, whose pair of feet shine with a mass of long rays from the jewels upon the crowns of his soldiers, causing rival heroes to lose their pride; he who,
through the hundreds of wonderful deeds of his son Soma, has, as it were, deluded the quarters of the world.
His younger brother, the illustrious King Mahādeva, has inscribed this panegyric upon the wall.
From Kailāsa, where the fame of Gaurī’s lord is sung by the young women of his retinue languid with playfulness,
to Suvela, which borders the shore exhausted by the waves of the tossing ocean;
from the easternmost mountain to the westernmost as well, [the earth] trembles at his command.
The sovereign lords, with their heads bowed in the form of cupped hands, uphold the command of the kings.
In battles, these heroes, having incurred debt to their enemies, instantly cast off various afflictions by producing the pleasure of service;
from this [king], they receive unconditioned happiness, and thus his fame—
It reaches out toward the circle of the quarters as if to bring the guardians of the directions to bear witness.
Hearing of his virtue— that which daily causes the ranks of those who have attained the path of a hundred thousand [arrows] through ease to remember the wonder of his satisfied and noble deeds—
those very enemies, now appearing as supplicants, shall meet him in great battles.
Even upon encountering his arm, the armies and the wretched alike go to their destruction.

[The city] where the rows of serpents are agitated by the sudden flight of flocks of mongooses terrified by the roar of the lion king echoing from the high, dense caves and hollows of the formidable trees;
[a city] where the floods of feverish terror swell whenever its pair of serpent-like arms are remembered.
Alas, the enemies, as they leap over the earth and its mountains, fall into a swoon.
Having observed that he has bestowed upon supplicants the wish-granting gem, the cow of plenty, and the celestial tree,
I suspect what [could possibly remain] of his entire—
Even the Lord of the Gods became a giver of his hand. || 12 ||
He has a name, Hemādri, who is the master of all auspicious undertakings;
and by his own generosity, he is indeed the master of all auspicious undertakings.
Therefore, in a lineage purified by irreproachable conduct and illustrious fame, there appeared one whose splendor was as bright as the moon;
Vāsudeva manifested here in a playful incarnation.
Therefore, the twice-born Kāmadeva manifested himself. || 94 ||
Then there was born to him a son of most excellent form, whose fame is sung throughout the entire earth as Hemādri;
for though equal in name, he surpassed his father in conduct.
For the Mountain of Gold does not seek praise from anything else. ||15||
That lord of the illustrious administration possessed a certain marvelous skill in writing,
by which the walls of the quarters were quickly filled with panegyrics of his fame.
Having wiped away with sacred ash the evil writing inscribed by the Creator upon the forehead of a person,
he then writes this auspicious one.
And the ritual rule also authorizes what is variegated. ||17||
Reflecting upon this again and again,
our minds are filled with wonder,
for he is capable of recollecting the knowledge acquired in his previous births.
That which, having been given, is forgotten in an instant. || 18 ||
I believe that the ocean, filled by the surging waves of the water offered by him,

never at any time— even at the end of a kalpa— assumes a state made perilous by the affliction of drying up; moreover, having thus determined the ocean to be his guarantor for its stability, the enemy of the Daityas [Vishnu] has remained steadfast.
Free from anxiety, one sleeps upon the couch-like bodies of the foremost of serpents. || 18 ||
How can we describe that wondrous essence which has produced a rain of gifts,
wherein the incomparable fame of other donors becomes like a mere row of grass;
for it swallows up the mud of the people's suffering when it falls upon the earth in abundance, and [satisfies] the needs of those who seek.
It wipes away the mark of sin inscribed upon the surface of the forehead and placed upon the palms of the hands. ||20||
Surely that host of gods, having been satiated by that, lost their appetite for the nectar of the moon;
may the waning of the moon be eclipsed by his fame.
Sins that have increased through rivalry bear fruit [in this way]. || 21 ||
The limit of heroes, a treasury of glories, the sole refuge of prosperities, the foremost among givers, the ancestral home of the arts,
a teacher of wit and disposition, the leader of the wise, and the unique abode of the doctrine of non-duality for the virtuous.
There has never been, nor does there exist, nor will there ever be another superior to Hemādri-sūri.
This one, renowned as Hemādri, surely bears the guise of a brahmin;
for he possesses noble progeny.
They say his right arm is the wish-fulfilling tree. ||23||
Then, observing that the three worlds were impoverished of the Dharma through the power of the Kali age,
he set his mind upon bringing them benefit.
And a beautiful wish-fulfilling gem appeared. ||24||
And therein,
having spoken of four sections— named Vrata, Dāna, Tīrtha, and Mokṣa— by means of four chapters (khaṇḍas);
The section on the remainder (pariśeṣakhaṇḍa) is now composed for the purpose of describing those remaining matters. || 25 ||

In this regard, first is the section on the deities, followed by the determination of time; then the ripening of karmas, and finally the compendium of characteristics. These are the four great topics here, presented in their proper sequence. (26)

[6] Therein, Hemādri, the presiding lord of the instruments of action, establishes the determination of time (kālanirṇaya), which is useful for the collection of rites such as the observances and gifts previously mentioned.
In that regard, the true nature of time is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"This blessed Time is beginningless, infinite, undecaying, and immortal;
because it is all-pervading, independent, and the self of all, it is the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*)."
There are many Brahmās, Rudras, and others such as Nārāyaṇa;
yet the Lord is indeed one, remembered as Time, the Seer, and the Sovereign.
By time alone they are created, and by that same time they are again swallowed;
this is the dissolution of the three—the Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, and Īśāna—into primordial nature (prakṛti).
Through the conjunction of time, rebirth occurs once again;
so too do the supreme Brahman, all beings, Vāsudeva, and Śaṅkara. Therefore, the universe is of the nature of time, and he alone is the Supreme Lord.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Time (kāla), which is without beginning or end, is remembered as Rudra and Saṅkarṣaṇa;
because of his reckoning of all beings, he is celebrated as Kāla."
Being without beginning or end, he is the Great Supreme Lord;
because he is subtler than even a moment, he is indeed more subtle than the subtle.
O fortunate one, the subtlety of that most subtle time, which is the supreme abode,
is difficult to discern even for yogins.
When a thousand lotus petals are indeed pierced by a needle,
an ignorant person thinks they are pierced simultaneously;
yet, O twice-born one, they are pierced in temporal succession— that is its subtlety.

[7] Although such a subtle entity, being without beginning or end, is indeed indivisible, nevertheless, its divisibility is established through the activities of the sun and other planets, which possess beginnings and ends. Since the continuum of these activities is without beginning or end—like the continuum of seeds and sprouts—it is possible for even time, though without beginning or end, to be delimited.
And so it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O twice-born ones, although that [time] is exceedingly subtle and likewise vast..."
The mental calculation should be understood by the wise according to the motion of the planets.
Likewise, the determination of time through such means as the closing of the eyes, which are perceptible to people like us, has been explained in that very same place:
"A *mātrā* equal to the duration of a short syllable is proclaimed to be a *nimeṣa*. A time even more subtle than this cannot be perceived, O best of the Bhṛgus."
Just as a substance cannot be perceived when it is extremely subtle down to the level of an atom,
so too two *nimeṣas* (twinklings of an eye) are to be known as one *truṭi*, and ten *truṭis* are recorded as one *prāṇa*.
Six breaths constitute one *nāḍikā*, and sixty of those are known as a *nāḍikā*;
sixty of those *nāḍikās* are always proclaimed to be a single day and night (*ahorātra*).
Thirty muhūrtas are likewise proclaimed to constitute a day and night;
among these, O Rāma, fifteen are said to always move by day.
But as the sun gradually advances toward the northern quarter,
O mighty-armed one, the day increases accordingly.
O Rāma, just as the day undergoes increase,
so too is the increase of the muhūrtas dependent upon it proclaimed.
O Rāma, as the days increase, so too does the decrease of the nights;
likewise, one should know that there is a corresponding decrease in the muhūrtas dependent upon them.
And when the sun gradually reaches the southern quarter,
a corresponding decrease in the length of the day should be understood to occur.
When that [day] decreases, its muhūrtas likewise decrease;
and those dependent on the night increase, and the increase of the night occurs in the same manner.
When the thousand-rayed sun enters Aries and Libra, day and night are equal;
that time is designated by the term *viṣuva*.

Thus, the time delimited by a solar motion whose constituent parts are two such motions—delimited by the time of actions such as the winking of an eye—is the object of the conventional usage "truti" (a moment). In this same way, other conventions such as *prāṇa* and *vināḍikā* are to be understood; and thus, by means of the constituent parts beginning with the *truti*, the day and night (*ahorātra*) is produced. And that [day and night] is shown to be of three kinds in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"The civil day and night (*sāvana*) would be from sunrise to sunrise of the sun."
Thirty minutes (nāḍīs) constitute one degree of the zodiac; the lunar day (tithi) is the duration of the moon's passage through that degree.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara, however, the day and night (ahorātra) is shown to be fourfold:
"A single lunar day (tithi) is proclaimed as a day in the lunar measurement,
and a single day and night is remembered as a civil day (sāvana)."
A solar day is said to be by means of the Sun's passage through its portion;
a sidereal day is recorded as being by means of the Moon's passage through a lunar mansion.
The definition of the lunar day (tithi) and its divisions is shown in that very same place:
"O Bhārgava, when there is a measurement of time by means of the motion of the moon and the sun, I shall then explain [the matter] based on their motion."
[9] By means of a complete circle (bhagaṇa), the twelve zodiac signs (rāśi) are to be known; and a thirtieth part of a sign is then designated as a degree (bhāga).
O Rāma, when the moon is at a distance of twelve parts from the sun, that is designated as a lunar day (tithi).
Also in the *Skandapurāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"O Goddess, the Great Kalā is said to consist of a sixteenth part of the *amā* [digit];
she is the supreme *māyā*, abiding as the sustainer of the bodies of embodied beings."
O fair-faced one, those very digits of the moon, beginning with the new moon and ending with the full moon,
are declared to be the sixteen lunar days (tithis).
In this way, the month has also been shown by the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) to be of three kinds:
the lunar month is from new moon to new moon; the solar month consists of thirty days;
and the solar month is also described by those who know it as being marked by the sun's transit (saṃkrānti).

In the expression "from the new moon" (*darśāt*), the ablative case is used with the elision of a verbal root; the meaning is that starting from the first day of the bright fortnight following the new moon, it ends at the new moon.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"The lunar month, beginning with the bright fortnight and ending with the new moon, consists of thirty solar days."
As long as the sun remains in a single zodiac sign, for that duration of time it is "with the sun" (sabhāskara).
In the Jyotiḥsiddhānta, however, four kinds of months are shown:
the first is the solar month (sāvana), the second is said to be the lunar (cāndra),
the third would be the sidereal (nākṣatra), and the fourth is the solar (saura) month.
[10] In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* as well, the fourfold nature of the month is declared: "O Rāma, the moon exceeds the sun by six zodiac signs within half a month; of this there is no doubt."
By means of twelve parts, in due order on each lunar day,
the moon is joined with the sun at the end of the dark fortnight.
Starting from one conjunction of the moon and sun, and continuing to the next conjunction,
that period is designated by the wise as a lunar month (cāndra-māsa).
Likewise, thirty solar risings are recorded in a *sāvana* month;
a *saura* (solar) month is proclaimed by the Sun’s transit through a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*);
and a *nākṣatra* (lunar/stellar) month is said to consist of the revolution through all the asterisms (*ṛkṣa*).

The lunar month, however, has been shown by the author of the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* to be of two kinds according to regional custom: the lunar month is also twofold, beginning either with the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣādi*) or with the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇādi*). Some do not accept the month that begins with the dark fortnight;
even for those who do accept it, it is not desired south of the Vindhya mountains.

And so it is heard in the Taittirīyaka: "Having completed the months with the new-moon sacrifice (amāvāsyā), they omit a day; for by means of the new-moon sacrifice they will complete the months. Having completed the months with the full-moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī), they omit a day; for by means of the full-moon sacrifice they will complete the months. Likewise, in this Mahāvārtika, [the term] *paurṇamāsa* is used because those learned in grammar have stated that it means "that in which there is a full moon" (*pūrṇamāso ’smin*).
And because of the scriptural illustration: "In the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the śrāddha should be performed day after day.
For this very reason, in order to include both types of lunar months:
In whichever month and on whichever day misfortune arises,
that month should be understood as the "limit of the joint" (parvānta) with respect to the occasional rite.

Thus, even by Jyotir-Gārgya it is stated in general that "the end of the lunar phase [is the time for rites]. Furthermore, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is said to be the annual one (*pratisāṃvatsarika*), and for the annual rite, the lunar month alone is prescribed;
for it is said in the scriptural statement: "In the annual ancestral rite (*pitṛkārya*), the lunar month is praised."
The number of days for each month according to the different measures is shown in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"In the case of the lunar measure (*māna*), a month consists of twenty-seven days;
in the remaining measures, a month is recorded as consisting of thirty days."

Some maintain that the word *māsa* should be understood as denoting all four types of months previously mentioned, just as words such as *go* have multiple meanings. Others, however, say: the word *māsa* specifically denotes the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*). This is because Vedic usage—such as in the passages, “A year consists of thirteen months,” “There is a thirteenth month,” and “The gods are worshipped in the half-month; offerings are made to the ancestors month after month”—refers exclusively to the lunar month. Therefore, like words such as *yava* or *varāha*, it does not have its primary application everywhere. This is confirmed by Amarasimha’s lexicon: “The two fortnights, bright and dark, are the two halves; the month consists of both. Otherwise, he would have simply said “lunar month” (*cāndramāsa*). Thus, it is established that among other designations, the word *māsa* refers specifically to the lunar month. Furthermore, the Purāṇas and other texts state, “A month consists of two fortnights. Nor is a commonality of “month-ness” (*māsatva*) perceived or logically possible across all four types of months. Since usage for other types of months can be explained through other means, and out of fear of postulating multiple powers (*śakti*) for the word, the lunar month alone is the primary meaning of *māsa*. On this point, some say: words such as *Caitra* and *Vaiśākha* denote a month associated with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) joined with a specific constellation (*nakṣatra*), such as Citrā, Viśākhā, or Anurādhā. This is according to Pāṇini’s rule: “Time joined with a constellation [is named], and when the full moon occurs in that [constellation], it is so designated as a name” (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 4.2.3). Here, “joined with a constellation” means joined with any one such as Viśākhā, which then receives the designation *Vaiśākha* and so on. And the conjunction with a constellation is the basis for the designation even if it occurs only partially, rather than in its entirety.

And so it is said in the *Śaṅkaragītā*: "When there is a connection with a lunar mansion by even half a quarter of the first [tithi], that tithi is joined even in its half; it does not, however, become the opposite."

The month in which that full moon occurs is designated by the term "Vaiśākha" and so forth; the rule "in the sense of a conventional name" (*saṃjñāyām*) establishes its status as a conventional (rūḍhi) word. And thus says Cyavana: "The last two months and the third [from the end] should be known as having three lunar days (*tribha*); Phālguna is also considered to have three."
"The remaining months are to be known as divided into two [parts] according to the arrangement beginning with Kṛttikā. Also, in the Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa:
"Two by two [are the parts] of the stars beginning with Citrā when joined with the full moon."
The months beginning with Caitra are to be known by groups of three, ending with the sixth and including the seventh.

Therefore, the designation of [the months] as Vaiśākha and so forth due to their conjunction with the asterisms Viśākhā and others means that conjunction with an asterism is to be respected. And thus says Viṣṇu:
"If the month of Māgha should be joined with Maghā, and if the month of Vaiśākha should be joined with Viśākhā..."

As for the example cited by the author of the *Vṛtti*—namely, "Pauṣī" from its conjunction with the Puṣya asterism—that was intended for the easy understanding of students. His intention was that this is not a case where the meaning of the constituent parts is lost through connection (as in the word *aśvakarṇa*), but rather, like the word *udbhid*, it has some basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) established in one way or another. Furthermore, the grammatical derivation of the base and suffix should be understood just as in the case of the word *go*: from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍo*, "that which goes" is a *go*. Consequently, regarding the word *vaiśākha*, there is no room for various speculative constructions such as whether it refers to the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the asterism, their conjunction, the full moon day conjoined with that asterism, the asterism conjoined with that [full moon], or the conjunction associated with that full moon; for the authority of traditional usage (*āgama*) prevails, and thus it is untenable to treat it as being equivalent to words like *aśvakarṇa*. Therefore, it is established that words such as *vaiśākhī* denote the time characterized by the full moon day conjoined with the aforementioned asterism, while words such as *vaiśākha* denote the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*) beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*pratipad*) up to the new moon (*darśa*), which contains that full moon day conjoined with the respective asterism. [Question: How then is the term *vaiśākha* applied to the solar month (*sauramāsa*)? [Answer: In that case too, the authority of traditional usage exists.

Regarding this, some say: [the term *vaiśākha*] is secondary (*gauṇī*) because of the fault of postulating multiple potencies (*aneka-śakti-kalpanā-doṣa*). For the usage of terms such as *vaiśākha* with respect to the lunar month is established among experts (*abhiyukta*) within the scriptures (*śāstra-sthā*), whereas it is not so established for the solar month. And the usage established in scripture is more authoritative than that which is merely worldly (*laukikī*), since it is likewise possible to explain it as being secondary. Thus they say: "The usage established in scripture is more authoritative because it is based on that [scriptural authority]; however, worldly usage may be interpreted even as being secondary."
That is incorrect, because there is no distinction between the two established usages. Thus says Gārgya Jyotiṣa:
"The solar month is prescribed for marriage and the like; the *sāvana* [lunar] month is remembered for sacrifices and the like;
and the lunar month is praised for annual rites and ancestral ceremonies."
Bṛhaspati says that in the month of saura Caitra, there is an abundance of success in wealth; Varāhamihira speaks of it [in the saura month];
Parāśara speaks of Caitra, while Pauṣa is said to bestow misfortune.
"The four months beginning with Āṣāḍha are not conducive to auspiciousness," as declared by certain twice-born ones, and so forth.
And Baudhāyana says:
"When Hari has fallen asleep in Cancer, the raising of Indra’s banner takes place in Āśvina;
one should awaken the Goddess in Libra, and Janārdana in Scorpio."
That should be known as the intercalary Āṣāḍha month, and Acyuta lies within Śrāvaṇa.

Therefore, Baudhāyana and others employ terms such as Śrāvaṇa and so forth for the solar month; thus, the established usage (*prasiddhi*) residing in both [the solar and lunar systems] is not restricted specifically to the solar month. This is resolved through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). Furthermore, because established usage is more powerful, the assumption of multiple denotative powers—as in the case of words like *akṣa*—is not contradictory. Indeed, the usage of terms such as Vaiśākha for the solar month is well-known even among cowherds and women, whereas it is known by only some for the lunar month. Therefore, it is established that the words Vaiśākha and so forth denote the solar and lunar months primarily (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*).

That is incorrect; for although both [systems] are established and there is no difference in their being based on scripture, the application of terms such as *vaiśākha* and so forth is universally prevalent and powerful in the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*), whereas it is not so in the solar month (*saura*). As for the claim that the application of terms like *vaiśākha* in the solar month is recognized even by cowherds and women, while in the lunar month it is recognized only by some, that too is false, because the opposite is actually observed. Thus says Pāṇini: "A time joined with a lunar mansion [is designated by a word formed from that name], and when the full moon occurs in that [month], it is a technical name [for the month]. Such a designation does not exist in this manner for the solar or the civil (*sāvana*) months; therefore, words such as *caitra*, *vaiśākha*, and so forth, denote specifically the lunar month. The seasons (*ṛtu*), however, consist of two months according to both the solar and lunar measures. Among these, according to the solar measure, [it is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
O Rāma, two solar months are designated as a *ṛtu* (season). Also, according to the *Cāndramānena* in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana*:
"One should perform all rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti during the lunar months and seasons."
But in their absence, the opinion of the astronomers is that [the rites should be performed] during the solar seasons.
That the *ṛtu* (seasonal period) has the moon as its cause is understood from the wording of the mantra:
"He who ordains the seasons is born again."
He who is born again and again, performing the seasons, is the moon;
because his births occur repeatedly, the season follows the power of the moon.
In the section concerning the Hotṛ priest, Tittiri speaks with reference to the Moon:
"He ordains the seasons"; thus, this Moon is the ordainer of the seasons.

[15] And those six seasons—comprising five or six seasons by the condensation of winter (*hemanta*) and cool season (*śiśira*)—are established by the Vedic revelation: "There are five seasons; winter and cool season are condensed into one. Furthermore, they begin with spring (*vasanta*), according to the revelation: "Spring is indeed the mouth of the seasons. Each of these consists of two months beginning with Caitra, as stated in the *Ādhvaryava* and other Śrutis: "Madhu and Mādhava are the two seasons of spring; Śukra and Śuci are the two seasons of summer; Nabhas and Nabhasya are the two seasons of the rains; Iṣa and Ūrja are the two seasons of autumn; Sahas and Sahasya are the two seasons of winter; Tapas and Tapasya are the two seasons of cool season."
The terms *madhu*, *mādhava*, and so forth, are employed for the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, and others in other texts:
"The month of Caitra is called *madhu*; Vaiśākha shall be *mādhava*;
the month of Jyeṣṭha is *śukra*; and Āṣāḍha is said to be *śuci*."
The month of Śrāvaṇa is Nabhas; Bhādra is desired as Nabhasya;
Āśvayuja is the month of Iṣa; and Kārttika is known by the name Ūrja.
The month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Sahas, and Pauṣa is called Sahasya;
the month of Māgha is declared to be Tapas, and Phālguna is remembered as Tapasya.

Furthermore, because Baudhāyana states that spring consists of either Pisces and Aries or Aries and Taurus, he accepts both the system beginning with Pisces (*mīnāditva*) and the system beginning with Aries (*meṣāditva*) as optional alternatives for spring. However, when an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) occurs, then according to the lunar measure (*cāndramāna*), a single season may consist of three months.
Thus it has been stated by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana:
"When the month of Caitra begins with Pisces and is intercalary, then..."
Even when Caitra is pure, there is springtime; even in Vaiśākha, there is the state of spring.
Is it not the case that this very [continuum] has arrived, having been uninterrupted for three months?
True; because there is no other possible course, that very [continuum] is accepted here.
But even in this case, why is an alternative [explanation] not accepted, just as in that previous instance?
[16] There are three months belonging to spring; having excluded either the first or the last, it is here stated that this alternative is indeed appropriate for solar months.
But he is not joined with those lunar months that follow after an intercalary month;
for those twelve months are indeed measured by the sun's transits.
In this system, two months are counted as each single season;
there are exactly six seasons there, beginning with Pisces or Aries.
But when the intercalary month (mala-māsa) arrives, there are thirteen months;
then, starting from that [intercalary] month, the [remaining] even-numbered months are optionally designated as such.
When the seasons are being performed, one month remains over;
is this month a non-season, or does it become a seventh season?
Or rather, it is considered that he may enter at any time among the natural seasons; for there is no time devoid of a season, nor is there a seventh season mentioned in the Veda.
In that context, "the season not being joined with the season" refers to the emptiness of the season;
"there are six seasons"—this is the scriptural authority for the seventh chapter.
Therefore, the Smṛti rule stating "two months constitute a season" must be set aside by the Śruti;
consequently, an intercalary month may occur at some point within those very seasons.
The season (*ṛtu*) should consist of three months, being that month in which this [spring] is included;
or else, a single month of sixty days may be of both natures.
Therefore, even here, the state of being spring (*vasantatva*) would belong to exactly two months.

An *ayana* consists of three seasons (*ṛtu*), and likewise, with reference to solar measurement, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "An *ayana* shall consist of three seasons. Furthermore, the year (*saṃvatsara*) is also of three kinds: lunar by lunar months, civil (*sāvana*) by civil days, and solar by solar days. Thus it is said in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"Due to the distinction between lunar, civil, and solar months, there are also three types of years known as lunar, civil, and solar."

And those [twelve months] consist of twelve months, according to the Vedic revelation: "Twelve months are a year. However, a lunar year may sometimes consist of thirteen months, according to the Vedic revelation: "They say there is a thirteenth month," for a thirteenth month is possible only within the lunar measurement. Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"When, at the end of a solar year, by the measure of the moon..."
Eleven days remain over, O descendant of Bhṛgu;
in two years and eight months, one month is thus left over.
The commencement of the lunar year (*cāndrasaṃvatsara*) is on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Likewise, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, regarding the sequence of the rules for the beginning of the year:
"In the month of Caitra, on the first day, Brahmā, while creating, brought forth [the world]."
During the bright fortnight, it is likewise complete when the sun has risen.
In this world, he likewise set in motion the calculation of time:
the planets, the *nāgas*, the seasons, the months, the years, and the lords of the days.
In the *Brahmasiddhānta*:

"From the rising of the sun at the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the days, months, years, yugas, and kalpas commenced simultaneously in Laṅkā at the start of creation. On that day, the solar year begins; furthermore, the spring begins either with Pisces or Aries, as both the commencement with Pisces and the commencement with Aries have been stated as alternatives. And since spring is the foremost of the seasons, it is logical that the beginning of the year itself constitutes the beginning of the season. As for what is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
When, at the commencement of the bright fortnight of Māgha, both the Moon and the Sun are situated in the constellation of Vāsava (Dhruva) and are conjoined with Jupiter,
then that is traditionally known as the beginning of the sixty-year cycle.

Thus, it should be understood that the fact that the years begin on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is for the purpose of explaining the auspicious and inauspicious results well-known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), and not for the purpose of the performance of religious duties (*dharma*). Regarding the sixty-year cycle beginning with *prabhava*, the five successive groups of five years are designated as *yuga* and are named respectively: *saṃvatsara*, *parivatsara*, *idāvatsara*, *anuvatsara*, and *udvatsara*.
Likewise, in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"The first is the *saṃvatsara*, and the second is the *parivatsara*."
The third is the *idāvatsara*, while the fourth is the *anuvatsara*;
the fifth is the *udvatsara*, and this period of time is designated as a *yuga*.

And thus, since time can be delimited in the manner described, it is established as a conclusion that even for that which is without beginning or end, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the performance of duties such as vows is appropriate according to the circumstances. In this regard, the application of time—such as the year and so forth—to the year-vow and other rites should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the solstice (*ayana*), he himself has said:
"The installation of deities, groves, ponds, and so forth, [should be performed] when the sun is facing north."
If one performs it facing the southern direction, one would not obtain that fruit.
In response to the inquiry as to where and for what purpose each of the solar, civil, lunar, and sidereal months is utilized, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Thus, four *māṣas* of the subtle time have been declared;
learn now which specific task is to be performed by which specific month."
Now, the determination of the solstices, seasons, and planetary motions is made according to the solar measure;
however, sacrificial sessions (satras) are determined by the civil (sāvana) measure.
[19] And because worldly activity consists of conventional linguistic usage.
By means of the lunar measurement, through the depletion and replenishment of the preceding period, there is a *yuga* for Rāhu; likewise,
there are the *nakṣatra-sattras* and the solstices (*ayanāni*) of the Moon.
One should perform [the calculation] by means of the mind, which consists of the collection of lunar mansions.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: In matters of marriage, vows, and sacrifices, the solar measurement is praised;
likewise, for the pārvaṇa śrāddha, the anvaṣṭakā śrāddha, and the annual śrāddha, the lunar measurement is desired.
In the *Jyotirgārgya*: "The solar measurement (saura-māna) is praised for weddings, festivals, and sacrifices.
Likewise, in another Smṛti:
In rites such as the Ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha and marriage, as well as in matters concerning debts, the solar and civil days are used;
however, for ancestral rites and the like, the lunar months are traditionally prescribed.
And so it is stated in the Jyotirgārgya: "The solar month is prescribed for marriages and the like; the *sāvana* month is remembered for sacrifices and the like;
and the lunar month is praised for annual rites and ancestral ceremonies (*pitṛkārya*)."

Regarding the term ‘ābdike’, it refers to the annual śrāddha performed on the anniversary of death; regarding ‘pitṛkārye’, it refers to the six-monthly śrāddhas and so forth. By the use of the word ‘ca’ (and), it is stated that for all divine rites (*devakārya*)—other than sacrifices—that are to be accomplished within a month or a year, the lunar month is recommended.
And it has been said by Pitāmaha:
“In rites for the gods and in rites for the ancestors, the lunar month is traditionally prescribed.”
In the Brahmasiddhānta:
"In the annual śrāddha ceremony, the month is traditionally held to be lunar."

Bṛhaspati says: "The solar day (māna) is prescribed for the rising of the sun; the lunar day for rites for the ancestors; the civil day (sāvana) for sacrifices; and the sidereal day (ārṣa) for all vows and similar observances."
Jyotir-Gārgya says:
The division of the lifespan, the performance of expiatory rites,
and even the propitiation of enemies must be carried out by means of the *sāvana* [civil] day alone.
Just as the Pāṇḍavas [determined] the month for the Kauravas according to the Brahmanical Siddhānta: "For a Brāhmaṇa, the month shall be defined by the new moon;
likewise, for a King and a Vaiśya, it is defined by the solar transits and the full moon."
The meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi) here has been shown by Śrīdhara.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "marriage, initiation, tonsure, vows, observances, consecration, house-building, shaving, journeys, Mahāṣaṣṭhī, Mahāsaptamī, Vijayadaśamī, Daśaharā, Yugādi, Mahājyeṣṭhā, etc.," these [ceremonies] are included. By the word "etc. in the phrase "in sacrifices, etc.," there is the inclusion of sacrifice, giving, fire-oblation (*homa*), *garbhādhāna*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarma*, debt, buying, selling, and legal transactions. Likewise, in the statement, "For rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkṛtya*) and so forth, the months are traditionally held to be lunar," the word "etc. in "rites for the ancestors and so forth" includes prosperity rites (*vṛddhi*), consecrations, annual *śrāddhas*, *pārvaṇa* and *aṣṭakā* offerings, the *devaśayana* rite, tonsure, vows, observances, consecrations, house-building, shaving, journeys, and festivals such as that of Śakra. Furthermore, from the first zodiac sign onwards, according to the sequence of following the *gocara* and *aṣṭavarga* charts, one experiences good and bad results through the connection with the transit (*bhoga*) of each respective sign.
"For auspicious rites, marriages, and the betrothal of daughters,
ten months are recommended, excluding Caitra and Pauṣa."

[21] Regarding the instruction on the month (*māsopadeśa*), the solar month (*sauramāsa*) is adopted because the civil month (*sāvanamāsa*) consists of a fixed thirty days; for the *puṃsavana* and other rites are prescribed in the sixth and eighth months starting from the day of conception (*niṣeka*). Furthermore, in injunctions such as "he performs the *agnihotra* for a month" and "one should sacrifice with the *Cāturmāsya*," it is impossible to adopt a month of indefinite days; therefore, by the word "fixed" (*niyata*), the civil month is understood. Likewise, in the rule "every month they perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*," and in the regulations for the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) prescribed in connection with lunar dates (*tithi*)—such as "in the second fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, during the sixteen lunar days"—the adoption of the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*) is necessary everywhere, since the rules for the white and dark fortnights would otherwise be untenable regarding the annual rites. On this point, the author of the *Paṇḍitaparitoṣa* has stated that by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), settled matters such as marriages and so forth, which have been enumerated, are to be understood. But how is this known? Because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) to refute the inclusion of unsettled matters. For instance, the solar month is prescribed for the "sleeping of the gods" (*devaśayana*) and other such events, while the adoption of the lunar month is seen in practice for rites like the "sleeping" based on lunar dates such as the twelfth (*dvādaśī*). As Gārgya says: [text follows].
The ritual of the double Āṣāḍha should be performed until the awakening of Viṣṇu;
once Hari has awakened, that ritual must be performed with the solar transit alone.

Moreover, even during the *dvirāṣāḍha* (the intercalary month), the practice of reckoning by the transit through a zodiacal sign (*rāśibhoga*) is observed, as in the statement: "Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer. Furthermore, the solar month is not used for ceremonies such as the initiation (*upanayana*) or the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), nor for the definitive calculation of years from conception, as seen in the words of Gautama: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception," "The first feeding of solid food occurs in the sixth month," and "A girl of eight years is a Gaurī, while one of nine years is a Rohiṇī. These [texts] employ the civil (*sāvana*) month; yet, within the civil month, there is no exclusion of the bright or dark fortnights. Since the lunar month is adopted when specific lunar days (*tithi*) are required, one can also argue for its use in such cases. Furthermore, because the rule for establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is prescribed in the lunar month—namely, "On that new moon day which coincides with the full moon of Vaiśākha, one should take [the fires]"—the application of the civil month to sacrifices and similar rites is not universal.
"In marriages, vows, and sacrifices, the solar measurement (sauramāna) is praised.
Thus, it shows that even in sacrifices, the solar measurement is indicated. [22] "By this rule, one should here offer the *śrāddha* for the three ancestors."
Whenever the sun is situated in Virgo, Aquarius, or Taurus during the dark fortnights.
"Due to the conjunction with Virgo while the sun is present, according to the instruction for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña),

the city of the ancestors remains empty until the appearance of Scorpio. Since the performance of ancestral rites is thus taught even by the solar measurement, it is not an absolute rule that the Śrāddha must be performed according to the lunar month.
In whichever zodiac sign the sun has entered when men meet with calamity,
it is in that very sign that the offering of funeral cakes and the rites of water-libation must be performed for them.
Thus, the statement of Vyāghra indeed indicates the solar measure (*sauramāna*).
Pracetās, however, says: "On whichever lunar day of the fortnight belonging to the month of the deceased, [the rite should be performed] every year."
"Even a grandson should cause [the gift] to be given right there, as far as he remembers them.

Nor is it an absolute rule that vows, observances, and so forth are performed according to the solar month (*saura-māsa*), because the commencement and conclusion of the Cāturmāsya vows are taught to depend on the period of Hari’s sleep (*hari-śayana*), and because the month-long fast (*māsa-upavāsa*), having begun on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, must conclude with such an eleventh day; thus, either the solar or the lunar month is fixed. Furthermore, even though the sleeping of the God (*deva-śayana*) and the festival of Śakra are prescribed in the lunar month, they are not absolute rules, for Viṣṇu sleeps in the month of Karkaṭaka.
One should awaken the Goddess during the month of Tulā, Janārdana during Vṛścika,
the Goddess Ambikā during Kanyā, and Purandara during Siṃha.
For, by virtue of such statements of Baudhāyana as, "When Viṣṇu is asleep, even if it be the month of Tāla or the month of Vṛścika," the solar [month] is understood. Furthermore,
they also recite:
There is no postponement on the Daśaharā days, nor on the four Yugādis;
likewise, the Upākarma is desired to take place on the sixth lunar day starting from the month of Vṛṣabha.

That too is inconclusive, because from such statements as Gobhila’s— "The commencement [of Vedic study] is on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada by means of the Hasta constellation, or having commenced it on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada according to the rule"— the lunar month is understood. Furthermore, there is the statement of Pitāmaha:
The bath performed in the month of Kārttika, and especially that in the month of Māgha,
as well as the observances such as the Kṛcchra penance, are to be measured by the lunar calendar (cāndramāna).

Thus, that [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for the *Padmapurāṇa* states: "The morning bath is prescribed during the months of Tula, Makara, and Meṣa. Furthermore, the lunar month (*cāndramāna*) is not inconclusive with respect to observances such as the *kṛcchra*; for instance, Manu, introducing the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, says:
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever throughout a month, one attains the same world as Candra.

By saying this, he prioritizes the solar month (*sāvana-māsa*). Furthermore, Yājñavalkya indicates the lunar fast (*cāndrāyaṇa*) with the rule: "One should take the ritual balls (*piṇḍas*) according to the increase of the lunar days (*tithi*). Likewise:
"But one who associates with an outcaste for a month or even half a month becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel."

Thus, he indicates the *sāvana* month. Otherwise, since the solar and lunar months consist of an indefinite number of days, it would be impossible to calculate the penance based on the conjunction of months—which is occasioned by a period exceeding a few days—in accordance with the root-month; therefore, it is appropriate to rely on the *sāvana* month, which has a fixed number of days. Likewise, even in a penance measured by a year, the *sāvana* month is to be taken. Therefore, the solar month applies to marriage and similar rites. As for the word "marriage" (*vivāha*), it should be explained otherwise, as it includes marriage and other such rites according to their specific enumeration. For instance, where a ritual injunction is designated by the enjoyment of zodiac signs such as Aries (*meṣa*) and so forth, there the rites are to be performed by resorting to the solar month; whereas if those same rites are designated by names such as Bhādrapada—as in "on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada"—[the lunar month is used].

Likewise, there are such statements as "the king should attend upon Śakra," and "the ritual of the banner of Śakra is performed in the month of Siṃha. In those cases, because there is no contradiction between the general and the specific according to the rule of general and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), the inclusion of both is easily accomplished. Where it is heard in a general sense that "ten months are recommended, excluding Caitra and Pauṣa," since the words *Caitra* and so on apply to both solar and lunar months, a doubt arises. In the case of marriage, the solar zodiac sign (*saura-rāśi*) is understood. For it is by virtue of that sign that auspicious or inauspicious results are heard of. Because of the statement, "The solar month is for marriage and the like," the solar month alone is appropriate. And when the solar Vaiśākha is taken, if a connection with the full moon joined with the *Citrā* constellation is observed therein, then—since it is entitled to the designation *Caitra*—it does not fall under the scope of the prohibition. This is because the solar [reckoning] is stronger due to its scriptural authority (*āgama-balīyastva*), and the prohibition is also justified by its connection with the full moon. Thus, even if *Caitra*-ness exists, it is practically non-existent. Similarly, although the phrase "the number of years beginning from conception" implies the adoption of the civil (*sāvana*) month, nevertheless, in rites such as initiation (*upanayana*), the adoption of the solar month is justified despite the contradiction, because the determination of the ascendant (*lagna*) and so forth must follow the auspicious or inauspicious results produced by the transit through the zodiac signs. With this intention, it was said: "The solar month is for marriage and the like"; however, this is not understood as a total exclusion of other months for marriage and the like. And thus Varāhamihira says: "The Southerners indeed desire marriage when Jupiter is in a favorable transit (*gocara*). He prioritizes the lunar month for the purification of Jupiter and the counting of years, saying, "Jupiter remains [in a sign] for a year" and "Mars [remains] for three and a half months. The civil and lunar measures are certainly possible here, because a civil year is delimited by twelve months of fixed daily sequence, and the transit through a sign by Jupiter is likewise delimited by twelve months of fixed daily sequence; furthermore, the purification of Mars is also required. Therefore, even regarding the transit through a sign, only the lunar month is adopted. Thus, in statements such as "a girl is married when Venus is in conjunction" and "a man [is married] when Jupiter [is in conjunction]," some texts prioritize the civil measure and others the lunar measure. In this way, it is shown that for sacrifices and the like, there is no fixed rule regarding the civil month and so on. Consequently, it is not the case that all lunar and other months are possible for all rituals simply by virtue of those statements; rather, whichever is praised in a particular context is what is recommended. Where, however, the lunar month is praised in one context and the solar in another—as in the case of the *Kārttika* bath—the performance is settled according to the logic of praising or censuring the "unrisen" versus the "risen" fire-offering (*anudita-anudita-homa*), similar to the option of Vedic schools (*śākhā-vikalpa*). Therefore, the statement that "by the word 'and the like' (*ādi-śabda*), marriage and the like are included as settled rules" is unseemly; the aforementioned view alone is more sound. We, however, say this: whatever other ritual action has the solar and other months assigned to it by another scriptural statement, that task is what is referred to by the word "and the like" (*ādi-śabda*). But where there is no reason for adopting a specific month, the lunar month alone should be taken, because the words *Caitra*, *Vaiśākha*, and so on, have their primary meaning in the lunar month alone.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Specific Uses of Years, Solstices, Months, and Particular Times," in the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time) within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri—the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the illustrious administrative offices of the Queen, and a master of all branches of knowledge.
[26] Now begins the second chapter.
Now follows the determination regarding the intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
In that regard, the nature of the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) has been shown by Laghu-Hārīta:
"That month is proclaimed as the beginning [of the lunar year] where Indra and Agni are sacrificed;
Agni and Soma are remembered [as the deities] in the middle, and Pitṛ and Soma at its conclusion."

"But when the sun should ever pass beyond that [month], the first is to be known as *malimluca* (the intercalary), and the second is remembered as *prākṛta* (ordinary). Here, the phrase "where Indra and Agni are offered" is an indicator for the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*); "Agni and Soma" indicates the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*); and "Pitṛs and Soma" indicates the new moon (*darśa*). By this, the lunar month is indicated. When the sun passes into another zodiac sign in a different month after that [indicated] month has elapsed, then the former is the *malimluca* and the latter is the *prākṛta*.
And likewise in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"A lunar month that lacks a solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*) is proclaimed to be an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). [Also] in the *Nandipurāṇa*:
When the sun enters [a new sign] on the day and night of the new moon, that month shall be pure; however, when it has passed, there shall be an intercalary month.

When the sun enters a zodiacal sign (saṃkrānti) either by day or by night upon reaching the new moon (amāvāsyā), then that lunar month shall be pure (*pavitra*). However, when the new moon has passed throughout the entire day and night and the sun enters a sign on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), then that lunar month shall be an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). As stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"Where two new moons occur devoid of a solar ingress."
That [lunar month] is to be known as *malimluca*; however, the latter is designated as *uttama*.
A lunar month that is overtaken by the sun is known as *malimluca*.
Varuṇa, Sūrya, Bhānu, Tapana, Caṇḍa, Ravi, Gabhasti, Aryaman, Hiraṇyaretas, Divākara, Mitra, and Viṣṇu—
these twelve names are the Suns who rise during the months beginning with Māgha.
The intercalary month, devoid of the sun and known as *malimluca*, is therefore sinful.
Indeed, throughout the months, twelve suns shine in their respective order;
however, when an intercalary month occurs, the sun shines as a single orb.
For a month that has transitioned due to the increase of lunar days (tithi) sometimes arrives at another time; it is called neuter (napuṃsaka).
Regarding the question of when that occurs, it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasiddhānta*:
"An intercalary month falls after thirty-two elapsed months, sixteen days,
and four ghaṭikās."
The meaning is that, starting from a past intercalary month, when thirty-two months have passed plus sixteen days and four *ghaṭikās*, an intercalary month occurs.
As for what is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Bhārgava, when, according to the solar measurement of the year..."
At that time, however, according to the Sāvana measurement, a period of six days is completed.
And those deficient nights, O Rāma, are said to be six in a year by the measure of the lunar month at the end of the solar year.
Eleven days remain over in two years and eight months, O son of Bhṛgu; therefore, one month is left over,
and that is called the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month), which is censured in rites performed for specific desires.
Likewise, in the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya*: "In the thirtieth month it occurs. And in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Every fifth year, two months are added."

"Due to the passing of time and the retrograde motion (*aticāra*) of those planets. Thus, all of this is impossible before thirty-two months; beyond that, it may occur. Now, one might object: in a single year, two months devoid of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) are stated in the *Jyotiḥsiddhānta*: "A month without a transit is clearly an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*); a month with two transits is sometimes called a 'destruction month' (*kṣayamāsa*). This destruction occurs within the triad beginning with Kārttika and not elsewhere; thus, there may be two such months even within a single year. Given this, how can it be said that an intercalary month does not occur before thirty-two months?

It is said: although it may happen that two months devoid of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) occur within a single year, nevertheless, only one of those two is an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). That which occurs after thirty-two months is the [intercalary] one; the other, though lacking a solar transit, is not an intercalary month because it is an excess of non-time (*akālādhikya*), whereas only an excess of time constitutes "impurity" (*mala*). Thus it is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Those who know time declare that the additional month of time is impure."
And so it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"That [month] is called an *adhimāsaka* (intercalary month), and it is censured in rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*).

Since the word *adhi*—by means of the figure of speech *lakṣaṇā* (indication) based on its component meaning of "excess"—does not itself convey the sense of excess, just as in the expression "thigh-flesh" (*ūrukam*), where the word *ka* indicates the word *kāsa* which denotes flesh, and thus conveys the sense of "flesh," this [intercalary month] is therefore exactly equal to a pure month.
And so Jābāli says:
"Even in a single year there may be two intercalary months;
the first month is auspicious, while the latter is the true intercalary month."

[29] When no solar transit (saṃkrānti) occurs within two months during the course of a year, the first of those two shall be the ordinary month (prākṛta), and the latter shall likewise be the intercalary month (adhimāsa).

The meaning is as follows: starting from the aforementioned *pūrvādhika-māsa*, that month which remains without a solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*) beyond thirty-two months is the *prākṛta* (ordinary) or *śuddha* (pure); that which follows it is the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month), meaning a *malamāsa* (defiled month). Thus, a month without a solar transit after thirty-two months is an *adhimāsa*; whereas a month without a solar transit prior to that is an ordinary month and not an *adhimāsa*. However, in this context, the mere chronological sequence of the months is not intended, because that would contradict the statements to be cited later. As for the statement that there may be two *adhimāsa*s within a single year, that refers to a month being *asaṃkrānta* due to the absence of a solar transit, according to such scriptural passages as "a month accompanied by the sun [is a *śuddha*]," and not because of its unfitness for ritual acts (*karma*). But when there is one month devoid of a solar transit during the six-month period beginning with Āśvina in one year, and another such month during the six-month period beginning with Caitra, then even though it occurs after thirty-two months, the former month is not an *adhika-māsa* (extra month), while the latter one is.
And so it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"An intercalary month shall not occur before Caitra, but may occur after it;
for in all the scriptures, the thirteenth lunar form is observed within that [lunar year]."

The meaning is that the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) is the [proper] form only in that latter month, and not even in the former one, because of contradiction. Regarding the phrase "prior to Caitra," it should be understood as beginning from Āśvina. For it is stated in the *Jyotiḥsiddhānta*:
"When the sun has entered Leo, Virgo, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, an intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not ordained."
But if this statement were intended to prohibit the mere presence of an intercalary month in general, then:
"If a month should occur without a solar transit while the sun is in Virgo, then rites for the gods and ancestors performed when the sun is in Libra yield inexhaustible merit for the performer. [30]

Otherwise, the traditional teaching of Jyotiḥpitāmaha would be contradicted and there would be a conflict with many authorities; therefore, it refers only to the subject matter as previously stated. However, when within a single six-month period beginning with Āśvina there occurs a pair of months devoid of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), then: "In that case, the first shall be the natural month, and the latter likewise the intercalary month."

This very point must be understood: in the six-year cycle beginning with Caitra, there is never an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), because such a month occurs on either side of a *kṣayamāsa* (a lost month), and it has been stated that a *kṣayamāsa* is necessarily restricted to the three months beginning with Kārttika. Likewise, there is also a "lost" month (*kṣaya*) known as a *malamāsa* that contains two solar transits (*saṃkrānti*).
Thus, it is said in the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya*:
"In whichever month there is no transit, or indeed two transits..."
That should be known as an intercalary month (malamāsa), occurring at the thirtieth month. Thus [it is said].

Regarding this, some say that the number of months is also included within the definition; that is not so, because in the defining statement "that is to be known," the term "thirtieth" is mentioned after the sentence is complete, and because of the previously cited authority. Furthermore, as for being "the thirtieth" in relation to something: is this definition based on the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) or something else? Not the first, because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*); nor the second, because it would involve self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), because it would apply to the month of creation and so forth (where there is no sequence), and because the month following an intercalary month would not be an intercalary month itself—thus the definition would be contradicted. Where, in a single year, there are two non-transitional months (*asaṃkrānta*) and one month containing two transitions (*saṃkrānti*), those two [non-transitional months] are designated as *saṃsarpa* and *āhaspati*, while the other is the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*).

Likewise, in the *Bārhaspatya-jyotirgrantha*: "The month in which there is no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or that in which there are two transits—these are the *saṃsarpi*, the *āṣāḍha* (intercalary), and the *adhimāsa* (lunar intercalary) months; they are all censured."

The Śruti also states: "He says, 'O Saṃsarpa, for Aṃhaspati! They say, 'There is a thirteenth month'; it is that very one which he thereby gratifies. In this regard, according to the Jyotiḥśāstra, all three [types of months] are censured in rites such as marriage; however, the *kṣaya-māsa* (intercalary month) and the *adhika-māsa* (extra month) are censured even in Śrauta, Smārta, and optional (*kāmya*) rites. This is because the *kṣaya-māsa*, being the lord of sin (*aṃhaspati*), is of the nature of temporal impurity (*kālamala*), and sin (*aṃhas*) is itself impure; furthermore, the *adhika-māsa* is impure due to its excess of time. Thus, it is said in another Smṛti:
"When the sun enters a zodiacal sign (*saṃkrānti*) during the day and night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)," [and so forth].
That month shall indeed be pure, for it becomes superior once [the previous one] has passed.

On this point, some say: one might set forth the *Viśvaprakāśa* in order to refute that view, [arguing] that the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) first receives the designation of Caitra and so forth. But surely, since the designations of the months beginning with Caitra are based on the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) such as Aries (*meṣa*), and because the intercalary month is devoid of such a transit, the conventional usage of "Caitra is the intercalary month," "Vaiśākha is the intercalary month," and so on, would not occur. For instance, if the words Caitra and so forth were applied by way of a universal (*jāti*) such as "Caitra-ness," then some recurring qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) must be accepted. Even if the terms were etymological (*yaugika*), the requirement for a qualifying attribute remains the same for the application of the word "Caitra" to a full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) marked by the Citrā asterism. Furthermore, no qualifying attribute other than the conjunction with the Aries transit is observed. Nor can "being subsequent to Phālguna" be the attribute, because there is no distinction between that and "being prior to Vaiśākha," which would lead to the same contingency; moreover, it would be redundant for both to serve as attributes, and if they were optional attributes, it would result in multiple meanings. Furthermore, if an intercalary month follows Phālguna, then the month following it would possess "Caitra-ness. Moreover, just as Caitra is subsequent to Phālguna, Phālguna is subsequent to Māgha, and Māgha is subsequent to Puṣya, then by this sequence, Vaiśākha would be subsequent to Caitra—thus there is the fault of a circular argument (*cakraka*). Therefore, the conjunction with the Aries transit and so forth is indeed the qualifying attribute. Furthermore, in the Veda, after enumerating the twelve names of the year as "Madhu, Madhava... and so on, another name, "Saṃsarpa," is mentioned for a year consisting of thirteen months; since this is a distinct number, it is appropriate that it lacks the previous designations due to the addition of Caitra and the others. To this it is replied: [32] If the intercalary month were indeed separate from the pure (regular) month, then this would be so; but it is not so.
However, that [period] is indeed included within the pure [count].
Thus it has been said: "Sixty days, according to Bādarāyaṇa, are declared to be a month."
"Thus, sixty days constitute a month, and half of that is the intercalary month. So it is said.

Nor should it be argued that here the word *māsa* functions as a *ekaśeṣa* (a single remainder for two), such that even in the absence of a dual ending, the duality of the months is understood, and thus the singular number alone serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the conjunction with the *saṃkrānti*; consequently, the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) would not be designated as Caitra and so forth. For this would entail the non-existence of the usage of Caitra and other months established by the entire world. Furthermore, even in that view, the fact that the term *saṃsarpa*—which denotes a specific portion—has a different referent [than the whole] certainly exists. Moreover, the Vedic revelation intends the month to consist of thirty days. Therefore, whenever and wherever this [intercalary month] is included within another, it is designated by that name; thus there is no fault. Now, since the intercalary month falls between two pure months, its designation is difficult to determine because there is no cause for deciding whether it belongs to the latter half of the preceding month or the former half of the succeeding one. It is said in reply: because the intercalary month belongs to the former half of the succeeding month, it receives the name of that succeeding month.
Thus it has been said:
"The first [month] is to be known as *malimluca*, while the second is remembered as *prākṛta*.

The 'first,' meaning the prior portion of the month consisting of sixty days, is to be known as *malimluca*—impure and unfit for ritual acts; the 'second,' meaning the latter portion, is *prākṛta*, which means pure."
In the science of astrology, even the Grandfather (Brahmā) has said:
"A month is declared by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa to consist of sixty days;
having discarded the first half, the latter half is recommended."

Thus, since it would follow that in all cases the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) belongs to the first half of the subsequent month, he states an exception in certain instances: [33] But when, in the middle of a year, a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) does not occur within two months, then the former shall be the natural (*prākṛta*) month, while the latter is the intercalary (*malimluca*) month.

When two months without a solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*) occur in a single year, then there is a reversal: the first half of the sixty-day month is "natural" (*prākṛta*) and pure, while the latter half is *malimluca* (intercalary); this is the meaning. The intention is that the two intercalary months occurring within one year bear the name of the preceding month because they constitute the latter half of that preceding month. And this is logical: the first part of an intercalary month is natural, and the latter part is *malimluca*, because it is an addition (*vṛddhi*), and by rule, an addition is dependent upon what precedes it. Otherwise, even the increase of lunar days (*tithi-vṛddhi*) would result in the subsequent day receiving the name [of the previous one]. However, regarding a single intercalary month, its designation as the subsequent month is stated by a more powerful scriptural injunction, such as "where Indra and Agni are sacrificed. For this very reason, it has been said:
If there should be two months in one [lunar] year, then the subsequent one is the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month).
[Objection: But would that not mean there would be fourteen months in a single year? To this, he says:
The scripture declares the thirteenth month, but a fourteenth month is nowhere seen at all.

In a single year, even when there are two intercalary months (*adhikamāsa*), there are exactly thirteen months; the intention [of this statement] is based on the scriptural declaration: "That pair of intercalary months which occurs within a year is called a *kṣaya* (destruction) month within the triad beginning with Kārttika. Some have provided the following explanation for such statements as "But when there are two months in the middle of a year": when two months without a solar ingress (*asaṃkrānta*) occur in one year, of those two non-ingress months, the first is the ordinary (*prākṛta*), pure (*śuddha*), and fit for ritual action (*karmārha*); however, the subsequent non-ingress month is the intercalary (*malimluca*) and unfit for ritual action, and it is not used for the installation or consecration of the Lord of Durgā or the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajrin*).

As previously stated, "The [days] are prohibited as before, and not by another [authority], nor is there a divine [exception]," this was said in such passages as "two months in one [place]" and so forth; however, that is incorrect because it contradicts many scriptural statements. For instance:
"In whichever month there is no solar transit (saṃkrānti), or indeed two transits..."
That month is to be known as a *malamāsa* (intercalary month), excluded from all religious duties.
When the sun transits after having passed the day of Sinīvālī,
that month is indeed "overstepped by the sun" (bhānulipta) and is unfit for all ritual acts.
In whichever year there are two solar transits [within one lunar month],
then that period of three months is indeed defective for all auspicious rites.
The months of Saṃsarpa, Aṃhaspati, and Adhimāsa are censured.
When two intercalary months (*adhikamāsa*) occur within a single year, that happens during the triad of months beginning with Kārttika, which is known as the *kṣaya* (destruction) period.
This [period] should be diligently avoided for three months during marriages, sacrifices, festivals, and auspicious ceremonies.
If the eighth lunar day occurs after sunrise on the seventh day,
one should perform the festival of Durgā then, and not on the following day.
Thus ends the statement from the *Nirṇayāmṛta*, and so forth. Therefore, the former explanation is superior.
As for the statement:
"An intercalary month does not occur before Caitra; however, it may occur after [Caitra]."
For in all the scriptures, that thirteenth form is indeed observed.
Furthermore:
"When the sun has entered Aquarius, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, an intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not ordained."

[The opponent argues: "Thus, both of those [statements] intend to show that the first halves of the months from Āśvina to Phālguna do not become *adhimāsa* (intercalary months), but they do not intend to say that *adhimāsa*s do not exist at all; for that would contradict the statement: 'Among the ten [months] beginning with Phālguna, and occasionally among Māgha, there occurs the state of being neuter (*napuṃsaka*). This is incorrect, as it refutes the opinion of Viśvaprakāśa because the wording is not straightforward, and because it is improper to abandon the parts expressed by the words 'previous' and 'subsequent' in order to grasp parts not so expressed. As for the claim that the two statements—'no *adhimāsa* before Caitra' and 'when the Sun has entered the signs of Aquarius and Virgo'—intend to show that the first halves of the months from Āśvina to Phālguna do not become *adhimāsa*, that is not so, because it would entail the necessity of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and textual supplementation (*adhyāhāra*), and because the contradiction with the statement 'among the ten beginning with Phālguna' does not apply even to our position, since we do not accept a prohibition of *adhimāsa* based on mere similarity of form. Furthermore, the criticism directed at our position is itself incorrect. It is logical that a general rule prohibiting a month without a solar transit (*asaṃkrāntamāsa*) should be set aside by a specific rule; moreover, this fault applies equally to your own position. Since we accept that the specific rule constitutes an exception (*apavāda*) to the posterior half of the month obtained through the general rule, the statement declaring three months to be defective refers specifically to auspicious rites such as marriages well-known in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*. Thus it is said in that very same work: 'In marriages, sacrifices, festivals, and auspicious ceremonies,' etc. Therefore, the former interpretation alone is superior."
That month in which two transits (saṃkrānti) occur is known as Aṃhaspati;
this can never happen during the seven months beginning with Caitra.
Whenever it should happen during the five months beginning with Ūrja that there are two intercalary months, then those two would occur within that same group of five months beginning with Arcā.
Thus concludes the determination of the nature of the intercalary month.
[36] Now follows the determination of what is to be performed and what is not to be performed during the intercalary month.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"An intercalary month (*adhimāsaka*) occurring within the year is a source of evil that destroys the fruit of sacrifices;
it is overrun by the Nairṛtas, Yātudhānas, and other such beings."
One should recognize a *malimluca* month as that which is overtaken by intercalary months and devoid of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*); it is censured for all ritual acts.
Satyavrata says:
But that month which is the *malimluca* (intercalary) is known as sinful;
it is excluded from all rites for the ancestors and the gods—one should avoid it.
Paiṭhīnasi says: All rites pertaining to the Śruti and the Smṛti are proclaimed [to be effective] in the twelfth year;
however, in the thirteenth year, all of them are designated as fruitless.
Therefore, one should never perform those [rites] in the thirteenth month;
by performing them, one would surely bring about misfortune and self-destruction.
Bhṛgu says: When two new moons occur while the sun remains in a single zodiacal sign,
that intercalary month (adhimāsaka) should be known as the destroyer of rites for the gods and the ancestors.
Also in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "A wise man should avoid a month that has no saṃkrānti for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, as it is defiled and impure."
Sumantu: [37] "One should never perform an optional rite (*kāmya-karman*) during the intercalary month;
those who know the divisions of time call that intercalary month the 'impurity' (*mala*) of time."
In the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa as well:
"The intercalary month (malimluca) is indeed impure, a source of sin;
it is censured by the ancestors and the gods. One should avoid it in all ritual acts."
In the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"When the moon enters the solar orb,
the sun undergoes its transit."
Then, that intercalary month was declared by Viriñci to cause defects in marriages, processions, festivals, and sacrifices.
In another treatise on astrology: "When the moon enters the solar disc,
the sun likewise performs its transit (saṃkramaṇa) following it."
At that time, the intercalary month was declared by the best of sages to be a destroyer of great sacrificial festivals.
Likewise:
"When the sun passes beyond the day of Sinīvālī,
that month is 'overstepped by the sun' (bhānulipta) and is indeed useless for all ritual acts."

Thus, when a general prohibition of all ritual acts has been established, a specific exception will now be stated. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says: "One should not perform any rite, whether prescribed or prohibited, during the intercalary month; except for occasional rites (naimittika), for those are specifically ordained for that very time."

[38] By the term "action and non-action" (*karmākarma*), optional action (*kāmyakarman*) is meant. For that is "action" because it is performed by those desiring fruits, and "non-action" because it is not performed by those not desiring fruits; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both action and non-action. Prajāpati has likewise stated: "One should never perform optional rites during the intercalary month, with the exception of occasional *śrāddhas*, for that [exception] is specifically prescribed therein."

On this point, some say that the commencement and completion of optional (*kāmya*) rites are prohibited during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). However, once an optional rite has been commenced, it should be performed even if an intercalary month falls within the period prior to its scheduled conclusion. Accordingly, for the *cāturmāsya* vows, there is no commencement in Āṣāḍha if it is an intercalary month, nor is there completion in Kārttika if it is an intercalary month; yet, if an intercalary month occurs in between, the performance must still take place. For this very reason, it is stated that even when an intercalary month falls in the interval, the commencement of the *cāturmāsya* vows is on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha coinciding with a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and their completion is said to be on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika coinciding with a solar transit. As it has been said: [The relevant verse follows.]
On the eleventh lunar day, during the sun's transit into Cancer,
and at the beginning of the month of Āṣāḍha, a man should devoutly undertake the performance of the Cāturmāsya vow.
Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Lord, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, awakens with a concentrated mind.
O Indra among kings, the twice-born should awaken the deity with the mantra;
this same sequence of ritual procedure applies when an intercalary month has fallen.
O King, even during the month of Adhimāsa, one should certainly raise Indra, Ambikā, and Hari in due order when the sun is in Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio.
This being the case, there is no contradiction with the designation "the four-month vow" (*cāturmāsyavrata*) when the performance of the vow extends over five months.
[39] "For four months of the rainy season, one should renounce liquor and meat;
by giving gold dedicated to Hari, a twice-born man becomes a knower of the Vedas."
That mortal who performs the worship of Viṣṇu for two seasons beginning with Āṣāḍha, even if he passes them by with only a quarter-effort, shall become an inhabitant of His abode.
Viṣṇu sleeps here on the foot of Maitra,
turns over in the middle of Vaiṣṇava,
and the slayer of the enemies of the gods [awakens] at the end of Pauṣṇa.
One awakens after four months.
