One should not argue that this contradicts such statements as [the previous one],
because the validity of a four-month period is established by the statement: "Sixty days are declared by Bādarāyaṇa to constitute a month."
In the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"Whatever *prārabdha* karma exists, it is not to be performed during an intercalary month (*malimluca*).
Those months which are called 'sunless' (*asūrya*), I do not approve of [performing rites] in them."
And likewise, the commencements and the completions of vows and sacrifices.

This is incorrect, because the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is prohibited specifically for both the commencement and the completion [of rites], and because the word "and" (*ca*) includes all optional rites (*kāmyakarman*). For it is said: "Any optional rite that was commenced prior to the intercalary month but remains unfinished shall, without doubt, be completed even when the intercalary month has arrived."

Thus, because the *Kāṭhakagṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states that even the completion of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) is prescribed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the following distinction of scope is established: by the statement, "Those months which are called 'sunless' (*asūryāḥ*)," the commencement and completion of optional vows and sacrifices are prohibited, but not those of obligatory vows and sacrifices (*nityavratayajña*). This is because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of restricting the many subsequent injunctions prescribing obligatory and occasional rites, such as: "One should perform obligatory and occasional rites with self-restraint even in an intercalary month. Therefore, it is appropriate that this single statement alone should be restricted to the subject of optional vows and sacrifices.

Now, is it the case that commencement prior to the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is prohibited here, or is it the completion of what has already been commenced? It cannot be the first, because that would contradict the statement: "What was begun prior to the intercalary month... Nor can it be the second, because since the prohibition of commencement itself precludes the possibility of completion, a prohibition of that completion would be redundant.

It is said: the completion of that very rite which was begun during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is prohibited therein. For if one, out of ignorance, begins an optional (*kāmya*) rite even during an intercalary month, an excess of fault would arise if its completion were performed then; it is for this purpose that this statement exists, and thus there is no contradiction. Vṛddha-Manu, Bṛhaspati, Paiṭhīnasi, and Jyotiḥ-Parāśara [state]:
"The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), consecrations, sacrifices, gifts, and vows..."

One should avoid in the intercalary month (malamāsa) the study of the Vedas, the performance of vows, the ritual release of a bull, the tonsure ceremony, the girdle-tying ceremony, auspicious rites, and consecrations.
In some places, the reading is "sacrificing, giving, and receiving.
This is an exception [to the general rule]:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at death, and at the birth of a son..."
"It should be given even during an intercalary month; what is given then brings inexhaustible merit.
And: "Whether Jupiter is in its infancy or its old age, or has set, one should avoid visiting a deity during these times, just as one avoids doing so during an intercalary month."

Regarding the phrase "the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)," it should be understood that the word "when there is necessity" is to be supplied as the remainder. Consequently, even during an impurity (*mala*), the *agnyādheya*, which serves as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), is not prohibited from being performed immediately after the extinction of the fires. Likewise, when the consecration of an image or similar object has been destroyed, its re-consecration is not prohibited. [41] Sacrifices (*yajña*)—whether optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*)—are prescribed in connection with spring and other seasons; thus, those which are performed during the subsequent period following a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) are considered as having been performed at their proper time. "Gifts" (*dāna*) refers to great gifts (*mahādāna*). Some say that this prohibition applies only to great vows (*vrata*). There is no prohibition against the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) performed on the eleventh day, because like the sixteen *śrāddhas* and others, it also benefits the deceased (*preta*); therefore, since it is not mandatory, the *agnyādheya* and so forth [are not prohibited] even at the beginning of the period following the setting of Venus (*śukrāstamaya*).

It is prohibited because it is stated, "as in the case of an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Regarding "visiting a deity" (*devadarśana*), it is well known that this is forbidden as in the case of an intercalary month. "Visiting a deity" refers to visiting a renowned self-manifested (*svayaṃbhū*) deity. Furthermore, this was intended first [in the previous rule], according to the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "When Venus has set (*naṣṭabhārgava*), seeing the beginningless deity is not auspicious. Thus, even during an intercalary month, one should avoid visiting sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) or shrines (*sthāna*) that have not been visited before.

On this point, some say: because the phrase "like impurity" (*mala iva*) is used as an established illustration, the prohibition against seeing the first deity during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is established by the logical necessity of the context. Others, however, apply the phrase "as in the case of an intercalary month" (*malamāsa iva*) specifically to rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*); that is, just as these [rites] are prohibited in an intercalary month except at times such as lunar or solar eclipses, so too should it be in cases such as childhood and so forth. According to that view, there is no prohibition against seeing the deity during an intercalary month. [This applies to] the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as sacrificial acts.
One should not perform great gifts or religious vows during an intercalary month.
The great gifts (mahādānas) are shown in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Manu said:
"Those great gifts which are here purifying and auspicious..."
O Acyuta, please tell me those secrets which are to be imparted.
Matsya said:
[42] I shall now duly declare to you, in their proper sequence, those sixteen great gifts which have not yet been mentioned and are secret.
The first among all gifts is that known as the Tulāpuruṣa;
next is the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
The gift of the wish-fulfilling tree, the fifth being the gift of a thousand cows;
likewise the gift of a golden cow of plenty and the gift of a golden horse.
Likewise, there was a chariot drawn by golden horses, as well as one with golden elephants;
similarly, there was the Pañcālāṅgalaka and likewise the gift of wives.
The twelfth is the Viśvacakra, followed by that which consists of the Kalpalatā;
then the gift of the seven oceans, and likewise the Ratnadhenu;
similarly, the Mahābhūtaghaṭa is proclaimed as the sixteenth.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, however, ten other great gifts (mahādāna) are shown:
gold, sesame seeds, elephants, a female slave, a chariot, land, a house,
a maiden, a tawny cow, and a milch-cow— these indeed are the ten great gifts.

In the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra*: "One should not perform the tonsure ceremony, the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, the establishment of the sacred fire (*agnyādheya*), the *mahālaya* rite, the consecration of a king, or rites for specific desires (*kāmya*) when the sun has transgressed [its proper path]."
Kauthumi says: "The annual Śrāddha and other such rites should not be performed during an intercalary month;
however, rites such as those for the increase of years (varṣavṛddhi) and consecrations (abhiṣeka) should indeed be performed in the intercalary month."
Hārīta says: "In an intercalary month, one should not perform a Śrāddha, nor likewise an Abhyudaya-śrāddha;
and similarly, no optional rite (kāmya-karma) except for that which belongs to the first year."
After the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, whatever śrāddha-related act there may be—
whether it be an iṣṭa (sacrificial) or a pūrta (charitable) one— one should perform it even during the intercalary month (malimluca).

The *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* (prosperity rite) is that which excludes the occasions for rites such as the *jātakarma* (birth ceremony) occurring within the first year. Others, however, explain it thus: "From the first year onwards" (*vatsarāt prathamād ṛte*) means that, setting aside the first year, the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* should not be performed in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). However, when an intercalary month occurs during the first year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (rite of unification with ancestors) is prescribed; the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* prescribed for the following day must then be performed even in the intercalary month. As it has been said: "A brother, a brother’s son, a *sapiṇḍa*, or even a disciple..."
Having performed the sapindikarana rite, one should thereafter perform the auspicious (abhyudayika) ceremony.

In this statement, the term *ābhyudayika* refers to the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*, as explained by Viśvarūpācārya in the section on partition (*vibhāga-prakaraṇa*). Others, however, explain it as a supplement to what follows: the monthly *māsika-śrāddha* for three generations (*caipuruṣika*) which is performed again every month during the first year after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must be performed even in an intercalary month (*malimluca-adhimāsa*). To state this, it was said, "from the first year onwards," and this will be explained further below. Regarding the non-transitional [intercalary] month, it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
In that case, what was given would be as if not given; what was offered would be as if not offered;
what was well-recited would be as if not recited; and no fast would have been observed.
One should not undertake a journey, nor a marriage, nor the laying of a foundation for a dwelling; nor should one perform the consecration of deities, palaces, villages, or trees;
nor should one acquire gold or fine garments—this is the settled rule.
Parāśara says: A lunar month that is overtaken by the solar month is known as *malimluca* (intercalary).
Whatever rite is prescribed for that [month], one should perform it in the subsequent month.
Prajāpati said:

One should regularly perform the Upākarma rite, as well as offerings to the gods (havya), offerings to the ancestors (kavya), and festivals on the lunar nodes (parva), on the northern [path]; if performed on the southern, that becomes fruitless.
Parāśara states: When the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) does not occur during either the bright or the dark fortnight,
then that monthly rite should be performed in the following month.
Thus, sixty days constitute a month, and half of that is the intercalary month (*malimluca*).
Having excluded that [half-month], the rites for the ancestors, the gods, and so forth, should be performed in the subsequent [lunar] period.
Satyavrata says:
When a doubling of lunar days occurs both within a month and within a year,
the latter should be known as the superior one, while the former is considered impure.
Regarding what should be performed during that intercalary month (adhimāsa), Śātātapa says:
"When two months having the same name should occur at any point within a year,
the rites for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) are to be performed in the first [month], and the rites for the gods (devakārya) in the latter."
Aṅgiras:
If there are two months bearing the same name within a single year,
the rites for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) should be performed in the former month, and the rites for the gods (devakārya) in the latter.
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), it is stated by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa that a month consists of sixty days;
rites for the gods are to be performed in the first [fortnight], and rites for the ancestors in both.

Statements such as these, which prescribe rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors during the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), should be understood as referring to those divine and ancestral rites that are mandatory (*avaśyaka*).
Bṛhaspati says: "One should perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites with self-restraint even during the intercalary month."
The śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha-śrāddha), the śrāddha performed during the "elephant's shadow" (gaja-chāyā), and likewise the śrāddha for the deceased (preta-śrāddha).

That which is *nitya* (obligatory) is that which is prescribed independently of the name of any specific month, and for the non-performance of which an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is traditionally taught on account of the lapse of the proper time. An example is: "He who performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt on either the new moon or the full moon day. It is such an obligatory rite that is meant here, not merely every obligatory act in general. Therefore, the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *agnihotra*, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and so forth, must be performed during an intercalary month (*malimluca*), because an expiation is prescribed for the transgression of its own proper time. And likewise, although the *soma* sacrifice is also obligatory, it should not be performed in an intercalary month; for even when the intercalary month has passed, there is no possibility of incurring an expiation here, since the specific time—such as spring—which is an essential constituent (*aṅga*) of the *soma* sacrifice, has not been transgressed. Similarly, this injunction—"one should perform [it] in the intercalary month"—applies to those necessary occasional rites (*naimittika*) like the *gṛhadāheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for a burnt house), which must be performed immediately after the occurrence of the cause and for which a prescribed time in another month is not available. This applies to occasional rites such as the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice upon birth) which, for the sake of protecting the infant, must be performed at a different time, setting aside the immediate time following the cause; just as its performance is deferred during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) lasting ten nights or more, so too may it be performed during the intercalary month if it falls within that period. Thus, the intended meaning of Bṛhaspati’s statement—"one should perform [it] in the intercalary month"—is to be understood as follows: whether a rite is obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), if its transgression entails an expiation, and if its performance in the intercalary month is necessary because the prescribed time in other months cannot be obtained, then all such acts should be performed in the intercalary month. This is the purport of Bārhaspatya’s dictum.
And so it is said in another Smṛti:
"One should perform that which is obligatory (*nitya*) even when there is no other way, and likewise that which is occasional (*naimittika*).

Since for an obligatory rite, if its primary time (*mukhyakāla*) has passed, no secondary alternative time is permitted—and thus the total omission would entail the necessity of a penance—that action must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), because it has no other recourse.
The *Gṛhyapariśi�ṣṭa* also states:
"Those who know the time of the month call the intercalary month the 'dirt' of time;
one should perform a special sacrifice there, except for those rites that are mandatory."

Apart from the obligatory injunctions for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites, one should not perform (*neheta*) special sacrifices (*viśeṣejyā*) during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). That specific sacrifice which, when performed in a pure month, does not involve a violation of the rule is a "special sacrifice according to the injunction" (*vidhiviśeṣejyā*), such as: "One should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma* every spring. Since the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which is prescribed for spring, is performed in the pure Vaiśākha by bypassing the intercalary Vaiśākha, it is effectively performed in spring itself; thus, there is no violation of the rule. By this, it is implied that an obligatory rite must be performed even during an intercalary month.
And it is stated directly in that very same source:
"The *avaṣaṭkāra* oblations, the seasonal sacrifices (*parvan*), and likewise the *āgrayaṇa*, should be performed during an intercalary month;
however, one should avoid optional (*kāmyā*) offerings."

The "offerings without the *vaṣaṭ*-call" (*avaṣaṭkāra-homa*) include the *agnihotra*, *upāsana*, *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth; the "parvan" refers to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*; and the "*āgrayaṇa*" refers to the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*. Although the *āgrayaṇa* is prescribed for the two-month period known as the rainy season—according to the rule "one should sacrifice with *śyāmāka* grains during the rains"—and thus does not become "without any other recourse" (*ananyagatika*) even in an intercalary month (*malimluca*) since its own proper time still occurs, nevertheless, in the event of famine when grains other than *śyāmāka* are unavailable, one must perform the *āgrayaṇa* out of necessity for the sake of survival rather than subsisting on *śyāmāka* food alone. Therefore, it is rightly stated that "the *āgrayaṇa* is likewise [necessary]" (*tathā*). However, when it is not necessary due to the absence of famine, then the *śyāmāka-āgrayaṇa* should not be performed in an intercalary month.
With this very intention, Paiṭhīnasi stated the following alternative: "In a month devoid of the *saṃkrānti*, one may perform the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice or not."

In the *Kāṭhaka-Gṛhyapariśi�ṣṭa*: "One should perform occasional rites (*naimittikī kriyā*) even during an intercalary month (*malimluca*), provided there is no other way [to perform them] for the sake of the impurity; likewise, rites such as the Soma sacrifice, though obligatory (*nitya*), [should be performed]."
One should avoid performing even those rites such as the Puṣṭīṣṭi, Āgrayaṇa, Agnyādheya, Cāturmāsya, and others,
as well as the Mahālaya, Aṣṭakā-śrāddha, Upākarma, and so forth— whatever actions are explicitly prescribed for specific months— during the *mala* (impure) period.
The "Mahālaya" is the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Beginning with the offerings of garlands and other items for the deceased, the rites of *śrāddha*, *piṇḍa*, and water-offerings,
ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, are to be performed as they arise in due course of time.
The fire-oblation with barley, rice, and sesame seeds, as well as rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*),

and the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day under the asterism Maghā performed for the purpose of averting impending calamity— these should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malimluca*), provided there is no other possible recourse.
Also in the *Bhṛgusmṛti*:

"One should not perform a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, nor a *soma* sacrifice, nor the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), nor the *mahālaya* rites, nor the consecration of a king, nor any optional rite (*kāmya*) when the sun has transgressed [its proper path]."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) also declared:
"If the month when the sun has entered Virgo should be without a saṃkrānti,
then rites for the gods and the ancestors performed when the sun is in Libra yield inexhaustible merit for the performer."
Jyotiḥparāśara also says:
"When the month dear to the Yātudhānas arises in Kanyā,
the rites for the gods and the ancestors are understood to take place in the following month."
Devala says: When the Sun is in Virgo during the month of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), the fortnight for Śrāddha is proclaimed.
Once the Sun has passed Sinīvālī and enters Virgo, [that period is designated].
At that time, because of the advanced age, the ancestral rites for the father had already passed.

"Passed" means having exceeded the fifth fortnight. And thus, as for what has been stated by some—that because the *śrāddhas* performed on the sixteen days on account of the transit into Virgo (*kanyā-saṃkrānti*) are occasional (*naimittika*), and because there is no prohibition of an occasional *śrāddha* during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), those [rites] should be performed; this was said by Prajāpati: "excepting the occasional *śrāddha*"—[this is refuted].
In the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "A month conjoined with the sun is not considered fit for ritual action by the wise."
Therefore, one should not perform a *śrāddha* ceremony there, except for that which is occasional (*naimittika*).
And the status of being a causal factor for the faithful person regarding the transit of the sun into Virgo is stated in the Purāṇas.
Those sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo are equal to the [six] seasons; what is given to the ancestors during them becomes inexhaustible.
Thus, that [objection] is refuted. And as Śāṭyāyani says:
"That which is the sixteenth lunar day in the latter fortnight of Nabhasya, if it should be conjoined with the sun's passage through Virgo, that is the time for the performance of the śrāddha rite."
And likewise, in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, there is the speech of Brahmā addressed to the ancestors:
“If a man should perform a *śrāddha* on even a single day during the fifth fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, while the sun is situated in Virgo (Kanyā).”

For one year, the ancestors will certainly remain satisfied. Whether the intercalary month (malamāsa) occurs in Nabhas or in Nabhasya, the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa) shall be the seventh; otherwise, it is indeed the fifth.
As for the statement of Jātūkarṇa: "Taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the limit, whichever shall be the fifth fortnight—
in that one should perform the Śrāddha, whether the sun enters Virgo or not."
This [statement] intends to introduce the subject (*pakṣa*) by considering the collection of passages previously shown;
and thus says Kārṣṇājini:
"Whether at the end, or in the middle, wherever the sun may pass through the maiden (*kanyā*)."
However, the fifth fortnight is to be honored with respect to the sixteen-fold śrāddha rites.
Bṛhanmanu also says:
"Whether in the middle or even at the end, whichever fortnight the sun enters [the sign], that entire fortnight is full; therein the Śrāddha is ordained."

Therefore, the Purāṇic statement beginning with “*kanyāgate savitari*” (when the sun has entered Virgo) should be explained as meaning that when the sun enters Virgo on any day within the fortnight, all sixteen days beginning with the first (*pratipad*) are to be accepted; it does not mean that the days prior to the entry are to be rejected. Alternatively, that statement may be intended to emphasize the preeminence of the fifth fortnight (*pañcama-pakṣa*). The *tīrtha-śrāddha* and the *gaja-chāyā-śrāddha*—both of these are neither obligatory (*nitya*), because there is no sin (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance, nor are they occasional (*naimittika*), because the conditions (*nimitta*) related to the sacred site (*tīrtha*) and the elephant’s shadow (*gaja-chāyā*) are not achievable through human effort alone. Consequently, they are mentioned separately. Here, “elephant’s shadow” (*gaja-chāyā*) refers specifically to the shadow of an elephant situated in the eastern direction; this is the primary sense to be understood, as stated by Viśvāmitra.
[50] Moreover, he who should offer milk-rice (paramānna) together with honey to the ancestors,
while standing in the shade of a lordly elephant, facing south, with his face toward the east;
When the moon is in the constellation sacred to the ancestors (Maghā) and the sun is situated in Hasta,
whatever lunar day it may be, that too is proclaimed as Gayā-chāyā.

Thus, that which is designated as *gajacchāyā* is secondary and impossible [in this context], because of the statement: "In an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the *haṃsa* indeed resides in the hand. Here, "*haṃsa*" refers to the Sun; "*kare*" means in the hand; and "*sthita*" indicates that the transition into Virgo (*kanyā-saṃkrānti*) is currently occurring. Consequently, since there is no intercalary month, the Śrāddha for the deceased—which is obligatory and thus applicable even during an intercalary month—is prescribed again for a specific purpose: namely, that when an intercalary month (*malimluca*) falls within the year, one should perform one monthly Śrāddha in that month, and then perform another additional one in the second month, even if that second month is pure (*śuddha*).
As Vasiṣṭha said:
"If an intercalary month should occur within the year, one should increase the duration of the monthly rite by one day."
Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
If an intercalary month should occur when the day for a Śrāddha has arrived, one should perform two Śrāddhas; by acting thus, one does not err.
Kauthumi says: One should give a water-pot for a year, or even well-stored food;
and even when the year has elapsed, one should perform the monthly rite every month.
Gabhasti says:

One should never perform a voluntary (kāmya) rite even during an intercalary month (malamāsa), with the exception of an occasional (naimittika) śrāddha; for that [śrāddha] is indeed prescribed for that very occasion.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is said to be occasional (*naimittika*).
According to the Dharma, it may be performed even in the previous month, provided there is an excess of time.
Viṣṇu: If an intercalary month falls within the half-month period for the monthly rite, one should increase the duration of that monthly rite by one day.

Someone explains this statement as follows: "'vardhayet' means 'one should interrupt [the monthly rites]'"—this must be disregarded, as its basis is merely a particular interpretation (*darśana*) not supported by the previously cited texts. Furthermore, in another *Smṛti* it says: "Even when increased by a year, the monthly rite is performed every month. Some hold that this refers to the monthly rites prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, because they belong to the category of *ekoddiṣṭa* monthly rites; however, that is incorrect, since even the monthly rites subsequent to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are prescribed as optional *ekoddiṣṭas*. As Kātyāyana says:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should not offer the monthly oblations;
rather, one should offer them according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Thus said Śaunaka."

And in this regard, there is one view that after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should not offer the monthly rites according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure; another view holds that one should offer them. However, it is not the case that one view is that the monthly rite should not be offered at all after the time of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the other is that one should offer it according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure. Thus says Jātūkarṇa:
"A son should perform [the rite] for his father who has joined the group of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*) according to the *pārvaṇa* method."
The eternal rule regarding every year and every month should be understood;
"situated among the host of ancestors" refers to one who has undergone the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. — Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
The thirteenth month is indeed an extra month [added to] the year;
it belongs to the Asuras and is therefore censured. Consequently, one should not perform a *śrāddha* in the thirteenth month, for [the offering] does not reach [the ancestors].

[52] Since the thirteenth month is censured due to its association with the Asuras, one should not perform a *śrāddha* during that intercalary thirteenth month; for even if performed, it does not bear fruit. Some read the text as "one should not perform the thirteenth *śrāddha*" and explain that this refers to the thirteenth *ṣaṇmāsika* (six-monthly rite) which falls within the intercalary month and must therefore be performed there. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the previously cited statements such as, "If an intercalary month should occur in the middle of the year... Others, however, read: "Therefore, one should not perform a *śrāddha* in the thirteenth [month] at the waning of the moon. That too is incorrect.
The śrāddha performed at the birth-rite (jātakarman) as well as the new-moon śrāddha (darśaśrāddha) must be performed even during an intercalary month (malamāsa), according to the word of Vyāsa.

This is because it contradicts the statement of Vyāsa, and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the New Moon *śrāddha*—which, like the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, must necessarily be performed immediately thereafter and is not fit for prohibition. Therefore, the reading seen in many texts and recorded by the Kashmirian [scribes], "Therefore, one should not perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day, nor does it [the recipient] attend," is superior. Accordingly, this very reading is adopted even in the works of Harihara and others. Māṇḍavya says:
"In the case of a fetus, a usurer, a funeral *śrāddha*, or a monthly *śrāddha* for a servant..."
"In the first [annual rite] and in the annual [śrāddha], an intercalary month is not prescribed. Thus it is said.
Yama says: Regarding a fetus, a usurer, a servant, the monthly *śrāddha* rite,
the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and obligatory rites, one should not avoid the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*).
Bathing at sacred fords, the recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings with barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth;
likewise, the birth-rite, the funeral rites, and the first anniversary śrāddha.

"The *maghā-trayodaśī-śrāddha* and the sixteen *śrāddhas*, as well as bathing, *śrāddha*, giving, recitation (*japa*), and so forth during lunar and solar eclipses— these should be performed even in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), whether they are obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*). Thus it is said.

[53] Regarding "in the womb" (*garbhe*), this refers to rites such as the *puṃsavana* performed according to the number of months of gestation; regarding "usurer" (*vārdhuṣike*), it refers to interest prescribed at a rate of one-eighth and so forth; regarding "servant" (*bhṛtye*), it refers to that which is determined by a period of time lasting a year or more. Some explain "monthly" (*māsike*) as referring to the twelve monthly [rites]. That is incorrect, because that very rite is prescribed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) by the rule "and the sixteen śrāddhas," and because it is counted among the sixteen śrāddhas. Jātūkarṇa says: "The twelve monthly [rites], as well as the first and the two half-yearly ones..."
And the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa—this indeed constitutes the sixteen-fold śrāddha.
In order to define the two *śrāddhas* prescribed by the term "six-monthly and annual," he says:
"When six months or even three [months] are less than a year by a single day,
then those two [intervals] constitute the six-monthly [rites]."

The meaning is that when six months or a year are less than one day or three days [respectively], then the *ṣāṇmāsika* (six-month) and *ābdika* (annual) *śrāddha*s should be performed. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"In the *asthisañcayana-śrāddha*, the monthly rites are performed at the three-fortnight mark."
And likewise, on two empty lunar days, one should perform the sixteen śrāddhas for the deceased.
"Of two empty lunar days" means that in each successive month—namely, the sixth and the twelfth—the [fortnightly] rites are deficient by one day each.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"For men who have abandoned their bodies, the sixteen śrāddhas must always be performed."
Likewise, in the fourth and fifth, as well as in the ninth and eleventh.

Then, for twelve months, the Śrāddha rites should be performed twelve times according to the number [of ancestors], as prescribed by the Śruti; therein, one should gratify the Brahmins with libations.

In that regard, "at the monthly *śrāddha* rite" means at the *śrāddha* rite performed on the new moon day; "in the obligatory [rite]" refers to the obligatory gift (*nityadāna*); "the *homa*" here refers to the domestic fire sacrifice (*aupāsana-homa*), because sacrificial materials such as barley, rice, and sesame seeds are prescribed for it; "funerary rites" (*antyakarmāṇi*) include cremation, the offering of water, the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), the collection of bones, and so forth. Even the *śrāddha* for a newborn (*jāta-śrāddha*) should be performed, just like the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).

The *śrāddha*, the naming ceremony (*jātanāma*), and those sacraments (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by vows (*savratāḥ*) must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malimluca*), but one should avoid optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*).

"Sanskāras" refers to the rites of first feeding (*annaprāśana*), going out of the house (*niṣkramaṇa*), and so forth; these include those accompanied by vows (*savratas*)—such as the intention "I shall perform the observances (*dhāraṇa*) and breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) beginning from the Lord's lying down (*janārdanaśayana*) until his rising (*utthāna*)"—as well as optional rites (*kāmyas*). The mention of *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offerings) is intended to indicate all ritual duties such as optional animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) and the like, since all optional rites are to be avoided because they are not mandatory. For this very reason, another Smṛti states: "One should avoid optional rites such as *iṣṭi* during an intercalary month. Hārīta also says:

"One should not perform the *śrāddha* for prosperity (*abhyudayika*), nor likewise any optional rite (*kāmya-karma*) during the intercalary month. The meaning is that any optional rite, such as an *iṣṭi* sacrifice and so forth, must not be performed in the intercalary month.
As for what was stated by Jyotiḥpārāśara:
The Upākarma, the Utsarga, the birth ceremonies, festivals, and the Aṣṭakās should,
when there is an increase in the month, be performed on the later [lunar day], with the exception of those rites dedicated to the ancestors (paitṛka).

"Parāḥ kāryāḥ" means they are to be performed in the subsequent month. In that context, by the term "the festival of birth," only the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice is intended, and not the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* or the *jātakarman*, for if those were also included, it would result in a contradiction with the Smṛti texts stating, "The *śrāddha*, the *jātakarman*, the naming ceremony," and so forth. The mention of rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) refers to those that are mandatory, and not solely to the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rite, since even the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and others are prescribed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). As stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at death, and upon the birth of a son..."
It should be given even during an intercalary month; what is given then produces inexhaustible merit.
In some places, the reading is "the śrāddha is inexhaustible. In the *Śātātapa-smṛti*:
"One should not avoid the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) for the annual śrāddha."
Paiṭhīnasi states: "The annual Śrāddha that is to be performed every year must be performed even during an intercalary month;
the annual Śrāddha on the anniversary of death should not be postponed."
The śrāddha performed at the birth-rite (jātakarman), as well as the new-moon śrāddha (darśaśrāddha),
and that which is prescribed for every year during the first half [of the month].
"In the first part" refers to the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). When there is a thirteenth month, how should the *śrāddha* be performed?
How should a wise man perform it at the two limits—the preceding and the following [months]?
In whichever zodiac sign the Sun has entered when the misfortune of the twice-born occurs,
it is in that very sign that the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya) should be performed on the anniversary of death.
These [rules] concern those who have died during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
As Paiṭhīnasi said:
"But for those who have died during an intercalary month, the annual *śrāddha*..."
It should be performed even during an intercalary month, but never for others.
Bhṛgu also says:
"The annual śrāddha for those who have died during an intercalary month (malamāsa) must indeed be performed in that intercalary month,
but never for anyone else."
Vyāsa says: If a Brāhmaṇa dies when an intercalary month (malimluca) has arrived,
how indeed should one perform the annual śrāddha in that month which is designated as "deficient" (ūna)?
In whichever zodiac sign the sun has entered when a calamity befalls a twice-born man,
in that very sign one should perform the offering of funeral cakes and the water-libation rites.
For those who die during an intercalary month (adhimāsa), one should rely on the solar measure;
that very [solar] month shall also be used for the śrāddha, the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa), and other such rites.
In another Smṛti, however, the second half-verse is recited differently:
"That very day [is prescribed] for him regarding the śrāddha, the rice-balls, the water libations, and so forth.
Others, however, say:
On whichever day one dies, marked by a specific month, fortnight, and lunar date,
they know that corresponding day each year to be his *kṣayāha* (the anniversary of death).

By reflecting on such statements, they say that the declarations of Śātātapa and others concern those who have died during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). When an intercalary month occurs for one who has died in such a month, the day of death is indeed touched by the intercalary month; it is not the case that it is touched by the pure (*śuddha*) month. Therefore, the annual *śrāddha* must be performed specifically on the day of the lunar decrease (*kṣayāha*) that falls within the intercalary month, and not on the day of the lunar decrease that falls within the pure month, because the latter is not of that nature. Furthermore, it should be understood that even when an intercalary month occurs, the *mṛtāha-śrāddha* must be performed on the day of the lunar decrease that is touched by the intercalary month, according to the principle of the omission of secondary qualities (*tadguṇalopa-nyāya*). The first annual *śrāddha* (*prathamābdika*) should be performed during the intercalary month.
And so says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"Even when the sun has not entered a new sign (saṃkrānti), the first annual rite (ābdika) must be performed by the twice-born;
likewise the monthly śrāddha and the sapindīkaraṇa."

Some explain it thus: the first *ābdika* (annual rite), the *nyūnābdika* (abbreviated annual rite), and the *tadābdika* (that same annual rite) are performed on the day prior to the anniversary of death, whereas the monthly rites (*māsika*) are performed on the very day of death. This is because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has already been performed previously at the end of twelve days or similar periods; however, when it is performed at the completion of the full year, there is no separate *ābdika*, as that too is accomplished by the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* itself. As it has been said: "The sixteenth rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is proclaimed for the completion of the year; by that very act, the *sapiṇḍatva* [unification with ancestors] is achieved, and by that very act, the *ābdika* is intended."

The word *piṇḍa* refers to the *śrāddha* performed at the completion of a year; "the sixteenth *piṇḍa*" means the sixteenth *śrāddha*. This [interpretation] is incorrect, because by the statement "the first is the annual (*ābdika*) one," there is no authority for taking the term *māsika* to include the annual, and because the twelve monthly *śrāddhas* must be performed precisely at the commencement of each of those twelve months. This will be demonstrated in the section concerning the determination of the time for the sixteen *śrāddhas*. As for what was stated by Satyavrata:
"And that *śrāddha* which is performed every year on the anniversary of the death of one's mother and father..."
It should not be performed during an intercalary month, according to the words of Vyāghra.

This refers to the first-anniversary *śrāddha* and other *śrāddhas* for one who has died at a time other than during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). Here, by the term "intercalary month" (*malamāsa*), the *adhimāsa* is to be understood.
As it is said: "When a single month is joined with two solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), the *śrāddha* pertaining to both months is recommended even in the intercalary month."

Because the annual *śrāddha* for one who died during a pure month is prescribed even in a *kṣayamāsa* (intercalary month). And thus, the *śrāddha* for the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurring prior to the *kṣayamāsa* should be performed both in the preceding pure month—because it is said, "In that case, the first shall be the ordinary one"—and in that *kṣayamāsa*, according to the statement, "When there is only one month. Therefore, when the month of death of one who died in an intercalary month is itself an intercalary month, the annual *śrāddha* must be performed in the intercalary month alone, neither in the pure month nor in both. However, when the month of death of one who died in a pure month is an intercalary month, if it is the first-year anniversary, it should be performed in the intercalary month alone, neither in the pure month nor in both; but if it is the second-year anniversary, it should be performed in the pure month alone, neither in the intercalary month nor in both.
In that natural month, however, one should perform the śrāddha as prescribed;
likewise, all the rites for prosperity should be performed, for the daily rite alone is always obligatory.

"In the *prakṛta* [or] pure [time], one should always perform the annual *śrāddha* according to the rule as only one, and not a second even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*); this is the meaning. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "The annual *śrāddha* should not be increased there on the day of death," the annual *śrāddha* is not to be performed in both places."
Regarding this, some say: having performed the annual *śrāddha* during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), one must perform that very same rite again in the following month. And so says Yama:
"If the first annual *śrāddha* falls upon an intercalary month, one should not perform it then;
rather, when the thirteenth month has arrived, one should perform the annual rite once more."

The meaning is that when the thirteenth month is completed, on the day of entering the fourteenth month, one should perform the *ābdika* (annual) rite once again. As for the statement, “The annual [rite] does not increase,” its meaning is: “it should not increase,” which means it should not be omitted. Therefore, this [statement] establishes that the *śrāddha* must be performed in both months. That is incorrect, because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for performing the *śrāddha* in both cases. However, the meaning of Yama’s statement is this: one should perform the first annual rite during an intercalary month (*malimluca*); the “second annual rite” (*punar ābdika*) refers to the second year’s rite, and that should be performed when the thirteenth month is completed, on the day of entering the fourteenth month. Thus, the meaning we have stated for the two statements—“the first annual rite” and “the annual does not increase”—is consistent with other scriptural texts (*vacanāntara*). Furthermore, since this is supported by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which is its source, there is no need to postulate another source; whereas the meaning you have proposed does not admit such support, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to postulate yet another foundational Smṛti. Moreover, in your view, the word *ābdika* would become redundant in the phrase “when the thirteenth has arrived. Even if it were said, “when the thirteenth is completed, one should perform it again,” the connection would still be with the first annual rite due to the context; however, if it referred to the second and subsequent annual rites, this fault would not arise. Therefore, it should be understood that Vasiṣṭha’s statement, “when the day of the *śrāddha* arrives,” refers to the monthly (*māsika*) rites. Furthermore, even if it refers to the annual rites, does it concern the annual rite for one who died in an intercalary month, or the first annual rite for one who died in a non-intercalary month? It cannot be the first, because it contradicts many general statements previously cited, such as: “It should be performed in that very zodiac sign,” “One should perform it in that very [month],” and “That indeed is his month, and that indeed is his day. As for the word “also” (*api*) in Paiṭhīnasi’s statement, “It should be performed even in an intercalary month,” it can be justified in this way: when the thirteenth month is a pure (*śuddha*) month, the annual rite should be performed there; and when the thirteenth month is an intercalary month, it should be performed there as well. However, since this contradicts the many previously cited statements, the word “also” (*api*) must mean “only” (*eva*), and furthermore, it would result in the performance of two *śrāddhas* on a single day. Alternatively, if one argues that based on the consideration of other texts, one is performed in the intercalary month and the other in the pure month, then by that very consideration, it would follow that they refer to the monthly rites. Nor can it be the second case, for the same reason already stated, and because of the forthcoming statement of Laghu-Hārīta: “Every year, in the twelfth month. If it is argued that the word “also” implies the *śrāddha* should be performed in both cases—even in a month without a solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*)—then after performing one annual rite in the intercalary month, the one performed again in the pure month would not be the first annual rite. Rather, when the thirteenth month is pure, the first annual rite should be performed there; and when the month of death is the thirteenth month without a solar transit, it should be performed there as well—thus the word “also” is properly justified.

Others, however, citing the reading, "One should not perform the first annual [śrāddha] in a *malimluca* [intercalary month]," explain it as referring specifically to one who has died during an intercalary month: "The first annual [śrāddha] for one who died in an intercalary month should not be performed in that intercalary month, because at the time of that first annual [śrāddha], an intercalary month is impossible. For indeed, in the third year, another intercalary month occurs distinct from the previous intercalary month; therefore, the first annual [śrāddha] for one who died in an intercalary month never actually falls within an intercalary month. Thus, the first half-verse is a restatement of a constant rule (*nityānuvāda*). The meaning is: when, with the passage of time, the second annual [śrāddha] arrives for one who died in an intercalary month, and that same intercalary month recurs, then one should perform the annual *śrāddha* prescribed for each year for that person who died in the intercalary month, even in that very intercalary month.
The annual *śrāddha* that is to be performed every year must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*);
the annual *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāhani*) is not to be postponed.

The first half of this verse also concerns the death of a thief; "annual" means the first-year anniversary rite; "should not be omitted" means it should not be interrupted; and "even in a pure month" is merely a reiteration of this point.

That is incorrect, because a purposeless, eternal restatement (nityānuvāda) is improper, as it would result in the verse being rendered meaningless. Therefore, the reading observed in many texts—“*ābdikaṃ prathamaṃ yat syāt tat kuryān mīlamluce*”—is the correct one. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement “it should not be performed in an intercalary month” (*malamāse na kartavyam*) is properly understood exactly as we have stated it. Consequently, it is established that the first annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) for one who died in an intercalary month should be performed in that very month when an intercalary month occurs, and the same applies to the first annual anniversary for one who died in a non-intercalary month. However, this must now be considered here: even when an intercalary month falls within the year, should the first annual anniversary be performed in the thirteenth month, or only when the intercalary month itself becomes the thirteenth month?
Regarding this, some say that this statement is intended to mean that if an intercalary month occurs, the first annual rite (*prathamābdika*) should be performed in the thirteenth month.
As Hārīta says:
"Every year, in the twelfth month, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍakriyā*) must be performed by the sons."
In some cases, it may even occur in the thirteenth year, excluding only the first year.

*Piṇḍakriyā* refers to the performance of the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death. When the twelfth month is completed, it means in the thirteenth month; however, in a year that includes an intercalary (*adhika*) month, when the thirteenth [solar] month is completed, it means in the fourteenth [lunar] month. Regarding the first annual rite (*ābdika*), even in a year containing an intercalary month, it must be performed when the twelfth month is completed—that is, it should be performed in the thirteenth month. This is the meaning.

That is incorrect; for if the phrase "in some [year]" were to mean "in a year containing an intercalary month," then when an intercalary month occurs in the interval, the first annual *śrāddha* for one who died in Kārttika would fall in the month of Āśvina.
[This contradicts the rule: "On whichever day of a month, fortnight, or lunar date a person dies, they know that corresponding day to be his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death) every year."

Thus, the statement of Vyāsa would be contradicted. However, if the meaning of the phrase "in some cases" (*kvacid*) were to be "in the case of the thirteenth intercalary month," then this statement would not suffer the contradiction characterized by restriction; therefore, this alone is the logical meaning. Furthermore, if the statement "every year in the twelfth month" is accepted in the sense we have stated, then [it follows that]: "The first annual rite (*ābdika*) must be performed by the twice-born even when the sun has entered a new sign (*saṃkrānti*)."

Since this very [text] serves as the root for the validity of the *śruti*, there is no need to postulate another root; however, in your view, such a postulation would indeed be required. Thus, first, it has been stated that because this matter is established by the word in certain cases, there is no restriction of the sentence "In every year, in the twelfth month" in our position. Now, however, it is said while granting [the opponent's point]: if an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs between [the anniversary and the next], and the *śrāddha* is performed in the month of Āśvina for one who died in Kārttika, there is a restriction of the rule "touched by the month, fortnight, and lunar day. Since the monthly rite is prescribed for both the intercalary and the pure months, in a year containing an intercalary month, thirteen monthly rites arise. Consequently, on the day of entering the thirteenth month, both the monthly and the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rites would coincide; and that is improper, because of the rule: "One should never perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day. If this [rule] applies to other cases, then in your view there is a restriction of two sentences, whereas in our view the restriction is merely of the word "thirteenth" as referring to the intercalary month—this is the distinction. Furthermore, are the two *śrāddhas* performed simultaneously or sequentially? They cannot be simultaneous, because of the prohibition against performing another rite in the midst of a rite; and if this [prohibition] applies to other cases, in your view there is a restriction of three sentences, whereas in our view the restriction is simply of the word "one"—thus that alone is proper. In the second case (sequential performance) as well, is the monthly or the annual performed first? It cannot be the monthly, because that would entail the sublation of the prescribed time for one [rite]. If that [prohibition] applies to other cases, the refutation is already stated. Nor can it be the annual, for the same reason. Moreover, since the annual rite is prescribed after the monthly, its sublation would also follow. And if that [prohibition] applies to other cases, in your view there is a restriction of four sentences, whereas in our view it is of only one—this is a great distinction.
Now, if an intercalary month should occur during the increase of the year,
then that additional [rite] must be performed in the twelfth month.
If it is argued that there is no fault here because, according to the statement of Satyavrata, the thirteenth monthly rite is prescribed within the twelfth month, we reply:
"And when the year is increased, there is a monthly rite for every month."

By such statements, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the monthly rite (*māsika*) performed every month; consequently, one must note that if the monthly rite were performed every month during thirteen months, the aforementioned defect would arise. Furthermore, in the passage "in the twelfth month of every year," the meaning "in the twelfth [intercalary] month" should be explained by reflecting on the statement "touched by the month, the fortnight, and the lunar day. Therefore, since this sentence can be justified without contradicting what it depends upon (*upajīvya*), it is not proper to contradict that which it depends upon. Moreover, in whichever month and on whichever day death occurs...
That month, however, ending with the full moon, is to be understood with respect to occasional rites (naimittika).

Thus, there would also follow the undesirable consequence of restricting the statements of Jyotir-Gārgya and others. Furthermore, since in our position the discussion at hand concerns the determination of what rites are to be performed and what are not during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), this statement is relevant to the subject under consideration; however, in your position, because one must determine the rites pertaining to other months even in a year containing an intercalary month, it is not so relevant—this is another distinction. Moreover, for one who dies in Caitra, if an intercalary month occurs in Jyeṣṭha and so on, the *śrāddha* would have to be performed in Phālguna; in that case, the rule "every year" (*pratisaṃvatsaram*) would be contradicted, as there would be no distinct years. And in the second case, due to its absence, the universal rule "every year" would be subverted.

Others, however, fearing the aforementioned objections, explain it thus: "But not even before twelve months; rather, on the anniversary day of death, [the rite] should be performed every month for a year."

Thus, there is an injunction that "the first [śrāddha] is to be performed there"; the meaning is that this rule applies, however, in the second year and subsequent years. For in this way, there is no contradiction with any of the scriptures. Otherwise, since the specific day of death would be established by other means, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the month; furthermore, the word "first" (*ādya*) would then have to refer to the second [year]. Therefore, it should be understood that when the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) becomes the thirteenth, the first annual śrāddha (*prathamābdika*) is performed precisely in that thirteenth month, even if an intercalary month has fallen in between. Others, however, say: "One should not perform that which is the first annual śrāddha during an intercalary month."

Having cited this recitation of Yama’s words, they explain this statement with the intent that the first annual rite (*prathamābdika*) must be performed even when an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) falls in between—that is, in the thirteenth month. Their meaning is as follows: "When an intercalary month (*malimluca*) occurs in the interval, whatever the specific month may be, on the day of death touched by the lunar fortnight and date according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the annual rite there; however, this refers to the second and subsequent annual rites, not the first. As for the first, it should be performed after the twelfth month has passed, upon the arrival of the thirteenth month, on the day of entry."

That is incorrect, because it would entail the faults of supplying numerous ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) and the like; because this sentence is not understood from any other statement; and because there is no evidence for assuming an intended meaning (*tātparya*) by accepting such ellipses for this specific purpose. Therefore, the reading seen in many texts—“*tasmād asya śrāddhasya ābdikaṃ prathamaṃ yat syāt tat kuryāt malimluce*” (therefore, one should perform that first annual *śrāddha* of this [deceased] in the intercalary month)—is the correct one. Consequently, it is established that when the intercalary month becomes the thirteenth, the first annual rite is performed in that thirteenth month, and not even when an intercalary month falls in between.
[64] Paiṭhīnasi:
"In an intercalary month, auspicious rites should not be performed by noble persons;
that which is inauspicious should not be performed by one who desires his own welfare."

Although here the optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) and the like are prohibited during the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) in general, nevertheless, their commencement and completion are prohibited specifically in the *adhimāsa*. However, in the case of a *kṣayamāsa*, it is only the first commencement that is prohibited; otherwise, if the month of Kārttika were to fall within a *kṣayamāsa*, there would follow the consequence that the Cāturmāsya vows already commenced could not be completed. Furthermore, if the month of Pauṣa were to fall within a *kṣayamāsa*, there would follow the consequence that the Māghasnāna vow, which was commenced in the preceding fortnight, would have to be commenced again. If its completion or commencement were to take place in the month preceding or following the *kṣayamāsa*, then the injunction for completion in Kārttika and the injunction for commencement in Pauṣa would be contradicted. Moreover, if the rite already commenced were left incomplete, there would be a contradiction with the intention of commencing again in another year a monthly vow that is to be accomplished over many years, as well as a contradiction with the statement of Kātyāyana: "From the commencement [of a vow] comes the rule, and from non-completion comes fault. As for the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), since there exists another pure month (*śuddhamāsa*) between them, the commencement and completion are possible there; thus, there is no contradiction in prohibiting those two in the *adhimāsa*. If it is asked: "Why should even the first commencement not be possible in a *kṣayamāsa*, since there too there is no other pure month between?"—the answer is: No.

"One should not perform great gifts (*mahādāna*) or vows (*vrata*) during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Because of this scriptural prohibition, [the opponent's view] would contradict [the injunctions for] the commencement and completion [of rites] other than the first one. Furthermore, it has been stated that if this [prohibition] were intended to forbid only the completion and so forth—excluding the first commencement—there would be a contradiction with the *saṃkalpa* (the formal resolve). This is because it has already been stated that there is a contradiction with the *saṃkalpa* and so forth if the prohibition were intended to apply to the commencement of optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) and the like in a deficient month (*kṣayamāsa*). However, if the prohibition regarding optional vows and the like in a deficient month is intended to apply only to the first commencement, there is no such contradiction.

Now, this being the case, when there is an intercalary Kārttika month, since the Kārttika vows must begin in the pure Āśvina, and once the pure Kārttika has arrived, it would follow that the vow of the month-long fast (*māsopavāsa*) must also be performed for two months; and that is impossible.

It is said: For if the rule for the commencement of the month-long fast (*māsopavāsa-vrata*) were prescribed for the month of Āśvina and its completion for the pure (*śuddha*) Kārttika, then it would indeed be so; but it is not thus. Rather, having stated its commencement on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, its completion on the subsequent twelfth day of the bright fortnight is declared in the *Viṣṇurahasya*: "Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should undertake this vow for thirty days."
Having thus performed this vow of fasting for a month for exactly thirty days— neither more nor less— the self-restrained person with conquered senses, [attains the goal].
Then, on the twelfth day, one should indeed worship the meritorious Garuḍa-bannered Lord;
one should honor him with flower garlands, perfumes, flowers, and ointments.
"And one should feed the best of the twice-born with gifts of clothing and the like;

one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and conclude the rite after prostrating. Thus [it is said]. Therefore, this vow should be commenced on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina and completed on the subsequent twelfth day of the bright fortnight; it should not be practiced for two months. Since the month-long fast (māsopavāsa) is an optional (kāmya) vow, and since it is prescribed that an optional vow commenced before the intercalary month (malamāsa) may be completed even during the intercalary month, there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, regarding the inquiry as to in which month the second anniversary, the annual śrāddha, and the *vardhāpana* (birthday celebration) should be performed for those who died during a *kṣayamāsa* (intercalary month) or were born therein—the following is stated to determine that distinction between the two months contained within the *kṣayamāsa*:
"The first half-tithi belongs to the former [month], and the second half-tithi belongs to the one following it;
these two months situated within the *kṣayamāsa* should be understood by the wise."

The meaning is that the first lunar month is the one occurring in the first half of the lunar day (*tithyardha*), and the subsequent month is the one occurring in the second half of the lunar day; thus, two months situated within the intercalary month (*kṣayamāsa*) are to be considered by the wise. Therefore, the distinction is as follows: for one who died in the first half of the lunar day, the annual memorial rite (*ābdika*) should be performed in the former month, and for one born there, the celebration (*vardhāpana*) should be performed in the former month; whereas for one who died in the second half of the lunar day, the annual memorial rite should be performed in the latter month, and for one born there, the celebration should be performed in the latter month. Thus [ends the work of] the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya, the sovereign of all the illustrious administrative offices (*sakalaśrīkaraṇādhīśvara*).

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, in the section on the determination of time (*Kālanirṇaya*), the determination of the intercalary month (*Malamāsa*) is completed.
Now begins the third chapter.
Next is the general determination of all lunar days (*tithis*).
A lunar day is of two kinds: complete (*sampūrṇā*) and partial (*khaṇḍā*). Among these, the complete lunar day is shown in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
All the lunar days, beginning with the first (pratipad), from sunrise until sunrise,
are renowned as "complete" (sampūrṇā), with the exception of the day of Hari (Ekādaśī).

The fullness of Harivāsara will be explained in the determination of Ekādaśī. When it is incomplete—that is, when it is a "khaṇḍā" (partial) day connected to two days—there arises a doubt as to whether, for the performance of vows and other rites, the earlier or the later [day] should be adopted; this determination is now made. Regarding this, the *Nigama* states: "The pairs of the Yugas, Agni, Yuga, Bhūta, Ṣaṇmuni, Vasu, and Randhra; the twelfth lunar day joined with the eleventh, and the full moon joined with the fourteenth. (Note: This verse provides the rule for determining the auspiciousness of specific tithis based on their conjunction with the preceding tithis.)
"Even when the new moon day (amāvāsyā) and the [preceding] lunar day form a pair, it yields great fruit;
this same pair, when reversed, is a great defect that destroys previously accumulated merit. Thus it is said.

‘Yugma’ is the second [lunar day], ‘Agni’ is the third, ‘Yuga’ is the fourth, ‘Bhūta’ is the fifth, ‘Ṣaṭ’ is the sixth, ‘Muni’ is the seventh, ‘Vasu’ is the eighth, ‘Randhra’ is the ninth, and ‘Rudra’ is the eleventh. Because of the designation that these are pairs of lunar days (*tithi-yugma*), the meaning is that among the lunar days starting from the second and ending with the first (*pratipad*), two consecutive days at a time constitute a mutually connected pair (*yugma*) which yields great fruit; however, they do not yield such fruit when separated by other intervening lunar days. By this, it is stated that within the aforementioned seven pairs, the preceding lunar day should be joined with the following one, while the succeeding lunar day should be joined with the preceding one.

In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, within the Dvādaśī-kalpa, it is recited: "yugmāsu kṛtarāmāsu. Here, "kṛta" refers to the fourth lunar day (caturthī), and "rāma" refers to the third lunar day (tṛtīyā). In that very same passage, there is an alternative reading: "yugmāni kṛtapuṇyāni," as well as "kṛtabhūtāni."

On this point, some say: the first lunar day (pratipad) joined with the new moon (amāvāsyā) is to be accepted, because of the statement, "The new moon may also be on the first day. As for the statement found in the Āpastamba, Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa, and Dvādaśīkalpa, namely, "The first day may be joined with the second, and the second with the first," that refers specifically to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) pratipad; for it establishes that the first day of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) must indeed be joined with the preceding [lunar day], according to the rule: "The pairing of the two lunar days—the new moon and the first day—yields great fruit."

But others say: here, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) joined with the first lunar day (pratipad) should be accepted, because of the statement, "The new moon day is [valid] even on the first lunar day. Furthermore:
"The fifth, the seventh, the tenth, and the thirteenth, as well as the first and the ninth—these lunar days (tithis) should be observed when they face [the preceding day]."
And because of this statement by Paiṭhīnasi:

"In this regard, some explain that [the day] which extends into the evening is 'saṃmukhā' (facing), based on the statement from the Skanda Purāṇa: 'That which is seen extending into the evening is called saṃmukhā.'"

That is incorrect, because it contradicts the statements that will be cited hereafter, and because it is logical that the statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa* refers to another subject. Therefore, in this context, the "face-to-face" (*saṃmukhā*) [first lunar day] is intended as that which is joined with the preceding [day], and even that must extend into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), according to the *Skanda Purāṇa* statement: "The first lunar day (*pratipad*) should be made face-to-face, which occurs in the afternoon. Any other first lunar day, whether bright or dark, should be accepted only when conjoined with the second; for the *Āpastamba* states: "The first lunar day may be accompanied by the second, and the second may be joined with the first," but it does not say that the bright first lunar day should be accepted when preceded [by the fourteenth]. Why, then, is there no such distinction in that very case?
The first lunar day (pratipad) that occurs in the afternoon should be made present;
the first lunar day shall be joined with the second.

However, this [rule] pertains only to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). In that case, there is no restriction that it must occur in the afternoon; furthermore, it is said that even the statement of Paiṭhīnasi refers to the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*). If this were so, it would entail the undesirable consequence of restricting the two statements—"the fifth and the seventh [tithis]" and "the *pratipad* should be made face-to-face"—to the first day of the bright fortnight alone. On the other hand, the restriction of the sentence "the *pratipad* should be accompanied by the second" is common to both fortnights, since you do not admit the exclusion of the subject matter of the *yugma-agni* rule, whereas we rely on the exclusion of the subject matter of the sentence "the *pratipad* should be made face-to-face."

Now, is it not the case that the restriction of the statement "the fifth and the seventh [cases]" is not a fault, because it is logical for a general rule to be subsumed by a specific rule? For if one were to refrain from such subsumption out of fear of restriction, it would follow that the principle of subsumption would be abolished everywhere.

It is true that there is no reason for such a restriction of the statement, "The first lunar day (pratipad) should be made present," and therefore this [rule] applies in both cases. Thus, on our position, there will be no restriction of the sentence, "The fifth and the seventh [lunar days]," nor will there result a restriction of the statement, "The first lunar day should be made present"; it is said that such a restriction of this [statement] is not logical.

If it is argued that for the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), being overlapped by the previous day (*pūrvaviddhatva*) is not otherwise established, and therefore there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) due to enjoining two matters—that it should be taken as overlapped by the previous day and that it must occur in the afternoon (*aparāhṇikī*)—whereas for the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*), such overlapping is already established and thus no prolixity arises in its case; to this it is replied: First of all, the afternoon occurrence of the first day exists by its very nature; consequently, the injunction "the first day occurring in the afternoon should have its face turned toward the six [preceding] days" does not entail prolixity. Therefore, this rule applies to both types of first days, and by this, the settled conclusion (*vyavasthā*) is established that the afternoon first day is to be taken as overlapped by the previous day, while any other is overlapped by the following day.

This is incorrect because it is impossible to perform the rite on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) when it is actually present [only for a portion of the day]. Consequently, if one were to prescribe that the rite must be performed on a *pratipad* that is actually present and likewise extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), there would be an unnecessary complexity; however, if the subject matter refers to the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) *pratipad*, this fault does not arise. Thus, even the forced restriction of the statement "the fifth and the seventh [lunar days]" is not a defect. Therefore, the conclusion is that the bright fortnight *pratipad* is to be taken as the earlier [part of the day], while the dark fortnight *pratipad* is entirely subsequent [to the afternoon]. By this, the argument of some who claim that the statement "the *pratipad* should be accompanied by the second day" refers specifically to the vows (*vrata*) of the *tilaka*, *aśoka*, and *karavīra* flowers—because those are prescribed only for the forenoon—is refuted. This is because other rites are also prescribed for the forenoon, and there is no reason to restrict the rule to those alone. Furthermore, if it is argued that it refers to all rites prescribed for the forenoon, that too is incorrect.
On whatever time a particular rite is performed, the lunar day (tithi) that extends throughout that time is the one to be observed.

Since the matter is already established by the general statement alone, what further purpose would there be? Moreover, if this were the case, the statement "the first lunar day (pratipad) should be made present" would result in being restricted to those rites prescribed for the afternoon; consequently, that statement too would become redundant, as its meaning is already established by the general rule. Furthermore, if it were so, the redundancy of all statements prescribing the taking of the day as either *pūrvaviddha* (deficient at the beginning) or *paraviddha* (deficient at the end) would follow, because the meaning of such rules is already established by the specific injunctions regarding the forenoon and so forth, and because it will be explained later that those statements prescribing *pūrvaviddha* or *paraviddha* apply only when the lunar day does not span the time of the rite on either of the two days. Therefore, the system set forth by us alone is logical.

But others say thus: "The eleventh, the sixth, the new moon day, and the fourth—these should be observed as fast days when joined with the following day; those [other days] are joined with the preceding."

According to this statement, the fact that the first lunar day (pratipad) is joined with the preceding day pertains specifically to the subject of fasting; however, the rule "the first lunar day should be accompanied by the second" pertains to matters other than that.

If this were the case, one might object: "In that event, there would result a contraction of the scriptural injunctions stating, 'The first day (pratipad) is also the new moon day,' 'And likewise the fifth day,' and 'The first day should be made to face [the previous day]'; whereas in our position, the contraction applies only to the statement, 'The first day should be accompanied by the second. Thus, there is a distinction; so how can this be a matter of subject-matter differentiation? To this it is replied: Even the contraction of many statements is accepted, because it is logical for a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) to be restricted by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*). Furthermore, no such contraction exists here. For while the statement regarding the "pairing" (*yugma*) declares that the first day is joined with the preceding day (*pūrvaviddha*), the statement "The first day should be accompanied by the second" declares that the first day is joined with the following day (*paraviddha*). When such a contradiction arises, since no specific ritual act is mentioned, there arises the expectation: "Which ritual act is to be understood here? Since the joining of the first day with the preceding day is prescribed specifically for fasting (*upavāsa*), it is that very act which is taken up in the "pairing" statement. However, in the statement "The first day should be accompanied by the second," the reference is to ritual acts other than fasting. Therefore, where is the contraction? There is none.

That is incorrect; for it will be stated in the latter quarter [of the verse] that "the first day (*pratipad*) would be accompanied by the second, and the second joined with the first," meaning that in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), these two—*pratipad* and the second—are indeed intended. Therefore, in the former quarter as well, those same two must be understood as the subject at hand. Furthermore: "The second, the fifth, the tenth, the thirteenth, and the fourteenth [lunar days], when observed as fast days (*upavāsa*), destroy the preceding and following lunar days."

Since this statement declares that the first lunar day (*pratipad*) alone, when joined with the preceding day (*pūrvaviddha*), is to be observed as a fast, it would be inconsistent to state that the first lunar day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) alone is *pūrvaviddha* if the rule regarding "paired days" (*yugma-vākya*) were restricted solely to the subject of fasting. If, on the other hand, that [rule] also pertains to the first lunar day of the bright fortnight, then in the passage "due to being pierced by the second and fifth," the second and third days must also be taken as belonging to the bright fortnight; thus, the meaning would be that the third day of the bright fortnight is to be observed as a fast when joined with the following day. And consequently:
"O best of the twice-born, one should avoid the third day known as Rambhā..."
In all other matters, she is praised when accompanied by her attendants.

By this statement, there would be no injunction for the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*) alone to be joined with the following day (*parayuta*) in all rites other than the vow known as *Rambhā-vrata*, because the general rule of being joined with the preceding day (*pūrvaviddha*), which is understood from many statements prescribing the first lunar day (*pratipad*) as joined with the preceding day, would be contradicted without cause by the statement "due to the conjunction with the second or fifth," wherein the words "second" and so forth appear to be common [to both white and dark fortnights]. Therefore, the systematic arrangement stated by us alone is logical: some say that the second lunar day is joined with the following day when it is the bright fortnight (*śukla-dvitīyā*), on account of the statement "the pair [of days] and Agni [three]," and its application to the bright fortnight is to be understood from its association with the fourteenth and full moon at the end of the fortnight (*pakṣānta*). As for the *Brahmavaivarta* statement, "the second is joined with the first," that refers to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-dvitīyā*). Others, however, say: the bright fortnight second is to be taken as joined with the following day, while the dark fortnight second is joined with the preceding.
In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken.

Thus, from the words of Mārkaṇḍeya: "Where each single lunar day (*tithi*) is to be taken as joined with the preceding [day] by one statement, it is said that 'the other [is joined] with the following'—in that case, a specific rule (*vyavasthā*) is established by this sentence. This being so, there is the presentation of the required meaning; however, it does not concern lunar days such as the fourteenth (*caturdaśī*) that are already regulated by the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights (*śukla-kṛṣṇa-vyavasthā*).
