As for the interpretation of some that this statement concerns the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*), [they cite]: 'The wise know two [days] in the bright fortnight and likewise two in the dark to be the beginnings of the Yugas.'"
In the bright fortnight, it should be taken in the forenoon; and in the dark fortnight, in the afternoon.

This [objection] based on the statement [of the Smṛti] is also refuted; for since it is possible for the text to be meaningful by supplying the required elements in the manner already described, there is no reason to restrict its scope solely to the *yugādi* (commencement of the ages) and similar occasions. As for the interpretation that the word "bright fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*) indicates rites for the gods (*devakārya*), because such rites are generally prescribed for the bright fortnight, and the word "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) indicates rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), because such rites are generally prescribed for the dark fortnight—according to the verse:
"The lunar day (*tithi*) on which the sun rises is to be known for rites for the gods;
the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be known for rites for the ancestors."
Thus, from the statement of Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:
"A lunar day (tithi) joined with the preceding [lunar day] is proclaimed to grant satisfaction to the ancestors,
but it is not recommended for the gods, except for that one dear to the Sun."

[73] Furthermore, that [interpretation] is also untenable because it would entail the improper application of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) without a valid reason. Since the meaning of another sentence is established by this very [text], which is consistent with its literal sense, such a statement is authoritative; therefore, the settled rule is that the second lunar day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇadvitīyā*) extends into the forenoon, while the second lunar day of the bright fortnight (*śukladvitīyā*) belongs to the following day. Others, however, say as follows: "But every second lunar day should be accepted as joined with the third, according to the statement 'The pairs [of lunar days] and the fires' (*yugmāgnī*).
As for that which is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:

"O best of the twice-born, the second [lunar day] should be made present for the commencement [of the vow]," as stated by Āpastamba: "The second [day] joined with the first. This refers to a case where the second lunar day extends into the forenoon of the preceding day;
likewise, it is so stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
O Lord, the practice that falls in the afternoon should be performed facing [the deity],
and the second [practice] of the forenoon should be performed in the same manner.

‘*Tādṛśī*’ means ‘facing,’ that is, *pūrvaviddhā* (preceded by the previous lunar day). Now, one might object: the second of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇadvitīyā*) should be taken as the preceding day; for it is precisely there that this specific rule applies: “It should be performed during the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇikī*). However, the second of the bright fortnight (*śukladvitīyā*) is only the succeeding day, and thus the restriction to the forenoon does not apply there—why should such a distinction not be established? The answer is: if that were the case, the scriptural statement “it should be performed during the forenoon” would result in an undue restriction (*saṃkoca*). But the restriction of the two statements—“the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) should be made facing the first (*pratipat*),” and “the second is joined with the first”—is common to both positions. For you, having accepted that the rule “*yugmāgnī*” (the pair of days and the fire) refers specifically to the bright fortnight’s second, you do not hear of its abandonment from that scope. For us, however, we do not hear of abandoning the scope of the statement “it should be performed during the forenoon. Furthermore, since a second lunar day exists by its very nature as being in the forenoon, the injunction of its being *pūrvaviddhā* avoids the aforementioned complexity (*gaurava*). As for the statement “in the bright fortnight, the lunar day is to be known [as the one to be observed],” it refers to other lunar days that require further specification. Therefore, the settled rule is: the second lunar day of the forenoon is to be *pūrvaviddhā*, while any other is *uttaraviddhā*. This [position of yours] is incorrect, because, just as before, the complexity remains impossible to avoid. Consequently, the correct settled rule is: the second of the dark fortnight is to be taken as the preceding day if it occurs in the forenoon, but the second of the bright fortnight is always the succeeding day. By this, what some have said—that the joining of the second with the first refers specifically to the *yamadvitīyā* (because on that day brothers are fed by their sisters), and not to the rules regarding *ekabhakta* (single meal), *ayācita* (unasked food), or *nakta* (eating at night)—since those are restricted to times when they pervade their own specific periods; nor does it refer to fasting (*upavāsa*), since that too is prescribed only for the *paraviddhā* (succeeding day)—is refuted. The acceptability of the *pūrvaviddhā* second of the forenoon has been stated, and that is also applicable to other rites besides the four starting with *ekabhakta*. Therefore, it is improper to resort to an unsupported restriction based solely on the *yamadvitīyā*; thus, the settled rule is exactly as we have stated it.
Others, however, state this rule: the eleventh, eighth, sixth, second, fourteenth,
new moon, and third [lunar days] should be observed as fasts when they are conjoined with the following day.

Thus, the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara-śivagītā*, namely the rule “yugmāgnī,” pertains to the subject of fasting (*upavāsa*). The passage beginning with “the second [lunar day] joined with the first” (*dvitīyā pratipadyutā*) and so forth, which prescribes the second lunar day as overlapping with the first, pertains to matters other than fasting. In that regard, there is this distinction: “It should be performed in the forenoon” (*pūrvāhṇikī ca kartavyā*). However, if one were to restrict the scope of these two statements—“the first lunar day should be made to face forward” (*pratipatsaṃmukhā kāryā*) and “the second is joined with the first” (*dvitīyā pratipadyutā*)—to matters other than fasting, even though they are applicable to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), it would result in an unwarranted limitation in the absence of a specific reason.

[Objection: But surely, even in your own view, the restriction of the statement regarding the pair of lunar days and Agni (the third) would entail a narrowing of its scope, since it can be understood as referring to anything other than fasting, and thus applies specifically to the bright fortnight.

[Reply: It is said in response: A restriction of this statement indeed exists in your position as well; for although this statement can be understood as referring to the fast on the second day of the dark fortnight, there is a scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) that it refers exclusively to the second day of the bright fortnight.

Now, even though there is no difference in the degree of restriction between the two positions, a great distinction exists between our position and yours: in your position, one must renounce many activities other than the fast on the second day of the bright fortnight, whereas in our position, one need only renounce the fast on the second day of the dark fortnight. Thus, there is a significant difference regarding what is much or little that is performed.

This is true; however, the distinction is that in your view there is a restriction (*saṃkoca*) of both statements, whereas in our view, the restriction applies only to the statement regarding the pair of lunar days and the fire (*yugmāgnivākya*). Furthermore, even here there is no restriction. To explain: by the *yugmāgni* statement it is said that the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) joined with the following day is to be accepted, while by the statement beginning with "the second joined with the first" (*dvitīyā pratipadyutā*), its being joined with the preceding day is stated. Moreover, no specific ritual act (*karma-viśeṣa*) is mentioned here. Therefore, when the question arises as to which ritual act is to be understood here, since it is stated that the second lunar day is joined with the following day specifically in the context of fasting (*upavāsa*), the *yugma* statement is thus understood [to apply to fasting]. As for the claim that the statements beginning with "the second joined with the first" refer to ritual acts other than fasting—whence would such a restriction arise?—that is incorrect, because it has been shown in the determination of the lunar day for fasting (*upoṣyatva*) that even a second lunar day joined with the first is fit for fasting. Therefore, the previously stated rule alone should be accepted. As for the third lunar day, it should be taken when joined with the second, according to the *yugmāgni* statement; and that too refers specifically to the *Rambhā-tṛtīyā*.
And so it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "O best of the twice-born, with the exception of the third lunar day known as Rambhā,
on all other occasions this [day] joined with a [lunar] Gaṇa is praised for all ritual activities."
The word "gaṇa" refers to the fourth [lunar day]. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"A third [lunar day] that is ever joined with the second [lunar day] is never [to be observed]."
This should be performed by those observing vows, O dear one, who are devoted to dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
"Except for the one named Rambhā, the third [night] which increases merit;
and thus has it been declared by the sages, O son of Kṛttikā."
Bṛhattapā, Rambhā, Sāvitrī, Vaṭapaitṛkī,
Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, Bhūtā, and the Ṣaṇmukhī lunar day must be observed.
Likewise: "O Brahmin, the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, the Rambhā-tṛtīyā, the Baṭapaitṛkī, and the Bṛhattapā— these should be observed on the tithis that are 'facing' (saṃmukhā)."
O twice-born one, the third and eighth [vows] should not be performed in the presence of others.
Every other [third] lunar day is indeed conjoined with the fourth;
likewise, it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"That third lunar day which is conjoined with the fourth bestows the fruit."
Āpastamba says:
"Or rather, that third lunar day which is face-to-face with the fourth is the bestower of fruits;
it ensures that women do not become widows and grants them sons and grandsons."
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "O Lord, the third [lunar day] must not be performed when it is defiled by the second;
for that lowest of men who performs it while it is joined with the second [day],"
By practicing this dharma here for one year, one is liberated from the desert.
Likewise,
O King, he who makes the third lunar day connected with the remainder of the second [lunar day] goes to the terrible hell called Kālasūtra, which brings about misfortune.
The wise declare that she who, being deluded, performs the second marriage while still joined with the remainder [of her first husband], shall attain widowhood.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Śikhidhvaja, a third lunar day must not be observed when it is joined with the second; if a woman or a man, being deluded, performs [the rite] thus," so it is said.
[77] O dear one, when the second lunar day is conjoined [with a Monday], the ancient dharma is destroyed;
widowhood and misfortune will surely come to pass—of this there is no doubt.

O Śikhidhvaja, even that second [lunar day] which appears as a mere *kalā* or *kāṣṭhā* must not be treated as the third; rather, it should be joined with the [preceding] lunar day (*gaṇa*) by one who desires the supreme secret and performs the vow.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa:
"The [twelfth day] should never be observed together with the second, nor ever with the third."

[Objection: Why should there not be a settled rule (*vyavasthā*) such that the injunction for the third lunar day conjoined with the second applies to the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) third, while the prohibition applies to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*) third? Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the *Rambhā* statement would become purposeless, because all vows would then apply there; furthermore, the statement regarding the third being joined with the second would be sublated in the dark fortnight, and the statement prohibiting conjunction with the second would be sublated in the bright fortnight—these are two further defects. [Reply: This is not so, because even in the bright fortnight, the third lunar day is accepted when it is joined with the following (fourth) day for the purpose of fasting (*upavāsa*). Thus, the *Rambhā* statement is meaningful as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule]. Nor should it be said that the defect remains because the general rule (*utsarga*) is indeed sublated by the exception; for in your own position as well, since the third lunar day joined with the fourth would otherwise apply to all vows, the *Rambhā* statement serves as its exception.

It is replied: In your position, partial contradiction (*pākṣikabādha*) exists even within a single statement consisting of two parts; for instance, the sentence "of the even-numbered days, of fire (third), of the even-numbered days, and of the lunar days" (*yugmāgniyugabhūtānām*), while being common to both the bright and dark fortnights, is said to refer only to the bright fortnight, and even there, while being common to all vows (*vrata*), it is said to refer specifically to the *Rambhā* vow alone—thus the contradiction is equal. Furthermore, in this context, the word "fasting" (*upoṣyāḥ*) in the verse "The new moon and the third day are to be fasted when joined with the following day" would become unintended, since one might still accept a third day conjoined with the fourth for other types of vows; therefore, the injunction and prohibition regarding the third day being joined with the second must refer to the second days of the bright and dark fortnights respectively. This is not sound. For if that were so, it would entail the contraction of many previously cited statements prohibiting the third day joined with the second; it would entail the contraction of the *Āpastamba* and *Brahmavaivarta* statements "conjoined with the fourth," and of the *Skanda Purāṇa* statement "it should be performed conjoined with the *Gaṇa* (the fourth). In our position, however, there is no such contraction, because we rely on the application of the prohibitions against the third day joined with the second and the injunctions for the third day joined with the fourth—even in the bright fortnight—by excluding them from the *Rambhā* vow. In your position, moreover, there would be a contradiction of the statements "in all other rites" and "except for the *Rambhā* vow. In our position, however, the contraction applies only to the "even-numbered days" rule (*yugmāgni*) itself by restricting it to the *Rambhā* vow; this is a great distinction. The statement "the new moon and the third day" establishes that specific lunar days are to have the following day (*paraviddha*) for fasting, but it does not prohibit having the following day for other rites. By this, the following view is refuted: that the prohibitions of the second day and the injunctions for the third day joined with the fourth pertain to fasting based on the statement "the new moon and the third day are to be fasted when joined with the following day," whereas the injunction for the third day joined with the second pertains to matters other than that, since statements such as "in all other rites, she conjoined with the *Gaṇa* is praised" declare that the following day is required even for rites other than fasting.

Now, if the statement regarding the pair of lunar days were to refer specifically to the Rambhā-Tṛtīyā, an inconsistency would arise; for one would have to admit that even another second day of the bright fortnight is joined with the third, since the word "Agni" is intended to include other third days as well. Otherwise, it would follow that only the Rambhā-Tṛtīyā could be considered "pierced by the next" (paraviddha).

That is incorrect here, because no specific ritual action (*karma*) has been mentioned; rather, upon considering other scriptural statements, it is accepted that on the occasion of the *Rambhā-vrata* on the third day of the bright fortnight, even if it is joined with the preceding day (*pūrvaviddhā*), it is to be taken, whereas the second day of the bright fortnight is to be joined with the following day (*parayutā*) in all matters. Thus, there is no fault in this interpretation. Therefore, the systematic rule (*vyavasthā*) stated by us alone is logical. As for the fourth day, it should be taken when joined with the fifth, according to the statement: "Of the pairs and the elements... This is the statement found in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa* and the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"The third day should be joined with the fourth, and the fourth day [should be joined with the fifth]."
One should never perform it joined with the third or the fifth lunar day.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O Lord, the fourth [lunar day] should indeed be observed in conjunction with the third.
This statement regarding the fourth being joined with the third refers specifically to the vow dedicated to Vināyaka.
And so it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"The third lunar day joined with the fourth is indeed the bestower of fruit;
and the fourth occurring on the third bestows the fruit of great merit."
O child, this [rite] which gratifies Gaṇanātha’s son should be performed by those observing the vow.
And here, by the force of the fourth epithet "Gaṇanāthasutoṣiṇī" (she who greatly pleases Gaṇanātha), it is understood that this pertains to the vow of Vināyaka.

Others, however, through a more thorough examination of the wording, assert that this refers specifically to the *vara-caturthī* (the auspicious fourth lunar day). In that case, since even the *caturthī* joined with Tuesday (*aṅgāraka-caturthī*) and others are even more gratifying, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in your position: namely, that the two injunctions for a *caturthī* joined with the third (*tṛtīyā-yuta*) and the prohibition of a *caturthī* joined with the fifth (*pañcamī-yuta*)—both of which were cited—would be sublated by applying them to the *caturthī* alone. In our position, however, the distinction is that the restriction applies only to the phrase "of the [days] joined with the yugas and the elements" (*yuga-bhūtānām*).

Somadatta, however, says: "By virtue of an excess of devotion and faith, all [observances] are exceedingly pleasing; yet in the absence of these, even the Māṣa-śukla-caturthī, known as Varacaturthī, is not [pleasing]. Therefore, it is proper that this refers specifically to the Sarvavināyaka-caturthī. Consequently, the meaning is that the Caturthī joined with the Tṛtīyā is highly pleasing, but not when joined with the Pañcamī. Others, however, say: "The Śukla-caturthī is joined with the subsequent [day], while the Kṛṣṇa-caturthī is joined with the preceding [day], according to the cited scriptural statement: 'In the bright fortnight, the lunar day (tithi) is to be understood [as ending with the next tithi]'."

That is incorrect, because the statement regarding the inclusion of the fourth lunar day joined with the third—as illustrated by the cited *Brahmavaivarta* passage—is understood to concern specifically the *Vināyaka-vrata*. However, the statement "the lunar day should be known as belonging to the bright fortnight" refers to other matters. Therefore, the previously mentioned rule of determination is superior.
Furthermore: "If the full Jayā (the third) is diminished while the fourth remains, that Jayā alone should be observed;
one should not perform it when pierced by the Nāga (the fourth)."

This statement refers to cases other than the Vināyaka-vrata; for if it applied to both cases, there would be the undesirable consequence of excessive complexity (*bādhagaurava*) and the prohibition would be rendered inconsistent, since the fourth lunar day joined with the fifth would already be applicable there. Therefore, the fifth lunar day joined with the fourth is to be accepted. Thus, in the *Yugma-vākya* (the verse on pairs), it says: "Of the pairs [of lunar days] and the [lunar] days. This is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
But the fifth [lunar day], O Lord, should be observed as joined with the fourth;
this is according to the Padma Purāṇa and the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa’s Dvādaśī-kalpa:
"The fifth, when conjoined with the fourth, should be observed, but not when conjoined with the sixth."
As for the statement from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*:

"The fifth lunar day, O Nārada, should be observed when joined with the sixth," that refers to the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), according to the scriptural injunction: "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be accepted."

Others, however, say: "This statement refers to when the fifth lunar day extends throughout the entire duration of the second day. Still others say: "The connection of the fifth with the sixth applies specifically to the worship of the Nāgas, because that [worship] is prescribed only for the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). Both of these views are incorrect. This is because, according to the reasoning already stated, the statement "the first day (*pratipad*) may be joined with the second" has been shown to apply specifically to the vows (*vrata*) of the *tilaka*, *aśoka*, and *karavīra* flowers; therefore, the established rule is that the bright-fifth (*śukla-pañcamī*) is joined with the following day, whereas the dark-fifth (*kṛṣṇa-pañcamī*) is joined with the preceding day.
But others say this: the statements from the Nigamas and other sources regarding the fifth lunar day being joined with the fourth refer to the subject of fasting:
"The eleventh, the sixth, the new moon, and the fourth—these should be fasted upon when joined with the following day;
the following days [should be fasted upon] when joined with the preceding."

For by this very statement, the fact that the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) is joined with the fourth (*caturthī*) in the context of fasting (*upavāsa*) is explicitly declared. Furthermore, in the previous arrangement, the restriction of the sentence "the fifth [day] must be observed" to a scope other than fasting would entail an unwarranted contraction (*saṃkoca*), even though it remains applicable to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Nor is such a contraction of the *yugma* and other rules a fault when they concern fasting, because it is logical for a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) to be subsumed (*upasaṃhāra*) by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*). In your own view as well, the contraction is no different, as it is restricted solely to the dark fortnight. Moreover, it was stated previously that in such cases, no such contraction exists.

The sixth [lunar day], however, should be taken when joined with the seventh; likewise, it is stated in the *Yugma-vākya*: "In the case of the pair [of days], [the sixth is excluded] for the two Munis. Also, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The sixth [day] should never be performed when pierced by the [seventh] Nāga."
Those who contemplate dharma and worldly prosperity should perform the sixth lunar day conjoined with the seventh.
Also in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:
"The sixth lunar day should never be observed when pierced by the Nāga [the seventh];
for if the sixth is observed when pierced by the Nāga, there will be a destruction of merit."
It should be performed together with the seventh lunar day; it bestows the fruit of great merit.
The Nigama states: "The sixth lunar day pierced by the Nāga [tithi], the Sun [seventh] pierced by Rudra [eighth],
and Viṣṇu [eleventh] pierced by Kāma [twelfth]— these days also are not to be accepted."

‘Nāga’ is the fifth [tithi]; ‘Rudra’ is the eighth; ‘Divākara’ is the seventh; ‘Kāma’ is the thirteenth; and ‘Viṣṇu’ is the twelfth. However, the seventh [tithi] should be taken when conjoined with the sixth. Thus it is stated in the Yugmavākya: “ṣaṇmunyoḥ” (the sixth and the seventh, the fourth and the fifth). This is also stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
[82] "O dear one, the seventh lunar day must always be joined with the sixth;
wherever there is both the sixth and the seventh, there the Sun is present."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa and also in the Dvādaśīkalpa Purāṇa:
"O dear one, when the sixth and seventh [tithis] coincide with one another,
it is likewise [so]."
O best of the twice-born, the seventh [lunar day] should always be observed when it is joined with the preceding [day];
the eighth should be accepted when joined with the ninth. Thus it is stated in the *Yugma-vākya*: "In the case of the Vasus and the Apertures.
This is also stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
The seventh [tithi] is not joined with the eighth, nor is the eighth joined with the seventh;
in all ritual observances, the eighth [tithi] is auspicious when it occurs later [in the lunar day].
In some places, however, the reading is "the eighth joined with the seventh. Also in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The eighth, when mixed with the ninth, should be observed by one desiring prosperity."
O Śiṇidhvaja, it should never be performed when conjoined with the seventh lunar day;
O dear one, the single eighth day of the dark fortnight should be observed when conjoined with the Sun.

Also in the Padma Purāṇa: "The eighth [tithi] joined with the seventh is not [to be taken]; the seventh is not joined with the eighth. The eighth should be performed together with the ninth; there is no doubt in this matter."
And this refers specifically to the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
for thus says the Nigama:
"The eighth day of the bright fortnight and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight."
"One should not observe it when overlapped by the previous day; rather, it should be observed when conjoined with the following day.
For this is the eternal law regarding such matters as fasting and other religious duties."

In some places, however, the reading is "in matters concerning fasts. The eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*) must indeed be joined with the seventh day (*saptamī*). And so it is stated in that very same source:

"The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣe caturdaśī*) should always be observed when joined with the preceding day; never when joined with the following day."
In matters such as fasting and other religious observances, this is the eternal law.
On both the eighth and ninth [tithis], during the pair [of days] in both fortnights, a great festival for Śiva and Śakti must be performed in the sacred field of Śiva (śivakṣetra).
And so it is stated in the Padmapurāṇa:
"The eighth [tithi] pierced by the ninth, and the ninth joined with the eighth."
The lunar day (tithi) of Umā-Maheśvarī is, for the most part, like Ardhanārīśvara.
On the pair of the eighth and ninth [lunar days], during the great enthusiasm,
there is a grand festival for Śiva and Śakti in the sacred field of Śiva, on both fortnights as well.
The ninth [lunar day] must indeed be taken when conjoined with the eighth; thus it is stated in the *Yugma* rule: "In the case of the Vasus and the Orifices.
Those desiring the fruit should observe the eighth day as pierced by the ninth.
This is according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, and the *Dvādaśīkalpa*.
O dear one, one should never perform the ninth [tithi] when it is pierced by the tenth;
as stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"When the ninth and the eleventh [tithis] are both pierced by the tenth..."
Then, it should be especially avoided, just as the water of the Ganges is avoided during the menstrual period.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa:
"The eighth should be observed together with the ninth, and likewise the ninth;
and the tenth, when overlapped by the preceding day, is to be accepted."
And so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O best of the twice-born, the tenth day should indeed be observed as being accompanied by Durgā.
When the tenth day extends across both days [of the lunar fortnight] and covers the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*), then either the earlier or the later [day] may be taken according to option."
And so says Aṅgiras:
"The tenth day should be observed in its entirety, whether joined with the preceding or the following [lunar day];
since it is not defiled by being joined [with the eleventh], it is therefore 'all-facing' (sarvatomukhī)."
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa:
"The Daśamī [tithi] should be made complete, whether by the preceding or the following [tithi];
since it is not defiled when joined [with them], it is therefore 'all-facing' (sarvatomukhī)."
The Ekādaśī joined with [the next day] is to be accepted, according to the statement in the Yugma-vākya: "The twelfth [day] is joined with Rudra [the eleventh].
"The Ekādaśī should never be observed when conjoined with the tenth;
O Lord, the Ekādaśī should not be observed when united with the Daśamī."
Thus, because of the prohibition in the *Brahmavaivarta* and the *Skanda Purāṇa*,
and also in the *Dvādaśī-kalpa* of the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"The third and the sixth [tithis] should not be performed when overlapped by the preceding [day]."
O King, for one who desires virtue, pleasure, and wealth, the eighth and eleventh lunar days are auspicious.

The remainder will be explained in the determination of Ekādaśī. As for Dvādaśī, it should be accepted when joined with Ekādaśī, according to the *Yugma* statement: "Dvādaśī joined with Rudra [Ekādaśī]," and:
"O Lord, Dvādaśī should always be observed as joined with Ekādaśī;
it should always be performed by wise men who are devotees of Viṣṇu."
And from the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O Sage, the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) should be observed when it is conjoined with the twelfth day (dvādaśī); indeed, the thirteenth day should be performed together with the twelfth."
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*. It is also said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) should be observed when it falls during the afternoon."
‘Aparāhṇikī’ means that it is overlapped by the preceding day.
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
“In this manner, the eleventh [lunar day] is to be accepted, and the thirteenth [lunar day] with the twelfth.”

And this refers specifically to the bright (śukla) thirteenth day, because it is traditionally taught that the dark (kṛṣṇa) thirteenth day should be accepted when it is joined with the fourteenth. To this effect, there is a statement from the Nigama:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the thirteenth of the dark fortnight..."
These should be worshipped joined with the supreme, and likewise, the supreme [syllables] joined with the preceding.

However, when the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇatrayodaśī*) does not extend into the following day, but rather on the preceding day it is already overlapped by a prohibited lunar day (*niṣiddhatithividdha*), Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says regarding that case: "The eleventh and the third [are to be taken as overlapped by the following]. Therefore, even if the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight (*śuklatrayodaśī*) occurs on the preceding day, it is not to be accepted as the earlier one. Others, however, say that this statement refers to both types of thirteenth days. Both of these views are incorrect; for if the two thirteenth days were to occur on the following day, then those joined with the preceding day would not be acceptable. Furthermore, in the *Nigama* passage, "the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight," the qualification "in the dark fortnight" would become redundant. Moreover, when there is doubt as to whether this refers to the dark thirteenth or the bright thirteenth, since the dark thirteenth is described as being taken when joined with the following day, while the bright thirteenth is taken when joined with the preceding day, and because the eleventh and others are prescribed when overlapped by the following day, the mention of the thirteenth day—by association with them—is understood to refer to the dark thirteenth when it is overlapped by the following day. Therefore, the previously stated rule alone is superior.
The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, however, should be taken as conjoined with the full moon. Thus it is stated in the *Yugma* passage: "The fourteenth and the full moon.
This is also stated in the *Dvādaśī-kalpa* of the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"In this manner, the eleventh [day] should be observed, and the thirteenth [should be observed] on the twelfth."
The [observance] should always be performed on the thirteenth day, but not when it is joined with the fourteenth;
likewise, the full moon day (pūrṇimā) should be joined with the fourteenth, provided that the fourteenth is conjoined with the full moon.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa as well:

"The third, eleventh, sixth, and fourteenth lunar days of the bright fortnight should not be observed when overlapped by the preceding day; they should be observed when joined with the following day."
In the *Padma Purāṇa* as well:

"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight—these should be observed when joined with the following day; the following days [of the dark fortnight] when joined with the preceding day."

In the Varāha Purāṇa: "The eleventh, eighth, sixth, and the thirteenth lunar day of the bright fortnight should be accepted when joined with the following [tithi], but not when joined with the preceding one."
Likewise: "The third, eleventh, sixth, eighth, and fourteenth lunar days,
when overlapped by the preceding day, are traditionally said to destroy wealth and progeny for one who performs [the rites]."
Likewise: when the eleventh coincides with the tenth, the eighth with the seventh, the sixth with the fifth, and the fourteenth with the thirteenth; [87]
"A person should not perform these rites on days that are pierced by the preceding [tithi]," so it is said.
The sixth [lunar day] pierced by the Nāga, Maheśvara pierced by the Sun,
and the fourteenth pierced by Kāma— these mixed days are remembered as impure.

"Maheśvara" refers to the eighth lunar day. Here, the eighth and fourteenth days are to be taken as those occurring in the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa). Furthermore, the fourteenth days of the bright fortnights of the months of Caitra and Śrāvaṇa are to be taken even if they fall during the night; specifically, that which is the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
That [day] which extends through the night is to be taken; the other is that which occurs in the forenoon.
Because of this statement:
"Since spirits and powers wander at night, bearing spears,
therefore, when that fourteenth day occurs, there should be worship of Him."

And thus it is said: the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī) must be joined with the preceding [tithi]. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "In the dark fortnight, both the eighth and the fourteenth days should be observed when joined with the preceding [day]; they are never to be observed when joined with the following day."

As for that which is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "O Lord, the fourteenth day joined with the new moon [is auspicious], as is the full moon joined with the fourteenth"; and that which is in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
The eighth, eleventh, and sixth days, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
the new moon, and the third day should be observed as joined with the following lunar day.
Thus, both of these refer to the subject of fasting:
"The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, the fourteenth of both fortnights,
the new moon, and the third— these should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day."
Thus, according to the statement from the *Padma Purāṇa*.
However, when the fourteenth days of both the bright and dark fortnights extend into the afternoon of the preceding day, then they should be accepted as joined with the thirteenth day;
so it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
"O Lord, O mighty-armed one, the fourteenth day should be observed by my devotees when it is joined with the thirteenth, provided it occurs in the afternoon;
it should never be observed when pierced by the new moon (darśa) nor when pierced by the full moon (rākā). Thus it is said.

The full moon day (pūrṇamāsī) joined with the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) is to be accepted; likewise, it is stated in the Yugma-vākya: "The full moon [is to be taken] together with the fourteenth. Also, in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The seventh day should be observed as joined with the preceding day by men who are engaged in a vow."
O protector of the earth, it is established as a certainty in the Purāṇa that this is the full-moon day.
And this refers specifically to the Sāvitrī-vrata:
"O best of sages, the new-moon or full-moon day should never be performed when pierced by the Bhūta-tithi,
with the exception of the supreme Sāvitrī-vrata."
Thus, according to the statement in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*: "The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, the full moon, and the fourteenth... [Note: The sentence is incomplete in the source text].
The new moon day and the third lunar day should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following tithis.
Thus, since the fast is prescribed for the full moon day following the Pratipad, and because there is scope on the preceding day even apart from the fasting of the Sāvitrī vow,
it is said: "The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, and the fourteenth of the bright fortnight..."

O protector of the earth, regarding the statements "the full moon day [is joined with the next]" and the pair of *Sāvitrī* statements, it is not proper for them to be set aside by the statement concerning the first lunar day (*pratipad*), according to the maxim: "In a conflict of contradictory properties, that which consists of the majority shall prevail. Apart from the *Sāvitrī* vow, the lunar day mixed with the first day (*pratipad*) is to be accepted, based on the scriptural injunction: "The lunar day in the bright fortnight should be taken when the sun has risen upon it.
However, the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) should be taken as joined with the first day; thus it is said in the *Yugma* statement: "The new moon day is [joined] even with the first day."
In the Padma Purāṇa as well:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight—
these are to be honored when joined with the following [tithi], while the following ones are auspicious when joined with the preceding."
Pracetas says:
"The sixth [tithi] that is pierced by the seventh, and likewise the eighth by the seventh;
the tenth pierced by the eleventh, and the fourteenth by the fifteenth."
O bull among sages, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) pierced by the [preceding] lunar day must not be accepted;
rather, those days should be observed as pierced by each subsequent one, according to the Kāṭhaka Śruti.
The statements, “the eighth [falls on] the seventh” and “the fourteenth [falls on] the thirteenth,” refer to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). As for the statement from the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:

“If one performs the new moon day (*darśa*), the full moon day (*pūrṇamāsa*), or the anniversary of a father’s death (*pitṛ-sāṃvatsara-dina*) as overlapped by the preceding [tithi], he falls into hell.”
Thus, this refers to the *sāvitrīvrata*. For there is a statement in the *Brahmavaivarta*:

"The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*) must never be observed. Indeed, O Śikhivāhana, the new moon day pierced by the fourteenth day should never be observed, with the sole exception of the *sāvitrīvrata*.
And because of the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:

others, however, say that the fact that the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is joined with the first lunar day (*pratipad*) pertains specifically to the context of fasting (*upavāsa*), since it is stated that for fasting she is joined with the subsequent day; whereas for all rites other than fasting, she is indeed joined with the preceding day.

That is incorrect, because it contradicts the scriptural statements: "It should not be performed when pierced by the [fourteenth] lunar day (*bhūta*)," and "The new moon is pierced by the [fourteenth] lunar day."
The sixth lunar day pierced by the Nāga, as well as the tenth and the eleventh, and the Sinīvālī pierced by the Bhūta— on these days one should not perform a religious vow.

This is also because it contradicts prohibitions. If it is argued that these [rules] refer specifically to fasting, we say no; for that would entail the unwarranted restriction of many scriptural statements and result in a lack of consistency between the two *sāvitrī* passages. Furthermore, in this way, rites dedicated to the gods (*devakārya*) would fall on an amāvāsyā joined with the previous lunar day (*bhūtaviddhā*).
And consequently:
"Sinīvālī is always used for ancestral rites (*pitrya*), while Kuhū is used for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*)."
Thus, the statement of Jābāla would be contradicted:
"Even among the *pratipad* days, if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) extends into the forenoon,
it must always be used for rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*), even if it is pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*)."

From this statement as well, it is understood that the rite for the gods (*devakārya*) may be performed even when [the time] is mixed with the first lunar day (*pratipad*). Therefore, the previously established rule is superior. Thus, the rule regarding the selection [of the correct lunar day] in the case of a conflict between two lunar days (*tithidvaidha*) has been set forth. Now, the determination of the scope of those statements that appear to contradict this is being made. In this regard, Uśanas and Vyāghra state:
"Dullness (*kharva*), pride (*darpa*), and likewise violence (*hiṃsā*)—these are the three characteristics of a lunar day.
Dullness and pride are great prides; violence occurs at the beginning of the period."

[91] ‘Kharva’ means equality (*sāmya*). However, the author of the *Ācārasāra* has explained it as: “‘Kharva’ is a slight decrease; ‘sarva’ is [the state when there is no change]. ‘Darpa’ means increase (*vṛddhi*), and ‘hiṃsā’ means decrease (*kṣaya*). These states of equality, increase, and decrease are in relation to the preceding lunar day (*tithi*). Pitāmaha says: “Kharva, darpa, and likewise hiṃsā—these are the three characteristics of a lunar day.
Kharva and darpa are to be honored in the subsequent [day], while one should honor hiṃsā on the preceding [day].”
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, however, the latter half [of the verse] is recited thus:
"Kharva and Darpa are to be made posterior; Hiṃsā belongs to the prior time.
Regarding this very contradiction, Vyāsa’s scriptural statement provides the resolution.
In rites such as the observances (niyama), the pairings beginning with the second [tithi] are to be honored;
in rites such as the Ekoddiṣṭa or the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, there are injunctions regarding decrease and increase [of offerings].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the case of observances and so forth" (*niyamādiṣu*), there is the inclusion of all rites other than those for the ancestors, such as vows (*vrata*) and fasts (*upavāsa*). By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "the *ekoddiṣṭa* and so forth," there is the inclusion of *śrāddhas* other than those that are constituent parts of auspicious rites such as marriage. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "at times of prosperity and so forth" (*vṛddhyādau*), there is the inclusion of the *śrāddha* performed for auspicious occasions. Thus, it is stated that in ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), there is an injunction regarding decrease and increase [of the lunar day]. An exception to this is found in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"On whatever time a particular rite is to be performed, the lunar day (*tithi*) must pervade that specific time."
Whichever lunar day (tithi) encompasses the time prescribed for a particular rite, that is the one to be observed.
Vṛddhayājñavalkya states:
"Whichever lunar day (tithi) extends through the time of a particular rite, one should perform that rite during that time;
its waning or waxing is no cause for concern."
Lunar days occurring in the forenoon are fruit-bestowing for rites dedicated to the gods;
likewise, those occurring in the afternoon should be known as auspicious for matters concerning the ancestors.
[92] This statement from the *Nigama* and the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* also refers to the same subject as the rule: "Whichever time of the ritual belongs to which day.
Now, one might ask: when the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) covers the odd-numbered day but is reversed on the even-numbered day, which [tithi] should be taken?

On this point, some say: "Only the pair of lunar days (yugmatithi) is to be accepted, because of the statement that 'the pair of lunar days yields great fruit,' and because of the hearing of a fault in the case of bypassing the pair—'This [fault] destroys the merit previously performed when the pair is reversed'—and because even a lunar day measured by only a few *ghaṭikās* is designated as 'complete,' and because the scriptural rule regarding the occupation of the time for the performance of the rite is applicable only by excluding the subject matter of the *yugma*-rule, and because it conforms to the practice of the learned; therefore, respect for the *yugma* alone is appropriate."

That is incorrect. Even if the scripture regarding the pervasion of the time of the rite (*karmakālavyāpti*) can be justified by excluding the scope of the *yugma* rule, and the *yugma* rule can likewise be justified by excluding the scope of the scripture on the pervasion of the time of the rite, nevertheless, it is more logical that the *yugma* rule itself should exclude the scope of the scripture on the pervasion of the time of the rite. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting even the specific injunctions for the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth. Furthermore, in certain vows, since the first lunar day and other dates are heard in the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), its subversion would result in a contradiction with a quality enjoined after the rite has originated; moreover, since the adoption of a lunar day occurring at the "superimposed" time of the rite—on account of its being described as "complete"—is improper when a lunar day occurring at the "primary" time of the rite is available. Nor is there any fixed traditional practice (*śiṣṭācāra*) in this matter, as people act in both ways. Moreover, when the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada occupies only the day and the seventh day is deficient by three *muhūrtas* (*trimuhūrtonā*) on the following day, then according to your view, the *amuktābharaṇa-saptamī* must be observed on the second day, because of the forthcoming statement: "Lunar days are meritorious during the days. Consequently, the *dūrvāṣṭamī* vow would also have to be performed on that same day, since this [seventh day] is designated as "preceded by the previous day" (*pūrvaviddhā*). And thus a contradiction would arise, because in the *amuktābharaṇa-saptamī* it is prescribed that only food cooked with fire is to be eaten, whereas in the *dūrvāṣṭamī* the eating of food cooked with fire is not prescribed. Therefore, a contradiction would occur for those who have accepted both vows. In our view, however, this fault does not exist; for, by considering the scripture on the pervasion of the time of the rite, the *dūrvāṣṭamī* vow is to be performed on the second day, since for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*) the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is prescribed. In this manner, contradictions should be pointed out in other lunar days as well. Therefore, because the specific times such as the forenoon established for the first lunar day and others are mandatory for the rites, one should accept the lunar day that pervades the time of the rite, disregarding the *yugma* rule. Thus, the settled rule is as follows: when the lunar day cannot—or can—pervade the time of the rite (such as the observance of rules) on both days, the *yugma* rule and others apply to that case. When the lunar day that pervades the time of rites such as the *ekoddiṣṭa* is possible—or impossible—on both days, the rule concerning decrease and increase (*hrāsavṛddhi*) applies. But when on one day the lunar day pervades the time of the vow or the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite and it does not exist on the other day, then, according to the statement "Whatever the time of a rite," the lunar day that pervades the time of the rite is to be accepted.
In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken.
This is also the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya.

Where one lunar day (tithi) is declared by one scriptural injunction to be acceptable as the preceding day, while by another it is declared to be joined with the following day, a rule for resolving that contradiction must be observed. Furthermore, an alternative interpretation shown in that regard has already been refuted previously.
As for the statement from the Viṣṇudharmottara:
On the waxing fortnight of the moon, the lunar day (tithi) is honored at its rising;
when the moon wanes, it should be observed during the afternoon.
"In the dark fortnight, the lunar day (tithi) on which the sun sets is to be known;
by that one should perform the rites, and one should not take into account the decrease or increase [of the tithi].
Both of these [statements] are to be explained as before.
As for the statement of Baudhāyana:
"The lunar day and the asterism upon which the sun rises during the waxing fortnight,
but [the one] facing the setting [of the sun] during the waning [fortnight]."
And as for the statement of the elder Vasiṣṭha:
"A lunar day (tithi) is honored when it rises during the waxing fortnight;
when the fortnight wanes, it should belong to the afternoon."
All of that pertains to the same subject matter as the statement regarding "arrogant speech.
Others, however, say it pertains to the same subject matter as the statement, "the lunar day (tithi) is to be known in the bright fortnight.
That is incorrect, because it would result in the metaphorical application of the terms "fortnight" to the waning and waxing of the moon.

As for the explanation that when the fortnight increases it consists of sixteen days, and when the fortnight decreases it consists of fourteen days, and that [the rule] is as before—this too is incorrect. Since a statement can be interpreted in two ways, it is proper to assume its intended meaning (tātparya) to be that which accords with other scriptural passages; thus, there will be no need to postulate another underlying *śruti* source, whereas in your position, such a postulation would indeed be required. Therefore, the previous explanation alone is correct.

Others, however, state the following rule: when a religious duty (*dharma*) is prescribed according to specific lunar days such as the *pratipad*, or according to specific times of day such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), the lunar day that extends throughout the forenoon and so forth is to be taken, on account of the scriptural statement beginning with, "Whatever the time of a rite... One might object: "But is this point not already established by the two injunctions regarding the [specific] times?"

True; however, this is contradicted by statements concerning decrease (*hrāsa*), increase (*vṛddhi*), and so forth. For this very reason it was said: "Decrease and increase are not the cause. Where, then, do they serve as the cause? It is replied: when two lunar days (*tithi*) occupy that same time, then, in the case of a decrease of the lunar day, the preceding one is to be taken, while in the case of an increase, the subsequent one is prescribed for sacrifice, according to the statement: "The dwarf (*kharva*), pride (*darpa*), and likewise violence (*hiṃsā*). But when there is equality of the lunar day, in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) the subsequent one is taken, and in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) the preceding one, according to the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya: "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day... and so on.
Now, an objection is raised: since sublation would apply equally to all three [types of lunar days], why is it that only the *kharva* (deficient day) is sublated?

To this we reply: because it is perceived first, because of the parsimony of sublation, because of the statement "decrease and increase are not the cause," and because the mention of decrease and increase refers to all lunar days (*tithis*). What, then, is the scope for the *kharva*? It is the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Thus says Pracetas:
When a lunar day (tithi) is diminished, it is considered Sinīvālī; when a lunar day is increased, it is considered Kuhū.
Even when they are equal, it should be known as Kuhū by those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

However, the claim that when neither of the two lunar days (*tithi*) exists at that specific time, the decision is made by considering the rule of the *yugma* (pairing), is incorrect. This is because it contradicts the statements of Vyāsa and the *Nigama*, namely, "In the case of the second and subsequent [days], the pairings [are authoritative]," and because the statement, "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day is to be known [as the one to be observed]," is compatible with the method we have described. Furthermore, there is no evidence to support the view that this statement overrides all others; for while the rules regarding *khara*, *vardhamāna*, and *kṣaya* are established by a single unified statement, and among those, *kṣaya* and *darpa* apply to all lunar days whereas *sarva* applies specifically to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), it is inappropriate to resort to such an asymmetry when the statement can be explained according to the aforementioned method. Therefore, the previous arrangement alone is superior. But when a lunar day touches upon a small portion of the ritual time on one day and not even a small portion on another day, then, by the principle "whatever is the time of a rite, that [time] belongs to it," only the day connected to the ritual time should be taken. However, when it is connected to a small portion of the ritual time on both days, then—according to the rules concerning decrease and increase (*hrāsa-vṛddhi*) as well as the rules of pairing (*yugma*) and so forth—the earlier or the later day should be taken as appropriate.

And in order to show that even when there is contact with only a single prescribed lunar day (tithi) that pervades the entire time for the performance of the rite within either of the two fortnights, the ritual performed is endowed with merit, Devala says: "The solar day upon which the sun rises is to be known as the complete lunar day for purposes such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation."
[96] However, in the *Paṇḍitaparitoṣa*, it is read as "in bathing, giving, vows, and so forth," whereas in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the reading is "in rites such as bathing and giving. Vyāsa says:
"The lunar day (tithi) which the rising sun encounters..."
That lunar day should be known as complete for the performance of acts such as giving gifts and Vedic study.
Devala says: Whatever lunar day the sun reaches at its setting,
that entire lunar day is to be known as valid for the performance of rites such as giving gifts and Vedic study.
In the *Paṇḍitaparitoṣa*, however, it is read as "in rites such as bathing and giving gifts. Also in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"When there is even a single *ghaṭikā* remaining for a vow, fast, or religious observance..."
The entire lunar day (tithi) is to be understood as applicable for rites for the ancestors when it falls in the afternoon;
as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"That lunar day on which the sun sets during that day and night [is the one to be observed]."
Likewise, one should perform the ritual acts; neither waning nor waxing [of the moon] is a cause [for alteration].
Also in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"In the case of a vow, a bath, a fast (nakta), and especially in rites for the ancestors..."
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun sets upon shall be the one that possesses merit.
When even a single *ghaṭikā* remains for the observance of a vow or fast, that lunar day (*tithi*) is valid at sunrise; however, in rites concerning the ancestors (*paitṛka*), the opposite is true.
"Viparītā" is that which pertains to the setting [of the sun].
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"When there is even a single *ghaṭikā* remaining for the vow, fast, bathing, and so forth..."
For śrāddha and other rites, that lunar day (tithi) which is present at sunrise should be accepted, provided it extends until sunset.
Vyāsa says: When even a single ghaṭikā remains for a vow, fast, ritual bath, or similar observances,
one who is not distracted should perform those rites by relying upon that very lunar day.
Baudhāyana also says:
"If even a small portion of a lunar day exists at the time of sunrise, it should be understood as full; however, it is not considered abundant without sunrise."

In this context, it should be understood that the statement regarding the completeness of the lunar day (tithi) at the time of sunset refers to a lunar day that is to be accepted when it is joined with the preceding one, whereas the statement regarding the completeness of the lunar day at the time of sunrise refers to a lunar day that is to be accepted when it is joined with the following one.
A specific detail regarding this is also found in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The day upon reaching which the sun (the lotus-lord) goes to his setting..."
That lunar day (tithi) on that particular day is said to be [auspicious] even if it lasts for only three muhūrtas.
In the *Śivarahasya* and the *Saura Purāṇa*:
"If that [period] during which the sun sets should last for three muhūrtas,
the wise know it to be complete for all religious duties."
In the case of a decrease, the [preceding] tithi should be observed; in the case of an increase, the subsequent one should always be performed.
For that tithi which possesses three moments (trikṣaṇā), its decrease or increase is not a cause for changing the observance.

‘Trikṣaṇāyāḥ’ means ‘of three muhūrtas. In the Skanda Purāṇa, however, the third quarter of the verse is read as: “tasyās tu trimuhūrtāyāḥ. Vṛddha-vaśiṣṭha says: “On whichever lunar day the sun sets during the period of three muhūrtas...”
One should undertake that very lunar day for sacrifices, giving, recitation, and other such rites.
Vasiṣṭha states an exception to this rule:
"A lunar day that is waning should not be observed even if it lasts for three muhūrtas;
however, a lunar day that is waxing should be observed even if it lasts for only three muhūrtas."

In this regard, the fact that the increase and decrease [of the lunar day] are the causes for accepting or rejecting a *tithi* lasting three *muhūrtas* has been stated in the words of Vasiṣṭha, while it has been prohibited by the statements of the *Śivarahasya* and the *Saurapurāṇa*. In that matter, the following settlement is established: the increase and decrease are the causes [for determining the *tithi*] in rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), but not in obligatory rites (*niyamādi*) and the like, because of the statement of Vyāsa and Nigama: "In the case of the second and subsequent [paired] *tithis*, [the rule applies]. This is also stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and the *Baudhāyanaprokta*: "When the sun has risen, the *tithi* is for the gods (*daivata*); when the sun has set, it is for the ancestors (*pitrya*). A *tithi* of two *muhūrtas* during the day is [sufficient] for offerings to the gods and ancestors (*havyakavya*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: when the sun has risen, the two *muhūrta*s of the subsequent time of the day belong to the gods (*daivata*), being dedicated to the deities; and when [the sun] has set, the three *muhūrta*s of the preceding time of the day belong to the ancestors (*pitrya*), being dedicated to the *pitṛ*s. Therefore, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) extends over that duration of time is to be accepted for the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*) respectively. Regarding this, some say: "The two *muhūrta*s" is a secondary rule (*anukalpa*); a lunar day that is waning should not be made [to count] as having three *muhūrta*s.
"A lunar day that is increasing and lasts for only two muhūrtas should not be observed," according to the statement of Dakṣa.

[99] This refers to the lunar day (tithi) connected with sunset, because it is stated that only a period of three muhūrtas connected with sunset is to be accepted; furthermore, this secondary alternative (anukalpa) is for the sake of obligatory rites (*avaśyakarma*). However, when [the tithi] is connected with sunset on an even day (*yugmadina*) but connected with both sunrise and sunset on an odd day (*ayugmadina*), then that [latter one] alone is to be accepted because of the excellence of being connected to both; for the one connected with the even day is unfit for the rite and is as good as non-existent. But when it is not seen before sunset on the even day, yet is completed before sunset on the odd day, then it has been stated by Jābāli and Vṛddha-Gautama:
During the days, the lunar days (tithis) are meritorious for the performance of rituals by day;
however, in connection with vows such as the "night-vow" (nakta), the conjunction with night is superior.

A vow (vrata) to be accomplished over a day and night must be performed on the *ubhayayoginī* [tithi] itself; one should not pay heed to its being a "pair" (*yugma*). Thus it is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya: "Whatever vow is to be observed during the day or night, if it falls upon a single tithi..."
In that state of union with both yoginīs, the observer of the vow should perform that vow.

Now, this being the case, when is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the vow of the seventh lunar day (*saptamīvrata*) to be made within the pair of the sixth and seventh days? It cannot be at the time of the seventh day and so forth, because it is prescribed that "the wise man should perform the resolve for the fast-vow and other such rites in the morning. Nor can it be in the morning [on the sixth], for it is said: "One should undertake the Saptamī-vrata on a day of the sun (Sunday), during the bright fortnight, when the northern solstice has begun, and under a constellation with a masculine name."

This is because the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) is heard [to be made] at the time of the seventh day and so forth through such statements; and because it is not on an odd-numbered day, since the even-numbered days are declared to be meritorious and a fault is heard [to accrue] from transgressing them.

On this point, some say: the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must be made on the morning of the even-numbered day itself, because of the declaration that even-numbered days possess merit; and because, as will be shown below, there are scriptural injunctions regarding the "completeness" (*sākalya*) of both the preceding and following lunar days, yet there is no completeness other than their respective fitness for performing their own specific rites. Therefore, it is understood that the rite belonging to the seventh day and so forth is to be performed at the time of the sixth day and so forth. Nor is there a restrictive rule that the formal resolve must be taken in the morning, since in vows such as the Bhīmadvādaśī, it is prescribed for the evening. Consequently, it should be known that the formal resolve occurs only on the even-numbered lunar day, and specifically in the morning, not at the time of the seventh day or subsequent lunar days.

But others say as follows: when the lunar day (tithi) connected with the time for commencing a rite on one day does not exist on the following day, then only that which is connected with the time for commencing the rite should be taken.
And so says Baudhāyana:
"Whatever time is prescribed for a particular rite, [that applies] at its commencement."
If it were already existing, my dear, it would not require the undertaking of an effort.

Thus, the statement regarding the auspiciousness of even-numbered days (*yugma*) and the statement regarding completeness (*sākalya*) are justified even by setting aside the scope of the injunctions of Baudhāyana and others.

Others, however, say that the statement of Baudhāyana and others refers specifically to a case where the time for commencing the rite on one day coincides with an even-numbered tithi, while the time for completing the rite on the following day coincides with an odd-numbered tithi. In this way, when a period of three *muhūrtas* is obtained through the statements concerning even-numbered days and so forth, it follows by implication that a tithi associated with an odd-numbered day is not to be accepted due to the defect of *vedha* (piercing/contamination). And this defect is shown in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
The Dānavas said:
O Brahmin, in what place shall our dwelling be?
Standing all without support, where indeed shall we eat our food?
Brahmā said:
"The first station is at the end of the second; the second is at the end of the Nāgas;
the third is at the beginning of the eighth; and the fourth is at the end of the tenth."
[101] Starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight, your station lasts until the fifth;
starting from the fourteenth, it lasts until the end of the thirteenth day of the following fortnight, which is the sixth.
This dwelling place of yours has also been proclaimed by you to be very firm;
thus were the lunar days (tithis) formerly ordained by Brahmā.
Indeed, when those [offerings] are given mixed together to the ancestors, they are likewise [efficacious];
for the various remaining times are proclaimed to be destroyers of sin.
"O protector of the earth, [the time] beginning with the seventh lunar day and starting from the full moon is established as auspicious;
however, it is the opposite for the Asuras, as was ordained by Brahmā in the past. Thus, the piercing conjunctions (*vedhayoga*) are shown in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
But of what nature is yoga, O best of Brahmins, and of what nature is piercing (vedha)?
Explain both yoga and piercing, by means of which a faulty fast is [remedied].
When this was asked, [he replied]:
"O King, whichever lunar day touches the morning while the sun is still visible on the horizon—that should be known as *vedha*; it is considered a conjunction (*yoga*) occurring at sunrise."
Thus it has been told. As for that which is in the *Brahmavaivarta*, Vyāsa said:
O King, four ghaṭikās constitute the determination of dawn;
it is said that here, the fourfold division of piercing (vedha) and the other [faults] is taught.
The *aruṇodayavedha* (piercing by dawn) lasts for three and a half *ghaṭikās*;
the *ativedha* (excessive piercing) lasts for two *ghaṭikās*, beginning from the appearance of the sun's light.
In that very [moment], even the Great Piercing (mahāvedha) is seen, and the sun is not seen;
therein, the wise prescribe the Fourth Yoga at the rising of the sun.
[102] That refers to the subject matter of the Ekādaśī vow according to the context. As for the statement: "The serpent [is satisfied] by twelve nāḍīs, and likewise the quarters by fifteen."
"The Bhūta [day] corrupts the subsequent lunar day by means of eighteen nāḍīs.

This should be understood as referring to the case where the lunar day (tithi) overlaps with the time of the ritual (karmakāla) on both days; however, it is not appropriate to regard this as the subject matter for fasting (upavāsa), because:
"If days that are uncorrupted (aviddha) cannot be found due to prohibitions..."
If pierced for five muhūrtas, the Ekādaśī lunar day must indeed be observed.
A man should fast on other days that are pierced by half of it; however,
if such unpierced days cannot be found, he may eat a small amount of milk,
curd, or fruit only once, for that shall constitute a fast.

This is according to the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. Furthermore, regarding a fast (*upavāsa*), even a penetration (*vedha*) of a single *ghaṭikā* is established by another scriptural statement: "It vitiates the subsequent lunar day. Nor is this [rule] restricted to the cases of *nakta*, *ekabhakta*, and *ayācita* (eating once a day, eating only one meal, and eating only what is offered unasked), because those are prescribed as to be performed invariably on a lunar day that extends into the evening (*pradoṣa*) of the first day; since such a condition would be impossible on the second day, it would follow that they must be omitted. As for the statement from the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
It may corrupt a lunar day by half a ghaṭikā, or a third part, or even slightly,
just as a single drop of liquor in a full jar of *pañcagavya*.
Thus, for the very reason already stated, this refers to the subject of fasting (*upavāsa*).

By this, the argument put forward by some—namely, that the statement "half a *ghaṭikā* or a third part" is to be understood as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to disparage the Vedas, otherwise the statement "an *nāga* [is defined] by twelve *nāḍīs*" would be rendered meaningless"—is refuted. For when a literal interpretation of the sentence is possible in the manner described, it is improper to assume it is an explanatory praise through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Others, however, say as follows: "First, regarding the eleventh day (ekādaśī), when it spans the time of the ritual (karmakāla) on both days, the preceding one is obtained in the case of a decrease (kṣaya). But as for the sixth and the full moon (ṣaṣṭhī-pūrṇimā), even by the rules of pairing (yugmavākya), the occurrence of the eleventh day is prohibited there due to their association. This is incorrect, because it has already been stated that the rules of pairing and so forth apply even when the time of the ritual spans both days; furthermore, the established arrangement of the scope of the rules of pairing, the rules concerning decrease, increase, and equality, and the rule concerning the span of the time of the ritual—as previously described—has not been refuted. Therefore, when a lunar day (tithi) occurs such that it spans the time of the ritual on both days, this [following principle] should be observed.

Others, however, say that this statement applies when there is no overlap with the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) even on both days. Still others accept it as applicable to both cases. Therefore, the rule regarding *vedha* (contamination) applies only to those lunar days (*tithi*) that possess merit in their own right; for those lunar days that possess merit through conjunction with a weekday, a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or a yoga, the defect of *vedha* does not occur. For if the defect of *vedha* were accepted in such cases, the ritual itself would be lost on the second day due to the absence of the lunar day conjoined with the weekday and so forth.
And it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta* regarding the fourth lunar day:
"That [fourth] which is joined with Tuesday yields fruit in exactly that same way.
The phrase "in exactly that same way" means by virtue of the qualities of the weekday and so forth, independent of the qualities of the pair [of lunar days].
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Where the tenth overlaps with the eleventh, that lunar day (tithi) should not be observed as a fast;
however, when it is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism, it is auspicious and grants all desires."
Gobhila says: O Nārada, whichever lunar day is conjoined with a [favorable] asterism or a yoga,
even if it lasts for only two muhūrtas, that entire day is praised as auspicious.

Since it has been established that this applies even to all [times] when an evil *yoga* is present, the fault of *vedha* (piercing/interference) does not concern only the lunar day (*tithi*). Therefore, a lunar day pierced by a forbidden [lunar day] is to be abandoned; however, any other [day], whether connected with sunrise or sunset, is to be accepted according to the scriptural statement: "That lunar day is to be known as complete.
Regarding an exception to this, Vasiṣṭha states in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"At the time of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) or at the death of men, the lunar day is considered to be momentary (*tātkālikī*)."
"In the rite for the ancestors (pitrya), the full [lunar day] is declared to be that which is touched at the time of sunset.

The meaning is this: whether for breaking the fast (pāraṇa) or for death, the lunar day is to be understood as being effective only at that specific moment; it does not follow that the entire duration of that lunar day must be considered [for the purpose]. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
For anointing the body, bathing in the ocean, brushing the teeth,
sexual intercourse, birth, and death, the lunar day (tithi) that extends through that specific time is the one to be observed.
On the first day of the month of Manu and at the beginning of the Yugas, during lunar and solar eclipses,
and on the occasions of Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti, the ritual act must be performed while it coincides with that specific time.

The meaning is that the rites such as bathing, giving gifts, and performing *śrāddha* on the anniversary of Manu and other such figures should be performed when they pervade the time of Manu and so forth, and not at any other time. In the same way, the phrase "and likewise on the beginning of a *yuga*" and so on is to be explained;
and when the time for a *nakta-vrata* has arrived, the lunar day (*tithi*) that pervades that specific time is to be taken.
The meaning is that the lunar day which pervades the time of that *nakta-vrata*, known as *pradoṣa*, is to be accepted.

Thus ends the determination of the general lunar days (*tithi-sāmānya-nirṇaya*) in the *Kālanirṇaya*, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri— the sovereign over all the illustrious administrative offices of the Great Queen, the supreme king of great kings, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
[105] This is the fourth chapter.
Now follows the determination of specific lunar days (*tithi*) according to specific vows.
Thus, in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*), as well as the Rambhā-tṛtīyā and the Vaṭapaitṛkī."
O Brahmin, the lunar day (tithi) should likewise be made present before one through great austerity.

O twice-born one, the third, eighth, sixth, and eleventh lunar days should not be performed as face-to-face rites (*saṃmukha*) on other occasions; such is the determination of the scriptures, O Brahmin.
"Saṃmukhā" refers to that which is overlapped by the preceding day; "Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī" is the eighth lunar day associated with the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow.

Some, however, explain "Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī" as Janmāṣṭamī, since even for this, the eighth day joined with Rohiṇī and overlapping the previous day is to be observed as the fast-day. "Rambhātṛtīyā" is the third lunar day associated with the Rambhā vow. "Bṛhattapā" is the lunar day associated with the Bṛhattapa vow, and that vow is expounded in the Śivarahasya.
Uttaṅka spoke to Bharata:
Listen, O Great King, to the single vow called *Bṛhattapas*,
by the performance of which Śiva, the Soul of the Universe, quickly becomes propitiated.
This *Bṛhattapas* vow dries up even the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils.

By such statements as these, some— failing to perceive this vow— conjecture the reading "bṛhattalpa" (the large bed) and explain it as the "uninhabited bed" (*aśūnyaśayana*), claiming it constitutes the meaning of the second vow.
Since that is not seen anywhere in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇas, or their commentaries, it does not deserve to ascend to the rank of authoritative evidence.
Saṃvarta says:
The Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, Bṛhattapā, Sāvitrī, Vaṭapaitṛkī,
Anaṅgatrayodaśī, and Rambhā should be observed when joined with the preceding lunar day.
The "Anaṅga-trayodaśī" is the thirteenth lunar day associated with the vow of Kāma.
Furthermore, Bṛhattapā, Rambhā, Sāvitrī, Vaṭapaitṛkī,
Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, and Bhūtā— these [observances] should be performed on the lunar day that is facing [the sun].
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "O child, the fourth [lunar day] falling on the third [tithi] bestows the fruit of great merit;
it should be observed by those observing the vow to please Gaṇanātha’s son."
The "fourth" (caturthī) refers to the fourth lunar day associated with the vow of Vināyaka. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight, the sixth day of Skanda, and the fourteenth day of Śivarātri."
These [fasts] should be observed as joined with the preceding day; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place at the end of the lunar day (tithi).
"Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī" refers to the sixth lunar day associated with the vow of Skanda. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Janmāṣṭamī, Rohiṇī, and likewise Śivarātri..."
The fast should be observed on the day that is pierced by the previous tithi, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place at the end of the tithi.
Vṛddhayama says:
The Śrāvaṇī, Durgā-navamī, Dūrvā, Hutāśanī,
Śivarātri, and the day of Bali (Navarātra) should be observed when joined with the preceding [tithi].

‘Śrāvaṇī’ refers to the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. ‘Durganavamī’ refers to the ninth lunar day associated with the Durgā-vrata and other such observances. ‘Dūrvā’ refers to the eighth lunar day of the Dūrvā festival. ‘Hutāśanī’ refers to the full moon day of the Holikā festival, as well as the lunar day associated with the Vahni-vrata. ‘Balerdina’ refers to the first lunar day (pratipad) of Bali. [107] In the Padma Purāṇa:
“The Śrāvaṇī, the Durganavamī, and likewise the Dūrvāṣṭamī...”
Śivarātri should be observed on the day overlapping with the previous tithi, as should the day of Bali.

In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*: "The eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja that is conjoined with the *Mūla* asterism is called the Great Ninth (*mahānavamī*), which is indeed very difficult to encounter in the three worlds."
When the sun has entered Virgo, the eighth lunar day joined with the bright fortnight and conjoined with the Mūla asterism is known as Mahānavamī.
By worshipping Ambikā, the Mother of the World, on the eighth and ninth days of the month of Āśvina, one indeed becomes free from sorrow.

The Dūrvāṣṭamī occurs on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada when the sun is situated in Leo. If Agastya rises before the eighth day, then it should be performed during the preceding dark fortnight.
Thus says Laugākṣi:
"The Udyānikā, the Śivapavitraka, and the Meghapūjā..."
One who desires auspicious results should not perform the Dūrvāṣṭamī, the Phalavirūḍhaka, the Jāgara,
nor any of the annual vows of women, when the sun has risen.
Thus concludes the determination of specific lunar days (*tithi*) according to specific vows.
Now follows the determination of the time for the *ekabhakta* (single-meal) vow.
Regarding that, the definition of *ekabhakta* is given in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
