That which is eaten according to rule after the half-day has passed is called *ekabhakta* (the single-meal practice); therefore, it must indeed take place during the day alone.
Devala says: That which is eaten according to rule after half the day has passed is called *ekabhakta* (the single-meal fast), provided it is deficient by no more than three mouthfuls.
And that [rite] should be performed when [the lunar day] extends through midday.
Thus it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"In the case of Ekabhakta, the lunar day should always be taken as that which extends through midday."
Baudhāyana says: For the fast, the lunar day (tithi) at sunrise is to be taken; for the night-vow, it is at sunset;
and for the vow of eating once a day, the lunar day that pervades midday is to be accepted.

And here, "midday" (*madhyāhna*) refers to the middle portion of the day divided into three parts. Now, one might object that the term "midday" is also employed for the second period of a day divided into four parts, as it is said:
"The forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) lasts for one and a half watches (*prahara*), and midday likewise lasts for one watch;
the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) lasts until the third [watch], and the evening (*sāyāhna*) follows after that."
Thus, according to the statement of Gobhila; likewise, it refers also to the third part of the day divided into five parts:
"When the sun has risen as far as the horizon lines and three muhūrtas have passed, that time is known as 'morning,' and it is the middle portion of the day."
The period of twilight (saṅgava) consists of three muhūrtas; midday is recorded as being equal to that.
Thereafter, three muhūrtas are prescribed as the afternoon (aparāhṇa).
The fifth part of the day is known as the evening (sāyāhna).
Whatever is prescribed for these [periods] should be performed by one who possesses discernment.
Thus, according to the statement of Parāśara, how is the definitive conclusion to be reached?

It is said: by its own inherent nature, the word *madhyāhna* (midday) refers to the middle portion in relation to the two parts—the preceding and the succeeding. However, compared to other divisions, this perception is delayed in the second of four parts or the third of five parts; therefore, this word *madhyāhna* applies to the third part of a threefold division. And thus says the Śatapatha Śruti: "To him, the gods brought food in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), humans at midday (*madhyandina*), and the ancestors in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*)."

Therefore, by reflecting upon the previously cited statements, the period after midday (*madhyāhna*) is the primary time, while the period following that until sunset is secondary (*gauṇa*), based on the statement, "When the time of midday has passed," and from the expression, "only during the day. Furthermore, regarding the requirement of "pervading midday," by reflecting on such statements as "whatever the time of a rite may be," and employing a *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) based on a single part—just as one says "the cloth is burnt" when a portion of it is burnt—the intended meaning is that the rite must pervade the midday period following midday. However, when two rites equally occupy a portion of the primary time, even if one also occupies the secondary time, then the rite that pervades both should be accepted.
Now, one might object: "Let it be so when there is a decrease in the lunar day (tithi); but what about when there is equality or increase?
For the three characteristics of a lunar day are *kharva*, *darpa*, and likewise *hiṃsā*.
Of these, *kharva* and *darpa* belong to the latter [day], while *hiṃsā* belongs to the preceding time."
If it is argued that this is because of the words of Vyāghra,

It is said: Just as there is a contradiction with the statement "Kharva and Darpa" when the *pūrvā* [tithi]—which pervades the entire time of the principal rite—is accepted by virtue of the rule "of that rite for which... and so forth, so too is there a contradiction when the *pūrvā*—which pervades only a portion of the two-fold time of the rite—is accepted. Furthermore, it was demonstrated in the section on the general determination of lunar days (*tithi*) that regarding the subject of vows, only the statement concerning the pair (*yugma-vākya*) applies, not the statement concerning "Kharva and Darpa. However, when the subsequent [tithi] pervades the greater part of the primary time of the rite, whereas the preceding one pervades a smaller portion—even though that smaller portion is secondary—then the subsequent one alone is to be accepted, because it pervades the greater part of the primary time of the rite.

Whatever time is prescribed for a particular action, that [time], being present at the commencement of that action, constitutes a constituent factor; it does not do so when the commencement has been abandoned.

And because of the requirement of this statement, the contradiction with the statement "the [time] prior to the [main] time is [also] Himsā" must be resolved here according to the principle for avoiding contradictions regarding the words "dwarf" (*kharva*) and "pride" (*darpa*). However, when both [times] do not pervade even a single part of the primary time, and the earlier [time] pervades a single part of the secondary [time], then the earlier one alone is to be accepted; for even though it does not touch a part of the primary time, it touches the secondary ritual time.

On this point, some say: "The *ekabhakta* (single-meal rite) should be performed precisely during the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*); for in that case, both [the primary time and the secondary time] will be favored. If the *ekabhakta* were performed at midday—which is the secondary time for the lunar day (*tithi*)—then the specific lunar day, which is established by the original injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), would be sublated by the quality of midday established by the subsequent injunction (*utpannaśiṣṭa*). But that is improper; for when the primary time is impossible, the adoption of the secondary time is resorted to in all cases. Therefore, the *ekabhakta* should indeed be performed during the secondary time. This is incorrect.
Whatever decrease or increase occurs on the lunar day and so forth during the following day,
that same amount must be taken into account on the previous day for one's own ritual, even if it was not perceived there.

According to this statement, whatever ritual action is prescribed for a particular lunar day is that day’s own duty; therefore, even if the midday time falls during another day, because that specific lunar day is obtained at that very moment, the *ekabhakta* (single-meal rite) must be performed on that very day.

But when [the tithi] pervades the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*) on both days, then the determination is made according to the rules regarding the pair (*yugma*) and so forth. Furthermore, this time refers specifically to the independent practice of *ekabhakta* (eating one meal). As for the *ekabhakta* that is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to another vow, because it is itself subordinate, it does not override the time of the primary rite according to the maxim of "the conflict between the quality of a subordinate and the primary. However, the *ekabhakta* that serves as a substitute for a fast (*upavāsa*) must be performed on the very day of the fasting tithi.

Now, one might object: if, in the vow of exclusive devotion (*svatantraikabhakta-vrata*), the day is taken as that which extends across midday (*madhyāhna-vyāpinī*), then even a day joined with a prohibited lunar date (*niṣiddhatithi*) would result; yet if the prohibited date is abandoned, a day extending across midday cannot be found. In such a case, what should be done? Should the scriptural injunction regarding midday be set aside, or the prohibition? It is replied: in this instance, it is proper to set aside the prohibition. This is because in prohibitions such as "the sixth day joined with the Nāga [fourth]" (*nāgaviddhā tu yā ṣaṣṭhī*), no specific vow is mentioned; therefore, the scriptural rule concerning midday—which pertains to a specific vow—is more powerful.

If it is argued that there is complexity because the prohibition would also sublate the statement regarding the pair [of days] when the prohibition is sublated, we say: no. Complexity-based sublation occurs between two rules of equal authority, not between a general rule and a specific rule, because the specific rule alone is more powerful.
If it is further objected:

"Just as the specific scriptural injunctions— such as 'For vows like the fast (upavāsa) and others, even a single ghaṭikā [of the lunar day] at sunrise shall suffice; that lunar day is the one to be observed there, but the opposite is the case for rites concerning the ancestors'— are set aside by the two statements regarding the prohibition of the pair [of days], so let it be here as well."
It is said:
"Fasts should be observed on [the lunar days] conjoined with the following day, while those conjoined with the preceding day are [considered as belonging to the preceding day].
Because this contradicts other scriptural statements such as these, there is an inconsistency regarding the application of the rule for the *yugma* (paired) days.
The Nāga [planet] corrupts the northern lunar day with twelve nāḍīs, the Dik [planet] likewise with fifteen,
and the Bhūta [planet] with eighteen nāḍīs.

Based on this statement, some maintain that on the second day, even if there is no midday (*madhyāhna*), the *ekabhakta* (single-meal fast) must be observed. That is incorrect, because when a [tithi] that pervades the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) is available, one should not resort to another.
For whichever rite is to be performed at a particular time, the lunar day (*tithi*) must pervade that specific time.
For whatever rite there is a specific time, the lunar day (tithi) that extends through that time should be observed;
for the *ekabhakta* fast, the lunar day that extends through midday is always to be taken.
Because of this statement, the systematic arrangement (vyavasthā) stated by us alone is logical. Thus ends the determination of the time for a single meal and the lunar day (tithi).
Now follows the determination of the time for the *nakta* fast. Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"When the vow of *nakta* has arrived, the lunar day (*tithi*) that pervades that specific time [is to be observed]."
For the *nakta* vow, the lunar day (*tithi*) that extends through the evening (*pradoṣa*) is always to be observed;
with the exception of Ekādaśī, all such days are traditionally held to be equal whether they fall in the bright or the dark fortnight.

However, for the *ekādaśī* observed as a *nakta* fast, that which extends into the *pradoṣa* (the evening) period is not to be accepted; this is because the *nakta* rite is prescribed there for those who are unable to perform the full-day fast (*upavāsa*). Therefore, the meaning is that it should be performed on the very day of the fast itself. Regarding the duration of *pradoṣa*, it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The period of three *ghaṭikās* prior to sunrise is called the *sandhyā*."
"The evening twilight (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*) lasts for three *ghaṭikās* from the time the sun is above the setting mountain;
it becomes the night (*pradoṣa*) consisting of three *muhūrtas* once the sun has set.

As for what was stated by Amarasiṃha, namely, "the beginning of the night is *pradoṣa*," that refers to a period of three *muhūrtas* by the term "beginning of the night" (*rajanīmukha*), in accordance with the preceding statement and because it is improper to assume multiple meanings [for a single word].
In the Viśvādarśa, however,
it is stated: "Pradoṣa is said to be the three ghaṭikās following sunset."

Regarding this, some say that the three *ghaṭikās* preceding [the main part of] evening (*pradoṣa*) and so forth are designated by the term "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*), and eating therein is forbidden; for it is said:
"One should avoid these four activities during the twilight:
eating, sexual intercourse, sleep, and the fourth, Vedic recitation."

By such statements as these, it follows that one should eat during the three *ghaṭikās* following *pradoṣa*. This is incorrect, because there is no reason to abandon the primary meaning of the word "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*), and the prohibition applies precisely to that time. For indeed, the primary time of twilight is well-known to all people as the period from the setting of the sun until the appearance of the stars; furthermore, it extends from the time when the stars first become slightly visible until the sun is seen. And it is during this very time that eating is prohibited. Thus, another *Smṛti* states:
The morning twilight is said to last for three *ghaṭikās* prior to sunrise;
the evening twilight lasts for three *ghaṭikās* after sunset.
And the rule is as follows:
The evening twilight lasts until the appearance of the stars;
that which follows it is known as night, and during that time one should avoid [certain] religious duties.

Or, even if the meaning of the word *saṃdhyā* (twilight) were three *ghaṭikās*, there would still be no prohibition regarding it, because that [prohibition] pertains to eating as prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*). However, when [the fast] does not extend into the *pradoṣa* (early night) on either of the two days, then it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "If it does not extend into the *pradoṣa*, then 'day-and-night' (*divānakta*) is prescribed;
when the shadow is double its own length and the sun has grown dim."

Regarding that, they say "naktaṃ naktaṃ" (night after night), but eating at night is not what is meant. Knowing this, the wise man who performs the act of eating in the evening while observing the *nakta* vow certainly obtains the full fruit of the *nakta* fast.

Now, some say: "The phrase 'it should not extend into the evening' (*pradoṣavyāpinī*) is merely an illustration; because eating at night on Sundays and other such days is prohibited, one should therefore perform the *divānakta* (day-night fast) even then. This is incorrect, because the prohibition concerns eating that has not already been established by a mandatory injunction, as was shown in the discussion regarding the determination of the time for oil-baths (*abhyaṅga*), where the prohibition is understood as an exception to what is otherwise enjoined. Furthermore, it would entail the fault of metaphorical interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, on Sundays and other such days, it should not be performed at night at all. However, in the *Sauradharma*:
But when the sun shines while casting double its shadow, one should know that it is night; "night" does not refer to eating at night.
This also has the same scope as the preceding [text]. In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"The wise declare that a night is a day minus one muhūrta."
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, I consider the night to be [the time for the *nakta* rite] from the appearance of the stars;

after the appearance of the stars is the primary time for the night," because of the expression "I consider," the other [time] is secondary, since it is taught as the opinion of another. By reflecting on this statement, what is intended in the *nakta* injunction is that the rite must extend through the evening (*pradoṣa*) subsequent to the appearance of the stars. On this point, some explain that "I consider the night to be [the time] before the appearance of the stars," arguing that there is no reason to bypass the first [option] and because of the proximity of the secondary time for the night.

To this it is replied: what is intended here by the word *nakta*—is it time, or is it eating? It cannot be time, because the period prior to the appearance of the stars is the *saṃdhyā* (twilight), and regarding that, the Veda prohibits its being designated by the term *nakta-kāla*, stating: "Neither by day nor by night [should one eat]. Nor can it be eating, because of the scriptural statement regarding the *nakta-vrata*: "When the *nakta-vrata* has arrived, the lunar day (*tithi*) that pervades that time [is to be taken]," and because the word *nakta* is not applied to eating merely through its connection with the time of the stars. In that case, an act performed at that time would not be *nakta*. Therefore, the meaning is simply that one considers eating to be *nakta* after the appearance of the stars; and the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) is observed to be exactly so. Thus, *nakta* occurs when the stars are visible.
Devala says:
For a householder, the wise have prescribed that the night begins with the appearance of the stars;
for an ascetic (yati), it is forbidden during the eighth part of the day, which for him constitutes the night.
In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Upon the sight of the stars, one should eat at night before the first watch;
the remainder is to be understood as in the determination of the time for *ekabhakta* (eating once a day)."
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the night-meal. Now follows the determination of the lunar day for fasting. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
"The second, fifth, tenth, thirteenth,
and fourteenth [lunar days], due to *vedha* (piercing/contamination), destroy the preceding and following *tithis* for the purpose of fasting (*upavāsa*).
However, in the case of fasting, the seventh day, due to *vedha*, destroys the subsequent day."

The meaning is that the lunar days (tithis) beginning with the second, due to being pierced (vedha), destroy their own preceding and succeeding days for the purpose of fasting; however, the seventh destroys only the succeeding one. By this, it is stated that the first and third days, when pierced by the second, are not to be fasted upon; the same should be understood for the fifth and subsequent days as well.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa, however, having recited the verse "The second and fifth [are spoiled] by piercing," it is further read:
"The third, the eleventh, the sixth, and likewise the eighth lunar day..."
These lunar days (tithis) are to be observed as fasts, excluding those that fall below the point of piercing.
In the case of a fast on the seventh lunar day, however, it destroys the merit of the following day due to overlap;
the rule for fasting is prescribed for both fortnights alike.

The meaning is that the second day and subsequent lunar days (tithis) should not be observed as fasts when joined with the third day and so forth. In this regard, fasting on the second day joined with the third is prohibited here [in this text], whereas it is prescribed in the *Bhṛgusmṛti* and the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, second, fourteenth, new moon, and third—these should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day."
Also in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the *Śaṅkarīgītās*:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, second, fourteenth,
thirteenth, and new moon days should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following [tithi]."

In this regard, the following rule is established: the second lunar day of the bright fortnight (śukla-dvitīyā) should be observed as joined with the subsequent day, whereas the second lunar day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-dvitīyā) is joined with the preceding day.
"In the bright fortnight, the lunar day is to be known as that on which the sun rises;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day is to be known as that on which the sun sets."
Thus, according to the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the prohibition against the third lunar day being overlapped by the second applies to contexts other than the Rambhā-vrata.
Accordingly, the *Nigama* states:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight, the Bṛhattapā, the Sāvitrī, and the Vaṭapaitṛkī..."

"The Anaṅga-trayodaśī and Rambhā [Tithis] should be observed as fasts when joined with the preceding [day]. Thus, other than Rambhā, the third lunar day (tṛtīyā) must indeed be joined with the fourth. And so says Gārgya:
The eleventh, the sixth, the new moon, and the fourth [lunar days] should be observed as fasts when joined with the subsequent day;
the subsequent days are preferred over those joined with the preceding day.

The word *parāḥ* means "the following. Here, although the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) is mentioned, fasting on the fourth (*caturthī*) is prohibited by the statement, "The second and the fifth [are spoiled] by piercing," yet it is enjoined by the statement of Gārgya.

Regarding this, some say: "The white (bright fortnight) fourth should be fasted upon when joined with the following [day], while the black (dark fortnight) fourth is joined with the preceding [day], according to the statement, 'In the bright fortnight, the lunar day (*tithi*) is to be known [as such]'";
however, that is incorrect.
The fourth [lunar day], however, when falling on the third, bestows the fruit of great merit;
it should be observed by those undertaking the vow, O child, so that Gaṇanātha may be well-pleased.

Because of this statement from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, the prohibition of fasting on a fourth lunar day conjoined with the fifth implies—by necessary implication—that the injunction for fasting on a fourth lunar day conjoined with the third refers specifically to the Vināyaka-vrata; for if it applied to other vows, the phrase "O Gaṇanātha, [this is] the Sutoṣiṇī [tithi]" would be inconsistent. Furthermore, all cultured authorities (*śiṣṭas*) perform the Vināyaka-vrata on the fourth lunar day conjoined with the third; the scope of the statement "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day is to be known [as such]" has been shown in the section concerning the general determination of lunar days (*tithi*). Therefore, the established rule is that the Caturthī for the Vināyaka-vrata is to be fasted upon when conjoined with the preceding [third], while other [Caturthīs] are to be fasted upon when conjoined with the following [fifth]. As for the fifth lunar day, it is to be fasted upon when conjoined with the fourth, according to the statement of Gārgya: "The Ekādaśī, Aṣṭamī, and Ṣaṣṭhī [are to be taken as conjoined with the preceding day]," and because of the prohibition of fasting on a day conjoined with the sixth in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*: "The Tṛtīyā, Ekādaśī, and Ṣaṣṭhī [are to be taken as conjoined with the preceding day]. The sixth lunar day, however, is to be fasted upon when conjoined with the following [seventh], according to statements such as: "The Dvitīyā and Pañcamī [are to be taken as conjoined with the following day]."
Likewise, in the Śivarahasya and the Saura Purāṇa:
"The sixth lunar day that is pierced by the fifth (Nāga), and the seventh that is pierced by the sixth (Śiva),
and the tenth that is pierced by the eleventh— these should never be observed as fast days under any circumstances."
Having thus ascertained the most precise lunar day from the sun and the moon,
the observer of vows should always fast on the Ekādaśī, the Tṛtīyā, and the Ṣaṣṭhī.

In this context, the prohibition of fasting on a sixth lunar day conjoined with the fifth applies to cases other than Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī, while the injunction for fasting applies when it is conjoined with the seventh.
Thus it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The eighth of the dark fortnight, Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī, and the fourteenth of Śivarātri..."
These [fasts] should be performed joined with the preceding [day]; the breaking of the fast should take place at the end of the lunar day (tithi).

The seventh [lunar day], however, should be observed as a fast when conjoined with the sixth, according to the statement of Gārgya: "The eleventh, the eighth, and the sixth," and because of the prohibition of fasting on a sixth that is pierced by the seventh (Nāga) found in the *Śivarahasya* and the *Saurapurāṇa*: "The sixth, the eleventh, the new moon, likewise the eighth, and the seventh—these five lunar days, when conjoined with the following day, are not to be observed as fasts."

Thus, because of the prohibition in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), however, in both fortnights, must be joined with the following [tithi]," as stated in the phrase "in both fortnights. Furthermore: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight should be observed when joined with the preceding [tithi]; they are not to be joined with the following for anyone."
For this is the eternal law regarding duties such as fasting and the like.
This statement refers to the subject of Rudra-vratas.
In all Rudra-vratas, the lunar day (tithi) should be observed as it appears face-to-face (saṃmukhā);
in other ritual procedures for vows, one should fast according to what has been specifically prescribed.

Because of this statement, the ninth [lunar day] is joined only with the preceding one, according to the statement: "The second and the fifth [are excluded] due to piercing (*vedha*). The tenth is also joined only with the preceding one, according to the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* statement: "The third, the eleventh, and the sixth. The eleventh, however, is joined with the following one, because of the prohibition of fasting on a day pierced by the tenth, as stated in passages such as "the second and the fifth [are excluded] due to piercing," and because of the injunction for fasting on the eleventh when joined with the following day, according to the statements of Bhṛgu and others: "The eleventh and the eighth. The remainder will be discussed in the section concerning the determination of the eleventh. The twelfth, however, is joined only with the preceding one, according to the statement of Gārgya: "The eleventh as well as the sixth."

On this point, some say: "The white (bright fortnight) thirteenth is joined with the preceding [day], and the black (dark fortnight) thirteenth is joined with the following," as was shown in the section on the general determination of lunar days (*tithi*); the same should be understood to apply to fasting (*upavāsa*) as well. Now, one might object: why is the second day not accepted in the case of fasting on the white thirteenth, given the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and the *Śaṅkaragītā*: "The eleventh, the eighth, and the sixth"?

It is said: "The second and the fifth [tithis] are [to be taken] from the piercing. Because fasting on the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the fourteenth is prohibited, one must necessarily fast on that same day when it is conjoined with the twelfth.
Furthermore, the sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the thirteenth of the dark fortnight—these, when conjoined with the following day, are to be honored.

Based on this scriptural statement, the following rule is accepted for the fast on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight: it is joined with the following [tithi], whereas the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight is joined with the preceding [tithi], just as in other vows.

Others, however, say: here, the prohibition of fasting on the thirteenth day conjoined with the fourteenth refers to the *anaṅga-trayodaśī*; whereas the injunction for fasting on the thirteenth day conjoined with the fourteenth refers to cases other than the *anaṅga-trayodaśī*, based on the scriptural statement (nigama): "The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the *bṛhattapā* [are to be observed]. Considering this statement, the previous arrangement [of the date] should not be adopted; furthermore, the prohibition of the fourteenth day conjoined with the thirteenth applies to both fortnights. As Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says: "The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, and both the fourteenth days in each fortnight..."
The new moon day and the third lunar day should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following days.
In the *Nigama* and *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, new moon, fourteenth,
and third [lunar days], when overlapped by the preceding day, are to be observed as fasts on the following day."

The Ekādaśī and other such days should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day; however, the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā) is joined with the preceding day. Even therein, there is a specific rule: the Rambhā-tṛtīyā is joined with the preceding day, while other Tṛtīyās are joined with the following day. The prohibition against fasting on the full moon and new moon days when they are joined with the fourteenth day applies to cases other than the Sāvitrī-vrata. Furthermore, the injunction for fasting on the first lunar day (Pratipad) when it is joined with the fourteenth is based on the scriptural statement: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight is the Vṛhattapā. As for that which is stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "The sixth, the eleventh, the new moon, and likewise the eighth, when joined with the preceding day..."
The full moon day (pūrṇimā) that is overlapped by the next [lunar day] is not to be observed as a fast, nor is the "five-day" period (pañcaka).
Thus, that [rule] pertains to the *sāvitrī-vrata*. Also in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"One should not perform a vow on a day when the moon is pierced by a lunar mansion (*bhūta-viddhā*) or on a *sinīvālī* day."
But with the exception of the Sāvitrī-vrata, O Śikhivāhana.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, the full moon, the fourteenth,
the new moon, and the third— these should be observed as fast days when joined with the following [lunar day]."
And other lunar days during the rainy season should be observed as fasts when joined with the preceding [tithi].

The statement, “other lunar days (*tithi*) are also to be observed,” refers to occasions other than those where the day overlapping with the following one (*paraviddhā*) is prescribed for fasting by another rule. This is because, as a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), its application is precluded in a domain already occupied by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*). However, this interpretation is not correct, as it would render the word *sarvāḥ* (“all”) redundant; for by the phrase “all other lunar days,” one already obtains all the days other than those prescribed for fasting when overlapped by the following day by another rule. If, however, the word *sarva-* is intended to ensure that even those days prescribed by other rules for fasting when overlapped by the following day may optionally be observed when they overlap with the preceding day (*pūrvaviddhā*), then the word serves a purpose. Consequently, this too is a specific rule, and thus lunar days other than the seven beginning with the eleventh (*ekādaśī*) may optionally be observed either overlapping with the preceding or the following day. In this regard, Bhavadeva has remarked concerning the conclusion of the *Jāghanī-adhikaraṇa*, where the author of the Vārttika states there is an option between the *jāghanī* (the tail) and the clarified butter (*ājya*): “But here it must be asked how there can be an option between the clarified butter prescribed as a general rule and the *jāghanī* prescribed as a specific rule, since that would lead to the destruction of the relationship of sublation (*bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva*) between general and specific rules everywhere. This is not so, because both are indeed specific rules. For instance, if in the injunction for clarified butter only the word *yajñāya* (“for the sacrifice”) were heard, while elsewhere the specific form of the *patnīsaṃyāja* were present, then the principle of general versus specific would indeed apply. However, after stating the general term *yajñāya*—namely, “this clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is taken for every sacrifice (*sarvasmai vā etad yajñāya gṛhyate*)”—there is the further utterance of the co-referential word *sarva-*. By this, it is understood that the word *yajña-* is intended by the injunction of study to refer to the entire range of sacrifices under discussion that are not already restricted by a substance prescribed at their origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). Therefore, since both refer to specific domains, there is an option.

That is incorrect. For if this statement were to apply to guests who are to be fed by others as prescribed by other texts, then there would result an inequality of injunctions (*vidhivaiṣamya*): in one case, a prohibition would depend upon the sublation of another scripture, while in the other, it would be independent. Furthermore, there would also be an inequality in that the injunction would be mandatory (*nityavat*) regarding guests to be fed by oneself, whereas it would be optional (*vikalpena*) regarding those to be fed by others. In the passage, "Indeed, that which is clarified butter (*ājya*) is taken for the sake of every sacrifice when [it is used] in the *bruvā* vessel," the injunction of clarified butter for a sacrifice where no material has been prescribed follows from the very same reason [just stated]. Moreover, if clarified butter were enjoined with reference to the sacrifice, then the qualification "for every" (*sarvasmai*)—intended to include sacrifices where no material is prescribed—would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because it would involve a qualified reference (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*). Therefore, the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of restating what is already established; its purpose is the praise of the clarified butter by means of establishing its connection with all sacrifices.

How, then, is the option between the tail (jāghanī) and the clarified butter (ājya) stated? It is said: because of the Taittirīya statement, “When the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) are offered with clarified butter, and the wife-offerings (patnīsaṃyāja) [are offered] with clarified butter,” clarified butter is obtained for the wife-offerings.

Now, it might be argued that this is a commendatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to the injunction for the recitation of the Ṛg-verses, and not an injunction for clarified butter in the wife-offerings. For it is heard thus: “A redundancy (jāmi) is indeed created in the sacrifice when the fore-sacrifices are offered with clarified butter and the wife-offerings with clarified butter; one offers the wife-offerings with a verse after having recited a verse, so that there is no redundancy.”

That is incorrect, because here we rely on an injunction due to the impossibility of the statements being mere restatements of established facts (*siddhavat-anuvāda*), as in the case of the rule, "One holds it above for the sake of the gods. However, the authors of the *Tantravārttika* consider that the use of clarified butter (*ājya*) is obtained from another scriptural passage stating, "He performs the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with clarified butter"; therefore, the mention of an option (*vikalpa*) there is appropriate. If it is objected: "Let it be so in that case, since the word 'all' (*sarva*) has a purpose as a matter of praise (*stuti*); but how can this be so here, where such is not the case?"

It is replied: The word *sarva* (all) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established, just like the word *ubhaya* (both) in the passage, “For whom both oblations (*havir*) should suffer damage. Now, if it is argued that the word *ubhaya* is used there to dispel the confusion regarding the first [day] being restricted—as in the case of the damage to the *Āgneya* oblation—then here too, since the plural number finds its application only in the three [days], the use of the word *sarva* will be for the purpose of dispelling the confusion that only the triad of lunar days beginning with the *pratipad* is intended. Alternatively, if it is argued that the purpose of dispelling such confusion is accomplished by other means here, then it serves no specific purpose; in which case, the same logic applies to the word *ubhaya*. Or rather, what is the use of this search for a specific purpose? The solution applicable to the word *ubhaya* is the very same here; so enough of this over-extension. As for the statement of Vṛddhagārgya regarding fasting on lunar days—that in the bright and dark fortnights, the first day is to be fasted upon by the subsequent day, and the subsequent day by the preceding—one should understand that even this refers to a subject matter that contradicts other scriptural statements. Now, this is considered: when a lunar day, having begun at sunrise and extended until the next sunrise, subsequently increases in duration and becomes a thirteenth day or similar, which one should be fasted upon—the previous or the subsequent? On this point, some say that the subsequent day alone should be fasted upon, based on the rule of the "pairing" (*yugma*) and other such injunctions.
Now, if a vow that was undertaken on a single lunar day extends across both day and night,
the observer of the vow should perform that vow on the other [day] when there is a conjunction of both.

On account of this statement, it is proper to perform the observance (*vrata*) on the preceding day itself by abandoning the paired lunar day (*yugmatithi*). For when the primary time is impossible—since a vow (*vrata*) to be accomplished over a full day and night (*ahorātra*) cannot be performed during a partial lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*)—and one might otherwise resort to taking another indefinite lunar day proximate to it, specific lunar days are restricted by such statements as "Of the pairs, fire, pairs, and elements... (*yugmāgniyugabhūtānām*). How then can it be said that, by the force of the rule on pairs, even a partial lunar day is to be taken while abandoning the complete lunar day? It is replied: [The text continues: ...It is replied: [The rule applies] when the primary time is impossible. When the primary time is possible, there is no abandonment of the complete lunar day; rather, the performance of the vow occurs precisely within that very lunar day. Therefore, it is established that the performance of the vow takes place on the preceding day by abandoning the paired lunar day, because the primary time is impossible. Thus, the meaning of the rule on pairs is that the performance of the vow occurs on the preceding day by abandoning the paired lunar day, since the primary time is impossible. Consequently, the statement that
Whatever decrease or increase occurs on the lunar day (tithi) and so forth during the following day,
that same amount must be taken into account on the preceding day for one's own ritual action, even if it was not perceived there.

By reflecting on this statement, it follows that whatever lunar day (*tithi*) increases on the following day, the other [shorter] lunar day exists on the preceding day as well. Consequently, since the preceding lunar day is also fragmented, it is proper to perform the rite on the following day alone, by abandoning the former in order to comply with the *yugma* (pairing) injunctions.
This has been stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A lunar day that is pierced [by another] should be avoided."
Even though it is devoid of virtue, wealth, and pleasure,
the wise should avoid a woman who increases her own faction at their expense.
Another Smṛti also states:
"Just as the intercalary month is the first [of two], so the following one is the true [month];
likewise, when a lunar day (tithi) increases, the preceding one is to be abandoned and the subsequent one should always be observed."

Since fasting (*upavāsa*) is accomplished over a full day and night (*ahorātra*), it must be performed on the preceding [lunar day], because that day pervades the entire ritual action (*vakalakarmavyāpitvāt*). This is according to the scriptural statement: "On whichever time a rite is prescribed, the lunar day (*tithi*) must pervade that specific time. As for the claim that even the preceding [lunar day] is merely a "fragmentary lunar day" (*khaṇḍatithi*)—based on the statement, "However much [of the lunar day] may exist at the beginning of the [following] lunar day"—and that the increase occurring on the subsequent day extends back from the rising of the preceding lunar day; that too is incorrect. For in that context, it is stated "in its own rite" (*svakarmaṇi*); whatever rite is ordained for a particular lunar day is the "own rite" of that day. Therefore, the fast (*upavāsavrata*) ordained for the thirteenth day is the rite of that very day, not of the twelfth. Consequently, the application of the decrease or increase of the twelfth day to the vow of the thirteenth day, based on the rule regarding one's own rite, lacks any authoritative basis. [The vow] lasts throughout the day and night.

Furthermore, since there is no reason for restriction if the statement "and that which... were to refer to matters other than the fast (*upavāsa*), any restriction based on a consideration of the verses concerning the *yugma* (paired days) and so forth would apply even to what is distinct from the fast. Now, it might be argued:
"A wise person should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the morning regarding the vow of fasting and the like."

Because of this statement, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must be made on the morning [of the first day]. And thus, if on the second day even a lunar day (*tithi*) suitable for the resolve is not obtained, one should take the previous lunar day; but if it is obtained—even if it only partially covers the entire day and night—the rite belongs to the second lunar day alone.
That too is incorrect, because it would result in the redundancy of the qualification "by day and by night," and because all vows are traditionally observed on the preceding day.
For whichever time a ritual action belongs to, the lunar day that pervades that specific time [is to be taken].
Thus one should perform actions; neither decline nor prosperity is the cause [for desisting].

Furthermore, since the priority or posteriority of a lunar day (*tithi*) based on its decrease or increase has been refuted as a determining factor when a time that pervades the period of ritual action (*karmakāla*) is available; and because the purpose of considering the absence of decrease or increase—which was shown in the general discussion on the determination of all lunar days—is inapplicable here; and because the statement "the lunar day is pierced by a thorn" (*tithiḥ saśalyā*) refers specifically to the *ekādaśī*. The term "pierced by a thorn" (*sāṃśalyā*) means overlapped by the tenth day (*daśamī*), while "devoid of a thorn" (*vihīnaśalyā*) means a complete *ekādaśī*; both types are to be rejected. When the *ekādaśī* increases slightly on the following day, this [statement] should be understood as having the same scope as the scriptural passage: "Where the *ekādaśī* is complete, yet it occurs again at dawn," and so forth. In this way, the contradiction with other statements is resolved, and there will be no need to postulate a separate root scripture (*śruti*). However, if it were applicable to all lunar days, such a postulation would be required—as in the case of the statement "as the intercalary month (*malimluca*) is prior," which does not have the same scope as "both full and deficient [lunar days] are to be honored," nor can it override the rule for complete lunar days. Therefore, it is established that in such a case, the preceding day alone is to be accepted. But when the subsequent day is to be observed and only a single *ghaṭikā* (24 minutes) exists on the second day, then those [subsequent ones] alone are to be observed, and not those overlapped by prohibited lunar days even if they are slightly diminished.
And likewise, in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:

"When there is even a single *ghaṭikā* remaining for the observance of a vow or fast, that lunar day (*tithi*) should be known as complete; however, for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*), it is that which falls in the afternoon."
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* it is also said:
"One may corrupt a lunar day by half a ghaṭikā, or a third part, or even slightly;
[the penance is] like a drop of liquor in a full jar of *pañcagavya*."
But when [the tithi] on the following day does not extend until sunrise, yet on the previous day it is indeed pierced by a prohibited tithi,
then Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"If days that are unpierced [by prohibited tithis] are not obtained..."

"The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) pierced by five muhūrtas is indeed to be accepted; a person should observe the fast on other days that are pierced by half of that [duration]. This means that if days not pierced by the prohibited [times] cannot be found, then those days possessing the aforementioned characteristics are to be accepted. Regarding the phrase "pierced by five muhūrtas," this includes the four ghaṭikās within the period of dawn (aruṇodaya). When there is a piercing greater than this and a pure lunar day is absent on another day, he says the same thing even then: The meaning is as follows: if days that are not pierced by the forbidden times cannot be obtained, then days characterized by the previously mentioned definitions are to be accepted. The expression "pierced by five muhūrtas" includes the inclusion of the four ghaṭikās within the period of dawn (aruṇodaya). When there occurs a piercing exceeding this [limit] and there is an absence of a pure lunar day on another day, then he says the very same thing.

"But in the absence of unpierced [roots], one should eat milk, curd, and fruits only once in small quantities; from that, it shall be a fast. Some say: "This should be understood as a substitute for fasting, with the exception of Ekādaśī. However, on Ekādaśī, the drinking of water alone is the substitute for fasting; for while eating is prohibited, even the drinking of water is shown to be a substitute for fasting."
In the Vāyuprokta:
"During prohibitions of fasting, one should partake of some food;
one does not incur fault thereby, and one obtains the fruit of fasting."
At night, one should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya) without rice,
or sesame seeds, milk, or water;
or else the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or even just air.
"In this matter, the latter [alternative] is praised as the superior one.
This is incorrect, because a prohibition does not apply when something is obtained through passion (*rāga*) or when it is obtained through a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*).
Thus concludes the determination of the lunar day for fasting (*upavāsa-tithi-nirṇaya*).
Now follows the determination of the proper times for fasting under the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and other observances.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*,
Rāma said:
O Lord of the gods, a lunar day has already passed when the eye [of the deity] was seen;
how indeed should one act? Dispel this doubt of mine.
The God of gods said:
"O Rāma, one should fast on the lunar mansion upon which the sun sets,
or on that with which the moon is conjoined at midnight."
In some places there is a different reading:
"O Rāma, that lunar mansion upon which the sun sets while one has fasted, or that with which the moon is conjoined at midnight."

The meaning is that one should fast on that lunar day (*tithi*) with which the midnight—the point of half-night—is conjoined by the moon and a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or on that lunar mansion itself. And so Sumantu says:
"When a lunar mansion is reached during the lunar day before midnight..."
One should perform that lunar mansion vow (nakṣatravrata); the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place once it has passed.

"Is attained" (prāpyate) means "is commenced. The phrase "when that [specific] constellation has passed" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Bṛhatpracetā says: "But the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should be performed after completing all the constellations."

On this point, some say: "In this context, *pāraṇa* refers to the completion of the vow (*vrata*), not to eating, because eating is a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*). Furthermore, the word *pāraṇa* is a form derived from the verbal root *pāra-tīra*, meaning 'the completion of an action. Since that [completion] consists of giving gifts, performing oblations, and worshipping the gods, and since these are prohibited from being performed at night except during a lunar eclipse, one must fast until the appearance of the stars. This fasting for the sake of the stars should be understood from the *Nakṣatrapuruṣa* and other such texts. When the disappearance of the stars cannot be reached by any means during the day, then it is only logical that one should perform the worship of the gods and so forth prior to the disappearance of the stars, and eat once the stars have vanished.
That is incorrect; for it is said:

"One should perform bathing, giving, and other such acts at night during the sighting of Rāhu, at the solstices (saṃkrānti), at marriages, after calamities, during times of prosperity, and during optional vows."

Because of such statements as these, since the performance of gifts and other rites is prescribed even at night for various optional (*kāmya*) vows, and since the *nakṣatrapuruṣa* vow and others are likewise optional; and because that which was said—namely, "when the conjunction with the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) occurs by any means during the day," etc.—is also incorrect, for in such a case, according to your own view, it is proper to adopt the lunar mansion belonging to the second day. Therefore, the settled rule is this: when the lunar mansion connected to sunset belongs to the very first day, then that [first day] alone is to be observed. When, however, it does not belong to sunset on either of the two days, then it is likewise [the first]. But when it belongs to midnight on the previous day and to sunset on the second day, then the one connected to the second day [is to be observed].

Whatever time is prescribed for a particular action, that [time] exists as a constituent factor when the action is commenced; it is not, however, a factor by means of a commencement measured [only] by its duration.
Because of this statement;
and as for the statement in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"That lunar day and that asterism on which the sun has risen..."
One should perform one's duties by means of that [knowledge]; neither decrease nor increase is a cause for concern.
That refers to the subject of vows other than the fast (*upavāsa*).
As for the statement of Baudhāyana:
"The lunar day (*tithi*) and the asterism (*nakṣatra*) on which the sun has risen..."
But when there is a decrease in the waxing fortnight, it is toward its setting.

It should be understood that this refers to the subject of ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*). For otherwise, if the statements of the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and Baudhāyana were to refer to the same subject, a contradiction would arise: because in one [text] the allowance for decrease and increase [of the lunar day] is permitted as a cause, while in the other it is prohibited. Nor can the reverse be the case, because it is more logical that the determination of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) follows the same principle as the lunar day (*tithi*), due to their association. Furthermore, the injunction regarding decrease and increase applies only to ancestral rites and not elsewhere; nor do both [texts] refer to the subject of fasting (*upavāsa*), since that is already governed by specific scriptural rules. Therefore, the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) stated by us alone is correct.

Thus concludes the determination of the proper times for fasting under the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and other observances. Thus ends [this section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the supreme lord of all the offices of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
The fourth chapter, on the determination of time (*kālanirṇaya*), in the section on residual matters (*pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), is completed.
[129] The fifth chapter.
Now follows the determination of Janmāṣṭamī.
That [tithi] which is conjoined with Rohiṇī, whether it be the earlier or the later part, is the one to be observed as a fast.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇurahasya:

The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, when conjoined with the lunar mansion of Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), should be observed as a fast even if it is obtained for only a single Muhūrta; it yields great fruit.
One should observe the fast on that most meritorious eighth lunar day when Rohiṇī constellation is joined with it for even a single moment during the day or night.
Furthermore, that [lunar day] conjoined with Rohiṇī is highly meritorious for fasting and other such rites; therefore, it alone should be accepted.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O best of the twice-born, when the asterism of Rohiṇī occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight..."
That lunar day is declared by name to be Jayantī, the remover of all sins.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, in youth, in middle age, or likewise in old age, that lunar day, when observed with a fast, destroys the evil accumulated over many lifetimes.
In the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā:
"Listen attentively, O King, as it is being told by me to you:
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O lord of men."
If the lunar day named Jayantī, which occurs when the moon is in Rohiṇī, can be obtained.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "When the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) occurs conjoined with the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī) during the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it destroys all sins."
One performs victory and merit [on that day]; therefore, they know it as Jayantī.
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Prauṣṭhapada, when conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism,
is the lunar day known as Jayantī."

The term "prauḍhapada" refers to the month beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapratipad), while "Śrāvaṇa" refers to the month beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (śuklapratipad). This being the case, only one eighth day is established [as the primary one] in the *Bhaviṣya* and *Viṣṇudharma* Purāṇas:
"Fasting on the Jayantī destroys even the greatest of sins."
Keśava should be worshipped by all with great devotion.

In the Vahnipurāṇa: "Where even a single digit of Rohiṇī is known to exist on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, that should be understood as the one named Jayantī; it must be observed with diligent effort."
O King, Govinda, when properly meditated upon on that lunar day, washes away the threefold sins committed by men throughout seven lifetimes.
And there, O protector of the earth, fasting on Jayantī is declared to destroy even great sins when performed according to the prescribed rite; of this there is no doubt.
O King, in the Tretā, the Dvāpara, and indeed in the ancient Kṛta Yuga,
this [day] was observed as a fast by the learned when it was conjoined with Rohiṇī.
Likewise:
"But Rohiṇī alone, even for a single digit, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight is Jayantikā.
When the conjunction with Rohiṇī occurs on both [days], excluding midnight, then the latter [day] alone should be observed as the fast."

"Even when accompanied by a lunar mansion, the eighth day joined with the seventh must not be observed [as a fast]," according to this scriptural statement. However, when the conjunction with Rohiṇī occurs at midnight on the preceding day, while on the following day it occurs after midnight has passed, then the preceding day alone should be observed as the fast.
Thus it is stated in both the Bhaviṣya and Viṣṇudharma Purāṇas.
When the eighth day of the dark fortnight coincides with Rohiṇī at midnight,
worship of Śauri performed on that occasion destroys the sins born of three lifetimes.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, conjoined with the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī)—
one who performs the worship of Hari there while observing a fast does not suffer.
This yoga occurs at midnight at the rising of the moon;
it is the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, conjoined with the asterism Rohiṇī.
If it should occur even by a single *kalā* before or after midnight,
then the Lord of the World, Hari, the Sovereign who bears the Kaustubha gem, was born there.
In the Vahnipurāṇa: "If Rohiṇī occurs at midnight on the eighth lunar day conjoined with the seventh,
that Aṣṭamī will be meritorious for as long as the moon and sun endure."
Likewise: "O best of kings, Govinda was born at midnight during the conjunction with Rohiṇī, possessing four arms and the form of a child."
Therefore, one should worship him there according to one's means.
In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, at midnight,
when the moon is situated in the sign of Taurus and in the lunar mansion named Rohiṇī..."
For it was from Vasudeva that Devakī gave birth to me through this yoga;
therefore, one who is pure and has properly fasted should worship me there.
In the Agni Purāṇa as well:
"Therefore, O best of kings, the eighth day of the dark fortnight should be honored;
when joined with the Rohiṇī asterism, it should be observed as a fast, destroying the entire flood of sins."
Likewise:
"Whether it occurs even half a *kalā* before or after midnight,
that [time] is called *Jayantī*, which destroys all sins."
In the Padma Purāṇa as well:
"The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) conjoined with the seventh (Saptamī) and accompanied by Rohiṇī should be observed;
one should perform the fast on that day and break the fast at the end of the lunar day."
And in the Viṣṇudharma:
"Jayantī and Śivarātri should be observed when conjoined with Bhadrā and Jaya;
having performed the fast, one should then break the fast at the end of the lunar day."
Bhṛgu also says:
"The Janmāṣṭamī, Rohiṇī, and likewise the Śivarātri, should be observed as joined with the preceding [tithi];
the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place at the end of the tithi."

When the eighth lunar day has commenced even for a single *kalā* after midnight, and Rohiṇī remains for half a *muhūrta* or a full *muhūrta* on the second day, then that second day alone is to be accepted.
And so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O best of the twice-born, if the asterism Rohiṇī (the constellation of Prajāpati) should occur for half a muhūrta on the second day, following an eighth tithi conjoined with the seventh,
then it is to be known as an 'eight-watch' [Aṣṭayāmikā] occasion; so it was declared of old by Vyāsa and others."
Also in the *Pādma*:
"Even if conjoined with [only] a single muhūrta, that [day] becomes a full Aṣṭamī;
how much more so when joined with the Navamī, which grants liberation to ten million lineages!"

When, due to the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), there is a conjunction of Rohiṇī and the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*) at midnight on two consecutive days, then the Jayantī vow is to be observed on the following day.
And so it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"The eighth day joined with the seventh must be carefully avoided."
Even when accompanied by a lunar mansion, the eighth lunar day joined with the seventh should not be observed.

However, when the conjunction of Rohiṇī and the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) occurs on the very second day, then the Jantūvrata is said to be performed on that same day. In that case, there is an even greater excellence if it coincides with a Wednesday or other such auspicious days. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "If the eighth lunar day exists at sunrise and the ninth lunar day persists throughout the entire [following] day..."
But if it should coincide with the conjunction of Mercury and be joined with the constellation Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī),
it may or may not be obtained even in a hundred years.
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The state of being a ghost is destroyed for those who have gone to the womb of ghosts by men who have observed the eighth lunar day conjoined with Rohiṇī in the month of Śrāvaṇa."
How much more so on a Wednesday, and especially on a Monday!
How much more so when joined with the ninth lunar day (navamī), which grants excellent liberation to ten million lineages!

Others, however, say this: when Rohiṇī is joined with the first half of the night and not the latter, and that [night] falls on a Wednesday or a Monday, then only the latter [half] is to be observed for the fast, not the former. This is because of the statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "If even a small portion of the eighth day exists at sunrise," and because of the statement from the *Padma Purāṇa*: "For those who have entered the womb of a ghost. Furthermore, the two statements—"on the eighth day joined with the seventh"—and "even if joined by a single muhūrta"—apply to cases other than Wednesdays and Mondays.

That is incorrect. Even though the statement beginning with "on the eighth day at midnight under Rohiṇī" finds its scope in cases other than those associated with Wednesday or Monday, and the statement regarding Wednesday and Monday applies only when Rohiṇī is conjoined on the second [lunar day], nevertheless, while the restriction of the Wednesday and Monday statements is possible because the lunar day can still pervade the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*), a restriction of the midnight statement would entail the sublation of that [midnight rule]. Therefore, the restriction applies only to the Wednesday and Monday statements, not to the midnight statement; for both types of cases are covered by the two scriptural passages: "on the eighth day joined with the seventh" and "even if joined for a single muhūrta. There is no evidence for restricting [the midnight rule] solely to the instances of Wednesday and Monday.

As for what has been stated by some: these two statements do not concern the fast (*upavāsa*), because the word *upavāsa* is not heard therein and they merely express completeness; rather, by considering the sentence "from midnight onwards," even if the fast was performed on the previous day, the fact that the feeding of Brahmins, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth—which are prescribed for the second day—is performed even after passing [the proper time], and is described as being "entire," indicates that the fast is accomplished precisely when the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) and the Rohiṇī asterism coincide, thereby making known the great fruitfulness of the fast.

That is incorrect, because the designation "completeness" is also justified as referring to the fast (*upavāsa*), since the contradiction with the statement "below and above midnight" has already been resolved. Therefore, the previously stated determination of the subject matter is the correct one.

On this point, some say: when there is a conjunction with Rohiṇī for only a short duration, it is called Jayantī-aṣṭamī; when there is a conjunction with Rohiṇī at midnight, it is called Rohiṇī-aṣṭamī.

That is incorrect, because the term *jayantī* applies even when conjoined with midnight, according to the cited scriptural passage: "Whether it occurs a *kalā* before or after midnight, that is declared to be named *jayantī*."

As for the statement made concerning Jayantī, "even a single moment [of it] may be obtained," that is also applicable when there is a conjunction with midnight; for there is no evidence that the word *jayantī* refers merely to the eighth lunar day joined with Rohiṇī for a short duration, since a consideration of all the previously cited passages leads to the understanding that it denotes the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight accompanied by Rohiṇī. When the word *jayantī* refers to a specific night characterized by the birth of Janārdana, [it is said]: "The asterism named Abhijit, the night named Jayantī, and the hour named Vijaya—therein was Janārdana born."
Thus, according to the statement in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "But when [the eighth day] is not joined with Rohiṇī, then:
'In the dark fortnight, both the eighth and the fourteenth days should be observed as joined to the preceding [tithi]; they should never be joined to the following.'"
Based on such statements as these, only that which is joined with the preceding day (pūrvaviddhā) is to be accepted.

In this matter, some must be addressed regarding the subtle calculation (*sūkṣmānayana*); yet those [nakṣatras] intended by that method are established by the gross calculation (*sthūlānayana*) as being situated in the middle of the latter half of Kṛttikā. And it is not possible for them to possess the primary status of Rohiṇī, for one thing cannot become another due to contradiction. Just as midday is indeed day and not night, therefore, the status of Rohiṇī belonging to the half of Kṛttikā through subtle calculation is merely a resemblance to Rohiṇī due to its connection with the results of Rohiṇī; it is like Devadatta’s being called a "lion. This being the case, when the primary Rohiṇī is available, the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) should be understood as being conjoined with Rohiṇī, because it is improper to resort to a secondary (*gauṇa*) designation when the primary is possible. Furthermore, it is proper to accept the lunar day (*tithi*), nakṣatra, and so forth, as established by the gross path (*sthūlamārga*), because they are the first to be perceived. Even the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) calculates the primary time through subtle methods, but it does not establish the primary essential nature [of the nakṣatra].
As it has been said:
"This gross calculation has been presented for the sake of the practical conventions of astronomers."
"Now I shall explain the subtle [calculations] composed by the Sage for the sake of establishing the results of marriage, journeys, and so forth.

Furthermore, there would be no systematic determination of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and planets regarding injunctions and prohibitions for unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*) other than through the coarse [calculation], because the subtle calculation required for what is specifically enjoined or prohibited by day, lunar mansion, and so on, would not be established; this would lead to contradictions in its parts and would oppose the uncontradicted practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Therefore, one must rely exclusively upon the coarse calculation.
Thus concludes the determination of Janmāṣṭamī. Now follows the determination of the time for the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on Jayantī.

And that [breaking of the fast] should be performed at the end of the lunar day (*tithi*), according to the previously cited scriptural authority. However, when the end of the lunar day or the end of the asterism (*nakṣatra*) occurs after midnight on the day of breaking the fast, then the breaking of the fast should be performed at midnight. As it is said: "When there is an overlap of the lunar day and the asterism, or when the end of the asterism is reached, or at midnight, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the following day."
Because of this statement, some here say: "The alternative 'or having reached the end of the lunar mansion' applies to cases other than Jayantī, Śravaṇa, and Dvādaśī;
for whatever lunar days are proclaimed as meritorious when conjoined with a lunar mansion..."
One should break the fast at the end of the asterism of Ṛkṣa (Mṛgaśīrṣa), except when it coincides with Śravaṇa or Rohiṇī.
Because of this statement; and also in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"One should never break the fast on the eighth lunar day or under the Rohiṇī asterism."
One would destroy previously committed karma and the fruit earned through fasting.

"The lunar day (tithi) destroys eightfold [the merit], and the asterism (nakṣatra) fourfold; therefore, one should diligently perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at the end of the lunar day. This is incorrect, because in the very section on the Jayantī vow, the Vahnipurāṇa prescribes the rule for breaking the fast either at the end of the lunar day alone or at the end of the asterism.
"O Bhārata, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at dawn or even at the end of the lunar day (tithi); this is recommended.
Likewise:
"This [day] joined with Rohiṇī should be observed as a fast by the wise."
Upon their separation, the sages who discourse upon Brahman broke their fast.
When a fast based on a conjunction has been undertaken, if even one [of the conditions] is separated, one should break the fast; thus the knowers of the Veda understand.

Therefore, it should be understood that the rule for breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) at the end of the lunar day alone or at the end of the zodiacal sign (*bhānta*) pertains to those who are incapable [of fasting], whereas the other rule pertains to those who are capable.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for breaking the fast on Jayantī.
Now, incidentally, follows the determination of the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the Jayantī vow.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, conjoined with the lunar mansion Prājāpatya (Rohiṇī),
should be observed every year for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).

From this statement, because it is joined with a distributive repetition (vīpsā)—just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring"—its obligatory nature (nityatva) is understood; therefore, like the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, its obligatory character is also accepted according to the principle that "when a single thing has a dual purpose, there is a distinctness of connection" (saṃyogapṛthaktva).

As for what has been said by some—that this [case] is not equal to that: in that [other case], once the fruit has been enjoined by another sentence, the rite associated with the repetition (*vīpsā*) is enjoined for the spring season as being devoid of the fruits of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth; therefore, the result of that sentence is simply the communication of its obligatory (*nitya*) nature. But this [present case], by stating "for the sake of the satisfaction of Cakrapāṇi," enjoins the vow with respect to the fruit characterized as satisfaction; therefore, since it is [already] optional (*kāmya*), it cannot communicate its obligatory nature, because if it were intended to convey both [meanings], there would be the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Consequently, the repetition "year after year" (*varṣe varṣe*) is for the purpose of increasing the fruit, not for the purpose of indicating obligatoriness, because otherwise there would be no consistency of meaning, since the eighth lunar day conjoined with the *Prājāpatya* asterism does not occur every single year.

Therefore, it is correct [to accept] the repetition (*vīpsā*), because otherwise there would be the consequence of the scriptural statement being purposeless. Nor should it be argued that the repetition is for the sake of a greater abundance of results; for even in your own view, this would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), since one injunction would be for the result and another for the repetition required to achieve that abundance. If you think that the injunction regarding the vow (*vrata*) pertains only to the result and not to the repetition of the vow—on the grounds that the abundance of results is established without such repetition, and thus the repetition is not intended to convey that—it follows that the purposelessness of the text is difficult to avoid. Furthermore, if it were for the sake of abundant results, the primary meaning—the necessity of performing it every year—would have to be abandoned. And there is no reason for such abandonment, since the meaning of this sentence is as follows: the vow enjoined by another text for the propitiation of the Discus-handed Lord (Viṣṇu) on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when conjoined with the *prājāpatya* constellation (Rohiṇī), must be performed year after year. Nor should it be said that it is improper to denote the vow by the word "eighth day" through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) while abandoning the primary meaning, because an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) must conform to what has been previously established, and this applies equally to you, who also accepts that the injunction regarding the vow pertains to the result. The only difference is that for you there is figurative indication in the injunction, whereas for me it is in the restatement; and as the Commentator has stated: "In an injunction, the secondary meaning of a word is not perceived. Therefore, the objection raised—that there is no logical consistency in the meaning otherwise—is refuted, as it is possible for even an obligatory rite (*nitya*) to have the attainment of satisfaction as its fruit.
By a person who observes the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated; there is no other path that is so beneficial in this regard.

Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. Furthermore, is the obligatory (*nitya*) rite intended for the fruit of destroying previously acquired sins, or for the purpose of avoiding the transgression caused by its non-performance? In the first case, its status as an obligatory duty remains intact [even if the fruit is attained]. "When the eighth day of the dark fortnight falls on a Monday and under the asterism Rohiṇī at midnight, worship of Śauri on that day destroys the sin born of three lifetimes."
Because of this statement, even in the second position, its eternality is not contradicted:
"For the sake of the satisfaction of the Son of Devakī, the vow originating from Jayantī should be performed with devotion according to one's means by devotees as well."
By failing to do so, one goes to hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
For it is heard that there is a great fault in failing to perform [this rite].
As for what has been said by some regarding this: "This [passage] is not sufficient to establish its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), because it can be explained otherwise; for instance:
'When the eighth day of the dark fortnight falls on a Monday and under the asterism Rohiṇī at midnight...'"
Worship of Śauri performed there destroys the sin born of three lifetimes.

And so forth. By this, it is stated that the vow—like a ritual expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—has as its fruit the destruction of sins accumulated over three lifetimes. The meaning is that if one fails to perform that vow, there is no destruction of sin; consequently, one goes to hell due to those very sins accumulated over three lifetimes.
This is just as in the statement of Yājñavalkya:
"Men who are devoted to sins and do not perform expiation..."
Those who feel no remorse go to terrible and dreadful hells.

Thus, in this case as well, there is no fall into hell resulting from the non-performance of expiation; rather, it is due to the existing sin itself, because by not performing it, there is an absence of the means for the destruction of that sin.

[140] That is correct, because its permanence is determined by the use of the distributive particle (*vīpsā*) in the sentence. Since the incurrence of sin (*pratyavāya*) is established upon the non-performance of the vow, it is possible for the statement prescribing the fault of not performing it to be taken in its primary sense. There is no evidence for abandoning that sense to postulate another meaning. Moreover, if this Jayantī-vow alone were the means for destroying sin, then such a conclusion might indeed follow; however, since there are other means for destroying sin, such as various expiations (*prāyaścitta*), how could one fall into hell simply by failing to perform this one? Thus, even regarding expiation, the rule "an expiation must be performed" implies that it is obligatory (*nitya*).
When a sin has been committed and is beyond doubt, one should not eat while remaining present;
for by eating, one increases the sin as long as it is not confessed before the assembly.

Since the necessity [of the vow] is understood from such statements as these, and since the sin incurred by its non-performance is established, the statement "those who do not perform the penance," which declares the fault of failing to perform it, can maintain its primary meaning. Therefore, there is no basis for abandoning that meaning and postulating another sense. Furthermore, as it has been said: if, because the vow is obligatory, one falls into hell upon its non-performance, then a penance is indeed prescribed to avoid that [fall], as in the cases of *vrātyatā* and the failure to maintain the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). And so it is with the non-performance of the obligatory Ekādaśī vow.

"On the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], having eaten during the day, one should perform the *aindava* penance; on the eleventh [lunar day], one should eat during the day, and at the *parvan* junctions, one should eat only at night.
This too is incorrect, because there is no prescribed penance for all such cases; were that the case, [it would follow that...].
A penance should be prescribed where no expiation has been mentioned;

for the removal of all sins, including those arising from minor offenses (upapātaka) and those for which no specific rule has been laid down, one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) must be performed.
Because this would lead to the consequence that such statements as these would be rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, as for what has been said by some others: "If there were a transgression (pratyavāya) in non-performance, an alternative rule (anukalpa) would also have been prescribed; for example: [as follows].
In the absence of these, the twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
likewise in the case of the obligatory Ekādaśī vow,
one who is emaciated, aged, or afflicted by illness may pass the time by eating only once a day or by eating only at night.
It has been stated that a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) is prescribed for one who is incapable, but such is not the case here.
That too is incorrect, because even in the absence of a prescribed alternative, the occurrence of demerit (*pratyavāya*) is inevitable when a compulsory rite (*nitya*) is not performed.
In another Purāṇa, a common alternative is shown:
If one is unable to observe the fast, one should feed a single Brahmin;
or else one should give wealth and so forth to that extent, and if [the Brahmin] has eaten, then double that amount.
"Or, through breath-restraint (*prāṇasaṃyama*), one should recite the Goddess a thousand times;
a sick man should perform them twelve times according to his ability.
Therefore, it is established that the result of the statement regarding going to hell is the understanding of its obligatory nature (*nityatā*).

In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the obligatory nature [of the Jayantī vow] is made explicit by demonstrating the great multitude of faults incurred through its non-performance. For it is said: "The sin that arises from eating the food of a Śūdra, or from eating while the food is in the hand of a corpse—that same sin is incurred by men when they eat on the day of Jayantī."
O best of sages, one who has eaten the flesh of a vulture, a donkey, a crow, or a hawk, or the flesh of bipeds, on the occasion of Kṛṣṇa’s birthday, the eighth day of the lunar fortnight—
O best of the twice-born, whoever has eaten on the day of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī has,
without a doubt, consumed the sins arising from the three worlds.

O tiger among men, neither the world of the slayer of a Brahmin, nor that of the drinker of liquor, nor that of the killer of a cow, nor even that of the killer of a woman, is attained by one who is averse to Jayantī.
O highly wise one, those who, knowing [the significance], do not perform the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī vow, they indeed become predatory beasts in the forest.
[142] He who does not observe the vow of Kṛṣṇa’s birthday on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa becomes a cruel rākṣasa.
