If one does not observe the eighth day (Aṣṭamī) during the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
the servants of Yama— armed with cruel weapons and possessing fierce countenances— will indeed torment that person.
When one does not perform the vow associated with Jayantī for Viṣṇu,
having fallen under the power of Yama, one endures the agony of hell.
When the day of Jayantī arrives, if one fills one's belly [with food],
the body will be tormented by the messengers of Yama even to the extent of a single sesame seed.
O King, that deluded soul who eats on the day of Jayantī finds no escape from hell, even though he may observe the Dvādaśī vow.
When one performs the Dvādaśī vow together with Jayantī,
his residence shall be in the city of Śauri until the dissolution of all beings.
"O great sage, it is proclaimed here again and again in the ancient texts:
'By him who eats on the day of Kṛṣṇa, one hundred and one generations of his family—both past and future—have been cast into a terrible hell. Thus [it is said].

As for the statement regarding eating that was mentioned, it is actually a prohibition of eating, similar to the injunction "one should not harm any living beings. If that is so, how can there be permanence (*nityatā*) regarding the Jayantī, and how can its recitation occur in the description of its greatness (*māhātmya*), given the lack of connection between the two? If it is argued that because it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of Jayantī, the prohibition is intended for that purpose, even then, the permanence of Jayantī cannot be established by that alone; for indeed, the permanence of a sacrifice is not established by a prohibition for the sake of the ritual, such as "one should not speak untruth. Furthermore, fasting (*upavāsa*) is defined as the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to abstain from food along with its attendant ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*). Once the cessation of eating is already established for the sake of fulfilling that resolve, what purpose would a prohibition serve? This objection is answered simply by not accepting such a prohibition. Therefore, just as in the case of "fire is not to be piled on earth, nor in the atmosphere, nor in heaven"—where, due to the absence of any prior possibility (*prāpti*), the statement functions as a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended to praise the depositing of gold—so too here, the prohibition of eating should be understood as being for the purpose of praising the obligatory vow (*nityavrata*) of the Janmāṣṭamī, since it is illogical for it to be a praise for a rule concerning an optional (*kāmya*) vow by merely stating the fault in non-performance. However, the fact that the sentences censuring eating are supplementary to the obligatory vow is quite clear; yet, because of the mention of a connection to a specific result, it is also understood that this vow possesses an optional aspect as well.
As it is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:

"The eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, when conjoined with the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), should be observed as a fast even if it is obtained for only a single muhūrta; it yields great fruit."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having worshipped that Lord Hari together with Devakī through this vow,
one abandons the terrible path of Yama and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, for those supreme men who indeed observe the Janmāṣṭamī vow and cause it to be observed,
their prosperity remains forever stable.
O Sage, if the remembrance of Vāsudeva occurs at the time of death after the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow has been performed, all one's undertakings are accomplished.
O bull among sages, he bestows dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation— whatever desired objects one wishes for, and even those others that are exceedingly difficult to attain.
Likewise:
"O sinless one, by my command, perform the Jayantī for the sake of liberation.
[From] the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
O son of Dharma, whether it be a man or a woman, my devotee who performs this annually according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit as described.
There shall be a lineage of sons, health, and incomparable good fortune;
thus, becoming devoted to Dharma, one who dies shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having enjoyed various kinds of pleasures for a hundred thousand years by divine measure, he has come here due to the remainder of his merit.
But in that place, O Pārtha, which is enriched with all desires, devoid of all suffering,
endowed with all dharmas, and crowded with all the inhabitants of Gokula;
In the lineage of the best of kings, one who is like the god of love is born;
and in whatever land this [image] is always kept, whether painted or set within a vessel.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, my auspicious birthday, adorned with every ornament, is celebrated by people joined in festive celebration.
There, no fear of enemy armies shall ever arise;
the rain-god shall send rain according to desire, and there shall be no fear from the sons of Diti.
In whichever house my account of Devakī’s deeds is honored,
there shall be every prosperity, and no fear from calamities or the like.
There shall never be fear from beasts, mongooses, or serpents, nor from evil diseases, sin, kings, or thieves.
Therefore, it is established that this vow is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). Thus concludes the determination of the obligatory nature of the Jayantī-vow.
Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya, the sovereign lord of all instruments...

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, in the section on the determination of time (*Kālanirṇaya*), this is the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of Janmāṣṭamī."
[145] Now begins the sixth chapter;
now follows the determination of the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī).
Regarding that, the greatness of Ekādaśī is described in the *Tattvasāgara*:
"Like a mother for all children, like medicine for the sick,
the lunar day of Ekādaśī was created for the protection of all the worlds."
Likewise: "He who observes the fast on the eleventh day is blessed and he is wise.
And likewise:
He who, having abandoned Ekādaśī, observes another vow,
is like one who discards a great jewel held in his hand and begs for a clod of earth.
Likewise: "By fasting on even a single Ekādaśī and worshipping Janārdana— even out of desire— one shall attain liberation from saṃsāra."

In another Purāṇa, however, the reading is "one should worship even with water. Furthermore: "Whether out of context, or out of hypocrisy, or out of greed, by bowing to the Lord of the Thirty-three on the eleventh day, one is liberated from all suffering."
For all embodied beings suffering in this most terrible state called saṃsāra,
this fast on the eleventh day has been fashioned as the supreme medicine.
For those people afflicted by the disease of saṃsāra who have committed sinful deeds,
happiness shall arise immediately through fasting on the eleventh day.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa, Vasiṣṭha says: "O King of kings,
by the fire arising from Ekādaśī, the fuel of sin—
even that produced over a hundred lifetimes— is reduced to ashes."
O King, there exists nothing so purifying for men as this day of Padmanābha, which brings about the destruction of sins.
O lord of men, sins remain within this body for as long as a living being does not observe the auspicious day of Padmanābha through fasting.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the eleventh lunar day.
O Lord, whatever sin has been committed through the eleven sense organs,
all of that shall go to destruction by fasting on the eleventh lunar day.
There exists no protection equal to Ekādaśī;
for she indeed bestows heaven and liberation, grants kingdoms and sons,
provides a virtuous wife, and confers physical health upon the body.
Neither the Gaṅgā, O King, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara;
neither the sacred field of the Kurus, nor the Revā, nor the Devikā;
nor the Yamunā and Candrabhāgā are equal to a single day of Hari, O King.
O King, even if performed under a pretext, it does not fail to reveal the end;
O Indra among kings, the state of Viṣṇu is indeed attained without effort.
For this [speech] is indeed equal to the wish-fulfilling gem, equal to an inexhaustible treasure,
resembling the tree of one's resolve, and likewise comparable to the Vedas and the Upaniṣads.

In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "O Brahmin, by performing this Ekādaśī vow, which serves as a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) that brings about deliverance from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), one shall attain liberation."
Whatever a man accomplishes in fourteen days,
he indeed attains by fasting on the fifteenth day of Viṣṇu.
Thus, in all the Purāṇas, this is the settled opinion of the sages:
by fasting on Ekādaśī, one is liberated from sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Brahmin, in this Kali age, for those who maintain no sacred fires and whose souls are purified by non-violence, there is no liberation from saṃsāra except through Ekādaśī.
From the Padma Purāṇa:
"We have heard from Yama that a human being who observes even a single Ekādaśī fast, even incidentally, does not go to the tortures of Yama."
Likewise: "O Vaiśya, whatever sin has been committed by human beings through the eleven organs,
all of that shall go to destruction by fasting on the Ekādaśī."
"There is no merit found in the world equal to Ekādaśī; even those who observe it under a pretext do not come under the power of the son of the Sun (Yama). — *Skanda Purāṇa*.
For indeed, even without the conjunction with a lunar mansion, the Ekādaśī always destroys the sins of men here,
just as a wicked king destroys his own realm.
Just as knowledge is [corrupted] by false knowledge, as purity by impurity, as discourse by fallacious argument, and truth indeed by falsehood; [148]
O fair-browed one, just as frost is destroyed by heat, so is the accumulation of wealth destroyed by misfortune;
just as a gift is lost through boasting, and austerity is lost through the cause of pride.
For as an untrained son, as cattle from a distant place, as a funeral feast by mere convention, and as wealth through non-increase; [so is it with that which lacks its own nature].
O lady of excellent complexion, O auspicious one, just as knowledge arises from diligent effort toward its fruits, so has this Dvādaśī been proclaimed for the destruction of multitudes of evil deeds.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—
these will cease to exist [as sins], for Tripuṣkara is indeed not like that.
Neither the sacred field of Naimiṣa, nor that known as Kaurava,
nor Prabhāsa, O Goddess, nor Gayā, nor the Revā, nor the Sarasvatī [is superior].
Neither the Kālindī, nor the Yamunā, nor the Devikā, nor the Kāñcanī,
nor any other collection of sacred fords is equal to a single day of Hari.
Neither charity, nor recitation, nor ritual bathing, nor any other meritorious deed anywhere,
O fair-browed one, led to liberation, except for the single day of Hari.
By fasting on this day even once, heaps of sins are destroyed.
On one side is the gift of the entire earth, and on the other is the day of Hari;
the wise have declared them not equal, for this day is considered superior.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "That man who, fasting, meditates upon Hari with devotion— reciting His prayers, intent on His rites, and with his mind fixed upon Him— "
[149] One who is free from desire attains the state of Brahman without doubt, just like one who knows non-duality.
In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"The eleventh day is of great merit and the destroyer of all sins."
But for a devotee, it is the kindler of the flame of devotion to Viṣṇu and the bestower of the ultimate goal;
by fasting with devotion on this day, a person shall not exist again in the cycle of worldly existence.
He who fasts on the eleventh day and eats on the twelfth day does not fall into a miserable state or the hells; of this there is no doubt.
Having committed thousands of sins, if one fasts on the eleventh day and worships Viṣṇu on the twelfth day, one shall not fall into an evil state of existence.

This lunar day is supremely meritorious and bestows satisfaction upon Viṣṇu, the Lord; on this very day, the Lord of the World, though formless, remains present in embodied form. Therefore, it destroys all sins and annihilates all suffering.
"That infinite and imperishable power consisting of Viṣṇu which exists,
she is to be regarded as the Ekādaśī, being in the form of a lunar day," as stated in the *Sanatkumāra-prokta*.
Having committed thousands of sins and even hundreds of killings of Brahmins,
one becomes pure by fasting with devotion on a single Ekādaśī day.
Whatever vow other than the Ekādaśī-vow is performed by men,
one should know that to be fruitless, like a sprout growing from saline soil.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "That man who, having reached the day of Viṣṇu, with senses restrained and intent upon fasting, should worship Madhusūdana."
He destroys all evils; what need is there for austerities or for sacrifices?
Those men who have taken refuge in Ekādaśī are the best among the best of men;
likewise, many beings whose banners are made of serpents,
wearing foremost yellow garments, go indeed to the abode of Hari.
"O Lord of the Earth, this power of the twelfth lunar day has indeed been proclaimed by me; it is known as the fire that consumes the terrible fuel of sin."
In the *Devīrahasya* and the *Skanda Purāṇa*,
sin is declared to be of various kinds: *pātaka*, *atipātaka*,
that which is designated as *upapātaka*, and *mahāpātaka*.
And all that miscellaneous [sin] goes to dissolution by fasting on the eleventh day,
just as a clay vessel situated in water dissolves away.
In the Vaiṣṇava Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, the great Tantra:
"What need has he who observes the fast on Ekādaśī for any other rite?
And what need has he who does not observe the fast on Ekādaśī for any other rite?"
Regarding the duties of the Sun:
the Lord placed the Agnihotra and other rites on one side and the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) on the other in a balance; therein, the twelfth day was found to be superior.
In the *Devīrahasya*: "Just as the Gāyatrī here is the shatterer of the cage of all sins,
so too is Ekādaśī the shatterer of the cage of all sins."
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That which arises from eating what should not be eaten, from approaching those who should not be approached,
from officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate, and from consuming things that should not be consumed."
Whatever [sin] arises from touching those who should not be touched, from reviling others,
from praising oneself, and from committing adultery;

Whatever sin or minor offense has been committed— whether through the non-performance of prescribed duties, the theft of another's wealth, or whether done intentionally or unintentionally— all that dissolves by fasting on the Ekādaśī day.
In the Vaiṣṇava Tantra: "The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is of great merit and is beloved by Viṣṇu, the Lord;
he who fasts on that day and worships Hari on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī)."
His sins are destroyed, devotion to Viṣṇu arises,
and he gains eternal knowledge by which a man is liberated from saṃsāra.
In the Skanda and Bhaviṣyat Purāṇas:
"Those who fast on the twelfth day, subsisting only on air and water,
or those who worship Hari with clove blossoms,"
Those royal swans of the ocean of washed-whitened milk cross to the further shore of the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The man who, endowed with devotion, observes the Ekādaśī vow,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu."
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The man who observes the fast on the eleventh day with faith is liberated from all sins and the like, just as a snake is freed from its skin."
He beholds neither calamity, nor hell, nor torment;
he is to be saluted and he is to be worshipped, for he is beloved by Vāsudeva.
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"The man who always performs the Ekādaśī vow with devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu and attains a form identical to that of Viṣṇu."
In the Āgneya Purāṇa:
"The man who always observes a fast on the eleventh day goes to the supreme abode where the Lord Hari resides."
In the Rudra Purāṇa: "The man who performs the fast on Ekādaśī with devotion goes to the realm of Viṣṇu and attains a form identical to that of Viṣṇu."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Just as the syllable Om is honored as the foremost of all the Vedas,
so too is the vow of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī-vrata) the most excellent of all vows."
Thus concludes the majesty of Ekādaśī.
Now follows the determination regarding the prohibition of the vow-formula (*vratavākya*) in relation to Ekādaśī.

In that regard, concerning Ekādaśī, some statements are intended for the prohibition of eating, while others are intended for the injunction of the vow. Among these, first, those intended for the prohibition of eating are cited.
Regarding this, Devala says:
One should not drink water from a conch shell, nor eat tortoises or pigs;
one should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the killing of a Brahmin,
they remain residing in food when the day of Hari has arrived."
One who eats on the day of Hari incurs those sins;
thus do the Purāṇas proclaim again and again, O fair-faced one.
"One must not eat, one must not eat on the arrival of the day of Hari (Ekādaśī). From the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Even a killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of a brother, or likewise a killer of a guru [is purified by it]."
But one who eats on the eleventh day shall fall from the world of Viṣṇu.
From the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "Any mortal in my kingdom who, being more than eight years of age and not yet reaching eighty, eats on the day of Viṣṇu, is a partaker of sin."
"He is to be punished by me, he is to be executed by me, and he is to be exiled from my country by me.
Also in the Viṣṇusmṛti:
"A man should never eat on the eleventh day."
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: He who eats on the day of Hari consumes only sin;
for on that day, all sins reside within the food.
He who eats them out of delusion is not liberated from his sins.
However, Kātyāyana has pointed out a specific fault for a widow regarding the eleventh day:
"If a woman who is a widow should eat on the eleventh day,
her merit would perish, and she would incur the sin of killing an embryo day after day."

And in this context, because of its association with established prohibitions such as “one should not eat tortoise or pork,” the intent of statements like “one should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight” is determined to be purely prohibitive. Furthermore, in these sentences, no grounds for an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), such as grammatical coordination with the word *vrata* (vow), are heard; therefore, these are prohibitions against eating.

On this point, some say: these statements also concern fasting alone, because in some cases they introduce the topic with fasting, in some they conclude with it, and in others they establish fasting both in the introduction and the conclusion; furthermore, if one were to posit a negative injunction (*nañartha-vidhi*), it would entail the necessity of postulating another root Vedic text (*mūla-bhūta-vedāntara*). To maintain a single source for the tradition, even the use of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is well-established within the system of the Smṛtis. Moreover, the statement in the *Smṛtis* of Devala and others—having first declared, "One should fast on the eleventh day," and then stating, "One should not eat on the eleventh day"—is intended either as a concluding summary or as an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, its placement within the section on fasting is also appropriate. Therefore, the view that such statements are solely concerned with an independent injunction of a negative meaning is refuted.

Others, however, say: "This is not correct; for when the primary meaning is possible, it is improper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor should it be argued that resorting to figurative indication is appropriate because it avoids the contingency of postulating another underlying Vedic source (*mūlabhūtavedāntara*); for [if that were so], it would follow that all injunctions and prohibitions would have a single purpose. Furthermore, there is no reason here to resort to *paryudāsa* (exclusion) based on grammatical coordination with words such as 'vow' (*vrata*).
[Objection: 'One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights...'"
This is the duty of the forest-dwelling ascetic; the householder, however, should always practice only the bright path.

Thus, this is an *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) that enjoins a vow (*vrata*) known as fasting (*upavāsa*), which consists of the resolve not to eat; for it is stated, "This is the duty (*dharma*) of forest-dwellers and ascetics," due to its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "duty. Indeed, no merit (*dharma*) arises from the mere abandonment of prohibited acts such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). From the performance of acts like the killing of a Brahmin, demerit (*adharma*) results; from their non-performance, there is merely the avoidance of demerit, but no further production of merit occurs. Even if a prohibition were understood as a positive duty when it is grasped by a specific injunction (*grāhaka*), a standalone prohibition does not become a duty in that way. Therefore, because of its coordination with the word "duty," it is understood that there is some positive entity to be enjoined. Just as in the case of the Prajāpati-vows, where the meaning of the negative particle is coordinated with the word "vow" (*vrata*), so too in all sentences prohibiting food on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), the coordination with the word "duty"—based on the principle of the "all-branches" (*sarvaśākhānyāya*)—will serve as the reason for resorting to *paryudāsa*, since the statement "this is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics" is the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*).

It is said: True. Where this obligatory vow of fasting on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), as enjoined by this statement, is prescribed in another Smṛti either in its primary sense or—due to the impossibility of the primary sense—by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), as in the Smṛtis of Kātyāyana and Devala:
"One should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights. And in the Viṣṇurahasya and Skanda Purāṇas: [similar injunctions].
"Having observed the Ekādaśī fast regularly on both fortnights," and so forth; as also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
a celibate student and a woman should always do so, as should a householder, but only during the bright fortnight.
In the Agni Purāṇa: "A householder, a student, and likewise one who has maintained the sacred fires,
shall not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding the suffering of those beings, radiated light from his body and illuminated them all. Then, by means of his transcendent wisdom (*prajñā*), he perceived that these five aggregates are all empty and thus delivered all those beings from their suffering. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Bhagavān, why is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara called ‘Avalokiteśvara’? The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “If there are many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of living beings who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon him, then Avalokiteśvara will immediately perceive their voices and deliver them all from suffering. Therefore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is called ‘Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if sons or daughters of good family wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should observe that all phenomena are empty in nature and should not give rise to perverted views. This is how one should observe the five aggregates as empty. Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not different from form, and form is not different from emptiness. What is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object. There is no realm of sight, up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness. There is no ignorance, nor the extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging and death, nor the extinction of aging and death. There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and also no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, the Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted dreams, he realizes *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequalled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra and all those present—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and mahoragas—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it.

Such is the statement. In this regard, since there is identity of action (*karmaikya*), it is appropriate to synthesize (*upasaṃhāra*) the specific details found in that Smṛti—namely, "This is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics"—with the specific details found in this [text], namely, "The student and the woman," and "The householder, the student, and likewise the one who has established the sacred fires. However, where there is no injunction for a fast-vow because a prohibition is certain due to the possibility of the primary meaning, how can there be a synthesis of what pertains to the vow? For a specific detail pertaining to the *agnihotra* is not synthesized with another rite in a different Vedic branch. If it is argued that the injunction for the vow will arise precisely from such a synthesis, we say no; for this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), wherein the synthesis occurs only when the vow-injunction exists, and the vow-injunction exists only when the synthesis occurs due to the identity of action. Furthermore, if there were synthesis everywhere, there would be the consequence of redundancy (*paunaruktya*), since other sentences enjoining the vow already exist in the *Devalasmṛti*. Nor should it be said that one sentence is the injunction of the vow and the second is for the sake of synthesis or for the sake of enjoining an accessory (*guṇavidhi*). This is because synthesis is untenable for something not present in the mind due to the intervention of prohibitions such as "One should not drink water from a conch-shell vessel"; moreover, since a distinct purpose is possible, it is improper to assume a purpose of synthesis. Nor is it an injunction of an accessory, because an injunction is untenable if its object is already established by other means, and because these are recited in association with well-known prohibitions such as "One should not drink water from a conch-shell vessel. By this, the argument that the presentation of the fast occurs in some cases in the introduction and in others in the conclusion is also refuted. Furthermore, its placement within the section on fasting is appropriate due to its connection with a single lunar day (*tithi*). Therefore, the view that such statements are intended solely as injunctions regarding the independent meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is correct. If it is asked, "How can there be an injunction for a fast-vow through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in sentences concerning students (*brahmacārin*) and others, given the impossibility of the primary meaning? It is replied: if the primary meaning of these sentences were accepted, their sense would be as follows: "For householders, students, those who have established the sacred fires, and women, there is a prohibition against eating on the eleventh day of both fortnights; therefore, for others, there would be no sin in eating. Moreover, for the householder, there would be a prohibition against eating only during the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), while there would be no sin in eating during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*), because a specific prohibition implies permission for the remainder. But if that were the case, [the text would be contradicted]. Thus...
A person should never eat on the eleventh lunar day.

This would contradict such statements as those cited above. Nor can it be argued that the general prohibition is restricted by a specific prohibition—just as the general rule "one divides the *puroḍāśa* cake into four parts" is restricted by the specific rule "one divides the *āgneya* cake into four parts"—because a prohibition, having cessation (*nivṛtti*) as its result, does not depend on a specific qualification, and thus restriction is untenable. Even if such restriction were possible, if the general prohibition "one should not harm any living beings" were restricted by the specific prohibition "a Brahmin is not to be killed," then the instruction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or others would become meaningless. If it is argued that the specific prohibition "a Brahmin is not to be killed" is intended to indicate the gravity of the sin, we say no; for there is no such difference. It is not possible for the transgression to be less for forest-dwellers and ascetics when eating on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) than for householders and others, nor for a householder’s transgression to be less when eating on a dark lunar day than on a bright one, since no greater expiation is prescribed for them. On the contrary, compared to householders and others, greater expiation is prescribed for forest-dwellers and others, according to the statement: "Purification is declared to be like cleansing. If it is argued that restriction is impossible precisely because of the instruction regarding expiation, we say no; for if expiation were not instructed, the same [general] contingency would apply. If it is argued that a generally prescribed expiation exists everywhere, we say no; for in your own view, this would lead to the contingency of mere mental construction (*kalpanā*), even when a direct prohibition exists. If it is argued that there will simply be an absence of restriction for what is explicitly heard (*śruta*), we say no; for if the purpose were not to preclude restriction, the word "human" (*mānava*) in the text would be redundant, since the scripture’s authority over humans is already established by the fact that humans alone possess the capacity for religious duty (*adhikāra*). As for the objection raised against the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—namely, that in the sentence "the householder and the student," the mention of the householder would be inappropriate because fasting would apply to both parties (as it would for the student), and because it would contradict future statements such as "the householder should always [fast] on the bright [fortnight]"—that is incorrect, because the lack of contradiction will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.

Others, however, say: those sentences which lack grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as *vrata* (vow) and the like, are intended solely as prohibitions (*niṣedha*). [Objection: Even in the case of the alternative of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is indeed no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because of the traditional rule: "In the absence of *nañ*, it [expresses] similarity, its opposite, and that which is other than it. Therefore, by considering other passages, [the sentence] would be intent on fasting (*upavāsa*), denoting a resolution (*saṃkalpa*) not to eat, which is distinct from eating. Otherwise, even in the case of "He does not perform the *ye yajāmahe* at the *anuyāja*s," there would be no mention of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) due to the presence of figurative indication. [Reply: If it is argued that even if figurative indication is accepted—because in the case of the prohibition alternative (*niṣedhapakṣa*), there would otherwise result the contingency of an eightfold fault-ridden option (*vikalpa*)—we say: No. For if that were so, there would result the contingency of figurative indication of rice (*vrīhi*) even in the sentence "One should sacrifice with barley" (*yavair yajeta*). Nor is there figurative indication of barley in the sentence "One should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), because the word "with rice" is recited in many sentences, and because of the eightfold fault-ridden option; rather, the assumption is that it is better to have a productive result (*abhyudayakāri*) from two sentences being enjoined. It is more reasonable for there to be figurative indication of rice in a single sentence concerning barley than figurative indication of barley in multiple sentences concerning preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, since accepting figurative indication out of fear of an option would lead to a lack of settled rule (*avyavasthā*), there is no figurative indication of *nañ* in the exclusion alternative; it is simply its primary sense. Thus, let it be an exclusion. To this it is replied: Even in the absence of figurative indication in the exclusion alternative, these are indeed prohibitions. For everything connects primarily with the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) when possible; thus, through connection with the finite verb—the primary element—it is a prohibition. But when connected with the meaning of a noun or a verbal root, it becomes an exclusion, not a prohibition. That [prohibition] occurs in connection with the finite verb; as it has been said: "And because of connection with the meaning of a noun or a verbal root, *nañ* is not a prohibitor. Therefore, this is accepted as a prohibition, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) in its connection with the perceived primary finite verb, and not out of fear of the contingency of figurative indication. As for what was said—that if figurative indication is accepted out of fear of an option, it results in the sentence concerning barley—that is addressed here.

Therefore, it is improper to accept that [prohibition] in either the sentence concerning rice (*vrīhi*) or the sentence concerning barley (*yava*), as there is no reason for such a restrictive determination (*vinigama*). Nor is the frequent recitation of the word *vrīhi* in many sentences a determining factor, because the word *vrīhi* occurring in the preparatory injunctions (*saṃskāra-vākya*) does not denote barley; rather, it is justified by its figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the mere material source of the offering substance. Furthermore, the statement "the householder and the student" is solely intended as a prohibition; it does not contradict the statement, "A person should never eat on the eleventh day," because there is no subsequent restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*). Nor is the mention of specific [categories] redundant.
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the ox, and the student of sacred knowledge—these three succeed only while eating;
for them there is no success through fasting.
[159] That householder who does not eat, as well as he who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni),
would become one who has violated his vow (avakīrṇin) through the neglect of the Prāṇāgnihotra.

This is because, upon reflecting on such statements as these, they serve to avoid the restriction of the term *mānava* (human). Nor can statements such as “one should not eat on the eleventh day” (*ekādaśyāṃ na bhuñjīta*) be taken as referring to occasions other than the eleventh day; for, considering the prohibitions against eating for householders and others, it would follow that “one should not eat on the eleventh day” would likewise refer to occasions other than that. Therefore, there is no fault in the statement “the householder and the student” being intended to dispel this misconception. Furthermore, those sentences which are seen to contain the word *vrata* (vow) are not intended as mere prohibitions, unlike the rule “one should not look at the rising sun.”
From the Matsya-purāṇa and Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa:
He who, having fasted on the eleventh day, eats on the twelfth lunar day—
whether in the bright or the dark fortnight— that is indeed the great Vaiṣṇava vow.
In the *Āgneya Purāṇa*: "One should not eat on the eleventh day; for this is indeed the Vaiṣṇava vow.

In this manner, other statements as well that are devoted to the injunction of vows (*vrata-vidhi*) are to be understood. Those statements yet to be mentioned which contain the word "fasting" (*upavāsa*) or the word "fruit" (*phala*) are also exclusively devoted to the injunction of vows; for if they were devoted to a prohibition, a connection with a fruit would be untenable. Furthermore, statements devoted to the injunction of vows are of two kinds: those devoted to the injunction of obligatory (*nitya*) vows and those devoted to the injunction of optional (*kāmya*) vows. First, examples of those devoted to the injunction of obligatory vows are cited.
In this regard, Nārada says:
"Men who are devoted to Viṣṇu and endowed with constant devotion should observe a fast on the Ekādaśī day in every fortnight."
The syntactical connection here is that one must always perform the fast.
Also, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having fasted on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) regularly during both fortnights..."
Also in that spoken by Sanatkumāra:
"The Ekādaśī should be observed with a fast throughout both the bright and dark fortnights. Likewise:
One should fast on the eleventh day and never let it pass; for thus it is said:
"That fool who does not perform the fast on the eleventh day..."
That man goes to the Raurava hell, which is shrouded in darkness.

From the hearing of the statements, "one should never, at any time, transgress [this]," from the hearing of the repetition "every fortnight," and from the proclamation of the fault incurred by non-performance, it is understood that the Ekādaśī vow is obligatory (*nitya*).
Likewise, in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"The twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) must not be observed for eating by those of good conduct as long as they live."
In the *Āgneya Purāṇa*:
"O King, having fasted on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight] for as long as one lives with virtuous conduct...
Thus, a specific fault is demonstrated in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa* regarding the transgression of the eleventh-day fast by ascetics (*yatis*) and widows.
O great sage, on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight],
a widow and an ascetic who do not fast are indeed cooked in the Andhatāmisra hell until the dissolution of all beings.
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight; this is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics, but a householder should always observe only the bright fortnight.

[161] From this statement of Gobhila as well, its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is understood due to the connection with the word "always" (*sadā*). "Always" means at all times; for there is the understanding: "One should not eat on the eleventh day. However, the connection with the word "always" does not apply to the householder alone. Thus, in other cases as well, the status of being a subject of fasting constitutes a specific variety of both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites; it is certainly not for the purpose of avoiding a conclusion [of the ritual], because of the connection with the proximate word "always. Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana, however, says: "He is a slayer of a Brahmin, he is a drinker of liquor, he is a thief, he is a violator of the Guru's bed."
He who, out of delusion, discriminates between the two Ekādaśīs, the bright and the dark;

This statement establishes its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). Although this [text] is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, because it is an independent *arthavāda*, it implies an injunction (*vidhi*), for such a passage would otherwise be untenable without one—just as in the case of the rule, "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood. Furthermore, since a fault (*doṣa*) is heard [in connection with non-performance], and a fault necessarily arises from the transgression of an obligatory scriptural rule, it implies an obligatory injunction; thus, the hearing of the fault is logically consistent only if there is an obligatory rule, and not if it were merely optional (*kāmya*). When the question arises as to what the object of that obligation is, rather than postulating some other matter and then imagining an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) for it to establish the necessity regarding that object—which would involve greater complexity—it is better to connect the fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī-upavāsa*), which is understood from another text and which requires specification of whether it is obligatory or optional, directly with the present injunction. This is because the word "eleventh day" is heard here in the text, bringing that practice to mind, and it stands in need of a verbal designation; therefore, by enjoining its obligatoriness, a connection is established, as this involves less conceptual construction (*kalpanālāghava*).
[Objection: Why is it not assumed that there is a prohibition based on hearing this censure?
[Reply: It is said: because that would entail the logical fault of assuming both the prohibited act and its prohibition (the principle of *kalpanā-gaurava*).

[Objection: Since the phrase "he who, out of delusion, investigates" indicates that investigation (*vicāra*) is what is prohibited, what is the object of that investigation? [Reply: We say it is the subject of Ekādaśī, due to its proximity.

Not so; for since that which has not been investigated cannot possibly be performed, it is impossible to prohibit investigation. As it has been said: "One who adopts anything without investigating would be thwarted. Therefore, the purpose of this censure of investigation is to foster a desire for fasting. Why then is it investigated? This matter has already been largely investigated. Thus, the meaning of the statement is: one should fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) without further deliberation; otherwise, there is the incurrence of faults such as the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Now follow the statements concerning the injunctions for the eleventh day. Among them, in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:

"He who desires residence with Viṣṇu and [the attainment of] learning for himself. However, in some versions, the word "son" (*putra*) is read in place of the word "learning" (*śruta*). This is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.
Kātyāyana says: He who desires union with Viṣṇu, prosperity, and personal wealth, and who,
being devoted to Viṣṇu, desires to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.
Whatever he desires—sovereignty, progeny, heaven, or liberation—[he attains].
"One should not eat during the latter half of these [days], nor on the eleventh day of either fortnight. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
If one desires abundant enjoyments as well as liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to attain,
one should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "He who,
having fasted on the Ekādaśī day, worships Govinda,
shall attain Nirvāṇa, which is free from burning and dissolution."

Viṣṇu says: Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva with offerings of incense, unguents, lamps, and food, as well as by satisfying the fire and the Brāhmaṇas. Having thus completed this vow, one becomes purified from sins; by performing it throughout one's life, one attains Śvetadvīpa itself. By observing it on both the eleventh and twelfth days for a year, one attains the heavenly world; by doing so throughout one's life, one attains the world of Viṣṇu, and so forth. Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
For this [vow] bestows heaven and liberation; it grants bodily health;
it indeed bestows a virtuous wife, and it grants a kingdom and sons.

For this mention of a fruit is not called an *arthavāda* on the grounds that it is for the sake of another—such as the hearing of [the hymn] *Apāpaśloka*—whereby its purpose would be the destruction of sin; rather, that "being for the sake of another" is intended to mean being for the sake of the destruction of sin. Furthermore, even that is not clearly understood from the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), but is based solely upon the *arthavāda*. And since that *arthavāda* is no different in the case of heaven and other such fruits, those very fruits are accepted [as the primary results]. This is just as in the case of the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, which, although it must necessarily be performed, is accepted as being connected to a fruit mentioned in an *arthavāda*. And here, thinking that because austerity is understood to be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of knowledge through the passage, "Brahmins seek to know him by means of Vedic recitation, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting," it serves the purpose of liberation through a traditional sequence, it is stated that [knowledge] "bestows liberation."
Thus concludes the determination of the prohibitory statements regarding the subject matter of the eleventh day.
Now, the person entitled (*adhikārī*) to this vow is defined.

In that regard, under the view that it is optional (*kāmya*), the one entitled is simply one who desires the respective fruit. Under the view that it is obligatory (*nitya*), Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana says: "Because it is favorable to the state of being obligatory, a person who possesses life is postulated as the entitled one; nevertheless, because the Dharmaśāstras pertain to those of the three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*), those outside the three classes are excluded."
But surely, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) that "this is the dharma of forest-dwellers and ascetics," why does this not also exclude householders and the like?

It is said: Because it is impossible for the words of the verb to be syntactically connected with the terms *vanastha* (forest-dweller) and *yati* (renunciant), a connection with the phrase “one should not eat on the eleventh day” is not possible when these two terms function as subordinate adjuncts to the word *dharma*. However, such a connection is possible as follows: “This is the duty (*dharma*) of the forest-dweller and the renunciant; one should not eat on the eleventh day. But this meaning is untenable, because an insentient *dharma* cannot possibly be the agent of fasting. For it is not the case that one eats thinking, “This is the duty of the forest-dweller and the renunciant,” whereby [the eating] would be prohibited for them. Therefore, there is no such meaning as corresponds to the syntactical connection [proposed], nor is there any word expressive of such a meaning that is actually possible. Consequently, the terms *vanastha* and so forth are for the sake of praise (*stuti*), intended to show: “Since this is a duty even for those in the highest stages of life, such as the forest-dwellers and renunciants, how much more so for others! Just as it is said: “The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (*satra*); how much more so, then, others?”

But even so, why does the determination that this refers to a forest-dwelling ascetic not follow from the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)? Because there is no doubt. For where there is doubt regarding the choice between ghee and oil—as in the case where it is said, "Ghee is indeed light"—a determination is stated based on the supplementary statement, "Ghee is indeed light. However, in the present case, since it is certain that the entitlement to fasting belongs to all who are alive, there is no need for a supplementary statement. But is it not the case that the text does not explicitly state, "One who is living shall fast"?
And that [truth] is also postulated.

But surely, rather than postulating a qualification (*adhikāra*), it is more parsimonious to rely on that [truth] based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice.

It is said: For fear of the complexity of conceptualization (*kalpanā-gaurava*), if one were to assume the two qualifiers—being a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and being an ascetic (*yati*)—as intended from the remainder of the sentence, a greater fault than that would result: namely, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). This is because it is impossible for the states of being a forest-dweller and an ascetic to coexist simultaneously in a single person; thus, they cannot function as qualifiers of the qualified subject in combination. If each were taken as a qualifier of the qualified subject individually, the syntactical split is evident: "the forest-dweller should fast" and "the ascetic should fast."

Now, if the sentence is completed with each individual subject, what constitutes a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)? For example, in the case of "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), even though the cleansing is enjoined for each one individually among the cups dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others, it is still considered a syntactical split.

True; in that case, when the direct verbal function (*śrauta tātparya*) of a single word has reached its conclusion, the implied function (*ārthika vyāpāra*), though differing with respect to each individual term, does not cause a split in the sentence. However, here it is not possible for the direct verbal function of any single word to apply commonly to both the forest-dweller and the ascetic, because the word "forest-dweller" does not denote the ascetic, nor does the word "ascetic" denote the forest-dweller; therefore, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). But surely, as in the case of the king and the domestic priest (*rājapurohita*), there can be a connection to the entitlement (*adhikāra*) even for the forest-dweller and the ascetic when they are expressed by distinct words?

Not so. For in that case, there is possible a single qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa) consisting of the desire for union (sāyujyakāmanā); but here, we do not see any single qualification of the qualified person that is common to both, distinct from the states of being a forest-dweller and a renunciant (yatitva). Furthermore, by resorting to the same logic as the "king and the domestic priest" (rājapurohita), it would follow that the entitlement belongs to the two acting together; thus, the injunction would be "the forest-dweller and the renunciant should not eat on the eleventh day," rather than "one should not eat on the eleventh day. [Objection:
But surely, because of the connection with both through syntactical ellipsis (anuṣaṅga), there is no fault of the referent being absent when the word is uttered twice.

It is said in reply: Where it is certain that there is a syntactical split (*bhinnavākyatva*), something is supplied (*anuṣajyate*) from a complete sentence to a deficient one, as in the case of "He sacrifices the *kapiñjala* birds to Spring. However, in this instance, because the two terms "forest-dweller" (*vana-stha*) and "ascetic" (*yati*) occurring within the compound are individually unfit for connection with the verb, there is no such supply. Therefore, since the word "forest-dwelling ascetic" cannot in any way serve to designate the qualified performer (*adhikārin*), it is established that householders and others are also entitled [to this practice].
But if this is so, does this not contradict the following statement?
Whether he be a householder or a student, if one practices austerity while fasting,
he becomes an outcast by neglecting the fire-sacrifice of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnihotra).
Thus it is said.

It is said: What is intended by this statement—is austerity (*tapas*) being prohibited, or is the necessity of the *prāṇāgnihotra* being enjoined? First, it cannot be an injunction for the *prāṇāgnihotra*, because that which is stated as a "reason-like explanatory passage" (*hetuvannigada*) cannot function as an injunction, just as in the case of the phrase "for by means of food, [the sacrifice] is performed. Even if the meaning of a reason-like explanatory passage were to be enjoined, there would still be no attainment of an injunction for the *prāṇāgnihotra*; rather, its very omission would be indicated as the reason. Consequently, through the abandonment of that [omission], the omission of the regular *agnihotra* itself would follow, which is an undesirable consequence. Furthermore, since the name "Agnihotra" is heard, the ritual details (*vidhyanta*) of the regular *agnihotra* are extended to it. When the substances such as milk and so forth are thus extended, the *prāṇāgnihotra* can be accomplished even with one of those substances—such as water—which does not conflict with fasting; therefore, the rule of the *prāṇāgnihotra* does not necessarily obstruct fasting. Alternatively, if it is argued that because a name occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) lacks the power to extend ritual details, the substances of the regular *agnihotra* do not apply, and instead the *prāṇāgnihotra* is understood as being offered into the mouth, whereby it is enjoined that "the *prāṇāgnihotra* must be performed with the substance used for eating," then, since eating is necessitated for the sake of accomplishing that [offering], it would indeed conflict with fasting.

It is said in reply: If the *prāṇāgnihotra* were to be performed with a substance intended for eating, then, because it would depend on that substance already procured for other purposes, it would not itself have the power to necessitate its own materials—just as in the case of the rule, "He pours out the husks with the cake-potsherd. This point has been established in the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras) based on the following example: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered; he himself should offer the first oblation with the words, 'Svāhā to Prāṇa! Therefore, this sentence—"The householder, the student..."—does not enjoin the *prāṇāgnihotra* as a mandatory duty. Nor does it prohibit fasting for householders and others, because it would contradict such texts as, "The householder should fast on the preceding day," and "The householder should always [fast] during the bright fortnight. Likewise, by excluding fasting specifically prescribed for particular times such as Sundays, it is understood that other forms of fasting are permitted. Consequently, in subsequent passages, we see a similar reference to the householder: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I create offspring'; he performed austerity (*tapas*). Since the householder is the one authorized by the Prajāpati-injunctions, the reference to his performing austerity indicates that austerity is appropriate for other types of householders as well. Indeed, it is heard in the Purāṇas that sages such as Vasiṣṭha, though being householders, performed severe austerities. Similarly, in the *Viṣṇudharma*, *Bhaviṣyottara*, *Matsyapurāṇa*, and others, vows characterized by frequent fasting are prescribed for householders. Likewise, in the Dharmaśāstras, penances consisting largely of fasting are recorded for householders. Even today, certain noble householders are seen to be devoted to fasting; thus, from the perspective of traditional conduct (*sadācāra*), it is understood that those householders who seek spiritual welfare are entitled to it. This being the case, general statements regarding austerity do not suffer from the defect of being overly restricted (*saṃkocaka*) when applied to the householder. For instance: "Austerity is austerity; there is nothing higher than austerity. For austerity is difficult to overcome, and therefore they delight in austerity. In this context, where a specific stage of life (*āśrama*) is intended to be expressed, that specific stage is mentioned; therefore, it is understood that austerity is common to all. Thus: "By austerity the gods attained the highest divinity; by austerity the sages found their status as seers. By austerity we shall drive away our rivals and enemies; everything is established in austerity; therefore they say austerity is supreme. And: "Those who are invincible through austerity, those who have gone to heaven through austerity, and those who have performed great austerity—even the gods go to them."
"Moreover, the gods accept the worship of a Brahmin who is endowed with austerity alone, and they fulfill his desires. Thus it is said.

As for those words of Mohinī which repeatedly state, "O King Rukmāṅgada, being a householder—and especially a Kṣatriya—you have no entitlement to fasting; rather, this duty of fasting and so forth belongs only to ascetics and widows; therefore, you must eat on the eleventh day, you must eat," these appear in the form of injunctions but are not in fact prescriptive. Rather, they are *arthavādas* (explanatory or corroborative statements) regarding the injunction of fasting performed by Rukmāṅgada, which has a meaning contrary to her own. Why? Because, after first negating the point she made with the words, "Do not speak thus, O auspicious lady, but what is appropriate for you," he subsequently enjoins the fast. This is just as in the case of the statement, "One may offer oblations of wild sesame gruel or wild millet gruel," which is an *arthavāda* for the injunction "One offers the Agnihotra with milk," because it first prohibits wild sesame and wild millet before enjoining milk: "Wild sesame and wild millet are indeed unfit offerings. Furthermore, if Mohinī’s position were the established conclusion, why would the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, having personally seized Rukmāṅgada—who acted contrary to her words—by the hand, desire his union with his own self? Moreover, since Mohinī’s activity was directed solely at sending men to hell for the sake of helping [the demons], Mohinī’s words regarding fasting result only in the attainment of hell and are not intended to be practiced. Therefore, it is established that even a householder is entitled to fasting and the like. By this, the status of the religious student (*brahmacārī*) is also explained.
Through various specific austerities and vows enjoined by the rules,
the entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born.
For, by such statements as these, his connection with asceticism is also understood.

If this is so, then what is the scope of the statement, "Or he may be a *brahmacārī*"? We say that its purpose is to prohibit asceticism (*tapas*) that endangers life. For instance, the compound *prāṇāgnihotralopena* is a *tatpuruṣa* containing a *dvandva*; the third case ending (*-ena*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇā*), and the word *agnihotra* is intended to indicate prescribed duties (*vihitakarman*) in general. Thus, the meaning becomes: "A householder who, while remaining a *brahmacārī*, practices asceticism by endangering his life or by neglecting prescribed duties, incurs the fault of being an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of chastity). And such is the construction: *prāṇāś cāgnihotraṃ ca* = *prāṇāgnihotre*; "by the neglect of those two. What is meant is this: there is no great fault for one such as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who performs asceticism even at the cost of obstructing the *prāṇāgnihotra* and other rites; however, for a householder and others, if either his life or his *agnihotra* and other duties are obstructed, then there is a fault.
Life is the cause for the maintenance of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; by killing it, what is not destroyed? By protecting it, what is not protected?
Thus,

by these two statements— "One should indeed perform actions here while wishing to live for a hundred years"— it is established that the activities of the vital breaths (prāṇa) are not to be obstructed. Even if it is said:
Whatever action, even if auspicious, causes the body to suffer, that should not be done to excess; this is called "effortlessness."

Thus, this [prohibition] is for the purpose of warding off extreme suffering, but not for the sake of avoiding suffering in general. Therefore, it is established that householders and students have the entitlement to perform fasts and other such observances.
Now, let it be granted that this applies to other householders; however, for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there is no such entitlement.
For it is said: "The one who maintains the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three [are exempt]."
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "They become pure only while eating; there is no success for those who do not eat."

It is said: What is enjoined by this statement—is the eating of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) being prescribed, or is fasting being prohibited? Even if eating is being prescribed, is it meant that one must eat at all times, or that one should eat when there is a desire to eat, provided there is no obstacle and food is available; or rather, is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) being enjoined for eating even in cases not permitted by other scriptures? Among these, the injunction to eat at all times is not desired precisely because it is impossible. Nor is an injunction appropriate for eating when there is a desire to eat, provided there is no obstacle and food is available, since that is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*). As stated by the author of the *Nyāyamañjarī*: "For an injunction such as 'one who is hungry should eat' or 'one who is dirty should bathe' is of no use. Nor can it be said that one must eat even when there is an obstacle, for that is impossible. Nor is eating being counter-exceptionally permitted in places, times, or conditions not authorized by other scriptures; for if that were so, it would follow that even during an eclipse (*sagraha*), in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), or at any time or place, even a pure person maintaining the sacred fires must eat stale food and the like. If you say, "Let it be so," alas, what a pity! Oh, how great is this greed for food, that eating even during eclipses and the like is taught—contrary to the consensus of all learned people—and that many scriptures prohibiting those specific instances, such as "One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun," are contradicted.
But surely, because they are general rules, they concern those who have not maintained the sacred fires.

It is said in reply: Why is this not accepted as having a scope distinct from what is prohibited? Just as prohibitory scriptures are called general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*) because they apply equally to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and those who have not, so too the scripture concerning eating is a general rule because it applies equally to both prohibited and non-prohibited objects. If it is argued that there is thus an option (*vikalpa*) between them, that is not so, because the injunctions are inconsistent (*viṣama-śiṣṭatvāt*). Furthermore, in the statement "they indeed succeed while eating," the injunction must be inferred because it is a descriptive statement (*vartamānāpadeśa*); whereas in cases such as "one should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun," the injunction is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, there is no option.

Surely the Venerable One is laboring in vain; for it is not said that one who maintains the sacred fires must eat during the *saṅgraha* and other such occasions, but rather that he must eat on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth.

It is said: what partiality is there in this? For just as the explicit contradiction of scripture is seen in the statement, "One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun," so too does the scripture exist that says, "One should not eat even at night on the eleventh day. Therefore, there is a contradiction; since the subject matter is already occupied by another scripture, this is not an injunction to eat. The fact that it functions as an injunction for a different subject—namely, "Only those who eat attain success"—has already been refuted previously. Consequently, eating is not enjoined by this [text] anywhere. But surely, [one might object]:
[170] Eating in the evening and in the morning is prescribed by the Śruti for the twice-born;
one should not eat in between, for this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice.

Thus, this injunction regarding eating can be refuted by the same alternatives as before. Who says that this is an injunction regarding eating? For, in the case of eating which is already established through natural desire (*rāga*), what is done here is merely a prohibition at other times than evening and morning; everything else is restated (*anūdyate*). Since it is possible for the passage to have the purpose of enjoining only a small portion [of details], it is improper to assume an injunction for eating qualified by time, because a restriction to two specific times would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, since the praise of similarity to the *agnihotra* is established by the mere fact that eating occurs only in the evening and morning and not in between, one need not assume a complete identity with it. These injunctions are accepted as being subordinate to another purpose by way of restating the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), just like such rules as "one should eat food facing the east."
Now, one might ask: how can there be a necessity for the morning and evening observances of one who has been initiated?
It is said in reply: even in that case, the undertaking of the observance is solely for the purpose of maintaining the body; it is not prescribed as a necessity independent of that purpose.

Others, however, say that the vow (*vrata*) is indeed mandatory. For, having prescribed the vow with the words, "One observes the vow at midday and at midnight," he further says, "But one must certainly not fail to observe the vow. Since the connection of the vow with the times of midday and midnight is already established by the preceding statement, this prohibition against the absence of the vow would otherwise be purposeless; it therefore leads us to understand that the state of being under the vow is indeed obligatory. As for the argument that the injunction is redundant because [the practice] is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), [that is refuted as follows].

That is not so; for even in the absence of hunger and the like, there is an injunction that one must necessarily eat at least a certain measure. Thus, the eating of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣa*) is also mandatory because it is prompted by the substance to be offered, even in the absence of desire and other such motives. As for the statement, "In the evening and morning for the twice-born," its purpose has been explained as merely enjoining a prohibition against eating in the interval; the same will also be said regarding the statement concerning those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Therefore, this [text] does not enjoin eating. [Objection: Granted, let it not be an injunction; yet it certainly grants permission (*abhyanujñā*).

It is replied: even so, one must still consider the alternatives as before. First of all, permission (*abhyanujñā*) cannot be granted regarding a matter already restricted by a scriptural injunction, such as fasting (*upavāsa*), precisely because that would contradict the injunction. Nor can there be permission regarding a matter not restricted by scripture, for that would be purposeless. If one desires to eat and obtains the opportunity, and there is no conflict with the rule, then one simply eats even without rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*); what, then, would the statement of permission accomplish? Furthermore, the position that it is a prohibition of fasting is even more flawed. For it has already been stated that where a scripturally mandated fasting is established, it cannot be prevented even by resorting to a rule permitting eating. How, then, could it be warded off by a prohibition? This is because a prohibition is dependent upon the prior establishment of a possibility (*prāpti*). In that case, there would have to be either an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of taking or not taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—"one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) shall fast, or he shall not"—or an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), as in the case of "one does not perform the *ye yajāmahe* formula at the *anuyāja* offerings"—namely, "those other than those who have maintained the sacred fires shall fast. Neither of these two is possible: because an option involves eight logical faults (*doṣa*), and because in the case of an exclusion, it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the fault of the connection being severed from the primary verb (*ākhyāta*).

[Objection: Surely those obligatory acts such as fasting are indeed permitted even for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); however, those which are performed out of a desire for spiritual merit (*śreyas*) are prohibited for him. But this is a well-stated argument; for even obligatory fasting cannot be prohibited by this [text]. How then can optional (*kāmya*) fasting be prohibited? Have you not heard this: "The optional is stronger than the obligatory"? [Response: What then is the interpretation of that statement? When there is a conflict between the performance of fasting and other such acts and the duties of one who maintains the sacred fires due to his diminished capacity, then for such a fire-maintainer, the Smṛti-based performance of fasting and so forth is prohibited by those very Vedic injunctions (*codanā*). It is for the purpose of establishing this that the statement exists: "One who maintains the sacred fires and an ox... [is exempt from fasting].
But would this not result in the statement being merely a restatement?

Do you still not understand that the statements of the *Smṛtis* are merely reiterative? If they are explained in this way, in accordance with the efficacy of other *dharma* rules, there will be consistency with the subject matter at hand. For instance, having introduced the topic with, "In such a manner one should ensure no obstruction to the self so that one remains capable for ritual acts," Āpastamba stated: "One who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and the ox. Therefore, it is established that even one who has maintained the sacred fires may fast on the eleventh day provided he is able to do so without neglecting the *agnihotra* and other rites. Likewise, fasting is prescribed for householders and others in the *Agni Purāṇa*.
"A householder, a student, and likewise one who has maintained the sacred fires—
none of these should eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight," so says Kātyāyana.
"A mortal who is more than eight years old but less than ninety years of age should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights.

And because of the traditional teaching that "in the case of the rules beginning with initiation (*upanayana*)," all such rules apply only after the time of initiation, the phrase "more than eight years" refers to the lack of entitlement even for one who has been initiated until the age of eight.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "Any mortal in my kingdom who, being more than eight years old and less than eighty, eats on the day of Viṣṇu, is a partaker of sin."
He is to be executed by me, he is to be punished by me, and he is to be banished from my country by me.
For this reason, O Brahmin, a man or a woman should observe a fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
This Ekādaśī vow is to be observed even by the devotees of Maheśvara (Śiva).
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The worship of the Liṅga, the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, and the observance of the vow during the three days of Śiva."
And death at Vārāṇasī—this liberation is fourfold.
Having said this, it was further stated:
"The eleventh, the eighth, and the fourteenth of both fortnights are declared by the sages, such as Śaunaka and others, to be the lunar days (tithis) sacred to Śiva."
"One should fast on the first of these [days], and likewise not eat during the day on the last two."
Likewise: "Whether a Vaiṣṇava or a Śaiva, one should observe the Ekādaśī vow;
fasting on Ekādaśī is to be performed even by the Sauras, because it is stated so in the Saura Purāṇa."
"Whether a Vaiṣṇava, a Śaiva, or even a Saura, one should perform this.
By this, it is established that the fast applies to the householder and others belonging to the three higher castes.
However, others say that there is no exclusion of the three castes here.
"Tell us the duties of those belonging to the castes, the stages of life, and others, without exception.

By reflecting on this statement, [it is clear that] all have the qualification [to study], especially because the term "mortals" (*martya*) is used here. As for the mention of the twice-born (*dvija*) through the expression "at every mouthful," that is intended to show their particular susceptibility to faults.
Others, however, say that since the qualification of even the student (*brahmacārin*) and others is established, the term is intended as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of human beings in general.
That is not so, because it would entail [the application of] secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); here, the qualification belongs only to those who have undertaken the vow without effort.
And thus it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"O Brahmin, without the Ekādaśī, there is no liberation from saṃsāra."
Nevertheless, there is this distinction: here, the effect must be produced by that which possesses the capacity.
But the wise do not consider the body here to be something that should be afflicted out of attachment;
for the body is afflicted by whatever action, even if it be most auspicious.
One should not exert oneself excessively; that is called "absence of strain.
For the body is the primary means for accomplishing dharma and the source of great merit.
If, out of foolishness, one does not destroy that [defilement] all at once,
but instead performs asceticism by means of self-affliction through grasping at a fundamental [view],
he shall obtain neither happiness, nor spiritual accomplishment, nor the supreme goal. [174]
Regarding the incapacity of the qualified person, a substitute is mentioned in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"When the body is incapable and a vow has presented itself,
one should have it performed by the lawful wife or by a son endowed with discipline."
Whether it be a sister or even a brother, his vow is not violated.
Kātyāyana says: "For the sake of a king and for the sake of a Kṣatriya, one who has fasted on the eleventh day [attains the same merit];
it is declared that the priest and the Kṣatriya receive an equal share from both."
By those two, the fruit of fasting is obtained simultaneously.
Listen: for one who fasts on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) with another person in mind, O brahmins, the full fruit belongs to the one for whom it was performed;
the performer obtains tenfold merit in this matter—of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmin, when one has fasted on the Ekādaśī even in the absence of food,
the full fruit of that fasting is obtained by him.
When a Brahmin, having fasted on the eleventh day, [is released] from the king's wrath,
the fruit of his fast certainly becomes fully realized.
For this reason, O Brahmin, a man or a woman should observe a fast on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) during both fortnights.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"But one who is unable to fast— whether he be a maintainer of the sacred fires (āhitāgni) or otherwise—
should have it performed by his son or the like, or even by a Brāhmaṇa."
Alternatively, one should give gifts according to one's ability to the foremost of Brahmins;
in that way, the entire fruit of fasting is fully obtained,
and even any fault regarding the food there vanishes at that very moment.
Kātyāyana also says:
"One who observes a fast for the sake of his father, brother, or mother, and especially for the sake of his teacher, shall obtain a hundredfold merit."
Even he for whose sake it was performed obtains the full fruit;
likewise, a woman who fasts on Ekādaśī for the sake of her husband [obtains the same].
The sages who see the further shore declare that her merit is a hundredfold;
her husband undoubtedly obtains the fruit of her fasting.
Likewise:
"If one is unable to perform it oneself, one should have it performed by a family priest;
one should give gold as a sacrificial fee according to one's own means and in a fitting manner."
Kātyāyana says:
Whoever performs the fast on the eleventh lunar day for the sake of their father, mother, or brother, and especially for the sake of their teacher; [attains the highest goal].
One who observes the fast shall obtain a hundredfold merit;
no sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is to be given here, for service alone is always prescribed.

Or, if there is an abundance of material wealth, one who fasts on the eleventh day undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the donor's fasting; the performer of the *nakta* rite likewise attains it— no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
It was stated by Manu:
"Or, having fasted on the eleventh day with compassion directed toward another,
O Brahmins, that which is performed for whomsoever it may be shall be as if performed for oneself first."
The performer obtains tenfold merit here; of this there is no doubt.
As for that which was stated by Manu: "For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even fasting";
and likewise by Viṣṇu:
If a woman observes a vow of fasting while her husband is still alive,
she shortens her husband's lifespan and goes to hell.
This refers to the case of fasting without the permission of one's husband and the like, and specifically concerns female practitioners.
As Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated:
"At her own will, she may undertake vows, fasts, and so forth, with the permission of her husband."
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Indeed, if a woman performs vows and other religious observances without being authorized by her father, husband, or son, it shall be fruitless for her."
One who is unable to observe the fast on every eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) should perform at least the practice of eating only one meal per day (ekabhakta), and so forth.
Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya:
"By eating only one meal, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked for..."
One should not remain without the twelve [observances] by means of fasting or giving.
