One who is a child, an elder, or ill may pass the day by eating only once, or by eating at night, or even with milk, roots, or fruits; yet he shall not be one who fails to observe the twelfth-day vow.
Baudhāyana also says:
"For those who are unable to fast and who live beyond eighty years,
the sage Baudhāyana declares that the practice of eating once a day and so forth should be performed."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa:
"Having worshipped the Lord Viṣṇu on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) at some time,
by one who has fasted, or likewise by eating only at night (nakta), or by eating only what is unasked for (ayācita)."
Or, O dear one, by eating but a single meal a day, one should not fail to observe the twelfth-day vow;
always adhering to that single rule, one does not sink in the ocean of existence.
One should practice the Dharma according to the strength of one's own physical capacity, and not by force;
whether fasting, or eating at night, or eating uncooked food, or even eating only once a day.
O dear one, one should worship Hari, the one who brings an end to worldly existence, twice a day;
by the offering of a single meal, the fruit of eating but once [a month] is said to be attained.
Now, know that the fruit is accumulated through the doubling of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The fruit of a fast is fourfold compared to a single night,
and that fourfold fruit is obtained even upon the breaking of a vow through a gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee.
He who observes the fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights should be known as one who,
even if of wicked conduct, is himself bathed and is Acyuta (the Imperishable).
The third vow, which takes the form of the Dvāpara age, is said to be observed at night;
it is meritorious when performed upon the appearance of the stars, with the meal taken before the first watch of the night.
Vyāsa: One who eats at night should practice these six: eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, truthfulness, moderation in food, performing fire-rites, and sleeping on the ground.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, in the *Dvādaśī-kalpa*: "Fasting is of four kinds: with betel and without betel, with food and without food, with sustenance and without sustenance."
As long as one has not performed his daily rites, as long as he has not worshipped Hari,
and as long as he remains without betel— only then is it called "true betel."
He who, having first worshipped Acyuta during the Pūrṇā period,
eats again during the Bhadrā period— that is called "eating together" (sabhojana).
Eating grass, grain, roots, milk, clarified butter, or fruits,
as well as fasting on the day of Hari— that is declared to be *sāhāra*.
If fasting is performed purely by these means, it is beneficial;
therefore, abstaining from betel, food, and meals is wholesome.
Baudhāyana also says:
"For those overcome by diseases, for those whose bodies abound in bile (pitta),
and for those over thirty years of age, the arrangement of eating at night and so forth is prescribed."
The reading "triṃśadvarṣāṇām" (of thirty years) also occurs in some places; in that case, the meaning is "of ninety years. In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One who is a child, an elder, or afflicted by illness should pass [the time] with one meal per day or eating only at night."
And one should not let the twelfth day pass by without observing the vow of fasting.
And this vow is to be observed during both fortnights;
thus it is stated in the Viṣṇurahasya and in the Skanda, Kūrma, and Nāradīya Purāṇas:
"As it is with the bright fortnight, so it is with the dark fortnight; there is no difference whatsoever."
Also in that which was proclaimed by Sanatkumāra: "As the bright fortnight is, so is the dark; as the dark is, so is the other. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.

"Whether it be the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, there is no distinction whatsoever. Thus it is stated. In the *Sauradharma*: "The eleventh day (ekādaśī) should be observed as a fast, whether it be in the bright or likewise in the dark fortnight."
In the *Viṣṇurahasya* and the *Saurapurāṇa*:
"Just as a fair-complexioned or dark-complexioned twice-born man who is well-versed in the Vedas, when properly honored,
delivers the donor, so too are the two twelfth lunar days (Dvādaśīs) remembered."
In the *Viṣṇurahasya* and the *Skandapurāṇa*:
"Just as oil from sesame seeds that are not white is indeed equal [to other oils],
and just as the milk of a black cow is equal to that of a white cow."
Likewise, the merit of both the bright and dark twelfth days is equal.
"Just as the New Moon (darśa) and the Full Moon (pūrṇamāsī) are equal in terms of merit,
so too are the two twelfth days (dvādaśīs), the bright and the dark, remembered by the sages as meritorious. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Just as the northern and southern solstices are proclaimed [to be equal],
one obtains equal merit from both the two twelfth days (dvādaśīs).
Likewise:
"Just as the lunar and solar eclipses are remembered by the sages as meritorious,
so too are the white and black twelfth days (dvādaśīs) meritorious and granters of satisfaction to Viṣṇu."
As is the twilight at evening and morning, so are the two oblations at evening and morning.
Likewise, the two meritorious twelfth days, the white and the black, are equal according to Dharma;
just as Viṣṇu and Śiva are both remembered by the sages as worthy of worship.
Likewise, the two twelfth days (dvādaśī), one in the bright fortnight and one in the dark fortnight, are declared to be most worthy of worship.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "One should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights;
he who worships Viṣṇu on the twelfth day shall partake in the fruit of liberation."
Also in the Viṣṇurahasya: "Thousands of hells difficult to cross have been described by you,
as well as the tortures inflicted by Yama’s servants in the terrible abode of Yama."
Tell me whatever there may be for the purpose of destroying that [obstacle] on the path of Yama.
Brahmā said:
Even those best of men who merely desire to observe the Dvādaśī vow in their minds do not behold the terrible ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Whether during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, one intent on the worship of Viṣṇu should not eat on the eleventh day of either half-month.
Just as a twice-born Brahmin who is fair or dark and is a knower of the Vedas, when duly honored,
delivers the donor, so too do these two twelfth days deliver him by their fruit.
For the destruction of all sins and for the gratification of Viṣṇu,
the meritorious twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast on both fortnights.
And because the hearing of the faults of sin is mentioned in the *Śuklakṛṣṇaviveka*.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* and the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He would be a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, ungrateful, and a violator of the Guru’s bed."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "He is a slayer of a Brahmin, he is a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
[181] In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"He is proclaimed to be the refuge of all sins here"—
this is the second half of those [verses].
He who, out of delusion, observes the two Ekādaśīs, the bright and the dark...
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:

"Knowing this, one should always fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), whether it be of the bright or the dark fortnight. One should not make a distinction between the two; by making such a distinction, one goes to hell."
In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"Whether it be the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, there is no distinction whatsoever.
He who makes a distinction is proclaimed a slayer of his ancestors."
From the *Tattvasāgara*:
"As is the white, so is the black; as is the black, so is the other. He who considers them equal is indeed called a Vaiṣṇava."
The waxing and waning of the moon's rays, as well as its white and dark phases,
are merely the numerical variations of the single essential nature of the eleventh day.
Therefore, qualities such as blackness or whiteness are said to belong to the moon;
consequently, there is no defect on the eleventh day by which it could be seen [as such].
Even if it were to possess a quality, even so there would be no fault;
for instance, blackness in sesame seeds or Brahmins and the like is not at all a fault.
As stated by Sanatkumāra:
O King, as for that ruler who creates a distinction between two Ekādaśīs,
I see no redemption for him until the dissolution of all beings.
[182] By this, it is established that the fast should be observed during both the bright and dark fortnights.
Now, there is a prohibition against fasting on Sundays and the like, as well as on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
During the dark fortnight, on the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), or during an eclipse, one who has sons should not observe a fast, for it leads to the loss of children, relatives, and wealth.

In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "On the day of the sun's passage (saṃkrānti), on the new moon, and during an eclipse, one who has sons should not observe a fast, for fear of the loss of children, kinsmen, and wealth."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "On the day of the sun's passage (saṃkrānti), on the waning of the day (dinakṣaya), and during eclipses of the moon and sun,
one who is endowed with sons and grandsons must not observe a fast."
One should not observe a fast or perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on a solar transit (saṃkrānti), during the dark fortnight, on Sundays or Fridays, or on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī).

In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "When two lunar day-ends (tithyanta) fall on the same weekday, that is a 'day of loss' (dinakṣaya). On such a day, one should perform bathing, recitation, and fire-offerings, but not observe a fast while in the householder stage of life."
In the *Sṛtimīmāṃsā*, Jaimini states:
"On the day of the sun [at the equinox], on the day of the solstice (*saṃkrānti*), and during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
a fast should not be observed by a householder who has sons."
Kātyāyana says: On the eleventh lunar days of the dark fortnight, likewise during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti),
and during eclipses of the moon and sun, a householder who has sons should not perform [the rite].
[183] The word "fast" (*upavāsa*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Gautama says:
"On the day of the sun (Sunday), on the day of the *saṃkrānti*, and on the eleventh days of the dark fortnight."
When a Śrāddha has been performed on a Vyatīpāta day, a householder who has sons should not fast.
On a Sunday, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), at the vyatīpāta yoga, or on the day of the loss of a lunar day (dinakṣaya),
a householder with sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast.

Nārada also says: A householder who has sons should not observe a fast on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), and likewise on Sundays,
a householder who has sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says: On a Sunday, on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
during the Vyatīpāta yoga, or when a Śrāddha has been performed, a householder with sons should not fast.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "O Yudhiṣṭhira, by fasting on a *saṃkrānti* and breaking the fast [on that same day],
or by fasting on the dark *ekādaśī*, one's eldest son perishes."

In these passages, the prohibitions against fasting on Sundays and other such days are intended to prohibit fasting specifically occasioned by Sundays and the like; they do not, however, intend to prohibit fasting occasioned by the Ekādaśī vow.
Thus says Jaimini:
"On a Sunday, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
A householder who has sons should neither observe a fast nor break one.
[184] This prohibition of fasting on account of that [occasion] has been declared;
it should not be understood as applying to incidental [fasting], because fasting is obligatory.

This prohibition concerns that which is caused by [other factors], such as Sunday and so forth; it is not, however, a prohibition against fasting on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) based on its conjunction with Sunday and other such days, because the meaning is that fasting on the eleventh lunar day is obligatory.
Kātyāyana also states: "This cited prohibition refers to fasting occasioned by those [other factors]."
For one who is engaged by another application, there is neither injunction nor prohibition.

Some, because this word occurs in the section on Ekādaśī and because it refers to the Ekādaśī mentioned in that context, maintain that since it does not—by way of syntactic connection (anuṣaṅga)—have as its referent the fast already established [for everyone], this passage is intended solely to prohibit fasting for one who has sons on an Ekādaśī joined with a solar transit (saṃkrānti) or similar occasions.

That is weak, because the proximity of the words [suggests] a rapid formation [of meaning]. Moreover, this is logical: since a lunar eclipse is impossible on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), how could the use of that word [“eclipse”] be justified? If it were intended to refer to a solar eclipse there, then there would be a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*), as a single utterance would have to intend two different meanings. Therefore, the previously stated interpretation alone is superior. Nor is it the case that the *saṃkrānti* and so forth are qualifiers of the eleventh day, for it has been stated—on account of the association with lunar and solar eclipses and because of the mention in the same grammatical case—that when the *saṃkrānti* and so forth occur on the eleventh day, the injunction for fasting is prescribed.
Likewise, it is stated by Sanatkumāra:
"When joined with Sunday, and likewise joined with a solar transit (saṃkrānti)..."
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), which bestows all prosperity, should be observed with a fast.
In the *Kātyāyana-smṛti*:
"When the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*) or a Sunday falls on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*),
that lunar day, which bestows great merit and removes all sins, should be observed as a fast."
Likewise: "When Vyatīpāta or Vaidhṛti occurs on the eleventh lunar day, that day should be observed as a fast;
it is highly meritorious and increases the abundance of one's sons."
Nārada said: An Ekādaśī that is conjoined with a Sunday and likewise associated with a Saṃkrānti should be observed with fasting; it increases one’s progeny and prosperity.
In the Skanda Purāṇa as well:
"O child, when the eleventh lunar day falls on a Sunday, one should diligently observe a fast; it increases one's sons and grandsons."

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Rāma, when the day of the eleventh lunar tithi falls on a Sunday, that day should be observed as a fast; it is highly meritorious and increases one's sons and grandsons."

Nor do these [rules] refer to anyone other than householders who have sons, because of the supplementary statement beginning with "increasing sons and grandsons. For Saṃvarta has stated that fasting is occasioned by such events as the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti): "The new moon day, the twelfth [lunar day], and especially the sun's passage into a new sign..."
These lunar days are praised, as is likewise Sunday.
In this regard, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, worship of the deities,
fasting, and likewise giving— each one is remembered as purifying.

The prohibition against fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of the dark fortnight, however, pertains specifically to householders who have sons. Accordingly, in those scriptural passages intended to prohibit fasting on the dark *ekādaśī*, specific qualifications such as "the householder with sons" or "the eldest son perishes" are heard, as is the censure: "due to the loss of children, relatives, and wealth," and so forth. Gobhila states: "One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight."
"This is the duty of the forest-dwelling ascetic; the householder always [observes] the Śukla [Ekādaśī].
This should be understood to apply likewise to the student (*brahmacārin*) and others as well. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:
"One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights."
"A celibate student, a woman, and a householder should always wear white. Thus it is said.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, at the commencement of the discussion on both types of Dvādaśī, Yudhiṣṭhira says:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, for what reason is the Dvādaśī not proclaimed by me?
Is it because she is not dear to you, O Lord, or is it because it is not proper to proclaim her?"
Kṛṣṇa said:

Just as the bright fortnight, so too the dark fortnight—the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is always dear to me. The bright fortnight should be observed by householders, for it increases worldly enjoyments and progeny.
Thus, Kṛṣṇā was taught in various ways by those seeking liberation.

Therefore, for a householder who has sons, the fast should be observed only on the Śukla (bright) Ekādaśī, not on the Kṛṣṇā (dark) one; however, there are certain occasional (naimittika) fasts on the Kṛṣṇā Ekādaśī as well.
This has been stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Then, the perpetual [observance] is declared to be white, while the occasional one would be black.
O Pārtha, the white [observance] must always be performed; it must not be abandoned even in times of distress.
A man who eats food on the white day indeed eats sin.

"Kṛṣṇā" means "occasional" (*naimittikī*), so called because it occurs on a specific occasion; the occasion here is its falling between the *Śayanī* (the day of the Lord's reclining) and the *Bodhanī* (the day of His awakening).
[187] That single Kṛṣṇa Ekādaśī which falls between the *Śayanī* and the *Bodhanī* is the one to be observed by a householder; no other Kṛṣṇa Ekādaśī should ever be observed.

Some explain that the absence of a son is the cause; thus the meaning of the scripture becomes this: for everyone, at all times, on both occasions, there is the avoidance of mere eating for the sake of observing the prohibition; for those other than householders who have sons, the vow of fasting must be performed on both occasions; for a householder, however, the vow is only on the bright fortnight between the Śayanī and Bodhanī days, even on the dark fortnight [in certain cases], and that too only for one who is without a son.

Now, one might ask: why does this [prohibition] not apply to a householder who has sons? For it is logical that the prohibitions against fasting on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight for such a householder pertain to cases other than the fasts specifically ordained by the *Śayanī* and *Bodhanī* injunctions.

It is said: By reflecting on the statement, "A householder should always observe the white [Ekādaśī]," the non-observance of fasting on all black Ekādaśīs would follow; however, since the rule for fasting on black Ekādaśīs applies specifically to those occurring between the Śayanī (Sleeping) and Bodhanī (Awakening) days—and because there is no possibility of such fasting elsewhere—the specific prohibition is logically applicable only to that black Ekādaśī on which a householder would otherwise be required to fast.

This very point has been stated by others, preceded by an objection: "These statements prohibit the fast for a householder who has sons; how, then, is this tenable? For the fast on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇaikādaśī) is established neither by scriptural injunction nor by worldly inclination, and a prohibition must be preceded by a prior establishment [of what is prohibited]. Since there is no status as a supplement to another injunction, and because there is no prior establishment [of the act], the prohibitory statements would result in meaninglessness as mere constant restatements (nityānuvāda)."

It is said: By such statements as "between the Śayanī and Bodhanī [Ekādaśīs]," there is an occasion for the observance of the fast on the dark Ekādaśī (Kṛṣṇaikādaśī) based on its connection with householders in general; with reference to that, the prohibitions against the fast on the dark Ekādaśī for a householder who has sons have been set forth.
Well then, since it is both enjoined and prohibited, an option (vikalpa) would result, just like the taking or not taking of the Śoḍaśī cup.

"Do not say that; for since injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) have different objects, a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) or a prohibition concerning a specific object (*viśeṣaviṣaya*) does not sublate [the general rule]. As for those injunctions and prohibitions which have the same object, they indeed form an option (*vikalpa*), like the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. This is incorrect, because of the contradiction with the established topic (*adhikaraṇa*) stating that "an option would arise when there is a prohibition of what has been obtained through an injunction initiated by a separate location of the prohibition. We, however, shall state later the resolution based on the theory of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). According to your view, there would result a contraction of the many prohibitions against fasting on the dark *ekādaśī* days for householders with sons, within the context of the dark *ekādaśīs* prescribed for fasting in the *Śayanī* (Sleeping) passage. In our view, however, the contraction belongs to the *Śayanī* passage itself, as it pertains specifically to those with sons.
The Grandfather [Brahmā] said:
"In this world, there are likewise the fathers of those [gods], the fathers of the [human] fathers,
and the maternal grandfathers of those, as well as whoever their progenitors may be."
Even their progenitors and the ancestors of their mothers go to the world of Viṣṇu by fasting on the day of Hari.
Thus, this very staff-banner has been placed by you at your feet—
that king by whom incomparable sovereignty over the world-protectors was attained.
"If you cause that one, the best among speakers, to waver from his fortitude when the day of Hari has arrived, then I shall be your servant.

In this context as well, the mention of the "day of Hari" (harivāsara) should be understood as referring specifically to the Ekādaśī observed by Rukmāṅgada. Therefore, it is established that for a householder with children, the fast is on the bright Ekādaśī, whereas for others, it is on both [Ekādaśīs].

Others, however, say: "The prohibitions against fasting on the single *kṛṣṇa* (dark fortnight) Ekādaśī pertain to optional (*kāmya*) vow-fasts, but not to obligatory (*nitya*) vow-fasts. For prohibitions are not postulated with respect to the latter, as that would result in a logical contradiction (*vikalpa*). Nor should it be argued that this constitutes a sublation of the fast enjoined by the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), because a prohibitive injunction depends upon a prior application of the rule; therefore, it is impossible for it to absolutely sublate it. Consequently, the claim that both Ekādaśīs may be fasted by anyone other than a householder who has sons is incorrect."

Others, however, say that the fast belongs exclusively to the Vaiṣṇavas. Nevertheless, they maintain that for a householder with sons, the fast is on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (śukla-ekādaśī) and not on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī). And thus says Gautama: "One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight; this is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics, but a householder [should fast] always only on the bright one."

That is weak, because there is no authoritative evidence for the claim that the fast belongs exclusively to Vaiṣṇavas. Nor is there any authority for the statement "that vow is Vaiṣṇava," since its purpose is to praise the Ekādaśī fast by way of proclaiming its connection with Viṣṇu:
"Whether one be a Vaiṣṇava or a Śaiva, one should perform the Ekādaśī vow."

This is because it contradicts the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, and because fasting on the Ekādaśī of Kṛṣṇa is heard of for Vaiṣṇava householders who have sons and have undergone the *Upanayana* ceremony and so forth. As for the statement, "A householder should always [fast] on the bright fortnight alone," its meaning is that this is not optional (*kāmya*); otherwise, there would be the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) arising from the prohibition of what has been enjoined. Therefore, it has been stated that all people have the entitlement to the obligatory vow and fast on both Ekādaśīs.
That is incorrect.
"Having sons, together with his wife, and likewise accompanied by his kinsmen, he should perform the Vaiṣṇava vow, which is desirable for both sides. Thus it is said.

Since there is a traditional injunction (smṛti) that permits the optional vow of fasting on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) for a householder who has sons—despite it being otherwise prohibited—and since in the *Bhaviṣyottara* Purāṇa Kṛṣṇa instructs Yudhiṣṭhira, a householder with sons, in the optional vow of both twelfth days (*ubhayadvādaśī*), the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) remains unavoidable even if the act is considered optional, because it is nonetheless prescribed. Therefore, out of fear of such an option, this must be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), just like the rule: "One does not perform the *ye yajāmahe* formula at the *anuyāja* offerings. Nor can it be argued that an exclusion involves a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as has been established; nor does the statement "nor is this a prohibition" serve to refute its status as an exclusion, because its intent lies in the phrase "of the fasting occasioned by that. Thus, being a restatement (*anuvāda*) while sharing the same function as a negative particle, it falls under the category of exclusion. By examining the aforementioned texts, it should be understood that the traditional injunction regarding the fasting on both eleventh days for Rukmāṅgada—a householder with sons—is specifically concerned with the optional (*kāmya*) context. Consequently, it is established that the prohibition against a householder with sons applies to the optional fasting on the dark eleventh day, but not to the obligatory (*nitya*) fasting on the eleventh day.
Now, regarding the occurrence of a Śrāddha on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), the duty of fasting is being stated: in that case,
when a Śrāddha is performed during a Vyatīpāta yoga, a householder who has sons should not fast.
Thus, likewise,
if a Brahmin, having performed a śrāddha, does not eat what has been offered to the ancestors,
the gods do not accept the havis offerings, nor do the ancestors accept the kavya offerings.

By such statements as these, the prohibition against fasting on the day of a *śrāddha* refers to occasions other than the obligatory fast of the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*). Thus says Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:
"When the obligatory fast coincides with an occasional *śrāddha*..."
Then, having smelled that which was used by the ancestors, one should observe a fast.
If the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) should coincide with the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
one should worship the ancestors and the gods and then smell the food that was offered to the ancestors.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "O Nārada, when the day of fasting arrives and a Śrāddha for the ancestors or another [rite] is to be performed, listen to how that should be done."
There is great sin in breaking a vow; however, one should feed those who remain after the meal.
The remaining food should be eaten together with those who are dear to the family.
In that regard, listen to what must be done as told by me:
having gathered all the food with the right hand, [one should proceed].
The smelling of the breath must indeed be performed; otherwise, there would be a breach of the vow, O best of sages, Nārada, if the smelling of the breath is not performed.
By the omission of the *śrāddha*, one becomes a slayer of his mother and a slayer of his father;
knowing this, the wise twice-born devised a remedy.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Guha, on whichever day the Śrāddha for one's father or mother occurs,
O dear one, on that very same day the Ekādaśī vow should be observed."
O Skanda, listen to that which must also be performed on other occasions;
for in such cases, O Guha, neither the ancestral rite (śrāddha) nor the fast is ever violated.
Thus, O Śikhivāhana, when a matter is disputed, this method is considered the supreme means, desired for the welfare of all men.
When the day of the śrāddha arrives and one must observe a fast,
then, having performed the śrāddha, one may consume whatever remains of the meal.
O Śikhidhvaja, having taken all that food with his right hand,
he smells it; by this means, O Śikhidhvaja, the purpose of the *śrāddha* for the ancestors is fulfilled, my dear, providing them satisfaction, and no violation of the vow occurs.
One should not observe a fast on the day of a Śrāddha, on one's birthday, on the Saṃkrānti, or during the Rāhusūtakam, if one desires one's own welfare.

In this context, the mention of "the faithful" (śrāddha) should be understood—by considering the preceding statement—as referring to occasions other than Ekādaśī. The phrase "on a Saṃkrānti" is a prohibition against fasting occasioned by that event; likewise, the phrase "on the day of birth," due to its association with the former, refers to occasions other than Ekādaśī.
Others, however, say it refers to fasting undertaken out of worldly attachment (rāga). Furthermore, having performed a Vṛddhi-śrāddha, fasting for six months is not enjoined.
The ancients maintain that this refers to one who has undertaken a vow;
others say that even one who has not undertaken it must perform it as an obligatory duty;
yet others state that it concerns the fast prescribed by worldly attachment (*rāga*).
That is not so, because it would be inconsistent with the statement, "The fast is not prescribed. Now,
if it is argued that this vow must be performed even during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like,
regarding that point, [it is stated] in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Even when one has fallen into the greatest calamity, or when joy has arisen, or during birth-impurity and death-impurity, the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) must not be abandoned. Thus it is said.
In this regard, there is a specific rule stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"During a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), a person, having bathed and bowed mentally to Hari, shall not eat on the eleventh day; thus the vow is not violated."
Then, having eaten on the eleventh day at the end of the period of impurity, one should worship Janārdana according to the prescribed rite and also worship the best of the twice-born.
"A man should never eat on the day of death or on the eleventh day;
however, having bathed and bowed to Viṣṇu, he may eat on the twelfth day. Thus it is said.
However, whatever vow was previously resolved upon by those firmly committed to their vows,
that should be performed by men, excluding the performance of śrāddha, giving gifts, and ritual worship.
Now, the ten observances for the tenth day according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
one should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils, honey, speaking untruths,
eating a second meal, and habitual indulgence on the tenth day.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "While fasting, one should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, millet, leafy vegetables, honey, food belonging to others, and women."

"Upavasan" means "intending to perform the *upavāsa* (fast). Consequently, the restrictive observance (*niyama*) must be undertaken on the tenth day itself. Likewise: "One should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils, eating a second time, sexual intercourse, gambling, drinking excessive water, and [the seventh], on the tenth day."
In some places, the word *ghṛta* is found in the position where the word *dyūta* occurs.
Devala says: On the tenth day, one should eat only a single meal, abstaining from meat and sexual intercourse;
on the eleventh day, one should fast during both fortnights.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: Bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, false speech,
physical exertion, travel abroad, sleeping during the day, and likewise the acquisition [of wealth].
One should avoid these twelve: sesame paste and lentils.
In the *Smṛti* as well:
"On the tenth day, one who has restrained his senses should take a single meal;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should thereafter chew a tooth-stick."
Thereafter, O Brahmin, the student (brahmacārī), having conquered his senses,
should pass the night; then, having bathed in the morning with a concentrated mind,
he should resolve upon the fast and drink water consecrated by mantras.
Now, the rules for the day of fasting (*upavāsa*). Regarding the nature of fasting, [it is stated] in the *Vṛddhavasiṣṭha*, *Kātyāyana*, and *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who, having turned away from sins, dwells together with the qualities [of virtue]..."

"That should be known as a fast (upavāsa), which is devoid of all enjoyments. Regarding this, "from sins" means from those things that ought to be avoided. "Of one who has turned away" (upāvṛtasya) means of one who has desisted [from them].
In that regard, Sumantu states the things to be avoided:
The non-performance of what is prescribed, the lack of restraint over the senses,
and the constant indulgence in what is forbidden must be avoided with great effort.

Hārīta states: "On the day of fasting, one must avoid conversing with outcasts, heretics, atheists, and the like, as well as lying and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (*ādi*), acts such as violence and sensory restlessness are understood.
The secondary virtues (*guṇas*) are described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
The recitation of that [mantra], meditation upon it, listening to discourses concerning it,
its worship, and the chanting and hearing of its name—
these are indeed the virtues declared by the wise to be produced by fasting.
In the Viṣṇudharmas: "That man who, observing a fast, meditates upon Hari with devotion— repeating His mantra, devoted to His rites, and with his mind fixed on Him."
One who is free from desire, like one who realizes non-duality, attains the state of Brahman without a doubt.
On that eleventh day, the cleansing of the teeth should be performed in the morning,
according to the Smṛti: "One should perform the morning Sandhyā worship preceded by the cleansing of the teeth."

But is it not the case that the cleaning of the teeth with a wooden stick is prohibited on the day of fasting by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha? For he says: "On the day of fasting as well as at a śrāddha, one should not consume a tooth-stick;
contact of the teeth with wood indeed destroys seven generations."

Not so; for since the scripture mentions a fault regarding the use of wood, the statement is intended to mean that one should not perform the cleaning of teeth with wood. Consequently, on the day of fasting, the cleaning of teeth should be performed with leaves or similar materials.

On this point, some say: here it is only the brushing of the teeth that is prohibited; the mention of taking a wooden stick by whatever means is intended merely as a deprecatory explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) and is not meant to be taken literally, because a prohibition, having cessation as its result, does not require a specific qualification. Indeed, it is impossible to turn away from a general rule without specifying a particular case, as in the prohibition against eating garlic and similar things. However, in the case of the injunctive statement, "One should place the sugar-cubes smeared [with ghee]," since the performance of the general rule cannot be carried out without a specific detail, that required specification is supplied by the supplementary sentence, "Ghee is indeed brilliance."
That is incorrect.

Whether wood is unavailable or forbidden, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with pure leaves or the like; furthermore, the scraping of the tongue should always be done [with such materials].

This is because of such statements by Paiṭhīnasi. As for the statement of Vyāsa: "On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth, and on the ninth, one should use a tooth-stick; on other days, however, one may always use leaves or wood, and the tongue should always be scraped."

Thus, in this context, the mention of "the specific day" (pratipad) is intended as an illustration for prohibited days such as those on which tooth-sticks are forbidden. He states another alternative: "In the absence of tooth-sticks, or likewise on a prohibited lunar day, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water."
Immediately thereafter, having performed the morning ablutions and other rites, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the fast.
Regarding this, Devala states the mantra:
"Having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day."
"I shall eat, O lotus-eyed one; be my refuge, O Acyuta.

In some places, however, the reading is "sthitvāham apare 'hani" (having stayed on the following day). Kātyāyana reads it as "sthitvāhani tataḥ para" (having stayed on that day thereafter). After the recitation of the mantra, he himself says:
"Having recited this, the wise man should then offer a handful of flowers.

By reflecting upon this, it is understood that one should form a hollowed palm full of flowers, resolve upon the fast with this mantra, and offer the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Viṣṇu. [In the] *Skanda Purāṇa*:
Thereafter, he should pass the night; then, having bathed in the morning with a concentrated mind and having made a formal vow (saṃkalpa) for the fast, he should drink water purified by mantras.
"Rātrim" means on the tenth night; the meaning is that one should drink water consecrated with the eight-syllable mantra.
And so says Mārkaṇḍeya:
"Consecrated by reciting the eight-syllable mantra three times..."
Desiring the fruit of the fast, one should drink water with a concentrated mind.
Having thus performed the worship of the deity, or even offered a handful of flowers,
one should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), utter the mantra, and present it to the deity.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, this verse is recited immediately after the line "puṣpāñjalim athāpi vā":
"Having worshipped the Lord of the gods with supreme devotion,
the wise man should spend a day and night endowed with fasting in order to obtain the fruit thereof."

The phrase "one should drink again" is stated for the purpose of drinking all the water contained in the vessel. Alternatively, at the conclusion of the worship of the deity and the sacrifice, having formed a full *añjali* of flowers, one should then worship the Lord of the Gods with that handful of flowers immediately following the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). As for the Śaivas, however, the mantra for the resolve is shown in the *Śivadharmas*:
"We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva;
may Rudra impel us."

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the solar [deity] should be made either by means of the *Sāvitrī* mantra or by name; for it is stated in the *Saura Purāṇa*: "One should perform the resolve either with the *Sāvitrī* or by name. However, when the tenth day extends slightly beyond midnight, one should perform the worship and the resolve after discarding the first four watches (*yāma*) of the eleventh day.
On the tenth day, due to the fault of association,
one should avoid the four watches following midnight for both the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and the worship (arcana).
Because of this statement: "But when the tenth [lunar day] persists even at sunrise, then [the worship should be] at night;
having fasted, being concentrated, and having abandoned the day, one should worship Viṣṇu at night and then perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa)."
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"Due to the fault of association with the preceding [day], the fast, as well as the ritual bathing and worship, should not be performed on the [following] day."
O twice-born one, those who know that avoid it and the four watches of the night as well.
Thereafter, those who have fasted should perform the ritual bathing, worship, and other rites.
One does not attain purity during the day; therefore, it is prescribed for the night. And the entirety of the daily duties should be performed at the beginning of the night.
On this point, Devala says:
"Taking a vessel of udumbara wood filled with water and facing north,
a twice-born man should either undertake a fast or make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) to do so."

"Audumbara" means made of copper. Taking that [vessel] filled with water while facing the north, one should undertake the fast (*upavāsa*); or rather, the meaning is that one should form the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), or simply perform the mental resolve alone. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"One should indeed undertake the fast, or else merely holding water."

Thus it is recited; therein, there is an option between water and a handful of flowers. Therefore, it is established that the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the fast is accompanied by the mantra according to the prescribed rule. Now, in cases where the rule for eating at night (*nakta*) applies, is the resolve to be performed with the mantra alone, or is the procedure for the fast (*upavāsa*) itself to be employed? On this point, some say it should be without the mantra because the mantra is not explicitly heard [in that context]. That is incorrect. For example: "The mortal who would observe the vow of fasting by means of a single meal," and likewise: [other citations].

"Having fasted by the *nakta* method, O Lord, for four [days] conjoined with Tuesday," and so forth—in passages such as these from the *Skanda Purāṇa* and others, it is established that the application of fasting (*upavāsa*) in *nakta* and other observances is for the purpose of indicating the duties of fasting according to the principle of the "Monthly Agnihotra. Since there is thus a transfer of ritual properties (*dharma-atideśa*), when the literal meaning of the mantra associated with fasting is absent, and a need arises to manifest the relevant subject matter, it is understood that the rite is to be performed with a mantra in which words such as "eating at night" (*naktāhāra*) have been substituted for [the word "fasting"] on the eleventh day and so forth. Therefore, it is proven that even in the case of *nakta* and similar observances, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must indeed be accompanied by a mantra.

Now, other observances to be performed by those intent on fasting are described: from the time of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) until the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*), one must not associate with heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) or engage in conversation with them. As it is said in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"One should avoid contact with heretics as well as even conversing with them."
For those intent on the propitiation of Viṣṇu, no task whatsoever should be performed while fasting.
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Therefore, one who is initiated (dīkṣita) should avoid conversation and touch with sinful heretics,
especially at the time of ritual action or during sacrifices and the like."
Regarding those heretics who perform actions prescribed by scriptures outside the Veda, an expiation for seeing them has been stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Upon seeing such a person, a wise man should look at the sun."
Regarding contact, the expiation is stated in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"Upon contact, however, a wise man, having bathed and become pure, [is purified] by beholding the sun.
And regarding conversation, the expiation is stated in that very same work: 1.
Having conversed with them, the wise man should contemplate the Pure-footed Acyuta;
and having made his mind fully inclined toward Him, he should properly recite this.
May the blessed Lord Viṣṇu bring to complete pacification all bodily ailments, injuries to the internal organs, and every form of speech directed against me here.
One should proceed [to liberation] when the Infinite is seated within the heart.
May he who is pure, consisting of Dharma, and immutable, perform internal purification and external purification within that stainless [body];
may I always remain truly pure.
May the sinless, unborn, and omniscient Lord Viṣṇu, whose self is infinite, who abides in the mind and perceives external afflictions, lead us to peace.
"Having conversed thus, this should be recited by heretics who have fasted;
having uttered 'Obeisance to the one whose feet are pure,' the initiated person should look at the sun.
Some authorities understand this to be the expiation for the violation of physical, vocal, and mental observances.

That is weak, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). Nor is the indicative mark of a mantra (*mantraliṅga*) an authoritative means of proof; for since it is weaker than syntactical connection (*vākya*), it lacks authority when there is a contradiction with syntactical connection. And the syntactical connection is contradicted by such [texts] as, "Having conversed thus, one should recite [the mantra]. Regarding the omission of speech, Yājñavalkya states this expiation:
"If there should be an omission of the words during bathing, giving, recitation, and so forth, one should indeed utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu."

However, in the case of a lapse in mental restraint (*mānasaniyama*), penances such as ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth are well known. Furthermore, one who is fasting should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Thus says Kātyāyana:
"A man should observe a fast accompanied by the practice of celibacy."
And the fast (*upavāsaka*) is a vow (*vrata*). In a vow, the fourfold set beginning with celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be observed.
And so Devala says:
"Celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, and the avoidance of meat."
These four should be practiced constantly among one's vows.
He himself states the causes for the failure of celibacy:
"Celibacy is indeed broken by looking at women, by touching them, and even by conversing with them; however, it is not broken by union with one's own wife during her fertile period."
He himself stated those things which spoil a fast:
"The fast is vitiated by drinking water repeatedly, by chewing betel,
by sleeping during the day, and by sexual intercourse."
And when unable [to fast], one may drink water repeatedly. As for the statement of Vyāsa:
"Flowers, ornaments, and garments, perfumes, incense, and ointments—these do not cause a fault during a fast, nor do the cleansing of the teeth and the application of collyrium."
Thus, that [rule] regarding merit concerns women.
Now, the observances for the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped Hari, one should offer the vow:
"O Keśava, by this vow, be gracious to me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance;
O Lord, be well-disposed toward me and grant the vision of knowledge."
Then one should perform the breaking of the fast according to the available means;
from that point onward, however, one may act as desired and according to one's preference.

But when the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is sufficient only for the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa), then, having performed all the rites such as bathing and so forth during the remainder of the night, the breaking of the fast should be performed in the middle of the twelfth day.
And so it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"When the twelfth day is very short on the day of the breaking of the fast..."
At the time of dawn, one should perform two rites: then the morning and the midday [rites].
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa as well:

"O best of Brahmins, when the Dvādaśī is short, the rites of bathing and worship should be performed at the break of dawn (aruṇodaya), accompanied by acts of giving, fire-offerings, and so forth. [202]
On the pure thirteenth lunar day, by breaking one's fast, a person undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the earth or even the merit of seven sacrifices and other rites.
For this reason, a Brahmin should perform his bath at dawn,
accompanied by the libations to the ancestors, even upon seeing only a small portion of the twelfth day remaining.
And so it is stated in the Śāradā-purāṇa:
"If all the daily rites are to be performed during the day,
and one does not achieve success on that very day, then they are prescribed for the night."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: For this reason, O Brahmin, one should perform a bath at dawn,
accompanied by libations to the ancestors, upon seeing that the lunar day is the twelfth.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "O King, on the twelfth day when it is short, at the break of dawn,
the ritual for bathing should be performed, accompanied by acts of giving, fire-offerings, and so forth."
In the *Kālikā-purāṇa* and the *Śāradā-purāṇa*:
"Where the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is very short, the ritual acts such as bathing and giving gifts should be performed during the night itself, accompanied by offerings and burnt oblations."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Where two or even three *kalās* of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) are seen,
the rites such as bathing and worship are prescribed for that night."
Kātyāyana says:
But if, in the performance of duties, even a small amount is omitted in its proper sequence,
then there will be a total failure of the rite, because otherwise the sequence is violated.
Jaimini says: "In that case, because of the connection with the daytime, there should be a reduction [of the rite] ending at that point.
Now, here too are the rules regarding the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*).
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: Brass, meat, liquor, honey, greed, false speech,
physical exertion, travel abroad, sleeping during the day, and the application of collyrium— these [should be avoided].
Sesame paste and lentils—these twelve things a devotee of Viṣṇu should always avoid on the twelfth lunar day; thus he is liberated from all sins.
Eating again, anger, carrying loads, physical exertion,
sexual intercourse, and fifthly, sleeping by day— these would destroy the fruit of fasting.
Bṛhaspati also says:
On the twelfth day, one should avoid these eight things: sleeping during the day, food from others, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, honey, eating from a bell-metal vessel, meat, and oil.
One should avoid bell-metal, meat, liquor, gambling, physical exertion, anger,
sexual intercourse, sleeping during the day, eating again, chickpeas, and *koradūṣaka* grain;
on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), one should likewise avoid these eight things, including bell-metal and honey, as well as food belonging to others.
Likewise:
bell-metal, meat, and lentils are to be avoided; as are physical exertion, sexual intercourse, violence, untruthfulness, oil, greed, the remains of offerings, and fasting.
The word "one should avoid" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Honey, meat, liquor, oil, physical exertion, anger, and sexual intercourse..."
On the twelfth lunar day, a Vaiṣṇava should avoid these twelve things: food from others, eating from a bell-metal vessel, betel nut, greed, and fasting.

In these statements, the connection with a fruit is heard in some cases as "the desired object is accomplished," in others as "one desiring the fruit of fasting," and in yet others as "they would destroy the fruit of fasting. Therefore, it is understood that these declarations concern the domain of optional rites (*kāmya*). Furthermore, even in those rules regarding the tenth day where no connection with a fruit is explicitly heard, it is nevertheless understood from their being recited in association with the subject matter of optional rites; thus, it is concluded that everything pertains to the domain of optional rites.
"In the first two days, [the meal] is at night; but in the middle two days, it is at night and in the morning."
"One who desires the fruit of the fast should abandon four meals.

Regarding this, some say: by this statement, the abandonment of the four meals that are auxiliary to the optional (kāmya) fast is enjoined; for the mention of "one desiring" (*prepsu*) is inappropriate in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) auxiliary, since in obligatory rites there is no performance [of an act] for the sake of a connection with a fruit.

That is untenable, because there is no evidence for its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*). For in this case, only syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) are conceivable; other means of proof do not even enter the range of suspicion. First, it cannot be an auxiliary by virtue of context, because a thing without a fruit becomes an auxiliary to something with a fruit when it occurs in proximity to it. And it cannot be said that the abandonment of the four kinds of food—which is connected by the word *phalepsu*, a synonym for *phalakāma*—is itself fruitless. Therefore, it is not an auxiliary by context. Nor is it so by syntactical connection, for the sentence expresses a connection with the fruit of the fast, but not that the fast is performed as a means to a desired end; this is because the connection is understood through the natural force of the words. Thus, its connection is only with the fruit of the fast. That too is not the case, because since a general fruit unspecified as "sons, cattle," and so on, is not required, it is impossible to connect it with that. Now, if it is argued that by the very power of the qualification of the fast in the phrase "one desiring the fruit of the fast," it is connected with whatever specific fruit belongs to that fast.

That is not so. If it is argued that [the injunction] connects with a specific fruit qualified by the fast (*upavāsa*), that is not correct. For if there were a connection with a specific fruit qualified by the fast, then—since that [connection] would necessarily be preceded by the cognition of a scriptural statement enjoining the connection between the fast and its fruit—it would be impossible to enjoin another means for a fruit achieved through the fast, because [that other means] would be dependent on the fast itself, making both option (*vikalpa*) and combination (*samuccaya*) with it impossible. Well then, let us assume the relationship between a quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit for the fast: "One who desires such a specific fruit should abandon four meals. This too is not tenable, because it would entail a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "fruit" (*phala*) as meaning "such a specific fruit. Therefore, the relationship between the quality and the fruit must be stated in this way: "When the very fruit accomplished by the fast is desired in a more excellent degree, then one should abandon four meals. Just as the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is enjoined for those desiring an excellence of the fruit accomplished by the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, so it is here as well. This being the case, the prefix *pra-* in the word *phalaprepsuḥ* ("desiring the fruit") also becomes meaningful as expressing excellence (*prakarpa*).

But surely, since the abandonment of devotion is itself of the nature of an action, how can it be enjoined for the sake of a result by one who does not accomplish another action? For example, in the case of the *vāravantīya* chant—which is of the nature of the act of singing—it was resorted to as a qualified injunction because it could not be connected to a result unless it accomplished the sacrifice under discussion.

It is said: since a factor (*kāraka*) that exists in its accomplished form cannot bring about a result unless it performs an action, it would require the accomplishment of the action at hand as a means, just as the *godohana* vessel [requires the milking action]. However, because an action is itself of the nature of action, it does not require the production of another action; rather, because it cannot bring about the result without depending upon that [action], it receives its designation by taking recourse to it.
Now, even without a connection to a specific desire (*kāma*), the practice of eating only one meal on the tenth day is enjoined by a statement in the form of an injunction (*praiṣa*), as follows:

"O people, stay awake during the day at dawn and eat only one meal"—this statement refers specifically to the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, not to every eleventh day in general, because it is recited within that specific context; for it says there:
"This [eleventh day] which is bright in Kārttika dispels the sleep of Hari."
"The eleventh day has arrived at dawn; do not take food for two days. Thus [it is said].

Now follows the determination of the eleventh day (ekādaśī). It is of two kinds: complete (saṃpūrṇā) and overlapping (viddhā). Some say that a complete ekādaśī is one that persists from sunrise until the next sunrise.
And likewise, in the *Jyotiḥsiddhānta*: "For all these [lunar days] are complete from one sunrise to the next. Also in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
"Starting from the time of sunrise, that lunar day which lasts for sixty nāḍīs is declared by the ancient sages to be complete. Thus [it is said].
This is not correct:
"All [lunar days] beginning with the first day (pratipad), from sunrise until sunrise,
are known as complete, with the exception of the day of Hari."
Because this contradicts the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, one may ask: "What then is a complete *harivāsara*? In response to this, it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* and the *Śivarahasya*:
"O Brahmins, when [the day] is joined with two *muhūrttas* prior to sunrise..."
On that occasion, the householder should observe the fast known as Sampūrṇaikādaśī.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The Ekādaśī that is accompanied by two muhūrtas prior to the time of sunrise is proclaimed as complete; any other is declared to be pierced (viddhā)."

[207] We shall explain completeness by another method further on. Regarding the complete Ekādaśī, there are two types: that which is *viddhā* (pierced) when there is no twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) on the following day, and that which is *viddhā* when a twelfth day exists. Among these, it is undisputed that the first type is to be observed by everyone, provided there is no twelfth day on the thirteenth day. Regarding the second type, where a twelfth day exists on the thirteenth day, some say: "The fast should be observed on the Ekādaśī and not on the twelfth day, because the primary time characterized as Ekādaśī is absent on the twelfth day. Indeed, the twelfth day should not be accepted merely for the sake of performing the ritual function of the Ekādaśī; for when the primary time is available, it is not logical for another time to perform that same function."
As for the statement:
"When the Ekādaśī lasts for a full day and night and the Dvādaśī exceeds it by even a single moment (kalā),
then, on the morning of the Trayodaśī, the Dvādaśī should be observed as the fast."
Thus, this refers to the case of an Ekādaśī pierced by the tenth tithi (daśamī-viddhā), as well as to the case where even a small portion of Ekādaśī exists on the twelfth tithi (dvādaśī).

Others, however, say: "If the twelfth tithi exists thereafter, the fast is on the pure twelfth and not on the eleventh; even if pierced, it should be understood as unpierced provided there is no twelfth tithi thereafter."
If the twelfth day (dvādaśī) extends beyond [the morning], it is as if pierced, even if it was not pierced [by the eleventh].
Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
And likewise in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"If even a single *liptā* [of the day] is conjoined with [the previous day] when the moon is increasing..."
Now, if the eleventh day does not exist, or if it is joined with the tenth day;
If there should be even a *kalā* or a *kāṣṭhā* of the twelfth [lunar day] on the following day,
twelve [instances of] the twelfth [lunar day] destroy [the merit] if the breaking of the fast is performed on the previous day.

In this context, by means of the censure of the former breaking of the fast, the latter breaking of the fast is enjoined; and since the breaking of the fast is logically impossible without a preceding fast, for the fast culminates in the breaking of the fast.

[208] This has been stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*: “The vow is to be understood as ending with the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*). By this, it is determined that the fast occurs on the pure twelfth day (*śuddhadvādaśī*); nor is there the fault of obstructing the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) which is enjoined by its originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), because it is declared therein that the twelfth day enters [the vow] through another opening. Those who have asserted that this statement refers only to the case of the subsequent eleventh day are ignorant of the context. For it is also the subject under discussion here that “or else, the eleventh day may not exist. And those who claim it refers only to the case of the eleventh day pierced by the tenth day (*daśamī-viddhā*) are likewise mistaken; for the phrase “joined with the tenth” is the subject under discussion there, and because it will be stated later that the presence of the twelfth day on the following day is irrelevant to the fast on the second eleventh day and to the fast on the pure twelfth day when there is a fast on the pierced eleventh day. Thus, this statement concerns the subject matter as described above.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "When the Ekādaśī is full and the Dvādaśī follows it,
one should indeed abandon the Ekādaśī and observe the fast on the Dvādaśī."
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*:

"If the Ekādaśī is complete and the following day is similar [in duration], the preceding one should be understood as being like the previous case; the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*) is highly praised."

"Uttarā" refers to the twelfth day; "sadṛśī" means having a remainder, implying that it may extend into the thirteenth day as well. "Pūrvā" refers to the eleventh day; "pūrvavat" means as before, i.e., without fasting on the tenth day.
As stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"When the eleventh day is complete and the twelfth day follows after it..."
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast there; in that case, the increase of the lunar day (tithivṛddhi) is highly praised.
Also in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"When the Nandā tithi is full and the Bhadrā increases, one should fast on that Bhadrā; the increase of the lunar day is praised."

In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "The twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast when it is pure; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the twelfth itself, even if only a single digit (kalā) or two digits of the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) have emerged."
O protector of the earth, that man who fasts on the twelfth lunar day when it consists of two kalās and performs the ritual breaking of the fast, does not enter a womb again.
In another Smṛti: "Where the eleventh day is complete and the twelfth day exists on the following day, there the twelfth day should be observed as the fast;
the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the twelfth day itself."
In the Bhāgavata and other Tantras: "If the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is complete and the twelfth (dvādaśī) follows, the complete ekādaśī should be abandoned;
the pure twelfth day should be observed for fasting, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the twelfth day alone."
"A living being does not enter the womb," so said the Blessed Lord Hari.
Therefore, some maintain that in such a case, the fast must be observed on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) alone;

others, however, state the following rule: when the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is complete, the twelfth day is absent, and the twelfth day exists on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), [then the fast is on the latter].
O Brahmin, when [the moon] is joined with two *muhūrtas* prior to sunrise...
When it is called "complete Ekādaśī," the householder should fast on that very day.
According to this traditional teaching (smṛti), householders must observe a fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī). Furthermore:
"If the eleventh day does not exist, or if it is joined with the tenth," and "The eleventh day shall be considered complete if there is a twelfth day following it."
Such are the scriptural statements:
"The twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast when it is pure;
the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) must take place on the twelfth day itself, even if the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) has emerged by even a single digit (kalā) or two digits."
O protector of the earth, that man who fasts on the twelfth lunar day when it consists of two kalas and performs the ritual breaking of the fast, does not enter a womb again.
Where the eleventh day is complete and the twelfth day occurs on the following day, one should fast on that twelfth day;
the breaking of the fast should take place on the twelfth day itself.
"The living being does not enter a womb [again]," so said the Blessed Lord Hari.

By reflecting on such statements, these [rules] concern those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). When a doubt arises as to where those other than householders and seekers of liberation should observe the fast—specifically when a doubt arises due to the contradiction of many scriptural passages—it is said:
"In that case, the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is to be accepted, and the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should take place on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*)."

According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), the fast is observed on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). However, if there is no overlap (*vedha*) with the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), or if the twelfth day is absent, or even if the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) is absent—since there would then be no basis for fasting on the twelfth day and thus no room for doubt—one should indeed perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the twelfth day of the second fortnight.

Thus, since the rule for breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) in the middle of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) is prescribed when there is the presence of a *dvādaśī* sufficient for two digits (*kalā*), it follows that one should break the fast on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) when there is a *dvādaśī* of less than two full digits. Consequently, in the absence of an unpierced (*aviddha*) *ekādaśī* on the *dvādaśī*, and given the presence of the *dvādaśī* on the *trayodaśī*, there is no basis for determining that householders and seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*)—as distinct from ascetics (*yati*)—should fast on that [the *dvādaśī*] alone, just as ascetics do on the *ekādaśī*. Furthermore, because there is no basis for determining a fast on the *dvādaśī* (as in the saying, "The living being does not enter the womb"), and because doubt arises, fasting on the *ekādaśī* would lead to a contradiction with many scriptural statements such as "or else, if the *ekādaśī* does not exist. Therefore, the meaning is that the *dvādaśī* is to be accepted. Even if the contradiction among many statements can be resolved through the determination of their respective scopes (*viṣayavyavasthā*), then doubt ceases due to the certainty of that determination. If resolution is impossible, then because they possess unequal strength, certainty is established by following the stronger authority, and thus doubt is absent. If they possess equal strength, certainty is established through an option (*vikalpa*), and thus doubt is absent. Since the production of doubt occurs only when one fails to consider the determination of scope and so forth—and because there is no difference in their status as Smṛtis for unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*) such that one side cannot be definitively chosen—the interpretation of this statement as being intended merely to remove the doubt created by many statements is not tenable.
When there is a dispute among Brāhmaṇas due to contradictions between many scriptural statements,
one should abandon the eleventh day and observe the fast on the twelfth day.

Thus, this traditional rule (*smṛti*) is established for widows and others distinct from householders and seekers of liberation; for, since there is no single consistent voice among the disputing and contradictory Brahmins who advocate fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), it follows that due to the contradiction of many statements, a widow and the like should abandon the eleventh day and fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). The compound *bahuvākyavirodhaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "those for whom there is a contradiction of many statements.
And regarding those statements which are ambiguous, one should fast on the twelfth day.

Even with such a statement, in the case of widows and others for whom sentences such as "Now, if the eleventh day does not exist" are ambiguous, it should be explained that "such a widow and others should fast on the twelfth day."

That is incorrect; for prior to sunrise, by reflecting on the preceding statements, it is understood from the subsequent [texts] that the fast applies to those other than householders. Furthermore, the explanation of the statement beginning with "due to the contradiction of many sentences" is also improper because it is not straightforward, given the conflict of the *jyotiḥśāstra* regarding the measurement of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the fact that [the statement] is appropriately straightforward as referring to cases of doubt concerning the overlapping of the tenth day (*daśamī-vedha*). As for the statement from the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Pradyumna:
"In all disputes, however, one should fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*)."
O Sage, the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day is my command;
one should not employ logical reasoning, for by such reasoning a man falls.

Thus, that too should be explained as having the previously mentioned piercing (*vedha*) as its subject matter. Alternatively, those [texts] concern cases where one is unable to determine the fixed rule regarding the subject matter; this is what was stated in the phrase "and in the case of doubtful statements. Since liberation is not established merely by fasting on an unpierced *ekādaśī*, the statement "the living being does not enter a womb" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Its utility through the purification of the internal being (*sattva-śuddhi*) is common to householders and others alike; therefore, there is no contradiction even if [the text] has the fruit as its primary purpose. Consequently, what has been stated is indeed superior. As for the second [type of *ekādaśī*], whether the thirteenth day lacks a twelfth day (*avidyamāna-dvādaśikā*) or possesses a twelfth day (*vidyamāna-dvādaśikā*), the rule applies to the former.
And so it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Where the Ekādaśī is complete and remains likewise at dawn,
the ascetic (yati) should observe the later day, while the householder (gṛhī) should fast on the earlier."
Also in the *Gāruḍa Purāṇa*:
"O Brahmin, when [the moonrise] occurs joined with two muhūrtas before sunrise, that is called 'Full Ekādaśī'; on that very day, the householder should fast."
Furthermore, when one *ghaṭikā* remains of the dawn,
fasting is prescribed here for those dwelling in the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*),
as well as for widows, provided that the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) does not follow thereafter.
And here, by the word "ca" (and), those residing in the forest and others are included. Pracetās says:
"If the eleventh day is extended [into the next tithi], especially so in the bright fortnight..."
The husband should perform the latter [rite], while the householder should observe the fast for the former.
The elder Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Where the eleventh day is complete and yet that same day recurs at dawn,
while the twelfth day is lost— how can there be a fast on such an occasion?"
Those intent on pleasing Viṣṇu should observe the fast on both lunar days there.

On that thirteenth day, however, when there is no twelfth day, then—by virtue of the distinction between the eligibility of those in the householder stage and those in the fourth stage previously mentioned—the two lunar days (tithis) are to be observed as fasts, and not just one; this is the meaning.

Others, however, explain [the text] as being solely intent upon fasting on two lunar days (*tithi*). This is because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate different classes of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*); because we observe a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) which is an exception to the *dvandva* compound prescribed for mutual conjunction; because there is the understanding that the two lunar days joined together are to be fasted upon; and because there is a scriptural statement regarding the qualified practitioner who desires the pleasure of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the interpretation that "one day joined with two lunar days is to be fasted upon" is not tenable, as it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *tithi* in the sense of a part of itself. Also, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "On the first day, the full [lunar day] persists, pervading the entire day and night."
And likewise, O dear one, it is seen again on the twelfth day.
O Śikhivāhana, if even a single ghaṭikā of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be seen,
it must be observed by householders and likewise by ascetics,
O Lord; indeed, those who desire liberation should always observe it conjoined with the twelfth day.

By reflecting on this statement, it is understood that in the phrase "again at the time of dawn," the established rule refers to a complete [tithi] that spans a full day and night, specifically to the single *ghaṭikā* existing on the second day, and so forth; however, in the sentence beginning with "starting from sunrise until sunrise," a complete [tithi] is not intended. Furthermore, in the phrase "again at the time of dawn," the established rule is stated as referring to the single *ghaṭikā* existing at sunrise, and so forth. If sunrise were the upper limit, then the word "dawn" (*prabhāta*) would be inappropriate as a synonym for sunrise; for Amarasimha and others have defined "dawn" (*prabhāta*) as "the break of day" (*aharmukha*), "the auspicious time" (*kalya*), and "the early morning" (*uṣaḥ-pratyūṣasī*). This word "dawn" is a synonym for "early morning" (*pratyūṣa*) and denotes sunrise. Moreover, in the Nāradīya statement cited in the context of the rules for the *dvādaśī* when it is short—having first mentioned "bathing at sunrise" (*aruṇodaya-snāna*), it concludes by saying "one should perform the bath in the early morning" (*pratyūṣe*). Likewise, in the Pādma statement read in that same context—"when it occurs"—it is stated that "bathing and other rites should be performed at the time of *uṣaḥ* (dawn). In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa statement "when it is short," [the term used is] "at sunrise" (*aruṇodaye*); therefore, the word "dawn" (*prabhāta*) is a synonym for the word "dawn" (*uṣaḥ*) which denotes sunrise, and the statement is likewise. The phrase "if there is no *dvādaśī* thereafter" would otherwise be untenable, because it is well-known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) that a decrease of six *ghaṭikās* may occur on the day immediately following a maximum increase (*paramavṛddhi*). It is argued: If the sentence "again at the time of dawn" could have the same meaning as the statement "on the first day, however, it is complete," then, since this is supported by the very Vedic source upon which it is based, one should not assume another source. Otherwise, that [source] would be required; furthermore, in your view, the word "time" (*samaya*) would be redundant, whereas in our view, by resorting to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) in "dawn-time" (*prabhāta-samaya*), there is no fault whatsoever. For this very reason, statements such as "she [the tithi] again at dawn" are similar to those; and "dawn" (*prabhāta*) is in the locative case. In the case of the *karmadhāraya* compound "dawn-time" (*prabhāta-samaya*), and because there is no reason to abandon the upper limit already stated in statements such as "all these are indeed complete," the restriction "excluding the day of Hari" cannot be the reason, as that would lead to unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and because it can be explained otherwise. Just as a complete lunar day (*tithi*) consists of sixty *ghaṭikās*, we see that the upper limit in the form of sunrise also applies to complete tithis. Nor should it be said that the statement "at the time of the sun's rising" contradicts the established fact that a tithi consists of sixty *ghaṭikās*. If both limits were applied, the word "complete" (*saṃpūrṇa*) would result in having multiple meanings, and if its meaning were restricted to consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās*, the previously mentioned faults would follow. Rather, for the purpose of determining the specific intended meaning, the two statements "before sunrise" and "at the time of the sun's rising" can be explained as referring to the tithi existing during the two *muhūrtas* prior to sunrise on both days. Thus, there are two kinds of complete *ekādaśī*: one that spans a full day and night, and one that exists starting from sunrise until the next sunrise. Even among these, the word "complete" is primary in the first case as it applies generally to all lunar days, but not in the second, as that would result in multiple meanings. The designation "complete" for a tithi existing even during the four *ghaṭikās* before sunrise is for the purpose of refuting the "piercing" (*vedha*) by sunrise, as is the phrase "excluding the day of Hari."

Others, however, say: "It is designated as 'complete' precisely when it is joined with the preceding limit; there is no requirement to grasp a second limit. Even in this view, the explanation is the same as before, following the previous method. Others, however, explain it thus: "If [the tithi] lasts for two *muhūrtas* prior to sunrise and also extends across the day and night, then—since the rule 'the first and subsequent [tithis] belong to the preceding [day]' excludes completeness common to all lunar days (*tithis*)—there arises a desire to know completeness by another means. And since the sentence is logically complete simply by providing what was required [by that desire]," [this is their position].

And so says Mārkaṇḍeya: "Where the eleventh [lunar day] is joined with the preceding [tenth], and that same [eleventh] occurs again on the following day, one who has desires should fast on the former; one free from desire, however, should fast on the latter."
Furthermore, if this were merely a statement regarding householders in general, then a desireless householder would not be required to observe a fast on the second Ekādaśī; for it is said:
"A desireless householder, however, should always observe the later Ekādaśī."
O best of the twice-born, let it be the twelfth day at dawn, or let it not be.

Thus, there would be a contradiction with the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*. Others, however, offer this explanation for the different readings of the terms *yati* (ascetic) and *gṛhin* (householder): if only the householder were to fast on the previous day and only the ascetic on the following day, then where would the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and others observe their fast?
