For the fast cannot be on the previous day, because of the injunction, "The householder shall fast on the previous day"; nor can it be on the following day, because of the injunction, "But the ascetic shall perform it on the following day."

[Objection: But surely the word *yati*, by its connection with the word *niyata* (restricted), denotes even those such as forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) who are restricted; and thus, if it is argued that for such a person there is fasting on the following day, [we reply:

No, because it would then follow that even householders (*gṛhin*) who are restricted would have to fast on the following day. And in that case, the scriptural statement, "The householder should fast on the preceding [day]," would be rendered inconsistent. [Objection: But the word *yati* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those other than householders; therefore, for forest-dwellers and others, there is fasting on the following day.

Not so; for since no contradiction has yet arisen, it is untenable for the word *yati* (ascetic) to function as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaka*). On the contrary, because it occurs in the concluding portion, the word *gṛhin* (householder) would instead function as a secondary indicator of those other than the ascetic; and in that case, there would be a contradiction with such statements as "Again, at the time of dawn... If you argue that the injunction is that the householder should fast on the previous day while the ascetic should fast on the subsequent one, and thus the forest-dweller and others may fast on another day—[we reply:]...

It should not be so, because the statement "the householder should fast on the previous day" would otherwise be rendered fruitless. For fasting on the subsequent day is occasioned by the presence of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) thereafter, according to the rule: "if there is a twelfth day thereafter. Since the twelfth day is absent thereafter, fasting on the preceding eleventh day (ekādaśī) would already be established for everyone; thus, the statement "the householder should fast on the previous day" would indeed be useless.
[Objection: Why could forest-dwellers and others not observe a fast on both days? [Response: That too is prescribed within this very context.
Where the eleventh day is complete and that same [eleventh] reappears at dawn,
while the twelfth day is lost— how can there be a fast on such an occasion?
Having begun thus:

"In that case, those intent on pleasing Viṣṇu should fast for two lunar days," according to this statement, let it be granted that fasting may apply to one with desires, such as a forest-dweller; however, it must be explained where fasting applies to one who is free from desire. Furthermore, even regarding fasting for two lunar days, it occurs only when there is a loss (*kṣaya*) of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*).
Where the Ekādaśī is complete [on one day] and that same [Ekādaśī] occurs again on the following day,
with the Trayodaśī at the time of dawn— on such an occasion, which [day] should be observed as the fast?
Having begun with these words, [it continues]:

"In that case, those intent on pleasing Viṣṇu should fast for two lunar days," according to the statement from the Skanda Purāṇa. Furthermore, the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day is prescribed for one who is free from desire.

Where the Ekādaśī is complete [on one day] and it occurs again at dawn, [that is the one to be observed]. Baudhāyana says: "Where even a minute fraction (kalā) of Ekādaśī exists and there is no Dvādaśī on the following day..."
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Even if there is but a single moment (*kalā*) of Ekādaśī, if there is no Dvādaśī following it," [the second half of this verse follows:
"for these [cases], the latter [portion of the day] is [to be observed]."
"In that regard, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day.
Thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"On the pure thirteenth day, however, breaking the fast yields the fruit of the entire earth."
Or indeed, a man undoubtedly attains even more than the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*:

"He by whom the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is fasted upon even when only a single digit (*kalā*) of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) remains shall be equal to one who has performed a hundred sacrifices; however, the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) must take place on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*)."
Baudhāyana says:
Having fasted on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) when it is joined with even a single digit of the eleventh day (ekādaśī),
a man who eats on the thirteenth day attains union with Viṣṇu.
In another Smṛti: "If the Ekādaśī is complete and the following day (Dvādaśī) likewise [extends],
it is declared that breaking the fast on the Trayodaśī yields the merit of a hundred sacrifices."
But is it not the case that a prohibition against breaking the fast on the thirteenth day is also seen?
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "Having thus fasted on the eleventh day, the breaking of the fast is prescribed on the twelfth."
One should not perform that on the thirteenth day, because of the occurrence of twelve twelfth-day fasts.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who, having fasted on the eleventh day, performs the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day,
for him twelve twelfth days are lost."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O best of kings, he who performs the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day destroys twelve Dvādaśīs; there is no need for further deliberation on this point."

It is not so; for the prohibitory statements regarding breaking the fast on the thirteenth day refer to those who have desires (*sakāma*). Thus, it is said: "On whichever Ekādaśī a fast might result in breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, one who has desires should not fast on that [Ekādaśī]. If the aforementioned prohibitions were intended for those without desires (*niṣkāma*), then the injunctions for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day would become purposeless. Therefore, the injunctions for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day concern those without desires. Likewise, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"The breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day should be performed by those who do not seek rewards."
In the Skanda Purāṇa as well:
"The breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day bestows liberation upon those free from desire.
Therefore, [the rules] regarding the stages of householder and ascetic are not to be followed literally.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Where the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is pure and the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is overlapped (*viddhā*), the former, when observed, bestows heaven; the latter bestows both heaven and liberation."
When a certain *dvādaśī* exists on the thirteenth day, it is the subsequent one alone that must be observed as a fast by everyone.
Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Where the *ekādaśī* is complete [on the eleventh], and it occurs again at dawn..."
But the ascetic should perform the *uttarā*; the *uttarā* bestows heaven and liberation.
If a certain twelfth day exists on the thirteenth day, it is the latter one alone that must be observed as a fast by all.
And so says Bhṛgu:
"Where the eleventh day is complete and it occurs again at dawn..."
A renunciant should perform the latter [observance], while a householder should fast on the former.
This is one statement:
"Where the eleventh day is complete and that same [eleventh] appears again at dawn,
there the second [eleventh] should be observed as a fast, provided that the twelfth day follows thereafter."

Thus, another [view]. On this point, some explain as follows: in the preceding verse there are two injunctions; by one of them, the first Ekādaśī is specifically prescribed for the householder, while by the other, the subsequent Ekādaśī is prescribed for the ascetic (yati). Thus, having fasted on the first Ekādaśī specifically ordained for the householder, the Ekādaśī pertaining to the presence of the twelfth day on the third day is then enjoined.
That is untenable. For instance, in the passage concerning the "twelve-twelfths" (dvādaśa-dvādaśī), the word "householder" is not heard at all.

If it is argued that it is accepted as pertaining to householders (*gṛhastha*) for that specific reason because there is no other subject matter [for it], then why does it not pertain to ascetics (*yati*)? Or, if it is argued that since the Ekādaśī pertaining to ascetics is already enjoined by another scriptural statement, the present statement regarding the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) would become redundant—being incapable of producing valid cognition because it is delimited by that same nature [of being already established]—then [the following applies].

It is said in reply: Even for a householder (*gṛhastha*), then, the subsequent eleventh day (*uttara-ekādaśī*) cannot be enjoined because it would conflict with the preceding [eleventh day], since there is a contradiction defined by their mutual exclusion. Consequently, the production of valid knowledge (*pramiti*) is impossible, and the futility (*ānarthakya*) of the injunction remains as it was. If it is argued that, despite the contradiction, the statement regarding the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) possesses purposefulness because it acts as a sublater (*bādhaka*) due to being a specific injunction (*viśeṣa-vidhi*), we shall state that in that case there is no such thing as "specific injunction" at all. Or, even granting that it is a specific injunction, it still cannot be understood as such on the grounds of mere redundancy; for its purposefulness is possible precisely through its nature as a specific injunction, acting as a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) of the general rule regarding the subsequent eleventh day. For instance, the injunction of the subsequent eleventh day for an ascetic (*yati*) applies only to cases where the twelfth day exists thereafter, and not otherwise.

But surely there is inconsistency because of the contraction of what is being summarized in the concluding summary. Ah, but in the case of an exception (apavāda) as well, there is indeed inconsistency for that which is being excepted.

But surely, even if there is inconsistency in the statement regarding householders—on the grounds that the rule "if the twelfth [lunar day] does not exist" would otherwise become devoid of scope—an exception is nevertheless accepted.
Well then, for that very reason, there is a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) of the treatise on asceticism. [Objection:

But surely, in the case of an exception (*apavāda*), a great range of application is covered by both the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception; whereas in the case of a restriction, a limited scope of application results. [Reply: True, but what fault lies in having a limited scope? On the contrary, due to the brevity of the statement, it is actually an advantage. As for the objection that there is a sublation (*bādha*) because of the resulting contraction [of the rule], it has already been stated that this is no different even in the case of an exception.

Now, restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) is indeed that which is performed by a specific scripture upon a general scripture that has already been promulgated—for example, the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) taught without reference to a specific context, which is common to all archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛti-iṣṭi*), is restricted by the scripture concerning the number seventeen that pertains specifically to particular rites such as the *adhvarakalpa*. However, the statement regarding the twelfth day (*dvādaśīvākya*) is not a specific sub-rule within the scripture for ascetics (*yati*), because it is understood as being common to both ascetics and non-ascetics; how then can there be a restriction in this case? If that is so, then an exception (*apavāda*) also occurs through the relation of the general and the specific—for example, the rule "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire" is set aside by the rule "one offers in water. But the statement regarding the twelfth day is not a specific sub-rule within the scripture for householders (*gṛhastha*), since it is common to both householders and non-householders. A "specific" is defined as that which exists, as it were, outside the scope of the general; therefore, it does not function as an exception. If, however, due to the lack of any other recourse, one were to assume that the statement regarding the twelfth day pertains to a specific sub-domain of the householder scripture and thereby treat it as an exception, then alas! why is it not likewise accepted that it pertains to a specific sub-domain of the ascetic scripture and is thus treated as a restriction?

[Objection: "In the case of an exception (*apavāda*), since there exists a dual range of application for the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception, two sentences are meaningful; however, in the case of subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*), because the single subject matter is subsumed, it follows that the two sentences become meaningless. [Reply: True; even in the absence of a dual range of application, they are indeed meaningful because of the existence of two injunctions (*vidhi*). Nevertheless, the nature of that which is being subsumed is enjoined by one [sentence] as having the form of the subsumption itself.

Now, one might object: the general injunction "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas" is restricted by the specific rule "Let it be given to the Gargas. In that case, since the performance of the act occurs exactly as long as the specific rule for the Gargas exists—and even when the general rule for Brāhmaṇas exists, because it is subsumed solely within the domain of the Gargas—there is no performance of the giving of curd to the Gargas beyond what is already required. Therefore, the general rule regarding Brāhmaṇas would have little purpose. On the other hand, according to the view of exception (*apavāda*), curd is not established for Brāhmaṇas by the specific rule alone, nor is buttermilk obtained for Kauṇḍinya by the general rule alone. Therefore, both rules serve a purpose.

It is said: In the case of *upasaṃhāra* (reiteration), two scriptural injunctions (*śāstra*) are purposeful; by one, the curd is enjoined, and by the other, its connection with the Gargas. In the case of the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) and so forth, the connection of the seventeen-fold number with the *sāmidhenī* verses—which serve as its medium—is stated by a sentence necessarily studied independently (*anārabhyādhīta*). Therefore, both scriptural injunctions are purposeful. As for the claim that when a specific injunction exists, the performance lasts only as long as that [specific rule applies], and thus both [injunctions] would be rendered useless—this can be said even in cases such as "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). For instance, if one accepts the originative injunction (*utpattivihita*) "he performs the Agnihotra" and relies upon the qualified injunction "he offers with curd," then the performance would last only as long as that [originative act]; even if both are accepted through a distinction between the originative and applicatory injunctions (*viniyoga*), the originative injunction would result in being purposeless. Therefore, since multiple scriptures are established through individual injunctions, a heavy burden should not be placed upon a single head. On the contrary, the two scriptures, which imply distinct performances, attain their own utility. If that were the case, there would be parity [between the two]. Consequently, because it is impossible to determine either the exception (*apavāda*) or the reiteration (*upasaṃhāra*), and because the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would arise if the sentence were intended to convey both meanings, the sentence regarding the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) does not have this as its subject matter. Thus, it is established that for a householder, the eleventh day is always the earlier [limit], while for an ascetic (*yati*), the later [limit] is the one.

In that case, what is the subject matter of the statement regarding the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*)? To this we reply: for instance, when there is a doubt as to whether forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others should observe the fast on the preceding day, the following day, or both, it is settled that they should observe the following day if the twelfth day exists thereafter, and otherwise the preceding day. Thus, by enjoining a required matter, the sentence achieves its purpose; furthermore, the restriction of the other [general] rule becomes complete. This is the opinion of Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana: "Where the eleventh day is complete and recurs again at dawn..."
The Uttarā must be performed by all [the lunar days] if the twelfth day follows thereafter.
Thus, the statement that this is based on the non-observation of Nārada’s words is to be disregarded:
"If the eleventh day [Ekādaśī] is followed by the twelfth day [Dvādaśī],
then the twelfth day should be observed for fasting there, if one desires the supreme state."
"Viṣṇu" refers to the twelfth day (dvādaśī); the third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment, meaning "conjoined with the twelfth.
This is also stated in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"When the eleventh day is full and the twelfth likewise follows..."
On the following day, on the twelfth [lunar day], one should likewise perform the worship and other rites.

The *ekādaśī* that is incomplete and pierced by the tenth day (*daśamī*) is of three types: (1) when it is joined with the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) at the end of the night; (2) when it occurs on the following day with the *dvādaśī* still present; and (3) [the third type]. Among these, the first is to be observed as a fast by everyone. Thus says Nārada:
"The lunar day (*tithi*) of *dvādaśī* which is joined with the remainder of the tenth day is not to be observed as a fast."
If on the eleventh day, at the end of the night, the twelfth day is not seen;
If, by chance, three lunar days should coincide on the Ekādaśī,
then the merit of a hundred sacrifices shall accrue from breaking the fast on the Dvādaśī.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa as well:
"Where the Ekādaśī touches two [days], Hari is present there; one who is devoted to Viṣṇu, whether having desires or being desireless, should fast on that very day."
That Ekādaśī which touches both the tenth and the twelfth [lunar days] is called "dvispṛk" (touching two).
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"An Ekādaśī pierced by the tenth [day], and which does not increase on the following day..."
Whether by ascetics or householders, that very lunar day is to be observed at its conclusion.
The injunction for fasting on a pure twelfth lunar day (*śuddhadvādaśī*), even at the end of the day, pertains to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
Thus say Sumantu and Satyavrata:
"Even at the end of the day, a pure twelfth lunar day alone [is to be observed] by those desiring liberation."
The tenth day (Daśamī) when pierced [by the eleventh] should always be observed as a fast; the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) itself should never be so observed.
In the Śāradā-purāṇa:

"The twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast when it is pure; when there is a loss of a day (dinakṣaya) on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), those seeking liberation must not fast on the eleventh lunar day if it is pierced by the tenth (daśāviddhā)."

As for the statement in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "If the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) occurs as one that possesses three days, the first [day] therein is not to be fasted upon; rather, the subsequent one should be fasted."
By considering the preceding statement, that [rule] concerns one who seeks liberation.
But when the end of the day has arrived, and the two days are complete,
O King, a pure Dvādaśī should always be observed as a fast.
Thus, the statement in the Viṣṇupurāṇa also refers to that same subject.
In the Skandapurāṇa: "If even a single ghaṭikā of the tenth day is seen on the eleventh day..."
And when the lunar day Ekādaśī does not arrive on the second day.
On the lunar day that coincides with the rising of the thousand-rayed sun,
that very day should be observed by the wise as being conjoined with the tenth day.
O General, [the battle] should never be commenced when the lunar day (tithi) is waning, nor when it is waxing;
rather, when it is waxing, one should act against the enemy, but when it is waning, one should cause [the retreat] to be made first.
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, when death occurs at the end of the day, the Ekādaśī joined with the tenth is not to be observed;
rather, that meritorious sixth, eighth, or Ekādaśī [of the following day] should then be observed."
The meaning is: "if the thirteenth [lunar day] occurs on the twelfth.
Also in the *Nigama*:
"The sixth and the eleventh days should not be observed when overlapped by the preceding day."

Others, however, say that if on the following day the Trayodaśī is pure and there is no Dvādaśī at all, then because there is no "loss of a day" (dinakṣaya), the meaning of the statement containing the word "always" (*sadā*) is that one should fast on the Ekādaśī even when there is such a loss of a day, provided it is joined with the Daśamī. But when in this very same situation there is no Trayodaśī on the Dvādaśī, but rather the Dvādaśī lasts until its own sunrise, then the Ekādaśī pierced by the Daśamī is to be fasted upon. And so it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"When the Ekādaśī is pierced and the entire Dvādaśī occurs..."
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "If the Ekādaśī is not obtained [in its entirety], the Dvādaśī shall be complete.
This is the second half of these two verses.
The sage Uddālaka declared that the tenth day (daśamī) should be observed when it is pierced [by the eleventh];
however, if days not so pierced are not available due to prohibitions.
The lunar day (tithi) of Ekādaśī should be observed when it is pierced by five muhūrtas;
on other days, a wise person should fast when they are pierced by half of that duration.

However, this is not tenable, because in such a case the eleventh day is obtained on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). That is incorrect; for, by including the piercing caused by the rising of the *araṇa* on the tenth day within the fivefold piercing of the *muhūrta*, and because in a waning period consisting of five *muhūrtas* and six *ghaṭikās* there is an absence of the eleventh on the twelfth day and an absence of the twelfth on the thirteenth day, it follows—upon a careful consideration of the statements already cited and those yet to be mentioned—that even a [twelfth] joined with the tenth is logically eligible for acceptance. Therefore, one should not resort to such a strained interpretation.
Likewise:
"If on the day of the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇāha*), the twelfth [lunar day] is not obtained even by a single digit (*kalā*)."
At that time, even if it is pierced by the tenth day, the lunar day of Ekādaśī should be observed as a fast.
Hārīta also says:
When there is not even two *ghaṭikās* of the twelfth lunar day on the thirteenth,
that very lunar day— the tenth pierced by the eleventh— is always to be observed as the fast-day.
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"When the eleventh day is joined with the remainder of the tenth, one should fast on that Ekādaśī,
provided that there is not even a *muhūrta* of the *tithi* on the thirteenth day."
In another Smṛti:
"The sixth and likewise the eleventh [tithis] should not be observed when overlapped by the preceding day;
however, the eleventh should be observed even if overlapped, provided that the twelfth does not follow."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"When Ekādaśī is conjoined with Daśamī and one must fast upon it,
provided that Dvādaśī does not exist for three ghaṭikās on Trayodaśī."
In another Purāṇa: "If even a small portion of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) cannot be obtained on the thirteenth day,
one should observe the fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), even if it is mixed with the tenth day (daśamī)."
In another Smṛti:
"If one observes the fast on the tenth day because the twelfth is not obtained,
then even that which is mixed with the tenth is indeed the Ekādaśī that fulfills dharma."
If the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is very short and does not exist even slightly on the following day, it should be joined with the tenth day (daśamī); there is no fault in this, according to the Creator.
The word "statement" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*: "O Sage, when there is not even a moment of the twelfth day on the thirteenth day..."
The lunar day Ekādaśī should always be observed as a fast even when it is mixed with Daśamī.
Likewise:
"If, on the thirteenth day, there should not be even a single moment of the twelfth lunar day,
then the eleventh day conjoined with the tenth must be observed as the fast."
Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha also says:
"If on the following day there should be even a very small portion of the twelfth lunar day, it must be observed as mixed with the tenth;
it destroys even the greatest sins."
If even a mere measure of the rising sun on the following day constitutes the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) while it falls on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī),
then one should perform [the rite] on that which is joined with the remainder of the tenth lunar day (daśamī).
If the eleventh and twelfth lunar days overlap such that three days are diminished,
one should not perform the rite on the twelfth day when it is joined with the tenth day on the following day.
From the Purāṇa:
"When the tenth and eleventh [lunar days] are mixed, the eleventh should not be observed even if mixed;
however, it should indeed be observed even if mixed if one does not find the twelfth day."
If, when the time for breaking the fast has arrived after observing the fast, one does not find the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
then even if the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is pierced by the tenth day (daśamī), that very [eleventh] day partakes of merit.
Even if the Ekādaśī is pierced [by the preceding day], if the Dvādaśī is not obtained [the next day],

it destroys twelve Dvādaśīs if the fast-breaking (pāraṇa) occurs on the Trayodaśī. Regarding this, some maintain that the mention of "two muhūrtas" or "one ghaṭikā" is not intended to be definitive, because other scriptural statements declare, "even by a fraction" (kalayāpi cet) and "if even a tiny bit" (svalpam alpāpi cet).
Others, however, say that the statement "even by a *kalā*" refers to one who desires liberation; for it is said:
"O protector of the earth, that man who performs the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day consisting of two *kalās*, having fasted upon it, does not enter a womb again."
This is because of the indicative mark [of the scripture].

And regarding its universal applicability, Vasiṣṭha, the knower of dharma, has declared: "O King, when there is even a single digit of the twelfth lunar day on the thirteenth, that lunar day is considered complete."
Thus, by stating [the rule] in its entirety, there would be the consequence of redundancy, and the mention of "muhūrta" and so forth would have to be intended as significant.
Others, however,
[hold that it applies] from after the two parts of the day until midnight, or if [it occurs] at night.
This is the time for feeding the twice-born, with the exception of children, the elderly, and the sick.

Thus they explain that because the prohibition of daytime eating—which is obligatory for two *muhūrtas*—cannot be set aside by the rule of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) during the middle of the twelfth day (unless it is for a specific desire), it does not apply to the one-day fast on the eleventh day undertaken by one desiring liberation; rather, this [prohibition] applies only to those seeking liberation, and not to all cases involving the thirteenth day.
Furthermore, this refers to those other than householders who have sons; for a householder with sons, however, fasting is prohibited when the eleventh day is deficient. As it is said:
"He who observes a fast when the eleventh day is deficient..."
His sons perish, just like one who offers the funeral cakes during the Maghā constellation.
Nor should it be said that this prohibition concerns a fast occasioned by the *dinakṣaya* (the overlapping of two lunar days), for that would result in the word "Ekādaśī" being rendered meaningless.

Nor should it be said that this is intended to demonstrate an excess of fault, because no such excess of fault is mentioned; furthermore, since the *dinakṣaya* is established as the primary factor (*prakṛta*) by the statement of Jaimini or the statement of Kātyāyana, it is impossible for it to be referred to by the pronoun "this" (*saḥ*).
For it has been stated thus by Jaimini:
"On a Sunday, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
a householder who has sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast. This cited passage is a prohibition specifically regarding fasting undertaken for those specific occasions.
It should not be accepted as being produced by a secondary connection, because fasting is constant.
Kātyāyana also says:
"On the dark Ekādaśīs, likewise during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti),
and during lunar and solar eclipses, a householder who has sons should not perform [the rite]."
This prohibition is declared for one who has undertaken a fast prompted by that [specific motive];
for one who has undertaken it for any other reason, there is neither injunction nor prohibition.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) also said:
"He who observes a fast on the day when the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) ends,
his sons perish, just like one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) under the asterism Maghā."

But when the end of the day has arrived, one who desires prosperity and abundance for oneself, as well as for one's sons and grandsons, should not fast on a [Ekādaśī] that is joined with the tenth day.

Thus, for a householder who has a son, when the fast has been prohibited on the preceding day, the fast must take place on the pure twelfth day (*śuddhadvādaśī*) itself in order to avoid violating the vow. Vyāsa also says:
"If a householder is to fast when the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is diminished [by the overlap with the tenth],..."
Whether due to the absence of food, being confined, or especially through mere intention.
There is a loss of Dharma and the continuum is surely destroyed;
his lifespan constantly diminishes for a year, according to the sacred tradition.
Likewise:
"On the dark Ekādaśīs, as well as during the sun's transit (saṃkramaṇa),
a householder who has sons should perform neither the breaking of the fast nor the fast itself."
And so Gobhila says:
"O Brahmin, when on the eleventh day the lunar day falls at the end of the day,
then one should indeed abandon the eleventh day and observe the fast on the twelfth."
In that regard, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices for one who breaks the fast on the thirteenth day.
The Grandfather also said:
"O child, when on the eleventh day the lunar day (tithi) should coincide with the end of the day,
one should fast on that twelfth day, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"Whether at waning or waxing, when the end of the day has arrived,
the meritorious twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī)."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa as well:
"When the end of the day has arrived, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast;
one should never observe it when it is joined with the remnant of the tenth day."
Likewise:

"When there is an increase or decrease of the lunar day, or when a loss of a day occurs, and in cases where the statements are ambiguous, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day. Thus it is said.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"When the end of the day has arrived, the tenth lunar day joined with the eleventh (Daśamī-yuktā) must not be observed as a fast;
rather, the pure twelfth (Dvādaśī) should be fasted upon, and the breaking of the fast (Pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth."

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "When a loss of the lunar day occurs, one who desires his own welfare should observe the fast on the twelfth day and perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the thirteenth."
If Ekādaśī is lost, one should fast on Dvādaśī as well;
having fasted, one should worship Viṣṇu during both fortnights.

O King of kings, the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) is highly praised for recitation of mantras (japa), fire-offerings (homa), giving gifts (dāna), the satiation of Brahmins (tarpaṇa), and even for breaking a fast (pāraṇa);
so it is stated in the Kūrma, Nāradīya, and Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇas.
When the tenth day is pierced by even half a *kalā* of the eleventh day,
one should then abandon that eleventh day and observe the fast on the twelfth;
the fast is on the twelfth day, and the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) takes place on the thirteenth.
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"If the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) does not extend upward [into the next day], one should then take the Dvādaśī;
here, the fast is on the Dvādaśī, but the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the Trayodaśī."
Acting thus with devotion, a person shall attain union with Viṣṇu;
but he who acts otherwise certainly goes to hell.
When the Ekādaśī is pierced [by the preceding day] and does not extend even into the next [the Dvādaśī],
then the Dvādaśī should be observed as the fast-day, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī.
Likewise:
"The eleventh day belongs to the sages, while the twelfth belongs to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
When the eleventh day does not exist [as a full lunar day], then the twelfth is to be observed as a fast."
Likewise,
in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "In this case, the fast is on the twelfth day, while the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) is on the thirteenth."

Who, even by the power of the Vedas, would observe the Anandā when it is pierced by the previous day? And who, O dear one, on account of a Vedic injunction, would indeed slaughter a cow in the Gosava sacrifice?
What observer of the vow would undertake the vow on a day joined with the remainder of the tenth?
Therefore, the Ekādaśī joined with the remainder of the tenth should be abandoned;
the pure Dvādaśī should be observed as the fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī.
But when, in this very context, the thirteenth lunar day exists alongside the twelfth, then the fast is observed on the twelfth alone.
And so Vyāsa says:
"When the eleventh is lost and the twelfth follows after it..."
One should observe the fast on that twelfth day if one desires the supreme goal.

"Luptā" means that which has gone to destruction. "Parataḥ" means on the thirteenth day; that is the meaning. When the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is pierced by the tenth (daśamī) and reaches only the sunrise [of the next day], and there is no twelfth day (dvādaśī), while the twelfth day exists on the thirteenth, then the fast is to be observed on the pure twelfth day alone.
Thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"O King, the pure twelfth day is always to be observed as a fast."
The tenth day mixed with the eleventh should never be observed at all.
In the Padma Purāṇa as well:
"If the preceding Ekādaśī is contaminated by Daśamī, the following Ekādaśī shall be omitted;
in that case, one should fast on the Dvādaśī, and never on the Daśamī."
"And when the tenth day pierces the eleventh by even half a *pala*, one should indeed abandon that eleventh day and fast on the twelfth.
Thus it is stated; and also in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
When the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) arising from the preceding [eleventh] is not obtained [in its entirety],
tell me, how indeed should the fast be observed by human beings?
When the day of fasting is pierced by the preceding [tithi],
and on the second day there is not even a slight portion of the Ekādaśī lunar day,
how is the fast ordained in that case? Tell me that, O son of Sūta.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, when the preceding day is not obtained on the twelfth [tithi],
even if it is only half a *ravicakra* in measure, then the following day should be observed as the fast-day.
One should observe the fast on a pure twelfth day and conclude it on that very twelfth day,
even if a single digit or even two digits of the [new] thirteenth day have emerged.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days coincide, Hari is present there;
therefore, even if it is a pure [eleventh day], it should be observed by those who desire the fruit of the twelfth."
When the Ekādaśī is lost and the Dvādaśī follows,
one who desires the supreme state should observe the fast on that Dvādaśī.

[234] In this regard, the statement beginning with "yadi" (if) is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), because upon examining the collection of cited texts, it is understood that all [classes of people] must observe the fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). However, when the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is pierced by the tenth day (*daśamī*) and the twelfth day lasts only until sunrise—or is equal to or less than it—then for householders (*gṛhin*), the preceding day is the fast. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"If even a small portion of the twelfth day is not obtained on the day of breaking the fast (*pāraṇāha*)," etc.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: If on the day of breaking the fast, even a fraction of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) cannot be obtained, [then the fast is broken on the following day].
This refers to the latter half of these two verses.
At that time, having fasted on the Ekādaśī lunar day when it is pierced by the Daśamī,
[it is stated] in the Padma Purāṇa: "Even if the Ekādaśī is pierced, it should be accepted provided there is no Dvādaśī on the following day."
One destroys twelve twelfth days by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day.
Even if pierced [by the eleventh day], it should be known as unpierced if the twelfth day does not follow;
likewise, even if unpierced, it is pierced if the twelfth day follows.
Hārīta also says:
"When on the thirteenth there is not even two *ghaṭikās* of the twelfth,
and the tenth is mixed with the eleventh, then that lunar day alone is to be observed as a fast."
Also in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"Where the tenth overlaps the eleventh, that day should not be observed as a fast, for it destroys one's lineage.
That very day should be observed [as a fast] if even a single digit of the twelfth is not present."
In the future,
even if the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is but a single digit (kalā) long, and does not increase further,
that very lunar day (tithi) must be observed as a fast by householders and those who have sons.
Regarding this very subject, for an ascetic or one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the fast occurs only on the subsequent day.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"If the preceding [eleventh] day is mixed with the tenth, the following eleventh day shall be observed."
O highly wise one, how should the fast on the eleventh day be observed?
O King, the twelfth day alone, when pure, should be observed as a fast by those desiring liberation;
and the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day there would be equal to a hundred sacrifices.

Whenever the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is pierced by the tenth day (Daśamī), then those desiring liberation should fast on the pure twelfth day (Dvādaśī). The breaking of the fast (Pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day; therein, the fruit becomes inexhaustible.
Regarding these statements from the Kūrma and Padma Purāṇas:
"If Ekādaśī is overlapped by Daśamī on the preceding day and there is no Dvādaśī on the following day,
then Dvādaśī should be observed as the fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on Trayodaśī."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "If the eleventh lunar day is overlapped by the tenth and the twelfth does not increase,
then the twelfth should be observed as the fast-day, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth."

By reflecting upon those cited statements, it is understood that they concern those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). However, when the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) is pierced by the tenth (*daśamī*) and the twelfth (*dvādaśī*) exists until sunrise, and the twelfth also exists [at that time], then the second [day] alone is to be observed as a fast, being both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*).
And so says Nārada:
"O Lord of the Thirty-three Gods, where the eleventh is joined with the twelfth..."
Having fasted on that [twelfth day], one should then perform the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day.
The Skanda Purāṇa also states:
"Where there is even a single digit of the eleventh day (ekādaśī) and no twelfth day follows,
one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day."
And in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One tithi, when joined with the [preceding] smear (liptā), attains increase;
the twelfth [tithi] is for the purpose of the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa), and the preceding day is not to be observed as a fast."
Baudhāyana also says: "Where the eleventh lunar day is complete and there is no twelfth day thereafter,
one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day."
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"In all cases, the Ekādaśī lunar day should be observed as mixed with Dvādaśī,
whether or not Dvādaśī exists on the Trayodaśī."
Likewise: "In all cases, men should observe the Ekādaśī that is conjoined with Dvādaśī;
whether it occurs in the morning or not, for fasting is obligatory."
Also in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"O Lord of the Gods, when the eleventh lunar day is joined with the twelfth,
one should fast on that [eleventh] and then perform the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth."
Nārada said:

Where the eleventh day (ekādaśī) extends into the twelfth (dvādaśī), and the twelfth day continues beyond it as well, one should perform the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on the twelfth day; one shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Where the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is joined with the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), Hari is present there;
the merit of a hundred sacrifices is gained by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*)."

Also in the Padma Purāṇa: "O King, for one by whom the twelfth day (dvādaśī), conjoined with even a single digit of the eleventh day (ekādaśī), has been observed as a fast— what need is there there for many sacrifices, such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and others?"
When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days coincide, Hari is present there;
by fasting for a single night, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
(From the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*).
O Lord of the Thirty-three, when the eleventh lunar day is conjoined with the twelfth,
one should fast on that [eleventh] and then perform the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth.
If the eleventh day follows the twelfth and there is no thirteenth thereafter,
the twelfth day should be observed as a fast with devotion, and the breaking of the fast should indeed take place on the twelfth.
Moreover, in this manner, among the various [observances], only the second [lunar day] should be accepted, because of the prohibition of that which is pierced by the tenth.
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid that which is pierced by the previous [day]."

In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "O twice-born one, the third and the sixth lunar days should not be observed when overlapped by the preceding day; likewise, the eighth and the eleventh, by those who seek dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa."

In this context, it is understood that the Ekādaśī and other such days should be observed when overlapped by the following day (*paraviddhā*), because a specific prohibition implies permission for the remaining cases; otherwise, one would have to say "it should not be observed," rather than saying "it should not be observed when overlapped by the previous day" and "the Ekādaśī should be observed when overlapped by the following day.
Thus, Sumantu and Sanatkumāra state:
"The third, the Ekādaśī, the sixth, the fourth, and the fourteenth..."
The new moon day and the eighth day should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following lunar days.
In the Śāradā-purāṇa: "The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, the full moon, the fourteenth,
the third, the fourth, the new moon, and likewise the [other] eighth."
Those [days] connected with the following [tithi] should be observed as fasts; those connected with the preceding [tithi] should not be observed.
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"The eleventh, the sixth, the fourteenth in the bright fortnight,
as well as the third and the fourth— these should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day."

And when the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is pierced by the tenth day (daśamī), and a small portion of it remains on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), with the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) occurring at the end of the night, then for those other than householders, the fast is observed there.
Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa: "In that case, the eleventh day exists there conjoined with even a fraction of the twelfth day."
Even at the end of the day, that meritorious tenth day (daśamī) must by no means [be disregarded].
Where the eleventh day touches three [lunar phases], Hari is present there;
breaking the fast on the thirteenth day is said to yield the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa and other texts:
"When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days extend into the remainder of the night and the thirteenth day follows,
this fast is recommended, provided that the lunar day is honored in this manner."
When the eleventh, twelfth, and especially the thirteenth lunar days coincide, it is called Trispṛśā; it destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who always worships with devotion the Ekādaśī, Dvādaśī, and especially the Trayodaśī, that man rejoices in heaven.
Having fasted on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) which is joined with even a single digit (kalā) of the eleventh day (ekādaśī),
Viṣṇu is pleased with that man who eats on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī).
The eleventh, the twelfth, and especially the thirteenth [lunar days] are significant;
by breaking the fast on the thirteenth, one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices.

In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days [overlap] and the thirteenth remains at the end of the night, that lunar day is said to be mixed with three; it is remembered as the destroyer of all sins."
"Fasting observed on that day destroys all sins—
especially on the eleventh, the twelfth, and the thirteenth," so it is said in the Purāṇas.
If the eleventh, twelfth, and the remainder of that [thirteenth] lunar day coincide on the same day,
even when there is a loss of a day (*dinakṣaya*), it should be honored on the latter part of that very day.
In the Skanda Purāṇa as well:
"Wherever the lunar day Ekādaśī is conjoined with Dvādaśī, even if it occurs at the junction of two days (dinakṣaya), that [Ekādaśī] is to be honored; never one joined with Daśamī."
When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days extend into the remainder of the night and the thirteenth day follows, that Ekādaśī should be observed with great effort; it increases immense merit.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"Even if there is but a single digit (kalā) of Ekādaśī, and the Dvādaśī lasts for the entire day,
and the Trayodaśī occurs at the time of dawn— that triad of days belongs to Viṣṇu."
"It is declared in the Smṛti that this fast, which removes all sins, should be observed."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: When the Ekādaśī is joined with even a single digit [of the lunar day] and the Dvādaśī diminishes,
that lunar day is highly meritorious, destructive of all sins, and should be observed as a fast.
Sumantu: When the eleventh lunar day is joined with even a single digit [of the twelfth] and the twelfth is thus suppressed,
that Ekādaśī should be observed as a fast by those desiring liberation, and the second day [should be observed for breaking the fast].
In this regard, fasting is prohibited for a householder who has sons.
Likewise, in the Padma Purāṇa:
"When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days extend into the remainder of the night, and the thirteenth day [follows],"
Therefore, those seeking the Soma must not fast for a day and night that does not touch upon the three pressings.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: One should observe a fast on the eleventh, twelfth, and especially the thirteenth lunar days, being endowed with sons and grandsons.
If the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) and the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) overlap with the remainder of the night, and the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) follows,
then breaking the fast on the thirteenth day destroys twelve Dvādaśīs.

This also refers to that same subject. When there is a prohibition against fasting on that very day, Vṛddha-Śātātapa has prescribed *nakta* (eating only at night) as a substitute for the fast on that same day:
"When the tenth day pierces the eleventh and the twelfth day has gone to its wane—that twelfth day is to be known as 'waning' (*kṣīṇā*); in that case, *nakta* is ordained."
Pracetas says:
When the eleventh, the twelfth, and the remainder of that [thirteenth] lunar day coincide,
one should perform ritual bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and the formal address to the Brahmins.
"Having performed the rites of the twelfth day, one should then subsist on the *nakta* meal. Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"When the eleventh day is pierced [by the preceding day] and the twelfth day has come to an end..."
That twelfth day should be known as exhausted; on that occasion, the nakta fast is prescribed.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Where a fraction of Ekādaśī remains and Dvādaśī has come to an end, one should perform the nakta rite there; fasting is not prescribed for the householder."
In the Padma Purāṇa:

"When the twelfth day (dvādaśī) diminishes while even a single digit (kalā) of the eleventh day (ekādaśī) remains, that diminished twelfth day is to be known [as the time for fasting]; in that case, the nakta rite is prescribed."

Now, one might object: "The statement 'it should not be observed by those desiring sons' is a prohibition of fasting for those seeking sons—those who desire offspring—not for householders free from desire or those possessed of other desires.
That is incorrect; this is not a prohibition against the desire for sons, but rather:
"Wherever there is an Ekādaśī that possesses the three-fold contact (trispṛś), Hari is present there."

Since the aforementioned statements establish that fasting on that day applies universally to all without distinction, the phrase "it should not be fasted by those desiring sons" serves as a restriction for a specific class of persons. Furthermore, by the term "desiring sons," only householders are intended, as the desire for sons is possible only for them; thus, it does not apply to everyone who possesses a desire for sons. [As stated: "Even on a day of the conjunction of two lunar phases (dinakṣaya), that auspicious lunar day which is most excellent for ascetics (yatīs) [is to be observed]."

Since such excellence is thus predicated of the ascetic (*yati*) alone, there arises a doubt as to whether the word *yati* in that context refers to one who is devoid of the desire for a son, or whether the word *sutārthin* (one desiring a son) is intended to imply the possibility of such a desire. In this uncertainty, it should be understood that the word *sutārthin* itself is used to imply that possibility. For it is said:
"The householder should perform the *uttarā* fast and observe the *pūrvā* fast.
This applies to the householder in general.

"One should not observe a fast while endowed with sons and grandsons"—in order for these two statements to have a single meaning, it is appropriate that they refer exclusively to those related to sons; furthermore, since being "related to sons" is not possible except for a householder, this [term] depends upon that status. Since its purpose is fulfilled by this much alone, why should one accept a specific qualification that is not required by the injunction and which results in a syntactical split (vākya-bheda), such as:
"That day on which there are two lunar terminations (tithi-anta) in a single weekday shall be a *dinakṣaya* (day of loss)"?
In that [stage], there is bathing, recitation, and burnt offerings, but no fasting in the householder's stage of life.
Thus, because a prohibition is seen for every householder at the end of the day,
others, however, say:
"When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days [overlap] and the thirteenth remains at the end of the night..."
One who is endowed with sons and grandsons should not observe a fast.

From this statement, the general desire for offspring expressed by the phrase "by those desiring offspring" is further specified by the phrase "endowed with sons and grandsons. Even for one who already has a son, on the occasion of the *trispṛśā* [tithi], he should either observe a fast at night or consume some small amount of food;
however, when fasting is prohibited, he should partake of some food. He does not incur fault regarding the fast, and he shall obtain the fruit of the fast.
This is in accordance with such statements as these.

Others, however, say: "We accept the conclusion here, but not the preparation of food (*bhakṣaprakalpana*). This is because the general rule, "But when fasting is prohibited, there is food," is set aside by the specific rule that ordains *nakta* on the eleventh day during a lunar conjunction (*parvan*). Therefore, the preparation of food is to be understood as occurring elsewhere, and that is of many kinds: *nakta* may consist of sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*) or rice-free gruel (*anodana*).
Fruit, sesame, milk, water, and clarified butter—
these constitute the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); or even air alone is praised here, each subsequent one being superior to the preceding.

Others, however, say: "The injunction for fasting at night here refers to those with specific desires; thus, the optional fast is prohibited by the statement, 'Fasting is not for the householder. Where even a single digit of the eleventh day extends into the twelfth, there the twelfth is lost, and for those seeking merit, no fasting should take place."

Because of this statement, because of the prohibition against perpetual fasting, and because of the consequence of [logical] optionality (*vikalpa*); likewise, there would be a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) in that a rule is prescribed as optional with respect to householders who have sons (in view of the prohibition), while it is prescribed as obligatory with respect to others. However, since desire for a result proceeds from passion alone, a prohibition is appropriate; thus, there is no optionality and no lack of uniformity in the operation of the injunction. Furthermore, when an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is possible and logical, and fasting has been prohibited, it is proper to prescribe "eating at night" (*nakta*) in response to the expectation of what one who possesses desire should do.
And so it is.
Even if a single digit of Ekādaśī is lost where Dvādaśī occurs,
one who is free from desire and devoted to Viṣṇu should observe the fast there.
Thus, the statement is appropriate.

That, however, is incorrect, because fasting is prescribed even for those who desire the avoidance of sin, those who desire union with Viṣṇu, and those who seek liberation. [244] When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days extend into the remainder of the night, and the thirteenth day follows...
A lunar day (tithi) that is conjoined with three [other factors] is declared to be the destroyer of all sins;
a fast observed on such a day is the annihilator of even the greatest transgressions.
"O King, when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) coincides with a *dinakṣaya* tithi, one should observe a fast; thus one shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu.
In some versions, the reading is "one who desires union" (*sāyujyam icchata*).
"If the eleventh day (ekādaśī), the twelfth day (dvādaśī), and the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) extend to the end of the night,
a fast observed therein bestows liberation alone.
Likewise:
"However, at the end of the day, a fast must be observed by those seeking liberation.

Since this [rule] is prescribed even for one who desires specific results (*kāmya*), the state of the alternative remains as it was; for in that case, the characteristic of the injunction—namely, its tendency toward engagement—is avoided. Therefore, what has been stated previously is indeed superior.

Others, however, say: "The injunction for the night (*nakta*) here refers to the case of incapacity. Nor should it be argued that because incapacity is equal for both the *viddha* (pierced) and *aviddha* (unpierced) [dates], this specific occasional injunction regarding the *viddha* date would be inconsistent with the subject of incapacity; for in the case of the *viddha* date, a substitute fast (*pratyāmnāya*) consisting of a single meal (*ekabhakta*) and so forth is indeed perceived to be difficult to accomplish, since the injunction prescribes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for fasting at night: 'But one who observes the fast by not eating during the day, being composed, should worship the God at night and perform the formal resolve then.'"

The same time is appropriate for its substitution as well; however, that [time] is not the time for *ekabhakta* (the single-meal rite). For it is said: "That which is eaten according to rule once the half-day has passed is called *ekabhakta*; therefore, it must indeed be during the day."

[245] Thus, since this [fasting] is prescribed for the day itself, it follows that at that time [of the conjunction], it occurs only at night. It is correctly stated that this refers to an incapable subject; for, while there is a general prohibition against fasting for a householder with a son at the end of the day—and specifically at this particular "end of the day"—and while the possibility of consuming food might otherwise arise due to the lack of restriction, the sentence is appropriately explained in its straightforward sense as being intended to establish a restrictive rule by providing what was required. Therefore, exactly what has been said is correct. By this, the following is refuted:
"On the Ekādaśī, the twice-born man should likewise observe the *nakta* fast according to the rule."
Beginning from the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it is prescribed for one year.

Thus, because the injunction for a *nakta* fast on the waning of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī-kṣaya*)—as stated in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*—and the mention of "Ekādaśī" in the cited verse conflict with the injunction for fasting on the preceding day, the general rule is set aside by the specific rule. Furthermore, since the prohibition of fasting is logically consistent through the provision of what was required [by the context], and because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of subverting the Ekādaśī established by its own originative injunction, [the following applies]: "Where even a single digit (*kalā*) of Ekādaśī is followed by Dvādaśī, that day is meritorious even at the junction of two days (*dinakṣaya*); it is the most excellent lunar day (*tithi*) for ascetics (*yatins*)."

And here, the mention of "ascetics" (yatīnām) is not for the purpose of excluding others. For if that were the case, since there would be no possibility of [the practice] applying to a householder who has sons, the prohibition [against it] would be illogical. Therefore, this is intended merely to demonstrate the superiority of ascetics. That is incorrect; for by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even at the end of the day" (*dinakṣaye ’pi*), it is shown that for ascetics, the second [lunar day] is also excellent even apart from the end of the day. As for the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"The sixth, eleventh, and eighth [tithis] should not be observed when overlapped by the preceding day;
however, one should observe the eleventh if the twelfth is diminished.
This statement refers to persons other than those desiring purity, those desiring union with Viṣṇu, and those seeking liberation (mumukṣus), in accordance with the cited scriptural passage.
[246] If the days are not pierced by prohibited [muhūrtas], they are indeed unobtainable;
however, the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) should be accepted even if it is pierced for five muhūrtas.
A wise person should fast on other days that are pierced by half of that [duration].
"By forbidden [days]" refers to the tenth and others; "unpierced" refers to the eleventh day and subsequent days.
If the eleventh and twelfth days extend into the remainder of the night and the thirteenth day begins, one who is endowed with sons and grandsons should not observe the fast.
When the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) and the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) touch the remainder of the night, and the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) follows,
such that it spans three days, one who desires a son should not fast during that day and night.

The meaning of such statements is that [the Ekādaśī] is not obtained as something to be observed (*upoṣya*), nor is it obtained in its own essential form (*svarūpa*). As for the interpretation made by some—that on the occasion of the loss of the twelfth day (*dvādaśīdinakṣaya*), a householder should observe the obligatory (*nitya*) Ekādaśī even if it is pierced by the tenth day (*daśamīviddhā*)—that is improper because there is no reason for such a restriction. Prohibitions against fasting on a pierced Ekādaśī will be cited below.
Among them, in the *Vāsiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"Where the tenth and eleventh days coincide, a wise man should not fast there."
One's offspring perish, and one does not go to the heavenly world.
In the *Vratākhaṇḍa* of the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Having fasted on the eleventh day out of delusion when it is joined with the remainder of the tenth day,
a man does not attain happiness in this world nor in the next."
Questioned by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Maitreya spoke to the lord of men regarding that for which they longed, which was the separation from their sons and from their wife.
O King, previously you, together with your wife, observed the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) when the tenth day still remained; this is considered the reason for this.
Therefore, O best of men, it is proper that the Ekādaśī be joined with the Daśamī;
one should strive not to perform it otherwise, for if the Dvādaśī is lost, it is fruitless.
And just as the eleventh day, O King, and the twelfth day are equal for men,
so too are they declared to yield the same fruit in this vow of the Discus-bearer.
I am neither a wanton wife nor am I unfaithful to my husband;
there is no impurity here by which some sin from another birth might be suspected.
Having heard the words of Rāma’s wife, Vālmīki, the bull among sages,
meditated for a long time and then spoke these words to her, O Great King.
O Goddess, having fasted on the tenth day preceding the eleventh, Janārdana was worshipped by you; this is the fruit of that deed.
The pure Ekādaśī should be observed as a fast; that which is joined with Daśamī should not be fasted upon.
By doing so, one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī.
Being thus questioned by the wife of Māndhātṛ, Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Goddess, the tenth and eleventh lunar days were formerly observed as fasts by you."
"Know this to be the truth, O devoted wife: by that very karma, you have now experienced separation from your husband, sons, and kinsmen."
Whatever sins may arise here in the three worlds,
the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) together with the tenth day (Daśamī) is indeed considered their bath.

The merit accumulated over seven lifetimes is destroyed; there is no doubt about this. Where the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is followed by the tenth (daśamī), there is the destruction of one's offspring, and moreover, one goes to hell.
The eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) that is pierced by the tenth (daśamī) should never be observed as a fast;
by fasting on such a day, a person loses the merit accumulated over a hundred years.
Likewise: "If one fasts on the eleventh day when it is pierced by the tenth, his lifespan is constantly diminished; this I, Nārada, declare."
Truly, truly, the lineage would perish, and not otherwise,
where the eleventh lunar day follows the tenth;
in that case, there would be the destruction of offspring, and thereafter, hell.
Likewise: "If the tenth and eleventh lunar days are joined even for a single moment,
a man who fasts on that [eleventh] out of delusion falls away from happiness and from dharma."
In the Kūrma and Nāradīya Purāṇas, as well as in the Viṣṇurahasya, it is said:
"By fasting on the eleventh day when it is joined with the remainder of the tenth,
a man is indeed liberated here from the merit accumulated throughout an entire year."
O Gāndhārī, if the fast is observed on the day joined with the remainder of the tenth lunar day, one's hundred sons are lost; therefore, one should avoid it.
Also in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"The fool who observes [the fast] when it is joined with the remainder of the tenth day,
his fruit from twelve years' practice of Ekādaśī shall be destroyed."
Those men who, through the delusion of ignorance, have observed the Daśamī-viddhā [Ekādaśī],
have gone to a terrible hell for nineteen yugas.
In the *Sauradharmottara*: "Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should then observe this twelfth day;
or one may observe it when mixed [with the eleventh], but never when joined with the tenth."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One who desires the continuity of his lineage should avoid even a full Nandā that is pierced by the preceding [tithi] by even half a pala,
according to all four rules."
One who desires prosperity should not observe a fast, nor keep a night-vow, nor eat only one meal, nor practice the ayācita vow on the Nandā tithi when it is overlapped by the previous day.
Also in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"If a remnant of the tenth day should still exist on the eleventh,
that lunar day is to be known as complete, being mixed with the time of the tenth."

Just as a jar filled to the brim with the water of the Gaṅgā would become entirely intoxicating liquor if it were joined with even a single drop of wine, so too would that entire [Ganges water] turn into liquor.
What man of deluded intellect would drink the fierce halāhala poison?
What observer of virtuous vows would fast on a day joined with the remainder of the tenth lunar day?
Knowing this, O best of sages, the day joined with the remainder of the tenth [lunar day] is avoided by all sages who desire Vāsudeva.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "O best of Brahmins, even when there is a *lava* (one-sixtieth of a minute) of overlap, if the tenth day extends into the eleventh,
one should completely abandon it, just as one avoids the water of the Gaṅgā when it is touched by a drop of liquor."
[250] During the dog's season, one should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); on the tenth day, one should abandon those who are defiled. Likewise:
"By fasting on the eleventh day conjoined with the tenth, one would remain childless."
The eleventh day mixed with the tenth destroys the merit produced by the eleventh day.
Kauśika says: "The tenth [lunar day] pierced by the eleventh destroys the sovereignty of the gods. Paiṭhīnasi says:
If the sixth lunar day is pierced by the seventh (Nāga), or the seventh by the eighth (Śiva),
or the tenth by the eleventh, a wise man should not observe a fast on those days.
Vārṣāyaṇi says:
An Amāvāsyā pierced by the tenth [tithi], or joined with the tenth and eleventh,
or pierced by the tenth, destroys all previously accumulated merit.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa as well:
"O Brahmins, wise men avoid this pierced Ekādaśī;
one who fasts on that day goes to poverty and indeed to suffering."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, Gāndhārī, who increases the Kuru lineage,
shall become the commander of the army, O Śikhidhvaja, due to her deluded state."
By that [act], her hundred sons will undoubtedly meet their destruction.
Thus, O Lord, Nandā should not be observed when joined with the tenth day;
even if a single digit or fraction of the tenth day is seen,
O General, Ekādaśī should never be observed [on such a day].
These statements refer to cases other than the permission for a pierced Ekādaśī. Kautsa also says:
"A certain woman, having fasted on a day pierced at the time of dawn..."
Her hundred sons were lost; therefore, one should avoid her.
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"If the tenth lunar day is seen at the time of sunrise,
the eleventh day should not be observed on that occasion, for it destroys virtue, desire, and wealth."
Likewise: "If the tenth lunar day is seen at the time of sunrise,
fasting on the eleventh day should always be declared to be the root of sin."
Likewise:
"O King, if at sunrise there should be even a mere trace of the tenth day,
one must observe it with great effort and avoid [the following day]."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa, the words of Mohinī: Mohinī said:
"When the sun rises having taken up the end of the tenth [lunar day]..."
That day of Hari, touched by him, was indeed given away to the Asura.
Indeed, that which is visible [on the ninth] but devoid of sunrise, and that which is visible but light [in duration],
they bestow [the merit of the fast] up to the tenth, provided it is touched by the day of Hari.
At the time of Agni’s installation, likewise during the bride’s attendance,
at the morning milking, and similarly upon the perception of birds;
At the conclusion of all the deities' rites, there is likewise the taking up of the broom;
so too at the time of opening the door when the hour for bathing has arrived.
When the sound of musical instruments is raised by ascetics and those initiated for sacrifice,
and where the tenth lunar day is overlapped by the eleventh—
if you have compassion for me, let a place be given for my residence.
I do not beg for the rising of the gods, nor do I beg for that day of Hari;
O best of deities, let the rising of Vainateya be granted to me.
O gods, those who have been scorched by the sage and those whose wealth has been exhausted—
let this remote forest be granted for the sake of rest and for the sake of contentment.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O lord of the earth, having heard those words of Mohinī, all the gods,
led by Digambara, deliberated for a very long time.
Indeed, for the purpose of establishing Yama, for the destruction of Vaikuṇṭha,
for the sake of showering heretics, and for the generation of sin.
O King, when Ekādaśī extends for three ghaṭikās prior to sunrise,
the gods— having placed Indra and the other deities at the forefront—
spoke to Mohinī indeed for the sake of maintaining the world’s perception.
O Mohinī, this place has been granted to you until the time of dawn;
it is indeed forbidden on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) and must end precisely at the conclusion of the tenth lunar day.
But this [place], favored by that Jambha, is not [attainable] even by gods or by men.
The sense is that one should abandon [the night] at the time of dawn (*aruṇodaya*). Dawn is also described in the Purāṇa:
"Four *ghaṭikās* in the morning are called dawn; for ascetics (*yatins*), this time for bathing is remembered as being equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā. Thus it is said.

By the phrase "the time for bathing for ascetics," it is implied that the four *ghaṭikās* prior to sunrise constitute the dawn (*aruṇodaya*). These prohibitory statements regarding dawn should be understood as referring to cases where even a small portion of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is seen on the twelfth day, and a small portion of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is seen on the thirteenth day; in such instances, [the eleventh day] must be abandoned. Alternatively, they pertain to the optional (*kāmya*) vow of the eleventh day. As stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"One who desires merit should avoid what is called a 'doubtful eleventh day' (*saṃdigdha-ekādaśī*)."
For the sake of the prosperity of one's sons and kingdom, one should observe a fast on the twelfth day;
by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
When the eleventh lunar day extends for one muhūrta before sunrise, it is called "Saṃyuktā Ekādaśī"; one should avoid it for the increase of dharma.
For the sake of increasing one's sons and grandsons, one should observe a fast on the twelfth lunar day;
by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
The complete Ekādaśī, beginning from the time of sunrise and lasting for sixty nāḍikās, must be observed by those who desire the fruits of dharma.
For the sake of the prosperity of sons and grandsons, one should observe a fast on the twelfth day;
if the breaking of the fast occurs on the thirteenth day, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
Kāṇva also says:
If the tenth lunar day coincides with the time of dawn,
one should fast on that twelfth day, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day.
Also in the *Purāṇa*:
"If, at the time of sunrise, the tenth day is joined [to the eleventh],
even by a mere half-measure of the sun's orb, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day."
In that regard, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day.
Gobhila says:
"If the tenth lunar day coincides with the time of dawn,
the Lord gave that Ekādaśī conjoined with it to Mohinī."
Viṣṇu said: When the tenth lunar day extends over the eleventh from sunrise,
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, gave it [as a fast] for the sake of pleasing the Dānavas.
Therefore, one should avoid the full Ekādaśī according to the most ancient tradition;
here, the fast is observed on the Dvādaśī, while the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) takes place on the Trayodaśī.
Also in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"When doubt arises due to the contradiction of many statements,
then the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is to be accepted, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day."
When the end of the day has arrived, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast;
one should never observe it when it is joined with the remainder of the tenth lunar day (daśamī).

These [rules] pertain exclusively to the optional Ekādaśī fasts. Accordingly, in those various scriptural passages, fruits such as "desiring merit" and "for the sake of the prosperity of sons and grandsons" are heard. Alternatively, the prohibitory statements regarding fasting on an Ekādaśī pierced by Aruṇodaya (the dawn) refer to Vaiṣṇavas; however, for Śaivas and others who have the authority to fast on Ekādaśī, there is no fault in fasting at that time. And so it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"If the Aruṇodaya should be joined with the remainder of the tenth day..."
A follower of Viṣṇu should not perform that Ekādaśī vow on that day.
The Determination of the Optional Ekādaśī, from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, in the section on Ekādaśī, regarding the censure of the piercing by the dawn (aruṇodayavedha).
Śaunaka said:
"O Sūta, please describe in detail the vow of Ekādaśī."
By which, when performed, there shall be the pacification of all the sins of men.
O Sūta, tell us what kind of Ekādaśī should be observed, how it should be observed, how Hari is to be worshipped, and what the fruit thereof shall be.
And for the sake of attaining the fruit of the vow, the ritual of its conclusion (udyāpana) must be performed;
therefore, O Sūta, tell all of that now as I listen.
Sūta said: In former times, Śūra, the father of Vasudeva, asked this very matter of the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, according to your own opinion.
Śūra said:
O Vyāsa, you have indeed described the Vaiṣṇava duties that grant liberation to human beings;
among all of them, you have declared the Dvādaśī vow to be the most important.
Of what nature is it, how is it to be performed, what is its fruit, and whose worship is to be practiced?
Tell us all this, for you are indeed my intellect.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, Vyāsa replied with an answer to that descendant of the Yadu clan; I shall relate that exactly as it was spoken, so listen to it, O Śaunaka.
Vyāsa said:
O hero, even if it is perfectly pure and free from thorns, a fast observed by one who possesses malice leads to the downfall of the performer into hell.
If it is observed with malice, even that which is otherwise virtuous results in the sinner's fall to the nether regions.
Whatever lunar day (tithi) may exist, even if it is but a small portion, at the time of sunrise, it should be considered full; it does not become abundant without sunrise.
If, in that case, the piercing of the tenth lunar day (daśamī-vedha), or even its excessive piercing (ativedha),
or a conjunction for a great piercing (mahāvedha) occurs, it will be fruitful for the Rākṣasas.
Therefore, this "thorn of the tenth day" must be abandoned on the twelfth day,
after those skilled in the movements of the moon and sun have properly purified the six-day period.
Therefore, those who possess arrows [of defilement] should be avoided by wise men seeking dharma, wealth, and pleasure;
likewise, even those who are free from arrows should be avoided.
When the faction advances to the forefront and attains growth.
Those expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas have declared that "piercing" (vedha) is a thorn;
it should be abandoned from afar, just as one would avoid the water of the Gaṅgā mixed with a drop of liquor.
Four *ghaṭikās* in the morning are called the dawn (*aruṇodaya*);
this is known as the time for ascetics to bathe, equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā.
They say that the night consists of three watches, excluding the four nāḍīs at its beginning and end;
those two twilights are designated as the beginning and end of the day.
They say that [a day] devoid of the piercing of the first tithi is "Asurī" and should be observed as a fast;
conversely, the three days characterized by the Asurī nature must be abandoned.
Nandā occurs in the morning, Bhadrā at midday, and Jayā at the end;
thus the three periods of the day belong to the gods. When the thirteenth day arrives, if the twelfth is obtained, then Nandā and Bhadrā belong to the asuras.
One destroys twelve twelfth days by breaking the fast on the thirteenth.
When the thirteenth day arrives, if the twelfth day remains for even a single moment,
then breaking one's fast on that thirteenth day yields the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
If the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) is passed over by men without the observances of fasting, it robs them of their merit;
and likewise, the Sarasvatī [robs one of merit] when one fails to bathe in her.
Therefore, one should observe Bhadrā when it begins on the day of Nandā and ends on the day of Jayā;
and on the full-moon day, one should by no means observe Nandā when it begins on the day of Bhadrā.
But those deluded sinners on earth who deceive others by means of false speech shall find refuge for a long time in Raurava.
Those of alienated intellect teach without understanding;
the ignorant in this world cause the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) to be observed when it is joined with the tenth (daśamī).
Those who cause the Dvādaśī to be observed, or observe it when it is joined with the Daśamī, should, for the sake of purification, look at its face and then gaze upon the sun;
or they should mutter the twelve-syllable mantra: "Namo Nārāyaṇāya."
When a sin has been committed, for that man in whom remorse indeed arises,
