the one supreme expiation is the constant remembrance of Hari.
How can these wretches possibly understand the concerns of living beings?
Fie on those evil ones of deluded intellect who cause the destruction of the Dharma!
The Blessed One has been violated by him who has made the twelfth lunar day joined with the tenth;
this has been correctly explained to you by me, O best of the twice-born.
Since the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa abides assuming the form of the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
therefore, without doubt, the twelfth day joined with the tenth (daśamī) must be abandoned.
Nandā is the body of the Lord, while Bhadrā is indeed the unborn and imperishable Self;
therefore, having abandoned the diseased limb, one should fasten the Self.
Having heard the dispute between two people, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day;
the breaking of the fast, however, should take place on the thirteenth—this is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
If a scripture establishes that the twelfth day is joined with the tenth,
I do not consider that to be a scripture, even if Brahmā himself were to speak it.
Behold the kind of audacity shown by those committing sins here;
how can they cause other foolish and wretched beings to do the same?
The twelfth day (dvādaśī) pierced by the tenth (daśamī) was fasted upon by Gāndhārī;
her hundred sons were destroyed. Therefore, one should avoid it.
For some, even at midnight, piercing by the tenth lunar day is desired;
at the time of dawn, there is no room for deliberation.
The teachers who are dear to Hari say that this is "piercing the skull" (kapālavedha);
that is not my opinion, because the night is held to consist of three watches (yāmas).
Therefore, the morning alone is the divine means for accomplishing dharma;
they say it is the primary [time], and thus renunciation and piercing [the vital point] therein are certain.
Sūrya said:
O best of Brahmins, what kind of piercing (*vedha*) might there be, and what kind of conjunction (*yoga*)?
Explain both piercing and conjunction, as well as their defective fasts (*upoṣaṇa*).
Śrī Vyāsa said:
O Sūrya, four ghaṭikās constitute the determination of dawn (aruṇodaya);
herein, the fourfold division beginning with piercing (vedha) has indeed been declared.
The *arayodaya-vedha* (the piercing by the rising of the sun) lasts for three and a half *ghaṭikās*;
the *ativedha* (excessive piercing) lasts for two *ghaṭikās*, beginning from the appearance of the sun's light.
Even the Great Piercing (mahāvedha) is seen there alone; the sun is not seen.
This yoga is prescribed as the fourth by the wise at sunrise.
The *yātudhānavrata* is for the *yoga*; the *mahāvedha* is for the *bāṣkala*;
the *ativedha* is for the demon Jambha; and *mohinī* is for the *vedhaleśinī*.
Indeed, whatever day of Hari was defiled by the tenth [lunar day] was formerly given to Mohinī by the gods; it is the reverse of that [which is pure].

It is better to abandon Ekādaśī than to perform it when joined with Daśamī; O Sūrya, this is my firm resolve. It is not auspicious if it is performed when even a portion of Daśamī remains—so what need is there for further words?

Having deliberated thus with those who are skilled, one should avoid the Ekādaśī that is pierced by the Daśamī during the increase of the fortnight— even if there is no Dvādaśī [the following day], and even if there is no Trayodaśī [the day after]. When the moon is waning, however, one should observe the Ekādaśī joined with the Daśamī.
According to this scriptural authority, even if the new moon or full moon occurs on the first day (pratipad), the twelfth lunar day alone is pure; however,
if there is a loss of a lunar day (tithi-hāni) and the Ekādaśī is "pierced" (saśalyā),
then the pure Dvādaśī should be observed for fasting, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī.

Accordingly, it should be observed; even if it is "devoid of a thorn" (*vihīna-śalyā*), it must be avoided if "the fortnight attains growth at the outset. Although this is a Smṛti rule, nevertheless, because the qualifying phrase "if the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī" would otherwise be inexplicable, and because the word *vihīna* can also mean "completely free from a thorn," [it follows that]: "If days not pierced by forbidden [times] cannot be obtained, then the Ekādaśī lunar day, even if pierced by five *muhūrtas*, must indeed be accepted."

Thus, even though a lunar day (*tithi*) is pierced by more than ten *ghaṭikās*—in contrast to the ten *ghaṭikās* prescribed in the traditional rules (*smṛti*) for permitting a "pierced" (*viddha*) day when there is no gain from the "unpierced" (*avidddha*)—it must still be avoided; this is how it should be explained.
And this very [rule applies]:
"If both the new moon (*darśa*) and the full moon (*pūrṇamāsa*) increase while being complete..."
"O best of kings, on the second day, that [lunar day] shall be a Pakṣavardhanī;
thus it is declared.
Now follows the description of the eightfold divisions beginning with the Unmīlinī.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "The vow of Ekādaśī is remembered as the most excellent of all vows;
I shall now fully describe it—listen to it at once."
This is the supreme purification for men from both dry and moist sins;
the wise know its essential nature to be superior even to bathing at sacred pilgrimage sites.
This is the essence, this is the truth, this is the reality, this is the vow;
this fasting on the eleventh day is the perfect expiation.
O best of the twice-born, a distinction regarding the twelfth days (dvādaśīs) is to be understood there;
eight are well-known, so listen to them as they have been described.
Unmīlanī, Vañculī, Trispṛśā, Pakṣavardhanī,
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī—
these eight twelfth days, O twice-born one, are highly meritorious and destroy all sins.
Likewise, four others are born through conjunction with lunar days (tithi);
by conjunction with lunar mansions (nakṣatra), they pacify powerful evil.
But when Ekādaśī is complete and increases once again, O best of the Bhṛgus, it is called Unmīlanī; it is said to be the destroyer of sins.
Fasting on the twelfth day and breaking the fast on the twelfth day itself—that is called Vañculī; it destroys ten thousand murders.
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) begins at sunrise and lasts for the entire day,
ending with the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) at dawn, that "Trispṛśā" is dear to Hari.
When the eleventh day (ekādaśī) has reached its full increase during the fortnight, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), setting aside the eleventh.
The eight twelfth days, when respectively conjoined with the lunar mansions Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī, and observed as fasts, yield equal fruits individually.
O Bhārgava, that first [confluence] purifies even the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
the second, called Vañculī, destroys ten thousand killings.
The Trispṛśā, when observed, dries up the four great sins;
the Pakṣavardhanī brings about the destruction of all impurities without exception.
Jayā, Vijayā, Pretamokṣā, and likewise Aparā Jayantī—
these deliver even those who have committed evil deeds from hell.
But the eighth day, O best of the Bhṛgus, is the destroyer of great sins.
Sins and the unbearable torments of Yama inflict suffering upon living beings in their bodies only so long as they have not undertaken this vow of Unmīlanī.
Whatever gift is given here, and whatever oblation is offered here,
the great seers declare all that to be inexhaustible in Unmīlinī.
[262] On the day when Vañculī arrives, the one whose banner bears Garuḍa comes from his own abode to the earth and accomplishes the desires of the people.
Beholding the mortal turned away from the *vañculī* tree, the son of the Sun,
filled with joy, enters into consultation with Citragupta.
"This dull-witted man, excluded from the vows of Viṣṇu, shall come under my power;
therefore, let him today wipe away the merit he has previously acquired."
In this very month, a severe headache assails them;
yet even those who have committed evil deeds go to heaven if they are devoted to Viṣṇu.
Twelve such twelfth days have been declared by those expert in the Purāṇas; even one of them, when observed, destroys previously committed sin,
while the same, when practiced in the opposite manner, destroys previously acquired merit.
O best of the Kurus, the day of Hari arrives with a vast expansion of merit during the bright fortnight, accompanied by special vows.
If even that which has arrived is abandoned by those excluded from merit,
then this very nectar, once obtained, slips from the hand in an instant.
Dharma is directly Janārdana in the form of Ekādaśī;
they say that the Vañculyunmīlinī vow is equal to his very body.
Abandoning Vañculī, the wicked will observe another lunar day;
and, O King, living beings with the eyes of the sun do not perceive this.
Fie on those base people who consider themselves wise, for they make of themselves a pit for all living beings by their own arbitrary decisions.
Those ignorant rationalists who cause [images] to be made while transgressing the scriptures—
without a doubt, the sin committed by that act goes to them.
Having become free from pride and following the scriptures, one should instruct them correctly; one must not act with a defiled intention.
The practice of all vows, bathing at all sacred fords,
and the giving of all gifts are equal to the Vañculī vow.
In that regard, by offering food to a Brahmin endowed with faith according to the prescribed rite,
a pure Brahmin attains the presence of Kṛṣṇa many times over.
There, one should worship the golden deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
by giving gifts of food according to one's capacity, one shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
A *vañculī* performed with devotion destroys the sins of three generations;
such indeed is the meaning of all the scriptures for all wise and virtuous people.
All that is beneficial and correct is contained in the vow of Vañculī:
fasting according to one's ability, giving gifts, and honoring Brahmins; by performing the Vañculī vow in this manner, a person attains a good rebirth.
Thus, having described in detail the greatness of the eighty-one [Ekādaśīs] beginning with Unmīlinī, it is concluded:
"In this way, this Ekādaśī vow indeed rests upon all excellent qualities and dharmas, and is truly endowed with its proper cause."
But he who, endowed with the scriptures, further purifies that which is dear to Hari, attains liberation.
Thus ends the determination of the eight types beginning with the *unmīlinī*.

Others, however, say: "When the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) exists following [the eleventh], the fast for all is on the pure (*śuddha*) twelfth; but in its absence, it is on the pierced (*viddha*) eleventh.
And so says the Śruti:

One should avoid the Ekādaśī that is pierced by the Daśamī during the waxing of the fortnight; when the moon is in its waning phase, one should observe the fast on the Ekādaśī even if it is joined with the Daśamī. "Laṅghayet" means "one should fast."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "If the eleventh day is overlapped by the tenth and the twelfth day occurs on the following day,
then that twelfth day should be observed as the fast, for it is the means of accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha."
That is incorrect, because even in the absence of a [thirteenth] twelfth day following it, the fast is prescribed on a pure (śuddha) twelfth day;
and so it is stated in the Kūrma and Padma Purāṇas:
"If the eleventh is pierced by the tenth, but there is no twelfth day following it..."
Having fasted there on the twelfth day, one should break the fast on the thirteenth day.

Other statements concerning this same subject have also been shown previously. Nor does this collection of statements refer to an Ekādaśī that is joined with the next day [the Dvādaśī], because of the statement: "One should fast on that Dvādaśī. For it would be more appropriate to say that the second Ekādaśī is to be accepted, rather than saying "Dvādaśī.
Some, however, claim that this collection of statements refers to the subject of renunciants (saṃnyāsins);
that is weak, as there is a lack of evidence. Nor...

"O King, the pure twelfth day alone is to be observed as a fast by those desiring liberation; the breaking of the fast, however, should be on the thirteenth day"—this statement is the authoritative proof. For by this statement, the fast on the pure twelfth day is not prescribed for renunciants (*sannyāsins*) specifically, but rather for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣus*). Nor is there a rule that only renunciants seek liberation. Furthermore, the fast on the pure twelfth day is also prescribed for Kṣatriyas and others.
"By Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—what else do you wish to hear?
By these words, it follows that the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) of Śūdras and others is not possible there. Furthermore, even for ascetics (yatins), the fast on Ekādaśī pierced by Daśamī is prescribed:
"Ekādaśī pierced by Daśamī does not increase on the following day."
That lunar day alone should always be observed as a fast-day by both householders and ascetics.
Thus, according to the statement of the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

Others, however, say that [the injunctions] regarding fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) pierced by the dawn (*aruṇodaya-viddha*) concern that specific case; that the prohibitions concern cases where it is pierced after that time; and that the injunctions for fasting on a pure twelfth day (*śuddha-dvādaśī*) concern those instances.
That is weak, because the prohibitions against fasting on an eleventh day pierced by the dawn have already been cited above.

Others, however, say that when the *śravaṇa* asterism occurs on both a pierced (*viddha*) Ekādaśī and a Dvādaśī, then the prohibitions against fasting on the pierced Ekādaśī and the injunctions for fasting on the pure (*śuddha*) Dvādaśī apply; whereas the injunctions for fasting on the pierced Ekādaśī refer to other instances of Ekādaśī. This is because, when the *śravaṇa* asterism falls on an unpierced Ekādaśī, there is an injunction to fast on the pure Dvādaśī. Thus, it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "When the *śravaṇa* asterism likewise occurs on an unpierced Ekādaśī, the meritorious Dvādaśī is to be observed as a fast; Hari is the deity for both."
In the *Skandapurāṇa*,
the fourth quarter of the verse is recited as follows: "Even when a scriptural debate has arisen."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "If Ekādaśī is pierced by Daśamī and Śravaṇa occurs likewise, one should fast on the Dvādaśī; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī."
Furthermore, the inclusion of such a passage within the section on the Ekādaśī fast would be purposeless.

Others, however, maintain that fasting on a pierced (viddha) Ekādaśī applies specifically to the case of a day-decrease (dinakṣaya), whereas elsewhere, fasting on a pure (śuddha) Dvādaśī applies to the case of a day-decrease; they argue that on a pure Dvādaśī, except when there is a day-decrease, one should fast [on the Ekādaśī] according to the statement, "it is joined with the tenth.
That too is incorrect, because it has already been shown that even when there is a day-decrease on Ekādaśī, the injunction for fasting on a pure Dvādaśī is established.

Others, however, say: "The collection of statements such as 'even if the Ekādaśī is pierced' is for the purpose of praising the pure Ekādaśī when there is no Dvādaśī on the following day. [The meaning is: 'If there is no Dvādaśī on the following day, even a pierced [Ekādaśī] should be accepted, how much more so one that is not pierced. Thus, even in the absence of having to postulate another root text, there would be no restriction on the prohibitions against fasting on a pierced Ekādaśī; and by examining the beginning and conclusion of the *Viṣṇurahasya* and other texts, this very meaning is understood. In that regard, one must consider how the statement, "O Goddess, [this is] the loss of a day," is to be interpreted.
Some, however, say that when the twelfth day exists on the following day, the fast on the second eleventh day applies to everyone and not otherwise;
and so it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"When the third day has arrived, if the twelfth day is seen [to follow]."
One should observe the second Ekādaśī, but one should avoid the first.
If the eleventh day is joined with the twelfth, and the twelfth follows thereafter,
then that eleventh day, mixed with the twelfth, is the one to be observed as a fast.

"Where the eleventh day is the twelfth, and the twelfth follows thereafter, there the second [day] should be observed as the fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should indeed take place on the twelfth."
That is incorrect, because when there is no twelfth day following, the fasting on the second eleventh day is prescribed;
and so it is stated in the Brahma, Vārāha, and Skanda Purāṇas:
"If [the Ekādaśī] is joined with the remainder of the tenth day and is increasing (vṛddhimatī)..."
Then, having fasted on the second day, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O best of sages, when the eleventh day is conjoined with the twelfth,
a man, having fasted on that [eleventh], should perform the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Even if there is but a single digit (kalā) of Ekādaśī remaining, provided that Dvādaśī does not follow;
in that case, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices, but the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) must be on the Trayodaśī."

Nor do these statements regarding the existence of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) on the following day [invalidate the rule], because of the statement, "The breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should be on the thirteenth day. Therefore, it must be said that the breaking of the fast occurs on the twelfth day, and not on the thirteenth.
Some maintain that this collection of statements refers to the subject of renunciants (*saṃnyāsin*).
However, when the twelfth day is overlapped by the tenth day (*daśamī-viddhā*), [the rule applies].
Those who desire liberation should fast on the eleventh day and observe the vow of that night.

If the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is pierced by the tenth day (Daśamī), even if it occurs later [in the day], then it should be fasted upon by one who desires union with Viṣṇu; however, the second [day] should be observed as the fast.
They say this is because of such scriptural statements.

But that is weak, for these two statements do not prescribe the fast on the second Ekādaśī for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), but rather for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣus*). Nor is the desire for liberation restricted to renunciants alone, since it is possible for householders and others as well. Now, one might object: "In those very texts that focus on breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, there is the hearing of rewards such as 'therein [is] the merit of a hundred sacrifices'; therefore, let there not be a settled rule (*vyavasthā*) that those [texts] intend optional (*kāmya*) fasting, while those focused on the injunction for fasting on the pierced day (*viddhā*) concern obligatory (*nitya*) fasting?"
Do not say so.
If, by chance, three lunar days should coincide on the Ekādaśī,
then the breaking of the fast on the Dvādaśī shall yield the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
Where the eleventh day is the twelfth, or where the twelfth day follows after it, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the twelfth; one shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
[268] Thus, because there is no difference in the scriptural declaration of the fruit even when the breaking of the fast occurs on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*),
furthermore: "In all cases, the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) should be observed by men when it is mixed with the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*)."
Whether the breaking of the fast occurs in the morning or not, it must indeed be done daily; however, for those free from desire, breaking the fast on the thirteenth day bestows liberation.

Furthermore, because the obligatory nature of breaking the fast on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī-pāraṇa*) is heard of in such passages as these, this [mention of results] is not a statement of reward (*phala-śruti*), but rather an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); this is my position. Others, however, say: in order to state the determination regarding the overlapping *ekādaśī*, one must first explain what kind of overlap (*vedha*) there is:
"When [the overlap] occurs on the *ekādaśī* after midnight..."
In that case, one should not undertake the fast if even a fraction of the tenth day remains.

Thus, from the consideration of the traditional Smṛti texts, it is understood that contact with the tenth day after midnight constitutes a *vedha* (defilement). "The eleventh day is declared to be complete when it is joined with two muhūrtas before sunrise; any other is proclaimed as *viddhā* (defiled)."

Since the *Smṛti* states that contact with the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*) during the four *ghaṭikās* prior to sunrise constitutes a *vedha* (defilement), and since the consideration of the *Smṛti* passage, "For this [eleventh] is always censured when touched by the tenth at sunrise," establishes that contact with the tenth at sunrise is a *vedha*, it follows that if contact with the tenth prior to sunrise were a *vedha*, then its occurrence at a time subsequent to sunrise would all the more certainly be a *vedha*. Otherwise, the statement "the remainder is touched by sunrise" would become meaningless; or, if it were not a *vedha*, there would be a contradiction with those scriptural passages declaring it to be a *vedha*.
The *aruṇodayavedha* (piercing at dawn) lasts for one and a half *ghaṭikās*;
the *ativedha* (excessive piercing) lasts for two *ghaṭikās*; the *prabhāvedha* (piercing by light) occurs from the sight of the sun;
and the *mahāvedha* (great piercing) is also seen therein when the sun is visible and not invisible.
O King, that lunar day which touches the morning while facing the mouth [of the sun] is to be known as *vedha*; this conjunction is recorded as occurring at sunrise.
Furthermore, from the observation of this fourfold traditional teaching, a gradation of defects appears due to the gradation of the objects [of the rules].

That is incorrect, because a defect in the time that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action does not produce a defect in the person; and because the ritual action, having no defect other than its failure to accomplish the fruit it is intended to produce, there is no possibility of a gradation of defects in the action—since even in the case of a slight piercing [of the rule], the fruit is not attained due to the deficiency of the action.
"One should never perform [the rite] on a day joined with the remainder of the tenth [lunar day]."
In ancient times, this [vow] was given to Jambha on the tenth lunar day conjoined with the remainder (the eleventh).
A twice-born man who has fasted but failed due to negligence should perform an expiation;
for one who does not perform the expiation, his merit is destroyed,
and he goes to the exceedingly terrible hell called Andhatāmisra.
If a man observes the Ekādaśī joined with the remainder of the Daśamī out of ignorance or delusion, this shall be the expiation.
Having performed that arduous penance there, a man should give a cow together with its calf;
half a suvarṇa of gold should be given, accompanied by a droṇa measure of sesame seeds.
Thus, when various kinds of defects have been removed by the prescribed expiation, the attainment of the supreme fruit of *Yama* occurs;
however, in the *Yoga* [system], there is the vow of the *yātudhāna*, while in the *Bāṣkala* [system] there is the *mahāvedha*,
and in the *ativedha* of the demon *Jambha*, there are the *mohinī* and *śilavedhanī*.

If it is argued that—since this expiation is prescribed as being applicable solely to cases where the piercing is merely defective (nindita-ativedha) by virtue of its association with the Jambha-asura—it follows that the degree of the expiation’s lightness or heaviness must be determined accordingly for major piercings (*mahāvedha*) and so forth; and since a disparity in expiations indicates a disparity in the ritual defects (*karmadoṣa*) termed "deficiency" (*vaiguṇya*), a gradation [of fault] is thus logical—[we reply: No.
For it is said: "The [day] joined with the remainder of the tenth [lunar day] must never be performed [as the eleventh]."

Thus, following the prohibition concerning general objects, since the deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "This [penance] was formerly given for Jambha," is understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the seizure by *Jambha*, it is impossible to establish a fixed rule regarding the scope of the penance.
Nevertheless, a penance must indeed be performed for the sake of purification through the vow;
for thus the continuity of Dharma becomes free from flaw.
One should feed thirty Brahmins and give a cow with her calf;
furthermore, half a *suvarṇa* of gold or a *droṇa* of sesame seeds should be given.

Furthermore, since no specific subject matter is indicated in this other *smṛti* passage, and because even if one were to assume a specific subject for the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it would be impossible to determine whether that same expiation applies to other cases as well or something else, there arises a circular dependency: the assumption of differences in expiation would depend on the assumption of differences in deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), and the assumption of differences in deficiency would depend on the assumption of differences in expiation. Therefore, it is not logical to assume a gradation of faults based on a gradation of expiations. Moreover, regarding the fourfold classification known as *vedha*, *ativedha*, *mahāvedha*, and *yoga*, the designation of these as "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*)—as in the statement, "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements"—is intended for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), namely, "this sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world. Similarly, it is possible that the designation of *yoga* and so forth is intended for the purpose of an explanatory censure (*nindārthavāda*), such as "the *yoga* is the vow of a demon (*yātudhāna*). Thus, it is not logical to assume a gradation of faults on the strength of those terms either. Therefore, in order to make all statements consistent, it must be stated as follows: Since the word "always" (*sadā*) is heard in the phrase "for [it is] by touching the sunrise," it is understood that contact with the tenth lunar day at sunrise is censured in the case of the obligatory or optional (*kāmya*) eleventh-day vow (*ekādaśī-vrata*). Furthermore, since the word "joined" (*saṃyukta*) is heard in the phrase "joined with the remainder of the tenth," and since the designation of *yoga* in the rule "contact at sunrise is called *yoga*" indicates a prohibition of contact with the tenth lunar day at sunrise.
When the sun rises having reached the end of the tenth [lunar day],
that day of Hari, touched by it, was given to the asura Jambha.

Thus, because another Smṛti text censures contact with the tenth lunar day at sunrise by associating it with the demon Jambha—stating, "In ancient times, this [day] was given to Jambha"—and since such censure must apply specifically to that instance, it follows that contact with the tenth at sunrise alone is prohibited; therefore, an overlapping (vedha) is determined. Consequently, among the contacts occurring prior to that, if the tenth lunar day is seen even at the time of dawn (aruṇodaya), it should always be known as the root of sin for those observing the fast on the eleventh day.
Thus, even when hearing such censure, regarding the contact with the tenth lunar day at dawn:
"O King, if even the mere scent of the tenth lunar day should be present at dawn,
it must be carefully observed and avoided."
And even though such a prohibition is heard, it is stated:
"If the dawn should be joined with the remainder of the tenth day,
the Ekādaśī vow must nevertheless be observed on that day by a Vaiṣṇava."
From this traditional teaching (smṛti), it is understood that the prohibition applies specifically to Vaiṣṇavas who desire union with Viṣṇu:
"When Ekādaśī extends for three ghaṭikās before sunrise,
it is called 'Saṃdigdha-ekādaśī' (the doubtful Ekādaśī) and should be avoided by those desiring dharma."
And thus:
"The hero is the best among the powerful, the righteous one is the most excellent among those who know the dharma."

Thus, because the word *dharma* is recited among the names of Viṣṇu, and because the Vedic mantra—"The gods sacrificed with sacrifice; those were the first laws (*dharmāṇi*)"—indicates that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word *dharma* through his praise as "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice," it is understood that the term *dharmakāṅkṣin* (one desiring *dharma*) signifies one who desires union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu. Consequently, the avoidance of fasting on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) when it extends for three *ghaṭikās* before sunrise is determined to pertain specifically to the desire for union with Viṣṇu. This remains so even though there are traditional rules stating that "four *ghaṭikās* in the morning are called the dawn (*aruṇodaya*)," and that "the dawn-penetration (*aruṇodayavedha*) consists of four *ghaṭikās*, and the [impurity] lasts for three and a half *ghaṭikās*," thereby defining the period of three and a half *ghaṭikās* as the time of dawn.
At the end of the night, during the half-watch when the celestial drums resound,
the study of the Sārasvata texts is said to take place at the break of dawn.

Thus, since the night at the end of which the eighth part coincides with the time of dawn (*aruṇodaya*) is recorded as being exactly twenty-seven *ghaṭikās* during the transit (*saṅkrānti*) of the Sun into Capricorn (*makara*), its eighth part cannot possibly extend for three and a half *ghaṭikās*. Consequently, there is no contradiction in designating an eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) that extends for slightly more than three *ghaṭikās* as "extending for three *ghaṭikās*" (*trighaṭikā-vyāpinī*). By stating "extension for three *ghaṭikās*," the logical possibility of contact with the tenth day (*daśamī*) at the time of dawn is established; whereas the mention of "three and a half *ghaṭikās*" refers to nights of exactly twenty-eight *ghaṭikās*, while for longer nights, it is stated that they extend for four *ghaṭikās*. Alternatively, the mention of "three and a half *ghaṭikās*" is intended to show that even within all four *ghaṭikās* of dawn, contact with the tenth day prior to those three and a half *ghaṭikās* does not constitute a taint (*vedha*). However, the avoidance of contact with the tenth day within two *ghaṭikās* before sunrise is [the stricter rule].
When Ekādaśī extends for even one muhūrta prior to sunrise, it is called Saṃyuktakādaśī; one should avoid it for the increase of dharma.

Thus, by the term *dharmavṛddhi* (increase of dharma), there is the intention to refer to the purification of the mind (*sattvaśuddhi*) which serves as a means for purity; because it is intended to consist of an excellence of dharma as indicated by the word "iti" in the passage, "If one should desire vast enjoyments and liberation, which is extremely difficult to attain," it pertains to the sphere of desire (*kāma*).
Starting from the time of sunrise, sixty *nāḍikās* constitute what is called a complete *ekādaśī*; it must be avoided by those who desire the fruits of dharma.

Thus, by considering another traditional text (smṛti) which states, "Even the 'great piercing' (mahāvedha) is seen there; the sun is observed [only] therein," if the tenth lunar day is heard to be even half a measure of the solar disc,
then the twelfth day is still to be accepted, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) takes place on the thirteenth day.

Thus, by examining other *smṛtis* as well, it is established—on the basis of the statement in the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika*, "And cattle and so forth are the fruits of dharma"—that the prohibition of contact with the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*) at the rising of half the sun is intended for the purpose of avoiding such contact. This is because the word "fruit of dharma" (*dharmaphala*) in the passage "If one should desire abundant enjoyments" is understood from the *smṛti* to denote enjoyment resulting from the dharma known as the fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*). If one were to accept that the words "desirer of dharma," "increase of dharma," and "fruit of dharma" possess meanings based solely on common worldly usage, several logical fallacies would arise: (1) the distinction between the "piercing" (*vedha*), "excessive piercing" (*ativedha*), and "great piercing" (*mahāvedha*)—defined respectively as the first, second, and third degrees of overlap—would become baseless; (2) there would be the undesirable consequence that even when a rite has been completed, its fruit might not be obtained due to obstacles, despite the fact that the overlapping time was within the two *ghaṭikās* following the commencement of the dharma (the *aruṇodaya-vedha*); and (3) since a completed action cannot be established as "dharma" in the sense of being "conducive to welfare" (*śreyaskara*), the term "desirer of dharma" would have no referent, and likewise the term "attainment of the fruit of dharma" would be redundant. Furthermore, the prohibitions against contact with the tenth lunar day at the time of sunrise (*sūryodaya*) apply universally to all cases. If one were to claim that the prohibitions against contact at the time of *aruṇodaya* apply only to those desiring specific fruits, this would render the terms "desirer of dharma" and so forth meaningless. Moreover, the verse stating, "The *saṃdigdhā ekādaśī* should be avoided by those desiring dharma," is followed by the injunction, "One should fast on the twelfth day for the sake of the prosperity of sons and kingdom. Similarly, the verse stating, "The *saṃyuktā ekādaśī* should be avoided for the increase of dharma," is followed by, "One should fast on the twelfth day for the sake of the prosperity of sons and grandsons. And the verse stating, "The *saṃkīrṇā ekādaśī* should be abandoned by those seeking the fruit of dharma," is followed by, "One should fast on the twelfth day for the sake of the prosperity of sons and grandsons. Since these latter verses are intended to prescribe fasting on the twelfth day for those desiring specific results when the *ekādaśī* is pierced by *aruṇodaya* and so forth, one should not suspect—on their authority—that the prohibitions regarding *aruṇodaya*-pierced days apply only to those desiring specific fruits. Finally, the verse "It should always be known as the root of sin" is merely a deprecation (*nindā*), and the phrase "This is the grace (*āśā*) of Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the word 'Sat' (*sad*)" can also be explained accordingly; thus, the prohibition of contact with the tenth lunar day at the time of *aruṇodaya* applies to all cases simply by the hearing of the word "always" (*sadā*). The verse, "A certain woman fasted on a day pierced at the time of *aruṇodaya*; her hundred sons perished; therefore, one should avoid it," is also merely a deprecation. However, the verse, "For this [day] touched by the sun at rising is always censured by the tenth lunar day," is indeed intended as a formal prohibition.
If unperforated days are not obtained because they are prohibited by [other rules],
then the Ekādaśī lunar day, even if perforated by five *muhūrtas*, must indeed be accepted.

Since there would otherwise be the contradiction of such statements, and because the word "always" (*sadā*) can be explained as applying when the Ekādaśī exists on the eleventh, the twelfth, or the following day, and because it is appropriate to explain it as referring to the subject matter of all obligatory and optional Ekādaśī fasts, it is proper to interpret it precisely as referring to the subject matter of all obligatory and optional Ekādaśī fasts.
When the eleventh day is pierced by the tenth from sunrise onwards,
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, gave it away for the sake of pleasing the Dānavas.

From the observation of this other Smṛti text, it is understood that the phrase "touching the sunrise" (*sūryodayaspṛśā*) refers to contact occurring at a time subsequent to sunrise. Therefore, it is established that the *vedha* (penetration/defect) applicable to all cases is precisely the contact with the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*) at a time after sunrise; whereas contacts with the tenth on the two *ghaṭikās* [or half-ghaṭikā] before dawn, or at the time of sunrise itself, pertain respectively to the desire for union with Viṣṇu, liberation, and the means for the Ekādaśī vow. As for the statement, "If even a fraction of the tenth is found after midnight, one should not begin the fast," this is to be explained as referring to the commencement of the vow on the first day [of the lunar fortnight].

This is untenable. Regarding what was first stated—that the defect of the time which is an auxiliary of the ritual (*karmāṅga*) does not entail a defect on the part of the person—that is incorrect. For when a ritual is performed at a time forbidden as an auxiliary of the ritual, every scriptural statement (*sarvavākya*) speaks only of a defect on the part of the person; and since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), it is impossible to abandon that [defect]. Furthermore, as for the claim that by the word *vaiṣṇava* one who desires union with Viṣṇu (*viṣṇusāyujya*) is denoted, that too is not so, because it also denotes those who desire the pleasure of Viṣṇu, devotees of Viṣṇu, and those who fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*). It is also improper to discard the meanings well-known in the world for the words *dharmakāṅkṣin*, *dharmavṛddhi*, and *dharmaphala*. Moreover, the gradation of piercing (*vedha-tāratamya*) is established through the gradation of the defects of the person. Furthermore, by virtue of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), it is understood that the prohibitions against the eleventh day being pierced by dawn (*aruṇodaya-viddha*) refer to those desiring other specific fruits. In the passage "it should always be known as the root of sin," the word *sadā* (always) is applicable to cases other than the favoring of the pierced day—as seen in the text: "For this [eleventh day] touched by sunrise is always censured as being joined with the tenth. Therefore, it is not proper to explain the word *sat* (good/true) as referring to Viṣṇu through such a strained interpretation (*kliṣṭakalpanā*). Consequently, what has been stated [by us] is indeed superior.
Now follows the determination of the time for fasting on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days.

When the eleventh-day fast (*ekādaśī-vrata*) and the twelfth-day fast (*dvādaśī-vrata*) both fall on a twelfth day that is mixed with the eleventh, then by means of a single fast, both the eleventh-day fast and the twelfth-day fast are purified. However, when a separate fast is required on the eleventh day because it is complete [in duration], and likewise a separate one on the twelfth, then two fasts must be performed. This is according to the injunction: "Having fasted on the eleventh, one should also fast on the twelfth; there shall be no omission of the rule here, for Hari is the deity of both. Furthermore, regarding the statement, "While the previous vow is not completed, one should not perform another vow," completion occurs through the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*). In the absence of that, if two fasts were performed, there would result an omission of the rule due to the non-completion of the previous vow. That too is indeed avoided by virtue of both having the same deity.
Thus, having abandoned the eleventh day, one should observe the fast on the twelfth;
one undoubtedly obtains all the merit arising from the previous day.

This is said with reference to one who is incapable of performing two fasts. When even a single fast is prescribed for one who is incapable of fasting, then what need is there to speak of one who is incapable of two? The vow of fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is obligatory (*nitya*), beneficial for all at all times; likewise, the vow of fasting on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is optional (*kāmya*), yet it is likewise prescribed for all at all times. In the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Pradyumna, Mārkaṇḍeya first stated that the fast is on the eleventh day and the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) is on the twelfth day; immediately thereafter, he stated that the fast is on the twelfth day and the breaking of the fast is on the thirteenth day. Having heard these two contradictory statements, Indrapramuṇa spoke.
"O King, it is proclaimed in the Purāṇas that the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) should not be observed [as a fast];
you too, O tiger among sages, have previously stated this—listen now to what I say."
O Brahmin, the twelfth day (dvādaśī), which is dear to Keśava, has been declared by you to be for breaking the fast;
yet the auspicious eleventh day (ekādaśī) has indeed been declared by you to be for fasting.
The breaking of the fast should be performed on the twelfth day, for the fasting was observed on the eleventh;
how can you practice what is forbidden according to the path established in the Purāṇas?
Thus questioned, Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O protector of the earth, to everything that has been asked by you, a virtuous man.
The world was destroyed by the wicked who were intent upon the discourse of sophistry."
O King, regarding the determination of the twelfth day, the three worlds are deluded in this matter;
indeed, O protector of the earth, most men of former times were likewise deluded.
They are lost; there is no stability in them, O King, for a secret does not reach those who are impure, just as medicine drunk into these bodies [is wasted] when they are defiled.
In those who are pure, that [meditative concentration] attains stability through the gathering of the Dharma;
for those with empty bodies, the three myrobalans become a medicine that leads to stability.
O lord of men, those who observe the fast on the fourteenth day out of devotion to Śiva—
O King, their going to hell is never seen anywhere.
[277] O lord of men, I have not observed anything censurable in those other men who practice devotion to Gopati and likewise observe the fast of the seventh lunar day with devotion.
O King, by fasting on the full moon day, they went to the world of Brahmā;
others, however, being virtuous and taking refuge in devotion to Śiva, [fasted] on the eighth day.
O best of men, having abandoned the mire of the Kali age,
men observe the Ekādaśī of the sages and the Dvādaśī of the Discus-bearer;
why then, O King, is the Dvādaśī not observed by people through fasting?
O King, this most excellent twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), which is devoid of both fruit and enjoyment and consists of liberation itself, was proclaimed of old.
The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is the body, while the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) is remembered as the person (puruṣa).
O King, by fasting on the twelfth day, thousands have attained perfection.
These fourteen powerful universal monarchs, lords of the earth, have attained incomparable sovereignty as cakravartins.
Those portions of Viṣṇu, possessed of great heroism and the destroyers of wicked Daityas,
have attained perfection by thousands through fasting on the twelfth lunar day, O King;
they have obtained incomparable sovereignty as universal emperors and unshakable prosperity.
Having observed the pure twelfth day (Dvādaśī) throughout their lives, endowed with their vows,
they attained the status of universal monarchs after having enjoyed pleasures and happiness.
Kuvalāśva, Bhavān, Gādhi, Hariścandra, Nala, Pṛthu,
Maruta, Bharata, and Kārtavīrya Haihaya.
Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Rāma, Kakutstha, and likewise Nahuṣa—
having fasted on the meritorious twelfth day and having avoided the subsequent one,
and having partaken of food, these attained the status of universal monarchs and the pleasures of heaven.
O protector of the earth, by fasting on the twelfth day of the month,
seven generations of the Janakas, joined together, attained supreme perfection.
The great protector of the earth, Purukutsa, attained perfection by fasting on the twelfth lunar day,
having cast off the difficult-to-overcome bondage of karma.
Māndhātṛ and Yauvanāśva, having fasted on the twelfth day and met their death in battle, attained the supreme state.
O protector of the earth, the unconquered Śākuntali, son of Duṣyanta,
attained that state of Viṣṇu by fasting on the twelfth lunar day.
O King, Vainya Purūravas, having protected the surface of the earth and having constantly worshipped the Supporter of the Earth on the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs),
went to the realm of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution.
O King, these royal sages and brahmins attained supreme perfection by fasting on the twelfth day; hear from me who they were.
Yājñavalkya, Raibhya, Māṇḍavya, the sage Kauśika, Bharadvāja, as well as Kaṇva, and Kumbhayoni, the treasure-house of asceticism.
O lord of men, eighty-eight thousand sages of sublimated vital energy proceed at the front of the chariot of the Enemy of Darkness.
O King, all of them attained supreme perfection by fasting on the twelfth lunar day;
they have gone with me—how could you have any doubt about this?
O King, the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day is proclaimed as the secret of Hari;
it is blameless in this world, auspicious, and dear to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Therefore, O King, no doubt should be entertained regarding the twelfth day (Dvādaśī);
it is declared to bestow special fruit and to destroy all sins.

Thus it is stated in the conclusion; therefore, there exists a distinct vow for fasting on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) that is different from the vow for fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), and thus everything is beyond reproach.
Others, however, say:
"O best of the twice-born, when the twelfth day in either the bright or the dark fortnight is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism..."
The fast is on the twelfth day, while the breaking of the fast is on the thirteenth day.

Although such Smṛti texts enjoin fasting on the twelfth day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, there is no authoritative evidence that this entails the performance of the specific ritual duty of fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*).
As has already been explained, the twelfth day conjoined with Śravaṇa is as follows:
"Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should subsequently observe a fast on the twelfth."

Based on this Smṛti, the fast must be observed even on the Ekādaśī; therefore, the fast is to be observed on both days only when that [Ekādaśī] is the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī. That is incorrect, because the optional lifelong fast is prescribed for the Dvādaśī even apart from the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī. Therefore, one should adhere strictly to what has been stated above.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the fasts of Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī.
Now follows the determination of the times for the Ekādaśī vow, such as the Naktam (evening) meal and others.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa:
"One should avoid a full [lunar day] pierced by even half a *pala* of the preceding *nandā*, even if it is full itself,
if one desires the continuity of one's lineage, even regarding the four observances."
One who desires sovereignty should not perform the fast, nor the night-vow, nor the single-meal vow, nor the vow of begging,
on a day when the moonrise is obscured by the previous tithi (pūrvaviddhā).
The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) joined with the twelfth (Dvādaśī) is recommended for fasting, as well as for eating only at night,
eating nothing at all, or always eating a single meal, as well as for worship.
O dear one, one should not offer food at night, nor food obtained by begging, nor a single meal;
giving gifts on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) when it is joined with the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) leads to misfortune.
Thus concludes the determination of the times for the *nakta* and other observances within the Ekādaśī vow.
Now follows the determination of the time for breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*), which is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the Ekādaśī vow.
Regarding this, the Kūrma Purāṇa states:
Having fasted thus on the eleventh day, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is prescribed on the twelfth;
one should not do it on the thirteenth, because of the loss of twelve twelfth-day periods.
In the Viṣṇurahasya:
"Those men who desire the increase of dharma must never break their fast on the thirteenth day after having observed the Ekādaśī fast here."
A fast broken on the thirteenth day destroys the merit of twelve twelfth-day observances, as well as one's dharma, progeny, wealth, and longevity.
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"When Ekādaśī is visible and Dvādaśī lasts for even a mere lava [of time],
it destroys twelve Dvādaśīs if the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is done on the Trayodaśī."
When the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is very short on the day of breaking the fast,
then one should perform both the morning and midday rites at the time of dawn.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "Then, O King of kings, on the twelfth lunar day of the dark fortnight at the break of dawn,
the rites of bathing and worship should be performed, accompanied by gifts, fire-offerings, and other such acts."
On the pure thirteenth day, however, by breaking the fast, a man undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the earth, or even something superior to all sacrifices.
For this reason, O Brahmins, one should perform the ritual bath at dawn,
even upon seeing that the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is but slightly visible, accompanied by the libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
For this twelfth day, when transgressed by men, causes great ruin;
it effects the destruction of dharma, just as the Sarasvatī [is fruitless] for one who does not bathe in her.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: One should not let two or even three *kalās* of the twelfth day pass by;
for a twelfth day that is exceeded destroys previously accumulated merit.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "The man who, having passed over the twelfth day, performs the breaking of the fast,
his vow of twelve years perishes at that very moment."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who, having bypassed the twelfth day, performs the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day,
for him twelve twelfth days are lost."
In the *Devīrahasya*:
"Indeed, for one who performs the ritual breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) after having passed the twelfth day,
all [acts] such as bathing and giving gifts become fruitless."
And it is not so:
whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches at its rising,
that entire lunar day is to be known as valid for bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and other such rites.
Based on this statement by Devala, one should not suspect that there is no fault in transgressing the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*). For Vasiṣṭha states in the *Nāradapurāṇa*:

"At the time of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) or at the death of men, the lunar day is considered to be momentary. The meaning is this: at whatever time the breaking of the fast or the death occurs, the lunar day is precisely that which exists at that moment; it does not mean that the entire duration of that lunar day must be understood [as the time for the rite]. However, where on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) there is only a small portion of the twelfth day sufficient for the time of breaking the fast, there the following from the *Padmapurāṇa* applies:
O King, Vasiṣṭha, the knower of dharma, has declared that when there is even a fraction of the twelfth day on the thirteenth, that lunar day is considered complete.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "One should pass over even two or three *kalās* of the twelfth day;
having fasted on the eleventh day, one shall attain the fruit of dharma therein."
Likewise: "If the remainder of the twelfth lunar day should extend beyond [midnight] and the thirteenth day follows,
there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices if the breaking of the fast occurs on the thirteenth."

This also refers to the case where the twelfth day (dvādaśī) extends into the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa). Thus, all those [texts] which are intent on prohibiting the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī), or which prescribe rules for breaking the fast on the twelfth day, all refer to cases where the twelfth day occurs on the thirteenth day.
And so it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"If even a small portion of the twelfth day is perceived on the thirteenth day..."
On the twelfth day, when breaking the fast, one should avoid the thirteenth day.
[283] For this twelfth day, when transgressed by men, causes great ruin;
it effects the destruction of dharma, just as the Sarasvatī does not bestow merit upon one who has not bathed in her.
Alternatively, if the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) does not exist, even for a moment, conjoined with the sun,
the vow should be completed on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) for the sake of increasing great merit.

In the case of other rivers such as the Gaṅgā and so forth, one should bathe on the opposite bank; however, in the case of the Sarasvatī, one must first bathe and then proceed to the further shore. Regarding the term *asnātā*: it refers to that [river] in which bathing has not been performed (*asnātā*, where the suffix *kta* is used in the locative sense). Just as the Sarasvatī, when bypassed—that is, crossed over without bathing—causes the loss of merit (*dharma-haraṇa*), so too does the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) cause the loss of merit if it is bypassed or transgressed. According to the Purāṇa: "The eleventh and twelfth days should be observed there as a fast; [only then is] the fruit obtained."
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) lasts for even a moment, one must not break the fast on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī).

Furthermore: "If [the twelfth lunar day] does not last for even a *kalā*, a *kāṣṭhā*, or a *mūhūrta* into the following day, it destroys twelve twelfth days; however, breaking the fast on the thirteenth day [is permissible]."
Thus, having restated the impossibility of the twelfth lunar day occurring on the thirteenth, those [scriptural passages] are intended to prohibit breaking the fast.
"Even if the Ekādaśī is overlapped [by the previous tithi], it should be accepted provided there is no Dvādaśī on the following day;
for a fast-breaking on the thirteenth destroys twelve Dvādaśīs."
Thus, since these [passages] have the same meaning as those beginning with "ityādi," there is no fault.

Others, however, state the following distinction regarding the censure and praise of breaking the fast on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*): the prohibition against householders breaking the fast on the thirteenth day is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of censure intended to show that such an act results in the loss of the merit of the twelfth day; conversely, breaking the fast on the thirteenth day applies to ascetics (*yatis*). For instance, when the twelfth day is exhausted, it is appropriate for householders who seek results, whereas ascetics—being indifferent to results—perform their duty simply because it is what ought to be done. The praise characterized by the attainment of the merit of a hundred sacrifices (*kratuśata*) applies only to ascetics; the meaning is not that various fruits of a hundred sacrifices actually arise from breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, as there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for this. Therefore, this is merely a figurative praise.

That is incorrect; for what is the meaning of the statement, "Twelve twelfth-lunar days (dvādaśīs) perish for householders"? Indeed, an action performed does not perish without the experience of its fruit. Therefore, it is impossible that the twelfth-lunar days perish either in their essential nature or in their results; rather, this is a threat intended to frighten one away from the fruit of transgression. To illustrate: "One should not say 'gire' [with the word] 'girā'; then the Udgātṛ priest would swallow his own self. Now, the swallowing of the Udgātṛ's own self is certainly not perceived through perception or other means of valid knowledge; rather, it is established that this is a censure against the use of the word *girā*. Similarly, the censure regarding the loss of the twelfth-lunar day applies to both ascetics and householders. For even in the case of an ascetic, the purpose is the destruction of accumulated demerit (*durita*) through the performance of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, as well as the avoidance of the transgression caused by non-performance. Therefore, when the twelfth-lunar day is lost, because there is no destruction of accumulated demerit and because the transgression caused by non-performance occurs, it is indeed improper for ascetics to break their fast on the thirteenth-lunar day (*trayodaśī*).
And so it has been said:
"By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil;
and by purifying knowledge through repeated practice, one brings it to maturity."
Through the knowledge of detachment and the casting off [of the mind], a person attains liberation.

As for what was said—that the statement "he attains union with Viṣṇu" is appropriate only for ascetics (*yatins*) and not for householders (*gṛhins*)—that too is incorrect. For it is heard in scripture that even a householder attains liberation through the performance of his prescribed duties; therein, the duties of a householder seeking liberation are taught. And it is heard [in the Śruti]: "He who conducts himself thus throughout his life reaches the world of Brahman; he does not return again. And Yājñavalkya says:

"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth—even such a householder is liberated. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, praise characterized by the attainment of the merit of a hundred sacrifices is indeed common to both ascetics and householders. Therefore, the very arrangement already stated regarding the injunctions and prohibitions for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day must be adopted. Now, when there is doubt concerning the religious duties of the eleventh day and so forth, those whose words are to be accepted and those whose are not are shown in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
Brahmā said:
"They always worship Viṣṇu through the actions of mind, speech, and body. [1]
For their word is to be accepted, for they are considered equal to Viṣṇu.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa,
the Blessed One said:
"Having indeed touched Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who are experts in the scriptures of Viṣṇu..."
One should diligently practice that which has been prescribed for those who have observed their vows and follow right conduct.
In the Skanda Purāṇa,
Maheśvara said:
"Those who know the Purāṇas together with the Itihāsas according to their true essence,"
The words of those who are devoted to virtuous conduct and are peaceful are like medicine.
Pulastya and Satyavrata—
those who are restrained in their duties, those who contemplate the meaning of the treatises on dharma,
and those who truly know the Vedas and the Śāstras— their word is medicine.
The Blessed One is Vedavyāsa. The words of those who know the truth of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, who contemplate the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras,
and who are devoted to virtuous conduct, are indeed medicine.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
[286] "And those who are knowers of logic, tranquil, conversant with the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras,
devoted to their own duties, and self-controlled— their word is medicine."
The meaning is that it should be accepted like medicine.
Āpastamba says:
"That which learned Brāhmaṇas declare is known as human dharma."
He who examines the instruction on Dharma given by the seers through reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras knows Dharma in its true essence.
The meaning is that, for that reason, his word is to be accepted.
In the Śāradā Purāṇa:
"Those who contemplate the meaning of the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras..."
Those who are indeed devoted to the conduct of the virtuous should diligently practice what has been so enjoined.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "That which is spoken by those who know the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, who understand the principles of the Smṛtis, and who are dear to Vāsudeva, shall be considered Vedic."
The meaning is that the speech of those other than those mentioned should be avoided. This has been established and stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya* and the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"O Sage, for those for whom the Vedas, the Brahmins, and Janārdana are not the cause, the Tantras and the Dharmaśāstras are the authority and the cause."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
One should avoid the speech of those who are devoid of Vedic study, who are bereft of purity and proper conduct, who are atheists, and who consider themselves learned.
One should avoid the speech of those who have omitted the Vaiśvadeva offering, those who are devoid of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), and those who are averse to the deities.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: One should avoid the speech of those who are averse to the deities, those who are devoid of japa and homa, and those who are lacking in devotion to Viṣṇu.
One should avoid the words of those who have no delight in the forest-dweller's life (araṇyaka), nor in sacred study, nor in the supreme abode, nor in the sun.
In the Vaiṣṇava Tantra: One should always avoid the speech of those who possess no great devotion toward their guru, their recitation (japa), and Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Those who are naked or non-naked, those who are rationalists (haituka), those who behave like herons (bakavr̥tti),
and those who revile the deities— one should avoid their speech."
In the Kālikā Purāṇa and in the Veda: "One should avoid the speech of those who have no faith in the deity, nor in the Vedic ritual."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "One should never explain the Veda, nor engage in Mīmāṃsā, nor likewise in the ritual sacrifice;
one should avoid the speech of those who are indeed devoted to dry logic."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The words of those who possess no devotion toward Viśveśvara, Viṣṇu, and Śiva should not be accepted for the sake of establishing a determination of Dharma."
Likewise:
"Those men who destroy the fifty Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas— one should indeed avoid their word."
And so says the Yogayājñavalkya: "The Purāṇas, the Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise the Pāśupata—these are supreme authorities; they must not be refuted by means of logical arguments."

Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Determination of the Ekādaśī, in the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time) within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the faculties of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge. [289]
Now begins the seventh chapter:
the section on the twelve [twelfth days] (*dvādaśī*). Now follows the determination of the *Śravaṇa-dvādaśī*.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*,
Śrī Rāma said:
"For those who are unable to fast, what would constitute a single day of fasting?"
"O Mahādeva, tell that great fruit to me who asks.
Śaṅkara said:
"O Rāma, that which is the Great Dvādaśī endowed with the hearing [of its merit]..."
Having fasted on that day, bathed, and worshipped Janārdana, [one obtains the fruit].
O knower of dharma, one obtains the fruit of twelve *dvādaśīs* without effort. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Supreme Person, O Sinless One, for those who are always unable to observe fasts, please tell me about this meritorious Dvādaśī.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In the month of Bhādrapada, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, when conjoined with the Śravaṇā nakṣatra, is meritorious, granting the fruits of all desires; it yields great fruit through fasting.
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers and fasted while consuming only what is naturally sweet,
one obtains the complete fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.
Likewise: "O Bhārata, when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
one who bathes at the confluence of rivers obtains the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā and other such sacred waters."
One who observes a fast attains [this]; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Yama said: When the Śravaṇa constellation occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
that highly meritorious twelfth day is known by the name Vijayā.
In the Viṣṇurahasya: "That twelfth day in the month of Bhādrapada which is joined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra is indeed highly meritorious; it is known by the name Vijayā."
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords;
having worshipped Acyuta with devotion, one obtains the merit of ten years.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, when conjoined with the Śravaṇā nakṣatra,
is to be known as the 'Great Twelfth' (Mahatī Dvādaśī), which yields great fruit for fasting."
Having fasted on that twelfth day at the holy confluence of rivers,
one obtains the fruit of twelve twelfth-day observances even without a boat.
If that same twelfth day should be conjoined with the asterisms of Budha and Śravaṇa, it is exceedingly great; whatever is given on that day becomes inexhaustible.
By worshipping Acyuta with devotion on that day, one obtains the merit of ten years;
furthermore, the fruit of gifts and performed rites becomes multiplied a hundred-thousandfold.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"If Wednesday occurs in conjunction with the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī,
that twelfth lunar day is proclaimed as the 'Exceedingly Great' (atyantamahatī) Dvādaśī."
O descendant of Bhrigu’s lineage, whatever bathing, recitation, charity, fire-offering, ancestral rite, or worship of the gods one performs on that day, all of it becomes inexhaustible.
O Rāma, having bathed on that day at any confluence whatsoever, he undoubtedly obtains the fruit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
All gatherings for listening always provide full nourishment,
especially when joined with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and particularly when associated with a religious vow.
If that same twelfth day should coincide with the lunar mansion Śravaṇa and the weekday of Mercury, it is exceedingly great; on that day, everything given here becomes inexhaustible.
Having worshipped Janārdana on the occasion of the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī conjunction,
and having given gifts to the Brahmins, one should remain fasting with the senses subdued.
At the confluences of great rivers, Yudhiṣṭhira performed the ritual giving of gifts every year according to the prescribed rules; thereafter, he met his end.
The supreme, imperishable abode is difficult for all human beings to attain;
there, the trees yield fruits according to one's desires, the rivers have mud of milk-rice (pāyasa),
and the delightful lotus ponds always contain pure water.
Having reached that region, the high-souled merchant,
his limbs adorned with highly polished gold,
spent an entire kalpa in the company of celestial beauties.
He always rejoiced, taking delight together with her.
When the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is conjoined with the asterisms of Budha and Śravaṇa, the water from the confluence is auspicious;
the giving of curd-rice is recommended, and the rule is to be intent upon fasting.
By Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumāra, Gādhi,
and by these and others, O Indra among kings, the Kāmadā Dvādaśī was observed.

That twelfth day which is joined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra and the day of Mercury is indeed called "Jayā" by the venerable sages; having fasted on that day properly and with devotion, a person indeed—
He attains perfection endowed with the qualities beginning with the power of the wish-fulfilling gem (aṇimā).
In the Pauṣkara and Pañcarātra [tantras], it is stated:
"Viṣṇu should be propitiated at the confluence of rivers on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), which is a Monday or a Śravaṇa-day, during the flood-tide that fulfills all desires."
And likewise, with reference to Śravaṇa-dvādaśī, it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa and the Viṣṇurahasya:
"On this [occasion], the fast is on the twelfth day, but the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the thirteenth;
even though it is forbidden, it must be performed—this is the command of the Supreme Lord."
And so says Mārkaṇḍeya:
"If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is found conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa and the Sun,
one should fast on that twelfth day and perform the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on the thirteenth day."
And this twelfth day (dvādaśī) becomes entirely meritorious by the mere conjunction with Śravaṇā, just as the eighth day (aṣṭamī) is by its conjunction with Rohiṇī.
And so it is stated in the Matsyapurāṇa:
"The twelfth day joined with Śravaṇā is an entirely most meritorious lunar day."
But it is not praised merely because it is conjoined with that [quality].

Some explain it thus: "When the full [period] is conjoined with Śravaṇā, then it is meritorious; however, it does not become meritorious merely by being conjoined with that [constellation] for as long as it is conjoined with Śravaṇā, but rather only when the full sixty nāḍīs have elapsed.

This is incorrect, because the meaning understood is that the entire period is meritorious when it is conjoined with Śravaṇā, and not that it is meritorious only for as long as it is actually conjoined with Śravaṇā.
Thus it is stated in the *Śaṅkaragītā*.
"The seven-day week of stars beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī do not purify the entire lunar day (tithi) merely by their conjunction. Thus it is said.

Therefore, it is determined that the lunar day (*tithi*) is meritorious only for as long as it is conjoined with the asterism (*nakṣatra*); by that logic, the same would apply even to the *Śravaṇa-dvādaśī*. To address this, it was stated: "The entire [lunar day] is most meritorious merely by being conjoined with the asterism; it is not the case that only the portion actually conjoined is praised. However, in the reading *śravaṇaspṛṣṭā*, by reflecting on the word *spṛṣṭa* ("touched"), it is understood that this implies a true conjunction with *Śravaṇa*. And thus, regarding the *Śravaṇa-dvādaśī*, it is said in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
O lord of men, when the conjunction of a lunar day and a lunar mansion occurs for even two moments,
that conjunction is to be known as lasting for eight watches (yāmas).
Therefore, our interpretation alone is correct.
As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Whichever lunar days (tithis) are declared meritorious on account of their conjunction with a [specific] asterism..."
One should observe that very vow among those [days], with the exception of Śravaṇadvādaśī.

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever rites are prescribed for whichever lunar days (tithis) are declared meritorious through conjunction with any particular constellation, those should be performed on those very days and not on other lunar days even if they are joined by that same constellation. For example, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, when conjoined with a meritorious asterism, is called Govinda-dvādaśī; the vow of fasting prescribed for it must be observed on that very day, and not on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) even if it is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism. This is the rule, with the exception of the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī; however, the meaning is that the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow may also take place on the Śravaṇa-ekādaśī.
And it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, the rule for your Dvādaśī has been declared in conjunction with the Śravaṇa asterism."
It pacifies all sins and bestows all happiness.
When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) coincides with the Śravaṇa asterism, it is called Vijayā; this lunar day is proclaimed to bestow victory upon devotees.
Also in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"When a Vaiṣṇava asterism is not found anywhere on the twelfth day,
then that Ekādaśī, which destroys sins, should be observed as a fast when it is conjoined with Śravaṇa."
The deity of both is Viṣṇu, the ancient Supreme Person;
no distinction should be made between them, for by making a distinction, a man falls.

Others, however, explain it thus: on those lunar days (tithis) which are declared meritorious due to their conjunction with a constellation, one should certainly perform that vow; however, the vow is not performed on the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī. For Vaiṣṇavas observe the obligatory and optional Ekādaśī vows; in that case, a fast on the Dvādaśī immediately following the Ekādaśī fast is impossible, because the vow must conclude with the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā), and because another vow is prohibited at the same time while a previous vow remains uncompleted.
This is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "A vow is to be known as ending with the breaking of the fast; at the conclusion of the vow, there is the feeding of Brahmins."
"One should not undertake another vow while the previous vow is still uncompleted. Thus it is said.

Therefore, for Vaiṣṇavas who have undertaken the Ekādaśī vow for some reason, a fast on Śravaṇa-dvādaśī is not appropriate; this is indicated by the phrase "except for Śravaṇa-dvādaśī," which serves as an illustration. This is because the collection of logical arguments is not equal, such as: "For those who have commenced vows on the Ṣaṣṭhī, Saptamī, or Caturdaśī, when a lunar day such as a full moon conjoined with a specific asterism (nakṣatra) occurs, the performance of the fast pertaining to that [conjunction] is certainly not attained [as the primary duty], since it is understood that a vow must be completed until its breaking (pāraṇā). Just as for those who have undertaken the vow of both [the Saptamī and the asterism], how can the fast be accomplished when the Aṣṭamī conjoined with Rohiṇī arrives?

That is incorrect, because the use of the restrictive particle *eva* would be inappropriate, and because it is improper to assume a secondary or indicative sense (*upalakṣaṇatva*) when the meaning is already established by the literal sense itself. Therefore, the previous explanation alone is correct. In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) joined with the *Śravaṇā* asterism on the eleventh day is said to be of great merit: "When the twelfth day, touched by *Śravaṇā*, touches the eleventh, that is indeed the Vaiṣṇava conjunction known as the 'Viṣṇu-chain' (*viṣṇuśṛṅkhala*)."
Having fasted there according to the prescribed rules, a man whose impurities are completely exhausted attains unsurpassed perfection, from which return to worldly existence is difficult to find.

“*Śravaṇāspṛṣṭā*” means joined with the *śravaṇā* [nakṣatra]. Although the word *śravaṇa* has three genders, by saying “*śravaṇāspṛṣṭā*,” it indicates that even through a slight conjunction with *śravaṇā*, one becomes fit for the fast of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and other rites. As stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
“If the eleventh and twelfth days, as well as the *vaiṣṇava* [nakṣatra], are present there, that is called ‘Viṣṇu’s Chain’ (*viṣṇuśṛṅkhala*), which brings about union with Viṣṇu.”
Having fasted there according to the prescribed rule, one shall certainly go to Śvetapura.
Here, the fast is on the twelfth day, while the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the thirteenth;
even though it is prohibited, it must be performed, for this is the command of the Supreme Lord.

In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: O King, if the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should touch the eleventh (ekādaśī), and the asterism Śravaṇa— the best among celestial bodies— is present, it removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.

However, for one who is unable to fast but has undertaken the vow of Ekādaśī, the fast itself is to be observed on the Ekādaśī day, while on the Dvādaśī day there is only the injunction for worship, according to the cited statement: "As long as the previous [vow] is not completed...
Likewise, in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"If, during the bright fortnight on the Dvādaśī, the asterism Śravaṇa occurs..."
Having observed the fast on the eleventh day, one should worship Hari there on the twelfth day.
Yama said: Wherever the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is found to be conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa,
one should fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) and worship Hari on the twelfth day.
However, he who is unable to observe two fasts and has not formally undertaken the Ekādaśī vow should fast on the Dvādaśī alone.
Thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"Having fasted on the meritorious Dvādaśī conjoined with the Viṣṇu asterism (Śravaṇa)..."
A person undoubtedly attains the merit arising from Ekādaśī.
Likewise, at the Vājapeya sacrifice, even one who is deficient in ritual action, having been consecrated,
obtains the entire fruit— even if he has not bathed and has not offered oblations.
The term *ahuta* is a bahuvrīhi compound.
Thus, by fasting on the twelfth day while excluding the eleventh,
one undoubtedly obtains all the merit arising from the preceding day.
However, for one capable of observing two fasts, fasting on both days is prescribed in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should likewise fast on the twelfth;
there shall be no omission of the rule here, for Hari is the deity of both."

"One should not undertake another vow while the previous one is still incomplete"—because of this prohibition, completion does not occur without the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*). In the absence of that, when there is a conjunction of two fasts, by the very force of the scriptural statement, the purpose of the *Śravaṇadvādaśī* vow and the purpose of the *Ekādaśī* vow are both accomplished through the single fast by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga*), even in the case of the *Viṣṇuśṛṅkhalā* conjunction.

On this point, some say: "If the conjunction with Śravaṇa occurs at the end of the upcoming day or during the night, then, because there is no conjunction [of the asterism] at dawn—according to the rule that 'the wise man should make his formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the fast, vow, and so forth in the morning'—that lunar day is not to be observed as a fast."

That is incorrect, because the entire lunar day (*tithi*) is declared to be meritorious through its conjunction with the *Śravaṇa* asterism. Therefore, just as there is merit even through a past conjunction with *Śravaṇa*, so too does merit exist through a future conjunction with *Śravaṇa*. Consequently, on this eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) joined with the *Viṣṇu-śṛṅkhala* [conjunction], since the day is meritorious at that very moment, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to undertake various *dvādaśī* vows is made. Likewise, regarding fasting under a specific asterism (*nakṣatra-upavāsa*), since the asterism connected to sunset is the one to be fasted upon, and even if it has not yet arrived in the morning, the formal resolve for the vow is appropriate precisely in the morning because the [asterism] is complete. Nor is there any contradiction in that case, as it is declared to be meritorious throughout the entire day and night.
