Therefore, by the logic of the statement: "On which [day] even for a single *muhūrta* during the day or night the Rohiṇī asterism is found conjoined with the eighth [lunar day], one should fast on that most meritorious [day]," the *dvādaśī* itself—merely by virtue of the conjunction with *Śravaṇa*—is designated as the "entirely obtained Vijayā" (*sakalā labdhavijayā*) and is fit for the performance of meritorious rites by those seeking merit.
Now follows the rule regarding the time for breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*). In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"When there is a restriction based on the lunar day (*tithi*) or the asterism (*nakṣatra*), the breaking of the fast occurs at the end of that lunar day."
Otherwise, by breaking the rule for the breaking of the fast, one would incur a violation of the vow.
Likewise: "Whichever lunar days (tithis) are declared meritorious when conjoined with an asterism,
one should perform the breaking of the fast at the end of that asterism, except in the case of Śravaṇa and Rohiṇī."

In the Vahni Purāṇa: "When a vow involving a conjunction of factors is undertaken, if even one of those factors is separated, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at that very moment; thus the knowers of the Vedas understand."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"When a fast occurs on the conjunction of a lunar day and an asterism,
the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) must not be performed until at least one of them has ended."
Thus concludes the determination of Śravaṇadvādaśī. Now follows the determination of Śivarātri, according to the Skanda Purāṇa.

The Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, the Skandaṣaṣṭhī, and the Śivarātri on the fourteenth day—these should be observed when joined with the preceding [tithi]; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place at the end of the lunar day.
Janmāṣṭamī, Rohiṇī, and likewise Śivarātri should be observed when overlapping with the previous lunar day; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place at the end of the lunar day.

The Śrāvaṇī, the Durgā-navamī, as well as the Dūrvā-aṣṭamī, should be observed when joined with the preceding [tithi]; likewise, Śivarātri and Baler dina (the day of Bali) should be observed when joined with Bhadrā and Jayā.
As for Jayantī and Śivarātri, they should be performed when conjoined with Bhadrā and Jayā.
Regarding this, some commentators on the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti* say:

"If this were a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibited fourteenth day joined with the thirteenth, then its scope would be restricted to the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, because that alone is prohibited when joined with the preceding day; whereas in other cases, such as 'the eighth and the fourteenth of the dark fortnight,' etc., it is the preceding day itself that is taken. Alternatively, if this were an exception (*apavāda*) concerning the fast regarding the fourteenth day joined with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), that is incorrect, because no such fasting is heard of in the scriptures.

If it is argued that [the term] is expressed by the word "Śivarātri," then in that case, it would apply only to those instances where fasting is prescribed on the thirteenth day and the vigil (jāgaraṇa) on the fourteenth. Alternatively, if the word "Śivarātri" denotes the vigil itself, then this [text] cannot be an exception [to the rule], because no fasting has been enjoined. [As it is said:
"Having eaten, one may perform the vigil during the Nakta, Candra, and other such purposeful vows."
Therefore, among all vows, the yoga of the night is preeminent.

Since the observance of the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) is prescribed for the [lunar day] joined with the previous [day] alone, this statement would be redundant. If it is argued that this statement serves the same purpose as that [previous rule], we say no; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the term "Śivarātri" is not intended to be significant in the statement. Therefore, where the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) does not exist on the second day, or exists only at the time of sunrise, the [fourteenth] joined with the previous [day] is prohibited; thus, when the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) would otherwise be taken, it is stated: "The Jayantī and Śivarātri should be observed when joined with Bhadrā and Jaya," or else:
The lunar day (tithi) of Ekādaśī, when pierced by five muhūrtas, is indeed to be observed;
on other days, a wise person should fast when they are pierced by half of that duration.

Now, regarding the acceptance of a lunar day (*tithi*) that is pierced by only half [of the previous day], where it is pierced by more [than half], and when the contingency arises of preparing some food—as prescribed by the rule, "But when fasting is prohibited, one should provide some edible"—this is stated: "Jayantī and Śivarātri. When the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) exists on both days, but does not exist on the night of the second day (and since keeping a vigil at night is enjoined), then one should fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and also fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*).
In this case, there is no omission of the injunction, for Hari is the deity of both.
According to this principle, because they share the same deity, the vigil (jāgaraṇa) should be performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) alone, due to their similarity; for as it is said:
"He who, firm in his vows and desiring liberation, constantly worships Śiva on the eighth or the fourteenth [day], shall obtain his desired fruit."
Thus, the Śiva-vrata is observed on the fourteenth day. Likewise:
"On a festival day, having failed to worship the Lord of Gods, the Guru, and the Fire with devotion..."
And having offered the bali-oblation there, one should recite [the mantra] of Śiva one hundred and eight times.

Thus, it is indeed observed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Furthermore, by the term *śivarātri*, fasting (*upavāsa*), worship of Śiva (*śivapūjā*), and keeping vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) are denoted. In the first alternative, whether there are two or one [of these], that which is prescribed for fasting applies equally to the other two as well. In the second alternative, if the two are denoted as distinct from fasting, then since one will occur on the new moon day, the second [night] alone would be intended. The third alternative, however, is tenable. If, in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*), there were a prescription of the specific time denoted by the term *śivarātri* as qualified by its attributes, then when the connection with the fruit of the *śivarātri-vrata* is stated in the injunctive statement of qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*), it would amount to stating the connection with the fruit of keeping vigil. Just as in the case of the originative injunction where, once the connection with time for all six sacrifices is understood, it is determined that "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—meaning that those very six denoted by *darśapūrṇamāsa* are enjoined for the fruit—so too would it be here. But such is not the case. First, regarding the instance where Durvāsas spoke to the hunter:
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, being oppressed by hunger and helpless, he did not obtain even the slightest bit of game for the sake of sustaining his life.
Having begun thus:
"O giver of honor, O lord of the earth, those very bilva leaves struck by the tip of the bow fell upon the head of Śambhu, O great king. [301]
O Great King, he remained right there throughout the entire night without weariness, full of egoism and desiring to catch a deer for the sake of his own belly;
the hunter stood for the remainder of the night with a fixed gaze and a motionless thumb.
Having said, "Thus, the fasting, the worship of Śiva, and the keeping of the vigil have become incidental to you," when the clear dawn had arrived, he saw Śaṅkara and bowed to him;
then, O King of kings, having bathed in the lake and worshipped Maheśvara, he departed.
O best of kings, it was completed with bilva leaves and roots and tubers.

When this much has been stated, by what specific distinction does the Blessed One declare that waking [at dawn] is connected to a single fruit? Furthermore, regarding the Lord’s own words to Pārvatī in the description of the vow (*vrata*) for the month of Māgha, beginning with: "The supreme vow is to be performed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha... and so forth.
O large-eyed one, on the thirteenth day one should observe a single meal;
O beautiful lady, O fair-faced one, one should remain fasting on the fourteenth day.

Having described the worship with bathing, perfumes, flowers, and so forth—beginning from the feet and extending to the adoration of all limbs—through this sequence of textual passages ending with the offering of *arghya* after encircling the cow-dung mandala with rows of lamps, [the text states]:
"O fair-faced one, he is indeed purified of the threefold sin."

Having thus stated this together with its excellence, and having prescribed the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) with the words, “A vigil should be performed there with songs, musical instruments, and auspicious rites,” and having concluded with, “The worship of the watches (*yāma-pūjā*) and bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) should be performed,” [it is established that] wherever there is a specific distinction based on predominance, therefore—according to the principle, “Or the primary [element follows the first injunction], as in common worldly practice”—the performance of all [elements] occurs on the very day of the fast (*upavāsa-dina*), whether all three or two [of them] are predominant in the first two cases.

Regarding the third position, however, in the passage: "By whom the worship of Kīnāśa was performed on the fourteenth [lunar day], as well as the vigil at night," since the vigil is specifically heard of as being at night, while the other [acts] are heard of as being on the fourteenth itself, there is no fault even if the worship is commenced during the day alone in accordance with the fourteenth when the lunar day belongs to the next fortnight. Furthermore, in another Purāṇa it is stated: "The worship of Yama is distinct from the daytime worship; therefore, the commencement of the entire worship should be during the day. In reality, however, these three alone are primary; this is indeed the correct position.
"O Goddess, my devotee who observes the fast on Śivarātri,
having performed it even once, enjoys divine, imperishable, and immortal pleasures, and attains the status of a Gaṇa, which bestows liberation and is a divine decree. Thus [it is said].
Likewise:
"I am pleased with you, a devotee of Bhava who has fasted on Śivarātri;
I grant you a boon that is difficult even for gods and dānavas to obtain."

Following these and other such plural expressions, the fast (*upavāsa*) itself is indeed primary; therefore, because all three are connected to the fruit [of the rite], this supreme vow should be performed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.

Thus, since in this context the term *vrata* (vow) denotes the primary elements, and since the vow is prescribed for the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), and since the "defective" fourteenth day joined with the fifteenth is accepted for fasting while elsewhere only the black fourteenth day joined with the "victory" (*jayā*) is accepted, and since here that [latter case] is impossible, one must necessarily perform the fasting, worship, and vigil on the same single day. When the sublation of either one of these times inevitably occurs, it is proper to sublate the latter—the time for worship and the vigil—because the fasting must be performed even before those two and thus involves no conflict with its own time. Furthermore, while the fasting extends across the entire day and night (*ahorātra*), the worship and vigil, being performed only during a portion of that interval, are not restrictive regarding the lunar date (*tithi*). Even though their status as primary elements is equal, it is logical that they alone should be sublated, rather than the time for fasting, because the latter is not contained within the other. This is seen where the vigil is observed without the fasting, as for example: [203] *...omitted...* [End of excerpt]
“Furthermore, whatever man, even if devoid of specific merit, performs the vigil (jāgara) there, he shall attain equality with Rudra.

In this regard, let there be the acceptance of that [lunar day] which is joined by the preceding one; for it is stated in such passages as, “Having eaten, [one should perform] the vigil and the night-meal (nakta),” and so forth.
Others, however, recite the following from the Purāṇa regarding a matter established by logic:
"O King, if the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha coincides with the fifteenth day."
"One who wishes to do what is pleasing to Śiva should never perform [the rite] on the night of Jayā.
This [argument] is unconvincing.
"Ekādaśī, Aṣṭamī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Caturdaśī in both fortnights, Amāvāsyā, and Tṛtīyā— these are to be observed as fasts when joined with the subsequent [tithis].

By such statements from Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha and others, which are presented in the context of determining the proper lunar day for fasting, just as the fast is prescribed on a Caturdaśī that is overlapped by Amāvāsyā, so too is it prescribed on that same day when it is overlapped by Trayodaśī.

The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight should be observed when they are joined with the preceding lunar day (pūrvaviddhā); they should never be joined with the following day (paraviddhā). This is the eternal law regarding the times for fasting.

Thus it is stated in the Nigama scripture; and since there is no distinction [otherwise], the fourteenth day of Śivarātri is taken as being joined with the preceding [tithi], by virtue of such previously cited statements as: "The Śivarātri rite should be performed on Jayantī when it is conjoined with Bhadrā. For this very reason, the primacy of the night for the Śivarātri vow is proclaimed in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Since spirits and powers wander about at night because [the Lord] holds the trident,
therefore, when that fourteenth day occurs, there should be worship of him.

"They wander at night" means "they roam. "The Śaktis" refers to the goddesses. "The Trident-bearer" is Śaṅkara; therefore, when that fourteenth day occurs, there is the worship of those Bhūtas, Śaktis, and Śivas. [This is stated] in the Nāgarakhaṇḍa.
O Lord of the Gods, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha,
I shall go to the surface of the earth at night, and not by day, during the Kali age.
And into all lingas, whether moving or stationary,
I shall undoubtedly enter for the sake of purifying the sins of the year.
Therefore, O best of gods, that man who shall perform my worship at night with these mantras will become free from sin.
Likewise: "The fourteenth day of Śiva that falls between the months of Māgha and Phālguna,
being conjoined with Anaṅga (the god of love), that lunar day should always be observed."
‘Agaṅga’ refers to the thirteenth lunar day. As for the statement:
“O King, if the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha coincides with the fifteenth day...”
One who desires to do what is pleasing to Śiva should never, under any circumstances, abandon the night sacred to Śiva.

"Jayā" refers to the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), and not that night during which the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*) is joined with the thirteenth. Thus, in this very statement, it is understood as "the night joined with Jayā.
Likewise, in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"O Goddess, when the thirteenth [lunar day] lasts for the duration of a daytime meal..."
The Śivarātri fast occurs during the night when the fourteenth lunar day is full.

By this it is stated that when the fourteenth night is not mixed with the thirteenth, but rather extends to the full duration of the day according to the measure of daytime consumption, then the vigil, fasting, and so forth should be performed. And thus, since the conjunction with *jayā* on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha is prohibited: "If the conjunction with *jayā* should occur before midnight, Śivarātri must be observed as joined to the preceding [day] by those dear to Śiva."

Some maintain that this statement refers to occasions other than the month of Māgha; for it is prescribed that the fast may be observed even on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight outside of Māgha during the Śivarātri vow, stating:
"One should undertake [the vow] at the beginning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the day of the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava), or in the month of Māgha; thus one should fast for twelve [years]."
By such [statements as these]:
"Or else, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha during the Festival of Lamps (dīpotsava),
one should perform the vigil (jāgara) here throughout all twelve months."
This is because the observance of the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) is also prescribed by the statement from the *Sahyādrikhaṇḍa*.

That is incorrect; for even though fasting is prescribed on a fourteenth day other than that of the month of Māgha, it is not designated by the term "Śivarātri," since the word "Śivarātri" is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) as referring specifically to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
And so it is stated in the *Skandapurāṇa*:

The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight between the months of Māgha and Phālguna is known as Śivarātri; it is the most excellent among all sacrifices. On that very point, it is also stated in the Sahyādrikhaṇḍa:
Because the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight between the months of Māgha and Phālguna bestows the fruit of Śiva,
it is renowned as Śivarātri by all the gods and asuras; it is my own form existing separately.
Likewise: "That which is the first fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, occurring at the end of the month of Māgha, is proclaimed as Śivarātri."
Also in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"The fourteenth lunar day (*tithi*) that falls in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha—
its night is declared to be the origin of Śivarātri."
In that [city], Hara always moves through all the lingas.
And likewise, in that very same work, regarding the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, it is said:
"Whatever lingas there may be here, whether mobile or immobile,
the Lord Hara transfers himself into them during that night."
Therefore, it is called Śivarātri; for that reason, it is beloved by Hara.
In the *Śivarahasya*: "O celestial sage, from that time forward, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha has become renowned as Śivarātri; it is dear to the enemy of Tripura."

Therefore, the determination of the subject matter here is as follows: when the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) extends across both days during the evening (*pradoṣa*), or when it occurs on the first day alone and the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) covers the full duration of the day, then the former [fourteenth day] alone is taken, according to the statement: "When the goddess [is present] on the thirteenth... When the fourteenth day extends across the evening on the first day alone and the thirteenth day covers the full duration of the day, then the former alone is taken. One should observe the fast for that Śivarātri fourteenth day which extends across the evening, because the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) takes place at night; therefore, one should fast upon it.
Thus it is stated in the scripture.

Now, if on the second day alone the [lunar day] extends through the *pradoṣa* period, then how is the decision to be made: is the earlier [day] to be accepted according to the statement, "If [it occurs] before midnight," or is the later [day] to be accepted according to the statement, "[It is the one] extending through *pradoṣa*"?

It is said: although the statement, "If [the fourteenth day] is before midnight," is applicable even when there is no pervasion of the *pradoṣa* period on the second day, and the statement, "[the day] pervading *pradoṣa*," is likewise applicable even when there is no conjunction with *Jayā* after midnight—nevertheless, in such a case, if one were to accept the second *caturdaśī*, it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of restricting the many statements previously cited that establish the *pūrvaviddha* Śivarātri; whereas if the first Śivarātri is accepted, that consequence does not arise. Therefore, that [first one] alone is to be accepted. Furthermore, since the former pervades the time for many ritual acts (*bahukarmakāla*) while the latter does not, that [first one] alone is to be accepted. When, however, the fourteenth day is absent during the *pradoṣa* period on both days, then by the rule, "If [it is] before midnight," the former alone is taken. As for the statement regarding the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, that serves to prohibit the conjunction with *Jayā* after midnight upon consideration of these sentences. The determination of the dark *caturdaśī* other than the one included within the Māgha-month Śivarātri vow is as follows: because of the rule, "The eleventh, eighth, and sixth [are to be taken pure]," it would follow that it is pierced by the new moon (*amāvāsyā*); yet, because of the rule, "In the dark fortnight, the eighth [is taken with the preceding]," it is pierced by the thirteenth (*trayodaśī*). When such a conflict arises, since worship is prescribed for the four watches (*yāma*) of the night and the practice of keeping vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) is prescribed, one should accept the day that pervades the time for the many ritual acts in accordance with those [prescriptions]. But when there is a distinction based on the pervasion of the specific time for that ritual act, then:
In all observances dedicated to Rudra, the lunar day (tithi) should be observed as it occurs face-to-face with the sun;
in other ritual procedures for vows, one should fast on the previously specified day.
Thus is the conclusion based on the statement from the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*.
On this point, some say:
"When the new moon day is sufficient for the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*), then the preceding [day] is [to be taken]; if not, then the following."
Having eaten during the day on the eighth lunar days of the bright and dark fortnights, having eaten at night on a festival day (parvan),
or having eaten both day and night on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, because of the prohibition against eating:
"O Goddess, when the thirteenth day [extends] according to the measure of daytime eating, Śivarātri shall occur during the vigil; [but] if the fourteenth day is full during the night..."

‘According to the measure of daytime eating’ means in accordance with the mealtime of the day; that thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) on which, when fasted upon, the prescribed breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at the end of the lunar period would not be possible at night is here referred to as ‘according to the measure of daytime eating.’

That is incorrect, because the word *bhukti*—just like the word *bhojana* (eating)—is established in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) even when referring to the occurrence of time, as in expressions such as “the *bhukti* of the lunar day, asterism, and weekday,” and so forth. Furthermore, if the word *bhukti* were taken to mean eating, there would be the undesirable consequence of a restriction [implied by the rule] “if it occurs before midnight”; however, if it is taken to mean the occupation of time, there is no such restriction. Therefore, it is this [occupation of time] alone that is expressed here by the word *bhukti*. Moreover, regarding the statement “when the goddess Trayodaśī [extends]...”, the meaning—that the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*), which is prescribed at the end of the lunar day, should be performed on the previous day when it is possible during the daytime—cannot be obtained without the difficulty of resorting to secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and other such devices. Furthermore, in your position, by the word “day” (*dina*), one would have to abandon the day connected with the proximate Trayodaśī and instead accept another day; for if it is said that when the Trayodaśī, which serves as the measure for eating on the second day, occurs on the previous day, then the full Caturdaśī occurring at night should be accepted, it would follow that whenever the Trayodaśī is limited to a duration of only a few *ghaṭikās* suitable for a meal, then the Caturdaśī overlapping with the previous day must be observed. Consequently, this would contradict the previously cited scriptural statements. If it is argued that the Trayodaśī on which eating is possible during the day after having fasted should be accepted, that too is not correct, because eating during the day is possible on every Trayodaśī once one has fasted.
Now, when a meal prescribed for the end of a lunar day (tithi) occurs during the daytime, then the preceding [time] should be taken.

That is not so, because it would entail [the application of] secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and because there is no sublation even in the case of eating at night. This is because a prohibition has as its object eating that is prompted by desire; for when what is prompted by desire is obtained and is touched by a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), a prohibition does not apply, lest there arise the undesirable consequences of a conflict between injunctions or an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of the killing of the Agniṣomīya animal and similar rites. This has been established in the discussion concerning the determination of the time for oil-massage and other such acts. Therefore, in order to avoid all these defects, it is proven that by the word *bhukti* (eating) only the pervasion of the time is expressed, and not the act of eating itself. And thus, regarding the Śivarātri, upon a comprehensive examination of all the scriptural statements, the hypothetical arrangement proposed by the commentator on the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti* is to be rejected. Furthermore, without any valid reason, there would result the sublation of the time for the worship of Śiva and the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*). Moreover, since it has been demonstrated that even the fast (*upavāsa*) is to be observed on the day joined with the preceding [tithi], and because it would entail the contraction of a great many scriptural statements, the term "Śivarātri" denotes the fast, the worship, and the vigil, as all three are perceived to be equally primary.
And so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In this manner, having fasted for twelve years observing the Śivarātri vow,
that man who keeps me awake during the night shall ascend to heaven."
He who worships Śiva and remains awake on the fourteenth day shall never again drink the milk from his mother’s breast.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "By the power of fasting and even by forceful vigilance,
one should likewise worship that *liṅga* on Śivarātri."
Then, having obtained the great kingdom of his father and grandfather, he...
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Having worshipped the self-manifested Liṅga while fasting and keeping a vigil,
even though he was unaware [of its power], the Niṣāda became free from sin and attained the state of a member of the Gaṇas."
Other statements as well, which establish the preeminence of these three, have been cited previously.

Thus [ends the section] in the work composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the sovereign of all the illustrious administrative offices of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
The determination of Śivarātri, within the section on the determination of time in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, is completed.
[311] Now follows the determination of the time for the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvan*).
In that regard, the *parvan* is twofold: the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). And their essential nature has been shown by Gobhila.
"That which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon is the full moon day (paurṇamāsī); that which is the closest proximity is the new moon day (amāvāsya). And another Smṛti states:
"When the moon should rise after the sun has set, that is the full moon day."
Regarding that, the etymological definition of *pūrṇimā* is found in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* and the *Matsya-purāṇa*:
"When the moon and the sun, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga,
gaze at each other fully in the afternoon, she is remembered as *pūrṇimā* because of her fullness (*pūrṇatvāt*)."
The etymological definition of *amāvāsyā* is found in the *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa*.

Those gods said, "Truly, he does not dwell at home today; he who has blown upon us no longer dwells [with us]. Having begun thus, they said, "The gods said, 'He shall certainly not be deprived of Soma for a year. Let us gather Soma for him. They gathered Soma for him. This King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon. When, on that night, he is seen neither in the east nor in the west, he comes to this world. He enters here the waters and the plants. He is indeed the food of the gods, for that which he dwells here as *amā* (at home) during that night is why it is called *Amāvāsyā*."

Regarding this, there are two etymologies for *amāvāsyā*: in the first sentence, it is explained that because the gods met with Indra—who had returned after his departure following the slaying of Vṛtra—they dwelt together (*amā saha nivasāt*) on that night, hence it is called *amāvāsyā*; in the second sentence, however, it is explained that because the moon (*vasu*), being in this world on this night, dwells together with it, it is called *amāvāsyā*.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Those known as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs are performers of sacrifice who are established in ritual."
Their mind-born daughter was a river named Acchodā.
Then, seeing her father named Amāvasu, she approached him;
seeking a boon, she chose him as her husband because of the torment caused by the flower-armed god of love.
But because that beautiful woman had fallen from yoga due to that transgression,
she first failed to touch the earth and then fell down upon the surface of the ground.
On whichever lunar day he formed the desire [to create], it was not directed toward that [specific] day;
yet by his power, it became renowned in the world as Amāvāsyā,
because it is beloved by the ancestors and renders what is given inexhaustible.

The purport of this *itihāsa* is as follows: she is called *Amāvāsyā* because her greatness is well-known for destroying pride and impatience, which cause the fall from the celibacy (*brahmacarya*) favored by the host of ancestors who are supreme self-restrainers.
This is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The ray of the Sun named *Amā*, standing at the head of the thousand [rays]..."
By whose splendor the sun is said to be the illuminator of the three worlds,
into that [splendor] the moon enters, whereby it is therefore known as the new moon (amāvāsyā).
In the Matsya, Vāyu, and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas:
"When the moon and the sun dwell together among the constellations,
this fifteenth night is therefore called Amāvāsyā."
The meaning is "together with the new moon.
From the Skanda and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas:
"The ray of the sun named Amā is established in the world of the Moon."
Therefore, Soma dwells in her on that new-moon day; hence she is called Amāvāsyā.
In the Matsya and Vāyu Purāṇas: "When the moon and the sun, having resorted to that new-moon day, behold each other's conjunction, that is then called *darśa*."
In the Bhagavatīpurāṇa: "The Sun increases the sixteen digits of the Moon during the bright fortnight;
during the dark fortnight, the nectar is consumed by the gods in succession through the nectar."
Agni drinks the first digit; Tapanas drinks the second digit;
the Viśvedevas drink the third, and Prajāpati drinks the fourth.
Varuṇa drinks the fifth, and Vāsava drinks the sixth;
the divine Ṛṣis drink the seventh, and likewise the eight Vasus drink the eighth.
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight, the Moon drinks even a single digit;
on the tenth, the Maruts drink it; and on the eleventh, Rudra drinks the digit.
Time drinks the twelfth digit; the Lord of Wealth drinks the thirteenth;
and Paśupati constantly drinks the fourteenth digit.
Then, on the fifteenth day, the ancestors drink that very digit;
when only a fraction remains and has been drunk, it enters the solar orb.
Because he enters [the moon] on the *amā*, it is therefore remembered as *amāvāsyā*;
in the forenoon he enters the sun, and at midday he enters the lord of the forest (fire).
In the afternoon, the water-born moon enters the waters, its own source;
having entered the new moon (*amā*) with a single remaining digit,
it produces the herbs— grass, shrubs, creepers, and trees.
The cows graze upon the land where the Tamoṣadhi plant grows, and they drink its waters.
Following that process, the milkiness arises from the cows;
that milk, having become nectar and purified by mantras, the twice-born offer as oblations in sequence with the utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*.
The Soma offered into the fires for Soma increases the Soma further;
thus the Soma wanes, and having waned, it is replenished again.
And those two, the full moon and the new moon, are of two kinds according to the Purāṇa:
Rākā and Anumati are remembered as the two types of Paurṇamāsī;
and Sinīvālī and Kuhū are the two types of Amāvāsyā.
In this context, Anumati and Sinīvālī occur when [the moon] is mixed with the fourteenth day, while Rākā and Kuhū occur when it is mixed with the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Thus says the Kāṭhaka Śruti: "That which is the full moon is Anumati; that which follows it is Rākā. That which is the prior new moon is Sinīvālī; that which follows it is Kuhū."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
They know that there are two full-moon days, namely Rākā and Anumati.
Rākā is that [day] when the moon is completely full, while Anumati is traditionally held to be that when it is deficient by a digit.
Furthermore, when that same [lunar mansion] is seen at night, it is celebrated as Rākā.
In the *Bhagavatīpurāṇa*: "When the sun has set and the full moon has arrived simultaneously, that night with the moon in the Uttarās is then called Pūrṇimā."
In the Matsya and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas:
"Because the ancestors, together with the deities, give their approval (anumanyante) to it,
therefore this first full-moon day is remembered by the name Anumati."
Because the moon shines exceedingly on the night of the full moon,
and because it delights [the world], the poets know her as Rākā.
The elder Vasiṣṭha says:
They call that new moon day Sinīvālī on which the moon is visible;
the great seers call that same day Kuhū when the moon has disappeared.
In the *Matsya-purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"The moon, having waned until only a remnant remains, enters the sun on the new moon day; therefore it is known as Sinīvālī."

*Sinī* means white, that is to say, covered with hair; *vālī* means having little hair. Thus, she who is both *sinī* and *vālī* is *sinīvālī*. "The size of *sinīvālī*" means the measure of a single hair-tip.
*Kuhū* refers to the duration of time indicated by the cry of a cuckoo; for this new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is traditionally known as *kuhū*, being named after that specific interval of time.
Likewise, the time for Anumati is said to be two lava-s until the end;
the afternoon time for Rākā should be known as exactly two lava-s.
Likewise: "Two *lava*s of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) constitute that time at the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*);
however, the time of the phase (*parvakāla*) is traditionally held to consist of two syllables, being merely the moment of *kuhū*."
Likewise: Anumati, Rākā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū—
of these, the time for two *lava*s is known as *Kuhū*, which is measured by a *kāhū*.
Thus, this time of the junctures between the lunar phases (parvan-sandhi) is indeed recorded as being two lavas in duration.
In the Bhagavatīpurāṇa: "Of Anumati, Rākā, and Sinīvālī—excluding Kuhū—their time is two lavas each; Kuhū alone is said to be of the measure of a single lava."

In that context, the injunction "one should sacrifice at the juncture" (*sandhau yajeta*) means that the sacrifice is to be performed at the juncture. Since the juncture itself is extremely subtle and thus unfit for the performance of ritual action, the word "juncture" (*sandhi*) indicates by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) the preceding and succeeding time which are suitable for the performance of the ritual action proximate to its own primary meaning. Objection: But in the phrase "one should sacrifice toward the juncture" (*sandhim abhiyajeta*), the word *abhi* has the sense of "above" or "upon"; since the sacrifice is to be performed on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), it is understood that the sacrifice must be performed after the juncture. Therefore, it would follow that the sacrifice cannot take place at a time prior to the juncture.

This is not a fault, because particles have multiple meanings; thus, the meaning of the sentence is "one should sacrifice aiming at the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) that is proximate. Otherwise, in the case of the word *abhiyajeta* [in the phrase] *pratipadam*, there would be the undesirable consequence of taking it to mean "afterwards" (*upari*). For if the *pratipad* had passed, it would follow that one must sacrifice on the second day, which is after that. Therefore, the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) "one should sacrifice at the conjunction" prescribes the sacrifice with respect to the time consisting of the preceding and following moments. For this very reason, another scripture states: "One should sacrifice around the conjunction. Thus says Baudhāyana.
Because the time of transition is subtle, it is called the "domain" (viṣaya) of the transition;
the ancients say that proximity is the domain, whether with what precedes or what follows.

Consequently, when the time for the performance of the ritual with all its constituent parts has arrived immediately following the *saṃdhi* (the junction), the Śruti prescribes a rule regarding the two days by way of a fixed arrangement: "On the previous day he prepares the fuel and the sacrificial grass; on the following day, having taken hold of them, he observes the fast. Likewise: "On the previous day he takes the fire; on the subsequent day he sacrifices. Gobhila also states that those two days are connected to the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and the full-moon/new-moon juncture (*parvan*): "The ends of the fortnights are to be observed as days of fasting; the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon."

The "ends of the fortnights" (*pakṣāntāḥ*) are the fifteenth days; on those days, the rites beginning with the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) should be performed. The "beginnings of the fortnights" (*pakṣādayaḥ*) are the first days (*pratipad*). This is the traditional teaching (*nigama*):
"One who contemplates the fortnights should perform the sacrifice at the end of one fortnight and at the beginning of the other."
The followers of Laugākṣi say: "The first and the last days of the fortnights are fit for sacrifice. Thus says Kātyāyana.
"Or [the phrase] 'at the beginning of the fortnight' refers to this," says Bharadvāja;
"for the beginnings of the fortnights are those that ought to be sacrificed upon."
Āpastamba also states:
"The initiation takes place on the new moon day, or on the day of the sacrifice following the full moon; the day of the Soma pressing is on the day of the sacrifice following the full moon.
Thus, he declares that the day following the full moon or the new moon—namely, the *pratipad*—is the day for the sacrifice.
Laugākṣi has shown a specific distinction here:
"They know that of the fast-day sacrifice there are four parts;
one should omit the last two parts, for they are the 'ears of the vow' in the journey."

[318] Regarding the *aupavasta* (the fast), they know it to have three parts; regarding the sacrifice (*yāga*), they know it to have four parts. One should "abandon" (*utsṛjet*) the "last two parts," namely the junctions of the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) and the first day (*pratipad*). One should abandon the last part of the fifteenth day for the ritual of the vow (*vrata-karman*), and the fourth part of the first day for the sacrifice. Others, however, citing the reading "one should abandon the other two parts," explain: the first quarter of the fifteenth day must be avoided in the fast (*upavāsa*) and the fire-consecration (*anvādhāna*), etc., while the final quarter of the first day of the lunar fortnight must be avoided in the sacrifice. This applies to cases other than when the fifteenth day is complete, because the fire-consecration is performed only during the first quarter of that day. Others, however, explaining this very same reading, state that since there is no reason to skip the first [quarter], the final quarter of the fifteenth day must be avoided in the ritual of the vow. And this applies to cases other than the *sadyaskālā* Full Moon sacrifice, because that is performed precisely on the fourth part of the *parvan*. How then [should one act] regarding the sacrifice having four parts? To this, Yajñapārśva [responds]:
The final quarter of the fifteenth day and the first three quarters of the first day of the lunar fortnight constitute the time for the *parvan* sacrifice; otherwise, it does not exist.
Kātyāyana says: "One should never perform sacrifices on the fourth part of the *pratipad*; the Rākṣasas plunder that [offering]. This is the eternal Vedic injunction."
Likewise:
"When three parts have passed away and only one part remains, that [fire] is to be known as spent; for no oblation is offered into ashes."

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the Vedic injunction (*śruti*) stating "one should sacrifice at the junction (*saṃdhi*)" when the time for the Smṛti-observance—such as the fourth part of the *parvan* day—is observed; for since the junction is extremely subtle, the performance of the ritual with all its constituent parts (*sāṅgaprayoga*) is impossible therein. Thus, the Smṛti rule refers to the limit of the vicinity of the junction required by the Vedic injunction. Nor should it be argued that the duration during which one is able to sacrifice is already established by the force of the injunction regarding the junction itself, making a separate prescription of a limit redundant. For if the determination were left solely to capacity, then for someone unable to complete the performance until the fifth *muhūrta* due to a lack of materials or other factors, the limit would have been reached at the fifth *muhūrta*. Consequently, rites such as the *pathikṛt* and *vaiśvānara*—which are prescribed for the occasion of a lapse in time (*kālātikrama*)—would not apply. Nor can it be said that the capacity of one who is able to complete the rite quickly serves to define the limit of proximity, and therefore others too must sacrifice there; for if that were so, one who completes it in four *muhūrtas* (when another could do it in three) would incur a lapse in time, leading to the undesirable consequence of the application of the *pathikṛt* and other such rites. Therefore, because capacity is not fixed in its measure, it cannot define the limit of proximity; thus, it is the Smṛti statement alone that defines the limit. For this very reason, Baudhāyana stated: "Indeed, the junction is not easily established. Moreover, even though an injunction is capable of implying a specific detail on its own, it accepts a specific detail brought forward by a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Just as in the sentence "He places the anointed pebbles," it accepts clarified butter (*ghṛta*) presented by the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), or as in "One should sacrifice with an animal," it accepts the goat (*chāga*) presented by the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇa*), so too here, the injunction "One should sacrifice at the junction" accepts the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth—which define the junction—as presented by the Vedic and Smṛti texts. Therefore, one should sacrifice at the time of the fourth part of the *parvan* and so on. Regarding this, some hold that the two Vedic injunctions—"One should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering] on the full moon"—and "One should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering] on the new moon"—refer to the junction defined by those times. Others, however, explain it as the fourth part of the *parvan*. Even so, the sacrifice must be performed during the day, because of the prescription of the day: "On the previous day he takes the fire; on the following day he sacrifices to the deity. To this effect is the Saṃkarṣaṇa-sūtra: "Or [the sacrifice is] on the day; it has been explained. Even then, it should be in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) alone, according to the Vedic text: "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods. Even then, it should be in the morning (*prātar*), according to the statement of Vṛddha-Śātātapa: "That which is the fourth part of the *parvan* and the first three parts of the *pratipad* should be known as the time for sacrifice, declared by the wise to be 'morning'"; and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "Sacrifice in the morning to the Aśvins"; and from the text: "May the Aṅgirases protect this sacrifice with the morning recitations (*prātaranuvāka*)," and "He should not eat in the evening of that day on which he intends to sacrifice in the morning," which establishes the connection of the sacrifice with the morning time. Likewise, Kātyāyana has stated: "Either immediately or in the morning," indicating the immediate time (*sadyaskāla*). Furthermore, another Vedic text states: "One should sacrifice where the sun rises in front of him after it has set behind him," from which it is understood that one should sacrifice at the time of sunrise. Āpastamba has stated that the procedure (*tantra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice begins only after sunrise: "When the sun has risen, he commences the procedure of the Full Moon [sacrifice]. As for the statement that the procedure of the New Moon sacrifice is performed before sunrise—"Before sunrise on the New Moon day"—that refers merely to the commencement before sunrise, not to the actual performance of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) itself; for if the performance were before sunrise, it would contradict the prescription of the day.
On this point, Gobhila states:

"There are three times for the full moon sacrifice: at twilight, or when the moon has risen after sunset, or when the moon rises high above the twilight. When the moon rises while the sun has set during twilight, that is the time; one should fast during that [latter] one. Likewise..."
"One should fast on the full moon of the twilight [month] until the following [full moon]," so say some. And there is another Smṛti:
"A wise man should observe the preceding [fast] when the moon has risen even a fraction deficient."
The word "one should fast" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Kātyāyana states:
"One should fast on both the preceding and the following full moon days."

In that regard, if the junction of the *parvan* occurs during the day, there is fasting on the preceding day and the sacrifice on that same day; if the junction of the *parvan* occurs at night, there is fasting on that same day and the sacrifice on the following day. And so says Baudhāyana:

Regarding this, he cites an example: after midnight on the full-moon day, the moon begins to wax; it remains full during that latter part of the night and throughout the entire day until midnight of the following night, which is the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*) for the new moon. After midday on that day, the sun overtakes the moon; it remains so during that afternoon and throughout the entire following day until midday. One should perform the sacrifice at this juncture.

The meaning of this is as follows: "In this regard, he cites a scriptural passage"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. "On the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām*) is the specification of the subject; "the moon is filled after midnight," which means that the full moon period (*paurṇamāsī*) commences. "He [the moon] continues through this latter part of the night," and subsequently "through the entire day," and "until midnight of the following night"; it persists until then and thereafter ceases—this is what is called the "conjunction of the night. Now, regarding the new moon (*amāvāsyā*): "on the day of the fast (*aupavasathīye ahani*), that is, on the day before the day of sacrifice, 'the sun takes over from the moon after midday,' meaning the new moon period (*amāvāsyā*) commences. He [the moon] continues through this latter part of the day, then through the entire night, and until midday of the following day"; it persists until then, and thereafter the first lunar day (*pratipad*) begins—this is what is called the "conjunction of the day. Having performed the ritual preparation of the fires (*anvādhāna*) on the day prior to this conjunction, one should sacrifice on the following day. Likewise, aiming for such a "conjunction of the day," one should sacrifice on that very morning.
Having thus cited the scriptural passage, he says— intending to explain the terms "midnight" (*madhyarātra*) and "midday" (*madhyandina*) as they occur therein—
"The night that occurs on the full moon is the junction, and the day [that occurs] on the new moon is the junction.
By this, it is established that the terms "midnight" and "midday" occurring in the scripture are intended to indicate the junctions of night and the junctions of day.
And the subsequent sūtra is intended to show that these two scriptural passages concerning the full moon and new moon days are illustrative in nature:
"There are two full moons and two new moons; [one should perform the sacrifice on] each preceding full moon and each succeeding new moon."

This is the meaning: there are two full-moon days (*paurṇamāsī*) characterized by the junction of night and the junction of day, and two new-moon days (*amāvāsyā*) characterized by the junction of day and the junction of night; among these, the junction of day belongs to the preceding new-moon or full-moon day, while the junction of night belongs to the subsequent one. Here, although the preceding new-moon day was mentioned and not the full-moon day, he expresses that [full-moon day] by way of a comparison: "the preceding, preceding full-moon day. The meaning is this: one should understand the preceding full-moon day to be like the preceding new-moon day. Consequently, it is established that on the full-moon day characterized by the junction of day, the sacrifice is performed and the fast is observed on the preceding day. Likewise, although the subsequent full-moon day was mentioned and not the new-moon day, he defines that full-moon day by saying: "the subsequent, subsequent new-moon day. This means one should understand the subsequent new-moon day to be like the subsequent full-moon day. Therefore, the meaning is that one should place the junction between the new-moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), which occurs during the night, between the fast and the sacrifice.

Āpastamba, however, says: "On whichever day the moon should rise full before [the end of the period], one should fast on that day as the *paurṇamāsī*, or when [one thinks] 'it will be full tomorrow'; the followers of the Vājasaneya school prescribe the third [day] as the *kharvikā*. On whichever day it is not seen, that day is the *amāvāsyā*, or when [one thinks] 'it will not be seen tomorrow'."

The meaning of the *kharvikā-sūtras* will be explained further below. Regarding the two sūtras, "On the day when the moon rises full in the east" and "On the day when it is not seen," this is their meaning: It is well known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) that the moon is always full during the *rākā* (full-moon) and entirely invisible during the *kuhū* (new-moon). If on the day when the moon rises full in the east—or when it is not seen—the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*) occurs in the afternoon or at night, then one should fast on that full-moon (*paurṇamāsī*) or new-moon (*amāvāsyā*) day. However, if the junction of the lunar phases occurs in the forenoon or at midday, then one should fast on the day when the moon becomes "filled" (full), or on the day when its observers would not see it; that is, one should fast on that *anumati* or *sinīvālī* day. The meaning of the two sūtras, "Tomorrow it will be full" and "Tomorrow there will be no observers," is as follows. And this has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*:
If the full-moon day (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night, then that Rākā day should be observed as a fast; it is characterized by the "overflowing of the full moon."
If the lunar festival (parvan) concludes either in the forenoon or at midday,
Anumati is to be observed as the fast-day there, characterized by its completion on the following day.

If the junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi) should occur in the afternoon or at night, then the new moon day (kuhū) must be observed as the fast-day; the definition "on whichever day it does not [end]" applies here.
When the junction of the lunar phases occurs either in the forenoon or at midday,
one should fast on that *sinīvālī* day, for the characteristic [of the moon] will not be visible on the following day.
Thus it has been stated by the commentators:
"If the full-moon day (parvan) concludes either in the afternoon or at night, then that day is to be observed as a fast;
for the full moon is characterized by its upward increase."
If a festival day (parvan) concludes either in the forenoon or at midday, one should fast on the preceding day;
that [preceding day] is characterized as being completed on the following day.
If a festival (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night, one should fast on that day;
however, if it does not possess the defining characteristics [of a full day], one should fast on the day [the festival actually occurs].
If the parvan ends either in the forenoon or at midday, then one should fast on that day when the moon is characterized by its not being visible tomorrow; such is the nature of Sinīvālī.
The *Gṛhyakārikā* also states:

"If the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) and the first day (*pratipad*) coincide on a single day, that [fifteenth day] is 'great' (*mahatī*); in that case, the fast (*upavāsa*) belongs to the nature of the fifteenth day, while the sacrifice (*yāga*) belongs to the thin [first] day.
Likewise, it was stated by Govinda Upādhyāya in the *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*:

On a day when the conjunction of the moon’s phases (*vikrama*) and the conjunction of the lunar mansions (*sannipāta*) occurs precisely at midday, the fast is observed on the preceding day; this is the scope for the scriptural injunctions: “Tomorrow the moon will be full,” or “Tomorrow it will not be seen. Where the conjunction of the phases and the conjunction of the mansions occurs in the afternoon or at night, the fast is observed on that very day; this is the scope for the injunctions: “The day on which the moon rises full in the east,” and “The day on which it is not seen.
This has also been stated by Devasvāmin.

If the junction of the lunar day (parvasandhi) should conclude in the forenoon, then it is most excellent; however, if it occurs in the afternoon or at night, one should fast on that day and perform the sacrifice on the following day.
Thus says Laugākṣi:
"If the junction of the lunar day concludes in the forenoon or at midday..."
Having fasted there on the preceding day, the sacrifice is intended for that very day.
If the festival day (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night, one should fast on that day;
the sacrifice is prescribed for the following morning.

Regarding this, some say that because there is no other restrictive statement concerning the twilight (*sandhyā*) at the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*), and because the word "night" (*rātri*) is generally employed there as well, that [twilight] too is included by the term "night.

That is incorrect, because there is no reason for the twilight and the night not to be distinguished, and because the performance of the sacrifice on the previous day during the twilight at the junction of the phases is already established by the very statement: "When the junction occurs [on the previous day]. By this, the two scriptural passages—"He should indeed fast immediately [at the junction]" and "He should indeed fast on the later [day]"—are also explained.
In the bright fortnight, the lunar day (tithi) is to be known as that on which the sun rises;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day is to be known as that on which the sun sets.

Statements such as these, which are established according to specific positions, refer to other lunar days (*tithi*). As for the statement, "The earlier, the earlier, the more meritorious the sacrifice," this explains that when the time prescribed by scripture has arrived, the more one sacrifices at the earlier [moment], the more praiseworthy it is; thus, it prohibits delay within that very same time. It does not, however, mean that the preceding day is praiseworthy in disregard of the prescribed time. If that were the case, then even on lunar days such as the fourteenth (*caturdaśī*), the more one performs the sacrifice on the subsequent day, the more exceedingly praiseworthy it would become. Therefore, the determination [of the proper time] is correctly made according to the divisions of the *parvan* junctions, such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so forth.

On this point, some say that by resorting to a threefold division of the day into forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and midday (*madhyāhna*), five *muhūrtas* each are to be understood here. But [one might object]: "In the case of the threefold division, if the junction of the lunar day (*parvan*) occurs during the final *ghaṭikā* of midday, then because the fourth part of the *parvan* would not exist during the morning, the sacrifice would fall into the third division [of the day]. In that case, the fourth part of the *parvan* consists of the first three *ghaṭikās* of the following day (*pratipad*).
That time of morning is to be known as the proper time for sacrifice, as declared by the wise.
This [statement] is contradicted.

That is incorrect. If it is asked, "How can there be an absence of the fourth part of the *parvan* at the time of morning, since the time of morning consists of only three *muhūrtas*?"—from where [is this known]? [It is said:
"But from the first appearance of the sun's rays, there are indeed only three *muhūrtas*."
But that which is remembered as morning is the fifth part of the day.

If it is argued that this is because of such a statement, we say no; for that [statement] relies on the position of a fivefold division [of the day]. Here, however, the morning time is defined as precisely that which is delimited by the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), since in the Vedic scripture cited by the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*: "By the Ṛgvedic hymns the divine Sun moves in the sky at dawn; by the Yajurveda he stands in the middle of the day; by the Sāmaveda he is glorified at sunset; with the three Vedas the Sun proceeds, never lacking them."

Thus, the entire period prior to midday is understood as the morning (*prātaḥkāla*). If there were another interval of time between the morning and midday, then while the Sun arrives at the times of morning, midday, and sunset accompanied by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas respectively, he would have to arrive during that intermediate period devoid of Vedas. In that case, the statement, “The Sun comes accompanied by the three Vedas, never devoid of them,” would be contradicted. Furthermore, from the variant reading in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), “by the *Ṛg* verses in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*)”, one understands the identity of the morning and the forenoon; for this very reason, after describing the first watch (*prahara*), the Smārta authorities say: “That same [watch], when joined with half [more], is designated as ‘morning’. Even so, if the morning were distinct from the forenoon, then a sacrifice commenced during that [morning] would take place in the forenoon. And as they also say: “It is declared that the deity is ‘morning’ (*prātar deva*); that [distinction] is not tenable.”

That too is intended only with reference to the commencement [of the rite]. If the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*) is a portion of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), then the term "morning" (*prātar*) is used in both statements with the intention of denoting the forenoon; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti: "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors. "They always perform the *caru* offering at the beginning of the fortnight (*pakṣādau*)";
"Others, however, who are wise, perform it in the forenoon even if [the day] is pierced [by an inauspicious conjunction]."

This is because of the statements of Kātyāyana and others; and also because it is seen in the passage, "Now, that which one offers in the morning before sunrise. In the sixth chapter, Jaimini stated: "Rites for the gods are to be performed during the northern course of the sun, during the bright fortnight, and on auspicious days, because of the observation of other purposes [in the texts]. Regarding this, the Commentator pointed out the observation of another purpose: "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods. And the teacher Karka said: "The New Moon sacrifice is to be performed in the forenoon. By this, the verse beginning with "In the morning, the wise have declared... is explained. Thus, it is established that in the context of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, there is a threefold division [of the day].

That is incorrect; for in this context, they say that the "forenoon" and "afternoon" refer to the intended divisions of the two parts—the preceding and succeeding portions—of what is divided into two.
However, the forenoon is prior to the turning point (āvartanā), while the afternoon follows it;
the midday, which is called the turning point, is the junction between those two.

Because of this statement, the words "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so forth do not refer to three sequential parts of a day divided into three sections. [As stated: "Whether the junction occurs at the turning point [of the sun], or even before it, that day is intended for the sacrifice; if it occurs after, then on the following day."

This is because of such statements [in the scriptures] and because of the consequence of contradicting the plural number that will be mentioned later. Furthermore, in the other view, since the time from the *āvartanī* (the turning point) until five *ghaṭikās* after midday constitutes the period, the sacrifice would necessarily fall on that very same day at the junction (*sandhi*). Nor should it be said, "Let it so happen," for in that case, the prescribed times such as the fourth part of the *parvan* in the morning would be impossible, which would contradict scriptural injunctions such as "the fourth part of the *parvan*" and so forth; this is because the morning time consists of three *muhūrtas*.
Thus Vyāsa says:
"The morning consists of three *muhūrtas*, and the *saṅgava* period is of the same duration."
Parāśara also says:
"When three muhūrtas have passed from sunrise, beginning from the first streak of light, that time is known as morning; it is the fifth part of the day."
In the Padma Purāṇa as well:
"From the first line [of dawn] until the sun [is visible], there are exactly three muhūrtas;
this is remembered as the time of morning (prātaḥ), and it constitutes the fifth part of the day."

In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*: "When the sun has risen from the first streak of light until it has remained for three *muhūrtas* in the east, that is declared to be the morning time; it constitutes the fifth part of the day."

Thus, in other sentences as well that convey the meaning of the word *prātaḥ* (morning), the morning time is stated to consist of three *muhūrtas*; however, it is nowhere heard that the morning time is the first part of a day divided into three parts. As for the usage found in the *Śruti*, that is not primary, because it is improper to assume multiple meanings [for a single term]. Likewise, the statement in the *Sthāpanāropaṇādi* that "the morning time consists of six *nāḍikās*" is to be understood in exactly the same way.

But surely the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*) consists of one and a half *praharas*, according to the statement: “That very [first] *prahara*, when joined with an additional half, is designated as ‘morning’ (*prātar*); here, ‘that’ refers to the *prahara*, and when an additional half is joined to it from above, it becomes one and a half *praharas*. Consequently, if the junction of the lunar day (*parvasandhi*) occurs during the final *ghaṭikā* of midday, then after five *ghaṭikās* have passed, both the morning time and the fourth quarter of the lunar day would coincide; thus, at that time, the sacrifice will be performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).

That is incorrect, because of the statement of Āpastamba: "One commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the full moon sacrifice when the sun has risen, and for the new moon sacrifice before sunrise.

If it is argued that this statement will apply to a case where the morning time, consisting of three *muhūrtas*, coincides with the occurrence of the fourth part of the lunar day (*parvan*), [we reply:]...

There is no reason for such a restriction [to a narrower time], for there is no cause for it. Nor should it be argued that, since the commencement of the ritual procedure (*tantra-prakrama*) for the Full Moon sacrifice occurs when the sun has risen, while the commencement of the New Moon sacrifice occurs before sunrise, one might therefore perform the latter after five *ghaṭikās* have elapsed. This is because the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), which impels a person toward the *bhāvanā* consisting of both the primary and auxiliary acts simultaneously, prohibits any delay in the interim. Therefore, although two scriptural statements indicate that the morning time consists of three *muhūrtas* and also of one and a half *praharas*, one must accept only the three-*muhūrta* duration in accordance with the statement of Āpastamba. Consequently, for the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice at this time, the division of time exactly as stated by us must be adopted.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a two-fold division where the junction (*sandhi*) occurs only one *ghaṭikā* after the [day] has turned, the sacrifice must take place on the very next day; thus, even there, because of the impossibility of the time, the contradiction with the scriptural injunction is exactly the same. [Response: Not so. Since the connection of the sacrifice with the time defined as "the fourth part of the *parvan*" and so forth is understood, it must be accepted that this [junction] is connected to the time of the sacrifice. If the sacrifice were performed on the day following the mere *parvan*, there would be no connection of the sacrifice with its proper time; therefore, the sacrifice takes place on the previous day itself, and thus there is no contradiction.
But in that case, would not the injunction for the sacrifice on the following day at the juncture of the afternoon be contradicted?

Not so. There is no contradiction here, for the term *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) is understood in this context as referring specifically to that afternoon on which the *parvan-sandhi* (the junction of the lunar phases) occurs, and the sacrifice is not performed on the following day during the fourth quarter of the *pratipad*. This is logical; otherwise, during the winter season, when that day is extremely short and the *āvartana* (midday point) occurs at slightly less than fourteen *ghaṭikās*, there might be a case where, due to the increase in the lunar day (*tithi-vṛddhi*), the fourth quarter lasts even sixteen *nāḍikās*. In such a case, if the *sandhi* occurred at a mere *ghaṭikā* after the *āvartana*, the sacrifice would wrongly result in being performed on the following day. But that is not correct, because the prescribed time for the sacrifice is possible on the previous day, and because of the prohibition "one must not sacrifice [on the forbidden day]," as well as the possibility of performing it on the previous day. Therefore, a restriction of the word *aparāhṇa* is preferable. Furthermore, you yourself must accept that the statement, "The divine rite is praised as being performed until the seventh *muhūrta*," refers to a time other than the morning, since it is a prescription for the morning period. Otherwise, if you accepted the morning—which consists of the third part of the day divided into three—as an auxiliary to the sacrifice, the sacrifice would still result in being performed [too late]. Consequently, in this context, *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa* should be taken as the preceding and succeeding halves of a day divided into two parts. Thus, when the *parvan-sandhi* falls within the *aparāhṇa* and subsequent periods, the sacrifice is on the following day; when it falls within the *pūrvāhṇa*, the sacrifice is on that very day. However, when the *parvan-sandhi* occurs precisely at the junction of the *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*, the sacrifice is on that very day; it is for the purpose of establishing this that the term *madhyāhna* (midday) is included. For the word *madhyāhna* here indicates the central moment of the day, setting aside the technical definition of midday. For this very reason, Śātātapa also uses the word "middle" (*madhyama*).
If the festival day (parvan) concludes either in the forenoon or at midday,
then fasting is prescribed on the preceding day, and the sacrifice is to be performed on that [following] day.
The forenoon consists of one and a half watches; likewise, midday is one watch;
the afternoon lasts until the third watch, and the evening is thereafter.
According to this statement of Gobhila, the fourth division [is established]; and that which is the three *muhūrtas* of morning (*prātaḥ*), so much indeed is the *saṅgava* period;
midday (*madhyāhna*) shall consist of three *muhūrtas*, and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is likewise.
The period of three muhūrtas at the end of the day, however, is excluded from all religious duties.

According to this statement by Vyāsa, the fivefold division is also, as previously stated, like the threefold division, applicable to other ritual acts (*karmāntara*). Furthermore, this twofold division has been adopted by all the authors of Sūtras and Bhāṣyas, as well as by many authors of Nibandhas; since it is also logical, it alone should be accepted. In that regard, when the twilight falls on the evening of the following day, the sacrifice (*yāga*) must take place on that very day, based on the statement of Laugākṣi, "In the afternoon or at night," and the statement of Gobhila, "The ends of the fortnights are to be observed as fasts; the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon."

Now, one might object: after sunset, at the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*), whether on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) before or after sunset, once the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) has concluded, it is precisely there—given its connection with the entire night—that milking and other rites are appropriate. This is because the Śruti states: "Since they dwell here together on this night, therefore it is called *amāvāsyā*; having caused him [the Soma] to be pursued by the cows, they gathered him together. Thus, it is said that the gods performed the gathering of Soma in the form of curds and so forth on the new moon when connected with the night. Nor is there a contradiction with the injunction, "The beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādayaḥ*) are to be sacrificed to," for that is possible there even when the time extends across both day and night. Nor is there a contradiction with the rule, "In the afternoon or at night," since that is also possible during the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), and because, being a Smṛti, it is weaker in authority.

It is said: because the word "night" (*rātri*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇaka*) for the lunar day (*tithi*), since the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) is also seen in some instances—such as in the passage, "On that very day he would not be seen in the east; on that day one should fast"—and since the word "day" is also seen elsewhere, such as in the passage, "When he is not seen either in the east or in the west during that night, on that day one should fast"—in the case of the statement, "And when he was not seen in the east or in the west during that night," one must explain whether the non-seeing in the east refers to the remainder of the preceding night, the non-seeing in the west refers to the beginning of the following night, or the non-seeing in both the east and the west occurs within a single [lunar day]. In the first alternative, it would be that very Amāvāsyā which occurs during the day. In the second alternative, since that same condition exists even during the following night, it would be that [night] itself. Now, if it should be argued that because the first lunar day (*pratipad*) exists during the following night, visibility occurs on the *pratipad* as well according to the scriptures.
The teacher Karka said: "Vision occurs immediately upon the commencement of the Śāstra. But Kātyāyana, however, says [it occurs] at the conclusion of the new moon day (amāvāsyā).

[331] "In the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes exhausted; and in the eighth part of the new moon (amāvāsyā), it is said that it becomes minute. This is incorrect. If, on account of its connection with the night, that which is prohibited by the scriptures is established, then—since the entry into the first day (pratipad) occurs before sunrise—the fast should not be observed there, because the fourteenth day exists even during the night of the preceding day; since the moon is present there as well, the fast should certainly not be observed then either.

And it is stated in the Smṛti: "If twice-born men perform a vihāra, a sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), or any other rite on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, which is the day of the spirits (bhūta), all that shall be fruitless."

‘Vihāra’ means the act of moving [the fires] for the sake of a sacrifice, such as the Āhavanīya and others; in that case, the omission of that [moving] would follow. Therefore, the statement “the ends of the fortnights are to be observed as fasts, and the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon” is indeed appropriate. Consequently, the sacrifice takes place on the following day at the junction of the night. Now, one might ask: why is the sacrifice not performed on the fifteenth day even when it extends into the night, if the first day (pratipad) has three muhūrtas, given the rule: “If the second day has three muhūrtas [the sacrifice is on the fifteenth]”? Why is the sacrifice not performed on the fifteenth day?

We reply that it is because of the understanding of a specific distinction (*viśeṣāvagamāt*). Although the scripture concerning the night-conjunction (*rātrisandhi*) finds its scope in a first lunar day (*pratipad*) that extends throughout the entire day, and the scripture concerning the three-muhūrta second lunar day finds its scope when the conjunction occurs during the day; and although there is no fault of relying on a sublation here—since this [latter rule] functions precisely by setting aside the statement "the beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādayaḥ*) are to be sacrificed"—nevertheless, because the scripture concerning the night-conjunction cannot be otherwise established, once the sacrifice on the following day is indicated by the rule "the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed," and since the fourth part of the *parvan* (the junction) is not obtained on the previous day in the morning, the sacrifice would not be obtained there either; therefore, as long as the scripture concerning the three-muhūrta period requires something to cause [the sacrifice] to be obtained on the preceding day, it considers the scripture concerning the night-conjunction and looks for another scope for itself, which we shall explain further below. Consequently, it is established that when the conjunction is at night, the sacrifice is on the following day; and even when the conjunction is in the afternoon, the sacrifice is on the following day.

[332] But surely: "On the fourteenth day, during the fourth watch, when the new moon (amāvāsyā) is not seen, and on the following day when the first lunar day (pratipad) has occurred— on that occasion, the ritual for the ancestors (kavya) and other rites should be performed."
Because of this statement, why is the previous [lunar day] not accepted? Likewise, there is another scriptural passage:

"If the fourteenth day lacks its final watch and the new moon (amāvāsyā) is not obtained, and if the first day (pratipad) occurs on the following morning, one should perform the rite on that very previous day."

Even if on the fourteenth day the new moon (amāvāsya) does not extend across all four watches of the night, but only a portion of them, nevertheless, if the first lunar day (pratipad) occurs on the following day, the meaning is that the fast (upavāsa) must be observed on the preceding day. According to the statement of Kātyāyana—"Having performed the full-moon sacrifice later, one should perform the new-moon sacrifice"—where the first lunar day occurs on the day of the fast, a three-oblation sacrifice is prescribed as an expiation (prāyaścitta).

It is said: since its existence on the first day is established even when the second day exists, Baudhāyana has stated here that the word "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) is otherwise explained; therefore, the sacrifice takes place on the second day.

Now, when there is no fourth part of the *parvan* on the morning of the previous day, and the fourth part of the *parvan* occurs on the morning of the following day, on which day should the sacrifice be performed? It cannot be on the previous day, because at that time there is no presence of the fourth part of the *parvan* or the like, and thus the time for the sacrifice is absent; furthermore, the conjunction of the *parvan* occurs in the afternoon. Nor can the sacrifice be on the following day, because even there the prescribed time is absent.

On this point, some say: the sacrifice should be performed on the following day, because the time prescribed for the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth is impossible on the preceding day, and because there is no rule prohibiting the performance of the sacrifice during the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*). As for this prohibition that acts as a restrainer:
"One should never perform sacrifices during the fourth part of the *pratipad*;
the Rākṣasas plunder it—this is the eternal Vedic injunction."
