It is said: this prohibition concerns the junction of the midday (*madhyāhna-sandhi*) and not the junction of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa-sandhi*), because the performance of the sacrifice is prescribed for the following day (*paredyus*) in that case.

[Objection: But surely, since the sacrifice is obtained on the following day precisely at the afternoon junction—and since the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is possible there, and because a prohibition must presuppose a prior possibility (of what is prohibited)—its consistency (*sāmañjasya*) lies in that very case. However, at the midday junction, since the sacrifice is prescribed for the previous day (*pūrvedyus*), there is not even a scent of the fourth part of the first lunar day; thus, the prohibition would be untenable.

To this it is replied: Regarding the injunction "the beginnings of the fortnights (pakṣādayaḥ) are to be sacrificed upon," there is a common applicability whether the lunar day (tithi) is complete or a partial one. In that case, since the fourth part of the *pratipad* occurs during the morning on the second day, the prohibition is indeed possible only because of a prior possibility [of performance]. However, by this much, one does not incur sin (*pratyavāya*) by performing the sacrifice in the fourth part of the *pratipad*, because the sacrifice is enjoined there by the rule "the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon. Furthermore, when there is a prohibition of what has been enjoined, there can only be an option (*vikalpa*). And this has been stated in the *Bṛhad-vārttika*:
Even if one has obtained some [result] through a ritual procedure that is equal in scope [to other methods],
it does not produce the thought of transgression (*pratyavāya*) because it relies upon an alternative option (*vikalpa*).
For in perception, affirmation and negation possess equal force and have a single object;
yet, for those who maintain the authority of one of these two through conceptual construction, [the other is sublated].
For those who have accepted prohibitions and do not perform [the forbidden acts], this fault does not exist;
however, in that case, the authority of an injunction is not based on its being characterized by a Vedic command (*codanā*).

"But on the view that the injunction is authoritative, since the prohibition has been set aside, there is no fault for those who perform the duty characterized by the Vedic command. Thus [it is said].

Nor should it be said that an option (*vikalpa*) is improper because the injunction "the *pakṣa* days and so forth are to be sacrificed upon" is applicable with scope across all four parts of the lunar day (*pratipad*), whereas the prohibition "one must not sacrifice on the fourth part" has no scope other than the fourth part of the *pratipad*. For even when a general rule has a broad scope, it is not absolutely sublated by a specific prohibition, since its application depends upon that very prohibition. As it was stated by the authors of the *Vārttika* in the *Ṭīkā* on that point: [334] "The general rule is not set aside by the specific prohibition; rather, its application is restricted to the remainder. Thus, the general rule remains operative insofar as it is not contradicted by the specific exception. Therefore, an option is indeed appropriate here.

Even though an injunction is weak internally, it becomes equal in strength to a prohibition because its own acquisition of existence is dependent upon that [prohibition]; this will be explained in the section concerning prohibitions and injunctions introduced by a specific context (*pradeśa*).

Therefore, since an absolute prohibition of that which is established by scripture is impossible, there arises an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of the rule: "One does not perform the *ye yajāmahe* at the *anuyāja* offerings. But this is not exactly like that; rather, an option can be avoided by resorting to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). To explain: the time directly enjoined for the sacrifice consists of the fourth part of the *parvan* day and the first three parts of the following *pratipad* day. Since this time does not exist on either of the two days during the morning, the sacrifice would otherwise be impossible. Furthermore, because a mandatory (*nitya*) enjoined rite cannot be abandoned, the force of the injunction regarding performance implies that one must sacrifice even if the time is somewhat deficient. Thus, it follows that one should sacrifice on the previous day in the morning—even if the fourth part of the *parvan* is absent—because the *parvan* itself exists; or else, on the following day, even if the first three parts of the *pratipad* are absent, one should sacrifice because the *pratipad* itself exists. Consequently, the possibility of performing the sacrifice even during the fourth part of the *pratipad* cannot be prevented even by the gods. Therefore, since an option remains unavoidable when one attempts to establish an exclusion through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is better to accept the literal meaning. Even though an option results from this, let the negative particle (*nañ*) be a direct indicator of a prohibition. Moreover, a prohibition is necessary because an exclusion is impossible. For instance, if the exclusion were based on the mere fact that the fourth part of the *pratipad* is to be avoided, then the injunction "one should sacrifice on the *pratipad* excluding its fourth part" would mean that the sacrifice could never take place during the fourth part of the *parvan*. If, on the other hand, it is said that one should sacrifice at the time enjoined as being "other than the fourth part of the *pratipad*," then consider a case where the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the afternoon: the enjoined time for the next day would remain there, yet nothing but the fourth part of the *pratipad* would be left; thus, what else could be prescribed by way of excluding that [fourth part]? Alternatively, just as in the rule "one should not look at the rising sun," where the negative particle is connected with the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) to enjoin a resolution (*saṃkalpa*) against looking, so too here a resolution against sacrificing might be enjoined. However, this is not the case here.

It is replied: It is appropriate that in that case, looking [at the sun] as established by desire (*rāgaprāpta*) is excluded. However, here, since the sacrifice on the following day at the juncture of the afternoon and the *parvan* is established by scripture (*śāstraprāpta*), it cannot be excluded. Nor can it be said here that there is an exclusion—just as there is an exclusion of the selection of a lineage-ancestor (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) by the stronger direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśana*) stating "one does not select a lineage-ancestor"—because both exclusions, which establish the fourth part of the lunar day (*pratipad*) and the afternoon juncture, are equally scriptural instructions. Furthermore, it is not possible here for there to be an exclusion—just as there is an exclusion of the formula "ye yajāmahe" (which applies to sacrifice in general) from the *anuyāja* offerings (which are specific sacrifices)—because the scriptural instruction regarding the afternoon juncture cannot be a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) with respect to the general rule of exclusion that applies equally to the morning, afternoon, and other *parvan* junctures. Nor does the rule of exclusion possess greater force due to being a revealed text (*śruti*), because its status as a *śruti* is unestablished. For the Commentator, having stated that the prohibition of the fourth part is based on the statement of Kātyāyana, recited the verse: "One should not sacrifice during the fourth part. Therefore, it is said, "This is an eternal *śruti*," with the intention that it is rooted in *śruti*.

But surely, since the injunction is explicit due to the hearing of the *tavya* suffix in the statement of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), whereas in the statement regarding the conjunction of the lunar days (*parvan*) such as the afternoon it is a delayed application because it is an existing description (*vartamānāpadeśa*) and thus its injunctive nature must be inferred—there is a disparity between the two cases.

This is not so. For while the doubt as to whether the *pratipad* (the first day of the lunar fortnight), the fourth part [of the moon], or the sacrifice itself is being excluded (*paryudasyate*) might persist for some time, the doubt as to whether there is a statement of a present action (*vartamānāpadeśa*) or a fifth verbal suffix (*pañcamalakāra*)—which would indicate a prohibition—is likewise removed. Furthermore, in the case of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the negative particle (*nañ*) would have to function as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), which is an additional fault. Therefore, since exclusion is impossible, a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is inevitable. Thus, the dilemma being established, the prohibition would concern the junction of the midday (*madhyāhna-sandhi*), while the injunction would concern the junction of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa-sandhi*). This is because Laugākṣi has established the performance of the sacrifice on either the preceding or the following day based on the distinction between the junctions of the forenoon and the afternoon, stating: "In the forenoon, or else at midday," and so forth. As for the statement, "The fourth part of the *parvan* (the full or new moon)," that too does not preclude the sacrifice during the fourth part of the *pratipad*. To explain: it does not first prohibit the fourth part, because that part is not enjoined and thus is not perceived as something to be prohibited. Nor does it exclude the other parts by implication through enjoining the preceding parts, because this sentence lacks an injunctive suffix and is therefore not perceived as an injunction. Nor can an injunction be inferred here—as in the case of the rule "one holds [the vessel] above for the gods"—because it is a restatement of an already established fact and is not contradicted by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If one were to assume that the purpose of this sentence is to enjoin the three parts of the *pratipad* by implication, thereby excluding the fourth part, it would contradict the scriptural passage permitting the fourth part as an option: "One should not sacrifice in the fourth part. Nor should it be said that the injunctive suffix is merely to be understood (*vijñeya*), for it could also be construed in the sense of "fitness" according to the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca*. Or, even if it were an injunctive suffix, it would pertain to the act of knowing (*jñāna*) and not to the act of sacrificing (*yajati*). If you argue that, like the verbs *nirvapati* ("he offers") or *ālabhate* ("he seizes"), an injunction residing in a verbal root—even if not explicitly required—effects the desired meaning, we reply: no. In those cases, the root-meanings themselves are enjoined; here, however, the root *yaj* is not enjoined. Therefore, the sentence "the fourth part of the *parvan*" is simply a descriptive reference (*anuvāda*) to what is already known from other sources. It serves to restrict the time for the sacrifice to the three parts of the *pratipad*, and as such, it is not a primary injunction. Consequently, the prohibition applies to the junction of the midday, while the injunction applies to the junction of the afternoon. Thus, the two rules are consistent.

It is replied: since that too is merely a strained interpretation, it lacks the capacity to subvert the scripture which clearly permits the fourth part [of the moon]. For instance, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*); in its impossibility, either the meaning of the verbal root is enjoined elsewhere, or something else is enjoined in relation to the meaning of the verbal root. However, where something entirely different is enjoined elsewhere, that is excessively strained. Now, if—avoiding that fault—it is argued that the meaning of the verbal root, namely knowledge itself, is enjoined, then how is the time obtained? Or, if it is argued that knowledge being enjoined consists in the refinement of the object of knowledge (*jñeyasaṃskāra*), and thus, being untenable without the application of the time—which is the object to be refined—to the sacrifice, it implies an injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*).

That is not so, because the postulation of the application of that which is to be refined through the refinement [itself] was already refuted in the *Saktu-adhikaraṇa* on the grounds that such a refinement is impossible.

Now, one might object: "Just as the application of the *phalacamas* and the *pūtīka* plants to the sacrifice was postulated—on the basis of the impossibility otherwise of the refinements consisting of consumption and pressing, as in the injunctions 'In the absence of soma, one should press the *pūtīkas*' and 'One should give it to him as a draught'—why is a rule for the application of time, which is to be refined by knowledge, not likewise postulated here?"

It is replied: In the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," since the application of Soma is already established, there is no contradiction in the rules for the purificatory acts of consumption (*bhakṣa*) and pressing (*abhiṣava*) through the names *somam abhiṣuṇoti* ("he presses Soma") and *somacamasa* ("Soma-cup"). Thus, once it is established that consumption and pressing are purificatory acts of Soma, it is easy to assume that a substance whose purificatory function is well-known (*nirūḍha-saṃskāra*) performs the same function as the previous substance by means of an injunction for the purification of another substance. However, in the present case, the purificatory act of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃskāra*) is not yet established; it cannot be sustained unless its application is obtained through another means of proof, according to the principle of the *saktu-adhikaraṇa*. Therefore, [the objection] is indeed correct.

Furthermore, when the substance *soma* itself has been enjoined but is occasionally unavailable, and the employment of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) would thus arise, the rule "one should press *pūtīka* plants" is merely a restriction (*niyamamātra*); it does not constitute a new injunction (*apūrvo viniyogaḥ*). However, in this case [of the time-injunction], the matter cannot be established without another enjoining factor. Therefore, just as in the passage "one meditates on the ocean with the mind, one meditates on the earth with the mind, and one meditates on the enemy with the mind," the injunction of the knowledge of time serves only as a remote auxiliary (*ārād upakārakatvam*); it does not have the function of bringing about the time itself. Or, let it be granted that since knowledge is already established when the causal complex for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) is present, the injunction of the knowledge of time is indeed an injunction of time. Even so, in the single compound word *yāgakālaḥ* (time of sacrifice), it is untenable for something to be the object of reference (*uddiśya*) and something else to be the thing enjoined (*upādīyate*), as is the case in expressions such as "one sacrifices the *sviṣṭakṛt* with three parts" or "the first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer. For just as one cannot enjoin a connection with "firstness" regarding the act of drinking qualified by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, so too it is not possible to enjoin a subsequent connection between the meaning of the word "time"—which is qualified by the fourth part of the *parvan* and other factors expressed by another word—and the meaning of one part of the compound *yāgakāla*. This is because the two words being compounded cannot be connected with another word until they have first related to each other, according to the maxim: "A complete word requires another word. If, on the other hand, it is argued that the connection of the sacrifice with the time expressed by another word—namely, "that which is the fourth part of the *parvan* and the first three moments of the *pratipad*"—is what is enjoined; [we reply:]...

It is replied: even so, because the word *yāgakālaḥ* (sacrifice-time) is a compound in which the sacrifice is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), a connection with that subordinate sacrifice would necessarily follow. Furthermore, actions are connected either with a result (*phala*) or with a factor of action (*kāraka*). Time is not the result of the sacrifice, because it is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*). Nor is it a factor of action, because there is no indication by means of a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*). Indeed, one does not see an indication by the locative case-ending for the fourth part of the lunar day (*parva-caturthāṃśa*) etc., as one does in the expression "one should sacrifice on the first day of the lunar fortnight" (*pratipadi yajeta*). Therefore, another difficulty arises: one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to assume the meaning of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Or, let it be granted that the time is prescribed; even so, the prescription of the three initial parts of the *pratipad* is not tenable. For here two times are taken up: the fourth part of the *parvan* and the three initial parts of the *pratipad*. Nor can both be prescribed by a single sentence, because if two times were prescribed by way of reference to the sacrifice (*yāga-anuvāda*), there would result the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). If it is argued that since time functions as a causal condition (*nimitta-svarūpaka*), what is prescribed is the connection with the two times, and not the two times themselves in relation to the sacrifice, then there is all the more reason for a syntactical split; for in that case, a difference in the connection of the sacrifice is perceived due to the difference in the times. If it is further argued that just as there is no syntactical split when the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is prescribed for each individual cup (*pratigraham*), so too here there is no syntactical split even though the sacrifice is prescribed for each respective time—[we reply: this is not so.

That is not correct. In that case, having established the connection between the cup (*graha*) and the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) by means of a single effort, once the purport of the scriptural injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*) has reached its conclusion, the various functional distinctions (*vyāpāra-bheda*) arising with respect to each individual cup do not split the sentence, even though they are produced separately. In this instance, however, there is no such word by which the connection of the sacrifice (*yāga*) with both the fourth part of the *parvan* and the three parts beginning with the *pratipad* could be enjoined through a single scriptural purport, because the two have been mentioned separately. Therefore, when multiple connections are enjoined for a sacrifice that is already established, there is a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), just as in the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the *revatī-vāravantīya* section and the *paurṇamāsī* section.
Now, why is it not accepted that, in that very same way, the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) is avoided by means of an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*)?

It is said in reply: If a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) were accepted, another sacrifice would result, and thus this injunction regarding time for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices would not be established. Since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are already established by other scriptural texts, if their connection to two times were made by a single sentence, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) has indeed been stated. Now, if it is argued that—just as in the case of "He measures half inside the altar and half outside the altar," where the syntactical split is avoided by figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) prescribing that he measures at the junction (*sandhi*)—so too here the syntactical split is avoided by figuratively taking the junction to be the combination of the portions of the *parvan* and the *pratipad* days.

That is not correct. In that case, when the junction-point (*saṃdhi*) is indicated, since the meanings of the words "inside the altar" (*antarvedi*) and "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*) are already established by implication, it is possible for them to be restated (*anuvāda*). Here, however, even though the time of the junction is indicated, a restatement of the fourth part of the lunar day (*parvan*) and the three parts of the first day (*pratipad*) is not established; for there is no implication of the two preceding and following parts, which are fixed and unequal.

Furthermore, what is the point of the laborious resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) for establishing the connection? Even though the injunction "one should sacrifice at the *saṃdhi*" (*sandhau yajeta*) prescribes the time of the *saṃdhi* by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), that time is unfit for the performance of the rite; thus, when an indirect indication of its proximity arises, one must explain why the sentence has arrived to prescribe the limits for proximity—both preceding and following—in response to the expectation as to what constitutes the limit of that time. If this sentence were intended to prescribe the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth—as in "the fourth part of the *parvan* and the first three parts of the *pratipad*"—then that too would now be untenable. If, on the other hand, it goes back to indicate that very same *saṃdhi*, then what is accomplished by it? Therefore, if one attempts to prescribe the connection of the sacrifice with two times, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is unavoidable. If, instead, the phrase "that which is the time of the sacrifice" (*yo yāgakālaḥ*) restates the time of the sacrifice and then prescribes both "the fourth part of the *parvan*" and "the first three parts of the *pratipad*," then there is first a split of the sentence in the qualified restatement "the time of the sacrifice. There is a second split of the sentence because both the fourth part of the *parvan* and the three parts of the *pratipad* are being prescribed simultaneously. Furthermore, there is another fault: the interpretation that the connection occurs through a transposition of those two elements. Alternatively, if the fourth part of the *parvan* or the three parts of the *pratipad* are restated and the status of being the time of the sacrifice is prescribed for both of them, then there is first a split of the sentence due to the qualified restatement "the fourth part of the *parvan*. There is a second split of the sentence due to the qualified restatement "the first three parts of the *pratipad*. There is a third split of the sentence because the status of being the time of the sacrifice is prescribed for both of them. Moreover, since there is no other means of prescribing the fourth part of the *parvan* and the three parts of the *pratipad*, they cannot even be treated as mere restatements (*anuvāda*); this is yet another fault.

Furthermore, because time is not something to be adopted (anupādeya), in sentences primarily concerned with the injunction of time, it is the ritual action itself that is prescribed with reference to the time. Therefore, if here the fourth part of the *parvan* were prescribed as the time for the sacrifice by referring to that portion, then—since the time for the sacrifice, being itself of the nature of time, cannot be adopted—the very status of being the object of reference (uddeśyatva) would result for it. Moreover, a mutual relationship between two objects of reference is impossible. Nor is there a single word intended to form a collective group (*samudāya*) of these two, by which the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) could be avoided through the prescription of the connection of the sacrifice with that collective.

[Objection: Is it not the case that by the word "time" (*kāla*), both [the sacrifice and the time] are referred to in a single form as "the time of the sacrifice" (*yāgakāla*), and thus their connection is enjoined?

[Response: That is not so, because it has already been stated that it is impossible to enjoin a connection between two things—the sacrifice and the time—by means of the compound "the time of the sacrifice."

Furthermore, if the time such as the fourth part of the *parvan* were first restated by the word "time of sacrifice" (*yāgakāla*), and then again by that very same word the connection of the sacrifice with that time were enjoined, then a syntactical split (*vairūpya*) regarding the *Vājapeya* would result. For it is not possible within a single sentence for one and the same thing mentioned in that sentence to be both restated with reference to something else and enjoined with reference to something else. However, if—in order to avoid this syntactical split—the connection of the sacrifice with time in its pure form is enjoined, without referring to the specific alternatives such as the fourth part of the *parvan*, [then there is no fault].

That is incorrect, because the [desired] result is established even without a prescription regarding the connection with time. Now, if it is argued that the word *tat* (that) refers back to the portions of the *parvan* and the first day (*pratipad*)—as in the statement "that should be known as the time for the sacrifice"—and thus the connection with the sacrifice is prescribed, even so, the aforementioned inconsistency remains exactly as it was.

Furthermore, this pronoun *saḥ* (that), being in the singular number, is incapable of referring to four temporal portions. If it is then claimed that it refers to each one separately by means of the principle of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word from a previous context), [the same objection applies].

Not so; for if, within a single sentence, the word were to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) with each individual term, such that multiple connections were grasped in a single location, this would result in the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Furthermore, since the word *saḥ* (that), which ends in the singular, is referred to by a plural in the rule "the first [words] are repeated with each subsequent word" (*ādyāḥ pratipadasvayaiḥ*), even its syntactic supply (*anuṣaṅga*) is not tenable. Just as there is no supply of the word *gacchatām* (of those going) in the phrase *saṃyajatrair aṅgāni* (the limbs with the sacrificers).

Furthermore, because the relative pronoun (*yat*) and the demonstrative pronoun (*tat*) are invariably connected, and since the word *yat* is heard in the phrase "the fourth part of the *parvan*" (referring to the *parvacaturthāṃśa*), it is appropriate that this very [part] be referred to by the word *tat*, and not the portions of the *pratipad*. If it is argued that the word *yat* is supplied there as well—on the grounds that what is directly stated (*śruta*) is more swiftly understood than what is supplied (*adhyāhṛta*)—even so, there can still be no reference to it. Or, let us grant the supply [of the word *yat*]; nevertheless, since the term "portions of the *pratipad*" ends in a plural suffix, how can there be a connection with this word *tat*, which ends in a singular suffix, even if it is supplied? If it is further argued that the aggregate of the *parvan* and the *pratipad* portions can be referred to by the word *tat* ending in the singular suffix— [The text continues: ...then [it must be said that] the word *tat* would refer to the whole, while the word *yat* refers to the parts; thus, the two words would have different meanings. Moreover, the word *parvacaturthāṃśa* is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of the two words *parva* and *caturthāṃśa*, and it denotes a single object. Therefore, it is logical that the word *tat* refers to that very same single object. Consequently, the word *pratipadbhāga* cannot be connected with the word *tat*. Furthermore, the word *pratipadbhāga* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of the two words *pratipat* and *bhāga*, and it denotes a portion of the *pratipad*. Since the word *parvacaturthāṃśa* denotes the *parvan*, and the word *pratipadbhāga* denotes a portion of the *pratipad*, they do not denote the same thing. Nor can it be by way of option; for an option is accepted only with great reluctance because there is no other recourse, even though it is accomplished through the difficulty of four pairs of contradictory operations—such as the manifestation and concealment of the injunctive capacity of two mutually opposed scriptural texts. What, then, is accomplished by this statement? Nothing at all. Rather, when the rule "the sacrifice should be performed in the third part of the *parvan*" has established the fourth part of the *parvan*, and the rule "one should sacrifice at the beginning of the fortnight" has established the *pratipad*, and the rule "sacrifice in the morning" has established the morning time, and the rule "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part" has prohibited the fourth part of the *pratipad* optionally according to the aforementioned method—then whatever mass of time remains, obtained from various scriptures, is all condensed and stated by a single ritual manual (*yājñika-kārikā*) for the sake of ease of memorization: "The fourth part of the *parvan*... Just as the meaning obtained from various scriptures such as "one digs up the altar with the wooden sword (*sphya*)" is restated in a condensed form: "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*)," so too the Vārttikakāra says: "The connection of the wooden sword and other implements with their functions, such as digging, is established there; thus, the term 'sacrificial implements' merely restates what is already obtained. Likewise, the phrase "the fourth part of the *parvan*" is also a restatement condensing various scriptures; it is not an injunction of any specific time by which it would, by implication, exclude the fourth part of the *pratipad*.

This is not a fault. For the authoritativeness of human statements is not destroyed merely by their being rooted in the Veda, since that would entail the lack of authority for all the Smṛtis. Even those who hold that human statements infer the knowledge of the speaker must, in some way, distinguish between injunctions, restatements, contradictions, and non-contradictory restatements within human speech; they certainly do not consider them all to be mere restatements. It is for this reason they say: "Having restated 'that which is characterized by the Vedic injunction,' it is enjoined that 'that is Dharma.'"
[Objection: If an object already obtained from another sentence can indeed be enjoined, then why is the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth not also enjoined?

[Reply: It is said: The fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth is not enjoined because it is not obtained from another sentence; rather, even if it were obtained from another sentence, it is not enjoined because, for fear of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of enjoining multiple things, it could at best be merely restated (*anuvāda*). Thus, it is not enjoined.

Now, if it is argued that since the time consisting of the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth is already prescribed by another scriptural statement, only the morning (*prātaḥkāla*) is what must be enjoined as the single thing to be performed, then why should the opposite not be the case? It is said in reply: because of the connection with the word *yaḥ* ("which") in the phrase "the fourth part of the *parvan*," that fourth part is not the object of the injunction; however, the morning time is enjoined precisely because it lacks such a connection. Furthermore, there is another difficulty: the fourth part of the *parvan* has already been prescribed by the rule "the first three *tithis* of the *pratipad*," and thus it would have to be referred to by the pronoun *saḥ* ("that") in the phrase "that is the time for the sacrifice. Therefore, the morning alone is the object of the injunction.

Furthermore, by the very same reason—namely, the fear of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and so forth—by which the three points of time are not enjoined, for that same reason not even a single time, such as the fourth part of the *parvan*, would be enjoined. To explain: regarding these three matters—the "fourth part of the *parvan*" and so on—is there first a connection with the action and subsequently a mutual connection among them (according to the principle of the red cow, *aruṇaikahāyanī*), or is there first a mutual connection among them and subsequently a connection with the action? Even if it were first connected with the action, would that connection with the action occur according to the principle of enjoining a qualified object (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), or would it be a connection with them by way of restating the action (*kriyā-anuvāda*)? If it were a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), then because this would entail a different ritual act (*karmāntara*), this injunction of time for the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices would not be established. If, on the other hand, by way of restating the action, a connection between the "fourth part" and the *parvan* is enjoined, then since multiple qualities are being enjoined while restating an already established action, there is at least one syntactical split; furthermore, even if their mutual connection were then enjoined, that same defect would persist. Alternatively, if—in order to avoid the syntactical split—one were to disregard the qualification of the "fourth part" and so on and enjoin the connection of the mere *parvan* with the sacrifice, then the sacrifice would be liable to be performed at any time during the *parvan*. Moreover, the mention of the "fourth part," whether as an injunction or as a restatement, would be rendered untenable and thus contradicted.

But even when touched by an injunction, it is touched only by implication (*arthāt*), not by direct scriptural statement (*śrutyā*); therefore, there is no fault of prescribing multiple things in that case.

Not so. For there is no logical inconsistency in the injunction regarding the whole [the sacrifice] without this particular part, such that it would necessarily imply this very particular part by implication (*arthāt*). Indeed, the inconsistency of something common does not, merely by being stated, terminate in a particular that has already entered the mind. If that were the case, the injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) would be abolished everywhere. For instance, in the case of "One should sacrifice with Soma," once the mere sacrifice has been enjoined and the injunction is concluded, the common requirement for a substance—which exists even without an explicit injunction—would terminate in the specific substance Soma as it has already entered the mind; how then could there be an injunction of a particular? Even in cases where a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result from enjoining multiple qualities in an action already established, one might simply say: let there be the injunction of only one quality, while the other specific quality is implied even by the necessity of the general [requirement]. Thus, it can be maintained.

[Objection: If this is so, then how can the fourth part of the *parvan* be enjoined for sacrifice by the statement, "The twice-born should perform the *iṣṭi* during the fourth part of the *parvan*," since the aforementioned defects apply equally there as well? [Response: It is said: In the phrase "the fourth part of the *parvan*," two word-meanings in the form of the *parvan* and its part, being mutually related and unified, are enjoined together for the sacrifice. Thus, because there is no division of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Now, one might object: "In the third part of the *parvan*,"—surely the mutual connection between these two parts of the *parvan* cannot be established without the operation of an injunction.
True, it is not established by this alone; however, there is indeed another injunction that prescribes their mutual connection, as follows:
"The last quarter of the fifteenth day and the first three quarters of the new moon."
This is the time for the Pārvaṇa sacrifice; otherwise, it does not occur.
Thus, a relationship is enjoined between these two [phrases]: "of the fifteenfold [stotra]" and "this foot.

Now, if this were so, would the sacrifice not also apply to the first foot of the fifteenfold stotra? If it is then specified as "the subsequent foot," there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

This is not a fault. Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice at the junction (*saṃdhi*)," since the time of the junction intended for the sacrifice is unfit [for the performance], it must be indicated by a time proximate to the junction. When there arises the expectation as to whether that proximate time is a *nāḍikā*, a *prahara*, half a lunar day (*tithi*), or a full lunar day, the "quarter of the fifteenth day" (*pañcadaśīpāda*)—being enjoined to fulfill the requirement for a specific kind of proximity—is established, by virtue of its reliance on proximity, as being much closer to the junction than what is distant.
But surely, in this sentence, not only is the connection between the *pañcadaśī* and the *pāda* perceived, but another connection, namely with the sacrifice, is also perceived.

This is indeed true; however, the injunction “the *iṣṭi* is to be performed during the fourth part of the *parvan*” is restated (*anūdyate*) because such a restatement is possible even for that which is yet to be attained. Therefore, in the sentence concerning the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), the purpose of the foot of the fifteenth day is enjoined. By the phrase “during the fourth part of the *parvan*,” only the connection of that [foot] with the sacrifice is enjoined. It has already been stated that although the fourth-part status of that *parvan*-portion is not explicitly enjoined, it is restated as being implied by the rules regarding the junction (*sandhi*). By the phrase “that which is the fourth part of the *parvan*,” only the connection with the morning time is enjoined, while everything else is restated. Consequently, since there is no enjoining of multiple meanings in any single instance, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

If it is argued that the connection of the fifteenth day’s quarter with the sacrifice—being established by another sentence—is not treated as a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) when that sentence is intent upon enjoining the connection with the sacrifice, then it follows that the connection of the fifteenth day’s quarter with the sacrifice can indeed be enjoined by the sentence, "That which is the fourth part of the *parvan*."

It is indeed true that it can be done; however, this specific time must be enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice. But since the syntactical unity (*vākya*) is established even by enjoining the general time consisting of the morning, such an injunction is not proper. This is because the specific time has already been secured through another sentence, and thus, although the fault of split-of-the-sentence (*vākyabheda*) is avoided in the case of enjoining a qualified entity, there remains an unavoidable degree of injunctive heaviness (*vidhigaurava*) compared to enjoining the essential nature alone, as well as a dependence on another sentence that provides that qualified element. However, where no suitable element for enjoining the essential nature alone is present, then even a qualified entity is indeed enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice, as in the case of the rule: "In the fourth part of the *parvan*."

Now, if the distinction between the time and the portion is established by one sentence, and the connection of that distinguished [portion] with the sacrifice is made by another sentence, then why is it not accepted that in this very manner the three portions beginning with the *pratipad* are connected to the sacrifice? For instance, [one might argue]: "The portion subsequent to the fifteenth day, and the first three from the beginning of the fortnight"—thus, by the force of implying proximity to the conjunction (*saṃdhi*), even the "portions" (*pāda*) starting from the beginning of the fortnight are established as being precisely the first ones in close proximity to the conjunction.

This is not so. Here, a connection with two parts of time is perceived; yet, when one connection is to be enjoined and the other abandoned, what logic is there in abandoning the first-perceived connection between the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) and the quarter (*pāda*), and instead enjoining the later-understood connection between the first part of the lunar day (*pratipad*) and the quarters? Furthermore, the connection between the fifteenth day and the quarter is established by the text, whereas the connection between the first part of the lunar day and the quarters must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*); this too constitutes its weakness. Moreover, even if the connection between the first part of the lunar day and the quarters were indeed enjoined as desired, by which sentence would that conjunction be enjoined? Certainly not by that very same sentence, because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Nor can it be by the statement, "The fourth part of the *parvan* and the first three parts of the *pratipad*," for it has already been stated that this sentence has fulfilled its purpose solely by enjoining the connection with the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*). And there is no other sentence by which the full extent of the connection for the three parts of the *pratipad* could be enjoined. Therefore, since the injunction of the three parts is impossible, only the prohibition "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part" remains as the prohibitor of the fourth part. Thus, it is said that this does not permit the optional attainment of even the fourth part of the *pratipad*. Consequently, it is established that according to the previously mentioned arrangement, the fourth part of the *pratipad* is not prohibited when the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the afternoon and so forth, but it is prohibited when the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*).
And so it has been stated by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana:
"If the junction [of the lunar day] should occur in the afternoon, one who performs the sacrifice on the following morning—
even if it falls in the fourth part of the *pratipad*— does not incur any fault."

Others do not accept this view of Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana and others. Why? Because if the fast were observed on both the morning and evening junctions (*saṃdhi*), and the sacrifice were performed on the second day, then since the beginning of the lunar fortnight (*pakṣādi*) and the fourth part of the first day (*pratipaccaturthāṃśa*) would both be possible, there would be no basis for the following regulation: "The beginnings of the fortnights are to be honored" and "One should not sacrifice in the fourth part," which would result in the simultaneous acceptance of two contradictory scriptures—one for when the junction occurs at midday and another for when it occurs in the afternoon. Furthermore, the two statements of Laugākṣi are not authoritative, because they are intended merely to establish the performance of the sacrifice on either the preceding or the following day, and thus lack the intent to establish a definitive rule regarding injunction and prohibition; moreover, such a distinction is impossible. For instance, if the junction of the *parvan* occurs immediately after sunrise and the sacrifice is performed that same day, one sees that the scripture concerning the beginning of the fortnight is favored by the prohibition [of sacrificing in the fourth part]. Likewise, even if the junction occurs in the afternoon, if the junction falls before sunset and the sacrifice is performed on the second day, one sees that both scriptures are favored. The same applies to a junction occurring at night.

Now, if it is argued that because there is no sacrifice in the fourth part of the *pratipad*, the scriptural injunction regarding the beginning of the lunar fortnight (*pakṣādi-śāstra*) is not favored during the morning junction (*pūrvāhṇa-sandhi*), then one must likewise say that since there is no sacrifice in the first part of the *pratipad* during the afternoon junction (*aparāhṇa-sandhi*), the scriptural injunction regarding the beginning of the fortnight is not favored. Furthermore, when the sacrifice is performed during the first three parts according to other scriptures, the meaning of the statement "the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon" is indeed fulfilled. Thus, in the case of the new moon and full moon sacrifices at the beginning of the dark fortnight, the sacrifice does not span the entire day; rather, the performance occurs in this manner within a single portion. As for the assumption of a sacrifice in the fourth part of the *pratipad* based on the apparent inconsistency of the prohibition "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part," that too contradicts this very section [of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras], which states that "there would be the loss of the *ārṣeya* (priestly lineage) here. For it has been stated there that since the rule "he chooses three *ārṣeyas*" exists alongside the prohibition "he does not choose four," it is impossible for the prohibition to be intended as a restrictive injunction (*kalpa-vidhi*). Similarly, here too, since the rule "the first three parts of the fortnight-beginning" exists alongside the prohibition "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part," it is impossible to assume another injunction based on that prohibition. Therefore, the statement "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part" is either a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), like "he does not choose four," or it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). In the latter sense, while the time for the sacrifice is declared to be the *pratipad* by the rule "the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon," the statement "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part" indicates that the sacrifice is to be performed on the *pratipad* excluding the fourth part. This very point is clarified in another Smṛti: "the first three of the fortnight-beginning" and "the first three parts of the *pratipad*. This being the case, the rule "the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon" and the rule "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part" will share a common scriptural source with the Smṛti concerning the three parts of the *pratipad*. As for the objection raised against the exclusion theory—that in the case of an afternoon junction of the *parvan* (lunar change) occurring when two lunar days (*tithi*) each consist of six *ghaṭikās*, even if the fourth part of the *parvan* is absent on the previous day, the sacrifice must be performed in the third part of the *parvan*; and even if the first three parts of the *pratipad* are absent on the following day, the sacrifice must be performed in the fourth part—this alternative resulting from the force of the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vacana*) cannot be avoided even by the gods. Furthermore, in the case of an exclusion, the negative particle (*nañ*) does not have its primary meaning, but functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

That is incorrect. For if the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) were not excluded—just as the third part of the full moon (*parvan*) is not—it might indeed be so. However, since there exists an exclusion here in the form of the statement, "One should not sacrifice in the fourth part," the sacrifice would necessarily fall on the third part of the *parvan* alone. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated in the *Ekādaśī-nirṇaya* that there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in an exclusion; by this very logic, even in the case of a prohibition, the sacrifice would fall on the previous day alone. For, since the sacrifice would otherwise be obtained optionally on either the third part of the *parvan* or the fourth part of the *pratipad*, the phrase "one should not sacrifice in the fourth part" prohibits the sacrifice specifically from the fourth part of the *pratipad*. Otherwise, regarding the taking of black gram (*māṣa*) as a substitute for mung beans (*mudga*), which was prohibited yet prescribed as a specific alternative, Jaimini stated in the sixth chapter: "The prohibition is overridden by the specific injunction of the Vedic text. And Kātyāyana stated: "[A prohibition is set aside] because of the cognition [of the injunction]. Even so, one could argue that the taking of the prohibited black grams should be permitted. But the resolution given there—that a prohibition of what is already established by the sense of the context is indeed a sublater—is equally applicable here. Therefore, the claim that the fourth part of the *parvan* is explicitly mentioned in scripture (*śruta*) is of little consequence.

That is not so; for Kātyāyana has stated, "This is the eternal revelation (śruti). As for what was said by the Commentator—that [the rule] is based on the statement of Kātyāyana—that is not contradictory even if it were a revealed scripture (*śruti*), because the phrase "this is the eternal revelation" is itself a statement of Kātyāyana. Only a mere indication has been shown here for fear of excessive prolixity. Therefore, it is established that the sacrifice must be performed at the time exactly as described.

Others, however, say: "The statement that 'one should not sacrifice during the fourth part of the [first] day' must be explained as referring to the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). Nor should it be argued that since the scripture concerning the junction of the forenoon and midday prescribes the sacrifice during the fourth part of the *parvan*, there is no possibility of the sacrifice occurring in the fourth part of the *pratipad* (the first lunar day), and thus the prohibition is redundant due to the absence of such a possibility—because a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility—since a possibility does exist even in the absence of that specific prescription, by virtue of the rule: "The beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādayaḥ*) should be sacrificed upon. Nor should it be argued that this [prohibition] is subsumed under the rule "the first three *pratipads* [are for the sacrifice]," because there is no contradiction since this [prohibition] serves to indicate another time, and it is therefore untenable for it to have the purpose of mere subsumption. Furthermore, if the four aforementioned times for sacrifice are not obtained on either of the two days, another time for sacrifice must necessarily be accepted. Yet there is no other scriptural authority (*śāstra*) that establishes such a time. This is because restrictive rules (*vyavasthā-śāstra*) are intended to establish a restriction and cannot serve to enjoin a previously unknown time; for if they were intended to serve both purposes, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result, and if they were intended solely to enjoin a time, the restriction would lack authoritative basis. Therefore, it is established that this [prohibition] merely indicates another time.

That is incorrect. For there would be the undesirable consequence of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) without a reason, since the connection with the time of sacrifice is established by the meaning of the scriptural injunction: "The second lunar day consists of three *muhūrttas*," and so forth; therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) either—this is trivial. Consequently, it is established that the sacrifice is not performed during the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*).

Now, one might object: since during the winter season the days are extremely short, the *āvartana* occurs at approximately fourteen *ghaṭikās* less a few moments; thus, when there is an increase in the lunar day (*tithi*), even the fourth part of the *parvan* may consist of sixteen *nāḍikās*. In that case, starting from the time of the commencement of the ritual (*tantra*), the fourth part of the *parvan* exists on the morning of the first day, and on the morning of the second day, the third part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) exists. Where, then, should the sacrifice be performed? On this point, some say: "Because the junction of the *parvan* falls in the afternoon, the sacrifice should be performed on the following day. That is incorrect.
The sacrifice should be performed by the twice-born during the fourth part of the lunar phase (parvan),
because the followers of Āśvalāyana condemn [the performance] when it is joined with the second day.

This is because of the statement of Hārīta, and because of the contradiction with such statements as, "The second [lunar day] is [valid] for three muhūrttas. However, the scripture concerning the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the afternoon applies only to those cases that do not conflict with the scripture concerning the three-muhūrta period.

Now, one might ask: why does the scripture concerning the three-muhūrta period not apply to a case where the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the forenoon, provided it does not conflict with the scripture concerning the junction of the afternoon?

It is said in reply: Since there is no possibility of a second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) occurring when the junction (*parvan-sandhi*) falls in the morning during the final three *muhūrtas*, the mention of "three *muhūrtas*" would be unintended [if applied to the morning]. Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of using the term "second day" to indirectly indicate (*lakṣaṇā*) a distant and purposeless morning junction; moreover, it would contradict many scriptural statements prohibiting sacrifice on a day when the moon is visible. However, if the subject matter concerns a junction occurring in the afternoon, the aforementioned defects do not apply; therefore, it is logical that this refers specifically to that case.

Furthermore, the distinction is this: proximity to the junction (*sandhi*) exists in my position, but it does not exist in yours. Therefore, because the prescribed time for the morning sacrifice occurs therein, the sacrifice should take place at that very time. However, when the fourteenth day lasts for two and a half *praharas* plus a little more, three *muhūrtas* on the fifteenth day, and three *muhūrtas* of the first day (*pratipad*) remain on the second day (*dvitīyā*), then the sacrifice is performed on the former [the fourteenth].
One should commence that very lunar day (*tithi*) upon which the sun sets while still possessing three *muhūrtas*, for the sake of sacrifice, giving, recitation, and so forth.
Because of this statement:
"Indeed,
the last quarter of the fifteenth day and the first three quarters of the lunar fortnight..."
This is the time for the Pārvaṇa sacrifice; otherwise, it does not exist.

It might be argued that a sacrifice performed at a time other than the sacrificial times thus established would be improper. This is not so; for just as sacrifices are prescribed for the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pakṣādi*) and so forth, yet by virtue of another scriptural injunction, the sacrifice is accepted even on the fourth part of the *parvan* (the junction) at a time distinct from those established sacrificial times, so it shall be here as well. However, when the full fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) and the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) conclude before sunset on the following day, or when there is an absolute waning of the second day (*dvitīyā*) and subsequent days, then the sacrifice takes place on the preceding day alone. And when the fourteenth day is complete and the second day is subject to waning: [The verse continues: *caturdaśī ca sampūrṇā dvitīyā kṣayagāminī |* [The sacrifice is to be performed on the previous day.]
The offering to the gods (iṣṭi) should take place on the fourteenth day, and the ritual for the ancestors (kavya) and so forth on the new moon day.

According to this statement: when the fourteenth day is full and the first day (pratipad) on the fifteenth day is less than three muhūrtas, while the second day on the first day is three muhūrtas long, then the sacrifice is performed on the previous day alone.
If the second day is three muhūrtas long and falls in the afternoon of the first day, the preparatory rite (anvādhāna) takes place on the fourteenth day, because the moon will be visible thereafter.
Because of this statement; likewise: "When the moon has set and the sun has risen after having waned."
"One should perform the rite on the *pratipad* and sacrifice on the fifteenth day.

When the *pratipad* on the fifteenth day exceeds three *muhūrtas*, and the second day (*dvitīyā*) on the *pratipad* likewise exceeds that duration or is even longer, then the performance must take place on the former day; for since those [three] *muhūrtas* still exist within the [preceding] days, the sacrifice is prescribed on the former day alone.
And it has been said:
If the new moon has risen on the first day (pratipad), one should add fuel to the fires on the following day;
if it ceases on the festival day (parva), however, the time for the Full Moon sacrifice is immediate.
Even the final day [is excluded]:

"When the moon has not yet set and the [new] moon day is not yet complete, it is considered the time for fasting; however, if on the first day of the lunar fortnight one should see the moon, or if the moon rises while [the new moon day] is deficient. Thus [it is said].
Now, as for this statement: "The sacrificial oblation (*caru*) and the rite for the ancestors (*kavya*) and so forth are performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)," likewise...
"One should perform the preparatory rite and sacrifice on the fifteenth day," and likewise:
"The anvādhāna should be performed on the fourteenth day, because the moon is visible thereafter."

Regarding the injunction for the sacrifice on the fifteenth day (the full moon) by such statements as these, let it be so provided that the morning exists within the fourth part of the *parvan*. Since it is prescribed that "the fourth part of the *parvan*" is the time for the sacrifice, it is argued that performing the sacrifice during the third or fourth part of the *parvan* is not appropriate.
"One should not perform the sacrifice where the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) is seen before sunset; there, the Viśvedevas turn their faces away."
This is merely that much.

If, however, [the rule] were heard [in the scripture], then it would have been stated that the sacrifice on the preceding day occurs precisely during the fourth part of the *parvan*; but here, because the performance of the sacrifice on the fifteenth day is prescribed under specific conditions such as "if the second [lunar day] lasts for three *muhūrtas*," a sublation based on following the fourth part of the *parvan* is not appropriate. Therefore, it is established that the sacrifice takes place at the time exactly as described. However, when the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the final minute of a summer day, and due to the reduction of three *muhūrtas*, the second part of the *parvan* falls in the morning and the second lunar day lasts for three *muhūrtas* on the following day, then the sacrifice is performed during the second part of the *parvan*.
And so says Āśvalāyana:
"The sacrifice should be performed by the twice-born during the third part of the lunar festival (parvan),
because the followers of Āśvalāyana condemn [the performance] when it coincides with the second day."

[355] However, when the entry of the fourth quarter of the *parvan* occurs on the previous day more than three *muhūrtas* after [the conjunction], and the fourth quarter of the *pratipad* occurs on the following day more than six *muhūrtas* after [the conjunction], then the sacrifice is to be performed on the following day;
but if the entry occurs before the *iṅkha*, it is on the previous day.
As Gārgya says:

When there is a conflict between two lunar days regarding the time for sacrifice, if six *kalās* are observed [of the later day], then that subsequent *parvan* should be performed; if [six *kalās*] are lacking, one should commence with the former.

The term *kalā* here means a *muhūrta*, and not a *ghaṭikā*, because that would contradict the scriptural injunction: "If the second [lunar day] lasts for three *muhūrtas*. The author of the *Smṛtipradīpa* has also stated that the word *kalā* in this context signifies a *muhūrta*. However, in the text of Parāśara, the reading is "ṣaṇmuhūrtas tu vidyate" (it exists for six *muhūrtas*).

Regarding this statement, some dispute its meaning. For they suggest that the meaning of the passage appears to be that when the moon is seen, the sacrifice must not be performed under any circumstances; rather, the sacrifice should take place on the day preceding that, while the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite) should take place on the day prior to that. However, this is incorrect. Āpastamba states that the sighting of the moon must be avoided on either the day of the *anvādhāna* or the day of the sacrifice by way of option (*vikalpa*), but he does not say that the sighting of the moon must be avoided on the day of the sacrifice as a rule (*niyamena*). As he says: [The text continues with the citation: "If the moon is seen on the day of the *anvādhāna*, one should perform the sacrifice on the following day. If it is seen on the day of the sacrifice, one should perform the sacrifice on the next day. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the phrase "on the day of the sacrifice" (*yajñe*) refers to the day of the *anvādhāna*, because the sacrifice itself cannot occur on the same day as the *anvādhāna*. Therefore, the meaning is that the sacrifice should be performed on the day after the *anvādhāna*, provided the moon is not seen on that day. Consequently, the view that the sacrifice must be postponed for two days is untenable. This is because the rule regarding the avoidance of the moon's appearance applies equally to both the *anvādhāna* and the sacrifice. If the moon is seen on the day of the *anvādhāna*, the sacrifice is indeed postponed to the following day. But if it is seen on the day of the sacrifice, the sacrifice is postponed to the day after that. Thus, the postponement extends over three days in total. Therefore, the view that the sacrifice must be postponed for two days is not correct. This is because the rule regarding the avoidance of the moon's appearance applies equally to both the *anvādhāna* and the sacrifice. But if it is seen on the day of the sacrifice, the sacrifice is postponed to the day after that. Thus, the postponement extends over three days in total. Therefore, the view that the sacrifice must be postponed for two days is not correct. On the day when [the moon] is not seen, that day is the new moon (amāvāsyā), or it is known as such because "one will not see [it] tomorrow.
Even the Vājasaneyins restrict the sight of the moon to one or the other of the two days, and not on both.
As they say:
Regarding this, some fast after having seen [the moon], and thus it is said: "One should fast at that very time when one can see him neither in the east nor in the west.
Kātyāyana also says:
"Some maintain that one should fast on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) when the moon is not visible, and on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) when it is full."

Likewise, a scriptural injunction regarding the prohibition of eligibility for the sacrifice is observed on the day the moon is visible, which prescribes the performance of the sacrifice.

"On the day when the moon rises in the west, they sacrifice, thinking, 'He will rise over these worlds. This is indeed the sacrifice named Sumanā; for one who has sacrificed today and the moon subsequently rises in the west, at that time there is prosperity for him in this world. On the day when the moon is not seen either in the east or in the west, on that day one should sacrifice."

Thus, regarding these conflicting scriptures, the established rule has been set forth in the investigation of the *parvan* according to the views of many teachers: one should sacrifice on the day when the moon is visible at the conjunction of the *parvan* in the afternoon or otherwise;
furthermore, it is heard in scripture: "One should fast on the later [day] until the [moon] has emerged."

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the question of whether one should fast on the preceding day or the succeeding day, where such a definitive knowledge does not exist—that is, where there is doubt—one should fast on the succeeding day alone. If, even in the face of such doubt, the succeeding lunar day (*parvan*) is to be observed for fasting, how much more so when, according to the established rule stated in the *Parvavicāra*, the succeeding lunar day is clearly determined? Therefore, the statement "if the second day lasts for three muhūrtas" must be explained in accordance with that very rule, and not independently. If, however, it were stated for its own sake (independently), then first of all, due to the difficulty of supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*), one would have to obtain the meaning of the verb along with the injunction; yet once that is obtained, nothing further can be accomplished without effort. For instance, if the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the fire-consecration (*anvādhāna*) were enjoined for the fourteenth day, the construction would be: "the fire-consecration should be performed on the fourteenth day, provided that the moon is seen later. To this, it is replied: why is the postponement of the fire-consecration not enjoined? For even if the second day falls in the afternoon of the first day (*pratipad*), nevertheless, because the moon is seen on the fourteenth day, the fire-consecration must be performed on the following day. This is because, just as the sacrifice is prohibited when the moon is visible, the fire-consecration is likewise prohibited. As it is said: "When one sees him neither in front nor behind, then indeed one should fast"—meaning one should fast on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) when the moon is visible—and also: "On the day it is not seen, that is the new moon. Therefore, since the moon is seen on the fourteenth day, it is logical to enjoin the postponement of the fire-consecration by abandoning that day.

[Objection: But in this case, since the moon is seen on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), the anvādhāna should be performed on the day following the fourteenth; thus, because the term "fourteenth day" is connected to both [parts of the sentence], there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda), as well as the assumption of a modification of the word "from the fourteenth day" (caturdaśītaḥ). [Reply: It is said in response: first, there is no assumption of a modification, because a mediated connection (vyavahitānvaya) in the phrase "because the moon is seen on the fourteenth day" is not faulty. "There is no contradiction in enjoining multiple meanings through both the word and its sense.
For it is only when there is a plurality of syntactic connections based on the literal word that a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) occurs,
as it has been said:
Kumārila [argues] that if there were a multiplicity of Vedic functions for words, there would be excessive complexity (*atigaurava*).

Therefore, because the second relationship is merely implied (*arthika*), even the fault of postulating a modification of the word (*śabdavipariṇāma*) does not arise. Just as in the case of the *rātrisatra*, where the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is already exhausted by its own purpose, the qualification "one desiring stability" (*pratiṣṭhākāma*)—serving the purpose of "stability"—does not divide the sentence when it occurs within the context of the eligibility (*adhikāra*), nor does it produce the fault of modification.

But surely, defects such as the assumption of an intervention are accepted only when no other alternative is possible; yet here there is indeed another alternative, namely, the injunction for the postponement of the *anvādhāna* on the fourteenth day.

It is replied: If, out of fear of postulating an intervention [in the sequence], you resort to the injunction for the postponement of the *anvādhāna* (preparation of the fire), then listen to how many faults would likewise attach to your position as well. [358] For instance, in that case, with which part is the phrase “because of the sight of the moon” (*somadarśanāt*) connected? Is it “because of the sight of the moon on the fourteenth day” (*caturdaśyām*), or “on the day following the fourteenth,” or “on the first day (*pratipad*) after the new moon (*amāvāsyā*),” or “because of the sight of the moon in a direction other than the one [immediately following]”? First, it cannot be “because of the sight of the moon on the fourteenth day,” because such a connection is entirely unaccepted by all authorities, and because the sight of the moon in such a context is accepted as a defect. How then could the *anvādhāna* be enjoined for that very same day? Nor can it be “because of the sight of the moon on a day following the fourteenth,” because there is no occasion when the moon is seen on a day following a fourteenth day that is suitable for the *anvādhāna*. Nor can it be “because of the sight of the moon on the *pratipad*,” for if that were so, one would have to say “because of the sight of the moon on a day further beyond” (*parātparataḥ*) rather than simply “beyond” (*parataḥ*). If you argue that the word “beyond” (*parataḥ*) indicates that same meaning through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then figurative indication itself is a fault. If, however, you claim that since the *pratipad* is also subsequent to the fourteenth day, the word “beyond” denotes the *pratipad* in its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), then the *anvādhāna* would be enjoined even for the fourteenth day if the moon were seen on the fifth day. If you argue that the connection is made with the explicitly mentioned “on the *pratipad*” in the phrase “the afternoon of the *pratipad*,” and thus it is said “because of the sight of the moon on the *pratipad*,” then, because the word *pratipad* would be connected simultaneously with the second case ending and the term “sight of the moon,” there would result a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and the postulation of an intervention; furthermore, the word “beyond” (*parataḥ*) would become redundant. Moreover, since the moon is never seen on the *pratipad*, the meaning would be impossible to conceive. Now, if it is argued that—since in the passage “some indeed fast having seen [it]” the sight of the moon on the fasting day is known to be a merit rather than a defect—the *anvādhāna* should be performed on the fourteenth day because of the sight of the moon on the fourteenth—then if one must explain the mention of the fourteenth day as being due to the sight of the moon at the time of the *anvādhāna*, it must be stated on which day this occurs. It cannot be on the fourteenth, because the moon is seen “beyond” that, which would mean the *anvādhāna* is enjoined for a later time. Nor can it be on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), because the phrase “because of the sight of the moon beyond” does not apply here, and because the moon cannot be seen on the new moon day immediately following a fourteenth day suitable for the *anvādhāna*. Nor can it be “because of the sight of the moon in a direction other than the one [following] on the *pratipad*,” because that would entail the same previous faults of syntactical split and postulation of an intervention. Furthermore, since the moon is invariably seen in a direction other than the one [immediately following] on the *pratipad*, the word “beyond” (*parataḥ*) would become a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) that adds nothing to the performance of the rite. If it is argued that the phrase “because of the sight of the moon in a direction other than the one following” is intended to exclude the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and the *pratipad* [of the dark fortnight], that is incorrect, because the moon is also seen in a direction other than the one [immediately following] during the day and night of the full-moon *pratipad*. If it is explained as “because of the sight of the moon in the first part of the night on the *pratipad*,” or “because of the first sight of even a mere line [of the moon] on the *pratipad*,” or “because of the sight of the moon on the white *pratipad*” (to exclude the black *pratipad*), then so be it. [359] However, the essential point remains: the *anvādhāna* is to be performed on the day when the moon is first visible. Thus, the text should be interpreted as: “The *anvādhāna* is to be performed on the fourteenth day because of the sight of the moon [on the following day]. But if that is the case, it must be specified on which day [the *anvādhāna* occurs]. It cannot be on the fourteenth, as the moon is seen “beyond” that. Nor on the new moon, as the moon is seen “beyond” that. Therefore, the interpretation must be as follows: the *anvādhāna* is performed on the day when the moon is first seen, and the phrase “because of the sight of the moon” refers to that specific condition.
