Likewise, the Smṛti states:
"On the day when it is not seen and when it is full..."
"That very same time is for the sacrifice; one should sacrifice with this oblation. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, even the fast (*upavāsa*) is prescribed for the day when the moon is not seen, by the statement: "One should fast only at that time when one can see neither [the moon] before nor after. Since the two [the lunar day and the fast] must necessarily coincide on such a day, if the moon should nevertheless be visible, then according to the maxim *aṅgaguṇavirodhe ca tādarthyāt* ("and in case of a conflict between a subordinate element and its quality, the quality is set aside for the sake of the purpose"), the very time of the subordinate element (*aṅgakāla*) must be abandoned. For if even the subordinate element must be abandoned due to conflict with the primary, how much more so the mere quality? For this very reason, Āpastamba restates [the rule]: "On the day it is not seen, that is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*); or [on the day] they will not see it tomorrow."

The meaning is that on the full new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) one observes the fast there, whereas on any other [new moon], the fast is observed on the preceding day, and the sacrifice is performed on the day the moon is not visible; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the time of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) in deference to the time of its subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).
Now, one might object: the text "On the day when the moon rises in the west, on that day they sacrifice" shows that the sacrifice is to be performed even when the moon is visible.

It is said: This scriptural passage (*śruti*) prescribes the sacrifice on the day of the moon’s rising, not on the day when the moon is merely visible. Nevertheless, the *śruti* states that the sacrifice must take place even before the moon has risen: “Having gathered him from the waters and the plants, he causes him to be born from the oblations (*āhuti*). And people do not see [the moon] on that very day when it has risen, but rather on the second day. Therefore, even when the lunar day (*tithi*) is incomplete, one must sacrifice in exactly that manner; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *śruti*. Furthermore, this is precisely according to the intention of such scriptures as: “He, having been born from the oblations, was seen afterwards. Alternatively, the meaning is that he was born from the oblations on the first day (*pratipad*) and was seen afterwards on the second day. For this very reason, the authors of the *Smṛtis* say that one should not perform the sacrifice on the day the moon is visible on the following day.
"The anvādhāna [should be performed] on the fourteenth day, after the appearance of the moon. Likewise:
"If the moon is seen in the western quarter on the day of sacrifice..."
In that case, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should give a staff to a twice-born man. Thus it is said.

Therefore, on the day when the moon is visible, the sacrifice must not be performed under any circumstances. Since the prohibition of the sacrifice upon the sight of the moon itself precludes its performance during the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipat*), that specific mention of the prohibition is intended to demonstrate its gravity. By this, the view that the statement "if the second lunar day [extends] for three *muhūrtas*" is an injunction for the postponement of the fire-kindling (*anvādhāna*) is refuted.

Furthermore, if there were no injunction for the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the *anvādhāna*, two disjointed connections would result: first, that because the moon is seen on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), the *anvādhāna* must take place on the day following the fourteenth; and second, due to the consequence of the fault you have mentioned. If, however, the afternoon of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) contains three *muhūrtas* of the second day (*dvitīyā*), then the *anvādhāna* should be performed on the fourteenth day, because the moon is seen on the following day—the first lunar day—during those three *muhūrtas* of the second day. When this meaning is accepted, there is no fault even in the injunction for the anticipation (*apakarṣa*) of the *anvādhāna*. For here, neither the word "first lunar day" (*pratipad*) nor the word "second day" (*dvitīyā*) is connected with the phrase "because of the seeing of the moon" (*somadarśanāt*), which would otherwise necessitate a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*), or the assumption of a disjointed connection. This is because such a connection is not obtained through the word "following" (*parataḥ*) alone. When it is stated, "The *anvādhāna* is on the fourteenth day, because of the seeing of the moon on the following day," the "day following the fourteenth" is understood as a lunar date (*tithi*). Since the moon cannot be seen on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) during the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the second day is taken; and since that too follows the fourteenth, there is no authority for taking any other lunar date by bypassing it. Moreover, the mere sight of the moon on the second day is not the reason for performing the *anvādhāna* on the fourteenth day, as that would contradict the rule regarding the three *muhūrtas*. Therefore, when the meaning is accepted as "the *anvādhāna* is on the fourteenth day, because of the seeing of the moon on the following day consisting of three *muhūrtas* of the second day," there is no fault. Since the perceived syntactical connection is thus maintained, and since the time of the primary rite is not sublated by the time of its subsidiary (*aṅga*), the injunction for the anticipation of the *anvādhāna* alone is logical.

Furthermore, if the sacrifice were accepted as taking place on the day the moon is actually seen, a contradiction with many scriptural statements would also result, according to the *Cārāyaṇīya-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*:
"As long as there is deficiency in the preceding [day], and as long as there is no rising after sunset—
for that duration they know the fast and the sacrifice."

The meaning is that the fast (*aupavasta*) should be observed as long as the waning of the full moon of the previous month has not occurred; and the meaning is that the time for sacrifice (*yāgakāla*) lasts as long as the moon, having set on the new moon day, has not yet risen on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).
When the moon is full, one should perform the fast and the sacrifice during the seventh week;
when the lunar node (*parvan*) has ended, one should perform the sacrifice at the conjunction of the moon and the sun.

Thus, the very meaning previously stated is clarified by this sentence: on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), when the moon is full, the vow known as *aupavasta* must be performed; immediately thereafter, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*)—when the moon and sun are at equal [longitude]—the sacrifice (*yāga*) must be performed. "If the moon is seen either risen or waning on the *pratipad* days, the sacrifice should not be performed; the Viśvedevas would turn their faces away."

If the moon, having risen on the first day of the new moon (*darśa-pratipad*), is seen deficient on the first day of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī-pratipad*), then the sacrifice must not be performed, because all the gods turn their faces away from it.
Likewise: "But if the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) is seen before sunset..."
No sacrifice would be seen there, and the Viśvedevas would turn their faces away.
An exception to this rule:
"Fullness is likewise seen during the first part of the night;
its reversal does not occur by day; therefore, the sacrifice takes place on the following day."
If fullness is not seen during the first part of the night,
or if [the moon] rises deficiently during the day, one should prescribe the sacrifice with the *iṣṭi* [rite] in that case.

On this point, some say: when the moon is visible on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), the non-performance of the sacrifice should be understood as optional; for if the New Moon sacrifice were prohibited solely by the sight of the moon even when the third part of the first day is obtained in the morning, then [the following verse would be contradicted]:
"If the moon is seen on the day of sacrifice, or if it is seen during the Vāruṇī [nakṣatra], one should offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis and give a staff to a twice-born man."

Thus, the statement of Kātyāyana would indeed be inconsistent in meaning. By the rule “if the second day [the new moon] lasts for three muhūrtas,” the anvādhāna (preparatory rite) is prescribed on the fourteenth day; since the sacrifice is then performed on the fifteenth day as a matter of course, the subsequent statement “if there is Soma (the moon) on the second day, the day of sacrifice, which is the first day of the lunar fortnight,” would be inconsistent, because that day is not the day of sacrifice. Rather, the morning of that day is the day of sacrifice at that time. Furthermore, the injunction “having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should give a staff as a gift to a twice-born” would also be inconsistent if it were prescribed for an occasion when no sacrifice occurs, as it would be arbitrary. However, if the occasional prohibition of the sacrifice is accepted upon seeing the moon, then even when the moon is visible, if the sacrifice together with the *vyāhṛti* oblation and the gift of the staff is prescribed by this very text, only then does it become meaningful; otherwise, it would not.

That is incorrect. To explain: is this an injunction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta-vidhi*) or an injunction regarding a specific occasion (*nimitta-vidhi*)? Regarding the first case, is the expiation to be performed when the moon is seen on the day of sacrifice, or is it an expiation upon the mere sight of the moon, or is it an expiation when the sacrifice is performed on the day the moon is seen? First, it cannot be the first alternative. For one who performs the sacrifice on the day the moon is seen out of ignorance, this [text] is appropriate as an injunction for expiation once the moon is subsequently seen; it lacks the capacity to render the Vedic and Smṛti prohibitions merely optional. Furthermore, expiation occurs upon the transgression of what is enjoined or prohibited. If this expiation were to apply when the moon is seen on the day of sacrifice, then a prohibition against that would have to be inferred. If, however, this were enjoined when the sacrifice is performed on the day the moon is seen, then since such a prohibition is already explicitly stated in scripture, no further inference is required; thus, the expiation applies precisely in that case. Nor can it be the second alternative, because that would entail the consequence that the prohibitions are not merely optional. Under the category of an occasion-injunction, is this enjoined with "the sight of the moon on the day of sacrifice" as the occasion, or with "the sacrifice being performed on the day the moon is seen" as the occasion? Neither is possible due to the aforementioned defects. In the second of these two positions, even the perception that "the sight of the moon on the day of sacrifice" is the occasion would be contradicted. Therefore, the prohibition against sacrificing on the day the moon is seen is not merely optional.

Regarding this, some say: "The sacrifice is always on the first day (*pratipad*) itself; the sacrifice is not on the first day when it is overlapped by the second day (*dvitīyā-viddha-pratipad*), nor is the sacrifice on the fourth part of the lunar phase (*parva-caturthāṃśa*).
As Kātyāyana says:
"One should always perform the rite that begins the fortnight at the very beginning of the fortnight."
"Only in the forenoon do some perform it; others, however, do so when [the moon] is pierced," thus [it is said].
The meaning is that others do not include the mention [of the word "others"] for the purpose of indicating an alternative, just as some recite "vaṣaṭ" while others recite "vauṣaṭ."

That too is incorrect, because it would entail the contraction of numerous Vedic and Smṛti statements—including those prescribing the sacrifice on the fourth part of the *parvan* day as the time for the preceding day's conjunction with the morning twilight, those prescribing the sacrifice on the second day when overlapped by the first, and the condemnatory statements regarding sacrifices on days when the moon is visible—and because it would lead to the contingency of various alternatives (*vikalpa*) marred by many defects. Furthermore, there is no injunctive suffix (*vidhi-vibhakti*) here, as it merely teaches a traditional practice (*ācāra*). Such a statement lacks the capacity to justify the introduction of so many alternative interpretations of the meaning of the sentence; therefore, this verse should be explained by eliding the initial vowel ‘a’ in the word ‘amanīṣiṇaḥ’. Consequently, the previously stated rule alone is correct.

Now, certain commentators on the Baudhāyana-sūtra maintain that even when the *parvan* conjunction occurs in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), one should fast on the preceding day and perform the sacrifice on that very day; furthermore, they desire the sacrifice to take place specifically in the afternoon, close to the conjunction. This is untenable, because it contradicts the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "Sacrifice in the morning" (*prātar yajadhvam*).
[Objection: But even if one sacrifices in the morning, does this not contradict the injunction to "sacrifice at the conjunction" (*sandhau yajeta*)?

This is not a fault. Since the rule of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi-śāstra*) refers to proximity, and proximity is relative, it can be said that the morning time is "near" in relation to something else; thus, there is no contradiction with the rule of euphonic combination. However, the afternoon can by no means be called "morning," and therefore, if one performs the sacrifice in the afternoon, there is a contradiction with the morning time; hence, it is not proper to sacrifice at that time.

Now, one might argue that as long as the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) is very close, the rule of conjunction (*saṃdhi-śāstra*) remains applicable; thus, when the conjunction occurs in the afternoon, the requirement for the sacrifice (*yāga*) would be immediately adjacent to it. Alas, in that case, even if the conjunction of the lunar day (*parva-saṃdhi*) occurs at night, the performance of the sacrifice would likewise have to take place right there. If, however, it is argued that because of the injunction regarding the day—namely, "On the previous day he takes the fire (*agni*), on the following day he sacrifices to the deity"—and because there is no direct injunction for the night, and since proximity to the conjunction can somehow be established on the day as well, the sacrifice is not to be performed at night.

Indeed, even when the sacrifice is performed at that juncture occurring in the afternoon, the performance in the afternoon is not [valid], because it contradicts the injunction for the morning and because there is no direct injunction for the afternoon; furthermore, since proximity to the juncture is possible even in the morning, [the afternoon is excluded].

Now, if it is argued that because "one should sacrifice at the juncture" is an explicit (pratyakṣa) injunction, the injunction based on the wording of a mantra—"Sacrifice in the morning"—is weaker as it is indistinct;
to this, the reply is that the statement "one sacrifices to the deity of the following day" is equally weak, as it too is indistinct due to being a mere descriptive reference (vartamānāpadeśa).

Now it is said: when there is a conflict, one considers relative strength and weakness. Since the day is also proximate to the junction occurring at night, there is no conflict between the rule concerning proximity (the *sandhi-śāstra*) and the rule concerning the day.
But then, for that very same reason, there would also be no conflict with the rule concerning the morning (*prātaḥ-śāstra*).

Furthermore, proximity (*sāmīpya*) is not the primary meaning of the word *sandhi*, but rather its secondary (metaphorical) sense; in that case too, the lack of clarity remains the same. Nor is it a defect for the injunction regarding the morning time (*prātaḥ-vidhi*) to be independent of the context (*aprakaraṇādhīna*). For it has been stated in the section on "Non-contradiction with the Learned" (*Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*) that even practices such as the Smṛti rules for sacrificial fees and conduct, though independent of the context, are stronger than the Śrauta rules dependent on the context because they require closer proximity to the performance manual (*prayogaśāstra*). Therefore, without subverting the prescribed place, time, and so forth, one adopts only as much proximity as is possible. Otherwise, if the morning time were subverted out of a mere desire for proximity, there would follow the undesirable consequence of subverting all other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Consequently, one should sacrifice during the morning time—which occurs near the *sandhi* and conforms to the prescribed times such as the fourth part of the *parvan*—and not otherwise.

But is it not the case that because of the prohibition of sacrifice at evening time in the statement, "There is nothing fit for the sacrifice to the gods in the evening," the remaining times such as the afternoon and so forth are understood to be permitted—since a specific prohibition is intended to permit the remainder—just as when it is said, "He sees with the left eye," it is understood that he does not see with the right?

This might be so if this were a prohibition (*niṣedha*), but it is not; rather, it is a restriction (*nirbandha*). For within a single sentence, there is the injunction regarding the morning time and the prohibition regarding the evening time; since this would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to its dual purpose, one must necessarily accept that one part is an injunction and the other is a mandatory restatement (*nityānuvāda*). In that case, if the prohibition of the evening time were accepted, then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), every time—such as the morning, the afternoon, and so forth—would incidentally (*pākṣika*) obtain as being for the sake of the sacrifice. Consequently, it would not be tenable for the morning time to be restated as having a permanent connection with the sacrifice.

Alternatively, if the injunction for the morning time is accepted, then since all times other than that are permanently excluded, the exclusion of the evening time as well is a permanent restatement (nityānuvāda).

Furthermore, because the statement "Sacrifice in the morning" (*prātar yajadhvam*) has the form of an injunction (*praiṣa*), and since an injunction consists essentially in instigation (*pravarttanā*), it is quite easy to conceive it as a mandate (*vidhi*). However, as for the phrase "there is not [sacrifice] in the evening," because it is a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), there is not even a trace of instigation, nor is there any such cognition; thus, this cannot be a prescription of a prohibition (*niṣedhavidhāna*), because a prohibition is not clearly understood, and because it would entail a contradiction with the plural injunctions previously cited that establish the sacrifice in the morning and the forenoon.

Now, it may be granted that this is so when there is a fourth part of the lunar day (parvan) at dawn; but when that is absent, how is the decision to be made—should the time of dawn be set aside, or the fourth part of the lunar day?

It is said: if the sacrifice were performed in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), the procedures (*tantra*) and times of the morning and forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa-prātaḥkāla*) would be sublated; however, if it is performed in the morning, there is only the sublation of the mere fourth part of the *parvan*. Thus, for the sake of minimizing sublation, that [morning performance] alone is appropriate. Therefore, it is established that even when the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the afternoon, the sacrifice must take place on the following day. But when the junction occurs at midday, the sacrifice takes place on that very day, according to the previously cited statements of Laugākṣi and others. On this point, some say: "If the sacrifice is completed on the first day (*pratipad*) before the [new moon] has entered..."
Having performed the sacrifice again in its entirety, one should then proceed; it must not be done otherwise.

Thus, because the statement of Garga prescribes the performance of the sacrifice again on the fifteenth day after the completion of the *iṣṭi*, it is logical that the sacrifice should take place on the second day itself. As for the scriptural rule regarding the midday conjunction (*madhyāhnasandhi*), it is applicable when the lunar day is decreasing (*kṣayagāminī*) and there is no time for the sacrifice on the following day; in such a case, it functions as an alternative (*vikalpa*) to the rule stating, "when the first day has not yet begun. However, when the lunar day is increasing (*vṛddhigāminī*) and the time for the sacrifice exists on the subsequent day, the rule concerning midday does not apply at all, and the restrictive injunction (*niyama*) that "the beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādayaḥ*) must be sacrificed upon" would otherwise be contradicted.

That is incorrect, because it contradicts many statements such as, "If the second [lunar day] lasts for three muhūrtas," and because an option (*vikalpa*) is also improper. Therefore, by reflecting upon this statement, one should perform everything except the conclusion during the morning; having paused, once the first lunar day (*pratipad*) has begun, the feeding of Brahmins and the completion of the final ritual act must be performed.

On this point, some raise an objection: since the principal rite along with its ancillaries (*aṅga*) must be performed in the forenoon alone, and since the satiation of Brahmins is an ancillary (*aṅga*), there would be a contradiction with the injunction that impels one toward the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which comprises both ancillaries and the principal—once the activity has commenced. Furthermore, in the *Yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa*, the Vārttikakāra stated in his commentary on the verse: "Even if [the time] is not fully occupied, it should be so; however, it is not perceived as such here," asserting that if the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) is not fully occupied due to the brevity of the ritual under the constraint of the forenoon injunction, nothing is wrong. Thus, he indicates that the completion of the *iṣṭi* may indeed take place in the forenoon. Therefore, when accepting the view that the full-moon sacrifice is to be completed in a single day (*sadyaskāla*), this statement is intended to show that there is no single-day performance in the case of fasting on the preceding day (the *pūrva-upavāsa* option), because on the second day the morning of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) still exists, making a repetition of the rite appropriate.

That is incorrect. Because it would entail a restriction of the sentence "having commenced, before [the sacrifice] has entered [the new moon]," and because the unity of time for the subsidiaries and the principal rite—though implied by the injunction of performance—is set aside by the force of the explicit statement, a restriction based on that [commencement] is not logical. Furthermore, it contradicts the Śruti text: "One should sacrifice on both sides of the conjunction (*saṃdhi*). For that text establishes that the sacrificial performance should proceed in such a way that it encompasses the conjunction on both sides. Thus, when the conjunction occurs in the afternoon or at another [specified] time, if the *anvādhāna* (preparation) is performed on that day and the sacrifice is performed on the following day, the performance indeed becomes centered upon the conjunction; hence there is no contradiction. However, in the case where the conjunction occurs in the forenoon, if one performs the *anvādhāna* on the previous day and completes the rite on that same day before the conjunction, the state of being centered upon the conjunction is lost. Therefore, the final ritual act—the act denoted by the word "completion," consisting of the satiation of the Brahmins—must simply be postponed until after the conjunction. By this much, the state of being centered upon the conjunction will be achieved in the performance; however, there must be no interruption in the middle. Why? We say: because of the authority of the scriptural rule regarding the performance being centered upon the conjunction.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that even when the *saṃdhi* (the junction) is postponed, everything is postponed for the sake of ensuring the continuity of the performance? [Reply: That is not so, because it would result in a contradiction with the time of the morning (*prātaḥkāla*). For continuity, though implied by the force of the injunction regarding the performance, is weaker than a ritual element whose time is explicitly prescribed. Thus, in such an example, having completed [the rite] at the morning time—excluding the final completion (*samāpti*)—one should stop, wait until the *saṃdhi*, and then on the following day, at the time of the *pratipad*, perform only the ritual element of the completion. Therefore, if the *saṃdhi* occurs at midday, the sacrifice (*yāga*) takes place on the next day. Even if the *parvan-saṃdhi* occurs in the forenoon, the sacrifice takes place on that very same day, according to the *Cārāyaṇīya-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*.
A sacrifice performed when [the time] is far distant, or likewise when it is too near,
is declared by the sages who perceive reality to be a cause of grief for you.
The sacrifice may also take place on the sixth and eighth [lunar days], as well as twice on the twelfth;
it occurs in the forenoon, prior to the conjunction of the sun and the moon.

The meaning of the sentence is that the sacrifice should be performed when there is a mutual conjunction of the sun and the moon in the forenoon on the sixth and eighth [lunar days] during the full moon, and on the twelfth [day] twice during the new moon.
Likewise:
"One who would perform the sacrifice after having postponed the arrived lunar day should offer the remnant of that lunar day."
One should not attend a sacrifice in vain, for no offering is poured into ashes.
The stated refutation is: "Having practiced [the path], but not yet having entered [the fruit]."

On this point, some say: During the summer season, because the days are exceedingly long, the *āvartana* (the sun’s turning point) occurs at slightly more than sixteen *ghaṭikās*. When there is a decrease in the lunar day (*tithi*), the fourth part of the *parvan* may sometimes consist of fourteen *ghaṭikās*. If, in that case, the junction of the *parvan* (*parvasandhi*) occurs in the forenoon near the *āvartana*, then—even though the fourth part of the *parvan* is absent at the time of beginning the ritual near sunrise—the sacrifice must take place on that very day. This is because the primary sacrifice (*pradhānayāga`) occurs in the morning when the [junction] is present; it should not be performed on the following day during the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*), due to the prohibition: "One should not sacrifice in the fourth part. For where there is a conflict with the specific time that constitutes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the primary sacrifice, it is proper to abandon the time of the auxiliary according to the principle of the conflict between the primary and its qualities (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*). Therefore, in this case, the sacrifice is not on the following day. However, even if in this same situation the third part of the *pratipad* occurs on the morning of the following day, the sacrifice is still not performed then. This is because of scriptural injunctions such as "if the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) lasts for three *muhūrtas*," and because it would contradict the numerous prohibitions against sacrificing on a day when the moon is visible. Therefore, in the aforementioned case, the sacrifice is indeed on the preceding day. Furthermore, regarding another scriptural statement:
"On the sixteenth day is the desired sacrifice; on the fifteenth day it is middling;
on the fourteenth day it is the inferior sacrifice; on the seventeenth day it is evil.
Therefore, one should not perform a sacrifice on the seventeenth day, but one should not fail to establish the sacred fires [on that day].

But surely, it is only the *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires) that is prohibited, not the sacrifice (*yāga*). If that were the case, then when the lunar day increases, the *iṣṭi* would simply not be performed. Therefore, it must be understood that starting from the day of sacrifice, the *aupavasatha* rite is not to be performed on the seventeenth day.
For this very reason, Baudhāyana says: "Therefore, the fourteenth and sixteenth days remain in their respective places, but not the thirteenth and seventeenth.
And likewise, there is another statement:
"Where the *aupavasatha* rite would fall on the thirteenth day after the day of sacrifice,
or even on the seventeenth, one should avoid that with great effort.

Now, since it is impossible for both the decrease and increase of two days to occur simultaneously, how can there be a prohibition against performing the *aupavasatha* rite on the thirteenth or seventeenth day at any time?
It is said: if there is no attainment [of the goal], then this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), like the expression "neither in the atmosphere nor in heaven.

Now, if the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice were performed on the day of fasting (*upavasatha*), it would contradict the injunction: "One should fast at the end of the fortnight (*pakṣānte*). For a fortnight consists of fifteen days; if one begins from the previous day of sacrifice (*yajaniya*) and the fortnight passes in fifteen days, this *ṣoḍaśī* remains redundant. Alternatively, if the fortnight is reckoned starting from the day after the previous day of sacrifice, then the status of the previous day of sacrifice as the beginning of the fortnight (*pakṣāditva*) is lost.

It is said: A fortnight (*pakṣa*) consists of fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), not fifteen solar days, according to the tradition of the astronomers (*jyotirvid*). Thus, lunar days are sometimes completed in fourteen days, fifteen, or even sixteen. Therefore, based on that tradition, the first day of the fortnight (*pratipad*) is designated by the term "beginning of the fortnight," and the fifteenth lunar day (*pañcadaśī*) is designated by the term "end of the fortnight. Consequently, even when that [fifteenth day] falls on the sixteenth solar day, the fast (*upavasatha*) is performed on that very [lunar day]. Alternatively, it should be understood that the first half of this statement refers to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the second half refers to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), since there also exists a view regarding the *sadyaskāla* (immediate) performance starting from the full moon. On the first day (*pratipad*), the ritual of the fast and the sacrifice take place; in that context, this prohibition is stated: "it is the seventeenth."
It has been said: "When [the moon] is equal, the fifteenth [verse] is the offering-verse (yājyā); in a full month, the sixteenth is the offering-verse;
whether it be deficient or even in excess, the seventeenth is never used as an offering-verse."

Now, since mere time is sublated by specific verbal designations, the mention of waning and waxing must refer to something else. One who does not know the waning and waxing of the lunar days within the lunar disc should be known as a *yātudhāna* (demon), like one who offers oblations into ashes.

Thus, this is the application of the rule for knowing the decrease and increase [of the lunar day]: that in the case of the decrease and increase of the subsequent day, one enters the preceding day during those two halves.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
Of the ghaṭikās that follow the tenth part, whether they be deficient or likewise excessive,
half of them should be subtracted and half added respectively.

"In the case of decrease or increase, that [correction] is on the first day. This means: of the subsequent lunar day (*tithi*), which is the *pratipad*, those *ghaṭikās* which are less or more than those of the preceding lunar day—after the [mean] equality—should be subtracted from the previous day in the case of decrease, and added in the case of increase. By this, it is stated that the knowledge of the *parvan-sandhi* (the junction of the lunar phases) must be performed. Regarding the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), however, Āpastamba has stated a specific rule:
"On the full moon day, the kindling of the fires, the strewing of grass, and the fasting may be done; or else, in the case of immediate performance (*sadyaskālā*), everything is performed at once."

The meaning of this is as follows: on a full-moon day that is performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*), the rites beginning with the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) are performed either immediately or on the preceding day; in that case, everything up to the satiating of the Brahmins is performed [on the same day], and therefore that constitutes a single [performance]. And it has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*:
"In the case of the *anvāhiti* offerings, the spreading of the grass and the fasting take place on the preceding day; this indeed is the rule for the full-moon sacrifice."
If the junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi) occurs before the turning point (āvarttana), then the entire rite is performed immediately;
"before the turning point" implies "after the time of saṅgava."
If the conjunction occurs after the moment of contact (saṅgava) and before the sun’s turning back (paryāvarttana),
that lunar day is to be known as the full moon for the purpose of the rule regarding immediate performance (sadyaskāla).
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana.
Furthermore, this state of being performed on the same day is optional, according to the statement: "It is performed either immediately or at that [later] time; both are equal."
And likewise Āpastamba states:
"The Vājasaneyins prescribe a *kharvikā* as the third [lunar day].
*Kharvikā* means "small"; and its smallness is due to its not extending beyond the [preceding] day.
And it has been stated by the author of the *Gṛhyārthasaṃgraha*:
"That day on which the junction of the parvan occurs before midday is this third [type]."
"That *kharvikā* is another [form] belonging to the Vājasaneyins; having fasted on that day, the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) takes place on the following day.

Some say that everything from "on the full moon day" up to "or immediately" constitutes one single sūtra, while others state: "In the *sadyaskālā* [form], everything is performed. Thus, they explain the meaning of the first sūtra as: "On every full moon day, the rites beginning with the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) are performed either immediately or on the preceding day"; whereas the second [sūtra] means: "The *sadyaskālā* is a modified form (*vikṛti*); in it, everything up to the satiating of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*) is performed, but not the concluding portion ending with the *iḍā* offering."

This is not correct; for in the case of the *sadyaskāla* (immediate) ritual when the junction occurs in the afternoon, it would contradict the Vedic injunction: "One should sacrifice on both sides of the junction. Furthermore, Vidhiratnakṛt has also stated:
"And the archetype (*prakṛti*) is never characterized by the *sadyaskāla* mode."
As it has been said:
"The wise do not praise a change in one's nature, whether it occurs all at once or gradually; this has been cited for the purpose of explaining transformation."
That is incorrect, because it would entail the contradiction of the context.

Thus it has been stated regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*). As for the ectype (*vikṛti*), although it appears that the same time characterized by the fourth lunar phase (*caturthāṃśa*) and so forth applies there as well—due to the extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) by the rule "The Darśapūrṇamāsa are the archetype of the *iṣṭi*s"—nevertheless, because Āpastamba prescribes the time again for the ectype, stating, "If one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, if with an animal sacrifice, or if with Soma, one should sacrifice on the new moon day or the full moon day," the completion of the sacrifice must occur on the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) itself. Therefore, where the fifteenth day and the first day of the next month (*pratipad*) are both complete, one should complete the ectype on the fifteenth day itself, and immediately thereafter perform the fire-consecration (*agnyanvādhāna*) and other rites for the archetype. However, when the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*) occurs in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) on a broken lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*), then because the prescribed time is impossible on the previous day, or even if possible, because it is impossible at the stage of commencing the rite, the principle that the primary act together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅgapradhāna*) must occupy the same time is not applicable. This is because Āpastamba ordains the connection with the prescribed time for the primary act together with its subsidiaries, stating: "The primary act along with its subsidiaries is designated [as occurring] in the same place, time, and agent. Furthermore, since the archetype was mentioned previously and Āpastamba himself states, "The unprecedented [rite] should be at the end," the archetype is performed first and the ectype follows immediately after. Thus, it should be understood that the performance of the ectype takes place during the three parts of the first day of the next month (*pratipad*) that are extended [to the previous day], which are sufficient for the subsidiaries and the primary act. But when the junction of the lunar phases occurs in the afternoon or at night, then the sacrifice takes place on that very day, because the prescribed time is possible on that day alone. Having all this in mind, it was said: * When the junction of the lunar phases occurs in the forenoon, the sacrifice is performed on the previous day. * When the junction of the lunar phases occurs in the afternoon or at night, the sacrifice is performed on that very day. * When the junction of the lunar phases occurs at dawn (*prabhāta*), the sacrifice is performed on the previous day. * When the junction of the lunar phases occurs at midday (*madhyāhna*), the sacrifice is performed on the following day. This is the established rule. It is not the case that the sacrifice is always performed on the previous day; rather, it depends on whether the junction of the lunar phases falls within the forenoon or the afternoon. When it falls in the forenoon, the sacrifice is on the previous day; when it falls in the afternoon, it is on the following day. This is the settled conclusion. If the junction of the lunar phase (parvasandhi) occurs prior to the turning back [of the moon], one should perform the primary sacrifice at that time and then the modified sacrifice; however,
if it should occur later than that, [the primary sacrifice must be performed first].
On that day, the modification [is performed]; on the following day, the original form.
Regarding this, some say:
"Those six muhūrtas on which there is an increase [of the day] on the following day are not to be accepted;
however, even three muhūrtas are to be accepted on which there is a decrease on the following day."

"One should not perform [the rite] for less than three muhūrtas; even in that case, one should indicate it as deficient. Thus it is said. "If the junction (sandhi) occurs after the time of saṅgava and before the sun's turning back [at midday], that full moon day (paurṇamāsī) is to be known as the lunar day (tithi) for the rule of immediate performance (sadyaskāla)."

By this very statement of Smṛti, since the lunar days (tithis) for the Agrayaṇa and other modified sacrifices (vikṛtis) are prescribed as being performed on the same day (sadyaskāla), when the first lunar day (pratipad) increases in duration on the second day, there is no status of being "same-day" (sadyaskālatva) on the preceding day. Likewise:
"If the second [lunar day] lasts for three muhūrtas and occurs in the afternoon of the first lunar day..."
The placing of the sacred fires (anvādhāna) should take place on the fourteenth day, after the appearance of the moon.

The prohibition of sacrifice shown in this statement—that it does not apply when there is an increase in the lunar day (*tithi*) on the first day of the fortnight—is the intended meaning of the two statements: "when [the day] is short, three *muhūrtas* in the afternoon must indeed be accepted.
To this, it is replied: as for what was said, that the statement "if the junction (*saṃdhi*) is after the *saṅgava* period" refers to the domain of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

That is incorrect. For this statement—whether read within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices or studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*)—in either case, its application to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) is not possible. Nor is it accepted or even found that its placement within the context of a specific modified sacrifice implies a scope covering all modified sacrifices. Furthermore, it is impossible for it to be read in the context of every modified sacrifice; therefore, this refers to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Nor is an exception to the rule of immediate performance (*sadyaskālatva*) possible there. In the absence of such an exception, would the sacrifice take place on the *pratipad* (the first day of the lunar fortnight) or on that very *parvan* (the full moon/new moon day)? It cannot be the first, because in such a situation, even if the *pratipad* occurs on the second day, since the second day (*dvitīyā*) lasts more than three *muhūrtas*, it contradicts the scriptural injunction: "If the second day is more than three *muhūrtas*... and so forth. Nor does this refer to the intention of the Vājasaneyins regarding the statement "it should not be performed for three *muhūrtas*," because that statement does not establish the meaning that when the junction of the *parvan* occurs before midday and the *pratipad* increases in length, the sacrifice should not be performed there, but rather only the fire-preparation (*anvādhāna*). Furthermore, the claim that the phrase "if the *pratipad* has three *muhūrtas* and the second day [has more]" is restricted by the rule concerning decrease (*hrāsa*) is refuted. Even the statement "six *muhūrtas* should not be taken" does not establish this meaning. Therefore, these two statements should be explained as follows: when even six *muhūrtas* belonging to the fourteenth-day (*caturdaśī*) period are to be taken for the fire-preparation, they should be taken if the [lunar day] increases on the second day; in the case of decrease, those too are to be taken. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the sentence "the second day is three *muhūrtas*" and with the prohibitions against performing the sacrifice when the moon is visible. Thus, in accordance with the lack of contradiction with other statements such as "it should not be performed for three *muhūrtas*," this should be explained as referring specifically to the fire-preparation (*anvādhāna*).

Others, however, say that the first statement refers to occasions other than the festival days. What need is there for more? Because of the contradictions with many other statements, their interpretation is not tenable.

The same should be understood regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). For this very reason, it is stated there as well: "The junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*) occurs fixedly at midday; having performed [the primary rite] on that day, one may then commence the animal sacrifice either immediately or after two days, and then the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). But if the junction of the lunar phases occurs before [midday], one performs the model sacrifice on that day, whereas if it were the animal sacrifice, it would be performed immediately. The phrase "immediately" (*sadya eva*) is used because, when the junction occurs in the forenoon, the prescribed time for the following day is impossible. This is the determination for modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) and animal sacrifices where no specific time has been prescribed; however, it should be understood that where a specific time or a duration of two days is heard in the scripture, the performance must be carried out exactly according to that.
However, a specific rule is shown in the Śruti regarding the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi:

"At whatever time the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs, one should sacrifice with that [new moon sacrifice]; or if it be the full moon (paurṇamāsī), one should sacrifice with that [full moon sacrifice] and then with the Pūrṇamāsa. The phrase "at whatever time" means before the turning of the sun; "with that" refers to the new moon sacrifice; "with this" refers to the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi. The meaning is: if the full moon should occur before the turning of the sun and be of the same-day performance (sadyaskālā), then one should sacrifice with that Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and then with the Pūrṇamāsa.
This has been stated by the author of the Vārttika:
"On the full-moon day, however, [the moon] may be full; on the second day, when the moon has waned, one should sacrifice with the Pūrṇamāsa first, and afterwards with the Darśa."
Here, by the word *ijyā*, the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice is meant.
The items to be avoided on the day of fasting (*upavasta*) are shown in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"Vegetables, meat, lentils, chickpeas, and *koradūṣaka* grains..."
One should avoid beans and honeyed foods on the day of fasting.
Regarding the means for knowing the *parvan* (the junction days), Gobhila states:
"One should study [the relevant texts] from those who know them, or one should ascertain the *parvan*."

Thus ends the determination of the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi-nirṇaya*) in the *Kālanirṇaya*, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the illustrious administrative offices of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.

regarding this, the Matsya Purāṇa states:
"During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat; however, one may eat after bathing once they have been released."
Having seen that the two [suns] had not yet set, they bathed on the following day.

One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or the sun until both have set; having seen them set, one should bathe and [then eat] on the following day.
In the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, one should not eat at that time when the moon and the sun are eclipsed."
But after both [the teacher and the disciple] have performed their ablutions, he should eat in his own home.
But where the reading is "one should do it afterwards," the word "eating" (*aśanam*) is supplied there as a modification.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Bhārgava, on whichever day of the moon or the sun..."
"But in that case, there may be an eclipse; one should not eat before the act of eating [has begun].
Thus it is said: "One should not perform [the rite] while there is an eclipse, nor likewise when [the moon] has set;
one should certainly not eat until its rising."
Having seen that [the food] has been released, one should eat after bathing according to the prescribed rule.
"In that regard," meaning during that day and night.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"On that day one should not eat as long as [the moon] has been eclipsed."
Having seen that it has been released, one should eat after bathing according to the prescribed rule.
Viṣṇu and Śātātapa state:
"One should never eat during the day or night when there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
however, having bathed according to the prescribed rule and seeing that [the eclipse] has been released, one may eat."
That person goes to the imperishable worlds of the sun and the moon;
with sins washed away and the self purified, he rejoices there like a god.
One should not eat before a solar eclipse during the day, nor after the waning of the moon at night;
one should not eat during the time of the eclipse itself, but should eat only after bathing once both have been released.
One may eat when the moon has been liberated, provided it is not the dead of night;

In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "O Nārada, Rāhu swallows the moon when it is below the midnight hour;
at that time, the virtuous should indeed partake of their meal once [the moon] has been released."
In the *Padma Purāṇa*: "If a lunar eclipse occurs either before or after midnight,
one should eat before the former [midnight] in the first case, and after the latter [midnight] in the second."
"In the former" means in the forenoon; "in the latter" means even in the afternoon. As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O dear one, when a lunar eclipse occurs after midnight..."
O dear one, food should be eaten in the forenoon; never, under any circumstances, in the afternoon.
O Śikhivāhana, when the moon is eclipsed before midnight, one must not take food during the day.
Mārkaṇḍeya says: If there should be an eclipse of the moon, one should eat before the first watch (yāma) in the case of the first [eclipse];
in the case of the first [eclipse], one should eat below the first watch.

"Āvartana" refers to the middle of the day. By this it is meant that one should eat after discarding the three *yāmas* (nine hours) preceding the time of the eclipse in which it occurs. In another Smṛti:
"When Rāhu swallows the moon and the sun at the time of twilight..."
At that time, one should not eat during the day, except for the sick, women, and children.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should not eat during the first four watches;
some sages, O descendant of Bhṛgu, say [one should avoid] three."
Vṛddhagautama says:
During a solar eclipse, one should not eat for the first four watches;
during a lunar eclipse, however, for three watches, except in the case of children, the elderly, and the sick.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: [382] If there should be an eclipse at evening, one must not eat in the afternoon;
if in the afternoon, not at midday; if at midday, not during the forenoon (saṅgava).
If it should be during the period of the junction (saṅgava), one should eat; there must not have been a prior act of eating.

This refers to cases involving children and the like, or those who are incapable; however, for one who is capable, the penance for eating [forbidden food] is stated in the *Kātyāyanasmṛti* and the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Having eaten during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one is purified by the *prājāpatya* penance;
having eaten on that very day [of an eclipse], one is purified by a three-night fast alone."
In another Smṛti:
"One should eat in the evening during the *saṅgava* period, and in autumn, before the *saṅgava*;
at midday, one should eat after that time; there is no fasting during an eclipse of the sun."

"During the autumn" means in the afternoon, because of the Vedic scripture stating that "the afternoon is autumn. The term "solar eclipse" is also an elliptical designation for a lunar eclipse; and this refers specifically to the householder who has sons.
Thus says Jaimini:
"On a Sunday, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
"A householder who has sons should not perform either the breaking of a fast or a fast. Thus it is stated in another Smṛti:
"On a Sunday, on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), and during an eclipse of the moon or the sun..."
Likewise, a householder who has sons should not observe a fast.

Now, one might object: when there is a solar eclipse at the time of twilight (*sandhyā*), then according to the aforementioned statements, there is no eating during the day, nor even at night—because of the rule, "Having seen [the moon or sun] set while not yet released, one should bathe and [fast] on the following day. Nor is there fasting for a householder who has sons, because that is prohibited for him. Therefore, when an eclipse occurs at twilight and the sun sets while eclipsed, what should a householder with sons do? It is said in reply: in that case, one should resort to the position stated by Mārkaṇḍeya and others, namely, "If the eclipse should occur in the evening...
Dakṣa says:
Bathing at every dawn, during the twilight, when the sun has risen,
and during an eclipse of the moon or sun, is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Viṣṇu says: At the solstices, at the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar or solar eclipses,
one who fasts for a day and night and bathes is liberated from all sins.

Regarding this, some explain that "having fasted for a day and night" means one has observed the fast on the preceding day. That is incorrect, because there is no authoritative basis for abandoning the day-and-night period associated with the lunar or solar eclipse and instead adopting another day-and-night period. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Always during the two solstices, as well as the two equinoxes,
during lunar and solar eclipses, during the vyatīpāta yoga, and on the festival days (parvan).
For one who, with a serene mind, fasts for a day and night and performs bathing, ancestral rites, giving, and recitation,
all that becomes inexhaustible for them.
Yama says: One who,
having observed a fast, bathes during the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar or solar eclipses, is liberated from all sins.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "Having fasted for one night in this manner and bathed, one should give according to one's ability;
[thereby] there is a withdrawal from the sheath of sin, as if from a silk garment."
Having fasted for three nights in this manner during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
one who bathes and gives gifts according to the rule rejoices together with Brahmā.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "When the moon or the sun is eclipsed at night during a great planetary seizure (mahāgraha), the merit is said to be inexhaustible; this is especially so when it concerns the sun."
"Seen" means fit for seeing. Vyāsa says:
"On Sunday there is an eclipse of the sun; likewise on Monday, an eclipse of the moon."
There, one known as Cūḍāmaṇi bestows infinite fruit.
Whatever merit is obtained on other weekdays during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
that merit is remembered as being multiplied ten millionfold during the eclipse of Cūḍāmaṇi.

Kātyāyana says: All waters on the surface of the earth, even those situated in wells, become equal to the waters of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā) during an eclipse of the moon or the sun; there is no doubt in this matter.
The "Svardhunī" is the Gaṅgā.
Vyāsa [said]: "Every gift is equal to land; all twice-born men are equal to Brahmā."
All the water of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā [is sacred] when the sun is seized by Rāhu.
The merit at the moon [festival] is a hundred thousandfold, and that at the sun [festival] is ten times greater than that;
but when the waters of the Gaṅgā are present, the merit is ten millionfold for the moon and one hundred millionfold for the sun.
Whatever fruit a person obtains from bathing in ten million Gaṅgās, that same fruit is obtained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu;
it is declared by the Sun himself to be ten times greater than that. [385]
And whoever bathes in the Jāhnavī during an eclipse of the moon or the sun has bathed in all sacred fords; why should he wander the earth?
(From the Devīpurāṇa).
An eclipse in the month of Kārttika at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is most excellent;
here, in the compound *gaṅgāyamunam*, the singular form is used according to the rule that "every dvandva compound may optionally be treated as a singular.
O great sage, an eclipse in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the Devikā is likewise proclaimed [to be excellent].
In the month of Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious; in Māgha, she is auspiciously present.
In Phālguna, the Varuṇā is meritorious; in Caitra, the Sarasvatī;
and in Vaiśākha, the most auspicious Candrabhāgā, the best of rivers.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Kauśikī is meritorious; in Āṣāḍha, the river Tāpikā;
in Śrāvaṇa, the one named Sindhu; and likewise in Bhādrapada, the Gaṇḍakī.
In the month of Āśvina, the Śarayū is most excellent; the Narmadā is even more meritorious;
and the Godāvarī is greatly meritorious when the moon is joined with Rāhu.
O great sage, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu and the world has become shrouded in darkness,
people attain their purposeful fulfillment through contact with the waters of the Narmadā.
Those people who touch or immerse themselves in the waters of the Revā when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu are not ordinary human beings.
By remembering [it], one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; by seeing it, the fruit born of the gift of a cow;
by touching it, that which is equal to a Gomedha sacrifice; and by drinking [its water], one gains the merit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
Having bathed there, one undoubtedly attains the merit of the Vājimedha sacrifice. This applies during an eclipse of the sun or moon, as well as during the northern solstice;
likewise, the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī are to be viewed in exactly the same way.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for the Śivāditya-maṇḍala,
a man shall obtain that as well when the maṇḍala has occurred together with the planets.
Whatever merit is proclaimed as being found in saline lands, in forests, or in sacred fields,
that shall become even greater here during an eclipse due to the greatness of the time.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The Gaṅgā at Kanakhala, Prayāga, Puṣkara, Gayā,
and likewise Kurukṣetra are meritorious when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu."
In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*: "When the sun is in Capricorn, a lunar or solar eclipse is rare even throughout the three worlds; yet, the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) at Gayā is rarer still."
Śātātapa says:
When Rāhu swallows the sun during the junctions of the lunar phases, that is to be known as the "Elephant Shadow" (gajacchāyā); what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony,
by that very act the entire earth is indeed placed into the hand of the brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu:
For a śrāddha offered at the sight of Rāhu remains as meritorious as the moon and stars,
and it reaches the ancestors, fulfilling all their desires.
One should indeed perform the Śrāddha ceremony even at the cost of all one's possessions during the appearance of Rāhu;
for by failing to perform that Śrāddha, one sinks like a cow in the mud.
Śātātapa says:
Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and the performance of Śrāddha at the time of an eclipse yield infinite merit;
any other night is demonic, therefore one should avoid it.
Devala says: Just as bathing and giving gifts are prescribed during a solar eclipse by day,
so too are bathing and giving gifts ordained for a lunar eclipse by night.
Regarding the *śrāddha* ceremony, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"An occasional (*naimittika*) *śrāddha* must be performed during lunar and solar eclipses and upon the death of a relative; otherwise, one would become a denizen of hell."
And optional *śrāddhas* are commended during eclipses and similar occasions;
as stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "When a distinguished Brāhmaṇa has arrived, or during a solar or lunar eclipse, or at the solstices..."
If one wishes, one may perform a Śrāddha ceremony during afflictions caused by planets at the time of one's birth star.

In this context, the meaning of "at will" (*icchayā*) is that one should perform every type of *śrāddha* at times such as during a solar eclipse, or otherwise, one may perform the *śrāddha* at the previously mentioned times at will—that is, with the desire for results such as heaven; it does not mean that one should perform it only if one wishes to do so, and omit it if one does not. Śātātapa says:
"In times of distress, when there is no sacred fire, at a holy ford (*tīrtha*), and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
"A twice-born man should offer an *āmaśrāddha*, and a Śūdra should always indeed offer one. In some places, the second half of the verse is read as follows:
"One should perform an *āmaśrāddha* or even a *hemaśrāddha*."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "In the absence of food, in the absence of a second [person], during travel, upon the birth of a son,
at a gathering, and likewise for women and Śūdras, the golden *śrāddha* should be performed."
Jābāli says: At the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the meritorious period consists of sixteen *kalās* on both sides;
however, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, it lasts as long as the phenomenon remains within the range of vision.

Regarding this, some say: Since the lunar and solar eclipses are established as the *nimitta* (occasion for ritual action), and since knowledge alone is the *nimitta*, one might initially conclude that it applies to all forms of knowledge. However, because of statements such as "as far as it is within the range of vision" (*yāvad darśanagocaraḥ*) and "upon seeing Rāhu" (*rāhudarśane*), and because the term "vision" (*darśana*) is used in its primary sense only with respect to visual knowledge—since only an object of visual knowledge serves as the *nimitta*—one should not perform bathing and other rites when [the sun] is obscured by Aries (*meṣa*) and so forth. This is incorrect, for if there were an intention to refer specifically to an object of knowledge produced by the eye, [the following would apply]:
"One should never look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun."
Neither when it is eclipsed, nor when it stands in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.

Since Manu thus prohibits a householder from seeing the sun eclipsed, it would follow that bathing and other such rites are impossible; yet, if that prohibition were set aside, the very same fault [of contradicting the primary rule] would arise. Nor should it be argued that if one intends to refer to scriptural knowledge, then bathing and other rites would still apply even when the eclipse occurs in another country. For it is said: "When there is a solar eclipse at night, or a lunar eclipse during the day, one should not perform a bath, nor should one ever give a gift."

Thus, because bathing and other such acts are prohibited there by the statement of the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata-nigama*, and because cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) perform bathing and other rites only while not looking at the eclipsed moon or sun; and...

Furthermore, when there is the state of being an object of knowledge produced by the visual organ (*cakṣurjanitajñānaviṣayatā*), bathing and such activities are not possible; and when bathing and such are performed, that [state of being an object of visual knowledge] does not exist. Thus, the sentence would have an untenable meaning. If, however, one intends to express "fitness" (*yogyatā*), then even when [the sun or moon] is covered by clouds and the like, bathing and so forth should be performed, because the fitness regarding its own nature (*svarūpayogyatā*) exists there as well. But if, due to the lack of fitness for that which is obstructed, there is no rule for bathing and so forth, then for one who does not look upward [at the sun], there would likewise be no requirement for bathing and so forth. Moreover, since learned people (*śiṣṭa*) perform bathing and other rites even when [the sun] is covered by clouds and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that the period of time during which the eclipse of the moon or sun is known from scripture is the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*). Some maintain that the intended meaning is the fitness for being an object of visual knowledge starting from the moment [the eclipse begins].

Others, however, explain [the matter] with the intention of referring to an eclipse and setting: as long as [the moon] is within the range of vision, it is a time of merit; but when it has set and is no longer seen, it is not then a time of merit. Accordingly, even during an eclipsed setting, the learned perform their baths and other rites only before [the end], and not after. As stated in the *Śivarahasya*:
One should perform recitation and other rites for as long as the eclipse of the sun or moon lasts;
one should neither bathe nor eat during that time, but should bathe and eat once both have been released.
In the *Śaṅkha-Likhita Smṛti*, however, the first quarter-verse reads: "As long as there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun. Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha states:
"The gods are satisfied at the time of contact, and likewise the ancestors."
In the middle age they are humans, but in the age of liberation they are Rākṣasas.

On this point, some say: "Since it is stated that the satisfaction of the gods and ancestors occurs at the time of contact (*sparśa*), therefore, as a means to achieve that, every rite dedicated to the gods and ancestors should be performed without distinction. This is incorrect.
"Bathing should take place during an eclipse and the like; in the middle [of the eclipse], there should be fire-oblation (*homa*) and worship of the gods."
[390] Thus, because of the statement in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* which prescribes [the rites] between the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the worship of the deity:
"When [the eclipse] is being swallowed, there should be bathing; when it is swallowed, the fire-oblation is prescribed;
when it is being released, there should be giving; when it is released, bathing is prescribed."
And because of this statement, therefore, this [rule] refers to matters other than the fire-oblation (homa) and the worship of the deities. [In the] Padma Purāṇa:
The merit at the time of eclipse (upamarde) during the grasping of the moon and sun is a hundred-thousandfold;
it is ten-millionfold in the middle, and infinite at the moment of release.
Śātātapa says:
At the beginning of the solstices, whatever desirable substance is always present in the house should be given away;
likewise at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
The meaning is that while the liberation [of Rāhu] is occurring, one is not yet liberated; for there is a statement by Vasiṣṭha: "But during the eclipse, [the impurity lasts] for that duration.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"For all castes alike, there is birth-impurity during the eclipse of Rāhu."
However, one should bathe with one's clothes on and avoid food from those in a state of birth-impurity.

"Sūtakānna" refers to food from one who is under the impurity of Rāhu (an eclipse). One should avoid cooked food prepared during the observance of a vow by one observing a vow, during a sacrificial session by those performing a sattra, or while a king is engaged in royal duties. As stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, as well as during the periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka)."
One who does not bathe meets with death; one who bathes incurs no sin.
In the case of both birth-impurity and death-impurity, there is no fault during an eclipse of Rāhu;
purity shall indeed exist only so long as the release [of the moon or sun] is not seen.
This refers to matters such as giving gifts and performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), but not to bathing alone:
"During an eclipse, impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) is prescribed; once it has ended, birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is recorded.
By the mere occurrence of their coincidence, one should perform the sequence of rites after sipping water."

Because this contradicts the statement in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, a sequence [of actions] is indeed appropriate for the performance of the rites of bathing, fire-oblation (*homa*), worship of the gods, and giving. Furthermore, if one were to perform only the bath, the first sentence alone would suffice to establish the bath, which would result in the redundancy of the second sentence. If it is argued that, in your view, since the bath is established by the second sentence alone, the first sentence would be redundant—[we reply: No. This is because the first sentence serves to demonstrate the connection with specific undesirable consequences for one who has not bathed; because the use of the terms "as long as" (*yāvat*) and "so long as" (*tāvat*) would otherwise be untenable; because the cited sentences prescribe bathing only during eclipses and similar occasions; and because there is an absence of impurity due to Rāhu (*rāhusūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtasūtaka*) [during such times].
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"If an eclipse of Rāhu should occur during a birth-impurity or a death-impurity,
that impurity does not exist as long as Rāhu has not released [the moon or sun]."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "During birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), as well as during an eclipse (rāhudarśana),
there shall be impurity only so long as the liberation [of the moon or sun] is not seen."
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"The abandonment of Smārta rites [occurs] during impurity (*sūtaka*), except for Rāhu.

The meaning is that, apart from the impurity caused by Rāhu, there is abandonment of rites during other instances of impurity. Others, however, explain it thus: "The abandonment of Smārta rites that occurs during impurity is [to be understood as occurring] except for the impurity caused by Rāhu. In some places, however, the reading is "except upon seeing Rāhu," but because that would entail the restriction of many statements, this does not refer merely to the subject of bathing.

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the time of death, and upon the birth of a son—even during an intercalary month—a gift should be given; what is given then produces inexhaustible merit."

In some places, however, the word "śrāddha" is read where "datta" occurs. On this point, Garga says: "Puṇya, Ājapada, Yāmya, Bhāgya, Paitṛka, Aindrāgna, and Agnidevatya—these seven are the groups of fires."
*Ājapada* is Pūrvabhādrapadā; *yāmya* is Bharaṇī; *bhāgya* is Pūrvaphalgunī;
*paitṛka* is Maghā; *aindrāgna* is Viśākhā; and *agnidevatya* is Kṛttikā. An eclipse of the Sun or Moon observed within the fiery (*ānala*) mandala—
One should know that it is terrifying to kings and causes many evils for the subjects.
The asterisms Ahibudhnya, Pūṣan, Mūla, Āpya, Śāṅkara,
Sarpadaivatyam, and Vāruṇa are known as the Vāruṇa Maṇḍala.

‘Ahirbudhnya’ is Uttarā Bhādrapadā; ‘Pauṣṇa’ is Revatī; ‘Apya’ is Pūrvāṣāḍhā; ‘Śāṅkara’ is Ārdrā; ‘Vāruṇa’ is Śatabhiṣaj; ‘Sarvadaivatyam’ is Aśleṣā. During an eclipse occurring within the orbs of the Moon or the Sun in these [asterisms], there will be the destruction of famine and disease for the people; this is the certainty.
The asterism Punarvasu belongs to the four [groups] beginning with Āryaman and the Bears (Ursa Major);
it is sacred to Soma, the Aśvins, and Vāyu, and constitutes the Maṇḍala.
The asterisms beginning with Āryamaṇ (Pūrvaphalgunī) and those beginning with Uttarāphālgunī, as well as ‘Saumya’ (Mṛgaśīrṣa) and ‘Aśvidaivatyam’ (Aśvinī),
produce war and fear for a long time, and bring about famine; moreover,
an excess of disease and weapons prevails within this region.
[393] Jyeṣṭhā, Brāhma, Maitra, the region of Indra (Pūrvāṣāḍhā),
Vaiṣṇava, and Vaiśvadeva constitute the mandala of Puruhūta.
"Brāhma" is Rohiṇī; "Maitra" is Anurādhā; "Prāgdeśa" is Abhijit; "Vāsava" is Dhaniṣṭhā; "Vaiṣṇava" is Śravaṇa; and "Vaiśvadeva" is Uttarāṣāḍhā.
When an eclipse occurs within this [group of] constellations, it brings welfare to the worlds.
It bestows bliss upon all beings, especially so.
Kāśyapa, however, having described these very mandalas, says:
"One should perform the Āgneyī pacification, and one should also perform the Vāruṇī pacification;
the Vāyavyā pacification is desired, and there one should perform the Māhendrī."

Thus he has described those various rites, such as offerings to the deities, oblations, and recitations. Therefore, kings should act accordingly for the welfare of the world, and likewise for the pacification of the evil influence of the planets upon the universe. As for each individual person, however, it is as follows: "If Rāhu should approach the moon in the place of the sun..."
And those people undergo the exhaustion of their karma and their afflictions.
A planet situated in the place of the Sun leads to the destruction of the father’s side;
a planet situated in the place of the Moon leads to the destruction of the mother’s side.
In whichever hour or under whichever lunar mansion the Moon is seized,
that person encounters a threat to life or meets with death.
For Rāhu overcomes both the moon and the sun upon whichever person's birth-star he eclipses;
one should know that for such a person there is fear of death and other calamities, as well as fierce mental anguish.
If the moon and the sun should eclipse the birth asterism of anyone,
there will be suffering for those born under that sign, and men will be devoid of peace.
For those whose minds are intent on transmigration and who experience the touch of obstacles throughout three lifetimes—
causing many diseases and deaths— offerings of gifts and the recitation of mantras must be performed.

Thus ends the section on the Determination of Time (*Kālanirṇaya*) within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the illustrious administrative offices of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
The Determination of the Time for Initiation.
[395] Now begins the tenth chapter.
Now follows the determination of the time for the Upākarma ceremony. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"The commencement of the study of the Vedas (upākarma) shall take place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa."
Or, in the absence of the medicinal herbs, on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

Regarding the "chapters," that is, the Vedas; on the "full moon of Śrāvaṇa" (śrāvaṇyām), meaning on the day joined with the asterism Śravaṇa; or on the fifth [lunar day] when it is joined with the asterism Hasta, the *upākarma* ceremony should be performed. Others, however, explain it as: "on the day joined with Hasta, or on the fifth [lunar day]. Regarding the phrase "when herbs have appeared," the term "of Śrāvaṇa" is connected with all [the preceding conditions]. Thus says Āśvalāyana.

Now, therefore, follows the opening of the term for study (*adhyāyopākaraṇa*). It should be performed when the herbs have appeared, or under the asterism Śravaṇa, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Hasta; so says the Nigama.
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform the Śrāvaṇī rite according to the prescribed rule.
The Upākarma ceremony should be performed when the sun is situated in Cancer,
on the fifth day of the bright fortnight under the asterism Hasta, or on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śravaṇa.
Kātyāyana:
Now, therefore, follows the Upākarma ceremony; it is performed under the asterism Śravaṇa, on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. Baudhāyana: [396]

Having performed the *upākarma* (commencement of Vedic study) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, one should study the *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters). The determination between these two fortnights is according to one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*. However, if in this month of Śrāvaṇa the herbs do not appear, or if there is some obstacle such as the inauspiciousness of a planetary transit (*graha*) or a solar ingress (*saṃkrānti*), or if for some reason the month of Śrāvaṇa is passed, then the rite should be performed on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada).
For this very reason, Śaumaka says: "They call that the *vārṣika* (the rainy-season rite).
That which occurs in the rainy season (*varṣākāla*) is "rainy-season" (*vārṣika*).
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (svādhyāyopākarma) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada.
"Proṣṭhapadī" refers to the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada.
Gobhila states: "The commencement [of Vedic study] is with the Hasta constellation on the day of the Proṣṭhapadī.
The meaning is: "having reached the day of the Proṣṭhapadī."
Manu also says:
"Having performed the Upākarma ceremony according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Proṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months."

By the word "api" (also), the months of Bhādrapada, the asterism Śravaṇa, and the fifth lunar day of the asterism Hasta are included. Thus says a verse from the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa: "If, in that month, the medicinal herbs do not appear due to lack of rain, then it is prescribed that [the rite] be performed in the month of Bhādrapada under the asterism Śravaṇa."
The meaning is that from the *upākarma* ceremony onwards, one should study the Veda continuously during the bright fortnights for four and a half months.
Vasiṣṭha states:
"Having studied for four and a half months, he performs the *utsarga*; or for five and a half months, or six and a half months."

Gautama says: Having performed the *upākaraṇa* ceremony on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, one should study the Vedic hymns for four and a half months, or for five months during the southern course of the sun. Hārīta says:
Having studied for four and a half months, or five and a half months, he performs the *utsarga* (concluding rite).
Kātyāyana says: "Having performed the *upākarma* (commencement rite) during the northern course of the sun, one who knows the Dharma should then study."

And this study for the purpose of memorization applies even to the householder. As Śaunaka says: "One who has returned home [from studentship] [should study] according to rule according to the procedure of a student; others say that even those of other classes [should do so]. Here, "others" refers to students. For this very reason, the injunction for study is placed in that context (the section on studentship) in order to indicate that the householder also has the qualification for the study of memorization.
The postponement of the *upākarma* due to the increase in the [lunar] period has been shown by Kātyāyana:
"There should be a postponement of rites such as the *upākarma* when there is an increase in the [lunar] period;
however, there is no postponement for the *yugādis* despite the increase of [other] festivals such as the royal consecration (*abhiṣeka*)."
As for the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga which establishes that there is no postponement:
"There is no postponement on the Daśaharās, nor on the four Yugādis;
for the Upākarma is desired from this [month] of Vṛṣa on the great Aṣṭamī."
That [rule] pertains to the Chandogas; for even when there is an increase in the duration of the month, their *upākarma* takes place only in Leo (Siṃha) under the asterism Arka (Hasta).
