As Gārgya says:
"When the sun is in Leo and the asterism is Puṣya, one should go outside at midday."
The Chandogas, having assembled, should perform the utsarga of all the Vedas;
the upākarma for the afternoon session should be performed under the asterism Hasta during the bright fortnight.
And this [rite] should be performed on the Śrāvaṇī day and so forth, provided it is not defective due to eclipses or other such occurrences.
Thus says the Smṛti:
"Those who know the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus Vedas perform the Upākarma rite in due order."
On days not joined with the transits of the planets, and during the asterisms of Hasta and Śravaṇa, as well as on the lunar festival days (parvan).
Likewise:
"At the time of a solar transit, during an eclipse, and likewise during birth-impurity or death-impurity, one should not perform a group bath (gaṇasnāna); such is the word of Nārada."
Moreover, if a ritual service should take place on an inauspicious lunar day,
the twice-born in that kingdom will be seized by suffering, grief, and disease.
Likewise:
"If the full-moon festival of Śrāvaṇa should be defiled by an eclipse or a solar transit,
then the Upākaraṇa ceremony shall take place on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa."
In the *Smṛtimahārṇava*:
"If a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or an eclipse occurs on a festival day (*parvan*),
that [rite] is prescribed to be performed in that same month on the fifth lunar day conjoined with the asterism Hasta."

Regarding this, some say: there is an option between [the day] conjoined with the *hasta* asterism and the fifth lunar day alone; however, there is no option here between a festival-day (*parvan*) conjoined with a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) and the other, because a fault is heard [in the scriptures] regarding that. Nor is there an option between [the day] conjoined with *hasta* and another lunar day, or the fifth day alone; for when the phrase "conjoined with *hasta*" requires a specific correlate, it connects only with the fifth day already mentioned. Otherwise, in this view, there would be the undesirable consequence of restricting the statement, "If the festival-day of Śrāvaṇa occurs," etc., which prescribes the *upākarma* rite on the fifth day alone when the festival-day is afflicted by the faults of a planetary eclipse or a solar transit.

[Objection: But in this way, the repetition of the fifth case-ending would follow, and that is faulty because it involves a restriction. [Response: Not so. Since the requirement for the phrase "joined with the hand" (hastayuktāyām) necessarily arises, there are two possible options for supplying the ellipsis; and since it is stated that one must supply what is already present in the mind, one supplies it accordingly. Nevertheless, when being joined with the hand is impossible, [one supplies] "alone" (kevalā).

That is incorrect. Since the phrase "or on the fifth" (*pañcamyāṃ vā*) conveys an alternative to another lunar day (*tithyantara*), it is more logical that the expression "conjoined with the *Hasta* [nakṣatra]" (*hastayuktāyām*) refers specifically to that [fifth day], given the requirement for its specification. Thus, since the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) in both cases must be of something already present in the mind, the distinction is this: in this case, the "fifth lunar day" (*pañcamīparva*) is taken according to the literal text, whereas in your position, it refers to the fifth day characterized by the absence of conjunction with *Hasta*. [Objection: Why does the alternative not apply to the fifth day of the month of *Proṣṭhapada* when it is conjoined with *Hasta*?

It is said: since one does not resort to a statement from another sentence when the requirement is met by what is contained within one's own sentence, and thus an option (*vikalpa*) being established, even a restriction (*saṃkoca*) that follows by force is accepted. Therefore, there is an option between the fifth day and other lunar days conjoined with the Hasta constellation. Even in that case, if a day conjoined with Hasta is unavailable, it is performed on the [fifth] alone; and this refers specifically to the Vājasaneyins. Accordingly, there is another statement in the *Smṛtimahārṇava*: "If a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or an eclipse occurs on the full moon day, the commencement (*upākṛti*) should be performed on the fifth day by the Vājasaneyins."

In this regard, some, considering the term "Vājasaneyins" to be indicative (upalakṣaṇa) because it is common to the preceding statement, maintain that the Taittirīyas also perform the *upākarma* on the fifth day.

That is incorrect, because it would entail *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication), and because an indirect indication is appropriate in this context. Furthermore, if *lakṣaṇā* were applied here on the grounds that the preceding sentence is common to all, then by the same logic of commonality, one would have to apply *lakṣaṇā* to the rule "he divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts" in the case of the rule "he divides the *āgneya* into four parts. Moreover, in this context, the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) is understood as belonging specifically to that month, not to any other month, because no other month is under discussion; therefore, this refers to the followers of the Vājasaneyins. Or, let us set aside the statement of the Vājasaneyins for a moment; nevertheless, the *upākarma* of the Taittirīyas does not necessarily follow from the previous sentence when there is the defect of the moon's transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurring during the period of the *graha*. For in the *smṛtis*, various times for this *upākarma* are prescribed, and it is proper to adopt a fixed option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) among them according to their respective *gṛhyasūtras*. Now, the *Taittirīya-gṛhya* does not explicitly state that the *upākarma* takes place on the fifth day. However, for those whose *gṛhya* does prescribe the fifth day, when an unrestricted option (*avyavasthitavikalpa*) might otherwise arise, this specific statement applies to establish a restriction—namely, that since the fifth day is available, no other time should be used. Thus, it provides what was required rather than prescribing a time not already applicable to the Taittirīyas' *upākarma*. Therefore, it is established that when the full moon of Śrāvaṇa is defiled by a lunar transit (*saṃkrānti*), the Taittirīyas should perform the *upākarma* on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada.

Regarding this, some say: "Even on a full-moon day (*parvan*) or during an eclipse, the *upākarma* should be performed under the asterism Śravaṇa even if it falls on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). However, one must certainly avoid nine days starting from the thirteenth day in all auspicious rites during lunar and solar eclipses."
Because of this statement, piercing (vedha) is also shown in another manner in another Smṛti:
"Piercing beginning with the twelfth [tithi] and ending with the third is prescribed for a lunar eclipse;
that beginning with the eleventh and ending with the fourth is proclaimed for a solar eclipse."
In the case of a partial eclipse of those two [the sun and moon], it is stated that there is a period of two days in both instances.

"In this case, [the suspension lasts] for two days, both before and after," according to the statement, "In the case of a partial eclipse of those two, it is for three days. That is incorrect, because:
"In the case of obligatory and occasional rites, in the recitation of mantras (*japa*), in fire-offerings (*homa*), and in sacrificial acts..."
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, no planetary affliction (grahavedha) is recognized.

Because of this statement, the asterisms Hasta, Śravaṇa, and the full moon (parvan) occurring at sunrise are to be accepted. And so it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "When the first day of the month coincides with the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā and is joined with the asterism of Tvaṣṭṛ (Śravaṇa), those who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas should perform the Śrāvaṇa rite."
Vyāsa says:
But that ritual act which is performed under the asterism of Uttarāṣāḍha—
any study undertaken during that year perishes at that very moment.
Whatever rite of Śrāvaṇa may be performed in conjunction with Dhaniṣṭhā,
one should know that rite, known as the Upākaraṇa, to be fruitful.
The *nigama* states: "An unfavorable planetary conjunction (*grahayoga*) kills the teacher; a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) kills the disciple;
and the star Uttarāṣāḍhā kills the austerity during the Vaiṣṇava *upākarma* ceremony."
When [the moon] is conjoined with Dhaniṣṭhā, the rite known as upākaraṇa should be performed.
In the Kālikāpurāṇa:
"On the fourteenth day, the two demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born;
they carried away the Vedas—the sacred revelations—from the lotus-born Brahmā as he was taking them into his possession."
Having slain those two Asuras who dwelt in the depths of Pātāla, the Lord,
the Teacher of the World, himself bestowed those Vedas upon him.
Brahmā had previously acquired the sacred learning on the day of the full moon;
therefore, the commencement of study (upākaraṇa) is not desired on that day when it is joined with a lunar mansion.
One should avoid an inauspicious time out of fear of improperly acquiring the Vedas.
Bṛhatpracetā says:
The introductory rite (upākaraṇa) should take place on the full moon day, specifically in the forenoon;
there, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas, dedicating the offering to the ancestors and the deities.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: When the end of the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, on the full moon day at the conjunction of the sun and the lunar mansion,
a wise man should perform his bath according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti.

Then he should satisfy the gods and the ancestors with excellent water. The Upākarma rite is prescribed for the daytime; the Brahmin should perform the libation to the sages and offer a Śrāddha ceremony dedicated to the Vedas according to his ability.
And on this occasion, the *upākarma* should be performed by the followers of the Taittirīya school during the *audāyika* parvan. This has been stated in the *Kārikās* of the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa*:
"The Taittirīyakas should perform the *Śrāvaṇa* [rite] during the *audāyika* parvan;
the Bahvṛcas should perform it under the asterism Śravaṇā, avoiding [times of] planetary conjunctions or transits."
Others, however, maintain that these should indeed be joined with the preceding day:
"The Śrāvaṇī, Durgā-navamī, as well as the Dūrvā-aṣṭamī,
Śivarātri, and the day of Bali (Vijayādaśamī) should be observed when joined with the preceding lunar day."
Because of this statement.

On this point, some say: "This is not tenable; for here it cannot be restricted that only the Taittirīyakas [perform] on the *parvan*, since the performance of the *upākarma* on the *parvan* is prescribed for other schools (*caraṇa*) as well. Nor is it tenable to construe the meaning of the sentence as 'only the Taittirīyakas should perform the *upākarma* on the *audayika-parvan*', because that would entail a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the restatement of a qualified subject. Furthermore, since the qualifiers have not been previously established, they cannot be restated; and in such a qualified rite, it is illogical to enjoin the Taittirīyakas, for it is the agent who is enjoined with respect to the action, not the agent within the action."

Furthermore, the *upākarma* rite and its time—the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*)—are prescribed solely in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*; therefore, they are not enjoined here in this *Kārikā*. Rather, what is indicated here is the connection of the full-moon time with the time of sunrise (*audayika*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*). In that regard, if another connection with the state of being at sunrise were indicated by the followers of the Taittirīya school, then the sentence would be split due to the expression of two distinct connections.

Furthermore, the Taittirīyakas are merely a constituent part (*aṅga*) [of the ritual], and there is no mutual relationship between constituent parts. Nor should it be argued that, according to the principle of the *aruṇa-ekahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow), there is subsequently a connection between the qualities [of the Taittirīyas] and [the rite] through that [constituent status]. For in that case, a purchase qualified by both the quality of redness and the substance of the one-year-old cow is enjoined; subsequently, because the substance and the quality mutually require one another and possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), a connection arises between them. In this present case, however, there is no injunction for the *upākarma* within the *kārikā*. Nor is there coreferentiality between the "full-moon day at dawn" (*parvaudayika*) and the "Taittirīyaka" even as substance and quality, nor is there a mutual requirement for a substance. Therefore, like the term "oblation" (*havis*) in the context of being "both," the word "Taittirīya" has its literal sense unintended and serves as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, the performance of the *upākarma* is established across all *Gṛhya-sūtras* according to the logic of the section on different Vedic branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*). Since there is no contradiction, the "full-moon day at dawn" prescribed for the Taittirīyas may be adopted by others as well.
And so it is ordained in the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "Whatever is not prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, provided it is not contradictory,
that should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other rites."

Since statements such as “the Śrāvaṇī, the Durgā-navamī,” and so forth do not specify particular rituals, their subject matter includes the offering of the *pavitra* to Hiraṇyagarbha, the *upākarma* which is an ancillary part [of that], and the *śrāvaṇī* rite performed for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*). Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the *upākarma* belongs exclusively to the Taittirīyas on the lunar day of the sun’s northern course (*audayika-parvan*).

That is incorrect. However, where there is no other possible recourse (*ananyagatipada*), the qualified entity is taken as the object of the injunction (*uddeśyatva*) for fear of rendering a word meaningless, as in cases such as "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa of eight years. But in the case of both words [in the present context], since their purpose is to dispel the misconception that the cause for the *āgneya* oblation is its destruction, there is no lack of other recourse. Nor is there a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), for that occurs when one intends to emphasize a qualification of the object of the injunction, but not when there is an injunction regarding a qualified whole. This has been explained at length by Bhavadeva: "For one who objects here, a solution must be stated by resorting to a qualified injunction, because it is what must be accepted. Furthermore, since the performance of the *upākarma* on the day of the full moon (*audayika-parvan*) is already established by the previously cited texts, its restatement (*anuvāda*) is appropriate; likewise, an injunction regarding the agent (*kartṛvidhi*) is also appropriate in relation to the ritual act, because an injunction applies to what is not otherwise established. Nor does the injunction of two relations constitute a syntactical split, because it relies upon a qualified injunction, and because the repetition is avoided through the difference in authors of the respective texts—otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total disappearance of all Smṛtis. Moreover, if this were not accepted, the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) and the purposeless restatement would both result.

[Objection: But surely, just as in the case of the injunction *vaiśvadevena yajeta* (one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva), where—due to the prolixity (*gaurava*) of a qualified injunction—it is accepted that the word *vaiśvadeva* functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the "umbrella-bearer" logic (*chatrinyāya*) to refer to the sacrifices under discussion, so too here, due to the prolixity of a qualified injunction, secondary indication itself must be accepted. [Reply: No; for even there, there is no secondary indication. For the application of the word *vaiśvadeva* does not arise from its connection with the Viśvedevas as deities, but rather from its connection with the Viśvedevas as performers. Thus it is heard in the Taittirīyaka: "Because the Viśvedevas sacrificed together, that is the 'Vaiśvadeva' nature of the Vaiśvadeva. That the basis for the application of a word resides in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is accepted everywhere, as in such cases as: "Because they ran the race (*ājim īyuḥ*), that is the 'Ājya' nature of the Ājyas. As for the mention of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in that context, it was made by way of an objection based on concession; for if one were to accept secondary indication because of a qualified object of injunction, it would lead to a lack of systematic consistency (*avyavasthā*). Furthermore, in that case (the Vaiśvadeva), although there is prolixity in a qualified injunction, there is the assumption of the extension (*atideśa*) of another ritual action, and the restatement (*anuvāda*) serves a purpose. Here, however, in a qualified injunction, there is merely prolixity; in its absence, there would be secondary indication, and the restatement would be purposeless—this is the disparity. Moreover, in a qualified injunction, the simultaneous connection (*pārṣṇika-sambandha*) of various qualities is possible. And the agent certainly has a requirement for a specific time for the performance of the ritual. Nor does the logic of the *śākhān-karādhikaraṇa* apply here; for if the time of the rising moon (*audayika-parvan*) were established for others by the rule alone—"They should perform the *Śrāvaṇa* on the day of the rising moon"—then the word *taittirīyaka* would be rendered useless. Nor is the time of the rising moon prescribed in the *Taittirīya-gṛhya*. If, on the grounds of the commonality of the narrative in the *Kālikā-purāṇa*, the *upākarma* for those other than the Taittirīyakas were also on the day of the rising moon, then the *upākarma* for the *Bahvṛcas* would also have to be on that very same day. However, the fact that they resort to a different time is the same in both cases, upon considering other scriptural passages. Furthermore, in this way, the word *bahvṛca* would also be non-significant (*avivakṣita*), since the aforementioned defect applies equally there if the word *taittirīya* were taken as significant. Therefore, the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) is as follows: when the *parvan* overlaps the time of the ritual on a single day, then for all of them the *upākarma* takes place then. But when it overlaps the time of the ritual on two days—or does not overlap at all—then for the Taittirīyakas the *upākarma* is on the day of the rising moon, while for others it is on another day.
Now follows the time for the conclusion [of the Vedic study].
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or else on the Aṣṭakā."
One should perform the formal ritual dismissal of the Vedic meters outside near water, according to the prescribed rules.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, or under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should perform the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) of the Vedas outside the village in the vicinity of water. The meaning is that one should now abandon the manner in which the study was conducted from the time of the *upākarma* onwards, but not entirely; for this very reason, Manu says immediately after the *utsarjana*: "A twice-born man should perform the *utsarjana* of the Vedas outside [the village] under the asterism Puṣya, or on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, in the forenoon."

If the commencement of the term (*upākarma*) is performed on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, then the conclusion (*utsarjana*) takes place on the first day of the bright fortnight of Puṣya during the forenoon; however, when it is on the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, it means it is on the [first day] of Māgha, because he himself has stated: "One should study for four and a half months. Baudhāyana says:
Having commenced the term on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, one should conclude it on the full moon of Taiṣa or Māgha.
Āpastamba:
One should cease [the study of the Vedas] on the full moon day of Taiṣya, or under the asterism Rohiṇī.
Here, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya, Rohiṇī is to be understood as belonging to the month of Pauṣa.
Kātyāyana says: Having performed the *upākarma* ceremony during the northern course of the sun, the knower of dharma should then study;
and the *utsarga* (concluding rite) for these [Vedas] is performed on a single occasion, either in the month of Taiṣya or in Proṣṭhapada.
Gārgya states the time for the suspension [of Vedic study] for the Chandogas:
"When the sun is in Leo and the moon is in the Puṣya asterism, one should go outside in the forenoon;
the assembled Chandogas shall perform the utsarga of all the Vedas."
In the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "If, in the month of Proṣṭhapada, [the moon] should be preceded by Puṣya from the asterism Hasta,
then on that Śravaṇa day, the twice-born should perform the formal abandonment (*utsarga*) of the Vedic hymns."
In the *Khādira-gṛhya-sūtra*: "One should perform the *utsarjana* under the asterism Puṣya, or on the day of the *upākarma*.
And these two rites must be performed every year."
As Kātyāyana said:
"The annual *upākarma* ceremony, performed according to rule by the twice-born along with the *utsarga*,
serves to restore the Vedic meters (*chandas*) to their full strength."
Whatever rite is performed by the twice-born with unexhausted meters,
even if they are merely playing, it always brings about their success.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Time," in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the departments of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
[407] Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Next follows the determination of the transits (saṃkrānti).
Regarding that, the divisions of the *saṃkrāntis* are stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"The twelve *saṃkrānti*-calculations are declared to be equal.

The term "*saṃkrāntikalpanāḥ*" means the divisions of the *saṃkrāntis*. The twelve [signs], beginning with Aries (*meṣa*) and ending with Pisces (*mīna*), are declared; and the meaning is that they are "equal" (*samāḥ*), that is, common (*sādhāraṇāḥ*), to the rites—both prescribed and prohibited—that are enjoined in connection with the *saṃkrāntis* in general.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "O twice-born one, these indeed have twelve names; hear them from me:
one is named Viṣṇupada, and likewise Ṣaḍaśītimukha."
The third is the equinox, and the other two are the southern and northern solstices.
They say that Viṣṇupada occurs in the signs of Aquarius, Taurus, and Leo;
Ṣaḍaśītimukha occurs in Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces, and Gemini;
the northern course (ayana) of the Sun occurs when it is in the abode of the Moon (Cancer); and the southern course occurs when it is in the abode of the Moon (Capricorn).
It occurs in Capricorn, Pisces, the equinoxes, and in Aries and Libra.

‘Ali’ is Scorpio; ‘go’ is Taurus; ‘hari’ is Leo; ‘strī’ is Virgo; ‘cāpa’ is Sagittarius; ‘śaśidhāmni’ is Cancer; ‘yāmya’ is the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana); ‘saumya’ is the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa); ‘jhaṣa’ is Capricorn; ‘aja’ is Aries; and ‘taulī’ is Libra.
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"The two solstices, the two equinoxes, the four *ṣaḍaśīti*s,
and the four *viṣṇupada*s— these are recorded as the twelve *saṃkrānti*s."
The two transits of Pisces and Cancer are the northern and southern solstices;
Libra and Aries are the equinoxes, and the others follow between them.
When the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, or Leo, this is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is even greater than that of the equinoxes (viṣuva).
The Sun’s transit through Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius is declared to be the Ṣaḍaśītimukha; it yields the fruits of the Ṣaḍaśīti through its qualities.

‘Between those two’ means between Capricorn (makara) and Cancer (karkaṭa); ‘the equinox’ (viṣuvatī). In some places, the reading is “then the other [equinox] in the middle of the sphere” (golamadhye), where ‘sphere’ (gola) refers to the zodiacal circle (rāśicakra).
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), there are the sixty-eight-year cycles (ṣaḍaśītayaḥ) in Sagittarius, Gemini, Virgo, and Pisces.
In Taurus, Scorpio, Leo, and Aquarius, Viṣṇupadī is traditionally taught. Likewise,
at the equinoxes (Viṣuva) in Libra and Aries, and in Pisces, Virgo, Gemini, and Sagittarius, there is the Ṣaḍaśīti.
The solstice occurs in the signs of Pisces and Cancer; in the remaining signs, it is the Viṣṇupadī.
In the *Devīpurāṇa*, seven names are stated for each [solar transit] due to its conjunction with specific constellations:
"She (the transit) should be understood as sevenfold, though she is but one;
listen to how each single [transit], such as Aries and the rest, is sevenfold—listen to the manner in which it is of seven kinds."
O King, the sevenfold Saṃkrānti is said to be composed of Rākṣasīs, namely: Mandā, Mandākinī, Dhvāṅkṣī, Ghorā, Mahodarī, Miśritā, and Proktā.
On Sunday she is Ghorā; on Monday, Dhvāṅkṣī; on Tuesday, Mahodarī;
on Wednesday, she is named Mandākinī; and on Thursday, she is Mandā.
Miśritā occurs on Friday, and Rākṣasī on Saturday;
these are the seven transits (saṃkrāntis), and their results are now described accordingly.
One should know that when the planets are slow, it is Dhruvā; likewise, when they are mild, it is Mandākinī.
One should recognize Dhvāṅkṣī by swift planets, while Ghorā is proclaimed for those that are fierce.
Mahodarī is to be known by slow-moving [planets], while Rākṣasī is by cruel asterisms;
when mixed, it is designated as Miśritā during the transit through mixed asterisms.

The "fixed" (*dhruva*) asterisms are the three Uttaras and Rohiṇī. The "soft" (*mṛdu*) ones are Anurādhā, Citrā, Revatī, and Mṛgaśīrṣa. The "light" (*laghu*) ones are Abhijit, Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya. The "fierce" (*ugra*) ones are the three Pūrvās, Bharaṇī, and Maghā. The "movable" (*cara*) ones are Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Svātī, and Śatabhiṣā. The "cruel" (*krūra*), or sharp, ones are Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, and Āśleṣā. The "mixed" (*miśra*) ones are Kṛttikā and Viśākhā.
These have respectively three, four, five, seven, eight, nine, and twelve *ghaṭikās*; that is the ultimate merit [of these timings].

In all transits (*saṃkrānti*), seven periods (*kāla*) are to be understood according to their respective order. The meaning is that the merit which is obtained during the performance of religious duties at the time of the ultimate, most subtle transit—such as that obtained from the *vasordhārā* sacrifice—is indeed obtained even during these *ghaṭikā*s. "In that [time] there is merit; that is merit. Likewise:
"The *mandā* is praised among Brahmins, the *mandākinī* among Kṣatriyas, the *dhvāṅkṣī* is to be known among Vaiśyas, and the *ghorā* bestows auspiciousness upon Śūdras."
Mahodarī brings victory to thieves and liquor-sellers;
she belongs to the Caṇḍālas and Pukkasas, as well as others who perform cruel deeds. For all craftsmen, she is the one who increases their livelihood when combined with them.

The meaning is that, O King, the *Mandākinī* [astrological configuration] is auspicious for a Kṣatriya. In the phrase "bringing victory to distillers (*śauṇḍikānām*)," one should understand it refers to the *Rākṣasī* [configuration]. Thus, whichever [configuration] brings victory to a person, when that has occurred, he should perform rites that are means for prosperity. Whichever [configuration] brings victory to whom, for that person, he should perform propitiatory rites (*śāntika*) for the sake of removing obstacles. He states another specific rule for the performance of propitiatory rites: "Kings cause affliction in the forenoon, but the best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*) in the midday."
Likewise, the Vaiśyas [should do so] in the afternoon, and the Śūdras at the setting of the sun.
At sunset, the Piśācas [are afflicted], and at midnight, the Rākṣasas;
at midnight during the Vyatīpāta yoga, the actors and dancers are tormented.
At the time of dawn, during a solar transit, it kills the people belonging to the owner of the cows;
at the time of twilight, it especially kills all wandering mendicants.
Wherever the transit occurs during the month of Bhāskara,
when Mars or Saturn is present, the wise declare that there will be fear arising from famine, drought, and thieves.
The sun's transit (saṃkrānti) may occur when it has arisen during Kintughna or Śakuna; while it is standing still during Kaulava or Taitila; and while it is asleep during Nāga or Catuṣpada.
For one who has perished, [the results] in the Viṣṭi-karaṇa, Vava, Vaṇij, and Bālava are, respectively,
desired and middling fruits, starting from Viṣṭi and the others in order.
Whatever kind of transit of the Sun occurs with respect to the Moon in a given month, they say that such is the auspicious or inauspicious result for human beings in that month.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "The sun's transition into a zodiac sign is called *saṃkrānti*;
it yields great fruit for bathing, giving gifts, penance, *śrāddha*, fire-offerings, and so forth. [411]
The meaning is that the *saṃkrānti* which is the Sun’s transition into a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) is said to yield greater fruit than the transitions between other planets. Śātātapa says:
"If a man does not bathe when the Sun’s transition has occurred..."
For seven births he shall be diseased and is born indeed destitute.
In some places, however, the second half-verse is recited differently:
"For seven future births, he shall always be diseased and a partaker of suffering."
Whatever offerings of *havya* and *kavya* are given by donors at the time of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*),
the Sun-god bestows them back eternally in birth after birth.
At the beginning of the solstices, one should always give whatever substance is desired among the planets,
as well as at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti* periods and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*:
"Regarding these bodies that have been described, beginning with the *saṃkrānti* [transits],
no obstacle exists for one who exerts himself during these times, which are designated as 'imperishable' (*akṣaya*)."
Whatever is given by men even without faith, even to unworthy recipients,
and even at an improper time— all that, being true, shall become inexhaustible.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Whatever is chanted or given during the equinoxes (viṣuva) becomes inexhaustible;
likewise at Viṣṇupada and at the beginnings of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods."
Bhāradvāja said: Whatever gift is given during the Ṣaḍaśīti, or whatever gift is given during the two equinoxes—
the end of the ocean may be seen, but the end of that merit is never seen.
Vasiṣṭha says: That which is given during the solstices, at the beginnings of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods,
and during lunar and solar eclipses, becomes inexhaustible.
At the solstice (ayana), the fruit is ten millionfold; at Viṣṇupadī, it is one hundred thousandfold;
and at the Ṣaḍaśīti, it is remembered by the wise as being eighty-six thousandfold.
A gift at the waning of the moon yields a hundredfold; at the end of the day, a thousandfold;
at the equinox, a hundred-thousandfold; but at the *vyatīpāta*, it is infinite.
— Vṛddha-vaśiṣṭha.
A man who, having fasted for three nights on the solstices and the equinoxes,
bathes and worships the Sun, shall obtain the fruit of all his desires.
Āpastamba says: On the solstices, on the equinoxes, and during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
one who has fasted for a day and night and bathed is liberated from all sins.
And this refers to those householders who have sons; for it is said:
"On a Sunday, on a day of the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a fast should not be observed by a householder who has sons."
Thus, because fasting is prohibited there for a householder who has sons; as stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"When the sun has returned to Libra, on the day of the equinox..."
Or fresh crops should be given to the Brahmins.
Likewise:
When the sun desires to enter Aries, one should discard the winter garment of ghee and diligently perform worship to the gods.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Gold, diamond, sapphire, ruby, and pearl—
these five jewels one should place upon the head of the deity."
In the absence of gems, however, having joined together one *karṣa* or even half a *karṣa* of gold during that very same northern course of the sun,
and having likewise worshipped it according to the rules with abundant clarified butter from a cow;
Having washed and rubbed it, one should then offer the "butter-blanket."
Having further given household utensils and having fed and honored the Brahmins together with the ascetics,
he should provide them with unrestricted provisions.
‘Kuliśa’ means diamond. ‘Having gratified’ means having worshipped with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The ellipsis is “he should prepare the food.
One should perform all this preceded by devotion after fasting.
Having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) mixed with sesame seeds, one should indeed complete the rite oneself.
A wise person should perform his bath with sesame seeds and likewise his body-anointing with them;
he should also perform the libation for both the deities and the ancestors with those same seeds.

‘Pārayet’ means he should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*). Here, no specific sequence between the sesame bath and the breaking of the fast is intended. ‘Ubhābhyām’ (with both) is the dative case used in the sense of purpose. He should always perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with those [sesame seeds] during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*).
He should indeed give them, along with gold, to the gods and to the Brahmins.
That man who, having fixed his mind upon Śambhu, acts thus with effort alone—
having reached the northern course of the sun— why should he grieve?
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"When the sun transits on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
that seventh day is indeed 'Mahājayā,' beloved of the Sun."
Bathing, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors, gods, and others—
all these are said by the one of great splendor, Tapana (the Sun), to be multiplied ten millionfold.
But that man who, being devoted to this [rite], bathes the Sun with ghee,
shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and thereafter go to the city of the Sun.
The devoted man who bathes the Sun with milk,
being liberated from all sins, attains the same world as the Sun.
By means of a variegated celestial chariot garlanded with networks of small bells,
he becomes equal to the sun in brilliance and equal to Atri in luster;
having remained there for a long time, he becomes a victorious king.
O Destroyer of Tripura, I have thus related this meritorious Saptamī;
by fasting upon it with devotion, a person shall obtain immovable auspiciousness,
and thereafter go to the Supreme Brahman, reaching which one does not grieve.
Viśvāmitra states the specific gifts to be given according to the specific solar transits (saṃkrānti):
"When the sun enters Aries, the gift of a ram yields great fruit;
likewise, when it enters Taurus, the gift of cows is prescribed."
The giving of clothing, food, and drink is prescribed for the sign Gemini;
however, the gift of a cow with ghee is highly praised for Cancer.
The gift of many years' worth of leaves is always prescribed for Leo;
likewise, upon the entry of Virgo, the gift of garments and fragrant substances is enjoined.
At the entry of the sun into Libra, the gift of grains and seeds is most excellent;
at the entry of the insects (the sun into Scorpio), the gift of garments and houses is likewise prescribed.
In this context, "insect" refers to the scorpion.
Upon the entry of Sagittarius (Dhanus), there is great fruit for garments and vehicles;
upon the entry of Pisces (Jhaṣa), likewise, there is the giving of wood and fire.
At the entry of the Sun into Aquarius, the gift of cows, water, and grass is prescribed;
indeed, at the entry into Pisces, the gift of unfading garlands is also most excellent.
O best of the twice-born, having bestowed these gifts at the proper time,
a man attains whatever desire is cherished in his mind.
Therefore, they indeed praise giving at the proper time.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O King, he who gives a cow made of sesame seeds during the northern course of the sun attains all desires and finds supreme happiness."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Brahmins, during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*), the gift of clothing yields great fruit;
by giving a bull preceded by sesame seeds, one is liberated from diseases."

In the *Śivarahasya*: "Formerly, at the transit of the sun into Capricorn (*makarasaṃkrānti*), when the Gosava sacrifice was performed, Śaṅkara caused sesame seeds to arise for the satisfaction of all embodied beings."
Therefore, on that day, wise men should perform a bath with sesame seeds and anointing with them;
likewise, they should offer libations of water and sesame seeds to the deities and the ancestors.
Sesame seeds should always be given to Brahmins during the northern course of the sun;
one should cause meritorious sesame seeds to be recited, and likewise, sesame seeds should be offered as oblations.
Those best of the twice-born who, on that lunar day, offer oblations of sesame seeds and honor the brahmins,
shine in the third heaven like those who have gifted a thousand cows.
Auspicious lamps made with sesame oil should be offered in the temple of Śiva;
the twice-born should worship the God according to the prescribed rite with rice mixed with sesame seeds.
Or, desiring the fruit of great merit, one should perform the consecration with ghee,
using a vessel filled with ghee while reciting the Sāvitra mantra day and night.
O Śambhu, one should offer a "butter-blanket" (ghṛtakambala) with cow-derived clarified butter;
having fashioned a beautiful image with ghee, one attains the increase of spiritual welfare.
And this transition (*saṃkrānti*) consists of extremely subtle moments of time.
Thus it is said in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"This coarse division has been proclaimed for one who desires liberation."
I shall tell you the number according to the ultimate truth, O best of kings.
When a healthy man is sitting at ease, as long as his eye remains steady,
the thirtieth part of that duration is proclaimed to be the *tatpara*.
A hundredth part of that [lava] is called a *truṭi*;
half of a thousandth part of a *truṭi* is the duration of time known as *ravisaṃgraha*.
At that time, when the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, had become liquefied,
even Brahmā, the best of gods, spoke in doubt:
Acts such as giving, study, and the recitation of prayers are clearly obtained through the fire-oblation;
otherwise, they could not be attained by any other means, even in the case of the streams of clarified butter (vasordhārā).

Therefore, since the performance of ritual acts is not possible within this extremely subtle [moment], the contiguous period must be taken; and in response to the question of how much of that period should be taken, Vasiṣṭha says:
"The moment of the transit (saṃkrānti) is so subtle that it is difficult to perceive even for those with the eyes of a physician;
yet by association with it, thirty nāḍīs [fifteen] before and [fifteen] after are rendered pure."

Thirty *nāḍīs* before and thirty *nāḍīs* after [the transit] constitute the auspicious time (*puṇyakāla*). Alternatively, it should be understood that there are fifteen *nāḍīs* before and fifteen *nāḍīs* after. For this being so, there is agreement with the statement from the *Devīpurāṇa* which is about to be cited. Jābāla states:
"At the transit (*saṃkrānti*), the auspicious time consists of sixteen *kalās* on both sides."
In this context, "kalās" refers to the channels (*nāḍīs*), in accordance with many scriptural statements. Marīci says:
"The sixteen channels which are to the east and west of the *saṃkrānti*."
Merely by the sight of Rāhu, it is proclaimed as a meritorious time.
Śātātapa says:
Sixteen nāḍīs before and sixteen after [the sun's passage] are known as the auspicious time for the solar transit (saṃkrānti), as proclaimed by the learned.

On this point, some say that the statement regarding the sixteen *ghaṭikās* of merit on both sides refers specifically to the *Viṣṇupadī*, because of the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The meritorious time for the *Viṣṇupadī* is sixteen [ghaṭikās] before and after [the sun's entry]. That is incorrect; for it is said:
"At the solstices and other such times, one should always give whatever wealth is desired during planetary transits."
And likewise at the commencement of the sixty-fourth year, and during the liberation of the moon and the sun.

Because of such statements and because the *Ṣaḍaśīti* prescribes a gift, yet since the moment is extremely subtle, it is impossible for it to serve as the basis for the act of giving; thus, when there is an expectation for a specific time, Śātātapa has stated: "The period prior to sixteen [nāḍīs] is to be known [as meritorious]. Therefore, it is logical that this statement refers to all transits (*saṃkrānti*) in accordance with that [definition], and not merely to the unmentioned *viṣṇupadī*. The interpretation of the sentence "The meritorious time is the *viṣṇupadī*" will be explained later.

Others, however, say that the statement, "Sixteen [nāḍīs] before [the sun's entry] are to be known," refers specifically to the *ṣaḍaśīti* occurring on the *viṣṇupadī*. As stated by Vasiṣṭha: "When the *ṣaḍaśīti* has passed, sixty nāḍīs are said to be meritorious; and sixteen [nāḍīs] before and after the *viṣṇupadī* are likewise called meritorious."
And here, because of the word "ca" (and), it is understood that in the *ṣaḍaśīti* as well, there are sixteen [breaths] both before and after; this too has already been refuted in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"The past and future enjoyment [is said to be] fifteen *nāḍīs*."

"Bhoga" (enjoyment) refers to the performance of prescribed acts such as ritual bathing and giving, or the avoidance of prohibited acts such as Vedic study, on the occasion of a *saṃkrānti* (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign), according to the traditional rule: "The root *bhuj* signifies both protection and eating.
Furthermore, there is the presence (*sāṃnidhya*) of the planets during the sun’s transit;
worldly affairs are characterized by [the positions of] the moon and the sun.
Time destroys everything, including Brahmā and the rest, both the moving and the unmoving.

Regarding the words *kāla* (time), *śabda* (sound), and *saṃkhyāna* (calculation): when the time of the *saṃkrānti* has arrived, it becomes "without sound" (*avikalate*), meaning that sound has departed.
The Goddess bestows the fruit according to the distinction between merit and demerit.
The "Goddess" is Durgā, whose essential nature is the time of the *saṃkrānti*; this very point was stated at the beginning of the section on the *saṃkrānti*.
O All-pervading Lord, the Goddess exists through the sequence of years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, and so forth, distinguished by both gross and subtle forms.
It is also stated at the conclusion of the chapter on Transitions (*saṃkrānti*):
"O child, the Goddess has passed away; she is proclaimed as subtle.
She is the accomplisher of all desires and the destroyer of great fears. Thus it is said.
Even a single act performed during that [time] shall yield millions upon millions of times its merit.
Indeed, from righteousness (dharma) increase longevity, ghee, sons, happiness, and so forth;
whereas from unrighteousness (adharma) arise disease, sorrow, and the like, especially when in proximity to the equinoxes and solstices.
Even when in proximity, a specific excellence of fruit is shown by the scriptural statement regarding the solstices (*ayana*) and the equinoxes (*viṣuva*).
Likewise:
"There is an option regarding the solstices; listen as I declare it to you."
As long as twenty *kalās* have been traversed, that merit belongs to the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*);
when the sun is devoid of its parts (*niraṃśa*) and unfavorable, it belongs to the end of the day in the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).

The meaning of the phrase "alternation during the solstices" (*ayaneṣu vikalpa*) is as follows: those fifteen *nāḍīs* which are generally obtained by dividing day and night at the equinoxes (*saṃkrānti*), and those twenty *nāḍīs* which are [obtained] at the night-equinox—these must be added together. Therefore, when the transit occurs before or after midnight, two days are meritorious. Alternatively, those fifteen [units] which exist during the solstices by way of the division into prior and posterior [halves] should be joined by dividing them into twenty *nāḍīs*; thus it is said that here there are twenty-five *nāḍīs* on both sides that are meritorious. Or else, as before...
The meaning is that there are ten times more merits on both sides.
Others, however, explain it thus: the merit lasts for as long as the twentieth part [of the day] remains after the moment of the transit.

Others, however, explain it as follows: the word *yāvat* (as far as) applies to the sequence, the totality, the injunction, and the transformation. As many *ghaṭikās* as are consumed during the movement toward the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*)—that is, as many *ghaṭikās* as there are in the twenty *ghaṭikās*—so much greater is that merit in the *uttarāyaṇa*; this is the distinction or specific detail. At the moment of transition (*saṃkrānti*), which is partless and devoid of portions, the Sun becomes free of portions. At the end of the day, in the *dakṣiṇāyana*, the *udagayana* is the day of the gods; and from that, the *dakṣiṇāyana* [is established]; this is a restatement of its essential nature. [This is stated] in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
The wise know that at the equinox there are six muhūrtas of merit, at the mouth of the Śaḍaśīti three, and likewise at Viṣṇupada three.

Thus, it should be understood that the mention of a short duration in the statements of Marīci and others is intended to demonstrate the excellence of the merit [accrued], and not as a restrictive rule. For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
"Whichever nāḍīs are proximate, those are remembered as the most meritorious."
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra):
A gift given at the equinox, at Viṣṇupada, at the beginning of the southern solstice,
when the six-aśīti-mukha has passed, and likewise at the northern solstice, yields abundant fruit.

In this context, by the word "middle" (*madhya*), the periods immediately preceding and following the *saṃkrānti* are intended, because the actual middle moment of the *saṃkrānti* is exceedingly subtle. Baudhāyana says:
"When the sun is about to enter [a new sign], when it has already entered, and likewise when it is in the middle of its transit."
When the six-month period of the sun's northward course has passed, and when that [period] has also passed.
Vasiṣṭha says:
The meridian moment of the equinox is meritorious; before Viṣṇu’s southern transit, when the Ṣaḍaśītimukha has passed, and when the northern transit has passed.
Laugākṣi says:
At the winter solstice, at Viṣṇupada, and likewise at the beginning, giving and other acts yield infinite fruit; however, at the equinox, they yield middling results.
The great seers indeed declare this regarding the past, the six-and-eighty-faced [year], and the northern course of the sun.
"When the sixty-fourth [day] has passed and the two equinoxes have occurred"—in some versions, the reading is "when the two equinoxes have passed.

"Merit will be found in the solstice and when the northern course has passed. Here, by the word "and," it should be understood that merit exists even when [the solstice] is yet to come. (From the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*).
Thirty nāḍīs in Karkaṭaka, and ten more in Makara;
this southern solstice will be meritorious, as will the northern solstice that has passed.

And here, by the use of the word "ca" (and), it is shown that during the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), the forty *ghaṭikās* following [the equinox] are also meritorious. A gift given at the midpoint is meritorious during the equinox (*viṣuvat*), as is one given previously during the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) or at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, and also when the *uttarāyaṇa* has passed.
Thus is the settled rule regarding gifts, at the time of the sun's passage into a new sign, and in sacrificial oblations.

Vasiṣṭha says: The two meritorious periods are the past and the future solstices, northward and southward; however, during an eclipse, that time is meritorious even when the sun has passed into the northern course.

In order to establish that merit is also attained in the future, it was stated: "and during the past northern course. Since it was said that there is merit during the past and future northern and southern courses, in response to the inquiry as to for how long a time this lasts, he says:
"Thirty *nāḍīs* are recorded for Cancer; twenty for Capricorn. For the present Libra and Aries, however, there are ten *nāḍīs* on both sides."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Brahmin, at the ends of the Yugas and likewise at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti, there are twenty [degrees] in Cancer;
the first thirty [degrees] are in Capricorn."
Vasiṣṭha says: When the Ṣaḍaśīti has passed, sixty nāḍīs are said to be meritorious;
and sixteen following the Viṣṇupadī are also so called.

In some places, however, the reading is "the sixty *nāḍikās* consumed. In that case, for each of the four *saṃkrāntis* known as the *ṣaḍaśītimukhas*, there are fifteen [nāḍīs] each; thus, there are sixty *nāḍīs* designated as meritorious (*puṇya*). Based on an analysis of this statement, some say:
"The consumption of the past and future is recorded as fifteen *nāḍīs*."
Thus, the statement from the Devīpurāṇa refers to the period of the Ṣaḍaśīti.

That is incorrect, because the statement from the *Devīpurāṇa* establishes [the fruit] of past and future enjoyments, whereas this [present passage] is intended to establish the remainder of past merit; thus, there is no inconsistency in their respective conclusions. Likewise, it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "When the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed, as well as during the northern solstice (*udagayana*), the fruit is abundant. Furthermore, in the *Devīpurāṇa*, there is one section concerning the general duties of the *saṃkrānti* (transit), and another concerning the specific duties of particular *saṃkrāntis*. This sentence is recited therein within the section on general duties.
The past and future experiences are known as the fifteen channels.

Thus, in that case, if one were to adopt the position of a summary (*upasaṃhāra*), there would also follow the sublation of the context (*prakaraṇabādha*). Therefore, this [statement] is not a summary intended to establish a specific merit for each of the fifteen *ghaṭikās* that have passed during the *ṣaḍaśītimukhīs*. However, if the meaning were that sixty *nāḍīs* of a single [period] are meritorious, then there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate another root scripture (*mūlaśruti*). But when this sentence is intended to establish a specific merit for fifteen *ghaṭikās* in each [period], then there is no need to postulate another root scripture.

By the statement, "The past and future [periods] are fifteen nāḍīs," merit is established even for the fifteen ghaṭikās that have passed; and by the statement, "When the Ṣaḍaśītimukha has passed, as well as during the northern transit (udagayana), there is abundant fruit," a specific result is established for what has passed. Since this is logically consistent with the very Vedic source upon which those [Smṛti texts] are based, [it follows that] when the Ṣaḍaśītimukha has passed, fifteen nāḍīs are traditionally taught [to be meritorious].
Thus, according to the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the former explanation alone is superior. Baudhāyana says:
"Merit is declared at the Viṣuvat [solstice]; it extends ten generations before and ten after."
The time of merit occurs at the sun's transition [into a new zodiac sign] for acts such as bathing, giving, and recitation.
Bṛhaspati says: "In the southern solstice, thirty auspicious nāḍīs will indeed occur; in the past, they occurred in the northern solstice—so say those who know the ancient lore."
Gautama says:
Sixteen nāḍīs before [the solstice] and sixteen after it;
these same [periods] apply first to the southern course and then to the northern course when it has passed.

In all transits (*saṃkrānti*), sixteen *nāḍīs* before and sixteen *nāḍīs* after are meritorious; these two groups, characterized by the pair of sixteens, are most meritorious during the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*). Regarding the phrase “and in the past northern transit,” the word “and” (*ca*) implies that it was also so previously. In some places, however, the reading is “those very ones are first in the south,” which is indeed easy to understand. It should be understood that the presentation of specific times for merit within these statements—by dividing them into earlier and later parts according to particular transits—is intended to demonstrate an excellence of merit and is not a restrictive rule (*niyama*). If it were intended as a restrictive rule, such as in the passage beginning, “A gift in the middle at the equinox (*viṣuvat*), at Viṣṇupada, and at the beginning of the southern transit,” then statements such as “The ones called meritorious and Viṣṇupadas are sixteen both before and after” and “The conjunction with that also purifies thirty *nāḍīs* below and above” would be inconsistent.
Gobhila states: "If the sun's transit (saṃkramaṇa) occurs at night, one should perform that rite during the day;
whether before or after [the actual time], the fruit is obtained due to its proximity."

Some explain this statement as referring to the Viṣuvad and Viṣṇupadī [solar transits] occurring at midnight, because on those two specific occasions, when they occur at midnight, both days are meritorious according to the established rule.

That is incorrect. For when the *saṃkrānti* occurs at midnight, there is no distinction between the two days—the preceding and the following—due to their proximity; and because the validity of the merit of both days applies to all *saṃkrāntis* occurring at midnight, except for the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) and the *Viṣṇupadī*. Therefore, this statement, "and its fruit [arises] from proximity," refers to every *saṃkrānti* occurring at a time prior to or subsequent to midnight. As Gārgya says:
"When the *saṃkrānti* should occur at a time before midnight..."
The Gārgyas, Gālavas, and Gautamas consider that day to be meritorious.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "If midnight has not yet arrived, the merit is that of the day;
but when midnight is complete, [merit accrues] at both sunrise and sunset."
The merit for half the day belongs to the Sun when the night has not yet ended;
when it is complete, it should be given to both; if there is an excess, it belongs to the following day.

"Not yet arrived" (*anāgata*) means that the time of transit has not come; the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter sense of the state of being, meaning that the time of transit has not been reached. "Rising" (*udaya*) refers to the morning twilight. "Setting" (*astamaya*) refers to the evening twilight. "Half of the measure" (*mānārdham*) is two *praharas*. "The sun" (*bhāskara*) is the day, both because it is characterized by the sun and from the etymological derivation "that which makes light. When this is incomplete—meaning when the night is not full—the "petal" (*dalam*) refers to half, i.e., the incomplete midnight. The meaning is that if the transit occurs during the twilights or at night, the merit belongs to the two *praharas* of the day. If it occurs at an incomplete midnight, the fault belongs to the two *praharas* of both the preceding and following days. If the transit occurs after midnight, the fault belongs to the two *praharas* of the subsequent day. At sunset, the two *praharas* of the previous day are to be taken; at sunrise, however, the two *praharas* of the following day are to be taken due to proximity. In some places, however, the reading is "when the night is past" (*atīte śarvarīdale*).

Others, however, read it thus: "But when midnight is not yet full, as well as at sunrise and sunset, there is half the merit of the sun [at midday] for the Blessed One; but when the night is full, [the merit is complete]."

By the phrase "at this incomplete midnight," it is already stated that "in the incomplete portion of the night. Nevertheless, that which is stated again is for the purpose of connecting it with merit; the meaning is that just as there is merit by day, so too there is merit even in the incomplete portion of the night.

On this point, some say: when the transit occurs at midnight, since the occasional rites such as bathing—which have the transit as their cause—must be performed only once for both days, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of them; it is not a case of equal option (*vikalpa*) between the two days, because that would be marred by the eight logical fallacies (*aṣṭadoṣa*). Therefore, one should understand that the merit of bathing and so forth is determined by a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*), whether on the previous day in the forenoon or on the following day. In this regard, the basis for the fixed rule is this statement:

"When the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed, when the two equinoxes (*viṣuvad*) have occurred, when the [southern] solstice (*ayana*) is yet to come, and when the northern solstice has passed, [there is] merit."

This statement does not refer specifically to the times of sunrise, sunset, midnight, or the [solar] transits (*saṃkrānti*), because it has been stated that those periods possess the merit of two watches (*prahara*). Nor does it refer to the transits occurring during the day;
for regarding a transit, the meritorious time consists of sixteen *kalās* on both sides.

This is because of the contradiction with the scriptural statement. Furthermore, if in the case of a transit (*saṃkrānti*) during the day, the syntactical connection were "when the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed," then one should have simply said "in the *ṣaḍaśīti*"; what is the purpose of saying "sixteen *kalās* on both sides"? If you argue that, given this [phrase], there would follow the undesired consequence (*prasakti*) that even a period of time exceeding sixteen *kalās* is meritorious, we say: no. Because for a transit occurring at night, merit is declared for two watches (*prahara*), and thus, when a specific duration is required elsewhere by implication, that [duration of sixteen *nāḍīs*] alone is appropriate, since that [nightly transit] is equal to sixteen *nāḍīs*. Therefore, the established rule (*vyavasthā*) is as follows: when the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed at midnight, the merit belongs to the following day; when the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*) have occurred, the merit belongs to the subsequent day. Thus, in the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), if it occurs at midnight, the preceding day is meritorious; in the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), if midnight has passed, the following day is meritorious. In this way, those transits and so forth which occur at full midnight are established by the sentence "when the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed" as belonging to the first half of the preceding day and the second half of the following day. However, regarding the *viṣṇupadī*, since there is no specific rule, it remains expectant of a determination and is therefore established by the immediately following sentence.
One should understand that merit is obtained at the outset if the lunar day remains undivided; however, if the Vyatīpāta yoga occurs at midnight, the special merit lies on the following day.

"One should know that the merit is at the beginning of the day"—this means that if at midnight the lunar day (*tithi*) has not changed and remains the same as that of the previous day, then the merit is at the beginning of the day; however, if at the time of the *saṃkrānti* (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign) the lunar day were different, then the merit would be established as being on the following day alone. Furthermore, once midnight has passed, whether the lunar day has changed or not, if the *saṃkrānti* occurs, the merit is to be known as being on the following day alone. This is incorrect, because in the case of the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, Viṣṇupadī, the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), the merit of the preceding period has already been established. Nor is the Viṣṇupadī dependent for its determination upon this rule, since a statement establishing its merit prior to the *saṃkrānti* has already been cited. There is no authoritative evidence for a restrictive rule that the dependence [of other cases] is resolved solely by the *Devīpurāṇa*. Nor is there any authority for the distinction that those statements concern daytime *saṃkrāntis*, while the *Devīpurāṇa* statement—"when the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed"—concerns midnight *saṃkrāntis*. Therefore, the rule "one should know the merit is at the beginning" applies universally to all *saṃkrāntis*. Consequently, by process of elimination, this [other rule] concerns daytime *saṃkrāntis*. Nor does its application to daytime *saṃkrāntis* contradict the statement: "The meritorious time of a *saṃkrānti* is sixteen *kalās* on both sides. This is because that statement is intended to establish a specific degree of merit. Nor is the statement "sixteen *kalās* on both sides" redundant when applied to daytime *saṃkrāntis*, as it serves to specify the exact number of *ghaṭikās*. Nor can it be argued that since two watches (*prahara*) are meritorious during nighttime *saṃkrāntis*, that same duration must be taken by implication whenever a specific detail is required elsewhere—even if obtained by implication, it is more appropriate to state it explicitly. Furthermore, the merit is not obtained from that [statement], because there is a difference between the "sixteen on both sides" and the "two watches. By this, the argument of some—who claim that the sentence "one should know the merit is at the beginning" refers specifically to the two equinoxes occurring at midnight, since that case requires a determination due to the need to establish a middle point, whereas the Viṣṇupadī is independent because its prior merit has been declared and thus does not require such a rule—is also refuted.

Others, however, say: "The statement ‘one should know the merit at the beginning’ may refer to all transits occurring at midnight; and the phrase ‘when the Ṣaḍaśītimukha has passed’ may also apply, as there is no contradiction. This is incorrect, because when a transit occurs at midnight during the latter part [of the day], yet on the lunar date (*tithi*) of the preceding day, there would result a contradiction between those two statements.

Since the establishment [of the rule] is accomplished by a single statement alone, there is no separate establishment from a second statement; therefore, others hold that the statement, "One should know merit at the beginning," refers to all transits occurring at midnight, whereas the statement, "When the six-aśīti-mukha has passed," refers specifically to transits occurring during the day.

That too is incorrect, because it will be stated later that for Capricorn and Cancer born at midnight, there is an absence of merit for two days; since there is no need for a formal rule in the absence of such merit, this statement does not refer to them. Rather, it is established that this sentence refers to transits occurring at midnight other than those of Capricorn and Cancer. Vasiṣṭha says:
"When a transit occurs during the day, the day is proclaimed as meritorious."
When a transit occurs at night, the merit for bathing and giving gifts lasts for half a day.
If the transit occurs below midnight, the rite is performed after midday;
if it occurs above [midnight], it is two *praharas* after sunrise.
If the sun enters [a new sign] at the completion of midnight,
they declare it a meritorious day of loss (dinakṣaya), with the exception of Capricorn and Cancer.

The statement regarding the merit of two *praharas* (six-hour periods) of the preceding and following days when the transit occurs before or after midnight applies only to the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and not to the *viṣṇupadī* or *ṣaḍī* transits. For it is said: "When the Sun’s transit occurs at night while he is in Sagittarius, Pisces, Gemini, or Virgo, [the merit belongs to] the preceding and following [days]."
The wise have declared that five nāḍīs in the forenoon are auspicious for Vedic and Smārta rites,
and likewise five in the afternoon.
This is because it would contradict the statements of the *Nigamas*. Nor does it refer to the solstice (*ayana*), for in that case the entire day is meritorious. And so says Yajñapārśva:
"The half-day preceding the transit (*saṃkrama*) is meritorious for bathing and giving gifts."
At night, when the sun enters a sign (saṃkrānti), the day [is meritorious] during the equinoxes (viṣuvat) and the solstices (ayana).

However, where the reading is "viṣuvaty ayane dina," the meaning there is that when the transit occurs during either day or night, half a day is meritorious for both the equinox (*viṣuvat*) and the solstice (*ayana*); under this reading, the application to the solstices is also accepted. As for the interpretation of some who claim that if the transit occurs during the day in either the southern or northern course (*dakṣiṇāyana* or *uttarāyaṇa*), the meritorious time is only the day—that should be disregarded because it is far-fetched.

[429] Others, however, considering the scriptural statement to be for the purpose of establishing a preeminent merit, maintain that when a birth occurs at any *saṃkrānti* either before or after midnight, the merit lasts for half a day. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Having passed through Sagittarius, Pisces, Virgo, and likewise Gemini..."
When it transits at night, it does so by way of a division into the preceding and the succeeding parts.
At the end of the day, five nāḍīs are remembered as most meritorious;
likewise, at sunrise, there are five for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.

Based on the statement, “The day of rising (*udaye*) is most meritorious,” some consider the following day to be the most meritorious. Regarding the statement, “If [the transit occurs] before midnight (*ardharātre*), however,” some explain it as follows: they say that if the transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurs when midnight is reached, then both days are meritorious—the first day being from the point of the sun’s turning (*āvartana*) onwards, and the subsequent day being prior to the turning—this being in accordance with the *Devīpurāṇa* statement, “But if it is exactly at midnight. However, having excluded (*muktvā*) Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*) when they are born at full midnight, there is no merit for two days; rather, the night is meritorious, and therefore the transit of those two occurs at that very time. As for what was stated here regarding the phrase “having excluded Capricorn and Cancer,” by this statement the merit of two days for Capricorn and Cancer is set aside (*paryudasyate*), but it is not said that the night is meritorious, because it is impossible for a single word to have two meanings. Indeed, when it is said, “Having eaten with Devadatta, the Brahmins should be invited for the meal,” it does not follow that another meaning is that Devadatta himself should be fed right there.

That is incorrect. Regarding the statement "excepting Capricorn and Cancer," its intent does not lie in the fact that those two days are meritless; rather, it lies in the fact that the night is meritorious. Otherwise, the presentation of their time as meritorious would not have been made, since the subject at hand is the presentation of the meritorious times for all transits (*saṃkrānti*). Likewise, regarding the example "excepting Devadatta," its intent does not lie in the fact that Devadatta should be made to recite; rather, it lies in the fact that he should be fed in that very manner. Otherwise, the presentation of giving food to him, even though he had been invited, would not have been made, since the subject at hand is the presentation of giving food to all those who have been invited. Therefore, because there is no intent toward two distinct meanings for a single word, there is no fault whatsoever. As for what was said—that only that which has already been established is excluded, and that the meritlessness of the two days has not been established because only the merit of half a day was mentioned, and thus the word "day" must be taken as indicating "half a day"—this is another fault.

That too is incorrect, because there is no fault in adopting a secondary (lakṣaṇika) meaning when the primary one is impossible. For it is not possible that while the transition (*saṃkramaṇa*) is imminent, merit belongs only to half of a single day, yet when it is remote, merit belongs to both days in their entirety; thus, the claim that "there is merit at night during the two solstices" is untenable. This is improper because there is no evidence to show that the statement, "excepting Capricorn and Cancer," intends to mean that "there is merit at night during Capricorn and Cancer. Indeed, if it were stated that "the two days [other than] Capricorn and Cancer are meritorious," this would only establish the absence of merit for those two days, but not the existence of merit at night. Furthermore, upon considering other texts, we find statements establishing the merit of each individual day—such as "in Capricorn, the subsequent day is meritorious" and "in Cancer, the preceding day is meritorious"—and there is no other text establishing the merit of the transit occurring specifically at night during Capricorn and Cancer alone. Therefore, when the transit occurs at midnight during either of the two solstices, the merit belongs to that very same day; it is not the case that there is merit at night throughout both solstices.
And on this point Baudhāyana says: "When the sun, having set, enters the stars— at either evening or at midnight— then another meritorious day begins."

On this point, some say: if, by the statement in this passage, “or at evening” (*pradoṣe vā*), the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of the Capricorn transit (*makara-saṃkrānti*) occurring at evening on the following day were to be established, then a contradiction would result with the following authorities: the statement regarding the merit of a near transit, “half a day,” etc., from the *Yajñapārśva-Vasiṣṭha*; the statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa*, “having passed through Sagittarius and Pisces,” etc.; and the statement from the *Devī Purāṇa*, “when midnight is not yet complete, even at sunrise or at sunset,” etc. Furthermore, there is another defect: in the statement beginning “when the sun has set” (*astaṃ gate yadā sūrye*), since both evening (*pradoṣa*) and midnight (*ardharātra*) are already obtained by the word “set” (*astaṃ gate*) alone, their separate mention would be redundant. Therefore, this statement should be explained as follows: the word “or” (*vā*) in the phrase “or at evening” (*pradoṣe vā*) is used in the sense of “like” (*yathā*), according to the lexicographical tradition (*nighaṇṭu*) which states, “*vā* is used in the senses of comparison and option. Thus, the meaning of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) is this: just as the first half of the previous day is meritorious at evening, so too is the following day meritorious at midnight. The second occurrence of the word “or” (*vā*) is used in the sense of “likewise” (*tathā*), because indeclinables have multiple meanings.

Others, however, fearing that the phrase "when [the sun] has set" would otherwise be redundant, explain it differently: just as the preceding day is meritorious when [the sun] has set and at dusk, so too, after midnight during the Makara-saṃkrānti, the subsequent day is meritorious.
Still others, in order to avoid the straightforward meaning of these statements, maintain that when the Makara-saṃkrānti occurs at dusk, there is merit on both days, with the choice being optional.

Others, however, say: because it is stated that the following day is meritorious during the *makara-saṃkrānti* at nightfall (*pradoṣa*), the statement "having passed beyond Sagittarius and Pisces" refers to the period prior to midnight, excluding nightfall.

This is incorrect; for if the word "prior" (*pūrva*) occurring in the sentence "having passed beyond Sagittarius and Pisces" were to refer to the period prior to midnight—excluding nightfall—during the *makara-saṃkrānti*, yet refer to the entire period prior to midnight during other *saṃkrāntis*, a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) would result.

Others, however, say that in the phrase "at midnight," the word "past" (*atīta*) must be supplied, because of the statement: "When both [days] are complete, [the gift] should be given; when there is an excess, on the following day. That is incorrect, because this refers to other [specific types of] transits (*saṃkrānti*), according to the statement: "They declare two days to be meritorious, with the exception of Capricorn and Cancer. In another Smṛti:
When the sun, having left the sign of Sagittarius,
enters Pisces at either evening or midnight, then the transit occurs on the following day.
If the sun's transit into Cancer occurs from Gemini,
whether at dawn or at midnight, one should perform the rite during the preceding day.

Therefore, for Capricorn and Cancer births occurring at midnight, there is no merit on either of the two days; rather, merit lies on the following day for the Capricorn transit and on the preceding day for the Cancer transit.

Some explain the statement "at midnight" as referring specifically to the Viṣṇupadī occurring at midnight; according to that view, merit exists on both days by way of this specific rule only in the case of the Viṣṇupadī.

Others, however, explain this as referring to the equinoxes occurring at midnight. According to their view, it is specifically at the equinox that merit accrues on both days by way of fixed determination. For this very reason, in the cases of Capricorn and Cancer, the transition (*saṃkrānti*) is characterized by the subsequent and preceding enjoyment [of the day].

Both of those [interpretations] are improper, because it has been established that even when the transit occurs outside the Viṣṇupadī, the merit belongs to two days according to the fixed rule; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of an unwarranted restriction in the absence of a cause, and there would be the undesirable consequence of the terms "Capricorn" (makara) and "Cancer" (karkaṭa) being mere figurative indicators (upalakṣaṇa) without a basis, since the statement is perfectly consistent with its literal sense according to the path shown.

Others, however, explain it thus: if the *saṃkrānti* occurs when midnight has fully passed, they say that two days are meritorious and fit for teaching and studying, "excepting" (meaning excluding) those two born at midnight—the Capricorn and Cancer transitions; for them, two days are not meritorious, but rather non-meritorious and unfit for teaching and studying. The meaning is that there is no study for two days during the Capricorn and Cancer transitions. And so says the *Smṛti*: "If [the transition] occurs by day, there is a pair of nights; if by night, there are two days."
The *saṃkrānti* known as *pakṣiṇī* should be understood as unfavorable for acts of giving, study, and ritual action.

By this statement, the impurity of the two days of Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*) is declared; that should be understood as referring to the acts of giving, teaching, and studying. "Giving" refers to the teaching of the Veda, and "studying" likewise refers to that same [Veda]. Regarding those ritual acts, it should be known that during these two days of giving, teaching, and studying, [the time] is not auspicious. Such is the established practice among teachers and students here: for they do not teach nor do they study during the two days of Capricorn and Cancer at night.

That is improper, because when inclusion within the context is possible, it is inappropriate to elevate [the subject] beyond it. Statements establishing the merit of bathing by day during both the two nights [of an eclipse] and during the day at the *saṃkrānti* have been shown; now, statements establishing the merit of bathing at night are presented.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, the words of Sumantu state:
"One should not perform a bath at night, nor especially a gift."
And one should perform occasional ritual bathing and giving of gifts during the nights.
On occasions of receiving a bride, marriage, the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign, a journey, illness, or childbirth,
as well as when listening to an ancient history (itihāsa), giving gifts at night is highly commended.
Viṣṇu [says]: "On occasions such as a marriage, a vow, the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), consecration, a seasonal festival, or a birth,
as well as at eclipses and the like, night is auspicious for bathing and giving gifts."
‘Ṛtu’ refers to conception; ‘pāta’ refers to the Vyatīpāta yoga.
Gobhila states: “At the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), at the sun’s passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), at marriage, at times of calamity, and on occasions of prosperity...”
One should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites at night during optional vows.
On this point, some say that these statements refer to transits other than those of the Sun. For this very reason, Gobhila stated:
"If the transit of the Sun occurs at night, one should perform the ritual during the day.
Furthermore: "The half-day preceding a transit is meritorious for bathing and giving gifts."
And as it is said: "When there is a transit of the sun at night, [the merit is] a day [at the equinoxes and solstices].

Furthermore, in those passages concerning nights, only the "transit" (saṃkrānti) is heard of, devoid of the specific name of any planet; therefore, this [rule] must refer to transits other than that of the sun. That is incorrect.
Bathing is recommended at the birth of a son, during a sacrifice, likewise at the transit of the sun, and upon the sighting of Rāhu; it is not so [recommended] otherwise at night.

This is because it contradicts the statement of Vasiṣṭha. Furthermore, regarding the opinion of Jitāmitra and others here—that since the night is not an auxiliary part of all rites, when bathing and other acts are somehow impossible during the day, one must necessarily perform bathing and so forth at night on the occasion of a *saṃkrānti* in order to avoid transgression; and that nocturnal statements are intended for this purpose alone—[they argue]:
