"When there is a transit (*saṃkramaṇa*) of the Sun at night, one should perform that rite during the day."
Thus, by the mention of "day," night is excluded; furthermore, it is because it is stated that when the sun transits at night, the merit belongs to the half-day.

And as for the opinion of others—that bathing, giving, and so forth, performed by virtue of being included within the time of the most subtle *saṃkrānti*, can be carried out even at night, which yields a superior fruit; whereas a night during which the *saṃkrānti* is not included is simply a time that is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*) of the ritual—otherwise, if the *saṃkrānti* occurred at night, it would be illogical to establish the rules for bathing and so forth on two days by excluding the proximate *nāḍīs*, given the scriptural statement regarding the merit of two watches (*prahara*). If one asks, "How is this known? it is from the very words of the *Purāṇas*. For it has been said: [The passage continues with the cited verses.]
"For from righteousness (dharma) indeed increase life-span, sovereignty, sons, happiness, and so forth;
whereas from unrighteousness (adharma) arise disease, sorrow, and the like, especially during the equinoxes and solstices. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, no one is capable of bringing about the proximity of any object whatsoever with a time that is extremely subtle; however, when an action is performed while including that [time], its proximity is established. Therefore, it might be argued that because the time of the *saṃkrānti* is included within the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) for bathing, giving, and so forth, its performance may take place at night. That too is incorrect, because the prohibition of the *saṃkrānti* [at night] does not negate the merit of the sixteen *nāḍikās* on both sides [of the transit], even in the case of a *saṃkrānti* occurring at night.
If the sun's transit occurs at night, one should perform that ritual during the day;
whether it is before or after [the actual time], the result is obtained due to its proximity.

This is because the statement [beginning with] "iti," which establishes the merit of the day proximate to a nocturnal *saṃkrānti*, lacks the power to exclude the night; and because the statement regarding "midday" (*dinārdha*), which establishes the merit of the midday of the proximate day, lacks the power to preclude the night. As for the meritorious time of a *saṃkrānti*: "Sixteen *kalās* on both sides [of the moment of transition], as well as fifteen *nāḍīs* of past and future [time], are traditionally taught [as meritorious]."
Whichever channels are situated nearby, those are remembered as the most meritorious.

Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of restricting such statements as these; and because there would be the undesirable consequence of restricting, without cause, those statements from the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* and other sources that prescribe bathing and other rites at night. Therefore, it is established that when the sun enters a zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*) at night, merit accrues both at night and by day, though the specific fruit differs due to the particularity of proximity.
Others, however, say: "In the two solstices (*ayana*) and the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*), there are five *nāḍīs* [of merit] on each of the two days.
Likewise, having passed through Sagittarius (*dhanus*), Pisces (*mīna*), Virgo (*kanyā*), and Gemini (*mithuna*)."
When it transits at night, it does so according to the division of before and after.
[436] At the end of the day, five nāḍīs are indeed remembered as most meritorious;
likewise, at sunrise, there are five for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:

"In the *viṣṇupadī* [transit of the sun], during the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, and in all *śrauta* and *smārta* rites, because of the proximity of night, there is merit only during the two auspicious days and five *ghaṭikās* [of the day]. When it occurs in the *viṣṇupadī*—that is, when the sun is in Sagittarius (*dhanus*), Pisces (*mīna*), Gemini (*nṛyuk*), or Virgo (*kanyā*)—[there is merit].
When the sun's transit occurs during the night, it falls between the preceding and succeeding days.
The wise have declared that five nāḍīs in the forenoon and likewise five in the afternoon are auspicious for rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.

Thus, according to the statement of the Nigama: even where there is no prohibition, the acceptance of the preceding and following *nāḍīs* remains the same because the time of the transit (*saṃkrānti*) is exceedingly subtle.

Gālava speaks of the most subtle merit of the equinoxes and so forth: "In a fixed sign, it is Viṣṇupada; in a dual-bodied sign, it is Ṣaḍaśītimukha; in Libra and Aries, it is the two equinoxes; when the Sun is in Taurus, it is the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*); and [when] in Cancer, it is the northern solstice (*saumyaka*)."
This has been explained by the preceding verses. Now,
it becomes clear that [the result] occurs in exactly the same amount of time as the degrees of precession (ayanāṃśaka),
provided the sun is in the signs beginning with Capricorn or Cancer, while the solstice is southern or northern respectively.
Then the times of transition (saṃkrānti), such as the equinoxes (viṣuvat) and so forth, are said to occur.

This is the meaning: there are thirty degrees (aṃśaka) for each zodiacal sign (rāśi), and the Sun traverses one degree per day therein. In that context, by as many degrees as the precession of the equinoxes (ayanacyuti) occurs, by that much future time of the Sun’s remaining portion (bhogyakāla), the precession of the Viṣṇupada and other signs occurs. Since the precession of the equinoxes occurs at twelve degrees, the meritorious time (puṇyakāla) occurs twelve days prior to the upcoming transit (saṃkrānti); during that time, acts such as giving (dāna) should be performed on account of the transit. This should be understood even when [the calculation] is deficient or excessive.
And so says Laugākṣi:
"Even prohibitions regarding journeys, being subtle in nature,
are unable to establish a firm footing."
Having reflected upon that which was taught to him by her,
they always have their desires completely fulfilled.
Jaimini also states that the time of the transit from one planet to another is meritorious:
"When the sun transits into a lunar mansion or a zodiacal sign, there are sixty nāḍīs before and after [the moment of transit]."
Furthermore, the sages have declared that for the Moon, three palas of a dharā constitute one auspicious nāḍī.
The four nāḍīs of Mars are with six palas;
those of Mercury are three manavas and seven palas; [those of Jupiter] are four and a half [nāḍīs] joined with seven palas.
And when Venus is in the fourth house from the Guru, there are four with Palāśa.
The two *nāḍīs* of the serpent, joined with seven *palas*, are declared auspicious for Saturn;
at the beginning, middle, and end [of these], one should perform recitation, giving, and fire-offerings.
By performing [this], one attains the abode of the lord of men.

When there is a transit (*saṃkramaṇa*) of the Sun into a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), the "nāḍīs of the Sun and Moon"—that is, sixteen *ghaṭikās*—before and after [the transit] constitute the time of merit (*puṇyakāla*). For the Moon, however, it is one *ghaṭikā* joined with thirteen *palas* (three *dhara*s and one *pala*). For Mars (*Maṅgala*), it is four *ghaṭikās* joined with one *pala*. For Mercury (*Budha*), it is three *ghaṭikās* joined with fourteen *palas*. For Jupiter (*Guru*, Bṛhaspati), it is four *ghaṭikās* joined with thirty-seven *palas*. For Saturn (*Śanaiścara*), it is "two-nāga nāḍīs"; since "nāgas" are eight, "two-nāgas" refers to twice eight.

Thus ends the determination of the *saṃkrānti* (solar transits) within the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time), in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the illustrious administrative offices of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of learning. [439]
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now commences the determination of the times for the *śrāddha* ceremony.
First, the determination of the time for the obligatory (*nitya*) *śrāddha*.

In this regard, the determination of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is first established. Thus, three divisions of the new moon day have been shown in the determination of the *ādiparvan*. Among these, when the new moon day is complete, the *śrāddha* should be performed in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), according to the Vedic injunction: "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors.
Likewise, Śātātapa states:
"That which is proclaimed as the *darśa-śrāddha* is declared to be the *pārvaṇa*."
However, that offering to the ancestors is praised when made in the afternoon.
Yama says: "One should offer [the oblation] to them at the end of the fortnight; for the ancestral rite (*paitṛka*) is performed in the afternoon.
But when [the new moon] spans two days, even then the *śrāddha* should be performed on whichever day it extends into the afternoon."
And so Kātyāyana says in the Chāndogya-pariśiṣṭa:
"The Śrāddha consisting of the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka is recommended when the moon has waned,
during the third part of the day, but not too close to the time of twilight."

The *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha is that performed immediately after the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. "When the moon has waned" means on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). "In the third part of the day" means in the afternoon, which is the third division of the day divided into three parts. Furthermore, when [the new moon] does not extend into the afternoon on either of the two days, even then the *Sinīvālī* associated with the preceding day alone is to be accepted. Thus he (the same author) says: "When [the new moon] fills the fourth watch of the fourteenth day..."
The new moon day (amāvāsyā) is desired for the śrāddha ceremony precisely when it is waning.
‘Kṣīyamāṇā’ means that on the following day it does not extend through the entire afternoon;
and thus Yajñapārśva also says:
“Where there is the fourteenth in one half [of the day] and the fifteenth in the other half.”
At the conclusion of the fourteenth day, however, one should perform the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
"In the latter half of the day. Vṛddha-Baudhāyana says:
"If the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] is seen during the fourth watch, and the new moon as well."
When the next day has dawned, one should begin; on that day, the rites for the ancestors (kavya) and others are performed.
And so Gobhila says:

"The full moon day (paurṇamāsī) is that which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon; the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is that which is the closest proximity. One should perform the new moon rite on the day when the moon is not visible in the sky; some say it may also be performed on the new moon day even while the moon is still visible. Vyāsa also says:
Sinīvālī is known as the night when the moon is visible, and Kuhu as the night when the moon has disappeared.
Sinīvālī is always used for rites pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya), while Kuhu is used for rites pertaining to the gods (daiva).

Therefore, it being established that the offering of the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* (the rice-ball meal) must be performed even at the end of the fourteenth day, some say: "This is not so; its offering does not take place on the fourteenth day. For it is prescribed immediately after the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, and the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed for the afternoon of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), according to the statement of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*: "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*."

As for the opinion that the word *amāvāsyā* is intended as an indirect indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*), that is not correct; for there is no evidence for such indirect indication, and it is improper to employ it in a primary injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, there is the scriptural text: "Therefore, on the previous day [the sacrifice] is performed for the ancestors, and on the following day they sacrifice to the gods; thus the sacrificer extends the sacrifice, having first completed it for the ancestors. Likewise, regarding the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), there is the statement of the authors of the Kalpasūtras: "In the afternoon they proceed with the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Since this refers specifically to that day of preparation on which the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs in the afternoon, it does not refer merely to the preceding day, nor can it serve as evidence for indirect indication.

Others, however, say that even on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) occurring within the period marked by the waning of the moon, the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* (the ancestral offering following the rice-ball rite) should not be performed, because it is prescribed to follow immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. And the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed for the new moon day when the moon is not visible. Thus says the Śruti: "When he is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he gives to them. There is also the statement of the author of the Sūtras: "On the day they do not see the moon, on that day one performs the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Nor is the term "not seeing" here intended merely as an indicator of the waning [of the moon], because the rule "when the night has waned" (*kṣīṇe rājani*) applies even when there is no visibility. Nor is the sequence [of rites] non-essential, as there is no evidence for such a claim. Now, if it is thought that this sequence applies only when both [events] occur on the same day and not otherwise—since the non-visibility of the moon occurs on the very day of fasting (*aupavasthya*), the two occur on one day; whereas at other times, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is postponed until the day of sacrifice (*yajanīyadina*)—[this is their view].
That is not so; for by the principle of the postponement of the primary [element], the *anvāhāryaka* (the rice-oblation) is also postponed. As for the statement of Laugākṣi:
"The *sinīvālī* [lunar day] should be used by twice-born men who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) in the rite for the ancestors;
the *kuhū* [lunar day] should be used by women, by Śūdras, and likewise by twice-born men who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anagnika*)."
[442] Let it be that this refers to the *piṇḍa* offerings of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *Anvāhāryaka*, and other rites for the ancestors.

This, however, is incorrect, because it contradicts the previously cited scriptural statements. As it has been stated: "The offering (*nirvāpa*) is not performed at the end of the fourteenth day. That is incorrect, because Kātyāyana, in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, while treating the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, says:
"Even when [the new moon] is visible, it is not with reference to the fourteenth day."
"One should wait for the new moon day, or one may perform the offering at its conclusion."

As for the claim that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed even while the moon is visible, that is incorrect. This is because of such statements as "some [say] when it is visible," which do not intend to refer to the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), but rather mean "at its end," that is, at the end of the fourteenth day. When, however, on the following day the new moon extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), then one should wait for the *amāvāsyā*; thus, the offering (*nirvāpa*) takes place even while the moon is visible. Anticipating the objection that this would contradict scriptural injunctions such as, "On the day they do not see the moon, on that day perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," the author himself, considering the scriptural statement regarding "non-seeing" to be an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the waning of the moon, says: "That which was stated—'on those days when the moon is not seen'—should be understood as an indication of that action [of non-seeing], just as the phrase 'when the night has waned' (*kṣīṇe rātrau*) is also [an indication]. Furthermore, the other position previously argued—that even on an *amāvāsyā* occurring within a day marked by the rising of the moon, there is no Piṇḍapitṛyajña or *Anvāhāryaka* [Śrāddha]—has already been refuted by the aforementioned statement of Kātyāyana, "even while it is visible," etc., as well as by Gobhila’s statement, "on one of the days when it is visible," and also by Hārīta.
At whatever twilight the moon is seen like a lotus stalk, the waning of the lunar day occurs during that afternoon; in that case, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) is certain.
In this context, the mention of "of the piṇḍas" intends not to exclude the Piṇḍapitṛyajña;
so says Kātyāyana again:
"When the fourth watch of the fourteenth day is being completed..."
"The new moon (amāvāsyā) is desired for the śrāddha at the very moment it is waning. [443]

Furthermore, on the day preceding the day of sacrifice, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and Śrāddha are prescribed, according to the rule: "Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors on the previous day. And when the new moon (Amāvāsyā) concludes at midday even though the first lunar day (Pratipad) occurs in the forenoon, then the sacrifice takes place on that very day; thus, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and other rites are performed on the preceding day when the moon has risen. This is because there is no evidence to suggest that the statement, "The Sinīvālī day should be observed by the twice-born who maintain the sacred fires for ancestral rites," refers to anything other than the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka-śrāddha. Regarding the question of when the waning of the moon occurs, he himself says:
"In the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes diminished;
indeed, in the eighth part of the new moon day, it becomes minute once again. Thus [it is said].

In this regard, those who know the movement of the planets describe how the waning of the moon occurs through twelve-twelfths of the zodiacal signs; thus, with each such subtraction of the moon, one lunar day (*tithi*) comes into being. Consequently, the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*) or the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) constitutes a twelfth part [of the cycle]. Among these, on the fourteenth day, the moon wanes at the end of its eighth part; then, during the eighth part of the new moon, having become minute, it is born again. The word *kila* here indicates that this is what is indeed proclaimed by the astronomers. On this point, there is the *Śatapatha-śruti*:

This very year is Prajāpati, consisting of sixteen parts (*kalā*). Its fifteen parts are the conjunctions (*saṃdhayaḥ*), while its sixteenth part is the fixed element (*dhruvā*). It is filled by the nights; that which wanes, having entered into all this world of living beings by means of that sixteenth part on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), is born again in the morning. Therefore, on that night, one should not deprive any living being of its life, even a lizard, out of reverence for this very deity.

The intention here is as follows: although one kalā perishes daily from the beginning of the first day of the dark fortnight through the fourteenth day of the Prajāpati in the form of the moon with sixteen kalās, such that fourteen kalās become exhausted by the end of the fourteenth day, yet on the third part of the fourteenth day, even the fifteenth kalā perishes. Thereafter, on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), having descended to the world of mortals with the sixteenth kalā—which is fixed and imperishable—it enters into all living beings. Then, on the third part of the new moon day, in the same manner, by means of that sixteenth kalā, it manifests once again in accordance with the day.
Kātyāyana states the time for the waning of the moon on a specific new-moon day:
"The new moon of Āgrayaṇī and likewise that which occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha—
those twice-born who know the movements of the moon declare this to be a special occasion."
This very day, in this very watch, the fourth part remains with but a fraction left;
at its very end, the moon goes to its waning.
Thus say those who know the wheel of the luminaries.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the moon is situated in Taurus (Vṛṣa), it is the new moon of Jyeṣṭha; and when it is in Scorpio (Vṛścika), it is the new moon of Agrahāyaṇī. These two are the positions of the moon’s highest and lowest altitudes. Due to their influence, there is a distinctiveness in the moon’s motion such that what occurs in the eighth watch on other new moon days happens, in these two specific new moons, in the very first watch. As for those who believe that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and other rites should be performed only upon the non-appearance of the moon and not even upon its waning, [the author] shows that the moon may sometimes not appear even on the second day in order to refute them.
In that year when there are thirteen months, the third [tithi] is not seen after the middle;
having thus understood the course of the moon.
When that [day] has ended, one should give [the gift] in the afternoon.

The meaning of this is as follows: In that year in which there is an intercalary month (*malamāsa*)—that is, when there is a thirteenth month—in that year, on the second lunar day following the third (i.e., the second day after the intercalary month), the moon is not visible; yet, for that reason alone, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, which is prescribed to be performed upon the sight of the moon, is not performed there. Therefore, having understood the course of the moon, one should perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites in the afternoon of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) mixed with the fourteenth day, even though the moon has waned. And thus is also the Śatapatha Śruti: [The text continues: "When the moon is not seen, that is the new moon. On that day, one should offer the sacrifice to the ancestors. It is not the case that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not to be performed simply because the moon is not visible on the second day; rather, it is taught that the rite must be performed on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day, even if the moon has set. This is the intent of the passage from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*. Thus ends the explanation of the meaning of the verse. Now, regarding the statement: "In the year in which there is an intercalary month," the term "intercalary" (*mala*) refers to the fact that the moon, having reached its conjunction with the sun, does not appear again for a certain number of days. Because it is a time when the moon is "impure" (*mala*), it is called an "intercalary month" (*malamāsa*). Regarding the phrase "on the second lunar day following the third": since the lunar day is determined by the appearance of the moon, and because the moon is not seen on that day, it is designated as the "second" (*dvitīyā*) lunar day. However, the name "second" is applied to it only because it follows immediately after the "third" day, and not because it possesses the actual characteristics of a second lunar day. Therefore, the meaning is that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not to be performed on that day. Consequently, one should understand that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites are to be performed on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day, in accordance with the rule: "One should perform the ancestral rites on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day. Thus, the meaning of the verse is established. Furthermore, the statement "in the year in which there is an intercalary month" implies that the performance of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not restricted solely to the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day; rather, it indicates that the rite may also be performed on the new moon mixed with the fifteenth day, provided that the moon is not visible on the second day following the intercalary month. This is the intended meaning. Now, regarding the statement: "Having understood the course of the moon, one should perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites in the afternoon of the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day, even though the moon has waned": this means that one should determine the course of the moon through calculation and observe whether the moon is visible or not. If the moon is not visible, one should perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day. If the moon is visible, one should perform it on the new moon mixed with the fifteenth day. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement: "And thus is also the Śatapatha Śruti": this is said to show that the aforementioned view is supported by scriptural authority. The Śatapatha Śruti states: "When the moon is not seen, that is the new moon. On that day, one should offer the sacrifice to the ancestors. Here, the word "not seen" (*adṛṣṭa*) refers to the non-appearance of the moon due to its proximity to the sun, and does not mean total invisibility. Therefore, the meaning of the Śatapatha Śruti is that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is to be performed on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day, even if the moon is not visible. It is not the case that the rite is omitted simply because the moon is not seen on the second day. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the commentary on the verse. Now, regarding the statement: "It is not the case that the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not to be performed simply because the moon is not visible on the second day": this means that the non-performance of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the second day is not based merely on the non-appearance of the moon; rather, it is because the second day lacks the essential characteristic of being a new moon. Therefore, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not to be performed on the second day. Consequently, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites are to be performed on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day, in accordance with the rule: "One should perform the ancestral rites on the new moon mixed with the fourteenth day. Or rather, he gives food to the ancestors every month on that single day when the moon is seen neither before nor after [the new moon]; for this King Soma is the food of the gods, and it is he who wanes during that night; when he has waned, he gives [the food] to them, and thus he brings about non-contention among them. Now, as for the statement "when he gives it while [the moon] has waned," those rules regarding *sinīvālī* and *niṣedhakā* apply to the *śrāddha* performed by one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragnika*).
Others, however, say that those statements refer to the *sinīvālī* that is pierced by the fourteenth day and enters the afternoon.
With this intention, Vṛddha-Manu said:
"The ancestors attend that lunar day (tithi) upon which the sun sets;
for it was given to them by the Self-Existent One during the afternoon."
If Sinīvālī extends into the afternoon, then she alone is to be accepted; otherwise, it is stated that Kuhū alone is to be accepted.
Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"But for the ancestors, [the day] which follows into the afternoon [is the one to be taken]."
She is to be accepted for ancestral rites, but not one who follows after the forenoon.
Even when there is a connection with the afternoon on both days, he (the same author) states the decision in the form of a doubt:
"Wherever the new moon might be mixed with the fourteenth day,
some know it as ending in the *kharvikā* [lunar day], while others call it *upendukā*."

On that day when the fourteenth tithi is present and the new moon (amāvāsyā) is very short, it is called *kharvikā*, because the word *kharva* signifies "small. By this very word "and" (*ca*), its unsuitability [for the ritual] is indicated. Therefore, some understand it thus: "it is not to be accepted"; others, however, understand it thus: "make use of the *upenduka* for the performance of the rite. Regarding this doubt, he states the resolution: "One should observe the increasing new moon on the following day; then the *pitṛyajña* should take place during three or even more watches [of the night]."

The meaning is that *kharvikā* occurs when there is an increase in the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and not otherwise. Now, however, even if it increases during the second fortnight, it is still considered *sinīvālī*. Paiṭhīnasi also says: "That new moon which increases at the rising of the sun is to be known as the 'later' one; what is given to the ancestors on that day becomes inexhaustible."

The meaning is that when the fourteenth day extends into the afternoon and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) increases [in duration], what is given to the ancestors on that [fourteenth day] becomes inexhaustible. Thus says Hārīta:
"The preceding [new moon] should be observed for three *muhūrta*s by the followers of the Ṛgveda, as well as the 'stunted' (*kharvā*) one."
The *kuhu* sacrifice is to be performed by the *adhvaryu* priests according to their desire with the chanting of *sāman* hymns.
The sacrifice should be performed by the twice-born during the second part of the lunar day (parvan),
because the followers of Āśvalāyana condemn [the performance] when it is joined with the second [tithi].
Baudhāyana says: Having fasted on the day of Sinīvālī and having performed the iṣṭi sacrifice,
the followers of the Taittirīya school should then perform the Pitṛyajña on the following day at its proper time.
[447] If the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs in the forenoon and not in the afternoon,
there is also the statement of Hārīta:
"Those who know the śrāddha rites understand that the śrāddha should be performed even on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad)."

Regarding this, Hariharācārya stated: "This statement has an unidentified source and is composed of mutually contradictory terms. To explain: the phrase "if [the new moon] occurs in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇe cet*) refers to the day of the first lunar day (*pratipad*). By the word "forenoon," either the third part of the day or its first half is meant. This being so, the claim that the rite would never occur on any afternoon is untenable; for when the fourteenth lunar day remains only in the forenoon of the *pratipad* day, there is a necessity for a connection with the afternoon of the fourteenth day, since there is no decrease in the lunar day (*tithi*) of more than six *ghaṭikās*. If, on the other hand, it were said that the rite must occur only in the afternoon of the *pratipad* day, then the phrase "if in the forenoon" would be redundant. Therefore, it should be explained as follows: when there is an increase in the lunar day (*tithivṛddhi*), the injunction for the *śrāddha* is prescribed for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) itself, as ordained by Manu following the *pitṛyajña*. Furthermore, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—which is not a subordinate part (*anaṅga*) of the sacrifice—is prescribed by the Śruti to take place in the afternoon and cannot be performed otherwise, because it occupies a long duration of time. Consequently, if the entire afternoon is occupied by that [sacrifice], what becomes of the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*? To answer this, he says "in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇe*), meaning not during the whole of the afternoon. Thus, the prescription of the *śrāddha* for the *sinīvālī* new moon (when it extends into the afternoon) concerns those who maintain the sacred fires (*agnimant*); however, for those without such fires (*anagnika*), the prescription of the *śrāddha* is for the *kuhvā* new moon (when it extends into the *kutapa* period).
And so it is stated in the Smṛti of Laugākṣi and in the Saura Purāṇa:
"The Sinīvālī [tithi] should be used by twice-born men who maintain the sacred fires for ancestral rites;
the Kuhū [tithi] should be used by women, Śūdras, and likewise by twice-born men who do not maintain the sacred fires."
Vyāsa also says:
"Sinīvālī, when the moon is visible, should be observed by Brahmins who maintain the sacred fires;
Kuhū, when the moon has vanished, should be observed by Śūdras and by Brahmins who do not maintain the sacred fires."
Baudhāyana also says:
"Sinīvālī and Kuhū are both mentioned in the Śruti regarding the rite of Śrāddha;
however, those who maintain the sacred fires should perform it on Sinīvālī, while those without fires should perform it on Kuhū."
*Kuhū* is that which extends through the time of *kutapa*.
Thus says Hārīta:
"The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), even if pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*) or mixed with the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*),"
In rites for the ancestors, the learned should perform [the ritual] at the time of Kutapa.
The definition of *kutapa* is given in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"There are always fifteen well-known *muhūrtas* in a day;
among these, that which is the eighth *muhūrta* is remembered as the time of *kutapa*."

This being the case, it is stated that when there is an amāvāsyā (new moon) connected with two days, that which extends through the *kutapa* period is the one to be accepted by those who maintain no sacred fires (*anagnika*).
For this very reason, Baudhāyana says:
"Where the fourteenth day persists beyond midday..."
She should be known as Sinīvālī, yet she is fruitless for rites dedicated to the ancestors.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"That new moon which begins after midday is to be known as pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta), and it shall not be considered the fifteenth day."
Kārṣṇājini also says:
"Those who, out of delusion or even through ignorance, perform the śrāddha rite on an amāvāsyā that is pierced by a lunar day [bhūta], their lifespan shall diminish."
[449] But when it does not span the time of Kutapa on either of the two days, then only that which is pierced by the [preceding] lunar day (bhūta) is to be accepted.
And so says Baudhāyana:
"If the new moon (amāvāsyā) lasts for even a single ghaṭikā on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipat), then..."
Even if pierced by a living being, it must be used in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
The meaning is that even a single *ghaṭikā* of the *pratipad* must not be connected with the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*). Jābāli also says:
"Even among the *pratipad*s, if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*)."
In rites for the ancestors, that [line] must always be made with the word *bhūta*.

But when the new moon (amāvāsyā) spans the time of Kutapa on both days, then—if during the forenoon—the later day is to be taken in cases of increase or equality [of duration], whereas in case of decrease, the earlier day is to be taken.
And so says Pracetas:
"Sinīvālī and Kuhū are declared by the Śruti for the performance of the śrāddha rite."
But if those two [the sun and moon] were to be eclipsed at midday, how then would the śrāddha and other rites be performed?
"Sinīvālī is traditionally taught to occur when there is a decrease in the lunar day (tithi), and Kuhū when there is an increase;
even when there is equality [of the lunar day], it should be known as Kuhū by those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. Thus says Kātyāyana as well.
One should observe the waning new moon on the first day;
one should observe the waxing new moon on the second day.
As for the statement of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "When the new moon occurs at the time of dawn, that moment should be known as supreme; what is given to the ancestors then becomes inexhaustible."
[450] This refers to the subject of the libations for one's ancestors and so forth. As for the scriptural statement:
"Even if it should be the new moon day (amāvāsyā) for only a single moment on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad)..."
"At that time, it should be known as the best; however, the remainder of the lunar day is treated like the full lunar day.
This refers to the *tulāpuruṣa* (weighing against gold) and similar rites.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
The lunar day (tithi) of the new moon, or the first day (pratipad), is said to remove all sins;
it is equal to the eclipses of the moon and sun for the performance of bathing, giving, recitation, and other rites.
In other places, however, the reading of the concluding statement is: "that gift is supreme.
Furthermore, it has been stated by Pracetas:
"If even a single *ghaṭikā* of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) should coincide with the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*)."
"Then the prescribed rite for the gods and the ancestors is considered futile.
This [statement] also refers to matters such as fasting, which primarily concern the deities and the ancestors.
Now, one might ask: why does it not refer exclusively to matters concerning the rites for the ancestors?
It is said: when [the new moon] extends into the afternoon (aparāhṇa) on the very same previous day, then it has been determined that it is indeed the former;
at that time, Sinīvālī is always for rites concerning the ancestors (pitrya), and Kuhū for those concerning the gods (daiva).

And because of this *Jābāli-smṛti*, the restriction (*parisaṅkhyāna*) that "in rites for the ancestors, [an Amāvāsyā] joined with Bhūta (the fourteenth day) is praised; therein, even one joined with Bhūta is to be honored during the [months of] Tulā and so forth" is appropriate. Nor does this refer to the absence of the overlapping of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) across two days, for the reason already stated applies. Furthermore, if the afternoon overlaps on both the preceding and following days, the rule "even an Amāvāsyā joined with Bhūta is to be honored" would not be tenable; for in that case, when there is equality or increase of the lunar day (*tithi*), the later one is to be taken, and when there is decrease of the lunar day, the earlier one alone is taken—thus, the restriction regarding Tulā and so forth would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, this refers to rites for the gods (*devakārya*).

Likewise, it is shown in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The sixth, the eleventh, the new moon day, the eighth joined with the previous [day], and the seventh joined with the following [day]—these five lunar days (tithis) are not to be observed as fasts. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, Pracetas said:
"The sixth [tithi] pierced by the seventh, the eighth likewise pierced by the seventh;
the eleventh pierced by the tenth, and the fourteenth on the thirteenth."
"The new moon day (amāvāsyā) pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta) is not to be accepted by the best of sages.

Thus, because it is taught that the new moon day pierced by the fourteenth day is unworthy for divine rites such as fasting, the new moon day pierced by the fourteenth day is indeed worthy of worship when conjoined with the zodiac sign of Libra (tulā) and so forth.
Hārīta records this in traditional law (smṛti).

In rites for the gods, [the day] mixed with the *pratipad* should indeed be honored; likewise, in the conjunctions of Tula and Makara, even if pierced by the *bhūta* (the fourteenth lunar day), it is to be honored.

Now, one might ask: even if this concerns rites for the gods, why not simply accept that its application occurs through exclusion (*bādha*) [of other times], rather than assuming it pertains to the time of ancestral rites (*pitṛkāla*)?

It is said: first of all, due to the fear of contradiction and prolixity, they are assigned to one and the same ritual act; nor is there any reason for preferential selection [between them]. For Kātyāyana states:
"The sixth lunar day pierced by the seventh (Nāga), as well as the tenth and the eleventh..."
Even a new moon day (amāvāsyā) that is pierced by the [preceding] lunar day must be avoided by the wise.
Having said this, it was further stated:
"In the signs of Libra, Capricorn, Pisces, Virgo, and likewise Gemini,
even the new moon day (amāvāsyā) that is pierced by the fourteenth lunar day (bhūta) should be diligently honored."

This is not so; because of their association, this [observance] also pertains to rites for the gods (*devakārya*). And that its subject matter consists of rites for the gods, such as vows and fasting, has been demonstrated in the general discussion on lunar days (*tithi*). Thus concludes the determination of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
Now, regarding the *aṣṭakās*:

by the term *aṣṭakā*, the eighth lunar days (*aṣṭamī*) of the dark fortnights (*aparapakṣa*) of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa are intended, according to the traditional teaching of Śaunaka: "The *aṣṭakās* are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. According to the view of some, there are only three *aṣṭakās* and three *anvaṣṭakās*. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"The new moon day (amāvāsyā), the three Aṣṭakās, and the three Anvaṣṭakās.
The Anvaṣṭakās are those that occur after (anu) or following the Aṣṭakās; they are the ninth lunar days subsequent to the Aṣṭakās.
[Thus it is stated] in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
"The new moon day, the three Aṣṭakās in the months beginning with Pauṣa,
the three Anvaṣṭakās, and likewise the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha— these are meritorious. Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
"When the Āgrahāyaṇī has passed, there are likewise three dark Aṣṭakās.

Now, although there is an Aṣṭakā in the second fortnight of Bhādrapada that is distinct from the four previously mentioned Aṣṭakās, its origin and praise are recounted in the *Padma Purāṇa* preceded by an ancient legend (*itihāsa*). [It says:
"They are known as the Agniṣvāttas, established in the sacrifice of the sacrificers."
Their mental daughter is the river named Acchodā.
Then, seeing her father named Amāvasu, she approached him;
seeking a boon, she chose him as her consort because of the torment caused by the flower-armed god of love.
Having seen that yoga, the beautiful woman, due to that transgression,
first failed to touch the ground and then fell to the surface of the earth.
Then, with her face cast down, dejected and ashamed due to the depletion of her ascetic power,
she too entreated him once more for the sake of her own prosperity.

While she was lamenting, her ancestors spoke thus to that poor woman; those illustrious ones spoke these words with voices auspicious with favor: [453] "Lamenting, that poor woman was addressed by her ancestors; those highly fortunate ones spoke as follows with words auspicious through their grace."
In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will be born from a mortal womb as an auspicious woman known by the name Satyavatī, the mother of Vyāsa.
"Due to your transgression against the ancestors, you shall obtain a miserable lineage;
therefore, you will inevitably become the daughter of King Vasu."
Furthermore, on the eighth day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, you shall exist in the world of the ancestors;
you will eternally bestow long life and health, and grant the fruits of all desires.

From the Brahmavaivarta and Vāyu Purāṇas: Now I shall explain Time, which is honored in the rite of Śrāddha by those who prescribe the rules for the Śrāddha dharma— whether it be performed for specific desires (kāmya), on particular occasions (naimittika), or as a constant obligation (ajasra).
The three Aṣṭakā rites, which bestow sons and have wealth as their root, are performed in the dark fortnight;
the first is declared to be under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā (the Aindrī),
the second under Rohiṇī (the Prājāpatyā), and the third under Uttarā Phalgunī (the Vaiśvadevikī).
The first [observance] should always be performed with cakes; another should always be with meat;
the third should be with vegetables—such is the rule regarding the substances.
The Anvaṣṭakā rite for the ancestors is indeed prescribed as a constant obligation;
furthermore, one should especially perform whichever other fourth lunar day may occur.
The wise should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) on those [lunar days] even at the cost of their entire wealth;
thus, one shall always be happy in both this world and the next.
For those who worship, there is constant prosperity; for the nihilists, there is a downward course. The ancestors [are pleased] at all times, and the deities on the days of the lunar phases.
All go toward such a man, like cows toward a watering hole—
those ancestors who would otherwise depart from him because they have not been honored with the Aṣṭakā offerings.
His world becomes futile, and what he has acquired perishes;
those who give to the gods go [to heaven], while those who do not give fall into the animal realm.

Here, the fourth [Aṣṭakā] is the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, according to the traditional teaching of Śaunaka: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. However, if one adopts the view that there are three Aṣṭakās beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, then the fourth is the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, in accordance with the historical account shown in the Padma Purāṇa. Furthermore, in the Brahmapurāṇa, when defining the deities and the substances for the libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) for the four Aṣṭakās in sequence, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is specifically mentioned.
On the first day, dedicated to Indra, one should satisfy the ancestors with vegetables;
on the second day, dedicated to Prajāpati, one should satisfy them with pure meats.
"On the third lunar day dedicated to Viśvedevas, one should offer cakes according to the sequence;
during the rainy season, on the fourth day, one should always offer vegetables in the middle."

In this context, the words *śāka* (vegetables), *māṃsa* (meat), and *apūpa* (cakes) are intended to indicate that all food fit for a *śrāddha* should have those respective substances as its primary component; they do not, however, intend to exclude other substances. For it is the established principle that a single injunction is understood as applying without subverting another single injunction, let alone without subverting many more. Indeed, it is observed that food in which vegetables are the primary ingredient provides satisfaction, whereas vegetables alone do not. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Agrahāyaṇa, as well as on the Anvaṣṭakā days. Indeed, the Śrāddha is also mandatory on the Aṣṭakā and Anvaṣṭakā days.
As Pitāmaha has said:
"On the new moon day, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the full moon day, and the Aṣṭakā days..."

"A learned man who does not perform the *śrāddha* falls into hell. Furthermore, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, it is stated that for one who does not perform the *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*, there is the attainment of an undesirable state in the form of rebirth as an animal, as expressed by the words: "Those who do not give go to the state of animals. And Viṣṇu, having enumerated: "The new moon days, the three *aṣṭakās*, the three *anvaṣṭakās*, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following [the latter], or the times of the ripening of rice and barley," said:
"Prajāpati has declared these indeed to be the obligatory times for *śrāddha*."
It is also stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of kings, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is always a time for the *śrāddha*;
likewise, O supreme monarch, the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the month of Māgha, and the month of Śrāvaṇa."
When the Pauṣṭhapadī has passed, as well as the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight;
when Āgrahāyaṇī has passed, likewise the three dark Aṣṭakās.
The first [offering] should be made with vegetables, and immediately after that with meat;
likewise, the third should always be made with cakes by one who possesses discernment.
"Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for the *śrāddha*;
one who does not perform the *śrāddha* on these occasions falls into hell. Thus it is stated in the *Devalasmṛti*.
"This ritual for the *śrāddha* has been proclaimed by Manu as the 'Mānava-śrāddhakalpa.
[456] 'The *aṣṭakā* may have many rice-balls (*bahupiṇḍā*), but the *aṣṭakā* itself does not consist of a single rice-ball (*ekapiṇḍā*).
In this context, the terms 'many rice-balls' and 'single rice-ball' refer respectively to the prohibition of the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure and the prescription of the *pārvaṇa* procedure."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The Śrāddha must indeed be performed during the winter Aṣṭakās;
it is prescribed that at the Anvaṣṭakās, it should be done in successive order, beginning with the Mothers."

On this point, there is a Smṛti text: "At the Anvaṣṭakās, at the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, and likewise annually—at these occasions the Śrāddha for the mother is performed separately; on other occasions, it is together with her husband."
The *Śaṅkhasmṛti* states: "Except for the Anvaṣṭakā rites, the Śrāddha for a mother, and the Ekoddiṣṭa performed on the anniversary of death, there shall be no separate rite for women."
In this *Viṣṇudharmottara*, a separate rule is stated for the *mātṛ-śrāddha*:
"And likewise, the *śrāddha* for women should be performed on the *anvaṣṭakā* days;
having offered oblations according to the *aṣṭakā* ritual, [one should perform] these five in sequence."
O King, the śrāddha for one's mother and grandmother should be performed according to the rules;
likewise, it should be performed for the great-grandmother, preceded by the Vaiśvadeva offering.
O King, the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be performed for him just as for his own father;
now learn from me the ritual procedure to be followed there once the Brahmins have eaten.
O King of kings, they should be one span in length and four finger-breadths in width;
one should have six furrows made there, each with a height equal to that [width].
At the base of each trench, having strewn grass around the fire and performed sacrifices to Agni, Soma, and Yama as previously prescribed;
One should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍanirvapaṇa) to men at the roots of the third kārṣū, first offering one to each according to the prescribed rule.
One should fill those three furrows with milk-rice;
and at the base of the three furrows, the offering for women should take place.
One should fill the trenches with curd, meat, milk, and water;
O best of men, this should be done here mixed with water. One should then offer it, saying: "May this be inexhaustible for you."
Thus concludes the determination of the *aṣṭakās*. Now follows the determination of the time for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
*Vṛddhi* refers to a time characterized by such occasions as the birth of a son.
And so says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
"The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed for the birth of a son, a marriage, and other such occasions. Jābāli says:
One should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha on occasions such as sacrifices, weddings, consecrations, the tying and untying of the girdle, the birth of a son, and the ritual release of a bull.

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The father should perform for his son, once born, the entire cycle of rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), as well as the *śrāddha* characterized by prosperity (*abhyudayika*)."

Kātyāyana also said: "In the rites of consecrating a son, the father should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to his own ancestors until the son's marriage; but in his absence, [the son should do so] according to the order of succession."
In this context, the *saṃskāras* (sacraments) are:

conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), birth rites (*jātakarman*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), tonsure (*cūḍā*), initiation (*upanayana*), the observance of vows (*vratacaryā*), study (*adhyayana*), the return home (*samāvartana*), marriage (*vivāha*), and the gift of a cow (*godāna*).

Among these, in the sacraments pertaining to a son ending with marriage, the father should offer [the *śrāddha*] to his own ancestors; in the remaining sacraments, the person undergoing the rite himself [should do so]. This has been explained in detail in the section on the *Śrāddhakalpa* while defining the qualified performer.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"At the weddings of daughters and sons, at the entry into a new house,
at the naming ceremony of children, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony and others;"
At the parting of the hair ceremony, as well as upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha class of ancestors.
"At the first sight of the son's face" means at the birth of a son; as stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Now, in rites for prosperity (*abhyudayika*), in auspicious ceremonies, and in those that are most splendid..."
At birth, at the initiation ceremony, at marriage, and for a son,
one should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed rule.
Vasiṣṭha says: On the previous day one should perform the Śrāddha for the maternal ancestors; likewise on the day of the rite, that for the paternal ancestors;
and on the following day, one should perform it for the group of maternal grandfathers.
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states an alternative procedure:
"If one is unable [to perform them] on separate days, one should perform the three Śrāddhas and the Tantric Vaiśvadeva on a single preceding day."
He states the performance of rites being carried out even on a single day according to their different times:
"The *śrāddha* for the mothers is in the forenoon, likewise that for the fathers at midday;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—these three *śrāddhas* are prescribed for the *vṛddhi* (prosperity) ceremony."
But in the event that even such a distinction of time is impossible, Bṛhan-Manu says:
"In the absence of different times for the three Nāndī-śrāddhas,
the wise man should perform them on the preceding day in the forenoon, beginning with the rite for the Mothers."

In the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*: "On the day before [the main rite], one should feed an even number of Brahmins during the performance of the Vedic ritual. Thus it is said: "They are called *nāndīmukha* [joyful-faced]. They do not perform the ancestral (*pitrya*) and divine (*daiva*) rites on the same day; for those who perform the ancestral and divine rites on the same day, their offspring become subject to premature death. Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors on the previous day. In that he performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the previous day, having redeemed the sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer extends it further. So says the *Brāhmaṇa*.

In this context, within the statement of Yājñavalkya—which serves as a general enumeration of all the times for *śrāddha* that will be described hereafter—the term "increase" (*vṛddhi*) is intended to indicate the entire range of times for *nāndīmukha-śrāddhas*; thus, the times for *śrāddhas* that are ancillary to ritual acts (*karmāṅga-śrāddha*) are also included.
Pāraskara states these [times]:
"At the time of conception (*niṣeka*), at the *soma* sacrifice, and likewise at the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*)."
The Śrāddha performed at the Puṃsavana rite is to be understood as a subsidiary part of the ritual, conducted like a Vṛddhi-śrāddha.

The period of impregnation (*niṣekakāla*) consists of sixteen nights, which is the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) of the wife. On a day therein conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion (*puṇyanakṣatra*), the *śrāddha* that is an ancillary part (*karmāṅga*) of the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) should be performed. The mention of a lunar eclipse (*somagrahaṇa*) is intended as an illustration for rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the *agnihotra*. Thus concludes the determination of the time for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. [460]
Now follows the determination of the *śrāddha* for the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Regarding this, Kātyāyana, in the same [work] belonging to the Vājasaneyins, states: "One should perform the *śrāddha* in the latter half of the month, or after the fourth day, on whichever day the necessary materials may be available. This means that in the dark fortnight—from the first day (*pratipad*) until the new moon—at any day after the fourth, on whatever day the requisite means for the *śrāddha* are obtained, on that very day one should perform the *śrāddha*.
Gautama also states:

"One should offer to the ancestors on the new moon day, or from the fifth day onwards of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), according to the *śrāddha* rite; or, when materials, location, and Brahmins are available, there is a restriction of time according to one's capacity. One view is that the *śrāddha* takes place on a single day during the dark fortnight; another is that it occurs every day. "A restriction of time according to capacity" means the determination of the timing based on one's ability. And in this context, the *śrāddha* is obligatory (*nitya*).
And so says Kātyāyana:
"One should not let the dark fortnight pass by even with mere vegetables.

As for the statements in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and other texts—such as "The first day [of the lunar fortnight] is for the gain of wealth, the second bestows bipeds," and so forth—which describe a connection with specific fruits for every single lunar day (tithi) within the dark fortnight, these do not diminish the obligatory nature (*nityatā*) of the *śrāddha* performed during that fortnight. This is because both its obligatory and optional aspects are logically consistent, much like the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Furthermore, when this [fortnightly *śrāddha*] is performed on a single day, it must be performed separately from the *amāvāsyā* (New Moon) *śrāddha*.

In this statement by Yājñavalkya— “The new moon day (amāvāsyā), the Aṣṭakās, the occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi), the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), and the two solstices (ayanadvaya)” — the new moon day is mentioned separately from the dark fortnight.

Therefore, that which has been stated by some—namely, "the *śrāddha* of the latter fortnight (*āparapakṣika*) is optional with the *śrāddha* of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)"—is refuted. Regarding the traditional text (*nigama-smaraṇa*) which says, "On whichever day it may fall in the latter fortnight, especially on the new moon," the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that since this applies even when the two are performed separately, it does not serve as authority for an option. However, some indeed hold that there is an option.
Āpastamba says: "It should be performed month after month; the afternoon of the latter fortnight is better, as is the latter part of the latter fortnight."

"The latter days. Here, "latter" refers to the tenth day and those following; this is not intended to state that any one of these is superior to the preceding ones, such as the ninth day and so forth, but rather to demonstrate that the subsequent ones are more excellent than the preceding. With this in mind, Manu stated, excluding the fourteenth day:
"In the dark fortnight, starting from the tenth day, excluding the fourteenth..."
"The lunar days (tithis) that are praised for the śrāddha ceremony are not like those others. Thus it is said.
In this regard, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) is not to be avoided at all times; rather, it is to be avoided only in the case of a *śrāddha* for the three deities other than those struck by weapons.
Yājñavalkya says:
"Indeed, starting from the first day (pratipad), one should avoid only the fourteenth day."
"But that which is offered there is for those who have indeed been slain by a weapon.
It will be stated that the mention of "weapon" (śastra) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for certain other causes of death as well.
Now follows the latter fortnight of Bhādrapada.

Although this latter fortnight of Bhādrapada is indeed included among the twelve latter fortnights by general statements such as, "One should perform the *śrāddha* during the latter fortnight; one should not let the latter fortnight pass even if it be only with vegetables," nevertheless, it is specifically mentioned in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts for the purpose of demonstrating its supreme merit and for the purpose of demonstrating the exceptional gravity of the transgression incurred by failing to perform it.
As it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
O King, according to the northern course [of the sun], the southern course would be superior;
for during those four months of the southern course, Keśava is indeed asleep there.
"The latter fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada is [auspicious],
and especially so from the fifth day onwards; even more so from the tenth day onwards, and even more than that, O King, is the thirteenth day when it coincides with the Maghā nakṣatra."

The southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is superior for the performance of *śrāddha* rites compared to the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*). Even within that southern solstice, the four months beginning from the full moon of Āṣāḍha—starting from the period of Upendra’s sleep—are superior. Superior even to all of those is the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) of the month of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada). Within that, too, the ten days following the fifth day are superior; within those, the five days following the tenth; and within those, the thirteenth day conjoined with the *Maghā* asterism. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja (Āśvina), the *śrāddha* should be performed day after day."
Or for a fortnight less a third part, or even for half a month,
one should especially offer śyāmāka grains, which are well-known and dear to the ancestors.
In this regard, it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa [463]:
"The Śrāddha ceremony is to be performed during the dark fortnight associated with the month of Prauṣṭhapada."

In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, however, it is stated that [the month] "is connected with Aśvayuj. This discrepancy between the two is resolved as follows: here, indeed, the Southerners (Dākṣiṇātyas) calculate the lunar month by beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, taking the full moon that gives its name to the month as the central constituent, and ending at the new moon. The Northerners (Auttaras), on the other hand, begin on the first day of the dark fortnight and end with the full moon that initiates the month's name. This being the case, according to Southern usage, when the full moon associated with Prauṣṭhapada occurs at the conclusion of the first fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, the subsequent fortnight falls within the middle of the month of Aśvayuj. Thus, this single fortnight receives two designations through two different systems of usage.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "During the rainy season, Yama releases the deceased ancestors from his abode back into the world of men, leaving his own city empty."
Afflicted by hunger and confessing their own misdeeds,
they long for milk-rice mixed with honey from their sons and grandsons.
Therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice mixed with honey,
clarified butter, and sesame seeds, as well as with cool water.
He who receives from him only as much as a mouthful,
or he who himself sustains his life by means of mere alms;

"As long as he maintains his body, he should perform the *śrāddha* every day by selling himself, using whatever wealth he has well-accumulated. This is the word of Brahmā addressed to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) here in Nāgarakhaṇḍa.
In the fifth fortnight of Āṣāḍha, when the sun is situated in Virgo,
whatever man performs a śrāddha on even a single day,
his ancestors will certainly remain satisfied for the duration of a year.
Śāṭyāyani said:
"That period consisting of the sixteen lunar days in the latter fortnight of Nabhasya, if it occurs while the sun is in Virgo, is the time for the performance of the Śrāddha rite."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* and the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, it is stated:
"When the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo, the ancestors— whether divine, terrestrial, or celestial, and whether stationary or moving— all desire the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*)."
The Lord Nārāyaṇa has declared that the sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo are equal to the [sixteen] seasons.
He who desires the fruit that is difficult to attain through the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices—
let him instead worship the ancestors with vegetables, roots, and grains when the sun is in Virgo.

Even though the sun’s entry into Virgo occurs within a single month, nevertheless, because the latter fortnight alone belongs to the ancestors (*paitra*) and in accordance with other scriptural statements, one should understand that the *śrāddha* rite is to be performed specifically during that period.
Also in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Those sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo..."
"Those [offerings] given to the ancestors are equal to the seasons; what is given becomes inexhaustible. Thus it is said.

In this regard, although the texts state that the fortnight (*pakṣa*) itself constitutes the time for the *śrāddha*, and while this fortnight consists of fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), it may occasionally consist of sixteen days due to the increase of a lunar day (*tithivṛddhi*). With the intention that there should be no loss of even a single day in that case, it is said here that "the sixteen lunar days" are to be taken; this is either to include the first day (*pratipad*) following the new moon (*āmāvāsya*), or the preceding full moon (*pūrṇamāsī*), for it is the latter upon which the *śrāddha* for the *nāndīmukhas* will be described. It should be understood that if the sun enters Virgo (*kanyā-saṃkramaṇa*) on any day whatsoever within this fortnight, the sixteen days beginning with the *pratipad* are to be adopted; however, it does not mean that the days prior to the entry are to be rejected.
For this very reason, Bṛhanmanu said:
"Whether in the middle or even at the end, whichever fortnight the sun enters [the sign], that entire fortnight is complete; the Śrāddha is prescribed to be performed therein."

In this context, the mention of the moon being in Virgo is for the purpose of demonstrating its superior merit, and not to suggest that one should abandon this [rite] even when the moon is no longer in Virgo. As stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"Even on another lunar fortnight, the Śrāddha is prescribed when the sun is situated in Virgo."
"One should perform it especially when the fifth [lunar day] falls while the sun is in Virgo.
This very same point is also stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Taking Āṣāḍhī as the starting limit, that which is the fifth fortnight..."
"In that regard, one should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha), whether the daughter is married or not. Thus says Kārṣṇājini:
"Sons, long life, health, and incomparable sovereignty [are obtained]."
By offering a śrāddha on the fifth day, one obtains abundant fulfillment of all desires.

Thus, it has been stated that when the Śrāddha is performed during the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, one attains distinguished and desired benefits. However, regarding the undesirable consequences of failing to perform it during that time, Kārṣṇājini says:
"The deceased ancestors indeed harm him who neglects the fifth [fortnight];
therefore, a wise man should not bypass the ancestral rite on the fifth."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "He who does not perform the *śrāddha* rite during the fifth fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha—
even if he is poor and offers only vegetables— shall fall into the state of an outcaste."
Those men who share with him his seat, his bed, his food, his touch, and likewise his conversation, are the most sinful of men.
"They will undoubtedly be devoid of progeny; neither happiness nor wealth nor grain shall ever accrue to them. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
If a householder does not perform the Śrāddha when the sun has entered Virgo, how can he have wealth or sons? He is tormented by the sighs of his ancestors.
If a man, thinking in his mind that ancestors do not exist,
does not perform a śrāddha ceremony there, they drink his blood.

Now, if by some circumstance the prescribed period for a *śrāddha* has been exceeded without one being performed, it is stated that the *śrāddha* occasioned by that lapse must be performed on the subsequent days, within specific time limits. As stated in the *Yamasmṛti*:
"When the Sun is in Leo, or during the rainy season when it is in Virgo, even one living at home with only vegetables [should perform the rite]."
One should give [the gift] between the two fifth [lunar days], on both fortnights.

The term ‘haṃsaḥ’ refers to the sun. The phrase ‘in the interval between the two fifth days of the fortnights’ means the intermediate period following the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada and preceding the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina; by this, the performance of *śrāddha* is permitted until the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
“As long as the sun does not abide successively in the signs of Virgo and Libra...”
At that time, it would be the proper hour for a funeral offering; otherwise, the city of the departed spirits remains empty.
Likewise:
When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons;
the city of the departed remains entirely empty until the appearance of Scorpio.
Then, upon encountering the scorpion, the ancestors departed in despair;
having uttered a most terrible curse, they returned once more to their own abode.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "If a man does not offer the *śrāddha* to his ancestors on the occasion of the moon's waning,
his ancestors, their bodies overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, become defiled."
Filled with the desire for their teacher, they await the fortnight of the ancestors,
just as farmers, unwearied by day or night, await the rain-cloud.
Even when the fortnight of the ancestors has passed, as long as the sun remains in Virgo,
the ancestors desire that the śrāddha be offered by their own sons.
Then, O King, even when the sun has entered Libra, some—
tormented by hunger and thirst— desire that a śrāddha be offered by those born of their own lineage.
When that period has also passed and the sun has entered Scorpio,
the ancestors, deprived of hope and destitute, then depart for their own abode.

O Lord of the Earth, for two months— while the sun is in Virgo and Libra— the ancestors of men wait at the doors of their homes, having become like the wind, afflicted by thirst and emaciated by hunger.
Sumantu said: O Great King, as long as the sun remains in the zodiac sign of Virgo,
gifts should be given during that time until it has entered Scorpio.
O King, on this fifteenth day of the month known on earth as Dīpānvitā,
whatever is given in the Mahālaya ceremony for the ancestors is indeed truly offered.
In this context, the *mahālaya* refers to the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) of the month of Bhādrapada.
As for that which was stated by Jātūkarṇa:
"The ancestors, having resorted to the fifth fortnight, long [for offerings]."

"Therefore, it should be given only there; given elsewhere, it is fruitless. This [statement] refers to the loss of the excellence of the result, not to the total abolition of the result altogether. Furthermore, it has been established in the *Malamāsa-nirṇaya* that this *śrāddha* of the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) must not be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Here, the following is considered: Is this the performance of a single recurring *śrāddha* of the latter fortnight, or are these the performances of distinct *śrāddhas*? Both of these two positions have been stated.
On this point, some first say: "This is the procedure for a single *śrāddha* alone, as Śāṭyāyani stated:
'The sixteen lunar days that occur in the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya—if they should coincide with the sun being in Virgo—that is the time for the rite of *śrāddha*.'"

In this context, according to the maxim that "when numbers are associated, there is a conjunction," it is understood that the lunar days (*tithi*) are to be combined in the *śrāddha*. Since this would not be possible if the *śrāddha* were not repeated, it follows that the *śrāddha* itself must be repeated. Just as repetition is accepted in the Soma sacrifice for the sake of completing the prescribed auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), so it is here as well. Furthermore, from the statement of Kātyāyana in the Vājasaneyi-sūtra—"For one performing the *śrāddha* in the dark fortnight, it may be performed on the fourth, or on whichever day [of the fortnight] falls"—it is understood that the fortnight (*pakṣa*) is an auxiliary element; and since a fortnight consists of fifteen lunar days, there is thus indeed a conjunction.
Likewise Gautama says:

"One should offer to the ancestors on the new moon day, or from the fifth day onwards of the dark fortnight, according to the *śrāddha* rite; or, when materials, place, and Brahmins are available, there is no restriction of time, depending on one's capacity. [469] Here, an option (*vikalpa*) between the days starting from the fifth of the dark fortnight and the new moon day is understood. Therefore, just as with the new moon day, the entire dark fortnight is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to a single *śrāddha*. Consequently, for the sake of accomplishing that, repetition (*āvṛtti*) alone is appropriate.
During the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, however, the Śrāddha should be performed day by day;
or else, it may be performed for three-quarters of the fortnight, or for one-third, or even for half.

Since the accusative case is heard in the statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa* cited above, it is understood that because of the comprehension of absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*), only a single *śrāddha* is to be repeated.

But if this were so, then even in the case of the text, “The cake on eight potsherds for Agni is constant on the new moon and full moon days,” there would likewise be a conjunction of times within a single sacrifice; consequently, the well-known division into six parts established by those learned in the *tantra* systems would be contradicted.

It is said: even in that case, there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*) because of the hearing of the word "and" (*ca*), and not two separate *Āgneya* offerings; however, the well-known status of the sixfold division is intended to refer to repetition (*āvṛtti*). But this has not been stated by some among the authors of commentaries (*vṛtti*) or sub-commentaries (*vārttika*) on the *Nibandhas*; therefore, this is a single performance (*prayoga*). Others, however, say: these are performances for distinct *Śrāddha* rites due to the difference in the *Śrāddhas*. "Whether at the end or in the middle, wherever the Sun enters Virgo..."
"That fifth fortnight is to be honored with respect to the sixteen śrāddhas. Thus it is said.

And here, a distinction between ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is understood through the number. This is not based on repetition (*abhyāsa*), as in the case of "he performs eleven *prayāja* offerings," where such an interpretation was adopted because another number was heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*). However, this cannot be based on repetition here either, since unity is understood from the cited sentences. This would indeed be so if those were originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) and this were an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for a rite already established; but that is not the case, because it is understood to be an originative injunction due to the hearing of multiple accessories. For this very reason, by statements such as "the second day leads to the acquisition of wealth" and "the second day with two feet [leads to] progeny," the connection with the fruit is stated for each individual lunar day throughout the entire dark fortnight. Therefore, these are the performances of distinct *śrāddha* rites.

We, however, say: since both types of statements cited have been shown to be non-contradictory (*anyathāsiddha*), both positions are logical. Therefore, according to the position that there is a single performance (*prayogaikya*), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given on the very day of completion, because the fee is an integral part of the performance; but if there is a division of performances (*prayogabheda*), it should be given every day.
Now follows the determination regarding the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*). In the *Manusmṛti*:
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism,
according to the *Yamasmṛti*.
And those who know the past recite the verses sung by the ancestors:
"May there be born in our lineage one who would offer [oblations] to us on the thirteenth day."
One should offer milk-rice with honey and clarified butter during the shadow of an elephant falling toward the east,
or with goat's meat and all types of metal during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
Then, having said, "There is a verse concerning the ancestors," Viṣṇu spoke:
"May there arise in our lineage some supreme among men who, being composed, [performs this] on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight during the rainy season."
He who performs a śrāddha with honey and milk-rice throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or on the day when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east, attains great merit.

Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi also says: "Whether it be a son or a grandson, he who would give [a cow] to us on the thirteenth lunar day during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism, [should give] one with all its limbs intact and made of copper."
Is he born as someone righteous who will increase his lineage?
In the Mahābhārata:
"May there be born in our lineage one who might give us, on the thirteenth lunar day under the Maghā asterism, milk-rice mixed with ghee while facing the south."
Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Yama have said:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
praise the son who has been born, just as birds praise the fig tree."
"With honey, meat, rhinoceros flesh, milk, or milk-rice,
he will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the asterism Maghā."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Whatever one gives while staying at Gayā, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism."
When the month of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, having reached the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism,
one should perform a śrāddha ceremony with honey or milk-rice (pāyasa).
And this lunar day is more highly praised than other lunar days in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Thus it is said in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Or he who would nourish his body every day by selling himself..."
He too should perform the śrāddha with various well-accumulated materials,
especially on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā asterism.
There is no time superior to this for ancestral rites (śrāddha) to be found elsewhere;
for here the ancestors themselves are present in person at the home, [receiving] immortal and inexhaustible [offerings].
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"O King, the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is superior to the northern course;
even during that, the Cāturmāsya period is more excellent when Keśava is asleep."
