"In the dark fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada, and especially therein; even better than that is the fifth lunar day, and better still the tenth, and even more so [the fifteenth]; moreover, O King, the thirteenth day conjoined with the asterism Maghā is highly recommended. Thus it is said.

In this context, "five-fold" means beginning from the fifth [lunar day], and "ten-fold" means beginning from the tenth; and that *śrāddha* is obligatory (*āvaśyaka*). For it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of kings, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is always the time for the *śrāddha*."
Likewise, O best of kings, the full moon days of Māgha and Śrāvaṇa.
When the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, as well as the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight,
and likewise the three Aṣṭakās and Anvaṣṭakās, O best of kings—
Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for the Śrāddha.
"One who does not perform the *śrāddha* on these [occasions] falls into hell. Thus says Viṣṇu.

Having enumerated "the new moon day, the three *aṣṭakās*, the three *anvaṣṭakās*, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following [that]," he stated this very same verse beginning with "these, however, are the times for *śrāddha*."
Now, here are the prohibitive statements regarding this matter. Jyotir-Bṛhaspati says: "The man who performs a Śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight..."
One should know for certain that death has come to his eldest son.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"A householder, even if he has sons, should not perform a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day,
nor should he observe a fast on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."
In the Vāmana Purāṇa: "A householder who has sons should not perform a Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day;
nor is fasting desired here, according to some, during either of the two solstices."
"Āpasamba: On the thirteenth day, one has many sons and many friends, and one's offspring are handsome, but they die young. Thus says Kātyāyana."
"Young men die there," so it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*:
"The man who desires liberation for himself along with his ancestors..."
For one who is childless, the thirteenth lunar day is prescribed for the Śrāddha;
if one who possesses a lineage should perform it on that day, the destruction of his lineage will occur.
Ānarta said:
"O great sage, why does the destruction of one's lineage occur when a śrāddha is performed on the thirteenth lunar day? Explain all of this to me in detail."
Bhartṛyajña said:
O best of kings, in a former age, during the Rathantara Kalpa,
there was a man named Sitāśva from the Pāñcāla country who was devoted to his father.
Indeed, he performs the śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day with honey, black pot-herbs, and exclusively with the meat of the rhinoceros, as well as with milk-rice.
[474] Once, being questioned again by the Brahmins who were filled with curiosity— "O King, while various kinds of food are present, from where [do these come]?"— he replied:
"Therefore, rhinoceros meat provides us with black potherbs;
they say that when offered by the twice-born at a śrāddha, it is an oblation that must not be refused."
"Thus it is being enjoyed by us; tell us the reason for giving that.
Having heard these words of those brahmins, the king said:
I shall speak even that which is unspeakable; listen with full concentration.
In former times, I was a cruel hunter, yet devoted to my father.
While wandering, I once reached the hermitage of Agniveśa at night;
I heard that brahmin, who was instructing his disciples, from a distance.
Agniveśa said:
When the moon is in the constellation of Maghā and the sun is situated in Hasta on the thirteenth lunar day, that shadow is to be known as the one called Kuñjarā.
She is also highly recommended for the śrāddha ceremony, as she brings satisfaction to the ancestors;
therefore, let the auspicious materials for the morning śrāddha be prepared now.
‘Paitryam ṛkṣam’ refers to Maghā; ‘haṃsaḥ’ refers to the Sun; ‘karaḥ’ refers to Hasta. The White-Horse said:
Having heard these words of that sage, I reflected as follows.
"And tomorrow morning, I shall perform the śrāddha rite."
Then, wandering in the forest at dawn for the sake of materials for the śrāddha,
I obtained rhinoceros meat, kālaśāka greens, and honey.
On the thirteenth day, with a concentrated mind, I fed those of my own caste, dedicating the meal to my own ancestors with whatever materials were available.
By such a śrāddha, the ancestors attained satisfaction for twelve years,
and I too became a king who remembered his former births.
Therefore, on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha, recollecting their power, I perform this śrāddha with faith by means of these very same offerings.
Having heard those words of his, other people on earth as well,
overcome by hunger, cursed those who perform the śrāddha on the thirteenth day.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, the gods Vasu, Rudra, and others, though prone to jealousy, became filled with joy for the performer of the śrāddha;
and vying with the foremost of the gods, they attained supreme perfection.
From this day forward, whoever shall perform a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day while the sun is in Virgo,
there shall be no exhaustion of that śrāddha.
Thus, by the curse of the gods, this great tithi was consumed;
from that time forward, no supreme śrāddha is performed on this day.
If one performs it out of negligence, that *śrāddha* is destroyed;
this *trayodaśī-śrāddha* is the cause of the extinction of one's lineage.
Therefore, O Lord, on that day, even without performing a śrāddha rite, one should offer honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa),
the meat of a rhinoceros (khaḍgamāṃsa), black potherbs (kālaśāka), and the meat of a porcupine (vārdhrīṇasa).
A *vārdhrīṇasa* is a large goat;
even in its absence, O King, the most excellent rice cooked with milk should be given to the Brahmins on that day for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Even in his absence, water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered. Thus it is said.

[476] On this point, some say: the statements prohibiting the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) lack authority altogether, because they contradict the words of Manu beginning with "whatever is mixed with honey. For the *Manusmṛti*, being as well-known as Vedic study itself and being recited by many through tradition, is impossible to have corrupted readings; furthermore, in case of conflict, it is more powerful than even direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), unlike those [texts] which are inferior, unknown even by name, not recited by anyone, possessed of unstable readings, and suspected of having their roots in error and the like. Thus, [the *Manusmṛti*] prevails over them.
For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"The authority of Manu's Smṛti is remembered because it is bound to the meaning of the Vedas;
however, that Smṛti which is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not praised."
Manu also said: "Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge."

It is replied: First, as for the claim that the *Manusmṛti* possesses greater authority than other contradictory *smṛtis* because it is rooted in the *Śruti*, that is merely a fabrication. The statement of Bṛhaspati, however, declares the lack of authority of the *smṛtis* of Buddha and others which contradict the meaning of Manu’s work; it does not apply to the *smṛtis* of Kātyāyana and others accepted by the learned members of the three *varṇas*, because the grounds for their authority—namely, their being connected to the meaning of the Veda—are present in those cases as well. Therefore, by the word "Manu" here, Kātyāyana and others who remember the meaning of the Veda are also implied. Alternatively, since the root *man* is listed in the *dhātupāṭha* in the sense of "knowing," the sage who possesses knowledge of the Veda's meaning is called "Manu. Consequently, even in the event of a contradiction with the *Manusmṛti*, it is not possible for the *smṛtis* of Kātyāyana and others to be lacking in authority.

Others, however, say: since it is impossible to prohibit any *śrāddha* whatsoever, the prohibitive statements lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). For instance, this is certainly not a prohibition of the obligatory (*nitya*) *śrāddha*.
Thus Manu says:
"One should offer the *śrāddha* every day with food, or even with water."
Or else, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors with water, roots, and fruits.
Dakṣa also said:
"He who eats without having bathed, without having offered oblations, and without having given gifts,
becomes a debtor to the gods and others, and goes downward along with his progeny."
In the *Paṇḍitaparitoṣa*, however, the fourth quarter is read as "he goes down to hell.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Therefore, when the son is satisfied, the gods, sages, ancestors, and deities [are satisfied]."
And one should nourish all living beings every day, just as one's own body.
Likewise,
one should perform the *svadhā* offering day by day, at least with a vessel of water; in this very manner,
one fulfills the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*).

Thus, since these statements prescribe the daily performance of the *śrāddha* for one who is alive, and state that failure to perform it leads to a downward descent, the performance of it on the thirteenth day cannot be considered a prohibition [of the regular rite]. Nor can it be a prohibition of the occasional (*naimittika*) rite; specifically, not of that occasioned by the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*).
For Yājñavalkya says:
"On the anniversary of death, however, [the offering] should be given every month for a year."
"And likewise every year, [the first rite] on the eleventh day.
Kātyāyana also says:
"Then, for one year, one should give food to the deceased on the very day the deceased passed away."
Among all types of ancestral rites (śrāddhas), that performed annually is remembered as the most excellent;
one should perform it with great effort, for by failing to do so, one goes to hell.

Thus, since the rites prescribed for the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and so forth in other *smṛtis* and *purāṇas* are required on those very occasions, their performance cannot be subject to prohibition. Nor can the occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as those for prosperity (*vṛddhi*) be prohibited. For it is said:
"If one should perform a Vedic rite without first performing the sacrifice to the Mothers (*mātṛ-yāga*), the Mothers, possessed by anger, desire to destroy him."
"A *vṛddhi-śrāddha* must indeed be performed for the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other such occasions.
In that regard, they say one should invite an even number of twice-born men, beginning with the mothers, and treating them like the mother herself.
Thus, upon the birth of a son, it should be performed by men in a manner equal to the birth-rite.

Since [the performance] is enjoined as mandatory—like the *jātakarman*—on occasions such as the birth of a son by means of such statements as these, its performance cannot be subject to prohibition. Nor does this apply to the *pārvaṇa* rite specifically occasioned by the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), for it is said:
"One who has sons should not desire a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day for the sake of his children's longevity;
he should not perform it for each individual ancestor, but rather he should perform the *pārvaṇa*."

Thus, because it is prescribed as necessary even for him, the meaning is that one should not perform the *pārvaṇa* for only a single group; rather, one should perform it for two groups: the paternal group and the maternal grandfather’s group. Nor is there a prohibition against offering a *śrāddha* to a single group, since there is no possibility of such a *śrāddha* being performed for that specific occasion alone.
"Wherever the fathers are honored, there the maternal grandfathers are certainly [honored]."

Thus, because the injunction for the *śrāddha* ritual is seen to apply only to two classes [of ancestors] according to the words of Dhaumya, nor does it apply to the optional (*kāmya*) rite, since that too is prescribed specifically in connection with the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*). Therefore, because no such subject matter is possible, the prohibitive statements lack authority.

It is said: There is sometimes a prohibition even of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, as in the case of *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) and so forth. Furthermore, even for a rite specifically prescribed on the occasion of the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), a prohibition is possible by means of a specific statement that qualifies that very occasion alone; for example, "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," where there is a prohibition of taking the cup. And since the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day is obligatory, even though its performance is established in some way or another, a prohibition is possible because the *Dhaumya-smṛti* suggests that one might, through delusion, proceed to perform the *śrāddha* of a single class [of ancestors]. Therefore, since there is no lack of scope, the authority of these prohibitive statements is accepted. Consequently, a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*) must be stated here.
In this regard, first, according to Śaṅkhadhara:

the scriptural injunctions regarding the performance of the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day under the asterism of Maghā refer to a *śrāddha* performed for two groups [of ancestors], whereas the prohibition refers to one performed for a single group.
For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini states:

"One should not commence a *śrāddha* for a single group on the thirteenth lunar day; those three [ancestors] of one who does so remain unsatisfied and will indeed harm his progeny. The meaning is that one should not commence it for a "single group"—that is, for the ancestors alone starting with the father—but rather one should perform it together with the maternal grandfathers and others; thus, when performing the *śrāddha* for six persons, there is no fault regarding the prohibition of the thirteenth day.

Others, however, say: there exist groups (*varga*) of those who have passed away and attained the state of ancestors—such as the group of paternal ancestors (*pitṛvarga*), the group of maternal ancestors (*mātṛvarga*), the group of maternal uncles (*mātulavarga*), and so forth. Alternatively, there are two groups: the group of *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the father’s side and the group of *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the mother’s side. Among these groups, when a man has obtained the entitlement for the *śrāddha* of all groups, he might perform the *śrāddha* for one particular group on another day, having considered some reason such as "I will perform the *śrāddha* for another group later," and so on. For this reason, one should not perform it on the thirteenth day of the month of *Maghā*; rather, it must be performed for all groups. This is because the thirteenth day of *Maghā* is the most excellent among the lunar days that cause the satisfaction of the ancestors, and because the *śrāddha* offered to all ancestors with substances such as honey-mixed milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is required. Since those to whom it is not given would become angry and destroy the progeny of the performer of the *śrāddha*, the scriptural restriction (*saṅkoca-śruti*) concerning the two groups is authoritative. Thus, it is established that the subject matter of the prohibitory statements is the performance of the *śrāddha* for only one group.
Others, however, say that the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* performed even by a householder who has sons is the subject [of the prohibition]. As Jyotir-Bṛhaspati says:
"If a man performs a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death."
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "A householder, even if he has sons, should not perform a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day,
nor should he observe a fast on the occasion of a saṃkrānti or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."
And they remember:
"A householder who has sons should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day;
nor is any fast desired during either of the two solstices."
Āpastamba says:
"On the thirteenth day, one obtains many sons, children who are handsome, yet they die young.
And Kātyāyana says:
"Young men die there.

Govindarāja, however, maintains that the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* is prohibited due to the defect consisting of the death of a son. For he says this: because this result is contingent (*niyogika*), it occurs only when it is desired, and not otherwise. As it has been said: "Knowledge is the result when it is desired; it will not come to one who does not desire it."

"Therefore, even when the *śrāddha* is performed, there will be no unintended result of action in the form of the death of a son; thus, the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* should be performed even by a householder who has sons. This is incorrect. For it is said: "A householder with sons should not perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*)."
In such prohibitive statements, the attainment of a specific undesirable result is intended;
one should know for certain that his eldest son shall meet his death.

By such statements as these, it is not the case that a *trayodaśī-śrāddha* in the form of a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) is enjoined for anyone upon the death [of a relative]; furthermore, no one desires the fruit of an action that is being prohibited, because its nature is harmful. Nor can a single sentence, when uttered once, convey the death of a son as something desirable to one person and as something undesirable to another; for that would entail the fallacy of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). However, the author of the *Paṇḍitaparitoṣaka* refuted Govindarāja’s view in this way: first of all, the word expressing desire (*kāma-pada*) is not heard here, as it is in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*). Nor is there any statement indicating a connection with a result, as in "one practicing malevolent magic should sacrifice" (*abhicaran yajeta*). Furthermore, neither ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) nor transformation (*vipariṇāma*) of the words is possible—as in the cases of the Viśvajit sacrifice or the Rātri-sattra—because the matter is established otherwise.

"By offering *piṇḍas* under the asterism Maghā, the eldest son perishes"—since such scriptural passages, which prohibit the *śrāddha* on festival days (*parvan*) by means of the principle of "present indicative" (*vartamānāpadeśa*), are properly explained as being merely deprecatory explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), how could there be here any attainment of a fruit? Far less, then, can there be any status as something desired for its own sake (*kāmyatā*). Thus he says: "For indeed, a declaration of fruit is not appropriate without the word 'desired' (*kāmya*)."
"By that which is taught as being present, the status of being an instrument is not understood.
Therefore:
"The man who performs a śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight..."
One should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death.

Thus, the justification for such Vedic passages as these is that they are *arthavādas* (explanatory or eulogistic statements), just like the Vedic injunction "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)," which is followed by the explanatory statement: "For one who gives silver on the sacrificial grass, there will be weeping in his house before a year has passed. Furthermore, one who speaks thus [regarding the prohibition of the *trayodaśī-śrāddha*] should not desire the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* if he has sons and desires their longevity;
he should not perform it alone, but rather should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite.

Thus, how is this to be justified? Therefore, one should not pay much heed to the commentary of Govindarāja, which is charming only when left unexamined. As for what has been said by some—that because the performance of *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the month of Maghā is of the nature of a religious duty (*dharma*), it is illogical that an undesirable result such as the death of a son should follow from its performance; and likewise, that it is also illogical to claim that the ancestors, being satisfied, bestow an undesirable result—[that too is incorrect].

That should not be said; for an object established by scripture cannot be overturned by mere reasoning, since that which is accessible solely through scripture is not within the domain of logical argumentation. As it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*, in the section on the Duties of Giving (*Dānadharma*):
"One who performs the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day shall become the most excellent among his kinsmen."
However, it is not necessarily the case that young men die in his house.

Thus, the refutation of the objection regarding the fault consisting of the death of a son—as stated by Āpastamba and others—has been performed; yet even that is not entirely settled. For by stating "not necessarily," the possibility of the fault occurring in certain cases is admitted. As for the interpretation of the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, who asserts that "they certainly do not die at all," that is incorrect, as it contradicts the cited scriptural statements. Therefore, a householder who has sons should not perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day.

That is incorrect, because it was already understood from the preceding statement that there is no fault even for a householder who has sons when performing the *śrāddha* with various kinds of materials.
However, some maintain that the subject matter [of the prohibition] refers specifically to the performance of *śrāddha* with substances other than milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like.

That is incorrect, because a fault is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* regarding the performance of a *śrāddha* even with substances such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Furthermore, from the preceding statement, it is understood that there is no fault for a householder who has sons when performing *śrāddhas* for multiple groups. However, Harihara has offered this refutation: "This is untenable, because it results in a sentence whose constituent parts are not syntactically connected (*apadārthavākyatva*). The word-meanings here are 'a son-bearing householder should not perform a *śrāddha*', whereas the sentence-meaning would be 'a *śrāddha* should not be performed with a substance other than milk-rice'."

He himself has stated such a rule: on the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the asterism Maghā, occurring within the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Śrāddha rite is both obligatory and yields great fruit. For this very purpose, the longing for a son among the ancestors is heard of at great length in the Puranic verses. In this regard, the prohibitory statements concerning the thirteenth-day Śrāddha—being of a general scriptural nature—fulfill their purpose by excluding the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada and applying themselves to the remaining eleven thirteenth days.

However, this [prohibition] is not particularly praiseworthy, because the prohibition of *śrāddha* specifically on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is clearly demonstrated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa-itihāsa*. Thus, it is established that such a prohibitory statement refers only to the *śrāddha* performed for a single class [of ancestors].
Accordingly, there is another scriptural passage:
"One who has sons should not desire a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day, for the sake of his sons' longevity."
One should not perform [the rite] for a single person alone; rather, one should perform the pārvaṇa rite.

Regarding this, some say: Is this a prohibition, like "silver should not be given on the sacrificial grass" (*barhis*), or is it a restatement of what has already been said, like "one should not say 'gira gira'? In the former case, it would be a prohibition against one who has no share; for when it is said, "one should not perform the *pārvaṇa*," how could there be any possibility of performing it for a single ancestor? It is called *pārvaṇa* because it is performed on a *parvan*, namely the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). And in that rite, there is the injunction for three ancestors. As Yājñavalkya says: "Two for the gods, three for the ancestors, or one for each of the two."
"Likewise for maternal grandfathers; or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single ritual procedure.

If it is argued that because of the scriptural injunction regarding its mandatory performance, there must be some way for even a single group to be included, we say no; for in that case, both groups must be included in every respect.
Thus says Dhaumya:
"Wherever the ancestors (pitaras) are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers (mātāmahas) must certainly be worshipped as well;
it must be performed without distinction, otherwise one goes to hell. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, for one who speaks thus, both prohibition and injunction must be accepted. First, if there were a prohibition, the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *pārvaṇa* would not be logical. Since the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* for those of many lineages is also obtained [by that prohibition], the injunction "one should perform the *pārvaṇa*" must be accepted. Nor is it logical to accept a second [rule] when the first is possible. If it is argued that, therefore, let this be merely a restatement—just as in the case of "Having performed the *aira*, one should sing; he should say 'girā gire'," and so on—[we reply: no, because a purposeless restatement is untenable. Indeed, a mandatory restatement (*nityānuvāda*) was accepted in the case of "One should choose the *hotṛ* priest by means of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*," only because no other recourse was available. But here, since another recourse exists, it cannot be so. Nevertheless, when it is said "one should perform the *pārvaṇa*," since the time of the thirteenth day is also commendable...

Because of the Smṛti text, "In the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, one should feed the Brahmins as in the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha]," it follows that the śrāddha possesses the procedural details (itikartavyatā) of the Pārvaṇa; this prohibition is for that purpose.
As for what was said—that because the time for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa is not fixed, it does not apply—[that is incorrect].

That is incorrect. For if this [offering] were to fall on the thirteenth day according to a fixed schedule, then the prohibition would apply only to that specific group, since there would be no other alternative. However, since it falls here even without such a fixed rule, the prohibition is appropriate. Therefore, this is indeed a prohibition against the *ekoddiṣṭa* and *sapindīkaraṇa* rites for a single group: "One should not commence the *śrāddha* for a single group on the thirteenth day. And:
"Those who are not satisfied there destroy the progeny of him [who performs it]."

[485] In that case, how should it be understood? Since satisfaction for others is impossible when [the rite] is performed in a combined manner (*sapiṇḍita*), this is not so, because even at that time the ancestors are beloved; at that time, all the maternal grandfathers and others desire satisfaction therein. Since the *śrāddha* cannot be performed on another day by excluding them, it is performed on the thirteenth day itself. With this intention, he says: "Those who are not satisfied there, they indeed harm the progeny of him [who performs the rite].
For this very reason, he says: "One should not perform [it] for only one [ancestor]; rather, one should perform the *pārvaṇa*."

One should not perform a *śrāddha* for a single individual alone; nor is a *śrāddha* for a single person ever prescribed anywhere except in the context of the *sapiṇḍana* rite. Therefore, this specific prohibition applies only to that [single individual], and it should be understood that the deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the death of a son also pertains only to performing [the *śrāddha*] for him, and not to the performance of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*.

As for the statement of Kātyāyana, "The young die there," its meaning is this: because the Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day has the fruit of inexhaustible satisfaction, even the young desire to die [in that state], yet they do not actually die. And so says Āpastamba:
"On the thirteenth lunar day, one obtains many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring; there is no death of children."
And it is said: "it becomes [so]," meaning "the death of one who has no son. Otherwise, the scriptural mention of having many sons and so forth would be contradicted, as it has been stated:
By performing [the rites] on odd lunar days and asterisms, one shall obtain all desires;
however, by performing the ancestral śrāddha on even days, one obtains abundant progeny.

"In even [days]" refers to the second day and so forth; "in odd [days]" refers to the thirteenth day, the first day, and so forth; "in asterisms" refers to Bharaṇī and the others. Furthermore, Yājñavalkya stated that the fruit of a Śrāddha on the thirteenth day is preeminence among kinsmen, but not the death of an eldest son.
And Vṛddha-Manu says: "On the twelfth day one becomes endowed with a beautiful form; on the thirteenth day, one has many offspring."
One obtains long-lived offspring, as well as wealth and mastery.

And likewise, having prescribed the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the month of Maghā, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "When men perform the *śrāddha*, the ancestors, being well-pleased, bestow offspring, nourishment, fame, heavenly bliss, health, and prosperity."
"And he who performs the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day shall become the most excellent among his kinsmen;
moreover, young men in his household will certainly not die [prematurely].
This [assertion] is incorrect.
For instance, as for what was stated there— that a *śrāddha* for a single group is nowhere prescribed without the *sapiṇḍana* rite—
that is incorrect, because even a *kṣayāha-śrāddha* (anniversary śrāddha) for a single group is ordained.
As the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
Yājñavalkya has prescribed the time for the ancestral rite (pitr-śrāddha) as the new moon day and so forth,
without distinction between that for one's father and that for one's maternal grandfather.
And that [simultaneity] is to be understood from the statement about to be spoken;
for a *tantra* may indeed exist through a difference in time and also through a difference in place.
Therefore, because of the injunction therein, simultaneity is perceived.
Because the time is one and the same during the new moon and other such occasions, the performance [of rites] together is appropriate;
however, on the day of death, since that [commonality of time] is absent, the performance together would not be fitting.

This is the meaning: By the statement of Yājñavalkya, "The new moon day (amāvāsyā), the eighth day (aṣṭakā), the occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi)," and so forth, the time for the *pitr-śrāddha* is generally prescribed as the new moon day and others. That [time] should be understood as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to both the *pitr-śrāddha* and the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* when they are performed simultaneously. This is because, within that very context, the rule regarding the commonality of the *vaiśvadevika* ritual—stated as "In the same way for the maternal grandfathers, or the *vaiśvadevika* is common"—is only logically applicable when there is simultaneous performance. Therefore, since the *paitṛka* and *mātāmaha* *śrāddhas* are understood to be performed at one and the same time, their commonality of ritual procedure (*samānatantratā*) is appropriate. However, on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), because the measure of lifespan differs for each individual, the *pitṛ-kṣayāha* (the father's anniversary) and the *mātāmaha-kṣayāha* (the maternal grandfather's anniversary) are distinct; thus, the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* does not share the same time as the *pitṛ-kṣayāha*. Consequently, a commonality of ritual procedure based on that [shared time] is not appropriate.

[Objection: But surely, by this very logic, because there is a difference between the *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death) of the father and that of the grandfather and others, one should not perform the *śrāddha* for the grandfather and others on the father’s *kṣayāha*.

[Reply: Not so; because of the extended injunction (*atideśa*), "one should perform the *śrāddha* as in the case of the new moon (*darśa*"), the grandfather and great-grandfather also possess the status of deities on the father’s *kṣayāha*. Nor should it be argued that, precisely because of the extended injunction "as in the case of the new moon," the maternal grandfathers must certainly be honored wherever the paternal ancestors are honored.

From this statement, it follows that the maternal grandfather and others also possess the status of deities. For Vyāsa says: "Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the offering for the three [ancestors] should be like that of the *darśa*."
Pāraskara says:
"For a legitimate son whose father has attained divinity, [the śrāddha] lasts for three generations;
in all cases, even for those of different gotras, it is performed on the single day of death for that one person alone."

For a father who has attained the state of a deity (*devatva*) through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite and has thus reached the status of a *pitṛ*, on the anniversary of his death (*kṣayāha*), an *aurasa* son must perform a *śrāddha* for three generations (*tripauruṣa*) dedicated to three deities (*tridevatya*). The meaning is that for those of different lineages (*bhinnagotra*), such as daughters' sons (*dauhitra*) and others, the *śrāddha* for childless maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) on their anniversaries of death and so forth is exclusively of the *ekoddiṣṭa* type. Consequently, although the rule "like the *darśa*" would extend the application by default (*atideśa*) to a *śrāddha* for six deities, the explicit mention again of "three generations" establishes an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) regarding the grandfather and the other ancestors on the father's anniversary of death.

Now, it might be argued that since the rule "that which pertains to three generations belongs to the legitimate son" (aurasa) is a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the three generations, and because the number "three" itself—being a qualification of the subject—is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), there can be no exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the maternal grandfather and others.

Do not say so. For on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), there is no possibility of performing a *śrāddha* for three deities. If it is argued that—on the basis of the statement, “It should be like the *darśa*, with reference to three,” a general entitlement to a *śrāddha* for three deities exists even on the anniversary of death after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony—then, in that case, by this very rule, there will be an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) regarding the maternal grandfather and others. Furthermore, if the mention of the number "three" in the phrase "for the legitimate son (*aurasa*), [the *śrāddha*] extends to three generations" were not intended to be significant, the entire sentence would be meaningless. Indeed, there is no such thing as a *śrāddha* that is both "three-generational" and "not three-generational," such that the rule could be meaningfully established as: "For the legitimate son, it is three-generational; for others, it is not three-generational. If it is argued that this is simply a prohibition of all *śrāddhas* prescribed for a single group (*ekavargīya*), we say no. This is because it was previously stated that the performance of *śrāddha* for a single group might occur due to delusion (*vyāmoha*); therefore, the application of the prohibition to that case as well would be unavoidable. If it is argued that the prohibition applies to both cases, we say no, because this would result in an inconsistency (*vaiṣamya*) in the injunctions. A prohibition of what is obtained through another injunction requires the sublation (*bādha*) of that other scripture, whereas a prohibition of what is obtained through delusion does not require such sublation. If it is argued that, to avoid this inconsistency, let the prohibition apply only to what is obtained through an injunction, we say no; for when a prohibition can be applied without sublating a scripture, such sublation is unjustified. Therefore, just as a prohibition does not apply when an object is obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*) and is touched by an injunction, the same holds true when it is obtained through delusion; thus, nothing is inconsistent. The prohibition of *śrāddha* for a single group even on the thirteenth day is established by the very words of Dhaumya: "Where the ancestors are worshipped... This is a specific prohibition intended to demonstrate a particular fault. And that specific fault is shown by the statement of Kārṣṇājini: "One should never perform a *śrāddha* for a single group."

As for the explanation made by splitting the vowel *a* [in the compound] to read it as "the death of one who has no son" (*aputramaraṇa*), that is incorrect; for even in the cited *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, it contradicts the statements of Itihāsa, Kātyāyana, and others. Furthermore, the explanation that the word "they die" (*mriyante*) has the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) is also incorrect, as it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). As for the mention of the fruit of having many sons and so forth on the thirteenth day, that refers to the *śrāddha* for multiple groups (*anekavarga*). Regarding the argument: "Since a prohibition (*niṣedha*) exists, a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *pārvaṇa* rite is untenable; therefore, both a prohibition and an injunction (*vidhi*) must be accepted, and since one cannot exist where the other is already established, this is not logical"—this too is incorrect. For there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) to the perception of both the injunction and the prohibition. Since the *śrāddha* for multiple groups (*bahuvarga*)—namely the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*—is obtained through the prohibition of the *śrāddha* for a single group (*ekavarga*), the injunction "one should perform the *pārvaṇa*" must be accepted in order to set aside that [prohibition]. Otherwise, even in your own position, this very [injunction] would be rendered useless. It might be argued: "If that were so, the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha-śrāddha*) would also be excluded, because it lacks the quality of being for six generations (*ṣāṭpauruṣatva*). If it is replied: "Even though it lacks the quality of being for six generations, it is called *pārvaṇa* because it is performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure," then the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* would likewise not be excluded, since that too is performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure.

It is said in reply: Since that which is performed on the thirteenth day lacks the status of being a primary *pārvaṇa* when performed according to the primary *pārvaṇa* procedure, it must be accepted as a *pārvaṇa* similar to a *pārvaṇa*.
Some maintain that while a *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is similar to a *kṣayāha-śrāddha*, it is not so in this case; thus, only that [the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*] is excluded, but not the *kṣayāha-śrāddha*.

This is incorrect, because it is also logical to exclude the *kṣayāha-śrāddha* and others when a *ṣāṭpauruṣa-śrāddha* (a rite for six ancestors) that is extremely similar [to the *kṣayāha-śrāddha*] cannot be obtained.
By this very [reasoning], it is established that others maintain that not even a single-group *śrāddha* should be performed at all.

That too is incorrect. For it has been stated that the prohibition concerns the *śrāddha* performed for a single ancestor out of delusion; therefore, by reflecting upon that, the *sapiṇḍana*, the *kṣayāha-śrāddha*, and so forth are not excluded. Nor does the statement "one should perform the *pārvaṇa*" [490] exclude the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* for many ancestors or the *kṣayāha-śrāddhas* and others, because it is logically established as a general injunction for the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). To explain: by the two scriptural citations from the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and the *Viṣṇusmṛti*, namely "the time for *śrāddha* is the new moon" and "the three new moons and the eight *aṣṭakās*," the obligatory *śrāddha* on the aforementioned thirteenth day is enjoined, and this is stated by the present text to be specifically a *pārvaṇa*. Thus, since this interpretation of the passage is consistent, there is no evidence that its purpose is the exclusion of other types of *śrāddha*. Consequently, this is established: the prohibition "one should not perform it for a single ancestor" refers only to the *ekoddiṣṭa* performed out of delusion. The phrase "one should perform the *pārvaṇa*" is, however, a specific injunction for the obligatory *śrāddha* ordained for the thirteenth day.
[Objection: But surely, even there, the *pārvaṇa* rite is established through extension (*atideśa*) alone; so what is the purpose of this specific injunction?
[Response: It is said: this *pārvaṇa* injunction is for the purpose of setting aside the *ekoddiṣṭa* that would otherwise apply to paternal uncles and others.
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is indeed for the parents alone;
however, for paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers, it is always the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

This [rule] should be understood as referring to the stepmother (*mātṛ-sapatnī*), because of its mention alongside paternal uncles and others. Āpastamba states the annual śrāddha for those who have no sons:
For those who have died without sons— whether they be women or men— an ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed for them, and not a pārvaṇa rite.
One should indeed offer the monthly Śrāddha to friends, kinsmen, and sapindas, as well as to women and unmarried maidens; the annual Śrāddha is to be performed otherwise than this.
Pracetas says:
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
the *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed for all those who are childless as well as for those who have no wives.
[491] "Of those without wives" means of those who have not performed the marriage ceremony.
Atri says:
"To a brother, a sister, a son, a father-in-law, and a maternal uncle..."
For an uncle or a preceptor, the śrāddha is ekoddiṣṭa, not pārvaṇa.

Thus, by these statements, it follows that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite applies to paternal uncles and others; therefore, the *pārvaṇa* rule is established for the purpose of overriding that. Consequently: "In the same manner, the *śrāddha* for paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers who are childless, as well as for a childless maternal grandfather, should be performed just like that for one's own father."
Thus, the statement of Jātūkarṇya should be understood as referring to the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī); the phrase "like for the ancestors" means according to the pārvaṇa rite.

As for the explanation that the statement "one should act like [the father]" is intended to indicate its mandatory nature (*avaśyakartavyatā*), that is incorrect. Since there is no reason to restrict the scope of "one should act like [the father]" to mere necessity, whereas the injunctions for the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for paternal uncles and others are restricted to occasions other than the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), and the restriction of Jātūkarṇya’s statement is to the thirteenth lunar day itself, it is appropriate to rely on the statement "one should perform the *pārvaṇa*" because it cannot be explained otherwise. Therefore, it is established that the prohibitory statements refer to the śrāddha for the single group (*ekavarga*) mentioned above.
Others, however, [state]:
"The śrāddha should be performed during the two solstices, likewise during the two equinoxes,
and on all the Yugādis, except for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa)."

Thus, based on the words of Pulastya and because the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is the beginning of a Yuga (yugādi), they say that the Śrāddha should be performed without the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa); for the prohibitive statements have as their subject matter the Śrāddha accompanied by the giving of rice-balls.

Alternatively, the prohibitory statements should be established as referring specifically to the *kāmya* (optional) *śrāddha*, because it is recorded in the Smṛtis that the fault lies precisely in the connection with desire (*kāma*) regarding the *śrāddha*. For instance, Vyāsa and Āpastamba, while proclaiming the fruits for the performer of the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight—such as the preeminence of one's kin and the birth of many sons—also point out the fault of the death of a son in that very context.
Thus concludes the determination of the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight. Now follows the determination of the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"On the days beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad), excluding the fourteenth day,
[the offering] is given there for those who have indeed been slain by a weapon."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya and Brahma Purāṇas:
"He whose young ancestors have died or were killed by weapons must perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), desiring their satisfaction."
In the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vāyu Purāṇas*:
"One should cause [the offering] to be given for those youths who have died in the house;
and for those indeed who were killed by a weapon, one should give it on the fourteenth day."
Vṛddha-Manu says:
"Excluding the fourteenth day, those experts in the Śrāddha rites perform the Śrāddha;
by this, his ancestors—and especially those who were slain by weapons in battle—are gratified."
And Manu, regarding the commencement of rites for specific desires, states:
"On the thirteenth day, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; on the fourteenth, one obtains good offspring; and his ancestors, as well as those who were slain by weapons in battle, are gratified."
The mention of "taking up a weapon" (śastragrahaṇa) is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "For those who have died through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, or hanging... [493]
"It is certain that on the fourteenth day, a *śrāddha* should be performed for the sake of satisfaction. Thus it is stated;
and also in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*:
"For those who have met an untimely death, or even died by the sword..."
And for those who have died from calamities or have met with death by poison, [one should perform the rites].
And for those consumed by fire, those who met death in water,
those killed by snakes or tigers, and even those by horns or by hanging—
O lord of men, a śrāddha for them should be performed on the fourteenth day;
when it is performed for them on that day, their satisfaction will then arise from that fortnight.

‘Apamṛtyu’ means untimely death; that is to say, death occurring even before one has reached old age. However, the death of those afflicted by yakṣas, bhūtas, grahas, and so forth, is called death due to calamity (*upasarga*). ‘Tatpakṣajā’ means that the satisfaction [of the ancestors] is as much as is obtained by performing the *śrāddha* on every day of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*).
Marīci also says:
[The [offering] for those who kill poisoners, serpents, beasts of prey, animals, and Brāhmaṇas...]
Rituals should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, they are censured.

Those who are killed by poison and the like are described as such. By this, it is restricted that for those killed by weapons and so forth, the Śrāddha occurs specifically at the time of the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), but not that the Śrāddha for those killed by weapons and so forth occurs *only* on the fourteenth day; rather, their Śrāddha certainly takes place even at other times. Pracetās also says:
"By climbing trees, by iron [weapons] and the like, by lightning, fire, poison, and so forth..."
"For those who have perished by [the claws of] beasts with nails or fangs, the fourteenth day is prescribed.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included means of death that share the same characteristics as those mentioned, such as climbing dangerous places like mountain peaks, being struck by one's own cart or pestle, hanging, falling from a stone, and so forth. As for the statement of Śākaṭāyana, which has a meaning contrary to what was said:
"For those who have perished by water or fire, or in a renunciate’s hermitage, at home, or on a road..."
"One should indeed perform the *śrāddha* for them, avoiding the fourteenth day. Thus [it is said].

This refers to living beings who have met their death through water, fire, and so forth, as prescribed for the purpose of atonement (*prāyaścitta*). However, the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) must be performed specifically for those who have died an "evil death" (*pāpamṛtyu*), because such deaths are listed among the examples in the statement of Pracetas beginning with "climbing trees" (*vṛkṣārohaṇa*). For this very reason, there is no *caturdaśī-śrāddha* even for women who have followed their deceased husbands according to the prescribed rite of entering the fire (*agnipraveśa*). Thus, it is established that based on the authority of the statements in the *Manu* and *Brahma Purāṇas*, the *śrāddha* on the dark fourteenth day is for those who have died by means of water, fire, and so forth—which are not [prescribed]—as well as for those who have died in battle or by fasting unto death (*prāyopaveśana*). Even for one who has performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony for such a person, only the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed.
As Gārgya says:
"But the Śrāddha performed on the fourteenth day after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa for one slain by a weapon must be conducted according to the Ekoddiṣṭa procedure."

Manu says: "For those who have been made into a single *piṇḍa*, a separate status is no longer possible after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, even if death occurs on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Even for a father who has attained equanimity but was slain by a weapon,
the sons must perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite on the fourteenth day during the Mahālaya."

The meaning is as follows: even for one who has attained similarity (*sārūpya*) by abandoning the state of a *preta* through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite performed together with the grandfather and others who have themselves attained the state of a *pitṛ* by abandoning their own *preta*-status—nevertheless, in the case of a father killed by a weapon, although the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha has been performed on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya*, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must still be performed on a subsequent day; for the satisfaction of the grandfather and others is not accomplished by the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha alone.

[Objection: If this is so, then even on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), when the *ekoddiṣṭa* has been performed, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha would also have to be performed for the sake of accomplishing the satisfaction of the grandfather and others.

Not so; for since it is not recorded in tradition that the grandfather and others are to be offered libations on the anniversary of the father’s death, the performance of the *śrāddha* would be for the sake of their satisfaction. However, regarding the *Mahālaya*, [it is said]:
"They long for milk-rice mixed with honey from their sons and grandsons;
therefore, one should satisfy them there with milk-rice according to the prescribed rule."

Since there is a traditional injunction that even the grandfather and others are to be offered libations with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, one must indeed perform a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha on another day for their satisfaction. However, for one whose grandfather was also killed by weapons or similar means, the grandfather’s śrāddha during the *mahālaya* period must be performed as an *ekoddiṣṭa* on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure applies to one or to two. This means that when either the father or the grandfather has been killed by weapons or similar causes, or when both among the triad beginning with the father have been killed by weapons or similar causes, a śrāddha for each is to be performed individually on the fourteenth day according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

The meaning is that it must be performed. Even when the Śrāddha has been performed for each of the two [grandfathers] according to the procedure for an *ekoddiṣṭa*, a Śrāddha must also be performed on another day for the sake of accomplishing the satisfaction of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*). When all three, beginning with the father, have been killed by weapons or other such means, separate *ekoddiṣṭa* rites alone must be performed.

On this point, someone says: because of the statement "in one or in two," it is understood that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite does not apply to the three—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. Therefore, when all three have been killed by weapons and the like, the *pārvaṇa* rite alone applies on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). And this is logical. For even though the specific time prescribed for the fourteenth day is available for all three who have undergone *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite—which is based on the impossibility of a single time due to the specific cause of being killed by weapons and so forth—does not apply. With this very intention, Aparārka also stated: "[496] And in that case, if only one has been killed by a weapon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rule applies, but not if all three; if all three are in that state, however, the *pārvaṇa* alone applies. The meaning of this is: "if all three are in that state"—that is, if all three have been killed by weapons—the *ekoddiṣṭa* rule does not apply, but rather the *pārvaṇa* alone applies there.

Others, however, say: "This is incorrect. Because the phrase 'in one or in two' is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), and because the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is based on the cause of being killed by weapons and so forth, it does not have its basis in the impossibility of [performing the rite at] the [prescribed] time; for such an impossibility is not explicitly stated in scripture. If the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* were based on that [impossibility], it would result in the rule having a foundation consisting of mere conjecture. For this very reason, Devasvāmin stated: 'Even when three [deceased ancestors] have been killed by weapons and so forth, only three separate *ekoddiṣṭa* rites should be performed, and not a *pārvaṇa* rite, because there is no scriptural statement to that effect.'"
That is incorrect, because if it were an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa), it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

In this context, since the meaning of the statement is understood to be that for those killed by weapons and the like, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is performed specifically on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), the *pārvaṇa* rite must be performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and other such occasions. However, regarding those who died by weapons and so forth specifically on the fourteenth day, a doubt arises as to whether the *pārvaṇa* or the *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed on their anniversary of death. To this, it is replied: although there is a distinction between the occasion of the fourteenth day and the occasion of the anniversary of death—according to the principle stated in the section on the conjunction of times in the *Śrāddhakalpa*—when multiple occasions coincide simultaneously, and when one occasion alone suffices for the performance of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) without conflicting with the *kutapa* period and other required times, leaving no room for a second, then because no specific distinction can be grasped when place, time, performer, and deity are identical, the occasional rites are performed by way of *tantra* (simultaneous performance). Thus, for those who, following the tradition of their family elders, have adopted the *ekoddiṣṭa* option even for the anniversary of death, for them the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone is to be performed on the fourteenth day, even though it is occasioned by the anniversary of death. On the other hand, for those who have adopted the *pārvaṇa*, that [performance] is maintained for as long as they live, just like the *uditahoma* (the offering made after sunrise); therefore, they must not abandon it even on the fourteenth day. As for the prohibition of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha on the fourteenth day, that refers to the *pārvaṇa* occasioned by the fourteenth day itself, and not to the *pārvaṇa* occasioned by the anniversary of death.

Now, one might object: in the statement "the *pārvaṇa* [is performed] on the fourteenth day," since the phrase "on the fourteenth day" specifies that which is occasioned by the fourteenth day, there would result both the necessity of supplying an unstated qualifier (*viśeṣaṇādhyāhāra*) and a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

This is not so. For the specific meaning is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors, and thus it does not provide ground for the faults mentioned. Otherwise, even the restrictive rule regarding threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth would not be connected with that which pertains to the *apūrva*. Furthermore, as for the statement in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* that the *pārvaṇa* performed on the fourteenth day is fruitless—that too refers to the *pārvaṇa* occasioned by the fourteenth day.

Now, a doubt arises as to whether he should perform two *śrāddha* rites—one on account of the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) as an *ekoddiṣṭa*, and one on account of the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) as a *pārvaṇa*—or only one; for since their constituent elements (*aṅga*) differ, they cannot be performed as a single ritual complex (*tantra*), as their specific characteristics are being grasped separately. In this regard, since the prohibition stating "one should not perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day" does not apply to *śrāddhas* based on distinct causes, he should perform both *śrāddhas*.

Not so; because the deity is one, when performing two principal rites together, the *pārvaṇa* rites themselves accomplish both occasional rites (*naimittika*) by subsuming the *ekoddhiṣṭa* rites within them for the sake of favoring the greater number of *śrāddha* duties. Therefore, there is no performance of the two *śrāddhas* separately.

But is there not also a *kāmya* (optional) Śrāddha on the fourteenth day? Since human activity is inclined toward desire and because the inclination for optional rites is intense, when a Śrāddha occasioned by the fourteenth day is to be performed, would it not follow that the rules of the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone apply? This would indeed be the case if no distinction were perceived here as favoring the majority [of cases]. Or, let there be two distinct Śrāddhas on this lunar day due to the difference in their respective occasions (*nimitta*). Furthermore, if a Śrāddha cannot somehow be performed on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya* fortnight, the Śrāddha must be performed on some other day within that fortnight; for even if the primary time is unavailable, the Śrāddha to be performed in that fortnight remains mandatory. Moreover, on other days, even for those killed by weapons, the *pārvaṇa* rite alone applies, since the *ekoddiṣṭa* is specifically prescribed for the fourteenth day. The reason why the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed for those killed by weapons on the fourteenth day is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: [The text continues with the citation from the Nāgarakhaṇḍa.]
Ānarta said:
Why is the fourteenth day prescribed for the *śrāddha* of those slain by weapons?
And what is the reason here for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite? Tell me this.
Bhartṛyajña said: O King, in ancient times, during the Bṛhat-kalpa, there was a great asura named Hiraṇyākṣa,
who was powerful, heroic, and a source of terror to all the gods.
Having performed various austerities when the month of Nabhasya had arrived on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Brahmā was thoroughly gratified by him.
Brahmā said:
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; ask for whatever you desire.
I shall grant it even if it is not to be given, and even if it is difficult for gods and asuras to attain."
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"O Lotus-born One, hungry ghosts, spirits, piśācas, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas constantly run toward me, famished."
"When the Śrāddha has been performed for the paternal side while the sun is situated in Virgo,
on this very day, their satisfaction for the duration of a year generally occurs.
Therefore, O Lord, provide a means for their gratification on this day."
Brahmā said:
Whatever man shall offer a śrāddha to his ancestors on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors, when the month of Nabhasya has arrived;
By my word, it shall undoubtedly come to pass for the pretas, the rākṣasas, and the bhūtas, as well as for those others whom you have mentioned.
For those who have died by an untimely death and those who have been slain in battles,
satisfaction shall come to them when the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is offered by their sons.
Having spoken thus, O King, Brahmā then vanished from sight;
Hiraṇyākṣa, too, filled with joy, departed for his own abode.
And regarding that which is given on that day for those slain by weapons—
an Ekoddiṣṭa performed with faith by men— I shall explain the reason for that to you.
And those who are slain by weapons in battle with a mind free from conceptual construction—
those mortals, while fighting, are not born again as human beings.

Those men who are slain with their backs turned, intent on flight, become pretas; so said the Grandfather. Even those who face their enemies, if they speak piteously while being struck, [become pretas].
Or they might feel regret, being shattered by those blows.
Manu, the son of Svayambhū, has declared that even they may become hungry ghosts (preta) here;
for sometimes even the minds of the brave undergo fluctuation.
Therefore, on that day, an offering should be given even for them, out of apprehension that they might have fallen into the state of a preta.
Since the state of being a preta arises for all embodied beings who have died by an untimely death, therefore that very day belongs to them.

O best of kings, I have specifically proclaimed that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is to be performed by men on that day as a *śrāddha*. I shall explain to you the reason why this is so after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony.
O King, if his father should ever have fallen into the state of a preta,
a śrāddha must be performed on that day for the sake of his satisfaction.
On that day, the ancestors beginning with the grandfather never deserve to receive a śrāddha offering;
if one should offer it out of delusion, it is seized by the rākṣasas.
O King, by the word of Brahmā and by the bhūtas, pretas, and dānavas,
only the ekoddiṣṭa rite is to be performed here, and not the pārvaṇa.
On the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors, when the sun is situated in Virgo—
for this reason, one should not perform the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha;
for when this day arrives, the śrāddha becomes fruitless.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Now follow the times for *śrāddha*, beginning with the solstices (*ayana*).
Regarding this, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
During the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on the three Aṣṭakās, and during the two solstices—
even water mixed with sesame seeds [is meritorious] at these times.
A man, being self-restrained, should offer [this] to the ancestors.
"He has performed the *śrāddha* for a thousand years"—this is what the ancestors declare as a secret.
Regarding this, they believe that the necessity of performing the *śrāddha* is expressed by the statement, "even water [is sufficient]. As for that which...

"The sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the two equinoxes (viṣuvat), the vyatīpāta yoga, one’s own birth star (janmarkṣa), and likewise an eclipse of the moon or sun—Prajāpati has indeed declared these to be the optional (kāmya) times for śrāddha.

This statement from Viṣṇu declares that eclipses and so forth are times for optional śrāddha. That [statement] is not capable of negating their obligatory (nitya) nature; for by the force of two [contradictory] statements, there is no contradiction between their being both obligatory and optional, as is the case with the Agnihotra and other rites.
Śaṅkha said:
That which is given during the shadow of an elephant, that which is given at the sight of Rāhu,
and likewise at the equinoxes and solstices— all this is said to be infinite in merit.

Regarding the two solstices (*ayana*) here: although the two solstices and the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) are already included by the very term *saṃkrānti* in this statement of Yājñavalkya, "the equinox and the sun's transition," the fact that they are mentioned separately should be understood as intended to demonstrate their superior excellence over other transitions (*saṃkrānti*), namely that the equinox is more excellent than the other transitions, and the solstice is more excellent than the equinox.
Thus it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O Lord of the Earth, the sun’s transition (*saṃkramaṇa*) is highly praised for a *śrāddha* ceremony."
Therein are two equinoxes and, in particular, two solstices.
The definition of the two equinoxes and the two solstices is given in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"When the sun enters Aries or when it proceeds to Libra,
then that time is called the equinox, which brings about imperishable merit."
O King, when the sun moves into Capricorn and Cancer,
that is designated as an *ayana*, and it is distinguished from the *viṣuva*.
And at this time, the *śrāddha* should be performed even without the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*).
As Pulastya said:
"The *śrāddha* [should be performed] during the two solstices (*ayana*) and likewise during the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)."
"And on the days of the solstices (saṃkrānti), the rite should be performed except for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa).

Thus, on these occasions, the Śrāddha should be performed without the offering of the rice-balls. This prohibition of the rice-ball offering applies specifically to the Śrāddha occasioned by these particular times; it does not apply by extension to the solstices and other such times when they coincide with the anniversary of death (mṛtāha) and so forth. For, by the rule "the Śrāddha on the two solstices," it is understood that the Śrāddha associated with the solstices and other such times is obligatory (nitya). And that which is obligatory by virtue of its own specific cause is more powerful than that which is obligatory by association with another. Furthermore, that which is obligatory in itself is stronger than that which is obligatory through association with something else.

Furthermore, regarding this, the qualification "except for the offering of the rice-balls" (*piṇḍanirvapaṇād ṛte*) attached to the *śrāddha* being enjoined here cannot reasonably refer to a *śrāddha* performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) or similar occasions that fall at that time by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). For if such a *śrāddha* were enjoined for these times, then it would follow that this is an injunction of the primary action (*bhāvārthavidhi*), which is a superior form of injunction. This is stated in the *Śātātapa-smṛti* and the *Liṅga-purāṇa*.
Indeed, the śrāddha must be performed even at the cost of one's entire possessions during the appearance of Rāhu;
for he who does not perform the śrāddha sinks like a cow in the mud.
This statement indicates the necessity of the *śrāddha*.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, having established the necessity of this *śrāddha* as being occasional (*naimittika*), its optional (*kāmya*) nature is also set forth:
"The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the three *aṣṭakās*, and [the days] in the three months beginning with Pauṣa..."
And three Anvaṣṭakās are meritorious, as is the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha.
The thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism, especially during the rainy season—
these are declared to be the daily, obligatory times for performing the ancestral Śrāddha rites.
However, a funeral rite for kinsmen must be performed during an eclipse of the moon or sun; otherwise, one would fall into hell.
Voluntary *śrāddhas* are recommended during eclipses and similar occasions;
likewise, at the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, [the merit] is infinite.
[503] On the occasion of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), an inexhaustible śrāddha should be performed, as it is on birthdays;
and it should especially be performed for the fulfillment of desires on all lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

And so forth, as stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "O son, [the merit is attained] upon meeting a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during eclipses of the sun or moon, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, at the transit of the sun, and during the *vyatīpāta* yoga."

"When there is an abundance of materials suitable for a śrāddha, or when suffering is manifested, or during afflictions by the planets at one's birth star, one may perform a śrāddha according to one's desire. Thus it is said.

In this context, one may perform a *śrāddha* at times such as a solar eclipse, or by "desire" (*icchayā*), meaning according to one's own inclination; or alternatively, one may perform a *śrāddha* at the aforementioned times "by desire," which means with the longing for results such as heaven. It does not mean, however, that one should perform it only if one wishes to do so.
These are the times for *śrāddha*, beginning with the solstices (*ayanādi*).
Now follows the time characterized by the availability of materials and Brahmins.
Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"When one is at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and when the requisite materials are available, one need not wait for a specific time;
having obtained a worthy Brāhmaṇa recipient, the Śrāddha is ordained to be performed immediately."

A "sacred place" (*tīrtha*) refers to Gayā and the like; "substance" (*dravya*) refers to food and the like. Upon encountering a Brāhmaṇa distinguished by such qualifications as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one should not wait for another time; rather, one should perform the *śrāddha* at that very moment. In this context, the word "immediately" (*sadyas*) indicates its obligatory nature.
As for what is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Upon obtaining a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, or during the solstices (*ayana*)."
When there is an abundance of materials suitable for a śrāddha, as well as when suffering is displayed;

"One should perform a Śrāddha at will during afflictions caused by planets at the time of one's birth-star. Here, the word "at will" (cecchayā) is contradicted by its obligatory nature; this has already been explained in the determination of the times for Śrāddha, such as the solstices and others, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
And when a learned Brahmin, a knower of the Vedas who is like a sacred fire, comes to one's house,
even with him alone one should perform an auspicious *śrāddha*, just as at the equinoxes.
When the acquisition of materials for a śrāddha is deemed appropriate by the virtuous,
the śrāddha should be performed by the best of the twice-born according to the pārvaṇa rite.

In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, even the optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* is mentioned for a time characterized by the availability of material wealth and a worthy Brāhmaṇa. For instance, immediately after the statement "Listen now to the optional [rites]," there follows this passage: "When wealth worthy of faith has arrived, or when a distinguished twice-born guest has come, one should perform the *śrāddha*, recognizing it as such, as well as during the *vyatīpāta* yoga and at the solstices (*ayana*)."
Thus concludes the determination of the time characterized by the perfection of the Brāhmaṇas.
Now, regarding Gajacchāyā (the Elephant’s Shadow),
as described in the Skanda Purāṇa and other texts:

"When the Moon is in the constellation presided over by the ancestors (Maghā), and the Sun (Haṃsa) is situated in the Kara (Hasta) constellation, and the lunar day belongs to Vaiśravaṇa (the thirteenth)—that is known as Gajacchāyā.

[505] Here, "Indu" means the Moon; "pitṛdaivatye" refers to the Maghā asterism; "Haṃsa" means the Sun; "kare" refers to the Hasta asterism; and "tithir vaiśravaṇīyā" refers to the thirteenth lunar day.

In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: "The thirteenth lunar day, when the sun is situated in the constellation Haṃsa (Śravaṇā) and conjoined with Maghā, is known as the Vaivasvatī Tithi; it is the shadow of the elephant."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The yoga known as Kuñjaracchāyā occurs on the thirteenth lunar day of the month of Magha,
when the moon is situated in the asterism of Maghā and the sun is positioned in the hand (the asterism of Hasta)."

This is the meaning: when the sun is situated in Hasta and there is a conjunction with Maghā presided over by the Moon on the thirteenth lunar day, that is known as the Gajacchāyā (Elephant-Shade) yoga; and it occurs during the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. The word *chāyā* is neuter according to the rule "vibhāṣā senāsurācchāya. Baudhāyana said: "That new moon day which occurs while the sun is in Haṃsa (Svātī) and is conjoined with Karā (Hasta), that should be known as Kuñjaracchāyā."

The *haṃsa* is the sun; because its presiding deity is the *haṃsa*, the lunar mansion *hasta* is also called *haṃsa*. "Endowed with rays" means possessed of the lunar mansion *hasta* joined with the moon.

"When Rāhu swallows the sun during the junctions of the lunar phases (*parva-sandhi*), that is declared to be the 'elephant's shadow' (*gajacchāyā*); one should perform the *śrāddha* rite at that time. Thus it is said.

‘Saiṃhikeya’ refers to Rāhu. ‘At the junctions of the lunar phases (parvasandhiṣu)’ means at the junctions of the new moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight. Now, regarding miscellaneous times, according to the Matsya Purāṇa:
Henceforth I shall proclaim that which was uttered by Viṣṇu:
the Śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the double transits of the sun, or any ordinary solar transit;
on the new moon day and the Aṣṭakā days, especially during the dark fortnight.
During the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī; when there is a gathering of wealth and Brahmins; during Gajacchāyā, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, Vaidhṛti, and on the day [of the week].
Likewise, [it is taught] on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, during eclipses, and likewise at festivals and the Mahālaya [rite].
(From the Brahmapurāṇa)
In this world, one should offer the *śrāddha* rite month after month during the fortnight of the moon;
furthermore, the *śrāddha* should be performed on the full moon day and when the moon is in its [specific] asterism.
It is proclaimed here that humans should perform the daily *śrāddha*,
and the wise should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* on occasions such as birth ceremonies and others.
When the sun has entered Virgo, for fifteen days,
that śrāddha is prescribed here according to the pārvaṇa rite.
Jātūkarṇa said:
During an eclipse of a planet, upon the birth of a son, during the Maghā constellation for ancestral rites, and during the two solstices;
Whatever is given daily in a conch shell and likewise in a lotus becomes equal to a thousand gold coins.

And here, because of the understanding of the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) that "it is always given," authorities declare the *śrāddha* and other rites to be obligatory on occasions such as lunar eclipses. Alternatively, the meaning is that it refers to the *maghā* asterisms situated in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, according to the rule: "Always, day after day, for as long as one lives, [one should perform] the ancestral rite during *maghā*.
He (the same author) also states the definition of the *śaṅkha* and *padma* [tithis]:
"The best of the twice-born call the new moon day, when the moon has waned, the *śaṅkha*."
"On the Aṣṭakā days, there shall be a lotus; what is given there is likewise inexhaustible.
Thus [it is said]. But Śaṅkha says:
"When Viṣṭi, Vyatīpāta, and likewise Sunday [occur together]..."
"That is called *padmaka*, and it is four times [the duration] of the *ayana*," so it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The latter fortnight of Āśvina and the first [fortnight] of Kārttika..."
But he who always performs the śrāddha ceremony shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
At the time when Janārdana, the soul of all, abandons sleep, a Śrāddha performed then yields infinite merit; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Likewise:
"O King, one should know that a śrāddha performed at the time of Rāhu’s appearance [during an eclipse] is inexhaustible;
it should be performed with cooked rice or with cooked barley."
O Great King, those two should by no means be excluded from the śrāddha ceremony under any circumstances.
Śātātapa says:
"The ancestors long for food during new water, at the first harvest of grain, upon the departure from home, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā constellation."
Therefore, one who is ever-striving should give to learned Brāhmaṇas.
The Grandfather said:
On the new moon day, during the vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day, and on the aṣṭakā days,
a learned man who does not perform the śrāddha falls into hell.
Thus concludes the miscellaneous times.
Thus concludes the time for the daily śrāddha. Now follows the time for the optional (kāmya) śrāddha.
In that regard, first are the lunar days (tithis).
Kātyāyana says:

Now follow the rites for specific desires: on the first day of the lunar fortnight, women of no beauty; on the second and third days, all desires; on the fourth, small livestock; on the fifth, sons; on the sixth, a share in ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*); on the seventh, agriculture; on the eighth, trade; on the ninth, single-hoofed animals; on the tenth, cattle; on the eleventh, servants; on the twelfth, wealth, grain, and family; on the thirteenth, preeminence among kinsmen and gold—yet young men die therein. On the fourteenth day, [the rite is for] one slain by a weapon; on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), everything. Thus it is said.
Āpastamba.

When performed on any day of the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa), one pleases the ancestors. However, due to the performer’s restriction regarding the specific time, there is a distinction in the fruit [obtained]. When performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females is born.
