On the second, thieves; on the third, those endowed with Vedic splendor (brahmavarcas); on the fourth, one possessing small livestock; on the fifth, one possessing honey and meat, having many children and never dying childless; on the sixth, for one of bad character; on the seventh, success in agriculture; on the eighth, prosperity; on the ninth, single-hoofed animals; on the tenth, success in trade; on the eleventh, iron, tin, and lead; on the twelfth, one possessing cattle; on the thirteenth, one with many sons and many friends, whose offspring are handsome, yet they die young; on the fourteenth, an increase in lifespan; and on the fifteenth, prosperity. By performing the Śrāddha constantly, one obtains all these benefits. Thus it is said.
[509] Viṣṇu presides over the office.

On the first lunar day (pratipad), beautiful women are obtained in the home; on the second, an excellent maiden; on the third, all desires; on the fourth, prosperity; on the fifth, victory at dice; on the sixth, agriculture; on the seventh, commerce; on the eighth, horses; on the ninth, cattle; on the tenth, cows; on the eleventh, sons endowed with Vedic splendor; on the twelfth, gold and silver; on the thirteenth, good fortune; on the fifteenth, all desires. For the Śrāddha rite for those slain by weapons, the fourteenth day is recommended.
Regarding the injunction that "one should perform the *śrāddha*," Hārīta states:

one desiring a son [should perform it] on the fifth lunar day; one desiring wealth on the sixth; one desiring cattle on the seventh; one desiring health for those killed by weapons on the eighth; one desiring an army on the ninth; one desiring food on the tenth; one desiring prosperity on the eleventh; one desiring a wife on the twelfth; one desiring fame on the thirteenth; one desiring power on the fourteenth; and one desiring well-being on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), while one desiring all things [may do so] on the new moon day. Paiṭhīnasi [states as follows].

On the fifth day, one desiring a son should sacrifice; on the sixth, one desiring cattle; on the seventh, one desiring prosperity; on the eighth, one desiring food; on the ninth, one desiring Vedic splendor; on the tenth, one desiring all things; on the eleventh, one desiring wealth; on the twelfth, one desiring land; on the thirteenth, mastery over women; on the fourteenth, for those killed by weapons; and on the new moon day, one desiring all things. Manu says: "Performing a *śrāddha* on the first day of the lunar fortnight, one obtains handsome sons."
On the second day, however, one should give maidens; on the third day, bards.
On the fifth day, one obtains small cattle; on the sixth, beautiful sons;
and on the seventh, a man gains either gambling or agriculture.
On the eighth day as well, the giver of a śrāddha always obtains trade;
on the ninth day he obtains single-hoofed animals, and on the tenth day, many hoofed animals.
On the eleventh day, one likewise obtains health and sons endowed with Vedic splendor;
on the twelfth day, gold, silver, and even base metals.
On the thirteenth day, there is excellence of birth; on the fourteenth day, one obtains good offspring;
and here, the ancestors who were slain by weapons in battle are gratified.
By offering these and other such extensive items that are dear to the mind on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight during a śrāddha, the giver attains all his desires.
"Bandinaḥ" refers to panegyrists.
[This is stated] in the *Brahma-purāṇa* and the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa*:
"When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, for fifteen days..."
There, the śrāddha is prescribed according to the pārvaṇa rite.
The first lunar day (pratipad) leads to the acquisition of wealth; the second bestows bipeds;
the third fulfills the desire for boons; and the fourth destroys enemies.
On the fifth day one attains prosperity; on the sixth, a man becomes nourished;
on the seventh, lordship over the Gaṇas; and on the eighth, supreme intelligence.
On the ninth day, one obtains women; on the tenth, the fulfillment of all desires;
and on the eleventh, one devoted to ritual action attains all the Vedas.
And on the twelfth day, the worshiper of the ancestors obtains progeny—
offspring, intelligence, cattle, growth, independence, and supreme nourishment.
A man devoted to faith who performs a Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day attains long life and sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
He whose ancestors were young men slain by the sword should perform the rite on the thirteenth lunar day if he desires their satisfaction.
A pure man who diligently performs a śrāddha on the new moon day attains all his desires and enjoys eternal heaven.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Women, beautiful forms, the birth of daughters in the home, as well as wealth,
all desires, fame, prosperity, victory at dice, and agriculture."
The giver of a śrāddha successively obtains trade, cattle, horses, as well as sons, gold, beauty, and good fortune.
O King, this [rite] should be performed starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight up until the thirteenth;
however, on the fourteenth day, it should be performed for those men who have been killed by weapons.
A person who always performs the *śrāddha* on the fifteenth days obtains all his desires;
therefore, O lord of men, it should be performed with great effort.
The Śrāddha should always be performed by those who know it on the fifteenth days.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*, it is said:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight when the sun has entered Virgo is a merit-bestowing destroyer of sins that increases the bliss of Śiva."
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods—
all these, when performed on that day, O Three-eyed One, truly become sources of great merit.
O Sage, a Śrāddha performed especially on that day and a Homa conducted according to the rules yield great fruit;
therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the Śrāddha on that occasion.
The wise know that on the fifth day there should be a single meal, and on the sixth day, eating only at night;
on the seventh day there should be a fast, and on the eighth day one should worship Śiva.
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion, one should perform the śrāddha for one's father;
having performed the śrāddha according to the rules, one should eat that which was enjoyed by the ancestors.
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there after having worshipped the Three-eyed One (Trilocana),
his ancestors shall remain satisfied for fifteen years.
Thus end the lunar days for specific desires.
Now, the asterisms. Regarding this, Manu says:
By performing [rites] on odd lunar days and under odd asterisms, one attains all desires;
and by honoring the ancestors on even lunar days, one obtains abundant progeny.
‘Yukṣu’ means on even [days], ‘ayukṣu’ means on odd [days].
Yama says:
By performing [the rite] on even days, one shall obtain all desires through the lunar mansions of the day.
By worshipping the ancestors during the Gajacchāyā, one obtains abundant progeny.
Yājñavalkya says: [One obtains] heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength, as well as sons, excellence, good fortune, prosperity, and auspicious happiness.
Likewise, the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], as well as trade and other such activities,
health, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly offers the Śrāddha ceremony bestows knowledge of the Dharma, success as a physician, base metals, cattle such as goats and others, horses, and long life.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī,
he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires.
‘Pravṛttacakratā’ means the state of possessing unimpeded knowledge; [it refers to] Viṣṇu.

Heaven under Kṛttikā; offspring under Rohiṇī; spiritual luster under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras); success accompanied by Indra under Raudra (Ārdrā); the earth under Punarvasu; nourishment under Puṣya; fortune under Sārpa (Āśleṣā); all desires under Pitrya (Maghā); good fortune under Bhāgya (Pūrva-phalgunī); wealth under Āryaman (Uttara-phalgunī); preeminence among kinsmen under Hasta; handsome sons under Tvāṣṭra (Citrā); success in trade under Vāyu (Svāti); gold under Viśākhā; good friends under Maitra (Anurādhā); agriculture under Mūla; success in sea-voyages under Āpya (Pūrva-āṣāḍhā); all desires under Vaiśvadeva (Uttara-āṣāḍhā); preeminence under Abhijit; all desires under Śravaṇa; strength under Vāsava (Śraviṣṭhā); health under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj); base metals under Āja (Pūrva-bhadrapadā); a house under Āhirbudhnya (Uttara-bhadrapadā); cattle under Pauṣṇa (Revatī); horses under Āśvina (Aśvinī); and life under Yāmya (Bharaṇī).

‘Saumya’ is Mṛgaśiras; ‘Raudra’ is Ārdrā; ‘Sārpam’ is Aśleṣā; ‘Pitrya’ is Maghā; ‘Bhāgya’ is Pūrvaphalgunī; ‘Āryamana’ is Uttaraphalgunī; ‘Tvāṣṭra’ is Citrā; ‘Vāyu’ is Svāti; ‘Maitra’ is Anurādhā; ‘Śākram’ is Jyeṣṭhā; ‘Āpya’ is Pūrvāṣāḍhā; ‘Vaiśvadeva’ is Uttarāṣāḍhā; ‘Vāsava’ is Dhaniṣṭhā; ‘Vāruṇa’ is Śatabhiṣaj; ‘Ājam’ is Pūrvabhādrapadā; ‘Āhirbudhnya’ is Uttarabhādrapadā; ‘Pauṣṇa’ is Revatī; ‘Āśvina’ is Aśvinī; and ‘Yāmya’ is Bharaṇī.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Indeed, heaven, offspring, as well as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*),
the accomplishment of fierce rites, the earth, nourishment, and likewise prosperity [are obtained]."
[514] All desires, good fortune, righteousness, preeminence among kinsmen, sons endowed with beauty, commerce, and abundance of wealth.
Gold, the kingdom of friends, a fruitful harvest,
profit from sea voyages, and likewise all desired objects.
Supremacy, as well as all desires, strength, and health;
base metals, a house, cows, horses, and even life itself.
By performing a śrāddha consecutively for each one among the host of lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī, a man undoubtedly attains [the desired result].
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"By worshipping the ancestors under the asterism Kṛttikā, a human being attains heaven;
one desiring offspring [attains them] under Rohiṇī, and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) one obtains brilliance."
One obtains valor under Ārdrā, and fields and such under Punarvasu; by always worshipping Puṣya, one gains nourishment; under Aśleṣā, excellent sons;
under Maghā, preeminence among one's own kin; and under the Phālgunīs, good fortune.
One who is inclined toward giving and possesses offspring indeed arises under the Uttarās.
A man who offers a śrāddha in the hand of a virtuous person attains preeminence among the good;
by offering it under Citrā, he becomes endowed with beauty and likewise obtains offspring.
Viśākhā bestows profit from trade, independence, and the desire for sons;
and for those performing rites under Anurādhā, it grants the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty].
In the Jyeṣṭhās one gains sovereignty; in Mūla, supreme health;
in the Āṣāḍhās, the attainment of fame; and in the Uttarās, freedom from sorrow.
By hearing [the teachings] under Śravaṇā, one attains auspicious worlds; under Dhaniṣṭhā, great wealth;
under Abhijit, knowledge of the Vedas; and under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), success as a physician.
One should acquire goats and sheep under Proṣṭhapadā, likewise a wife under Uttarā;
similarly, one should acquire base metals under Revatī and horses under Aśvinī.
Likewise, by performing a *śrāddha* under the asterism Bharaṇī, one obtains excellent longevity;
therefore, the knower of truth should perform rites for specific desires under these asterisms.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Now hear from me those optional *śrāddhas* which Yama proclaimed to Śaśabindu, categorized individually according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*s)."
But that wise man who constantly performs the śrāddha rite during the conjunction of Śrāddhā is born from the wives of Agni, freed from all feverish distress.
One desiring offspring should perform [rites] under Rohiṇī; under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one gains brilliance;
under Ārdrā, one achieves success in cruel deeds and should perform the ancestral Śrāddha rite.
A man performing a śrāddha under Punarvasu shall obtain a son who possesses a share of the ancestral field;
furthermore, a person desiring prosperity should perform a śrāddha under Tiṣya.
By worshipping the ancestors under Āśleṣā, one obtains heroic sons;
by performing the Śrāddha rite under Maghā, one becomes preeminent among one's kinsmen.
A man who worships the ancestors during the Phālgunī constellations attains good fortune;
he who is disposed toward giving and performs these rites under the Uttarā constellation gains progeny.
He who offers libations to the ancestors with his own hand becomes happy in assemblies;
and he who performs [the rites] under Citrā shall behold handsome sons.
He who performs [a śrāddha] under Svātī shall obtain profit in trade;
a man who has established the sacred fires and performs a śrāddha under Viśākhā shall obtain sons.
One who performs [the rite] under Anurādhā shall set in motion the wheel of the earth;
and he who does so constantly under Jyeṣṭhā shall obtain supreme sovereignty.
Under Mūla, they desire health; under Āṣāḍhā, Maheśvara [is propitiated];
under the Uttarā-āṣāḍhās, a man shall be freed from sorrow.
By hearing [this] in the worlds of Manu, one shall attain the supreme goal;
under Dhaniṣṭhā, one shall obtain a share of a kingdom and abundant wealth.
Performing a *śrāddha* under the asterism Abhijit, one obtains the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs; performing it under the asterism of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), one attains success in medicine.
One devoted to Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā shall obtain much livestock consisting of goats and sheep; by not transgressing against Uttarā-proṣṭhapadā, one shall obtain cattle by the thousands.
One who performs the Revatī rite obtains wealth consisting of many base metals;
one enjoys horses under Aśvayuj; and under Bharaṇī, one attains an excellent lifespan.
By performing this rite of faith, Śaśabindu obtained this entire earth and,
being preeminent, ruled over it for a hundred thousand years.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having performed [the rite] under the asterism Kṛttikā, the best of the twice-born obtains heaven;
under Rohiṇī, offspring; and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), spiritual luster."
One attains success in fierce deeds and valor under Ārdrā;
under Punarvasu, success in fields; and under Puṣya, one obtains nourishment.
Likewise, one obtains all desires under the Āśleṣā asterism, good fortune under the Maghā,
wealth under the Pūrvaphalgunī, and the destruction of sins under the Uttaraphalgunī.
Under Hasta one attains preeminence in birth; under Citrā, many sons;
under Svāti, success in trade; and under Viśākhā, gold.
In Maitra (Anurādhā), there are many friends; likewise in Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā), one obtains a kingdom.
In Mūla, one gains agriculture and knowledge; in Āpya (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), one attains success from the ocean.
One obtains all desires under the Vaiśvadeva constellation, preeminence under Śravaṇa,
likewise desires under Dhaniṣṭhā, and supreme strength under Vāruṇa.
In Revatī there are many cattle, and likewise horses in Aśvinī;
but in Yāmya (Bharaṇī), he who offers a śrāddha there finds his very life.

Other statements from the *Brahmapurāṇa* regarding this matter are not recorded here; although they differ in specific details, their meaning in every respect does not exceed what has been stated previously.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Performing śrāddhas under the Maghā asterisms, one shall obtain all desires."
By him, the ancestors are always worshipped in person.
Thus end the asterisms for specific desires. Now, the days of the week. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

One who performs a *śrāddha* constantly on Sunday attains health; on Monday, good fortune; on Tuesday, victory in battle; on Wednesday, all desires; on Thursday, desired knowledge; on Friday, wealth; and on Saturday, long life. "On Tuesday" (*kauje*) means on the day of Maṅgala; "on Thursday" (*jīve*) means on the day of Bṛhaspati. [This is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
[518] Therefore, O King, I shall now describe the optional *śrāddhas* performed for those purposes:
namely, for health, for good fortune, and likewise for victory in battle.
A man who always performs the śrāddha on the days of the Sun and the other [planets] in this manner shall obtain all desires, as well as knowledge, wealth, and even life itself;
he attains these in due order— of this there is no doubt.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: On Sunday one gains health; on Monday, good fortune;
on Tuesday, victory everywhere; and on Wednesday, all desires are fulfilled.
One shall obtain the desired knowledge from Jupiter, wealth indeed from Venus,
and furthermore, long life and very rare health from Saturn.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*,
Brahmā said:
"Those men who perform a *śrāddha* when the day of the Sun (Sunday) has arrived..."
Seven births have arisen for you, existing without contradiction.
Wherever the constellation Pañcatāra occurs for the Bull-bannered Lord,
that day on the day of the God of gods is remembered as bestowing sons.
In this case, there should be a fast, and likewise a śrāddha ceremony should be performed;
or else, the consumption of the middle-sized rice-ball (piṇḍa) is prescribed.
Fasting indeed, one should worship the Lord of Rays with devotion,
using incense, garlands, and offerings endowed with divine fragrances.
Having thus worshipped Vivasvat,
O hero of great intelligence, he sleeps upon the ground at night right before him, reciting the Śveta hymn.
Having risen in the morning and performed his ablutions, and having offered the supreme *arghya*,
he should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas with *karavīra* flowers mixed with red sandalwood.
Having worshipped the three-eyed Īśāna, the lord of the planets and spirits,
and having also honored Vīra, one should then perform the Śrāddha ceremony.
O God of excellent vows, one should fashion the divine image there with five Brahmins— both celestial and terrestrial—
with their divine limbs.
Having designated the Brahmins as paternal ancestors and the Earth-dwellers as the slayers of Andhaka,
one should then perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha in this manner, which is dear to the Sun.
Then, when the śrāddha ceremony is completed, O observer of excellent vows, one should eat the central pinda while standing before the God of gods, reciting the mantra.
O Lord of Gods, this is that very *piṇḍa* which you have always desired;
I eat it before you so that I may have offspring.
"By the grace of that god, whatever my mind desires shall be attained;
for when Bhāskara is thus worshipped here, he becomes the bestower of sons."
Therefore, this lunar day (vāra) is proclaimed as the "son-bestowing" day of the Lord.
Thus, whatever man here always worships Bhāskara on this day,
being intent upon fasting during the śrāddha ceremony, he certainly obtains a son.
Wealth, grain, gold, health, and supreme happiness—
he himself attains the heavenly world and thereafter becomes a king among men.
In brilliance he resembled a twice-born brahmin, in luster he was like a jambū fruit;
in valor he was equal to the Lord of Rays (the Sun), and in depth he was like the one born from a jar (Agastya).

‘Non-hostile’ (*avirodhinaḥ*) means free from enemies. The four constellations named Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Hasta each consist of five stars. He whose banner is a preeminent bull (*gauḥ*) is ‘Govṛṣadhvaja’; for we see that words signifying excellence, such as *vṛṣa*, *vyāghra*, *puṅgava*, and *kuñjara*, appear as the final members of compounds in words like *Bharatarṣabha*. ‘God of gods’ (*devadevaḥ*) refers to the Sun. Here, fasting is on Saturday and the *śrāddha* rite is on Sunday; this will become clear from the passage beginning with “having risen in the morning. The consumption of the middle *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) here is understood to be performed by the sacrificer alone, whereas in other *śrāddhas* it is prescribed for the wife and thus belongs to her. Others, however, argue that since both husband and wife who desire a son have joint entitlement, and because of the specific mention [of the act], the consumption of the *piṇḍa* belongs to both; moreover, in other rites for obtaining a son, both are seen to consume the remainder of the oblation (*havis*). For example, in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: “Having cooked rice with milk, they should eat it with clarified butter,” and so forth. Likewise, in that same text, after the oblation: “Having offered and taken out [the portion], he eats; he gives [the remainder] to the other. ‘Lord of cattle’ (*gopatiḥ*) is the Sun, and he should be worshipped in the sky according to the method described in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* using an image of gold or similar materials. ‘White’ (*śvetaḥ*) refers to the six-syllabled solar mantra known as Mahāśvetā: *Oṃ śvaścolkāya namaḥ*. The offering of the *arghya* water should be made upon the sacrificial ground while facing the Sun situated in the sky. Because of the repetition of the word “having worshipped” (*pūjayitvā*), another object of worship is indicated; thus, the five deities—the planets, Bhūteśa (Śiva), and the others—should be worshipped on the pedestal with their own names preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending in the dative case. The ‘divine Maṅgas’ are a specific class of Brāhmaṇas known as Bhojakas, well-known in the northern regions; others are ‘terrestrial. Here, having seated the Maṅgas in the place of the Vaiśvadeva deities, one should seat other Brāhmaṇas in the place of the ancestors. Thus, the mention of repetition here is for the sake of attaining a specific fruit. ‘Radiance’ (*prabhā*) is brilliance; ‘twice-born’ (*dvijaḥ*) is the Moon. ‘Luster’ (*kāntiḥ*) is splendor. ‘Jambūka’ is Varuṇa, according to the Vedic text: “Varuṇa is indeed Jambūka. And Varuṇa is the Sun, as seen in the statement: “Varuṇa shines in the month of Māgha. ‘Lord of cattle’ (*gopatiḥ*) means Paśupati, that is, Śambhu. ‘Born from the jar’ (*kalaśodbhavaḥ*) is Agastya, and he is intended here as being exceedingly profound due to his drinking of the very deep ocean.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"When the fourth lunar day occurs conjoined with a white Tuesday,
a Brahmin who performs a *śrāddha* with faith does not become a *preta* after death."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "If the Moon [is in conjunction] on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), or the Sun on the seventh,
or if there should be a Tuesday on the fourteenth or the fourth."
Then, by one desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors, a *śrāddha* should be performed;
for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
the ancestors rejoice in heaven, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
For indeed, for as long as that time lasts, such is the fruit for the one who performs the act of faith.
Thus end the days for optional rites.
Now follow the optional rites for miscellaneous times.
Regarding this, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
"O Lord of Men, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight in every month..."
Likewise, one should perform the rites on the Aṣṭakās; now hear from me the times for optional rites.
Upon learning that a distinguished person worthy of the *śrāddha* has arrived, or a twice-born man,
one should perform the *śrāddha*, as well as during the *vyatīpāta* yoga or at the solstices (*ayana*).
O protector of the earth, when the equinox occurs, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
it is equal in all the zodiacal signs as the sun moves through them.
One should perform it likewise at the onset of the month of Nabhasya during afflictions caused by the stars and planets.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The Śrāddha should be performed on the new moon day, month after month, when the moon has waned."
Likewise, learn from me the times for which the *aṣṭakā* sacrifices must necessarily be performed:
upon obtaining distinguished Brahmins, during solar and lunar eclipses,
at the two solstices (*ayana*), at the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), at the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*), and during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, O son.
When there is an abundance of materials suitable for a śrāddha, upon the manifestation of suffering,
or during afflictions of one's birth star or house, one may perform a śrāddha according to one's desire.
Viṣṇu also said:
At the transits [of the sun], at the equinoxes, especially at the two solstices,
during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, at one's own birth-star, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses.
Thus Prajāpati has declared these times for the *śrāddha* as being conducive to the fulfillment of desires;
whatever *śrāddha* is offered during these occasions leads to infinite results.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "One who is always pure should diligently perform the *śrāddha* on the new moon day;
he attains all desires and, at the end, enjoys heaven."
One should offer clarified butter on the new moon day; this is the great means for the nourishment of Soma.
Thus nourished, Soma shall sustain the three worlds.
Constantly worshipped and praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas,
he is honored with all kinds of beautiful flowers and every kind of desirable provision.
Seated in a celestial chariot, he was entertained by thousands of Apsarases with dance, instrumental music, and song; devoted to his father and firm in his vows, he remained there in play.

The gods, gandharvas, and hosts of siddhas always praise him. One who is devoted to the ancestors shall obtain all desires by worshipping the ancestors and the gods with devotion on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), because on this day the fruit is inexhaustible.
Likewise: "Bringing about nourishment, progeny, memory, intelligence, sons, and even sovereignty,
one who performs [the rite] on the full moon day attains everything in its entirety."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The rite for the Nāndīmukhas should be performed every year on the full moon day when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo, according to the words of Varāha."

On whichever day during the month of Bhādrapada the sun enters the zodiac sign of Virgo (Kanyā), one should perform the *śrāddha* for the *nāndīmukha* ancestors on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) occurring within that same month. This is obligatory because of the scriptural injunction stating "year after year" (*pratyabdam*). Furthermore, by the term *nāndīmukha*, those who are beyond the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) are intended here; for immediately following this very statement in the same Purāṇa it is said: "Those who are above the grandfather—those three are the *nāndīmukhas*."

"Because they are auspicious, you should have the notion that their faces are serene. In this context, by the word "grandfather" (pitāmaha), the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) is implied, as stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather."
"For these three ancestors are proclaimed as the 'Tear-faced' (aśrumukha);
those three who preceded them are remembered as the 'Joyful-faced' (nāndīmukha). Thus it is said.

Now, since this statement regarding the *nāndīmukha* ancestors is intended to form a single syntactical unit with the injunction for the *śrāddha* occasioned by the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) are not to be understood by the term *nāndīmukha* in other types of *śrāddha*. Furthermore, what is the purpose of the designation *nāndīmukha* applied to these? Just as in the passage "the ancestors have gone" (*pitaraḥ gatāḥ*) and so forth, the word "and" (*ca*) is used to enjoin the perception of non-difference (*abheda-dṛṣṭi*) between the [ordinary] ancestors and those [specific ones], so too here the word is used to enjoin the perception of non-difference between the Pitṛ-gaṇa mentioned in the section on the divisions of the Pitṛ-gaṇas belonging to the Vārāha-kalpa and the Pitṛ-gaṇa known as the *nāndīmukha*. By this, it is shown that the derivation of the word *nāndīmukha*—from the phrase beginning "because their faces are serene" (*prasannamukha-saṃjñāḥ*)—is intended because of their connection with a joyful countenance (*nandana-mukha*). Therefore, it is not for the purpose of teaching the perception of non-difference. Furthermore, just as in the case of the monthly *agnihotra* sacrifice of the Kauṇḍapāyinas, the use of a word from another context (*para-śabda*) applied elsewhere indicates a transfer of properties (*tadvadbhāva*) for the sake of extending the rules of the regular *agnihotra*, so too here the word *nāndīmukha* is intended to extend the well-known rules of the *nāndīmukha* performed at times such as the birth of a son. This has already been answered above: for this word "other" (*para*) is not used with the intention of expressing similarity to another, but rather because of the connection with a joyful countenance. Thus, we consider its purpose to be purely commendatory (*praśaṃsā*).
Hārīta says: The Aṣṭakā rites, the first [funeral offerings], rites for prosperity, pilgrimages, and the attainment [of goals]—
this is remembered as the constant purpose of the monthly offerings, which exceeds [the requirements for] the ancestors.
In the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vāyu Purāṇas*:
"Now I shall proclaim Time, which is honored in the rite of *śrāddha*—
whether performed for specific desires, on special occasions, or as a constant duty— by those who follow the prescriptions for the *śrāddha* ceremony."
And the three Aṣṭakā rites shall have the propitiation of the ancestors as their root.
Thus end the optional rites with miscellaneous timings. Now follows the general determination of the lunar day (*tithi*) for the *śrāddha*.
In that regard, if the lunar day on which the *śrāddha* is prescribed spans two days, then the *śrāddha* should be performed on the day during which it extends through the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).
And thus says the Nigama:
"Lunar days (tithis) occurring in the forenoon bestow the fruits of rites for the gods;
likewise, those occurring in the afternoon should be known as bestowing auspicious results for the sake of the ancestors."
Dakṣa says:
Rituals for the gods should be performed in the forenoon, those for humans at midday, and those for the ancestors in the afternoon; these duties should be carried out with diligence.
But when [the tithi] extends into the afternoon on both days, then the former alone is to be accepted.
As Bṛhanmanu says:
"The ancestors honor that day upon which the sun sets."
For the lunar days were bestowed upon them by the Self-born One during the afternoon.
Manu also says:
"The ancestors attend that [time] at which the sun sets,
for it was by the Self-born One himself given to the ancestors during the afternoon."
The meaning is that for the ancestral rite (*pitṛkārya*), that [day] in which the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) persists until sunset is recommended, but not one connected merely with sunset.
And so too Hārīta says:
"The afternoon belongs to the ancestors; it is that which follows after the afternoon."
She is to be accepted for the ancestral rites, provided she does not follow after the forenoon.
But when [the tithi] is not found to extend into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) on either of the two days, then too it is the former [day]. Thus said Vṛddhayājñavalkya:
"For rites for the gods (*devakārya*), the lunar day (*tithi*) is to be known as that upon which the sun has risen."
Regarding rites for the ancestors, the lunar day (tithi) on which the sun sets is to be known [as the one to be observed];
this is stated in the *Śivarahasya* and the *Saurapurāṇa*.
"Those desiring the fruits of the gods should fast on that very lunar day morning after morning."
For the great seers have declared that the ancestral rite (paitra) is the root for the purpose of satisfying the ancestors.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa it is also said:
"The wise know that the end of the lunar day (tithi), known as the 'divine' (surākhya), is indeed to be observed as the fast;
whereas the root of the lunar day, known as the 'ancestral' (pitrya), has been declared by those learned in the scriptures who are experts in time."
Regarding rites for the ancestors (pitrya), it is stated by the ancients that one should touch [the moon] at the time of its setting;

in that case, the lunar day belonging to the rising [period] is not to be taken. For rites for the gods (daiva), however, the lunar day belonging to the rising [period] is to be taken. Gobhila also says:
That [lunar day] which extends through the evening (sāyāhna) is declared to be the one for the Pārvaṇa rite;
that too must be accepted as connected with sunset and endowed with at least three muhūrtas.
Thus says Baudhāyana:
When the sun has risen, that is the time for offerings to the gods; when the sun has set, it is for the ancestors.
For two muhūrtas after sunrise and three muhūrtas before sunset, that is the tithi for offerings to both the gods and the ancestors.
Manu says: "The ancestors attend to that [lineage] in which the sun sets,
for it was given to the ancestors by the Self-born during the afternoon."

From the statement that "only that which extends into the afternoon and is connected with sunset should be accepted, and not that which is devoid of it," it is understood that [the rite] should not be performed at all due to the absence of the prescribed time and the resulting lack of qualification. True; however, in reality, even when [the period] lasts for only three *muhūrttas*, one should take as much of the lunar day (*tithi*) and so forth as there is on the following day—whether it be a decrease or an increase—even if it was not visible on the preceding day, for the sake of one's own ritual duty.

Because of this statement, since it is possible [to perform the rite] even in the afternoon by calculating an extended duration, [the tithi] should be accepted as occurring on the following day when there is a decrease, equality, or increase of that day. And so Vyāghra says:
"Diminution (kharva), pride (darpa), and likewise violence (hiṃsā)—these are the three characteristics of a tithi."
The two later [periods], Kharva and Dapa, are to be honored; indeed, violence belongs to the earlier period.

Regarding the distinction between the subject matter of these statements: for a *śrāddha* on a specific lunar day (*tithi*), one should accept a lunar day that extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and a lunar day that extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
"The wise know the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*) to be of two kinds—two in the bright fortnight and likewise two in the dark fortnight;
those in the bright fortnight are to be accepted when they fall in the forenoon, and those in the dark fortnight when they fall in the afternoon."

Based on such statements as these, the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) are shown to be the first and latter parts of the day, according to the rule: "The forenoon is indeed until midday, and the afternoon is likewise thereafter. This is the conclusion; the rest is as before. However, when both [the lunar days] occupy an equal time and a single portion of the day, then—whether there is an increase, decrease, or equality [of duration]—only the latter [lunar day] is taken, and not the case where "only the latter is taken upon an increase, while upon decrease or equality the former is taken," because the statement "the former must be performed" and so forth refers specifically to the lunar day of death, and because there is no reason to bypass the first [lunar day].

Whatever time is prescribed for a particular action becomes an integral part of that action when it is present at its commencement; however, it is not so if the commencement has already been abandoned.
Because of such statements as these, furthermore, in the case of *ekoddiṣṭa* and other types of *śrāddha*, that lunar day (*tithi*) which extends through midday (*madhyāhna*) should be accepted.
And so says Vṛddhagautama:
"In an *ekoddiṣṭa*, the lunar day should be that which extends through midday."
[528] That lunar day which extends through the afternoon shall be the one for the *pārvaṇa* rite. Baudhāyana also says:
"The lunar day that extends through midday, whether it belongs to the preceding or the following [lunar phase],"
In that [lunar day], offerings should be given to the ancestors; neither decrease nor increase is a cause for concern.
And so says Hārīta:
"The *āmaśrāddha* is performed in the forenoon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday,
the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) in the morning."
In the case of a *daivika* śrāddha, however, the lunar day (*tithi*) that extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) should be taken;
for according to such scriptural statements as, "For whatever rite there is a specific time, the lunar day must extend over that time," and because that [forenoon] alone is prescribed for it.
And so Manu says:
"The *daivika* śrāddha is in the forenoon, the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon,
the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi-nimittaka*) in the morning."
The definition of the *daivika-śrāddha* as stated by Pāraskara should be accepted:
"That which is performed with the deities in view is called *daivika*;
one should perform it diligently on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions, just like the daily *śrāddha*."

This is the conclusion; the rest is as before. Even when, due to the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*), both [days] cover the entire period for the ritual, or due to its decrease, neither touches the period for the ritual, then the latter alone is to be accepted.
"That lunar day, lasting two *muhūrtas* or three [parts] of the day, is for offerings to the gods and ancestors:
the rite for the gods when the sun has risen, and that for the ancestors when the sun has set."
For vows such as fasting, even a single *ghaṭikā* [of the lunar day] is seen at sunrise;
that lunar day is to be known as the one for [deities], while the opposite is for the ancestors (*paitṛka*).
Because of this statement.

Now, one might object: by virtue of this very statement, even when [the moonrise] extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), and even when at its rising it covers two and a half *muhūrtas* thus extending into the forenoon, why is not the later [lunar day] accepted? For the general rule, such as "of whichever rite... and so forth, applies here.

It is said: True. Where the lunar day (*tithi*) extends across both days [of the ritual period] or does not touch the time of the rite at all, there arises a doubt as to which lunar day should be adopted; and when there is a need for a scriptural statement to resolve this, the lunar day prescribed by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) is adopted, because a specific rule takes precedence over a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*). However, in the present case, since the prescribed lunar day is obtained within the very same day during the prescribed time for the rite, there is no doubt as to which lunar day should be adopted, and thus there is no occasion for a decisive statement. This concludes the general determination regarding *śrāddha*. Now, the time for the *preta-śrāddha*:

In that regard, Āśvalāyana—establishing the designation of *navaśrāddha* for those performed during the ten-day period for the deceased who have not yet been formally named (un-named) and for whom the rites are being carried out—considers the time for *navaśrāddha* to extend up to the end of the tenth day, stating: "The *navaśrāddha* lasts for ten days, while that mixed with the new [impurity] lasts for six seasons. Thus, Bhartṛyajña, in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, describes the division of place and time according to the number of days and states that the *navaśrāddha* also includes the eleventh-day rite:
"Listen now to these three [rites] intended for the purpose of the collection of bones (*sañcayana*)."
In whatever place death may occur, one should perform the śrāddha rite in that very place.
Then there is the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the path where rest was made;
thereafter, the third *śrāddha* is prescribed at the place of the funeral pyre (*sañcayana*).
Likewise, it is performed on the fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth days.
Indeed, those nine *śrāddhas* take place on the tenth and eleventh days;
when the Vaitaraṇī [river] has been reached, one then attains satisfaction.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "O twice-born ones, on the third day, the *śrāddha* for the deceased should be performed on the funeral pyre; at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), they declare that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is to be performed in the home."
Kātyāyana said: That which is given here for a living being on the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh day, is called the *navaśrāddha*.
Vyāsa says:
That which is indeed offered on the first, seventh, ninth, and eleventh day after birth is called the *navaśrāddha*.
Śaṅkha says:
One may perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day even if one is impure;
there is purity for the performer at that specific time, but he remains impure thereafter.
"Ādyam" means the first. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"In the case of immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca), [the offering] should be given on the eleventh day for the deceased."
That very day [is auspicious] for him regarding the funeral feast, the bed, the seat, and so forth.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "And for the deceased, one should feed the twice-born at the door of the house on the fourth day;
on the second day, the rite of shaving (kṣurakarma) should be performed by the kinsmen."
On the fourth day, he should perform the collection of the bones with all his kinsmen;
he should feed an even number of pure Brahmins with faith.
On the fifth, the ninth, and likewise on the eleventh day, one should feed an even number of Brahmins; they know that to be the *navaśrāddha*.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
on the fourth day for Brāhmaṇas, on the fifth day for kings,
on the ninth day for those of the Vaiśya caste, and after the tenth day for Śūdras.
Atri says:
For the sake of the deceased, one should feed Brāhmaṇas at the end of the period of impurity;
however, for the purpose of the *navaśrāddha*, one should feed one on the eleventh day.

This being the case, it is understood that the feeding of Brahmins, which is prescribed at the end of the period of impurity following the *navaśrāddha* on the eleventh day, constitutes a separate rite (*karmāntara*). Bṛhaspati states: "On the fourth day, food indeed should be given to the Brahmins by the kinsmen."
One should give cows, gold, and wealth according to one's ability for the sake of the deceased.
"On the fourth day" means on the day of accumulation (*saṃcayāha*). "One should diligently give that which was desired by him while he was alive"—the meaning is:
one should give whatever was "desired" (*iṣṭam*), that is, whatever was cherished, "by him" (*tasya*), the deceased, while he was "alive."
Thus ends the time for the nine *śrāddhas*.
Now, regarding those well-known as the sixteen *śrāddhas*:
The time for the *śrāddha* rites for deceased persons (*preta*). Regarding this, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"For men who have abandoned their country, sixteen *śrāddhas* must always be performed."
Likewise, in the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and the eleventh.

Then, over the course of twelve months, the śrāddha rites should be performed twelve times according to the number [of months] as prescribed by the Śruti; on those occasions, one should feed Brahmins.
Jātūkarṇya says:
The twelve monthly [śrāddhas], the first, the two half-yearly ones,
and the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa— this constitutes the sixteen śrāddhas.
He provides a definition of the two *śrāddhas* prescribed by the term "six-monthly" (*ṣāṇmāsika*):
"When six months are less than a single day, or when [the period] is less than a year by three [days],
then those two are the six-monthly *śrāddhas*."

The meaning is that when six months or a year are deficient by one day or three days, then the *ṣāṇmāsika* (six-month) and *ābdika* (annual) *śrāddhas* should be performed. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"At the collection of the bones, the *śrāddha* is performed, as well as the monthly ones at the three-fortnight mark."
And likewise, on two empty lunar days, one should perform the sixteen śrāddhas for the deceased.
"Of two empty lunar days" means that [the rites] are performed on a day less than the sixth or the twelfth month; such is the meaning.
Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"The six-monthly and annual Śrāddhas should both take place on the very preceding day."
The monthly rites should be performed on their own respective days, and also on the twelfth day.
Likewise: "One should perform the sixteen śrāddhas prior to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa;
all of them indeed should be performed according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the twelfth day, at the end of the month, after three fortnights,
and thereafter every month for as long as a year, the rite should be performed by the twice-born."
After that, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should be performed in due order.
Once the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed, the pārvaṇa śrāddha is prescribed once again.
From that point forward, having been released from the state of a preta, he attains the status of a pitṛ.
Vyāghrapāda says:
On the eleventh day, in the fourth month, and in every subsequent month,
as well as annually on the anniversary of death, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Kātyāyana states the specific rule regarding the *śrāddha* for one who has died with the sacred fires (*agnimat*):
"The *śrāddha* for one who maintained the sacred fires should be performed on the eleventh day after the cremation;
however, they always perform the obligatory (*dhruva*) rites on the anniversary days of his death."
Those [rites] after three fortnights are "uncertain" (adhruva). For this very reason, Jātūkarṇya says:
"The Śrāddha which occurs after three fortnights should take place on the actual day of death;
however, for a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni), one should perform it before the cremation."
Hārīta, however, has stated alternative time-periods for monthly rites in cases where one lacks the capacity:
"The primary *śrāddha* is performed month by month; if that is not possible, one should perform it every season, or every twelve days, or all twelve on a single day."

In the subsequent section, the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite upon the occurrence of an anniversary will be discussed; its basis for the postponement of the monthly (*māsika*) rites and their repetition will also be explained therein. Here, however, it is established that the monthly rites must be performed precisely at the commencement of each month. For a monthly rite is so called because of its connection with a month, and this connection with a month is possible even through a connection with a day falling within that month. Thus, since there is no reason to bypass the first month, it is concluded that the performance must indeed begin with the month itself. Consequently, the sequence prescribed in the *Kalpasūtra*—"one should offer the sixteen *śrāddhas* in order: the first monthly, the deficient monthly (*ūnamāsika*), the second monthly, the three-fortnightly (*traipakṣika*), the third, fourth, fifth, deficient sixth-monthly, the sixth-monthly, the seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh monthly, and the annual (*ābdika*)"—is also rendered consistent. Otherwise, that sequence would not hold, as the deficient sixth-monthly occurs after the sixth month, and the same applies elsewhere. As for the statement that "thereafter, in twelve months, the *śrāddhas* are performed in a number of ten," implying that the monthly rite should be done at the end of the month, that should be disregarded as it cannot withstand scrutiny. Therefore, both by logical consistency and in accordance with traditional practice, it is established that the monthly rites commence with the month itself.
Thus are the times for the sixteen śrāddhas as they are well known.
Now, regarding the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*:

when the ten monthly rites have been performed at their proper times and the full year has elapsed, thereafter is the standard time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*).
And likewise, in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, after describing the monthly Śrāddhas, it is stated:
"Then, when a full year has passed, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa is duly performed by men; the procedure for that is now declared."

[535] Regarding the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* performed by one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*), which has as its presiding deity one who likewise maintains no fire, and concerning other occasional times, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "O bull of the Bharatas, the sacrificer who maintains no fire should indeed perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the deceased who maintained no consecrated fire (*anāhitāgni*) once a full year has elapsed."

And it was said by Pulastya: "One who maintains no sacred fires shall, according to dharma, perform the sapinda-rite for his father and mother when a full year has elapsed, or on whatever day an auspicious occasion (vṛddhi) occurs."

“*Vṛddhi*” refers to an auspicious occasion (*abhyudaya*) such as the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the investiture of the sacred thread (*mauñjī*), or marriage. This is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical term), including every ritual action that serves as the cause for a *nāndīśrāddha*. This will become clear from Uśanas’s statement, “Upon the occurrence of [events] such as the study of the *Svapnādhyāya*,” and from Śāṭyāyana’s statement, “The *nāndīmukha* belongs to the performer. The meaning is this: on whichever day an *vṛddhi* occurs, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* by anticipation (*apakṛṣya*) prior to that day, and then perform the *śrāddha* known as *nāndīmukha*, which is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of that [sapiṇḍīkaraṇa]. By this, it is also shown that for one who has commenced the entitlement [to the rites] and has completed the *pretaśrāddha*, there exists an entitlement to the *nāndīmukhaśrāddha* as an ancillary part of the *caula*, *mauñjī*, marriage, or the establishment of the sacred fires (*adhāna*).
Laghuhārīta says: "A brother, or a brother's son, a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the prosperity-rite (abhyudaya)."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is established as taking place after one year;
however, if there is to be an occasion for a prosperity-rite (*vṛddhi*), one may perform it even before that."
Intending to refer to the postponement [of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*] prior to the *nāndīśrāddha*, which is an ancillary part of the *ādhāna*, Uśanas says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father [is normally performed] in the annual [śrāddha] during the year of death;
however, upon the occurrence of the *ādhāna* and other such rites, this [should be done] even before that year."

In that case, since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is being postponed, according to the principle that "when the final rite is postponed, all preceding rites are likewise postponed," one must postpone and perform the prior monthly (*māsika*) and other offerings before performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
Vṛddha-Śiṣṭha also says:
"One should not perform the *sapiṇḍana* without having first offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*."
But once that [impurity] has been removed, the deceased no longer remains a *preta* and attains the state of a *pitṛ*.
This applies only to the case of reduction; however, in the absence of reduction, that [order] is established simply by the prescription of the sequence.
For this very reason, Śāṭyāyani says:
"All the *śrāddhas* for the deceased, as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
Having drawn [the deceased] away, one should perform [the rite]; then, while performing it, one should offer the Nāndīmukha.
As for the statement of Laugākṣi: "For one whose sapiṇḍīkaraṇa takes place before a year has passed,
the monthly offerings and the water-pot (udakumbha) must also be given for that year."

However, that [rule] should be explained as referring to the re-performance mentioned by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*—namely, "one should perform those very same rites again"—by means of the principle of postponement (*apakarṣanyāya*), even when the monthly rites (*māsika*) have already been performed. Regarding the phrase "having postponed," Uśanas says:

"But he who performs the *śrāddhas* for the deceased without being governed by the rules for prosperity (*vṛddhi-śāstra*), that performer of *śrāddhas* is cooked in a terrible hell together with his ancestors."

The meaning is that one who would postpone the *śrāddhas* for the deceased when an occasion for prosperity (*vṛddhi*) has not yet arrived—this non-postponement without a *vṛddhi-śrāddha* applies to those who are capable. However, in the case of those who are incapable, there is postponement even without the presence of an occasion for prosperity.
Regarding the alternative times for such postponement, Gobhila says:
"When a year, six months, or three fortnights have elapsed, or on whatever day an occasion for prosperity may occur."

On this point, some maintain a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*) that the two options—"at the completion of a year" or "on the day when an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) occurs"—apply exclusively to those who do not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*), whereas the two options—"after six months" or "after three fortnights"—apply exclusively to those who do maintain a sacred fire (*sāgnika*). To support this, they cite the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "For one who maintains the sacred fire, the time for the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite in connection with rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), and works of public utility (*āpūrta*) is after three fortnights;
however, one may also perform the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at the completion of the full year."

They also cite the statements regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnimat*). Regarding this, the following must be said: let those alternative views—such as the three fortnights and so forth—which possess the qualification of "one who maintains a fire," remain as they are; let them be the primary options (*mukhyakalpa*) for one who is capable of performing it at the end of the year. However, for one without a fire, let those alternatives, being necessitated by incapacity and having attained syntactic unity with the view of the year-long interval mentioned in the relevant *Gobhila* sūtra, remain as secondary options (*anukalpa*). As stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* may take place when the year is complete, or even on an auspicious occasion (*abhyudaya*)."
According to the opinion of some, however, it should be on the twelfth day, or likewise on the eleventh.
Thus ends the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*).
Now follows the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*).
Regarding this, Laghuhārīta says:
But when there is no fire, O hero, the householder should then perform [the rite];
if the deceased possessed the sacred fire, the sapindikarana should indeed take place at the end of three fortnights.

In this case, if the householder performing the *śrāddha* is devoid of the *āhavanīya* fire, while the deceased possesses the *āhavanīya* fire, then the performer should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for that deceased person after three fortnights have elapsed from the day of death.
Likewise: "O King, when the sacrificer possesses the sacred fires and the deceased does not possess them..."
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed by the sons on the twelfth day;
here, it should be understood that this refers to the twelfth day starting from the anniversary of death.
Kātyāyana says:
Having first performed the rites on the eleventh day according to the rules prior to the new moon,
a Brahmin possessing the sacred fires should perform the sapindikarana for his mother and father.

The intention here is as follows: On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) must perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha. These rites have as their deities the father and others together with their wives, provided they are deceased. However, it is not possible for those two (the parents) to serve as deities in the *darśa-śrāddha* and other such rites if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed, because tradition records that this rite occurs at the time of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Therefore, thinking that the omission of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and the śrāddha should not occur, a fire-maintaining Brahmin, having completed the funeral rites on the eleventh day, should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of his mother and father on whichever day falls before the end of the ten-day period.
For this very reason, Prajāpati said: "A son who maintains the sacred fires (agnimān) shall not perform the Pitṛyajña as long as the sapinda-rite has not been completed;
by performing neither the Pārvaṇa nor the Abhyudaya rites, he does not obtain the fruit."
The mention of "Brahmins" (*vipra*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), since the same principle applies to Kṣatriyas and others as well.
Hārīta states another view:
"But that new moon day which occurs on the tenth day after the anniversary of death..."
On that day, a son who maintains the sacred fires must indeed perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for her.
The meaning is: starting from the day of death, on whichever day becomes the tenth, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) that follows it—on that day [the rite should be performed].
For this very reason, Jābāli says:
"A son who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the preceding new moon."
After ten nights have passed, and likewise another [rite] when the year is complete.

The meaning is that starting from the day of death, during the first *daśāha* (ten-day period) following that [period], a son who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his parents. The mention of "ten nights" is intended to indicate the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). Thus, three times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of one who maintains the fires have been stated: the twelfth day; any day prior to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurring after the ten-day period; and the new moon itself after the ten-day period. These are the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of those maintaining the fires. This applies to members of the three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*).
Now, regarding the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a *śūdra*:
with the phrase "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed" recurring [from the previous rule], Viṣṇu states:
"For *śūdras*, it is declared that [the rite] should be performed on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras."

The elders maintain that this refers to a Śūdra who performs the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*); by the force of the scriptural statement, the performance of the *śrāddha* is accepted even in the midst of the period of impurity (*āśauca*).
Thus ends the section on the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a Śūdra.
Now follows the determination of the annual time-periods. Among those, first is the determination of the anniversary of death (kṣayāha). In the Brahmapurāṇa:
Every year, on the anniversary of the day of their death, one should perform the rite for one's mother and father,
as well as for a childless paternal uncle and for an elder brother.

By the statement that "the *śrāddha* for the mother and others must be performed," it is implied by the sense that the duty falls upon sons and others. This is intended as an illustration of anyone who possesses the qualification [to perform the rite]. In the phrase "of the brother," the words "who is sonless" (*aputrasya*) are to be supplied. By the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya*), however, it is shown that the annual *śrāddha* is not mandatory for the younger brother.
And so it is said:
"The father shall not give [the *śrāddha*] for his son, nor likewise the elder brother for his younger brother."

Thus, because the restriction regarding eligibility has been removed, even the youngest son must perform the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) on account of an unrestricted eligibility such as affection (*sneha*).
And so it has been said:
"Out of affection, they may both perform [the rite], provided it is without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "O beautiful lady, he who does not perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of his father's death,
nor likewise for his mother at the end of the year on the anniversary of her death— "
O Great Goddess, neither I nor Hari accept his worship.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"Of all *śrāddhas*,
that which is performed by the wise on the anniversary of death is always considered the best, O best of birds."

O tiger among birds, he who does not perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of his father’s death, nor on the anniversary of his mother’s death at the end of the year—[541]—his ancestors remain unsatisfied for that entire year. Thus it is said. Furthermore, O best of birds, one should always perform the śrāddha with great care; otherwise, the ancestors do not accept it. One should offer food and drink with devotion to those who have passed away. By performing the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, one attains the highest state. Therefore, O bird, you should always perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of your parents’ deaths. By doing so, you will obtain great merit and reach the supreme goal. Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled “The Description of the Śrāddha Rite,” in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, within the section on the duties of householders. 542. What is the time? What is the place? And what is the fruit? Tell me all this in full. Viṣṇu said: Listen, O bird, I shall explain in detail how the śrāddha rite is performed, by whom it is performed, and what its fruit is. It should be performed with devotion using the best of grains, meat, and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar. One should offer these with devotion to the ancestors. O best of birds, neither I, nor Hari,
nor Brahmā, nor Rudra, nor any other hosts of deities accept his worship.
Therefore, O tiger among birds, a man— especially one who subsists on food— should diligently perform [the rite] every year on the anniversary of the day of death.
O Lord of Birds, that householder who does not perform the śrāddha for his mother and father every year on the anniversary of their death;
He goes to a terrible hell known by the name Tāmisra;
thereafter, he becomes a wicked-souled boar or a bird in a city.

In this context, by the term *mṛtāha* ("the day of death"), the lunar date (*tithi*) occurring on the day of death is intended, because at the end of a year, the actual day of death is impossible [to coincide]. For those same days do not revolve; indeed, individual days have neither specific names nor marks. Therefore, the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) would fall on whichever day [one might happen to be]. If it is argued that "the day is the reckoning of the end of the year," we say no; for this would render the inclusion of the word *mṛtāha* purposeless. Thus, the lunar date occurring on the day of death is what is intended. The mention of "day" (*ahaḥ*) is also a figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the night; therefore, even for one who dies at night, the lunar date that is obtained is the one used. And so, it is established that the annual rite should be performed at the end of the year on the lunar date associated with the day of death.
And in this regard: whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches upon rising—
that entire lunar day is to be known as valid for acts such as giving gifts and Vedic study.
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches when it sets.
That lunar day (tithi) which is known as complete should be understood as such for the performance of acts involving giving and study.

Thus, according to the statements of Devala and others, just as a lunar day (*tithi*) that is not actually present at the time of a ritual action is accepted by imagining it to be complete, it is not so with the lunar day occurring on the anniversary of death; rather, it is the lunar day existing precisely at the time of death that is to be accepted. Therefore, in the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*), the lunar day denoted by the term "death-day" should be understood as being that which exists at the moment of death.
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
"In the case of breaking a fast or the death of men, the lunar day is remembered as being that which exists at that very moment."
In the rite for the ancestors, when touched at the time of sunset, it is called "full."

"Immediate" (*tātkālikī*) means that for those two—the breaking of a vow such as fasting or death—the lunar day (*tithi*) belongs precisely to the time [of the event]; it is not, however, one that exists at a different time, such as one measuring three *muhūrtas* during the morning and so forth. In the case of ancestral rites (*pitrya*), such as the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) and others, even if the lunar day only touches the end of the day at the moment of sunset, it is declared to be "complete" (*sampūrṇā*) because it occurred at the time of death. This is what is meant: when the annual anniversary is to be performed on the lunar day coinciding with the time of death, if that day exists at the end of the day even at the hour of sunset, then—considering that it exists during the *kutapa* and *aparāhṇa* periods—one should perform the *śrāddha* at the *kutapa* time on that very day characterized by it. Alternatively, here the term "day of death" (*mṛtāha*) is intended to signify the full day and night (*ahorātra*) as distinguished by the three characteristics.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"On whichever day, touched by a particular month, fortnight, and lunar date, a person dies; they know that corresponding day each year to be his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death)."
The term "of such a nature" (*tathābhūtam*) refers to that which is endowed with the three characteristics mentioned.

Regarding this, Vyāsa states that for ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) lasting a year and so forth, only the lunar month (*cāndra*) is to be taken: "In marriage and similar occasions, the solar month is prescribed; in sacrifices and similar occasions, the civil month (*sāvana*) is prescribed."
"In the annual rite for the ancestors, the month is traditionally held to be lunar. Thus says Laghuhārīta:
"Since the sun revolves like a wheel by the power of time..."
Therefore, the annual Śrāddha should be performed, marked by the specific month.
The mark of the month must indeed be made starting with Pauṣa, Māgha, and so forth;
for it is by that procedure that the month is proclaimed.

The designations such as Pauṣa and so forth belong exclusively to the lunar month; for instance, that full moon night (paurṇamāsī) which is conjoined with the constellation Puṣya is called Pauṣī, and the month in which that occurs is the Pauṣa month. The same applies to Māgha and the others.
Thus said Pāṇini:
"A time conjoined with a lunar mansion [is named after it], and the name is applied when the full moon occurs on that day. (Pāṇini 4.2.3).

Furthermore, neither the solar nor the civil [days] possess such a designation, nor is there such a rule regarding the conjunction with the full moon; therefore, at the beginning of the annual cycle and other such occasions, only the lunar month is to be accepted.
As for the statement:
"In whichever zodiac sign the sun has entered when a human meets their end..."
The ancestral rite (pitṛkārya) on the anniversary of death should be performed in that very zodiacal sign.
This refers to the case of one who dies during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*).
If there is a deficiency caused by the intercalary month, one should rely upon the solar measurement;
that very day shall be the [proper] time for his *śrāddha*, funeral cakes, water libations, and so forth.

Now follows the determination regarding the conflict of dates for the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*). In that regard, when there is a conflict of lunar days (*tithi*) concerning the *śrāddha* for the anniversary of death, the day that pervades the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) is to be accepted.
As Vyāsa says:
"Whichever time belongs to a particular rite, the lunar day that pervades that time [is to be taken]."
In that manner one should perform actions; neither decline nor prosperity is the cause [for changing one's course].
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"At whatever time a rite is to be performed, the lunar day (*tithi*) must pervade that time.
Furthermore, the annual rite is of two kinds: the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Among these, the afternoon is the time for the *pārvaṇa*, and midday is the time for the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
And so says Vṛddha-Gautama:
"In the case of a rite for a single ancestor (ekoddiṣṭa), that lunar day (tithi) which extends through midday shall be used;
however, in the case of a rite for ancestors (pārvaṇa), that lunar day which extends through the afternoon shall be used."

On this point, some say: when there is equality of lunar days (*tithi*) such that both lunar days are connected with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), then for the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) which follows the procedure of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, the earlier lunar day alone is to be taken. Even though it is possible for the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) to extend into the following day as well, nevertheless, because there is no reason to bypass the first, the śrāddha must be performed on the very first day. Sumantu says: "If the lunar day of the anniversary of death should span two days..."
"One should offer the funeral ball in the east"—thus was spoken by the descendant of Aṅgiras.
Vṛddhayājñavalkya states:
For rites dedicated to the gods, the lunar day (tithi) on which the sun rises is to be known;
for rites involving the ancestral cakes (piṇḍa), the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be known.
In the *Śivarahasya* and the *Saura Purāṇa*:
"For those desiring divine rewards, the lunar day (*tithi*) should be observed as fasting at its end during the morning;
for the great sages have declared the ancestral portion (*paitra*) to be the root for the satisfaction of the ancestors. [545]
"Root" means the commencement.
Also in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"The wise know that the end of the lunar day, called *surā*, is indeed to be observed as a fast."
The root of the lunar day is declared by those learned in the scriptures and skilled in the knowledge of time to be the ancestral (paitra) period.
This is the traditional teaching: lunar days occurring in the forenoon are productive of fruit for rites dedicated to the gods;
likewise, those occurring in the afternoon should be known as bringing happiness for rites dedicated to the ancestors.
In this context, "afternoon" (aparāhṇa) should be understood as one of the various afternoons that will be described in the section on subtle time;
likewise, it is stated in the *Śivarahasya*, *Brahmavaivarta*, *Saura*, and *Nāradīya Purāṇas*:
"The new moon day, the full moon day, and the anniversary day of the father..."
"One who does not observe [the fast] when it is joined with the previous [tithi] falls into hell.
Thus, it is established that when there is equality of the lunar days (*tithi*), the earlier one is to be accepted.
However, regarding inequality, Baudhāyana says:
That lunar day on which the sun rises is the day-and-night (ahorātra) for the waxing fortnight;
however, in the waning fortnight, it is the one on which the sun sets.
Referring specifically to the day of waning (*kṣayāha*), he himself said:
"When the lunar day (*tithi*) of one who has passed away extends into the afternoon of two days,
it should be observed as the former on the day of waning, but on the day of waxing, the latter should be performed."
As for what Vyāghra stated regarding the adoption of the subsequent lunar day even when there is equality of duration—
"The three characteristics of a lunar day are deficiency (kharva), pride (darpa), and injury (hiṃsā).
Deficiency and pride are to be honored as belonging to the subsequent day, while injury belongs to the preceding time"— [546]

Thus, this general rule concerns lunar days other than the day of death; when there is an increase in the length of a lunar day such that it pervades the entire afternoon of two consecutive days, the later day is to be taken.

That is incorrect. For when, due to the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*), both [days] completely pervade the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), then even in the case of such an increase, the previous lunar day is rightly to be taken. This is because, as in the case of equality, there are numerous scriptural statements such as, "If it should pervade two days," and because of the principle stated in the rule, "Or the first [day] should be determined; transgression occurs only for a specific reason. Likewise, it will be stated that when there is equality in the pervasion of only a portion of the afternoon on two days, the previous one is to be taken. Similarly, when there is equality in the pervasion of the entire afternoon on two days, even in the case of an increase, the previous one is to be taken; in that case, the previous lunar day alone is to be accepted. Even if you argue that statements such as "If it should pervade two days" are applicable to cases other than the equality of a *kṣayāha* (the day of death), and that the *Kharva-śāstra* is applicable to cases of equality other than the general case of the day of death, yet all the scriptures must be set aside in favor of many other scriptures—this is not so. For the same logic applies to the case of increase as well. The statement, "When the lunar day of the deceased pervades two afternoons," refers to a situation where two lunar days equally pervade two portions of the afternoon. Otherwise, since it is impossible for both afternoons to be fully pervaded during a *tithi-kṣaya*, the injunction "In the case of decrease, the previous one should be performed" would be untenable. Furthermore, it is not proper to assume two separate sentences, as this would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Even if you think that a syntactical split is not a fault because the text is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), nevertheless, an assumption contrary to the principles of numerous scriptural statements is devoid of authority.

Others, however, say: when the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs on two days and is connected with the afternoon (aparāhṇa) on both, then in the case of decrease (kṣaya) the first day is taken, and in the case of increase (vṛddhi) or equality (sāmya), the second.
Regarding the rites of ancestral offerings (śrāddha), Śruti declares: "Sinīvālī and Kuhū are prescribed for the rite of śrāddha.
If these two [lunar phases] should fall at midday, how then could the śrāddha and other rites be performed?
When a lunar day (tithi) is diminished, it is known as Sinīvālī; when a lunar day is increased, it is remembered as Kuhū.
Even when they are equal, those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas should understand that it is Kuhū.
Because of this statement, it is the same even in other *śrāddhas*, since that [other *śrāddha*] is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *pārvaṇa*.
And so it has been said by Vyāsa:
"In the second and subsequent [rites], such as those involving rules (*niyama*), there is the worship of pairs."

"Because of the injunction regarding increase and decrease in the case of the expansion of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other rites. This is incorrect, because it contradicts the many statements cited above. Therefore, when a lunar day (*tithi*), due to its increase, occupies the entire afternoon on two days, then the former [day] alone is taken; but in the case of equality, if it occupies the entire afternoon on both days, that [rule] does not apply here. When neither of the two occupies the entire afternoon, then whichever one occupies a greater portion of the afternoon is to be accepted.
And so says Hārīta:
Regarding the afternoon for the ancestors, however, that [lunar day] which extends into the afternoon is to be accepted for ancestral rites;
one that follows after the preceding afternoon is not to be taken.

But when [the moonrise] occupies the entire afternoon on the second day, whereas on the previous day it occupied only a portion of it, then the second day alone is to be accepted because of its utility for the rite; for that time which is prescribed for a ritual action is an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) only if it exists at the commencement of that action, not if the commencement has already been abandoned.

Thus it is from the statement of Viṣṇu. In another place as well, it is stated that only the lunar day (tithi) associated with the yoga of Ārdrā is to be taken: "Even if the new moon (amāvāsyā) is pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta), or if it is mixed with the first day (pratipad), it should be accepted by the wise for rites pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya) during the time of Kutapa."
In the Matsya Purāṇa as well, the commencement [of the rite] is prescribed specifically at the Kutapa time:
"Since the sun always becomes dim at midday, therefore the commencement made then is distinguished as yielding infinite fruit. Thus it is said.

Nor should it be said that this specific rule—"even when the new moon [amāvāsyā] is pierced by the [preceding] lunar day"—applies only to the new moon and not elsewhere; for it is understood from the general rule regarding lunar days: "Whichever lunar day extends through midday, whether it be the preceding or the following one. However, when both [lunar days] equally occupy a portion of the afternoon, then, in the case of an increase in the lunar day (*tithivṛddhi*), the following one is to be taken; whereas in the case of a decrease (*kṣaya*) or equality (*sāmya*), the preceding one is to be taken. Thus it has been said:
When the lunar day (tithi) of one who has died extends across two afternoons,
it should be performed on the earlier one in the case of a decrease (kṣaya), but on the later one in the case of an increase (vṛddhi).

And from the cited statement, "The Darśa and the Pūrṇamāsa," even when there is equality [of duration], the former alone is to be taken, according to such statements as, "That which extends over two days. However, the *Kharva-śāstra* should be understood as referring to occasions other than those, in accordance with the many statements concerning the day of death (*kṣayāha*). For this very reason, the mention of *kharva* need not be made in the cited statement. When the former [tithi] extends through the afternoon (*sāyāhna*) and touches the afternoon of the following day, then the former alone is to be accepted. As it was said by Manu: "If the lunar day of the day of death should extend over two days..."
It should be performed as one that is pierced by the previous [tithi], provided it lasts for three muhūrtas.
And on this point Baudhāyana says:
"The rite for the gods is performed when the sun has risen, and that for the ancestors when the sun has set;
that lunar day which lasts for two muhūrtas during the three parts of the day is suitable for offerings to the gods and the ancestors."
