The meaning of this is as follows: when the sun has risen, for the two *muhūrtas* of the day that follow, it is "pertaining to the gods" (*daivata*), meaning it belongs to the deities; and when the sun has set, the three *muhūrtas* of the day belonging to that time are "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*), meaning they belong to the ancestral deities. Therefore, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) extends over such a duration of time is to be accepted, respectively, for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*). Thus, it being established that for these purposes the period of three *muhūrtas* prior to sunset is to be accepted, there is the statement found in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "In the case of vows, fasts, ritual baths, and so forth, even a single *ghaṭikā* [of the lunar day] which may occur..."

"That lunar day (tithi) is to be taken [as the one for the rite] when it occurs at sunrise, but the opposite in rites for the ancestors. Here, "the opposite" refers to that which is connected with sunset.
And as for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
"That which remains as even a single digit (kalā) at the time of sunset on that day is the one to be accepted for the annual śrāddha, and no other; [any other] causes the loss of sons.
And as for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"In the rite for the ancestors (pitrya), when touched at the time of sunset, it is called 'full' (pūrṇā).

This [statement] is intended as a praise for that [lunar day] which extends through three muhūrtas of the afternoon of the preceding day; it is not for the purpose of including one that lasts for only a few ghaṭikās, because such a duration is insufficient for the performance of the ritual, and because on the following day there is the availability of a time that covers the afternoon sufficient for the ritual. For this very reason, Hārīta says:

"The afternoon belongs to the ancestors; that [tithi] which follows the afternoon is to be accepted for rites for the ancestors, but not the earlier one which follows the setting of the sun. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa as well.

When even a single ghaṭikā remains for the observance of a vow, fast, or religious restriction, that lunar day (tithi) is to be known as complete; however, for rites pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya), it is the afternoon portion that is authoritative.
And words such as "astam" (setting) refer specifically to the afternoon;
thus says Vṛddha-Manu:
"The ancestors attend upon that time at which the sun goes to its setting."
For the lunar days were granted to them by the Self-Existent One in the afternoon.
Manu also says:
"The ancestors worship that [day] on which the sun sets;
for it was given by the Self-Existent One to the ancestors during the afternoon."

However, the inclusion of the [tithi] connected with sunset is not appropriate here, because the performance of a *śrāddha* is prohibited at the time of sunset. Furthermore, even in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), if a *śrāddha* were performed when the lunar day (*tithi*) that serves as the occasion for the *śrāddha* is absent, then the statement "they wait upon her" would be untenable; moreover, since the afternoon has already been assigned [to another purpose], the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) stating the reason—"because they wait upon her"—would be inconsistent, and the injunction "they wait upon her" would lack coherence. Moreover, by the word "sunset" alone, the afternoon is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—just as in the expression "he stands in the fire"—in the following passage: "By the *Ṛgveda* the god moves in the sky at dawn; he stands in the *Yajurveda* at midday; he does not set in the *Sāmaveda*; never empty of the three Vedas, the Sun moves. If only the phrase "he sets" were intended there, then since the Sun has no connection with the deity [the sacrificer] during the afternoon, the concluding statement "he is empty of them" would be impossible. Therefore, the meaning of "he sets" (*astam eti*) must be understood as "he goes near the setting," that is, into the afternoon. Thus, wherever in the *Smṛti* a *śrāddha* is prescribed for a lunar day connected with sunset, it should be understood that the *śrāddha* is prescribed for that very lunar day which extends into the afternoon. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statements regarding the *kutapa*, *rohiṇa*, and *aparāhṇa* periods.
On the day at the time of sunset, whatever lunar day (tithi) remains even by a single digit (kalā), that alone is to be used for the annual śrāddha; any subsequent day causes the loss of one's sons.

If, based on this statement, it were held that the lunar day (*tithi*) which exists at the very time of sunset is the one to be taken for the annual *śrāddha*, then by the force of that statement, the *śrāddha* would necessarily occur at the time of sunset itself. If it were argued that it is not performed then because of the prohibition of the *śrāddha* during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) period and its vicinity, then—since the lunar day of death is absent during the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*)—the purpose of the injunction "that very same [day] is for the annual [śrāddha]" would not be fulfilled if the rite were performed then. Consequently, the performance would instead take place on the other lunar day, which is the one prohibited as being a source of the loss of sons.
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches at its rising,
that entire day is to be known as valid for bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and other such rites.
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches at its setting,
that lunar day is to be known as complete for the performance of rites such as giving gifts and Vedic study.

If it is argued that, because these two statements by Devala declare both lunar days (*tithi*) associated with sunrise and sunset to be "entire" (*sakala*), an action performed at any time during them is considered as if performed according to the prescribed rule—this is not so. For just as the previous day’s [lunar day] is "entire" through its connection with sunset, so too is the subsequent day "entire" through its connection with sunrise. Since it exists on both days at the time of sunset, it cannot be determined which one is intended for the annual rite (*pratyābdika*); thus, it would be impossible to prescribe whether the earlier or the later is to be taken, and to prohibit the other on the grounds that it causes the loss of a son. Furthermore, if this metaphorical "entirety" defined in such a way were accepted, then all lunar days would be "entire" simply by virtue of being connected to sunrise and sunset, and there would never be an "incomplete" (*khaṇḍa*) lunar day. In that case, since all [lunar days] would be "entire" and would therefore pervade the entire time required for any ritual action, [the distinction between complete and incomplete days would vanish].
"Whichever time is prescribed for whom, the lunar day (tithi) that extends through that time is the one to be used.
That lunar day which extends through midday shall be the one for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
that which extends through the afternoon shall be the one for the *pārvaṇa* rite."

Since there would be nothing to be set aside by such a collection of statements, they would indeed be purposeless. Furthermore, here, is the prescription for the annual *śrāddha* at the moment of sunset intended as an exception to the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), or rather as an exception to the three *muhūrta*s—namely, "two *muhūrta*s of the day" and "the third part of the day"—which amounts to an exception to three *muhūrta*s? In the first case, there is a contradiction with the Vedic scripture stating, "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors.
As it is said in another *smṛti*:
"The afternoon belongs to the ancestors, that which follows the afternoon..."
That which is to be accepted in the rites for the ancestors is not that which follows after them.

Thus, even when the lunar day (*tithi*) is complete, the *śrāddha* would still be applicable at the time of sunset. Furthermore, by the term "annual" (*pratyābdika*), is a *śrāddha* meant, or some other rite? Even in the case of it being a *śrāddha*, as long as it is determined—on the basis of other authorities—that it refers to either the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha-śrāddha*) or the *śrāddha* on the third day of the month of Akṣaya, it cannot in any way be contradicted by the Vedic injunction that "the afternoon belongs to the ancestors. In the second alternative, this is the distinction: if the *śrāddha* were performed in the afternoon in the absence of the specific lunar day, the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death would not have been performed.
On whatever day of a month or fortnight, touched by a specific lunar date (tithi), a person dies;
they know that corresponding day of each year to be his anniversary of death (mṛtāha).

This is because of its definition as such. Furthermore, it should not be argued that even so, since the day is touched by the lunar day (*tithi*) existing at the end of the day, that day would become his "death-day" (*mṛtāha*), and thus the *śrāddha* would also apply there. For it is said:
"For one who is without the sacred fire (*anagnimat*), [the death-day is] when he departs; for one with the sacred fire (*sāgni*), it is from the time of the consecration rite (*saṃskārakarman*)."
Purification occurs after the collection [of the bones] and cremation; however, the anniversary of death is according to the lunar day.

Thus, it is stated that the "day of death" (mṛtāha) is determined by the lunar day (*tithi*) present at the time of death, and not by the conjunction of the lunar day with the actual moment of death. Otherwise, if two lunar days were to coincide on a single day, the *śrāddha* would have to be performed on both; or else, since there would be no distinction, it would not be performed anywhere at all. Furthermore, in such injunctions as "one should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) on the preceding [lunar day]," the locative case indicates that the lunar day serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). If the *śrāddha* were performed without that specific lunar day, one should know that the rite is as if unperformed, for:

"A rite performed at the wrong time, devoid of the prescribed rules and purity, should be understood as not done at all; the sacrifice must be performed again, by the force of the scriptural injunction."

Thus it follows; therefore, the meaning of the phrase "touched by the month, fortnight, and lunar day" is this: on whichever month, in whichever fortnight, and on whichever lunar day a person died, that is his "day of death" (*mṛtāha*) as long as those [periods] remain current. Regarding the term "time of sunset": does it refer to the evening twilight, or to a time before or after it? In the first case, the word "day" (*ahni*) would be inappropriate; for the elders employ the word "day" when the solar disc is perceived in its entirety. In the second case, every moment from midday onwards would constitute the "time of sunset."
At its rising, the sun should shine with increasing rays until midday;
thereafter, it goes to its setting with diminishing rays.

This is because the *Purāṇa* establishes that the time connected with the setting of the sun occurs after midday; were that the case, there would be no contradiction with the Vedic injunction, "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors. Nor is the third position tenable, as the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "on the day" and "at the time of sunset" would be untenable. Therefore, this is the meaning of the statement: on the day, at the time of sunset—that is, during the day, at the time of sunset which is proximate to the setting, namely the fifth division known as *sāyāhna* consisting of three *muhūrttas*—whatever portion, even if only a fraction of a moment (*kalā*), exists upon its commencement, that alone is to be accepted for the annual rite (*pratyābdika*), because it pervades the *aparāhṇa* consisting of the five *muhūrttas* suitable for the *śrāddha*. Any other [time], such as the preceding one which resides only in *sāyāhna* and does not pervade the *aparāhṇa* fit for the *śrāddha*, is the cause of the loss of sons and should not be accepted. In this sense of the statement, nothing is illogical. Nor is there any pointlessness or contradiction with other texts. Alternatively, when the [tithi] pervades the entire time of sunset as commonly known in the world on the first day, but pervades only a portion of it on the second day, then the *śrāddha* is restricted to the second day by way of an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding lunar day (*tithi*). Thus, the view of the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*—"even a lunar day touched by sunset is to be taken as the previous one"—is faultless. Nor should it be argued that the *śrāddha* cannot be performed because of the absence of a time joined with the lunar day in the *aparāhṇa*, since there is no possibility of the lunar day's conjunction in a time other than the latter half of the fourth watch (*prahara*). As Vasiṣṭha says in the *Nāradīyapurāṇa*: [He] who performs the *śrāddha* on the day when the moon sets while the tithi is still present, even if it is only for a moment, he obtains the fruit of the *śrāddha* for a year. Thus, there is no inconsistency. Furthermore, the *Smṛtyarthasāra* states: "If the tithi extends into the *aparāhṇa* of the following day, the *śrāddha* should be performed on that [following] day. This is because the *aparāhṇa* is defined as the time from the end of the fourth watch until the setting of the sun. Therefore, the view that the *śrāddha* must be performed on the day when the tithi exists during the *aparāhṇa* is established. Consequently, the view of the *Smṛticandrikā* and others—that the tithi touched by sunset is to be taken as the previous one—is not contradicted by the aforementioned texts. This is because the term *aparāhṇa* here refers to the period beginning from the end of the fourth watch, and since the conjunction of the tithi with that specific time is possible, there is no lack of opportunity for performance. Thus, the view of the *Smṛticandrikā* and others is indeed consistent with the authoritative texts. Therefore, the correct conclusion is that the *śrāddha* should be performed on the day when the tithi exists during the *aparāhṇa*, starting from the end of the fourth watch. This is the final determination. *Note: The original text contains a lacuna marked by brackets [554]. The translation reflects the available content.*

"For men, on the occasion of a fast (pāraṇa) or death, the lunar day (tithi) is considered to be that which exists at that specific moment. For rites pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya), however, the lunar day that touches upon the time of sunset is declared to be 'full' (pūrṇā).

The meaning is this: when the lunar day of death touches upon the time of sunset, that lunar day is declared to be "full" for ancestral rites such as the annual śrāddha (ābdika-śrāddha) to be performed on that day. By the phrase "touches upon the time of sunset," it should be understood that even if only a single minute (kalā) of the lunar day remains at the moment of sunset, the lunar day of death is still considered full.
As for another Smṛti text:
"The five nāḍīs at the end of the day are declared by the wise to be meritorious for rites pertaining to the ancestors as well as for those pertaining to the gods at sunrise."

Thus, the meaning is as follows: in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), the five *nāḍīs* (twenty-four minutes) occurring at the end of the day associated with the lunar date (*tithi*) prescribed as the proper time are meritorious; they bring about the merit produced by the conjunction of that specific *nāḍī* and *tithi*, but not those fewer than that. In rites for the gods (*daiva*), the five *nāḍīs* occurring at sunrise associated with the *tithi* prescribed as the proper time are meritorious; they bring about the merit produced by the conjunction of the *tithi* even for the *nāḍīs* following them, but not those fewer than that. This very point is stated [in the Smṛticandrikā]: "By performing the *śrāddha* on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) for the sake of gaining wealth, on the second for obtaining bipeds, and so forth—'A pure man who performs the *śrāddha* on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) with effort attains all desires'—this refers to the duality of the lunar dates beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) which are prescribed as the time for *śrāddha*, but it does not refer to the duality of lunar dates prescribed as the time for other types of *śrāddha*. For this statement is intended to specify a particular rule regarding that very context, having introduced the ancestral *śrāddha* as 'on the day of the dark fortnight, [the time] conjoined with sunset. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the previously cited statement of Vasiṣṭha."
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:

"When there is even a single ghaṭikā remaining for the observance of a vow or fast, that lunar day (tithi) should be known as complete; however, for the sake of the ancestors, the afternoon portion is what matters."

The meaning is that when one *ghaṭikā* of the afternoon remains close to the time of twilight (*saṃdhyā*), that lunar day (*tithi*) should be understood as being complete for the purpose of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). However, when the conjunction with the lunar day occurs on the previous day before sunset, and on the following day it lasts for three *muhūrtas* after sunset, then the latter day is the time for the *śrāddha*.
And so Sumantu says:
"The rite for the gods (*daivata*) is performed when the sun has risen; the rite for the ancestors (*paitrya*) when the sun has set."
"That lunar day (tithi) which lasts for two muhūrtas at either three times of the day is suitable for offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya). Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the sun has risen, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) related to the day and constituting a part of the rite for the gods (*daivakarma*) lasts for no less than two *muhūrtas*, that [day]—like a complete lunar day—renders the entire day a time for the offering of oblations (*havyadāna*); therefore, one should perform the rite for the gods on that day. When the sun has set, whichever lunar day constituting a part of the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*) continues for three *muhūrtas*, it renders the day connected with it a time for the offering of ancestral oblations (*kavyadāna*); therefore, one should perform the annual *śrāddha* and other rites related to the ancestors on the day associated with that [lunar day]. By this, it is implicitly stated that if the subsequent lunar day does not continue for three *muhūrtas* beyond sunset, then the preceding lunar day, which is setting, alone is to be accepted.

And thus, as it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "One who performs the New Moon (darśa), the Full Moon (pūrṇamāsa), and the anniversary day of a father's death (sāṃvatsara-dina) when they are overlapped by the preceding [tithi], falls into hell."

On the following day, it should be understood that [the rite] is to be performed if there is no occurrence of three *muhūrtas* after sunset. However, when the lunar day (*tithi*) occurs on the previous day as one setting at sunset, and on the following day—before the sun has set—it does not extend for three *muhūrtas* but instead sets [at sunset], then that very [previous day] is to be accepted for the *śrāddha* and other rites, because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that "for the *śrāddha*, that which sets at sunset is to be taken. But when the lunar day does not set at sunset on either of the two days, then the annual *śrāddha* must be performed on the following day alone—even in the absence of the specific quality of "setting at sunset"—according to the principle of omitting secondary qualities (*guṇalopa-nyāya*). This is because, otherwise, by transgressing the time of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) conjoined with the lunar day, a transgression (*pratyavāya*) would result.

That is incorrect; for in the case of accepting a lunar day (*tithi*) that is joined with the previous one for the annual *śrāddha* based merely on the contact of sunset, [the following rule applies]:
"When the lunar day of the anniversary of death extends over two days, it should be performed as joined with the previous day, provided it lasts for three *muhūrtas*."

This is because it contradicts the statement of Manu. Furthermore, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* passage, "the observance of vows and fasts," establishes that only the lunar day (*tithi*) belonging to the afternoon (*aparāhṇika*) is to be accepted. There is no evidence for the continued application of the rule "one *ghaṭikā*" [to this case] due to its contradiction with other statements; moreover, since an interpretation is possible through the method already stated, and since it is logically consistent as referring to cases where the performance of the *śrāddha* on the following day is impossible, the explanation of the *Sumantu* passage as referring to the three *muhūrttas* following sunset is also untenable.
That too is incorrect; for, upon examining the word "day," it is understood that a period of two muhūrtas is connected with the day.

Others, however, say that on the second day, if it extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) for three *muhūrtas*, it should be observed as overlapping with the previous day, based on the statement of Manu: "If it should be for three *muhūrtas*. The statement of Hārīta, "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors," refers to occasions other than the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*). This being the case, there is no contradiction with the following authorities: Sumantu’s statement that "it must span two days"; Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya’s statement that "the lunar day (*tithi*) is to be known for divine rites"; the *Śivarahasya* and *Saurapurāṇa* stating "having fasted every morning"; the *Nāradīyapurāṇa* stating "the end of the lunar day"; Baudhāyana’s statement that "for the gods, when the sun has risen"; the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* stating "in the case of vows, fasting, bathing, and so forth"; Vyāsa’s statement that "at the time of sunset"; and [the rule] that "for ancestral rites, at the time of sunset."

In our view, there would be the parsimony of subverting only ten statements—namely, the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "The Darśa and the Paurṇamāsa," and the statement of Manu cited in the Śivarahasya; however, in your position, there would be the burden of subverting many more. It might be argued: "Even in your position, there will be the burden of subverting eleven statements—namely, Vyāsa’s statement, 'Whatever the time of a rite'; Skanda’s statement, 'For at whatever time a rite [is performed]'; the Nigama statement, 'Likewise, those belonging to the afternoon'; Hārīta’s statement, 'The afternoon belongs to the ancestors'; the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa statement, 'Vows, fasts, and observances'; the two statements of Laghu and Vṛddha Manu, 'On which day the sun sets'; the statement of Vṛddha Gautama, 'Pervading the afternoon'; the two statements of Baudhāyana and Laghu-Viṣṇu, 'The prescribed time'; and Baudhāyana’s statement, 'Pervading midday. Thus, in your case, there will be the burden of subverting eleven such statements. In our position, however, there is parsimony regarding the subversion. To this we reply: Although there is no difference between the two positions in terms of the subversion of many statements, the time when the moon is joined by the previous day (pūrvaviddhā) and extends for three muhūrtas is accepted because it accords with established practice (ācāra).

That is incorrect, because of the duality of established practice (*ācāra*). In your position, there would also be a contradiction of a single scriptural statement regarding the rule for the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) on the day of death; therefore, because it contradicts many statements, this position is not superior. Furthermore, just as in the case of the *śrāddha*, where the hearing of the injunction to accept a lunar day (*tithi*) lasting three *muhūrttas* leads to the acceptance of a contradiction of the scripture concerning the time of the rite (*karmakāla*), so too [it is said]: "On whichever lunar day the sun sets during its three *muhūrttas*, one should commence that very lunar day for sacrifices, gifts, recitations, and other rites."

Because of this statement, and because one hears that even in other ritual acts (karmāntara) a lunar day (tithi) of three muhūrtas is to be accepted, it would follow that [the rule for the *darśa*] would be sublated; therefore, to accept such a disparity is improper. Furthermore, the fault in accepting such a position in that case as well has already been stated.

Others, however, say that regarding the *kṣayāha-śrāddha*, because of conflicting practices and conflicting scriptural statements, one should adopt the lunar day by relying on the practice handed down through tradition. For them, these traditions were handed down through succession and were also performed by their ancestors; as it is said: "They would not be at fault for those practices, but not for others.
And so Vyāsa says: "Reasoning is unstable; the scriptures are diverse..."
He is no sage whose view is not divided;
the truth of Dharma is hidden in a cave,
and that is the path by which the great man has gone.
Thus, whatever is appropriate here should be accepted.

Thus concludes the determination regarding the two-fold nature of the day of death (kṣayāha). Now follows the determination of the time for the annual śrāddha (sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha) when the day of death is unknown.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa,
Aruṇa said:
O Lord of the Immortals, how indeed can a man of great wisdom, who does not know the day or even the month of his parents' deaths,
perform for them the annual *śrāddha* according to the prescribed rite?

In this context, the phrase "of the parents" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for others as well, because the same practice is observed when the month and day of the śrāddha for others are unknown.
Āditya said:
O son of Vinatā, O King, that man who does not know the day of his death should perform the annual śrāddha on the new moon day.

The meaning is that for one who has died—whether he was away from home or not—if the specific lunar day (*tithi*) is unknown but the month is known, the annual anniversary rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) should be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) of that month.
Thus said Bṛhaspati:
"If the day of death is not known when someone has passed away while abroad..."
If the month is recognized, then [the anniversary] should fall on the day of death during the new moon (darśa).

"At that [time] of the new moon"—that is, on the new moon day of that month; "on the anniversary of death"—the word "that which is to be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis; "when he has gone abroad"—this is an indicative mark for any cause of ignorance [of the date].
Thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Even in the absence of a journey abroad, those two [rites] may occur when they have been forgotten."
At that time as well, those two should be accepted as before, however, on the anniversary of death.

Regarding this very subject, Marīci states that the *śrāddha* should be performed on the eleventh day when an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen and the day of death is unknown: "When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen and the day of death is not known,
it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight."

In this context, by the statement "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*), it is understood that the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is also permitted, since the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is described as being more praiseworthy. Consequently, when an option between the bright and dark eleventh days (*ekādaśī*) arises, the following rule applies: once the month and the fortnight are known, if only the lunar day (*tithi*) is unknown, the *śrāddha* must be performed on the eleventh day of that specific fortnight within that month, because there is no reason to abandon the identified fortnight. If even the fortnight is unknown, it should be performed on the dark eleventh; in its absence, even on the bright eleventh. Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
That man who knows only the day but not the month,
yet performs [the rite] in Mārgaśīrṣa, Bhādrapada, or Māgha—
and especially the *bhojaka* who always worships me— [attains success].
But for one whose day of death is known but not the month, the *śrāddha* should be performed on that same day in either Mārgaśīrṣa, Bhādrapada, or Māgha.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"When the month is not known, but the day alone is known..."
Then that day should fall either in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or in the month of Māgha.

But when both the day and the month of one who has died while traveling abroad are unknown, then the annual rite for him should be performed on the day and in the month corresponding to the time of his departure. Thus he [the author] says:
"When, moreover, the day and month of death are not known..."
The day and month of departure, however, should be determined according to the direction previously stated.

In all instances, by the word *dina* (day), the lunar day (*tithi*) is to be understood. The meaning of the phrase "by the aforementioned method" is as follows: when the date of departure is unknown but the month is known, one should perform the annual rite on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurring within that month. When the date of departure is known but the month is unknown, one should perform it on that very same lunar day during either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha. However, when both the date and the month of departure are unknown, one should perform it on the lunar day and in the month corresponding to the time of hearing the news of the death.
Thus says Pracetas: "When [the details] are fully known, [it is done] on the new moon, or on the day of hearing [the news]."
"On the day of hearing" means on the lunar day when the news of death is heard.
Also in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Upon hearing the news of death, those two [the eleventh and twelfth days] are to be observed according to the sequence previously mentioned."

[561] If the lunar day (*tithi*) of death is remembered but the month is forgotten, the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) should be performed on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurring within that month. If the lunar day is remembered but the month is forgotten, it should be performed on that very same lunar day in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha. If both the lunar day and the month are forgotten, it should be performed on the new moon of either Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa.
This has been stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"If one does not know the day of death, nor the month in any way whatsoever..."
Therefore, one should perform the śrāddha on the new moon day in either the month of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa.

The term ‘kathaṃcana’ means by some sign indicative of the departure for death; that is to say, when no news of death nor even news of life is heard from an absent person, and there has been no return for fifteen years, then after that period, having fashioned a representation of the body with *pālāśa* twigs or *kuśa* grass and performed the cremation rite according to rule, one should perform the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) on the day corresponding to the month, fortnight, and lunar date of that [death].
Thus says Jātūkarṇya.
If a father has gone abroad and there is neither news of him nor his return,
after fifteen years have passed, one should make an image representing him.
Then, one should perform his consecration according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should carry out all the remaining rites beginning with that very [consecration].
Thus concludes the determination of the time of transmigration regarding the lack of full knowledge of the destruction of the elements.
Now follows the determination of the *maghā-śrāddha*.
In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
Performing śrāddha rites under the Maghā constellation, one shall obtain all desires;
by him the ancestors are always worshipped as if visibly present.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who performs the *śrāddha* on the Maghā constellation:
his ancestors are satisfied and his progeny shall become inexhaustible.
O King, by this very same yoga, those who give clothing, vehicles, sandals,
and especially food during a *maghā-śrāddha*,
their ancestors remain satisfied for thirteen years.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
gaze upon the son who has been born, just as birds watch for a pipal fruit.
"With honey, meat, rhinoceros flesh, milk, and milk-rice,
he will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism."
By giving according to the prescribed rule under the asterism Maghā, one obtains four boons;
the ancestors, when honored, bestow wealth, food, sons, and long life.
Śātātapa says: [One should perform ancestral rites] under the Maghā asterism, when a son is born,
during an eclipse of a planet, and during both solstices.
Likewise, what is given in a conch shell, in a tooth, or in a lotus becomes equal to a thousand gold coins.

"Whether divided or undivided, they should always perform the *śrāddha*; however, on the occasion of the *maghā* asterism and elsewhere, there is no entitlement to perform it separately without [the others].
Thus said Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha.

“They lament one who gives cow-derived curd that is not mixed [with other substances], as well as various kinds [of food], during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism. [563] These statements refer to *śrāddha* rites devoid of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). Likewise, there is a statement in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
O Bhārata, by fasting on the day of the sun’s transit, by breaking the fast [on that same day],
and by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) under the Maghā asterism, the eldest son perishes.
And likewise, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "For one performing a *śrāddha* under the Maghā asterism, the eldest son perishes;
as does one who observes a fast on a solar or lunar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."
As for the citation from the Purāṇa given by Ācārasāra—
namely, "By offering the funeral cake (piṇḍa) under the Maghā constellation, one obtains four boons"— that refers to a subject other than a householder who has sons.
Others, however, say: this is merely a prohibition against the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) alone; that is possible, and so it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When the day of the Śrāddha has arrived, even if one is unable to provide the materials or a priest, only the cake itself should be offered, even if one must remain without food."

[Objection: "But surely the prohibition should apply in both cases. [Reply: No, because it is improper to invalidate multiple [scriptural injunctions]. Therefore, the *maghā-śrāddha* should also be performed together with the *sapiṇḍana*.
That is incorrect; since there is no reason for a definitive distinction (*vinigama*), the prohibition applies to both.
Others, however, say that by virtue of the same logic as the *trayodaśī-śrāddha*, the *maghā-śrāddha* is also prohibited when it pertains to a single ancestor (*ekavarga*).
That is incorrect.

For by the force of such scriptural statements as, "One should commence for a single class of ancestors on the thirteenth lunar day with the offerings of *śrāddha* food," that specific rule is demonstrated; however, this [present case] is not tenable due to the absence of such a statement. If it is argued that the reasoning is the same, we reply that because of that similarity, the prohibition—"one should not perform the *maghā-śrāddha*"—is logically understood to refer to the *sapiṇḍana-śrāddha*, since it is heard in scripture that "the son perishes through the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*)," and not through the performance of the *śrāddha* itself, as the necessity of performing that [latter] has already been shown.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the Maghā-śrāddha.
[564] Now follows the determination of the timing for śrāddha in the event of impurity (aśauca) and other such causes.
Regarding this, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"But when impurity arises while a Śrāddha for the ancestors is to be given,
the Śrāddha is offered to them once that period of impurity has passed."

The meaning is as follows: when impurity (*āśauca*) arises for those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* prior to the primary time, then—whether because that time has drawn near or because it has been defiled by impurity—the ancestral rite (*paitṛka-karma*) must be performed immediately after the period of impurity has passed.
As for the statement of Atri:
"If that day should be defiled by something such as birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), [then the rite should be performed later]."
"One should perform it again on that very same day immediately after the period of birth-impurity. Thus [it is said].

In that regard, concerning a *śrāddha* defiled by birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the position that "one should perform it after the period of impurity has ended" is indeed not in contradiction with the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. However, the position that "one should do it on that very same day" must be understood as referring to the primary time (*mukhyakāla*) when there is an obstruction caused by other incidental factors mentioned by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). This should be postulated in order to avoid contradicting the aforementioned statement. Furthermore, this alternative position applies specifically to the monthly *śrāddhas* performed on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*); for even if the specific time touched by the month is unavailable, that which is touched merely by the lunar day (*pakṣatithi*) of the fortnight is to be accepted. Therefore, Devala says:
If an obstacle arises when the Ekoddiṣṭa has arrived,
one should diligently perform the Śrāddha on that same lunar day (tithi) in another month.

The meaning is that in the month immediately following, on "that lunar day"—namely, the anniversary of death—on whichever fortnight (whether bright or dark) the person died, one should perform the *śrāddha* for that which was passed over due to an obstacle. Regarding the phrase "if he is wise," one should understand that the words "due to a cause other than impurity (*āśauca*)" are to be supplied as a supplement, so as not to contradict the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. When an obstacle arises due to the cause of impurity, even in the case of the monthly rites, one should follow the instruction of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, which prescribes that the performance of the *śrāddha* occurs immediately after the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) has ended.

For this very reason, Devasvāmin has also stated: "This statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga concerns the period of impurity due to birth (sūtaka); however, regarding the obstruction of that day due to another cause, there is the statement from another Smṛti: 'But when the Ekoddiṣṭa rite has arrived, if an obstacle should arise,' and so forth."
Vyāsa states: "When an obstacle to the Śrāddha has arisen due to death or birth occurring in the interim,
some wise men say that one should perform the Śrāddha on the new moon day."

"In the event of birth or death occurring 'in the interval' (antarā) means that if a birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka) occurs prior to the commencement of the cooking during the performance of a Śrāddha ceremony. Some maintain that this refers to the annual Śrāddha (sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha), performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) once purification has occurred. That is incorrect;

for the wise say: 'When a monthly or annual [Śrāddha] is due, and a birth or death-impurity occurs in the interval, they declare that it should be performed upon purification, or even on the new moon day.'"

Since the monthly rite is also prescribed by this statement from the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, the mention of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is an elliptical indication for both the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-ekādaśī*) and the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī*). For this very reason, Marīci says:
"When an obstacle to the Śrāddha has arisen and the day of death is unknown..."
It should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.

The grammatical connection is: "especially on that Ekādaśī which falls in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). Since for ancestral rites (pitṛkārya) only the dark fortnight is to be accepted, it should be understood that the superiority of the new moon day (amāvāsyā) over even the dark Ekādaśī in ancestral rites is established by the maxim of the "stick and the rice-cake" (daṇḍāpūpanyāya). In this context, the time immediately following purification is superior because it is proximate to the primary time; the time of the new moon is inferior to that, as it lacks proximity to the primary time of the new moon—this is how it should be considered.
And likewise, regarding that [inferiority], Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"One who has become pure should give [the offering] on whichever lunar day (tithi) arrives."

"That lunar day (tithi) is to be observed by him, and never any other. This is the meaning: one who has become pure must perform the rite; if purity is not possible during the primary times, then the lunar day that follows immediately after purity is "attained" (prapadyate)—that is, it becomes available—and it should be understood as the constituent part of his obligatory duty, rather than the primary lunar day itself, which, if defiled by impurity, should never be performed. He states the same:
"The interruption of the lunar day must not be made at will, except in the case of impurity."
"The *piṇḍa* and the *śrāddha* must be offered; one must never cause an interruption.

[Regarding the term] "at will" (*yadṛcchayā*), it means according to one's own desire. It is logical that when there is an affliction caused by death or birth-impurity (*mṛta-sūtaka*) on the anniversary of death, the *śrāddha* should be performed after that period has passed and the impurity has ceased. However, this does not apply if the knowledge of the impurity occurs before the commencement of the cooking or even before the invitation; it cannot be done at a later time. And so it is stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
When the Brahmins have been invited and the śrāddha rite has commenced,
[one should consider] the invitation of a Brahmin who has desisted from his Vedic study.
While the ancestors remain embodied, no impurity (aśauca) exists anywhere,
even for those who give or receive [the offerings] during birth or death.
There shall never be any fault regarding those who partake in faith-offerings and the like if it is unknown;
however, once it is known, the act of penance and so forth shall fall upon the eater alone.
If the donor passes away while the Brahmins have consumed only half of the food,
then those twice-born ones, being composed, should leave the remainder of that leavings behind; having sipped water with the water belonging to another, they become pure.
If an impurity (sūtaka) occurs between a wedding and a sacrifice,
it has been declared that the remaining food should be given by others.

This, however, refers to the subject of birth and death distinct from the donor, the recipient, and the house. Regarding the statement, "One should not touch the donors and the recipients," there is a specific fault [in that case].
Kratu said:
"A substance previously intended for giving does not incur fault when it is being given."
This has been stated: when the qualified performer is defiled by impurity (*āśauca*), the *śrāddha* must be performed after the primary time has elapsed and the impurity has ceased.

However, since the householder possesses the qualification for the rite only together with his wife, when she is defiled by the impurity resulting from the appearance of her menses, and it follows that the *śrāddha* should be performed only upon the cessation of that impurity after the primary time has passed, the husband alone—even while still subject to the impurity of her menses—must perform an *ām-śrāddha* (a *śrāddha* with raw food) at the very primary time itself. Thus says Uśanas: [The text continues with the citation of Uśanas.]
"One who is without a wife, one who is traveling abroad, and one whose wife is in her menses—these should not perform [the śrāddha] with cooked food; for them, raw food (āma) is prescribed.
Regarding this rule for the *āma-śrāddha*, Hārīta states an exception preceded by a summary:
"When there is an obstacle to faith for the twice-born, the *āmaśrāddha* is prescribed;
it may be performed on the new moon day and so forth, even if it occurs outside the monthly or annual periods."

The meaning is this: when an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen—such as the appearance of menstrual blood in the wife—it is proclaimed that an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food) should be performed; however, this applies only to those occasions such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and not to the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) performed on the day of death. Nevertheless, it must be performed precisely when that obstacle has passed. And since there is no other wife eligible for joint performance due to the defilement of the primary wife by menstruation, it should be performed at the very time the obstacle in the form of the menstrual flow ceases. As it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
On the fourth day, a woman who has reached her menses becomes pure after bathing;
for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day.
In another Smṛti:
"When the day of death has arrived, if his wife is in her menses, the Śrāddha should not be performed then; one should have it performed on the fifth day."

However, for one who has taken another wife while still possessing the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*), the rite must be performed at the primary time itself, because the qualification has not lapsed.
Regarding one who is unable to perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food), he prescribes a *hemaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with gold):
"In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born priests, during travel abroad, or upon the birth of a son..."
One whose wife is in her menses should perform the Hemaśrāddha.
In this context, the substance intended is that which is to be eaten, and the twice-born is the eater.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for *śrāddha* on occasions such as impurity (*āśauca*).

Now, regarding specific types of *śrāddha*, the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), midday (*madhyamāhna*), and afternoon (*sāyāhna*) are prescribed, while the evening (*sāyaṃkāla*) is prohibited; the same applies to other ritual acts as well. Therefore, the section concerning the times beginning with the forenoon is commenced for the purpose of distinguishing between them.
In this regard, it is clearly understood that by the power of convention, the day is divided into two parts: the first half is the *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon), and the latter is the *aparāhṇa* (afternoon).
And so says Manu:
"Just as the dark fortnight is distinguished from the bright fortnight..."
Thus, for one who is faithful, the afternoon is superior to the forenoon. So it is said.

[569] Now, one might object: "In this context regarding the *śrāddha*, only a difference in the division of the day into forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is being stated; it is not being asserted that the first part of a day divided into two is designated 'forenoon' and the second part is designated 'afternoon'. To this it is replied: The first and second halves of a month divided into two are the two fortnights (*pakṣa*); these are used here as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Due to a lack of complete similarity (*asārūpya*), this implies that even for a day divided into two, the first and second parts are designated 'forenoon' and 'afternoon' respectively. In that case, the status of being an example is justified by a mere partial similarity (*vaiśiṣṭhya-mātra*), despite the lack of complete similarity. True; nevertheless, because no other divisions are mentioned and in order to conform to total similarity, the intended division is understood. One must accept this [interpretation] precisely so that there may be no contradiction of that [intended meaning].

[Objection: Surely, by the expressions for the three or four parts of the day intended in the *darśa* [sacrifice], let the division based on etymological derivation (*yaugika*)—which is rooted in the postulation of similarity with the illustrative example—be sublated. [Response: True. Because a technical term (*pāribhāṣika*) taught by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) possesses no other scope and is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), it is stronger than that which is etymological or conceptual; thus, sublation would indeed occur. However, it is precisely for the sake of ensuring that the etymological meaning is not sublated by the technical definition that the meaning established through etymology has also been technically defined. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The forenoon indeed extends up to the turning [of the shadow], and the afternoon follows after that."

One opinion holds that *aparāhṇa* is the second part of the day divided into two parts, with the turning point (*āvartana*) being the midpoint of the day. Now, another opinion is stated: *aparāhṇa* is the third part of the day divided into three parts. Regarding this, there is a Śruti passage: "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors; therefore, one gives [the offering] in the afternoon. Here, the impression arises that the Śruti, having conceptualized three parts of the day—consisting of fifteen *muhūrttas*—each measuring five *muhūrttas*, and named 'forenoon' and so forth, assigns them respectively to rites for the gods, humans, and ancestors. The instruction that the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* prescribed for the time of *aparāhṇa* must be performed by a human in the third portion of the day will be shown in the section on the regulation of time. That [instruction] should also be understood here as an illustration of another sense of the statement that *aparāhṇa* is the third part of the day divided into three. This is the view that *aparāhṇa* is the third part of the day divided into three. Furthermore, another view holds that *aparāhṇa* is the third part of the day divided into four unequal parts. And thus says Gobhila:
"The first watch lasts one and a half [hours], and midday likewise lasts one watch;
from there until the third [watch] is afternoon, and after that is evening."

The meaning here is that they say the portion of the day starting from sunrise and measuring one and a half *praharas* is the *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon); the portion of one *prahara* following that is the *madhyāhna* (midday); the portion of half a *prahara* following that until the end of the third *prahara* is the *aparāhṇa* (afternoon); and the portion of exactly one *prahara* following that is the *sāyāhna* (evening). Thus, the view is that the *aparāhṇa* is the third part of a day divided into four parts. In this regard, there is another view that the *aparāhṇa* is the fourth part of a day divided into five equal parts. Concerning this, there is the *Śatapatha-śruti*:

The sun indeed is all the seasons: when it rises, that is spring; when it is the time of the cows being gathered, that is summer; when it is midday, that is the rainy season; when it is afternoon, that is autumn; and when it sets, that is winter.

Thus, when a day consisting of fifteen *muhūrtas* is divided into five parts, there arise five periods—morning (*prātaḥ*) and so forth—each measuring three *muhūrtas*. Here, although this fivefold division is heard as a subordinate element to the injunction regarding midday (*madhyandina*), which is mentioned immediately after the Vedic text stating, "Therefore, one should study at midday itself," and is thus connected to that specific time, it nevertheless attains a connection with all ritual acts because it is relied upon as the indicator of the duration of time required by the rites prescribed for the morning and other times. For this very reason, this fivefold division, whose constituent parts measure three *muhūrtas*, is observed to be common to all. And so it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration.
Midday consists of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise.
Then the evening consists of three muhūrtas, during which one is excluded from all ritual acts. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, Parāśara states that this division is useful solely for the performance of those rites prescribed for that specific time:
"From the first line [of dawn] until the sun [appears], there are exactly three muhūrtas;
this is remembered as the morning (prātaḥ), and it constitutes the fifth part of the day."

The period of twilight (saṅgava) consists of three muhūrttas; midday is likewise considered to be the same duration. Then follow three muhūrttas of the afternoon, which is distinguished as the most excellent.

"Furthermore, the fifth part of the day is known as the evening (sāyāhna). Whatever is prescribed for these [periods], that a wise man should perform. Thus, the "line" (*lekhā*) refers to the portion of the rising solar disc that is first perceptible, appearing like a streak; "from the sun" (*ādityāt*) means from the rising of the sun. Consequently, it is stated that the three *muhūrtas* beginning from the line—that is, starting from sunrise—are designated as "morning" (*prātaḥ*).
For it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"When the sun has risen from the first streak of light until three muhūrtas have passed,
that time is known as 'morning' (prātaḥ), and it constitutes the fifth part of the day."
The meaning is that whatever rite is prescribed for these times, such as the morning and so forth, one should perform each of those at the times as they have been described.

Now, the divisions (*kalpa*) of the forenoon, midday, afternoon, and evening—measured by the elaboration of the aforementioned statements—are being distinguished. Since the morning (*prātaḥ*) and the time of the gathering of rays (*saṅgava*) each constitute a single division, they are inherently distinct; therefore, only the divisions of time beginning with the forenoon are discussed here. In that regard, when the day is divided into three parts, the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) begins from the moment the twelve-fold solar disc becomes visible and lasts until the completion of the first half of the eighth *muhūrta*. When divided into four parts, it begins from that same point and lasts until the completion of the first half of the third quarter of the sixth *muhūrta*. However, when divided into five parts, the forenoon must be described as the period of six *muhūrtas* starting from sunrise. For in that case, the meaning of the word "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) must be explained through its etymological function (*yaugikī vṛtti*), and it is appropriate to state that this meaning is not preoccupied by contradictory designations such as "midday. Although the first six *muhūrtas* of the day do not conflict with the two designations of "morning" and "time of the gathering of rays," nevertheless, these do not contradict the etymological application, and thus they do not act as obstacles to the application of the name "forenoon."
Thus ends the fourfold classification of the forenoon. Now follows the ritual procedure for midday (*madhyāhna*).

When the day is divided into two parts, the period of midday is that which, on both sides of the moment of midday, is sufficient for the performance of the rites prescribed for midday. Due to necessity, a different technical designation is applied [to this period].

This is my acceptance. In a threefold division, midday (*madhyāhna*) begins from the sixth *muhūrta* and ends with the conclusion of the tenth *muhūrta*. In a fourfold division, it begins from the latter half of the third quarter of the sixth *muhūrta* and extends until the completion of the first quarter of the tenth *muhūrta*. In a fivefold division, however, it begins from the eighth *muhūrta* and lasts until the conclusion of the tenth *muhūrta*.
Such is the fourfold distinction regarding midday.
[573] Now, the divisions of the afternoon:

in a two-fold division, the afternoon begins from the latter half of the eighth *muhūrta* and extends until the commencement of the evening twilight (*paścimasandhyā*). In a three-fold division, it begins from the eleventh *muhūrta* and extends until the end of the evening twilight. In a four-fold division, it begins from the latter half of the second quarter of the tenth *muhūrta* and extends until the conclusion of the first quarter of the twelfth *muhūrta*. In a five-fold division, it begins from the tenth *muhūrta* and extends until the conclusion of the twelfth *muhūrta*.
Thus ends the fourfold distinction regarding the afternoon. Now follow the ritual procedures for the evening.

In a twofold or threefold division [of the day], the period for the performance of rites prescribed for that time extends until sunset; in a fourfold division, it begins from the tenth muhūrta and lasts until sunset; in a fivefold division, the afternoon (sāyāhna) begins from the thirteenth muhūrta and lasts until sunset. This is the analysis of the afternoon.

Furthermore, these periods such as the *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon) and so forth should be adopted according to availability, without overstepping the applications that will be described hereafter, or else according to the sequence of their relative excellence; for whichever time is more subtle in comparison to another is the more excellent. Indeed, when a large duration of time is established as being the *pūrvāhṇa*, its single part is also necessarily established as the *pūrvāhṇa*. This is just as when a specific flow of water beginning from a cave in the Himalayas and ending at the shore of the eastern ocean is established as the Gaṅgā, it is necessarily established that even a single portion of the flow existing within it is the Gaṅgā. Otherwise, how could there be the fulfillment of what is enjoined—such as "one should perform a bath in the Gaṅgā" or "one should perform the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) in the afternoon"—by performing it in only a portion of that [time]? Moreover, we observe certain words that are common to both a whole and a part thereof. As has been stated by the Teachers: [The original Sanskrit text follows: ete ca pūrvāhṇādayo vakṣyamāṇaviniyogānatikrameṇa yathālābhaṃ grāhyāḥ, praśastatāratamyakrameṇa vā, yo yaṃ kālam apekṣya sūkṣmaḥ sa tasmāt praśastaḥ | mahāvadhivacanena hi mahataḥ kālasya pūrvāhṇatve pramite tad ekadeśasyāpi pramitam eva pūrvāhṇatvaṃ, yathā himavatkuharād ārabhya pūrvasamudrasīmno jalapravāhaviśeṣasya gaṅgātve pramite pramitam eva tadantarvarttinaḥ pravāhaikadeśasyāpi gaṅgātvam, katham anyathā “gaṅgāyāṃ snānaṃ kuryād aparāhṇe pitṛyajñam ācaret” iti vihitasya tadekadeśānuṣṭhāne vihitasiddhiḥ | dṛśyante ca kecit samudāyaikadeśayoḥ sādhāraṇāḥ śabdāḥ | yad uktam ācāryaiḥ |
"Just as the word 'water' (toya) is applied both to a single drop and to a collection, because it consists of substances that are conjoined, so too is the *sūktavāka* the term for that [collection].

Therefore, it must be stated that the intermediate limit-statement possesses purposefulness either by excluding a portion of the forenoon as determined by the statement of the major limit, or by being intent on conveying its own denotation as something exceedingly praiseworthy. In that regard, in the first case, there would be both futility and sublation of the statements concerning the major limits; therefore, it is concluded that the intermediate limit-statement is for the sake of indicating [the time] as more praiseworthy.
Now follows the time of Kutapa.
In the Skanda and Vāyu Purāṇas:
"That moment when the Lord of Rays (the Sun) shines with his full splendor upon the earth is known as *kutapa*;
what is given at that time yields great fruit."

‘Kuḥ’ is the earth; ‘Gopatiḥ’ (the Lord of Cows) is the Sun; ‘with cows’ means with his own rays; at whatever moment he ‘heats,’ that is, makes warm, ‘in its entirety,’ meaning the whole earth, ‘that time’ is to be known by the name ‘Kutapa. By this, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word ‘Kutapa’ has been established: “This Kutapa has been defined. Indeed, because all shadows contract, the Sun heats the entire earth only at the very middle of the day; therefore, the middle of the day is determined to be the ‘Kutapa. And although it is measured by a *muhūrta*, it is referred to by the word ‘moment’ (*kṣaṇa*) using a figurative sense (*upacāra-vṛtti*), considering its brevity. For it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa itself: [The text continues with the citation from the Vāyu Purāṇa.]
"From the seventh muhūrta onwards and before the ninth muhūrta, that time is known as *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors during that time becomes inexhaustible. Thus it is said;
and also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
The muhūrtas of the day are always declared to be fifteen;
among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is known as the time called *kutapa*.

As for the ten items beginning with the sword and the vessel, since they are situated within the discourse on the midday [offering], it is impossible to separate them; therefore, they are written here in connection with the midday [ritual].
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"Brahmins, blankets, cows, silver, fire, and guests as well..."
Sesame seeds, darbha grass, and midday—these nine are traditionally known as the Kutapas.
Also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Midday, a sword, a vessel, as well as a Nepalese blanket,
silver, *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth."
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; since these eight cause torment for one who possesses such [sin], they are therefore renowned as "kutapas."
In the Kauśītaki school, however, it is read as "likewise another, the black blanket (kālakambala)," thus [referring to] the kutapa.
Now, the application of these times, such as the afternoon and others, in the Pārvaṇa and other Śrāddhas is described.
Regarding this, Śātātapa and Hārīta state:
The *āmaśrāddha* is performed in the forenoon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday,
the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) in the morning.
Manu also said: "The Śrāddha for the gods is in the forenoon, while the Pārvaṇa is in the afternoon;
the Ekoddiṣṭa is at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (vṛddhi) is in the morning."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"A wise man should perform the Śrāddha during the forenoon of the bright fortnight;
however, in the dark fortnight, he should perform it in the afternoon, but must not let the Rauhiṇa [period] pass."

[576] Here, in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* or *ekoddiṣṭa* *śrāddha* should be commenced specifically during the first half of the *kutapa* period within the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). In the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* or *ekoddiṣ�ṭa* *śrāddha* should be commenced specifically during the second half of the *kutapa* period within the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). This statement is intended to establish the first half of the *kutapa* for the *pārvaṇa* and the latter half for the *ekoddiṣṭa*; for otherwise, the forenoon and afternoon would already be established by other injunctions, namely that the midday and afternoon apply to the *pārvaṇa*. Alternatively, by the phrase "in the bright fortnight," the forenoon is prescribed with reference to the *daivika* (deity-oriented) *śrāddha* ordained for that fortnight; and by the phrase "in the dark fortnight," the afternoon is prescribed with reference to the *paitṛka* (ancestor-oriented) *śrāddha*. Thus, since there is no conflict with other injunctions and a valid application exists, the prescriptions regarding the midday and afternoon will not be sublated. Among these, the application of the afternoon is now analyzed.
Śātātapa says: "That which is declared as the Darśa-śrāddha is proclaimed as the Pārvaṇa;
therein, an offering in the afternoon is praised for the ancestors."

Regarding the *darśa-śrāddha* performed by those without sacred fires (*anagnika*) who omit the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, or by women, *śūdras*, and others: the latter portion of the afternoon, divided into two parts, should be taken as it occurs, beginning from the second half of the *kutapa* period. This is because, in the case of a *darśa-śrāddha* performed by those without sacred fires, the occurrence of the new moon (*kuhū*) coinciding with the *kutapa* period has been shown in the determination of the two-fold Amāvāsyā. Furthermore, regarding the *darśa-śrāddha* performed by those with sacred fires (*sāgnika*), or by those without sacred fires who do perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*: since there is an injunction that the performance must follow the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* to be performed in the afternoon—as stated by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* in the rule, "On the new moon day, they perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the afternoon"—one should follow that accordingly and take the third part of the day, divided into three, as it occurs until the twilight (*āsandhya*).
And so Manu has said:
"The Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha is recommended when the moon has waned,
during the third part of the day, but not too close to the time of twilight."

Likewise: "A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) at the waning of the moon, shall perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month. Thus it is said.
And this should not be said:
"But one who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) and the rite called libation (tarpaṇa),
should always perform the Śrāddha known as Piṇḍānvāhāryaka on the day of the new moon."

Thus, according to the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, the *anvāhāryaka* (the monthly śrāddha) follows immediately after the *tarpaṇa* and *pitṛyajña* which are included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and not immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Therefore, the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) need not be observed in accordance with that [specific rule]. For Laugākṣi says: "Having performed the rites up to the end of the fortnight, the one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) should perform the *vaiśvadeva*;
thereafter, the wise man should perform the *pitṛyajña*, and after that, the *anvāhāryaka*."

Therefore, following the analogy of the Darśa-Śrāddha and Pitṛyajña which are to be performed after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the third part of the day—extending up to, but not including, the time close to the evening twilight (saṃdhyā)—should be taken as the period for [the Śrāddha].
Thus ends the application of the afternoon time. Now follows the application of the forenoon time.

In this context, regarding the statement "the *daivika* śrāddha is in the forenoon," since there is nothing further to be said concerning the forenoon—which is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *daivika* śrāddha—it is stated with reference to that which is a constituent part of the *āmaśrāddha*. Regarding that, some have determined that the injunction "but the *āmaśrāddha* is in the forenoon" applies exclusively to the *āmaśrāddha* performed by the twice-born (*dvija*), and not even to the *āmaśrāddha* performed by a Śūdra. He [the opponent] thinks as follows: if it were to apply to both types of performers, there would arise an inequality—namely, that in one case (the twice-born) it would constitute an absolute sublation (*atyantika-bādha*) of the afternoon time, while in the other case (the Śūdra) it would enter as a merely optional (*pākṣika*) rule. For instance, in the *āmaśrāddha* of the twice-born, the afternoon time is derived through extension (*ātideśika*), whereas in the *āmaśrāddha* of the Śūdra, it is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*). Thus, in the *āmaśrāddha* of the twice-born, the injunction for the forenoon, being stronger than the extended rule, would effect an absolute sublation of the extended afternoon and establish the forenoon; however, in the *āmaśrāddha* of the Śūdra, because it possesses equal force with another direct injunction, it would effect only an optional sublation of the directly enjoined afternoon and then establish itself. Hence, there is an inequality. But how is it that the afternoon time is extended (*ātideśika*) in the *āmaśrāddha* of the twice-born, yet directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) in the *āmaśrāddha* of the Śūdra?

It is said: The primary *pārvaṇa* rite, consisting of the feeding of Brahmins, is obligatory (*nitya*) and pertains exclusively to twice-born (*dvija*) performers, not to Śūdra performers; for since the Śūdra is prohibited from performing a *śrāddha* consisting of feeding Brahmins, and because an obligatory *āma-śrāddha* (using uncooked food) is prescribed for him, there would arise an inconsistency if the rule regarding cooked food were also to apply to him—since that would involve overriding the prohibition for the Śūdra while being independent of it for the twice-born. Thus, the primary *pārvaṇa* consisting of the feeding of Brahmins is both obligatory and restricted to twice-born performers. However, the *āma-śrāddha* prescribed for twice-borns on account of specific causes such as the impossibility of cooking is non-obligatory (*anitya*).
And likewise Sumantu says:

"O lord of men, O mighty-armed one, Brahmins and others who lack a wife due to traveling abroad and other such reasons would still have the entitlement [to perform rites] even in the absence of cooked food."
And the wise know that for Śūdras, the funeral rite (śrāddha) should always consist of uncooked food.
O Uśanas! When a disruption of one's own place or time has arisen,
the twice-born should perform an *āma-śrāddha* (a rite with raw food), whereas for a Śūdra it should indeed always be performed in that manner.
Pracetas says:

In times of distress, when there is no fire, at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, the twice-born (dvijas) should perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a rite with uncooked food); indeed, a Śūdra should always perform it in this manner.
[579] A *tīrtha* (auspicious occasion) is the cause when there is an inability to cook; likewise, an eclipse of the moon or sun is the cause even in the absence of an eater.
Similarly: "A woman, a Śūdra, and a Svapaca are also [causes for a *tīrtha*] during the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*)."
One should always perform the *āmaśrāddha* according to the *pārvaṇa* rite.
"Self-cooker" (*svapaca*) means one who cooks for himself, that is, one who is without a wife. Jamadagni:
"As long as he is not joined with the sacred fires, whether his fires have been extinguished or even [if they have not been established]."
Then one should perform the *āmaśrāddha*; in that case, the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) should be done with the hand.
Hārīta says: "In the event of an obstacle to a Śrāddha for the twice-born, an Āma-Śrāddha (a Śrāddha with raw food) is prescribed;
this applies to the obligatory rites on the new moon day and so forth, except for those performed monthly or annually."

The phrase "except for the monthly and annual [rites]" means that this rule applies with the exception of the *māsika* (monthly) and *sāṃvatsarika* (annual) rites. This being the case, the ritual details (*dharma*) taught in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as those beginning with the afternoon, must apply only to the obligatory (*nitya*) rite consisting of the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, and not to the optional (*anitya*) Śrāddha performed by the twice-born (*dvija*). This is because of the contradiction between the obligatory and the optional (*nityānitya-saṃyoga-virodha*). For example, the ritual details taught in the archetype, such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, apply only to the obligatory Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice in its *agniṣṭoma* form, and not to the optional forms such as the *atirātra*. Similarly, the purchase of Soma (*kraya*) and other elements apply only to the obligatory Jyotiṣṭoma accomplished through the Soma substance, and not to the optional one accomplished through the *phalacamasa* cup; rather, they apply there only by extension (*atideśataḥ*). Therefore, in the optional Śrāddha performed by the twice-born, this afternoon time applies only by extension. However, in the Śrāddha for a Śūdra, since it is occasional (*anaimittika*) and thus obligatory (*nitya*), the afternoon applies by direct injunction (*upadeśataḥ*). Consequently, the morning time, which is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*), is an alternative to the afternoon in that case. But in the Śrāddha for the twice-born, the morning time—being extended from the archetype—sets aside the afternoon. Thus, this rule for the morning, applying to both cases, becomes confused by the disparity of the injunctions: in one case it is obligatory, while in the other it is merely optional. Being thus troubled by this inconsistency, the rule seeks to find a single consistent scope. It therefore avoids the Śūdra’s Śrāddha, where an improper option would result, and indicates that the rule applies only to the Śrāddha of the twice-born. And this being so...
That period which is declared as Kutapa after midday—
whatever is given to the ancestors at that very time in an unbaked earthen vessel becomes inexhaustible.

Thus, regarding the statement of Vasiṣṭha which mentions the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) as opposed to the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), that too is properly reconciled when it is understood to refer to the *dvijāma-śrāddha* (the funeral rite for twice-born ancestors), excluding the *śūdrāma-śrāddha*. This statement merely reiterates the afternoon time, since the afternoon is already obtained here by the general rule. Therefore, the *śūdrāma-śrāddha* takes place during the afternoon starting from the latter half of the *kutapa* period, whereas the *dvijāma-śrāddha* occurs in the forenoon.
This concludes the application of the forenoon.
Now follows the application of the midday.

And in that regard, although in the passage "The *ekoddiṣṭa*, however, at midday," five *muhūrtas* beginning with the sixth are taught as the time for the *ekoddiṣṭa* by virtue of being "midday," nevertheless, because of the supreme excellence of the *kutapa* [period], one should strive to accomplish the commencement of the *śrāddha* during the *kutapa*.
This is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Because at midday the sun always becomes weak..."
Therefore, undertaking an action therein is distinguished by its yielding of infinite fruit.
Gautama states that just as the commencement of the *śrāddha* at the *kutapa* hour is distinguished, so too is its conclusion at the *rauhiṇa* hour:
"Having commenced the *śrāddha* at the *kutapa*, the wise man should perform it until the *rauhiṇa*;
knowing the rule and adhering to the rite, he must not overstep the *rauhiṇa*."

*Rauhiṇa* is the ninth *muhūrta*. The phrase "one should not let [the time] pass" is intended to praise the completion of the rite within the *rauhiṇa* period; it is not a prohibition against exceeding *rauhiṇa*, because that period, being part of midday and afternoon, is itself an integral part of the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states that the five *muhūrtas* beginning from *kutapa* constitute the constituent parts of the *śrāddha*: "The four *muhūrtas* that follow the *kutapa* *muhūrta*—these five *muhūrtas* are indeed desired as the abode of *svadhā*."

The intention of the phrase "the abode of *svadhā*" is that this time applies to the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites characterized by the utterance of *svadhā*, but not to the divine (*daivika*) rite or the *nāndī-śrāddha* characterized by the utterance of *svāhā*, for those two are prescribed specifically for the forenoon and the morning respectively.
Thus concludes the application [of the time] for midday.
Now follows the application for the morning.

In this context, the injunction "in the morning [the rite] caused by prosperity (*vṛddhi*)" is a rule regarding the time of morning; it does not refer to the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* performed on the occasion of a son's birth. For, since it is prescribed immediately after the occurrence of the cause consisting of the son's birth, and because the time of birth is itself indefinite, it is concluded that the [time for the rite] must likewise be indefinite.

Now, one might ask: why is a *śrāddha* rite, even when prescribed for a specific occasion (*nimitta*), not postponed until its own proper time—just as the *vaiśvānarīyeṣṭi* is—simply because there is no cause for postponement? Know this: impurity (*āśauca*) is not the cause for postponement; for the *vaiśvānarīyeṣṭi* was not postponed merely to remove the defect of impurity, but rather due to a conflict with its intended purpose. Now, it may be argued:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors..."
Except for the offering of funeral cakes to the deceased, one should suspend [all other rites] even during the period of impurity.

On account of such prohibitions, there is an elevation [of the time for the *śrāddha*]. In that regard, because the occasional injunction (naimittika-vidhi) stating "one should perform a *śrāddha* when a son is born" is a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*), it overrides the prohibition; thus, the extensive range of scriptural statements is intended to show that impurity (*āśauca*) persists because the [period of] time has not yet elapsed.
On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather..."
Furthermore, beings are born there on that day and they experience it;
therefore, that day is meritorious and increases the merit of the ancestors.
Also in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"When a son is born to the twice-born, both the gods and the ancestors come;
therefore, that day is meritorious and always to be honored."
Therein, one should give gold, land, a cow, and likewise a horse;
as well as an umbrella, clothing, a garland, a bed, a seat, and a house.
Hārīta also says:
"And when a son is born, on account of the joy of the ancestors, that day [is auspicious] for the son.

Because of the "joy of the ancestors" (*pitṛṇām āmodāt*), there arises an excess of delight; thus, "meritorious" (*puṇyam*) means purifying, in the sense that it is a time of merit (*puṇyakāla*) for acts such as giving.

In this context, since the day of the son’s birth and so forth is not defiled by impurity (*āśauca*), the *śrāddha* occasioned by the birth must be performed at that very time; it is not to be postponed until after the period of impurity has passed. Although the statements of Śaṅkha and others suggest that the entire day is meritorious (*puṇya*), it should nevertheless be understood that [the rite] must take place specifically before the cutting of the umbilical cord. Thus says Hārīta: "They perform the purificatory rites for the sake of merit prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord, but once the cord is cut, there is impurity."
