"Saṃskāra" refers to the birth-rite (*jātakarma*); "acts for the sake of merit" refers to gifts of molasses, sesame seeds, oil, cows, land, gold, clothing, grain, and so forth.
Manu also said:
"The birth-rite is ordained for a male before the cutting of the umbilical cord."
"Vardhana" means cutting. Jaimini also says:
"As long as the umbilical cord is not cut, so long does the state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) not apply."
"After the umbilical cord has been severed, the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) is then prescribed.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The *śrāddha* must indeed be performed during the birth of a son while the umbilical cord is still unsevered."
Or else, it should be performed by those of self-restraint once the period of impurity has passed.

Satyavrata says: On the day of a son’s birth, until the cutting of the umbilical cord, that day is meritorious; on that occasion one should perform the *jātakarman* and the *āmaśrāddha*, and give vessels together with gold. By this, there is no requirement for the time of morning purification. And so says Atri:
An increase in prosperity may indeed occur in the forenoon, except for that occasioned by a birth;
however, upon the birth of a son, a wise man should perform an immediate *śrāddha*.
Prajāpati also states:
"When the umbilical cord is severed, there is impurity; therefore, the *śrāddha* must be performed precisely before the cutting of the navel-string.
And because this is an occasional (*naimittika*) rite, it should be performed even at night.

As Vyāsa has said: "One should not perform a ritual bath at night, nor should one give gifts during the nights, except on occasions of an eclipse, a wedding, a solar transit (saṃkrānti), a journey, illness, or childbirth."
"Gift-giving should be known as occasional (*naimittika*); it is not even faulty if performed at night. What is given on the birth of a son or during a journey at night is inexhaustible.
This [gift] must be performed even when there is a coincidence of impurity (*āśauca*) caused by another period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurring at that same time.
Regarding this, Prajāpati said:

"When a birth has occurred during a period of impurity (sūtaka), if another birth of a son takes place, the performer attains immediate purification; he is purified by the preceding period of impurity."

"Of the performer" means of the one who performs the *jātakarma*; in the case of another rite, however, the meaning is that once the previous impurity (*janmāśauca*) has ceased, the performer becomes pure. If, moreover, it were not performed at this time due to the lack of the necessary materials, the officiant, or other factors, or because of the onset of another period of impurity, then upon the cessation of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), it should be performed on some day, specifically in the morning. Now, one might ask: why should this rite, having fallen away from its own proper time, be performed at another time? For rites contingent upon specific occasions such as eclipses are not performed even when their designated time has passed.
This is indeed true; however, this is established by means of scriptural authority (*vacana*). And so it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The *śrāddha* must indeed be performed at the birth of a son while the umbilical cord is still uncut."

[585] "Or rather, it should be performed by those of self-restraint once the period of impurity has ceased. Now, one might ask: is not the cessation of impurity also a time for this [rite]? But why is it that this [cessation] is impossible at a time prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord?
We say: because of the statement of Vaijavāpa.

"The birth-rite (*jātakarman*) must be performed according to the rules immediately after birth; if, by chance, it has passed its time, it should take place once the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) has elapsed. Thus ends the application [of the rite] to the morning time.
Now, regarding the prohibited times:
on this matter, Vyāghrapāda says—
"The abandonment of Smārta rites during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), except in the case of Rāhu [an eclipse]."
If one goes to perform a Śrauta rite at that very time, one shall attain purification.

Aparārka maintains that during an impurity other than that caused by Rāhu, one should not perform Smārta rites such as the Śrāddha; however, Śrauta rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Agnihotra should be performed after bathing. He explained this with the intention that the term *sūtaka* (impurity) is applied even during birth-impurity (*janmāśauca*) prior to the release of the moon or sun from an eclipse by Rāhu.

Others, however, explain it thus: "In *sūtaka*," meaning during the impurity caused by birth, the abandonment of all ritual acts (*sarvakarmaparityāga*) must be performed; and that [abandonment] means, according to the rule "except for the sight of Rāhu," setting aside optional rites (*kāmyakarman*). In that case, under the first explanation, it is established that no *śrāddha* should be performed during the impurities of birth or death; and under the second explanation, it is established that no *śrāddha* should be performed during the impurity of birth. Furthermore, the word "act" (*karman*) refers to ritual acts other than the offering of funeral cakes (*pretapiṇḍa*) to the deceased. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi in this regard: "Giving, receiving, burnt offerings (*homa*), Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarman*)."

"One should terminate the period of impurity (āśauca), with the exception of the offering of rice-balls for the deceased (pretapiṇḍa)," so say Manu and Śātātapa. "One should not perform a Śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas."

"Or even during both twilights, and when the sun has set. It is called *rākṣasī* because powerful *rakṣas* demons roam therein; on such a night, the *śrāddha* is plundered by those demons. Furthermore, the *śrāddha* should not be performed during either of the two twilights.
Regarding the measurement of the twilights, Yājñavalkya says:
"The morning twilight is said to last for two muhūrtas prior to sunrise;
the evening twilight lasts for three ghaṭikās after the sun has set."

The statement, "when the sun has indeed set," is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the time near the twilight (*sandhyā*); by this, the time near the evening twilight is also obtained. Thus, by this [text], the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* prescribed for the morning—which would otherwise apply during the morning twilight and its proximate time—is prohibited; and the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] prescribed for the afternoon—which would otherwise apply during the evening twilight and its proximate time—is prohibited. However, as for the middle twilight and its proximate time, since it is the period of *kutapa*, there is no prohibition anywhere. (From the *Skanda Purāṇa*).
One should never perform the worship of the ancestors during the twilight;
that time is declared to belong to the Asuras, and one should avoid performing the Śrāddha rite then.

By this prohibition against proximity to the *saṃdhyā*, for one who is unable to begin or complete a *śrāddha* before the evening time, that portion of the evening other than the vicinity of the *saṃdhyā* is permitted. As for the statement: "The *sāyāhna* [evening] of three *muhūrtas* is excluded from all ritual acts."
Thus says the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"If a man performs a *śrāddha* when the fourth watch has arrived,
that *śrāddha* becomes demonic (*āsura*), and the giver shall go to hell."
Thus says the statement of Baudhāyana:
"If the sun has become dim during the eighth part of the day, that Śrāddha becomes Āsura; it does not reach the ancestors."
This statement by Harīta refers to one who is capable of both beginning and completing the *śrāddha* before evening.
Thus Vyāghrapāt said:
"One who knows the rules, is endowed with faith, and properly employs worthy recipients..."
"One who performs it at any time other than night attains unsurpassed welfare.
Thus [it is said]. Viṣṇu states an exception to the prohibition against performing [the rite] during the night, the twilight, or times proximate to them:
"Indeed, the wise should not perform a Śrāddha during the twilights or at night."
"And for those two as well, [the rite] should be performed if there should be the sight of Rāhu.
Here, "sight of Rāhu" refers to an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Thus ends the section on prohibited times.
Now, regarding the prohibited times for the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*): on this matter, Pulastya says:
"The *śrāddha* [should be performed] during the two solstices (*ayana*) and likewise during the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)."
And on all the beginnings of the Yugas, except for the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa).

On these occasions, the *śrāddha* is to be performed even "without the offering of the rice-balls" (*piṇḍanirvapaṇāt ṛte*), that is, excluding the giving of the *piṇḍas*; this is the understood remainder of the sentence.
As stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The *śrāddha* on the two solstices (*ayana*) and likewise on the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)."
And on the days of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the rite should be performed, with the exception of the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa).

On the third day of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of Kārttika, as well as during the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), men should perform the śrāddha rite during the bright fortnight according to the prescribed rules.

In this context, although the solstices (*ayana*) and other such times are already included by the phrase "at the transits" (*saṃkrāntiṣu*), their explicit mention again is for the purpose of highlighting that the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) performed at those specific times is extremely censurable. By the phrase "according to the procedure for the transit," the absence of the offering of funeral cakes is indicated. The entire passage beginning with "on the third day of Vaiśākha" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all the beginnings of the *yugas*, because of the statement of Pulastya: "and on all the beginnings of the *yugas*.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, after reciting the two verses from the *Matsyapurāṇa* beginning with "the *śrāddha* during the two solstices," it is stated as follows:
On the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada, on the new moon day of Māgha,
and likewise during the sun’s southern course, a Śrāddha ceremony should be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa).
And when a learned Śrotriya, one who knows the Vedas and understands the sacred fires, comes to one's house,
then with him alone one should perform the most excellent Śrāddha on the Viṣuvat day.

Regarding the phrase "the Viṣuvat is the last," even a Śrāddha performed on account of the arrival of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*śrotriya*)—which is superior to and more excellent than the Viṣuvat-Śrāddha—should generally be without rice-balls (*apiṇḍa*), according to the reading [of the texts]. Bṛhat-Parāśara states:
"On the anniversaries of the Yugas, under the Maghā asterism, at the Viṣuvat, and likewise at the solstices (*ayana*)."
And one should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) under the asterism Bharaṇī.
Regarding the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada conjoined with the asterism Maghā, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"On that occasion, a great worship should be performed for the ancestors and the deities;
however, one who has an eldest son should avoid the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) during that asterism."

"Even there"—that is, even on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada—when the lunar mansion presided over by the ancestors (the *pitṛ-daivata-ṛkṣa*), namely Maghā, occurs, a "great" ancestral worship characterized by the *śrāddha* rite must be performed. However, if the performer possesses an eldest son and that first-born son is living, then while performing the *śrāddha* on that occasion, he should avoid the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*); the meaning is that he should perform the *śrāddha* without the *piṇḍas*. By the term "possessor of an eldest son" (*jyeṣṭhaputrī*), the defect—characterized by the destruction of the eldest son—is indicated for the offering of *piṇḍas* occurring at the time of Maghā, at the time of the thirteenth day, or when both coincide.

Likewise, in this *Mahābhārata*: "O Bhārata, by fasting on the day of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*), by breaking the fast [on that same day], and by offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) under the asterism Maghā, the eldest son perishes. Thus it is said.
In the *Jyotiḥparāśara*:
"When a marriage has been performed, one should indeed avoid [the following] ten months;
however, in the case of a sapinda relative, one should avoid six months for the offering of funeral cakes, and likewise six for the tying of the sacred girdle."
The exception to this rule is as follows:
during the Mahālaya festival, at a Śrāddha for Gaya, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
and likewise at the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for any mortal whatsoever.
"Even one who has performed the marriage ceremony should always perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa)," so says Bṛhat-Śātātapa:
"That śrāddha which is prescribed as being devoid of the offering of the rice-balls..."
In this case, the recitation of the *svadhā* formula is omitted, but the scattering of food (*vikiro*) is not omitted;
likewise, the offering of imperishable water, the sacrificial fee, and the expression of great goodwill are performed according to the rule.
Thus ends the prohibited times for the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Now, regarding the prohibited times for rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*),
Gārgya says:
If the consecration (saṃskāra) takes place when the period of impurity has already ended, one should not purify the day at all.
However, if the rite of consecration is performed during the midst of the period of impurity,
then the day must be purified there according to the circumstances.
If the deceased is consecrated again after the period of impurity has ceased,
the day must be taken as the starting point only after first purifying it, provided this occurs more than a year later.
One should perform the funeral rites during the northern course of the sun, as that is most excellent;
even then, one should avoid the waning fortnight and the day of the waning of the lunar day.

In this context, there are two types of funeral rites for the deceased: one for the actual body, and another for a substitute image (*pratikṛti*). Regarding the rite for the actual body, there is no opportunity to examine whether the day is auspicious or inauspicious. However, for the rite of the substitute image, there are three times: during the period of impurity (*āśauca*), at the end of a year, and beyond a year. Among these, when the rite of the substitute image is performed during the period of impurity, it should be carried out—if possible—at a time avoiding the lunar days, asterisms (*nakṣatra*), and so forth that will be mentioned below. When the rite of the substitute image is performed outside the period of impurity but within a year, then the purification of the commencement time must certainly be performed according to the method to be described. Even when it is performed after a year has passed, the time must likewise be purified; however, in that case, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) are especially meritorious when accomplished. A day of lost lunar reckoning (*dinakṣaya*) must be avoided in all cases.
Marīci says:
One who maintains a household should not perform a śrāddha on the Nandā day, on a Saturday, on the fourteenth lunar day, or at Tripuṣkara, for fear of the loss of sons and wealth.

The sixth, eleventh, and first lunar days are called *nandā*. "The day of Bhārgava" refers to Friday. The asterisms named Kṛttikā, Punarvasu, Uttaraphālgunī, Viśākhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvābhādrapadā are known as the "tripuṣkaras. Here, by the word *śrāddha*, the funeral rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*) are intended. Among these very [days] beginning with *nandā*, he states which are most inauspicious: "On the eleventh day, on a *nandā* day, on a *sinīvālī* day, on a day of Bhṛgu (Friday), on the fourteenth day of the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), and under the Kṛttikā asterism—these are the tripuṣkaras."

In this context, the phrase "one should not perform a *śrāddha*" is to be supplied. The connection is that [it should not be performed] on the day of Sinīvālī or on the day of Bhṛgu. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"One should not perform [a *śrāddha*] under the constellation under which a man was born."
O Bhārata, one should not perform [the rite] under the two Proṣṭhapadas, nor under Āgneya;
one should likewise avoid all the Vāruṇas and the Pratyari.

In this context, the birth asterism (janmanakṣatra) belongs to the performer of the Śrāddha; the two "Proṣṭhapadas" are those called Bhādrapada; "Āgneya" is Kṛttikā; the "Vāruṇas" are Ārdrā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla; and the fifth, fourteenth, and twenty-third asterisms from the birth asterism are the "Pratyari. [592] Jyotiḥparāśara states:
For human beings, it is not recommended [to perform rites] during the Sādhāraṇa, Dhruva, Ugra, or Maitra asterisms.
The funeral rites may somehow be performed at Tripuṣkara and at Yamaladhiṣṇya.

The *sādhāraṇa* [asterisms] are Kṛttikā and Viśākhā; the *dhruva* [asterisms] are the three Uttaras and Rohiṇī; the *ugra* [asterisms] are the three Pūrvas, Bharaṇī, and Maghā; the *maitra* [asterisms] are Mṛgaśirā, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Revatī; the *tripuṣkara* [asterisms] have been mentioned; and the *yamaladhiṣṇya* is Dhaniṣṭhā, because it is stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "One should avoid [these] when the Moon is in the fourth, eighth, or twelfth [house]. Mṛgaśirā and Citrā are included among the *maitra* [asterisms]. In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"One should avoid [these] when the Moon is in the fourth, eighth, or twelfth [house]."
One should perform rites for the deceased during Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, and likewise during Parigha.
On the day known as Viṣṭi,
on a Saturday, especially on the thirteenth lunar day, and likewise during the three birth-constellations;
The tenth and the nineteenth asterisms from the birth asterism constitute the "three birth stars.
Kāśyapa said:
Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Maghā, Śleṣā, Mūla, and the two [asterisms] with two quarters [Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Pūrvabhādrapadā].
The five asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā are unfavorable for rites performed for the deceased.
The two Phālgunis, Rohiṇī, Anurādhā,
Punarvasu, the two Āṣāḍhas, and Viśākhā— these are the double-footed [nakṣatras].
One should avoid these when they are even slightly afflicted, provided that other options are available.

Thus, when it follows that the performance of *preta*-rites is prohibited in these cases, Gobhila states an exception: "On a Nandā day, on a Friday, on the fourteenth lunar day, and during the three birth-constellations,
the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is not prohibited from the eleventh day onwards."
"Trijamāni" refers to the three birth-stars (janmatārā). Vaijavāpa says: "When the eleventh day has arrived for the deceased who has been directly cremated..."
Nothing whatsoever, such as the lunar mansion, the lunar day, or the day of the week, needs to be purified.

If funeral rites for the deceased must occur by chance on a day of solar transit (saṅkrānti), the anniversary of death (yugamanvādi), or the new moon (darśa), one need not scrutinize the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) or other such factors.
Thus concludes the prohibited times for the rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*). Now, the following is considered:

Do the *śrāddha* rites—performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, on the anniversary of death, during the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, on the *aṣṭakā* days, at the *ayana*, at the *saṃkrānti*, during eclipses, at the beginning of the *yugas* and *kalpas*, and at the "elephant's shadow" (*gajacchāyā*) and other such times—differ with each occasion, or not? To that end, this is deliberated: Are the statements specifying these times injunctions for the origination of the ritual acts (*karmotpattividhi*), or are they injunctions for subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*) regarding time within a ritual act already established?
Thereupon, Somadatta said:

Although, in the case of an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), there arises both an injunction regarding the verbal root’s meaning and an injunction regarding the sentence-meaning, nevertheless—because the injunctive power is transferred to the qualifier and because of parsimony (*lāghava*)—these are indeed *guṇavidhis* and do not bring about a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*). Consequently, due to the unity of the action, even when the optional times (*kāla*) occur at different moments, the performance takes place at one time rather than at all of them; how much less, then, could there be separate performances for times that occur simultaneously? Thus, when times coincide, the *śrāddha* should be performed only once. For it is not proper for the principal act (*pradhāna*) to be repeated merely to conform to subordinate qualities such as "at will" (*kāmarūpa*); however, the repetition of the oblation (*homa*) in accordance with times such as evening and morning is justified because the occasion (*nimitta*)—defined as living during those specific times—is itself repeated.

That is incorrect. For where there is proximity to a pure originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*), in those sentences containing qualifiers (*guṇa-yukta-vākya*), there is an injunction of only the qualifier due to the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of that [originative act]. Here, however, because there is no pure originative injunction, there is no fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in an injunction qualified by the *udagana* and other factors. If one were to assume a pure originative injunction, then everywhere the injunction of the qualified would be lost, and in some cases a distinction [between rites] might arise merely from the qualifiers. Therefore, because it is an injunction of the qualified, there is a distinction between the *śrāddhas* for each time; and since eclipses (*uparāga*) and so forth are the occasional causes (*nimitta*), when they differ, the distinction is clear. Thus, it is established that when that specific time arrives, that particular *śrāddha* must be performed. Now, a doubt arises regarding the coincidence of times and the coincidence of occasional causes: at that time, among the various *śrāddhas* belonging to those respective times and those respective occasions, should only one be performed, or should all be performed separately, or rather, should they be performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*)?
Regarding this, Śivadatta says:
"One should never perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day," because of this statement by Hārīta; thus, [the rite] is indeed one and the same.
But Śaṅkhadhara and others say:
"This is not tenable; [it applies] when many, or even two, have passed away at the same time."
Having performed the cooking by means of the tantra, one should perform the śrāddha separately for each.
In cases of simultaneous deaths, one should first perform the rite for the one who died earliest, then for the second, and then for the third; this is the sequence.

Thus, because Bhṛgu has prescribed numerous *śrāddhas* with different causes even on the same day, and because he has prescribed various *preta-śrāddhas* for different occasions such as the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*) and others, the aforementioned prohibition refers specifically to the repetition of a *śrāddha* initiated with faith when it has only a single cause. [Objection: Let it then be that the scope of the cited specific statement excludes other cases; consequently, when the time for a monthly (*māsika*) *śrāddha* coincides with the time for a *śrāddha* due to an astronomical anomaly (*vyatīpāta*) or the like, there would be no performance of the *śrāddha*. [Response: No. Even in such a case, since the *śrāddha* is commenced with faith, the prohibition does not apply. Therefore, the performance of the *śrāddha* must take place. Furthermore, this is because the rule regarding the non-performance of multiple *śrāddhas* on a single day applies only to those performed for the sake of a single cause. Since the *māsika* and other *śrāddhas* have distinct causes, they are not subject to that prohibition. Thus, the *śrāddha* should indeed be performed. This is established by the following verse: "Even when many *śrāddhas* are to be performed on one day, whether by the rule of the *Pārvaṇa* or otherwise, one should perform them all according to the prescribed procedure. Therefore, it is concluded that the *śrāddha* must be performed even when its time coincides with another. Moreover, the prohibition against performing multiple *śrāddhas* on a single day is intended to prevent the confusion of rites and the resulting failure to observe the proper sequence (*krama*) and other ritual details. It does not, however, prohibit the performance of those *śrāddhas* that have separate, independent causes. Consequently, even if a monthly *śrāddha* and a *śrāddha* for an astronomical anomaly occur simultaneously, both should be performed. This is consistent with the principle that when multiple rites are enjoined for a single occasion, they may be performed together provided their respective procedures do not conflict. Thus, the performance of the *śrāddha* is mandatory in such instances.

No; for if the prohibition were to apply even when the *śrāddha* has a different occasion, it would follow that there could be no *vṛddhi-śrāddha* at the birth of a son occurring after a [funerary] *śrāddha*.
If you argue that the subversion of established practice (*ācāra*) applies only to cases other than that, we say no;
for it would then follow that one who has already performed a *śrāddha* would be deprived of faith (*śraddhā*) during a solar eclipse, which would result in a subversion of prior practice.
If it is argued that [the Smṛti] has as its object only that which is distinct from those [Vedic injunctions], we say no;
for this would entail the sublation of even those Śrāddha injunctions that have different causes but occur at the same time, since they too exist.
If it is argued that sublation occurs because those are general statements and customary practice (ācāra) is weaker [than specific Śruti], we reply: [no].

No; for if the scope of the cited statement were distinct from that [of the general rule], there would be a contradiction with the practice of the plural number and the necessity of postulating another underlying *śruti*. However, if the scope is as we have stated, there is neither contradiction nor the need to postulate a *śruti*, because it is rooted in logic (*nyāya*). Furthermore, if both *śrāddhas* were performed simultaneously, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the prescribed times such as *kutapa* and so forth. If they were performed at once, there would be a contradiction with those scriptural statements prohibiting the performance of another rite during the course of one—such as "While one [rite] is being performed, one should not perform various other rites"—and with the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) which prohibits delay. Therefore, since it is established that all [rites] must be performed, the position favored by Viṣṇudharma, namely that they should be performed separately (*pṛthak*), is adopted.

As for the statement that there is a *tantra* (common) performance of the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices due to the absence of apprehension of distinctions such as identity of place, time, and agent—that is appropriate only for subsidiaries grasped by a single performance-injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*), but not for independent primary rites (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, the claim that there is *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) to the permanent (*nitya*) *apūrva* from the *darśapūrṇamāsa* performed for the sake of a desired *apūrva* is also appropriate only when there is identity of the action (*karmaikya*). For those very same aggregates of the *āgneya* and others which serve the purpose of the desired *apūrva* are themselves those serving the purpose of the permanent *apūrva*, since their identity is understood from the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*). As for the conventional usage of "difference" (*bheda*) in that context, it is based on a distinction in the temporal determination of cognition caused by the connection with limiting conditions (*upādhi*) in the form of desire or occasion (*nimitta*), and not based on a real difference in the entity; however, the difference between *apūrvas* is real, arising from the difference in qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, this difference between *apūrvas*, though merely conditional (*aupādhika*), was examined under the section on the definition of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) because it must be produced as a consequence.
Is it not the case that [the two acts] are distinct because of the perceived difference in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the respective meanings of their original bases?
No; because in that case, the action is one and the same.

Since the obligatory performance is accomplished by the very same Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices performed for the sake of the desired transcendental result (kāmyāpūrva), no separate performance is carried out. However, when the actions are distinct, since one transcendental result cannot be established by another, a separate performance must be undertaken for the sake of that other result.

That is incorrect. Even when there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karman*), if there is unity of place, time, and agent, all the rites are accomplished through a single performance (*tantra-anuṣṭhāna*), and thus the production of all the *apūrvas* occurs simultaneously. At that time, no distinction is perceived such as, "this one has produced a specific result. Furthermore, even when there is a difference in the sacrifice (*yāga*), because a single performance is accepted for the *sānnāyya* offering when the deity is the same; and because it is established in the eleventh book (*Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra*) that in cases such as crossing a river in a dream, being rained upon, or encountering impurity (*amedhya*), when multiple instances of the same cause (such as seeing several impurities) coincide, and when the repetition of the occasional rite (*naimittika*)—consisting of the recitation of mantras like "The mind is poor, the eye [is poor]"—would otherwise be required for each individual cause, a single performance of the occasional rite takes place due to the absence of any perceived distinction. Therefore, when there is a coincidence of occasions for *śrāddhas*, a coincidence of times, and unity of place, agent, and deity, because no distinction is perceived, they must be performed by way of a single performance (*tantra*). Thus, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform these *śrāddhas*—the one occasioned by the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṅkrānti*), the one occasioned by the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and the one occasioned by the *vyatīpāta* yoga*—by way of a single performance. *(Note: The term *vyatīpāta* refers to a specific astronomical conjunction considered inauspicious.)*
Thus concludes the determination of the conjunction of time.
Now follows the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

In this regard, for the sake of its utility, an investigation into the Vaiśvadeva cooking is undertaken: whether the cooking for the Vaiśvadeva and other rites and that for the Śrāddha are one and the same, or whether they are distinct. On this point, first of all, there is only a single cooking for the daily Śrāddha—which is included within the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña)—and for the Vaiśvadeva and so forth; this is because the daily cooking performed every day serves the purpose of accomplishing all rites produced from the food. However, regarding the specific case of impurity (aśauca), since the Vaiśvadeva and other such rites do not exist prior to the eleventh day, at that time there is no question whatsoever of whether the cooking for the *nava-śrāddhas* is one or many. As for the Śrāddhas on the eleventh day, the Vaiśvadeva must be performed with a separate cooking.
In the case of an ekoddiṣṭa rite, however, one should discard the remainder of the food among the Brahmins.

Thus, because Devala has prescribed that all remnants of food (*annaśeṣa*) should be given to the Brahmins in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites known as the "nine *śrāddhas*," and because this "newness" (*navatva*) will be explained in the context of the *preta-śrāddhas*, the determination [of the procedure] for the annual (*sāṃvatsara*) and other rites—which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*—is made precisely by the determination of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, there arises a doubt regarding the cooking intended for the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*. In this regard, the teacher Karka established a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *śrāddha* should be performed with cooking separate from that intended for the *vaiśvadeva* rite, and he stated the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it should be done with the very same cooking used for the *vaiśvadeva*. The refutation of the reasons for both the prima facie and the final positions favored by him has been set forth in the *Śrāddhakalpa*. However, the reason for his own final position which was stated by Karka—the fact that "separate cooking is not mentioned"—is now being challenged on the grounds that it is unproven (*asiddha*).
One should prepare cooked food for the sake of the ancestors and likewise for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva;
the Vaiśvadeva offering is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is the Darśa offering for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva.

This is because the separate preparation of food (*pṛthakpāka*) is mentioned in the statement of Laugākṣi. Although in the first half of this verse it might appear that one should prepare a single cooking for both purposes—since it says, "one should perform a single cooking for the sake of both"—nevertheless, the distinction between the two types of cooking is clarified by the second half: "The *vaiśvadeva* is not for the sake of the ancestors. The food cooked for the purpose of the daily obligatory fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) known as *vaiśvadeva* is called *vaiśvadeva*; it is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is it for the sake of the *darśa-śrāddha*. However, it is not the case that it cannot also serve the purpose of the *nitya-śrāddha*, because there is a certainty that the sacrifices performed daily—designated by the terms *deva*, *pitṛ*, *bhūta*, and *manuṣya*—are accomplished through a single cooking. The food cooked for the *darśa-śrāddha* is called *dārśa*; that is not for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. By the word *darśa*, all *śrāddhas* ending with the *ekoddiṣṭa*—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—are indicated, since they share the same procedural framework (*itikartavyatā*) as the *darśa-śrāddha*. Furthermore, by the word *vaiśvadeva*, the *bhūtayajña*, *pitṛyajña*, and *manuṣyayajña* are also implied. But how can there be a suspicion that something intended for one purpose serves another, especially without *adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā* (indication based on the substrate), given that one does not accept an application (*viniyoga*) unless there is a reason for it?

True; however, it is not here that the possibility of one thing having a different purpose than it actually has is suspected or refuted. Rather, the suspicion regarding the *tantratā* (simultaneity) of the offerings (*nirvāpa*) and the cooking (*pāka*) is rejected, as is the possibility of something intended for one purpose being applied elsewhere through *prasaṅga*. In this regard, the suspicion of *prasaṅga* arises because, when actions performed at proximate times can be accomplished by a single means, there is an economy in the employment of the instruments. Here, that which was stated by a portion of Laugākṣi’s statement—“the *vaiśvadeva* [offering] is not [part of] the *darśa*”—should be understood as applying only when the *vaiśvadeva* is performed either before or during the *śrāddha*, and not even after it; for Paiṭhīnasi says: [Textual fragment omitted] Thus, the *vaiśvadeva* should be performed before the *śrāddha*. However, if the *vaiśvadeva* is performed after the *śrāddha*, then the *vaiśvadeva* offering is indeed part of the *śrāddha*. This is because the *vaiśvadeva* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, and since the *śrāddha* is the primary rite (*pradhāna*), its own *vaiśvadeva* offering must necessarily be performed. Therefore, the *vaiśvadeva* is certainly part of the *śrāddha* when it is performed after the *śrāddha*. Consequently, the *tantra* (common procedure) of the *nirvāpa* and *pāka* is established. Furthermore, since the *vaiśvadeva* is a subordinate element of the *śrāddha*, the *tantra* of the *nirvāpa* and *pāka* is established even when the *vaiśvadeva* is performed after the *śrāddha*. Thus, the *tantra* of the *nirvāpa* and *pāka* is established in both cases. For this reason, it is said: [Textual fragment omitted] Therefore, the *tantra* of the *nirvāpa* and *pāka* is established in both cases. "He who performs the Vaiśvadeva after having extracted [the portion] from the *pitṛpāka*—that *śrāddha* becomes *āsura*; it does not reach the ancestors.

Now, one might object that the word "having extracted" (*uddhṛtya*) is redundant; [but this is not so], for an oblation cannot be performed without having first cut off a portion (*avadāna*), and a cutting-off is precisely the extraction of a single part from the whole.

Not so. For here, by the word *pitṛpāka* (food for the ancestors), the food is designated in its state of having the ancestors as its deities through formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). And from that state, the extraction of a portion is nothing other than the removal of that deity-status; it is not merely a physical division. Furthermore, the removal of that deity-status is only possible once the connection with the previous deity has been severed. Therefore, this act of extraction is conveyed by the verb *uddharati* (he extracts) precisely as the removal [of the food] from the ancestors as deities. And this [extraction] is impossible either before or during the *śrāddha*, because it would contradict the specific resolve (*saṅkalpa*) consisting of the mental intention: "I shall prepare this food for the ancestors at the time of the offering. It is not possible even at a later time, for it is impossible to cut away from what has already been relinquished in favor of the ancestors, since its status as being dedicated to them has already been established. Indeed, it is impossible to make something already established into something unestablished.
Now, do we not say that what is already accomplished is made unaccomplished? Rather, it is said that it is destroyed.
Not so; because a destroyer is impossible. If it is argued that extraction for the sake of another deity is the destroyer, [we reply: no.
No; for there is no evidence that it [the subsequent injunction] destroys the connection with the previous deity, since its purpose is merely to establish a connection with a subsequent deity.

Now, one might argue that because the destruction of the previous connection is necessary for the establishment of the subsequent connection, the former's destruction is inferred, given the contradiction between two connections in a single substrate; thus, the "cutting off" (āccheda) taught by the scriptural statement is the destroyer.

Not so. For being "dedicated to that deity" (tad-daivatyatva) consists precisely in the state of being relinquished with reference to that deity; and since that [status] comes into existence only after the completion of the act of relinquishment and then perishes, what is there to be destroyed by the act of taking away? Furthermore, what is the intended meaning of the doctrine of "extraction" (uddhṛtyavāda)? [Objection: But in this way, even for a substance relinquished with reference to a deity presiding over an image or the like, the connection with the deity would come into existence only after the relinquishment and then perish; consequently, because that substance has been accepted [by the deity], there would be no fault of stealing the property of a god in the event of its misappropriation.

Not so. First, regarding that substance which has been relinquished for the sake of being enjoyed by an image and the like, because its dedication to that deity results in the fruit of enjoyment, it remains undestroyed as long as that enjoyment lasts. For if it were destroyed, it would be difficult to maintain the persistence of the contingent (*naimittika*) state once the cause (*nimitta*) has ceased. However, in the case of a substance whose enjoyment is complete, let there be a prohibition against taking it—treating the deity’s ownership as a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), as in the case of *nirmālya* (remnants of an offering). Thus, since the connection with the ancestors (*pitṛsambandha*) of the cooked food (*pāka*) perishes after the *śrāddha*, what destruction could destroy it? In reality, however, there is no connection with the ancestors at all in the remnants of the *śrāddha*; what, then, is there to be destroyed? For in the case of a remnant of what has been used, that [connection] is merely a secondary characteristic. And this [characteristic] does not deserve to be revoked while in that state. Now, why is it not explained as "having set aside from the remnant of the ancestral cooking, one should divide"? Because it has already been stated that the word "having set aside" (*uddhṛtya*) would be meaningless. Therefore, the meaning of the scriptural statement—"He who performs the *vaiśvadeva* rite after setting aside [food] from the cooking intended for the ancestors, his *śrāddha* becomes demonic (*āsura*)"—refers to a case where the ancestral rite has not yet begun, or has begun but is not yet completed. And this is logical. Even common people consider any act improper if something prepared for a specific purpose is given to another without first being offered to that [intended recipient], even if it is a worldly matter; how much more so when something is prepared for the ancestors or the deities, yet is given to another beforehand? But when it is given to that [intended recipient] and then given to another, no one considers it defiled or improper. Furthermore, it has been stated that even after the *śrāddha*, the food intended for the *śrāddha* may be employed in the *vaiśvadeva* rite.
And so Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Having performed the Śrāddha according to the rules, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites; thereafter, one should give alms and likewise utter the syllable 'dhanya' and so forth."

Here, by the word *adyataḥ* (from that), the meaning of the preceding verse is stated as a reason; by the second [word], it is stated that [the Vaiśvadeva is performed] from the food remaining after the *śrāddha*. Therefore, this is the meaning: since the *śrāddha* would become *āsura* if the Vaiśvadeva were performed with food extracted from the *pitṛ-pāka* (the cooking for the ancestors) prior to the *śrāddha*, for that reason, having completed the *śrāddha*, one should take a portion from the food remaining after that *śrāddha* and perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites. Nor should it be argued here that because the food (*anna*) has not been introduced as the subject matter, it is unfit to be referred to by the pronoun *tat*; for in the preceding verse, "having extracted [food] from the *pitṛ-pāka*," there is an introduction of the food (*anna*). And a pronoun refers to what is proximate; nor is there a rule that proximity must be through physical presentation, since it is accepted that proximity consists in being present in the mind. Here, by the word *ādi* (etcetera), all daily obligatory rites (*naityaka-karma*) accomplished with food are included; therefore, even the daily *śrāddha* (*nitya-śrāddha*) must be performed from the remnant of the cooking used for the [ancestral] *śrāddha*. Thus, if one performs the Vaiśvadeva at the end of the dismissal of the Brahmins, then it is done with the very cooking intended for the *śrāddha*; but if one performs the Vaiśvadeva at any one of the three times prior to the dismissal of the Brahmins according to the method to be described, then it is done with a separate cooking. On this point, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, having cited the statement of Laugākṣi—"One should prepare the cooking for the sake of the ancestors... the Vaiśvadeva is not for the *darśa* [śrāddha]"—and having explained that food prepared for the *darśa-śrāddha* does not serve the purpose of the Vaiśvadeva even when the *śrāddha* has been performed, and having stated that this refers specifically to the *darśa-śrāddha* involving the sacred fire (*sāgnika*), he set forth the following reasoning: "For since the Vaiśvadeva is prescribed for one who possesses the sacred fire (*sāgnika*) even before the *darśa-śrāddha*, it is improper to perform the Vaiśvadeva at the end of the *śrāddha* with the remnants of the *śrāddha*. This very reasoning establishes a meaning exactly opposite to what he intended. For if there were no Vaiśvadeva at a later time, there would be no possibility of its being accomplished by the remnants of the *śrāddha*, and thus a prohibition would be illogical. Therefore, this prohibition must apply to the earlier time alone, and consequently, this [prohibition] would concern both those with and without the sacred fire (*sāgnika* and *anagnika*). Now, if it is argued that although a prohibitive injunction is untenable due to the lack of such a possibility, it may be a perpetual restatement (*nityānuvāda*), then two faults would follow: first, the status of a restatement, and second, futility (*ānarthakya*). Furthermore, there is an inconsistency: if this concerns those with the sacred fire, it would depend upon both the Vaiśvadeva performed at the earlier time and the one performed at the later time. In that case, it would be a prohibitive injunction regarding the earlier time, but a restatement of a prohibition regarding the later time. Therefore, let the statement of Laugākṣi—"the Vaiśvadeva is not for the *darśa*"—be taken as concerning both those with and without the sacred fire, based on the prohibition against using a single cooking for the Vaiśvadeva performed at times prior to the dismissal of the Brahmins along with the *śrāddha*. As for the one who thinks that the statements prescribing the performance of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites with the remnants of the *śrāddha*—such as "Having completed the *śrāddha* according to rule, then the Vaiśvadeva etc."—apply to *śrāddhas* like the annual ones which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *darśa-śrāddha*, whereas the statement "the Vaiśvadeva is not for the *darśa*" applies only to the *darśa-śrāddha* itself—he should be informed as follows: All these general rules are taught in connection with the *darśa-śrāddha* itself; there is no "unattached" (*anārabhya*) teaching. Or, even if such a teaching existed, nevertheless, according to the maxim "or in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of the double mention," as in the case of "the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood," there is a rule that it must go to the archetype; thus, it finds its place in the *darśa-śrāddha* alone.

Now, if it should be argued that the *anārabhyavāda* (independent injunction) applies to the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) because the *prakṛti* (archetype) is already occupied by a rule taught in connection with it (*ārabhyādhīta*) which contradicts it—that is not so;

for the contradiction with the rule taught in connection with the archetype has already been resolved by the previously stated determination of the scope (*viṣayavyavasthā*). Therefore, one should not say here, "This injunction pertains to the Darśa-Śrāddha, this one does not.
Regarding a difference in the cooking prior to the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), there is another Smṛti text:
That which is given to the sick, to those who have renounced the world, or to fools, does not constitute the Vaiśvadeva offering; nor does that which is cooked for the purpose of a śrāddha ceremony.
Likewise: "The food cooked for the ancestors should not be given to the domestic fire, to children, to deities, to an ascetic, or to a student, as long as the funeral cakes have not been offered."
Pracetas also said:
"Having performed the *bali* offering from the household cooking and having completed the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*),
one should first offer that grain which has been set aside for them."

The term *gṛhya* refers to the purpose of domestic rites; here, *bali* means the *vaiśvadeva* offering. Having "completed" (*nirvartya*)—that is, finished—the *pitṛyajñiya*, which is the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* together with its ancillaries, "then" (*tataḥ*), immediately thereafter, one should "offer" (*nivedayet*)—that is, give—that food which has been set aside for the sake of the *śrāddha* "to them" (*tebhyaḥ*), meaning to those intended as the recipients of the *śrāddha*, "first" (*agre*), before [others]; by implication, after that time, one may give it to others as well. This concludes the determination regarding the Vaiśvadeva cooking. Now, the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is being made.

In this regard, first, concerning the doubt as to whether or not the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice should be performed by one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*) prior to the *śrāddha*: the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows. Since the injunction for the *vaiśvadeva*—namely, "one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* oblation"—establishes that the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one without a fire must be performed at some time, its performance at the time preceding the *śrāddha* is also necessarily established as an alternative possibility.
As for the prohibition of performing it at that earlier time found in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"If the daily oblation is performed at the beginning of the *śrāddha*... [603]... [the text continues with the refutation].
The gods do not accept the sacrificial offerings, nor do the ancestors accept the ancestral oblations.
Thus, there is also the prohibition made by Vṛddha-Gautama:
"He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite without first performing the ancestral Śrāddha—
that Śrāddha becomes as if unperformed and does not reach the ancestors."
Thus, it should be understood that this applies specifically to the performance of the *vaiśvadeva* at a time preceding the *śrāddha* cooking, and not to its performance with a separate cooking.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states that once the *vaiśvadeva* has been performed, the remainder of the food is unfit for the *śrāddha*:
"One who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*) may perform the *śrāddha* even without having performed the *vaiśvadeva*."
"If the offering is made into a worldly fire, the remainder does not reach the ancestors. Thus it is said.

And regarding this very point, the statement of Paiṭhīnasi—"having set aside from the *śrāddha* cooking," and so forth—is shown. For this is not a prohibition of the performance of the *vaiśvadeva* after the *śrāddha*, because even for one who considers that the verb *uddhṛ* in the phrase "having set aside from the *śrāddha* cooking" denotes merely a separation, there would arise a contradiction with the requirement to perform the remnants of the *śrāddha* as established by such statements as "having completed the *śrāddha* according to rule. Therefore, for one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*), the *vaiśvadeva* oblation before the *śrāddha* using a different cooking is not prohibited by anyone; thus, it must be performed by him as well.

It is said: Just as, because the Vaiśvadeva is prescribed to be performed with the food remaining from a *śrāddha* after the *śrāddha* has concluded, the injunction that it be performed with a portion extracted from the *śrāddha* cooking is interpreted as referring to times other than that; likewise, since the Vaiśvadeva is entirely prohibited before the *śrāddha*, those same rules must be interpreted as referring to times other than that. Thus, for one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagnika*), the Vaiśvadeva may be performed even with the *śrāddha* cooking after the *śrāddha* has concluded; however, during the *śrāddha* itself, it is never to be performed with the *śrāddha* cooking, but only with a separate cooking; and prior to the *śrāddha*, it is not to be performed at all.

Now, if all prohibitions regarding what ought to be performed were restricted to the Vaiśvadeva rite occurring in the middle of the Śrāddha, or restricted solely to that one rite, or restricted solely to those who lack the sacred fires (*anagnika*), three types of restriction (*saṅkoca*) would result. To explain: the agent-in-general—which is implied by the action in general, implied by the number denoted by the verbal suffix, or directly expressed by the verbal suffix, and which pervades both specific agents (those with and without sacred fires)—would be restricted to only one specific case, namely the agent who lacks sacred fires. This is because the Vaiśvadeva performed by an agent possessing sacred fires is necessarily preceded [by the Śrāddha], and thus cannot occur at the intermediate time. Thus, there is a restriction of the agent. Furthermore, the action-in-general in the form of the Vaiśvadeva—which is understood from the word "Vaiśvadeva" alone and which pervades multiple individual Vaiśvadeva actions occurring at both earlier and intermediate times—would be restricted to only the single instance of the Vaiśvadeva occurring at the intermediate time. Thus, there is a restriction of the action. For this very reason, there is a restriction of time. In this way, three restrictions would result. Moreover, if this were the case, the requirement that the Vaiśvadeva performed by an agent possessing sacred fires must be accomplished using the cooking of the Śrāddha food would not be set aside. And if the sentence prohibiting precedence were restricted solely to those without sacred fires, there would indeed be a restriction of the agent.

To this, it is replied: First, this must be considered—whether the prohibition that the Vaiśvadeva oblation is not to be performed before the Śrāddha is to be explained as applying exclusively to those with or without a sacred fire (*sāgnika* and *anagnika*), by being construed as a single syntactical unit with another statement—"it should not be performed after taking [food] out from the Śrāddha cooking"—for the sake of establishing the general agent implied by the general action; or whether, in order to favor the literal sense of the text, it is to be taken as a prohibition of the Vaiśvadeva rite in its own nature, applying exclusively to those without a sacred fire? In this regard:
Because of independence, because of the abandonment of what is heard, because of the transition to another thing to be enjoined,
and because of the consequence of meaninglessness, this [injunction] does not form a single syntactical unit with anything else.
Nor is its prior connection with a single person who maintains the sacred fires perceived [by this cognition],
because it is sublated by the instruction regarding a previous time.
In this case, the fault of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) would clearly follow regarding the positive concomitance (anvaya);
for otherwise, that would indeed constitute a single sentence once the concomitance has been ascertained.
Nor is it possible for one who knows the multitude of faults to establish a logical connection by identifying the Bhāṣya as having a single unified meaning after having set forth those defects.
Nor is it held that there is support for what is to be inferred by means of a directly perceived injunction;
for the inferred general agency contradicts the heard prohibition.

The sentence, which is already established even by the prohibition of the *vaiśvadeva*’s essential form, requires syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with another sentence; and that other sentence likewise [requires it]. In the case of such syntactic unity, one must assume an injunction prohibiting the performance of the *śrāddha* cooking, by abandoning the status of being merely a prohibition of the *vaiśvadeva*’s essential form as heard in the text. This being so, even the charge of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) does not apply, because its purpose is fulfilled by those very [prohibitions] that forbid the performance of the single cooking. This is the meaning of the first verse. The second and subsequent verses, however, have their meanings clearly evident. Therefore, this prohibition—that the *vaiśvadeva* is not to be performed before the *śrāddha*—refers exclusively to one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*). As for the prohibitions regarding the performance of the *śrāddha* cooking, they refer to both those with and without a sacred fire (*sāgnika* and *anagnika*). Among these, since the *vaiśvadeva* is entirely prohibited for one without a sacred fire (*anagnika*) prior to the time of the *śrāddha*, it refers to the *anagnika* as the performer during the intermediate period; whereas for the *sāgnika*, he is the performer during the earlier period. Consequently, the aforementioned defects of over-narrowing (*saṃkoca*) do not apply. However, the restriction of those [prohibitions] to the earlier period for the *anagnika* is indeed justified by the specific scriptural statement. Thus, for the *anagnika*, the *vaiśvadeva* is under no circumstances to be performed prior to the *śrāddha*; for even the rules prescribing the *vaiśvadeva* for the intermediate and later periods apply exclusively to the *anagnika*, thereby precluding the *vaiśvadeva* from the earlier period for him. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, the prohibition is meaningless, because it is heard in another Smṛti text. Thus, if even one who asserts a connection based on the commonality of the agent cannot obtain syntactic unity with another sentence, how much less could one who asserts a connection with a specific individual—the one without a sacred fire—obtain it?
Regarding the necessity of performing the Vaiśvadeva rite during the course of a Śrāddha, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations into the fire prior to the feeding of the Brahmins;
it is traditionally taught that one should perform the Bhūtayajña and other rites after having completed the Śrāddha."

By the statement, "prior to the feeding of the Brahmins," it is said that one should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. By the statement, "having performed the *śrāddha*, the *bhūtayajña* and so forth are prescribed," it is stated that the *bhūtayajña* itself is to be performed at the conclusion of the *śrāddha*. Thus, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* demonstrates that, by implication, the offering of the *bali* should be performed immediately after the Vaiśvadeva. This is one time for the Vaiśvadeva performed without the sacred fires (*anagnika*). A second [time] is also mentioned in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Having gratified the ancestors according to the rule, one should offer the *bali* according to the injunction."
Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, followed by the recitation for the Brahmins.
The word *bali* is also explained in that very context:
"O Hero, know that whatever a wise man should offer upon the ground with the mantra 'burnt by fire' (agnidagdhā) at all times during the rite of *śrāddha*, that is always called *bali*."
By this, it is stated that one should perform the Vaiśvadeva after the offering of the *vikira* oblation and before the recitation of the *svastivācana*. This is the second time.
A third time is also mentioned in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other sources. Regarding this, Manu says:
"The remnants, however, should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic *bali* offering—thus the law is established.
(3.246) The commentary on this by Medhātithi is stated as follows:

While the twice-born are eating, that food which remains stuck to the vessels used as the locus of eating or has fallen upon the ground must not be wiped away from that place until the Brāhmaṇas have departed. Then, once the Śrāddha rite is completed, one should immediately thereafter perform the Vaiśvadeva oblation, the daily rites, the feeding of guests, and so forth; this is because the word *bali* is intended to indicate these [other duties].

Others, however, say that the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings) alone is most commonly designated by the term *bali*; therefore, the offering into the fire (*agnau homaḥ*) prior to the *śrāddha* is not contradictory. Nor should it be argued: "In a rite intended for the ancestors (*pitrya*), once the *vaiśvadeva* has begun immediately thereafter, how can another rite be performed in the midst of it?"—just as, when Brahmins have been invited on the previous day, the performance of the morning and evening *homa*s is not contradictory even if the *śrāddha* itself has not yet been performed. In exactly the same way, for one who maintains the perpetual sacred fire (*sadāgnika*), the performance of the *vaiśvadeva-homa* in the interval is likewise not contradictory. Therefore, when the *bhūtayajña* is postponed, according to the principle of postponing the subsequent based on the initial, only those ritual elements following the *bhūtayajña* are postponed, and not those preceding it, such as the *vaiśvadeva* and so forth.

To this it is replied: if the *vaiśvadeva* oblation were performed before the *śrāddha*, and then the *śrāddha*, and then the *baliharaṇa*, then the *devayajña* and *bhūtayajña* would be separated [from their proper sequence]. Consequently, the established order—consisting of immediate succession—between those two as propounded by such scriptural injunctions as "One should perform the *vaiśvadeva* and likewise the *bhautika* offering," would be subverted. Indeed, even the principle of "anticipation up to the end" (*tadantāpakarṣa*) is resorted to precisely for the sake of not subverting the established order; therefore, to avoid that subversion, the "postponement up to the end" (*tadantotkarṣa*) must also be resorted to in certain cases. Nor does this result in a contradiction with the rule regarding the "postponement starting from the beginning" (*tadādyutkarṣa*); for that rule applies only where the postponement of a preceding item results in the subversion of its own internal order and time. However, when the *vaiśvadeva* is performed even after the *śrāddha* has been completed, there is no subversion of its own order and time. Therefore, the performance of all the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) occurs subsequent to the *śrāddha*.
Thus ends the commentary composed by Medhātithi.
This same point is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The remnants of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed."
"Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite once the ancestral rites (pitṛkarman) have been concluded. Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O mighty-armed one, having performed the Śrāddha and having dismissed the Brāhmaṇas..."
Then, O lord of men, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites. In another Smṛti it is said:
"When a man desires to give a Śrāddha to the ancestors..."
"Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite once the Śrāddha ceremony has been completed.
Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"Having performed the Śrāddha according to the rules, one should thereafter perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites."
"Then one should go for alms, and thereafter give betel nut and other such items.
Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya regarding the conclusion of the Śrāddha:
"Thereafter, one should perform the daily rites and likewise feed the guests."
Then that man should eat that food together with his servants and others.

"Daily rites" (*nityakriyā*) refers to those consisting of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, the offering of bali, the daily *śrāddha*, and so forth. Thus, for the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*), there are three times: one immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire), another after the scattering of food (*vikira*), and the third after the dismissal of the Brahmins.
This concludes the determination of the times for the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one who maintains no sacred fire.
Now follows the determination of the times for the *vaiśvadeva* performed by one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*).

Its performance is neither in the middle of the *śrāddha* nor at its conclusion, but rather when the *śrāddha* has not yet been performed; for since the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed before the *śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* must be performed even before that.
Thus says Devala: "But when the *vaiśvadeva* has not been performed, the *sthālīpāka* is prescribed."
But elsewhere than at the piṇḍayajña, it is prescribed for the afternoon.

[609] Here, the rites accomplished by means of the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice-offering) are designated by the term *sthālīpāka*. These, being distinct from the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, are performed even when the *vaiśvadeva* has not yet been performed. However, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is performed later in the afternoon, after the *vaiśvadeva* has been completed. Furthermore, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* was mentioned by Manu as preceding the *śrāddha*:
"A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the *pitṛyajña* at the waning of the moon..."
"One should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha every month.
Regarding this very point, Laugākṣi states clearly:
"Having performed the rites at the end of the fortnight and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one who maintains the sacred fires..."
"Then the wise man should perform the Piṇḍayajña, and thereafter the Anvāhāryaka.
Here, "end of the fortnight" (*pakṣānta*) refers to the *agnyanvādhāna* (the ritual preparation of the fires), and "Anvāhāryaka" refers to the *darśaśrāddha*.

Now, one might ask: since the Vaiśvadeva is prescribed precisely between the end of the fortnight and the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, its performance by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) is already understood; for what purpose, then, is the term "one who maintains the sacred fires" explicitly mentioned?

No; this is for the purpose of excluding the performer of the *sthālīpāka* and *piṇḍapitṛyajña* at the beginning of the fortnight (*pakṣādi*) who is without a sacred fire (*anagnika*). Therefore, even he must perform the *vaiśvadeva* at the very same times prescribed in the preceding section for those without a fire. Gobhila also stated in the sūtra regarding the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), the benediction (*svastyayana*), and the meaning of the sentence: "In every variety of *śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* occurs only at the beginning. In the Śruti as well, the *vaiśvadeva* is heard of as occurring at the beginning for one who possesses the sacred fires: "They should not eat what has not been offered, nor should they give what has not been offered. Even for one with the sacred fires, in certain specific *śrāddhas*, the *vaiśvadeva* occurs only afterwards.
And so it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"When the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha or likewise the *ekoddiṣṭa* has arrived, the Vaiśvadeva rite should take place first; on the eleventh day, however, it should be performed afterwards."

In this context, the mention of "parvan" (festival days) is intended as an illustration for *śrāddhas* dedicated to multiple deities. Consequently, the settled rule is that for *śrāddhas* other than those on the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*), the Vaiśvadeva offering must be performed first by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*); however, it is performed afterwards specifically on the eleventh-day *śrāddha*.
Thus says Śālaṅkāyana:
"One who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering indeed before the *śrāddha*."
Except for that which pertains to the eleventh day, for that is prescribed at the very end.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva rite performed by one who maintains the sacred fires.
Now follows the determination of the time for the *bhūtayajña* and other rites.

Regarding this, the teacher Karka maintains that at the very same time as the *vaiśvadeva*, immediately following it, is the offering known as the *bhūtayajña*. As for the offering (*bali*) mentioned by Manu at the conclusion of the *śrāddha*—in the passage, "Then one should perform the domestic offering"—that is intended for the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*), not for the *bhūtayajña*. For this very reason, Pāraskara, after describing the dismissal of the Brahmins, states:
"Having dismissed them, one should worship the household deities with the offering of the *bali*."
Śaṅkhadhara also [states]:

"At the very same time as the Vaiśvadeva, immediately following that, the Bhūtayajña is also performed; never indeed should an interruption by another rite be made between the Vaiśvadeva and the Bhūtayajña, because of the scriptural injunction regarding non-interruption.
For it is thus:
"The sacrifice to the gods (devayajña) is prescribed first, and the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña) is the next.
Likewise: "One should offer the bali to the beings from the remainder of the food offered to the gods."

Furthermore, as for the statement regarding the *bhūtayajña* at the end of the *śrāddha* when the *vaiśvadeva* has already been performed previously, its purpose is to indicate that even though the *bhūtayajña* was performed immediately after the *vaiśvadeva*, it must be performed again for that specific duration as an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. Likewise, as for the statement regarding the *gṛhabali* at the end of the *śrāddha* when the *vaiśvadeva* has already been performed previously, that too is intended to mean that although the *gṛhabali* was performed at the time of the *vaiśvadeva*, it must be performed again for that specific duration solely as an integral part of the *śrāddha*.

This is untenable, because it contradicts the fact that the *bhūtayajña* and other rites—which serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—cannot simultaneously be subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*.

If you argue that, as in the case of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), there is no contradiction in a single thing serving both purposes, we say no; for since no scriptural statement (*śruti*) or other evidence is observed that establishes the *śrāddha* as the primary purpose, the principle of "separateness of connection" is not established here.
Now, it might be argued that this is indeed a separate ritual act, enjoined as having the status of an auxiliary to the *śrāddha* established by the context.

That too is not correct, because the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings), which serves a human purpose, is recognized as being identical [to the one previously mentioned], just like the *vaiśvadeva*. Otherwise, in the case of the injunction "one should then perform the *vaiśvadeva*," there would follow the undesirable consequence of enjoining a separate *vaiśvadeva* as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. And this is not tenable due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*). For when only the sequence is enjoined, there is the merit of parsimony (*lāghava*) and the favoring of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Therefore, even the lack of intervention by another scriptural statement (*vacana*) should be accepted as being of that same nature. And such a scriptural statement has been shown by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*.
"One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation into the fire prior to the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas;

however, after performing the Śrāddha, one should perform the Bhūtayajña and so forth. One should not conclude from the mere mention of the "oblation" (*āhuti*) here that the subsidiary *bali* offerings of the Vaiśvadeva must be performed afterwards; for in the second half of the verse, it is specifically the Bhūtayajña and the others that are prescribed as occurring immediately after the Śrāddha. Precisely for this reason...
"One should perform the Vaiśvadeva and the daily bali offering.
Thus, within the very section on Śrāddha, the *Matsya Purāṇa* has stated the immediate succession of these two.
This concludes the determination of the time for the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) and the others.
[612] Now follows the determination of the times for the obligatory *śrāddha*.

Although the obligatory *śrāddha* has already been determined within the section concerning the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) and so forth, it is introduced again here in order to state certain specific details.
In that regard, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Then one should perform the daily rites and likewise feed the guests;
thereafter, the man should eat that food together with his servants and others."

‘Then’ (*tataḥ*) means by that food remaining from the *śrāddha*; ‘the daily rite’ (*nityakriyām*) refers to that which is accomplished with food. Therefore, the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*) must also be performed with that very same [food]. Alternatively, the daily *śrāddha* should be performed with a separate cooking (*pṛthakpākena*), because since it is of the nature of a *śrāddha*, there is the possibility of employing a separate cooking that possesses the characteristics of a *śrāddha*. For this very reason, regarding the daily *śrāddha*, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: “Not with a separate cooking, say others. The meaning of this is: the daily *śrāddha* should be performed with a cooking separate from the cooking for the *śrāddhas* of the new moon (*darśa*) and so forth; however, others say this is not so, meaning that the daily *śrāddha* may also be performed with the remains of the cooking intended for the *śrāddhas* of the new moon and so forth. And this is optional (*aniyata*) when another *śrāddha* has already been performed.
As it is stated in that very same place:
"Some men desire the daily rite for the ancestors;
others likewise do not [desire] it for the ancestors; one should perform the remainder as previously described."

"Of the ancestors," "the daily rite" (*nityakriyā*) refers to the *nityaśrāddha*. Regarding this alternative for the *nityaśrāddha*, the following arrangement applies: in the case of *śrāddhas* performed on common occasions such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), as well as in *nāndīmukha* and *tīrtha-śrāddhas*, the *nityaśrāddha* need not be performed because it is accomplished by occasion (*prasaṅgasiddhatayā*), since the deities of the *nityaśrāddha* are already intended to be worshipped there. However, in the case of annual *ekoddiṣṭa* rites and others, the *nityaśrāddha* must certainly be performed, because there is no rule that all the deities of the *nityaśrāddha* and so forth are necessarily intended to be worshipped in those specific rites. "The remainder," such as the *vaiśvadeva* offering and other rites, "one should perform as before"; the meaning is that one should perform them according to the established rules.
Thus it is said in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"One should not perform the daily *śrāddha* where it might be accomplished incidentally;
when another *śrāddha* has been performed elsewhere, one must not omit that [daily one], because of its obligatory nature."

Thus ends the determination of the time for *śrāddha* within the *Kālanirṇaya*, in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the faculties of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
[614] Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Next, the auspicious lunar days (puṇyatithi) in their sequence beginning from the first day (pratipad).
In that regard, first is the meritorious *pratipad*. In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"O mighty-armed one, in ancient times, the *pratipad* in the month of Caitra was meritorious;
on that day, the best of men who, having seen the Sun, performs an ablution [attains great merit]."
O King, tiger among the Kurus, no misfortune, no mental anxieties, and no physical ailments shall befall him who performs his ablutions in that [tirtha].
For that divine *nīrājana* rite is indeed the destroyer of all diseases;
O King, the monarch should adorn everything, including cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
Then, with all these—powders, garments, and so forth—one should lead [the image] beneath the archway;
likewise, O scion of the Kuru lineage, one should provide a feast for the Brāhmaṇas.
"O descendant of Kuru, O King, these three lunar days were previously proclaimed for the months of Kārttika, Āśvayuja, or likewise Caitra," as stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Since she was proclaimed by Brahmā as the most excellent of lunar days (tithis),
and since she was established at the very beginning, she is therefore called Pratipad.
For these three lunar days were proclaimed of old, O joy of the Kurus:
in the month of Kārttika, in the month of Āśvina, and in the month of Caitra, O Bhārata;
on whichever lunar day occurs in Kārttika, bathing and giving gifts yield a hundredfold merit.
O Bhārata, by worshipping and offering oblations to Agni even at the commencement of the rite,
one obtains all kinds of grain and immeasurable wealth through the sacrificial offering.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "At the beginning of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, on the lunar day [of the full moon],
the procession and worship with flowers and garments should be performed at night for the sake of desired happiness."
Having honored [the deity] with unwashed garments, one shall indeed go to the abode of Brahmā.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"In the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there are indeed two observances:
the 'Lustration of Women' (nārī-nirājana) in the morning, and the 'Auspicious Garland' (maṅgala-mālikā) in the evening."
If, however, the first lunar day (pratipad) is very short, then one should perform the Nārīnirājana on the second day; at that time, the Maṅgalamālikā rite should be performed in the evening.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"Having arrived either in the morning or during the two ghaṭikās of the first lunar day (pratipad),
the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) should be performed on that day, and the auspicious garland (maṅgalamālikā) in the evening."
And so it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"If the auspicious ghaṭikā of the first lunar day (pratipad) should be obtained in the morning,
then one should perform the Maṅgalamālikā rite on the second lunar day in the evening."
When the Nārī-nīrājana ceremony takes place on the new moon day at the end of the month of Āśvina,
there will be disease among women in that region, as well as famine.
At the beginning of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, during the two ghaṭīs of the new moon,
one should not perform the Maṅgalamālikā ceremony at all for fear of the ruin of the country.
