In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "On the first day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, Satyavat was defeated and Śaṅkara was conquered; yet on that occasion, Pārvatī obtained victory."
Therefore, I am Śaṅkara, who suffers, while Gaurī dwells in eternal happiness;
for that reason, men should engage in gambling there at dawn.
In that gambling match, for whichever side there is victory, their year shall be auspicious;
but defeat will be adverse and cause the loss of gains.
One should listen to songs, instrumental music, and the like while well-anointed and well-adorned;
and one should especially enjoy a meal together with hundreds of kinsmen.
On that night, a very beautiful bedchamber should be prepared,
adorned with perfumes, flowers, garments, and divine jewels.
Encircled by a garland of lamps and likewise perfumed by the king,
that night should be spent together with beloved women;
and the twice-born, kinsmen, and relatives should be honored with new garments.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*: "On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), having worshipped Brahmā with lamps mixed with molasses and unwashed garments, one shall indeed go to the abode of Brahmā."
A person should adorn that place with perfumes, flowers, and new garments;
on that first lunar day (pratipadā), he shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
This lunar day is of great merit, characterized by offerings of clarified butter;
it is indeed eternally dear to Brahmā and is celebrated as the Bāleyī.
He who honors the Brahmins on this day, and especially himself,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa, Trivikrama said to Bali:
"O tiger among men, there shall be a great festival for you known as the Vīrapratipadā; on that occasion, people, joyful and well-adorned, will [greet] you."
They will truly worship with offerings of flowers and incense;
there, a preeminent festival shall take place day and night.
Thus ends the Puṣya-pratipad.
Now follows the Puṇya-dvitīyā; regarding this, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
On the second day, one should worship Umā, Śiva, and Agni;
sacrificial food (haviṣya) should be offered as the oblation (naivedya), along with perfumes and ritual worship.
In this regard, the worship of *damanaka* in the month of Caitra and so forth is commenced in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The second lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina is indeed meritorious;
a gift bestowed on this day is said to yield infinite fruit."
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vṛścika,
he who does not perform the worship [of his brother] shall see his brothers perish throughout seven lifetimes."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Having performed the worship of Brahmā according to the rules on the second lunar day when it falls on a Thursday, one should eat only at night; thus one obtains the desired prosperity."

‘Vidhi’ is Brahmā. His worship should be performed with the Gāyatrī or with another mantra as prescribed in the section on the subtle (vraścana-prakaraṇa). Thus ends the auspicious second lunar day (Puṇyadvitīyā). Now begins the auspicious third lunar day (Puṇyatṛtīyā).
On the third day, one should worship the Goddess together with Śaṅkara,
using fragrant flowers, incense, and the *damanaka* flower adorned with beautiful garlands.
In this context, the month of Caitra is the subject under discussion.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "The third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha is meritorious."
Indeed, that [time] yields infinite fruit for acts such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "O tiger among the Kurus, this great lunar day in the month of Vaiśākha,
which is the third, is inexhaustible in the world and is saluted by the gods."
Whatever gift is given, whether it be small or great, all that is imperishable because of this; therefore, she is remembered as Akṣyā.
The third lunar day (tṛtīyā) that is specifically conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
and especially if a third lunar day conjoined with both Mercury (Budha) and Śravaṇa is obtained,
bathing, fasting, and other such observances performed on that day are proclaimed to be inexhaustible in their merit.
Likewise:
"The gift of water is praised, and likewise that of sweetmeats;
O King of kings, so too is sandalwood [praised] on the third lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha."
The word "to be given" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Likewise, molasses and cakes should be offered in the month of Bhādrapada;
furthermore, milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered on the third lunar day for the pleasure of Vāmadeva.
O King, on the third day of the month of Māgha, the giving of molasses and salt brings auspicious merit to both women and men.
The third lunar day, when joined with Rohiṇī and especially conjoined with Mercury, is said by him to yield very great fruit when it is being recited.
Thus ends the Puṇyatṛtīyā. Now follows the Puṇyacaturthī, as described in the Varāhapurāṇa.
"On the fourth [lunar day], however, the worship of Gaṇeśa and especially of Pārvatī should be performed"— this is understood as the continuation [of the rule]. Thus it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa.
On the fourth lunar day, one should perform worship of Gaṇeśa and offer sweetmeats such as *laḍḍukas* for the destruction of obstacles and the fulfillment of all desires.
And on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, this worship is performed with *damanaka* plants.
In the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"O King, she is considered to be of three kinds on the fourth day: Śivā, Śāntā, and Sukhā."
In the month of Bhādrapada, the bright fortnight is auspicious and honored among the worlds.
O King, by the grace of that elephant, bathing, giving gifts, fasting, and likewise the recitation of mantras performed therein shall become multiplied a thousandfold.
In that place, O tiger among the Kurus, women always honor their mother-in-law and father-in-law with jaggery, salt, and cakes.
Indeed, all those women shall become fortunate through the gladdening of Vighneśa;
a maiden, however, should worship him especially according to this rite.
O Lord of the Earth, that fourth lunar day which falls in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha should be known as always bestowing peace; it indeed constantly brings about tranquility.
Acts such as the gift of knowledge are known to yield a thousandfold merit.
Especially for women, O King, who worship their teacher with jaggery,
salt, and ghee, O Hero, descendant of Kuru, they shall become fortunate.
"When the day of Mars falls on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, it should be known as the one that bestows happiness; it is celebrated by the name 'Sukhā'.
All rites such as ritual bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, performed then, are said to be inexhaustible. Thus [it is stated].
Yama: If the conjunction with Bharaṇī occurs on the fourth lunar day during the day of Saturn,
then by worshipping the god Yama, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the Puṇyacaturthī. Now follows the Puṇyapañcamī, as described in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
O King, the fifth lunar day is beloved and increases the joy of the nāgas.
Those men who bathe the nāgas with milk on the fifth day grant fearlessness and protection of life to their own families.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Then, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, the fair-faced Śrī,
by the command of Keśava, descended from the world of Viṣṇu to the human realm."
Therefore, one should worship her there; Lakṣmī does not abandon him.
This Śrīpañcamī should be observed, for it grants access to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"When Janārdana Kṛṣṇa has fallen asleep on the fifth lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada,
one should then mentally worship the Goddess who resides upon the branches of the *snuhī* plant."
A man who places *picumarda* and *palāśa* leaves inside his house and worships the Goddess shall not encounter any fear from snakes.
O lord of men, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
fierce serpents should be drawn with cow dung on both sides of the door.
O Hero, one should worship according to the rules with curds, dūrvā sprouts, and kuśa grass,
as well as with offerings of perfumes and flowers, and by the satiation of brahmins.
O hero, those who here worship the nāgas with devotion at that [place] shall never have any fear of serpents.
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the fifth day, a man endowed with faith,
having painted the nāgas with colors such as white and black,
should worship them with perfumes, flowers, clarified butter, guggulu resin, and milk-rice.
The serpents, Takṣaka and the others, being pleased with him, depart quickly;
for seven generations of his lineage, there shall be no fear of snakes.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "The meritorious fifth day of the month of Bhādrapada is declared to be Nāgapañcamī. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
The bright fifth day of the month of Mārgaśīra and that of Śrāvaṇa are meritorious;
through bathing and giving gifts on these days, they yield great fruit and bestow the world of the Nāgas.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having propitiated the excellent Śrī,
on the fifth day worship with kunda flowers is for the sake of prosperity through the Kunda [goddess]."
Thus ends the Puṇyapañcamī. Now follows the Puṇyaṣaṣṭhī, according to the Brahmapurāṇa.
Skanda was born on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month named Caitra;
he was consecrated by Brahmā himself to the generalship of the gods,
conquered the Daitya Tāraka, and pierced Mount Krauñca with his spear.
Therefore, in every case, Skanda must indeed be worshipped according to the prescribed rite with fragrant garlands,
lamps, ornaments, garments, food, and cocks;
together with cock-shaped toys, bells, chowries, and mirrors.
It should be understood that this applies to all the "White Sixth" (Śukla-ṣaṣṭhī) days. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O bull among the Bharatas, this which is the sixth day in the month of Bhādrapada..."
All acts such as bathing and giving charity performed on this [day] are said to be inexhaustible.

O King, on the sixth lunar day one should subsist on fruits, especially during the month of Kārttika, O Monarch; remaining self-controlled, celibate, and composed, throughout both the dark and light fortnights.
He who, on the sixth [lunar day], eats only fruit and observes the practice of eating only at night,
attains supreme renown exceedingly both in this world and the next;
especially one fallen from his kingdom regains his own kingdom before long.
Likewise:
"The sixth [lunar day] in the month of Bhādrapada is for the propitiation of the Sun and for the imperishability of merit.
O bull among the Bharatas, this which occurs in the month of Bhādrapada as the sixth [tithi]..."
O King, this [river] is auspicious, peaceful, and virtuous, removing both merit and sin;
it is said that whatever bathing, giving of gifts, or other acts are performed here, all become inexhaustible.
Those who behold the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma) residing here in the southern region are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
In each and every instance, one should always behold Kārttikeya; indeed, he who,
having gone toward the southern direction, performs this three times and worships the Lord of the Gods with faith, shall go to the abode of peace.
The fruit of those who go to the north of the Vindhya mountains after having said three times, "I have gone toward the southern direction," is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"That sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa is dear to Hari."
That day on which the sacrificial fire is offered oblations is known as Mahāṣaṣṭhī.
Thus ends the Puṇya-ṣaṣṭhī. Now follows the Puṇya-saptamī, as described in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
He who, having fasted properly on the sixth day, worships the Tortoise on the seventh,
becomes free from disease, attains wealth, and obtains his desired fruit.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, that seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is renowned as Aparājitā; it destroys even the greatest of sins.

O Hero, that seventh day in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Nandā; it is auspicious and bestows all joy. It is said that rites such as bathing and giving gifts performed on that day yield inexhaustible merit.
Likewise: "The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Nandā; it bestows bliss.
It is declared to be named Jayantī, remembered as meritorious and a destroyer of sins."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Because the Sun-god, mounted upon his chariot, [appeared] at the beginning of that Manvantara on the seventh day of the month of Māgha, it is therefore called Rathasaptamī."
Thus, O Hero, this seventh [vow] called Rathāhvā has been described;
it is renowned as Mahāsaptamī, the destroyer of great sins.
Viṣṇu:
The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to an eclipse of the sun;
bathing on that day at the time of sunrise yields great fruit.
Likewise: On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, at the very moment the sun rises,
bathing there according to the prescribed rite destroys even the most heinous sins.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, which is Koṭibhāskarā,
one shall attain longevity, health, and prosperity by performing ritual bathing and the offering of water (argha).
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
If Sunday should fall on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, that seventh day is named Vijayā; what is given on that day yields great fruit.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, when the constellation consists of five stars—
namely Rohiṇī, Aśleṣā, Hasta, Puṣya, and Maghā."
O Lord of Gods, when the constellation of the Sun occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight during its first quarter, then that day is said to be auspicious;
the wise have declared that the bathing of the God with clarified butter should be performed then.
Thus, O Hero, this seventh [vow] named Bhadrā has been described;
by fasting upon it, even a timid man may attain the world of Brahmā.
"The asterism of Savitṛ is Hasta; likewise, it is the conjunction with the first quarter.
Similarly:
"If, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, the asterism should be Hasta..."
That seventh lunar day, occurring on a Tuesday, is of great merit and destroys all sins.
Having fully worshipped the Lord of Gods, the sun Citrabhānu, on that day, one is liberated from the sins committed during seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
And he who observes the fast on that day with a restrained mind,
his soul purified of all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
When the sun enters [a new sign] on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
that seventh day is indeed Mahājayā, beloved of the Sun.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods—
all these are said to be multiplied ten millionfold, according to the word of Bhāskara.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The seventh lunar day (saptamī) conjoined with the asterism Revatī and the Sun is of great fruit;
that seventh day on which Revatī occurs together with a Sunday."
Thus ends the Puṇyasaptamī. Now follows the Puṇyāṣṭamī. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Punarvasu,
one who bathes according to the prescribed rite at dawn shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
One should worship Durgā with *aśoka* flowers and drink the buds of the *aśoka*.
Those who, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra under the asterism Punarvasu,
drink the eight buds of the *aśoka*, shall never experience sorrow.
O Aśoka, beloved by the auspicious ones and born in the month of Madhu, I, tormented by grief, drink from you; make me forever free from sorrow.
[627] Thus ends the mantra for drinking.
In some places, the reading is *harābhīṣṭa*. [This is found] in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
In the month of Pauṣa, the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight is known as Mahābhadrā, which yields great fruit.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, Mahādeva said:
"O Goddess, when the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa falls on a Wednesday..."
Then she, being of great merit, was celebrated as Mahābhadrā.
O Goddess, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, libations, and feeding Brahmins performed there for my pleasure shall become a hundred-thousandfold in merit.
In some places, the reading is "bathing and likewise giving gifts" (snānaṃ tathā dānam).
Therefore, O Goddess, I am always to be worshipped on that [day] by men according to the rules,
with offerings of perfumes and flowers, and with the satiation of Brahmins.

O Goddess, when in the month of Pauṣa, on the eighth lunar day, the meritorious asterism presided over by Yama arises— namely, Bharaṇī, so called because it belongs to the realm of Yama— then [one should perform the rite].
At that time, however, that highly meritorious day is known as Jayantī Aṣṭamī.
O Goddess, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and libations performed on that day all become entirely multiplied ten millionfold.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"When the eighth day of the dark fortnight falls on a Rohiṇī while the sun is in Leo,
worship of the Sun performed on that day destroys the sins born of three lifetimes."
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"Whoever offers water to Bhīṣma on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
is instantly released from the sins committed throughout the year."
In some places, however, it is read otherwise:
"Those men who, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, offer water and perform a *śrāddha* for Bhīṣma, shall possess progeny."
To him of the Vaiyāghrapadya lineage and the Sāṅkṛtya pravara,
who is childless, I offer this water for Bhīṣmavarman.

Thus ends the section on the water-offering (*jalamātra*). On this point, some say: "One should perform the *śrāddha* facing east, because Bhīṣma was an incarnation of a Vasu, and thus his divinity is established. Nor should it be argued that, even though he was an incarnation of a Vasu, since he was a Kṣatriya and is understood to be the father of all people, one should perform the *śrāddha* facing south; for if one were to prioritize his status as a Kṣatriya, it would result in a contradiction with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*). For it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa who performs the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) for one of a lower caste... [and so forth].
He attains that state both in this world and in the next.

Because Marīci and others have prohibited the performance of *aurdhvadehika* (post-mortem) rites for a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya through such passages as these, there is no contradiction with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) if the rite is performed while honoring his status as a deity; for the conduct of the learned is indeed observed, as even Brāhmaṇas perform the *śrāddha* for Bhīṣma.

This is incorrect, because upon examining the wording of the mantra, "Bhīṣmavarmaṇe," one understands that he is honored as a Kṣatriya, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "For a Kṣatriya, [the name] ending in *varman* is prescribed.
[The mantra says: "In the month of Māgha, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, [offer] water to Bhīṣmavarmaṇe..."

[629] Thus, it is understood in this very same way even from the prescriptive statement (*vidhivākya*). Nor should it be said that the word *varman* is prescribed only when the word *deva* has not already been established; for if one were to say that the prohibition against prescribing words such as *bhrātṛpāla* and others applies to *kṣatriya* in general, while its scope is restricted to *kṣatriyas* other than those [specifically mentioned], then one must also state that because of the prohibition of a specific agent in the form of a Brāhmaṇa at a *kṣatriya*-śrāddha, this rule refers specifically to the Bhīṣma-śrāddha. If that were so, the opposite contingency would follow. Nor should it be said that since this prohibition depends on the prior establishment of the [Brāhmaṇa’s] eligibility, an option (*vikalpa*) is possible, and thus a Brāhmaṇa also has the right to perform the Bhīṣma-śrāddha. That is not so, precisely because of the fear of such an option; rather, one should resort to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), just as in the case of the injunction: "One performs the *ye yajāmahe* at the *anuyāja* offerings. Furthermore, there is no fixed practice (*śiṣṭācāra*) [of Brāhmaṇas performing it]; and even if such a practice existed, it is set aside by the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "Dharma is that which is ordained by Śruti and Smṛti; in the absence of that, the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is authoritative."
When the sun has entered Virgo during the dark fortnight, the eighth lunar day is especially distinguished;
it is called Aṣṭakā, and one should not neglect it even with mere vegetables.

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, there are three Aṣṭakās in the dark fortnight: the first is dedicated to Indra (*aindrī*), the second to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā*), and the third to the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevī*). The first is performed with vegetables, the second with meat, and the third with cakes. [Also stated] in the *Śivarahasya*.
In the latter fortnights of the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa,
there are indeed three Anvaṣṭakās, designated as "prior" and "intermediate," occurring respectively under the asterisms Puṣya and the others in sequence.
Āśvalāyana says: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and dewy seasons; these are the deities."
In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, however, it says:
"There are twelve full moons, twelve aṣṭakās, and twelve new moons.
The term "aṣṭakā" means the eighth days of the dark fortnights.
In the Mahābhārata it is declared that what is given on the Aṣṭakā days is infinite; likewise,
when the eighth day of the bright fortnight is full and conjoined with the son of the Moon (Mercury).
In that [age], those who observe religious vows shall not have their prosperity impaired.
‘Śaśiputra’ is Budha.
This is the Puṇyāṣṭamī. Now follows the Puṇyā Navamī.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "On the ninth day, the goddess Gaurī should always be worshipped with meditative concentration;
she will become the bestower of boons upon all the world—of this there is no doubt."
Some, however, say that the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina should be observed,
because of the praise found in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "The third day in Vaiśākha and likewise the ninth in Āśvayuja."

That is incorrect. Upon hearing the praise [of the rite], an excellence of the fruit is understood, but not that it refers specifically to the ninth day (*navamī*), as there is no evidence for such a restriction. As stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"On the ninth day, one should worship the Goddess, the great slayer of Mahiṣa."
Through offerings of saffron, agallochum, camphor, incense, food, banners, and libations,
as well as with *damanaka* and *marupatra* flowers, one shall attain the state known as Vijaya.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the exceedingly powerful Bhadrakālī is worshipped in the sovereign authority over all the Yoginīs."
Therefore, one should worship her there with devotion on all the ninth days, observing a fast and having subdued the senses, with various kinds of offerings.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina; on that day, the fruit is ten-million-fold. Likewise:
O lord of men, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, a gift given becomes multiplied ten millionfold. He who,
with a concentrated mind, observes the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika [attains the same merit].
One who bathes, gives gifts, or pays homage obtains inexhaustible fruit.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is for the festival of the ancestors;
bathing, offering oblations, and giving gifts on that day yield infinite fruit."
Thus ends the meritorious ninth day.
Now follows the meritorious tenth day:
the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is remembered as the "Mouth of the Year" (Saṃvatsaramukhī).
One should perform a bath in it, and especially offer gifts.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the tenth lunar day conjoined with the asterism Hasta,
it removes ten sins; therefore, it is known as Daśaharā.
One should perform a ritual bath in it, and especially offer gifts.
Manu has stated the ten evils:
harshness, falsehood, slander in every respect,
and incoherent prattle— this constitutes the fourfold nature of speech.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules, and consorting with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— these are the three types of mental action.
In the future,
if Tuesday should fall on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
that lunar day, conjoined with the asterism Hasta, should be known as the remover of all sins.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara: On the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, on a Tuesday, when the moon is in the Hasta constellation,
the descent of the Gaṅgā is remembered as the remover of all sins.

The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, conjoined with the Hasta nakṣatra, is the destroyer of ten sins; when joined with an auspicious day (Maṅgalavāra), it is the remover of all sins—this is the meaning. Immediately after the statement, "It is especially excellent when the Hasta nakṣatra occurs," it is recited thus: "That very day is remembered as Daśaharā. A man who bathes in the Gaṅgā even once during this conjunction shall have his purpose fulfilled;
on that occasion, the Gaṅgā indeed removes the ten sins—of this there is no doubt.

In this context, the destruction of light sins should be understood, but not the destruction of heavy sins, because that would result in the futility of the injunctions for heavy expiations regarding those [heavy sins].
And so says Gautama:
"Sins are heavy and light."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika—
performing vows and other rites on that day, one obtains the highest fruit."
Thus ends the Puṇyadaśamī. Now follows the Puṇyaikādaśī, according to the Vārāha Purāṇa.
A wise man, beginning from the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, should perform the ritual of eating only at night on the eleventh lunar day according to the prescribed rules for one year.
O best of givers of wealth,
that Lord Brahmā, being pleased, granted to him who had performed that vow the eleventh lunar day as his source of riches.
To him who remains disciplined and pure, eating only food not cooked by fire in that [city],
the god Dhanada, being pleased, bestows wealth.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "The eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight under the Puṣya asterism is most meritorious and destructive of sins. In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, when the lunar mansion is indeed Punarvasu, that day is known by the name Vijayā; it is the most excellent of all lunar days.
He who gives a prastha of sesame seeds and he who likewise remains devoted to fasting on that day for an entire year— the fruit of these two is recorded as equal.
In that [tirtha], Hari, the Lord of the world, the God who is the sovereign of all gods, swiftly approaches him as he arrives; therefore, it is remembered that the fruit thereof is infinite.
O best of beings, when the Puṣya asterism occurs on the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight,
that day is declared by Viṣṇu to be the destroyer of sins.
Having propitiated Govinda, the Lord of the lords of the worlds, in that [place], one is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
For one who performs the fast there after bathing completely,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever gift is given with Janārdana in mind,
or whatever oblation is performed on that [day], its fruit is declared to be inexhaustible.
Thus ends the Puṇyaikādaśī. Now follows the Puṇyadvādaśī, as described in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Fasting on the eleventh day of both fortnights,
he who worships Viṣṇu on the twelfth day shall partake in infinite fruit.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Hari with *campaka* flowers.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
And whatever is given on the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs), especially those that are bright (śukla),
and even more so, O best of the twice-born, when they are joined with the Śravaṇa asterism.

[635] Especially on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight, when it is joined with Mercury and in every respect associated with the constellation Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), occurring in the month of Caitra, it shall yield great fruit.
The "star of fortune" (bhāgyarkṣa) is Pūrvāphālgunī.
In Vaiśākha it is conjoined with Hastā; in Jyaiṣṭha, with Svāti;
likewise in Āṣāḍha, with Jyeṣṭhā; and in the month of Vaiṣṇava (Śrāvaṇa), with Mūla.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, which belongs to Viṣṇu,
as well as in the month of Bhādrapada,
the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is meritorious when conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa and the nakṣatra Āja (Punarvasu).
"Ājarkṣa" refers to Pūrvābhādrapadā.
In the month of Kārttika, [this lunar day] conjoined with Revatī bestows inexhaustible fruit. — Viṣṇu.

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva on the twelfth day with garments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, as well as by gratifying the fire and the Brahmins. Having perfectly completed this vow, one becomes purified of sin; by performing it throughout one's life, one attains Śvetadvīpa. By doing so on the twelfth day of both fortnights for a year, one attains the heavenly world (svargaloka); by doing so throughout one's life, one attains the world of Viṣṇu. [As stated] in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"The twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada yields great fruit."
And for those who offer oblations there, the fruit shall be a hundred thousandfold.
In the Viṣṇudharma:
"When the full moon of Māgha has passed,
that twelfth lunar day of the dark fortnight which is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism is called Tiladvādaśī."
[636] O King, on that day one should perform a bath with sesame seeds, an oblation with sesame seeds,
and a libation with sesame-water; likewise, a lamp should be offered with sesame oil, and sesame-water should be given,
as well as sesame seeds should be bestowed upon the Brahmins.
O Prajāpati, when the moon is situated in the Mūla constellation during the month of Māgha,
one who has fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight with senses subdued,
and who consumes only sesame seeds on the twelfth day, is liberated from all sins.
One who rubs himself with sesame, one who bathes with sesame, one who performs oblations with sesame, one who offers water with sesame,
one who eats sesame, and one who gives sesame— these six uses of sesame are destroyers of sin.
Having performed the Ṣaṭtila rite repeatedly, one is liberated from all sins;
for three thousand years, one is honored in the heavenly world.
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): If Jupiter and Mars are situated in Leo and the Sun is in the constellation Anurādhā during the bright fortnight;
The application [of the term] is that a lunar day (tithi) joined with the Karabha yoga and having an identical designation is called Vyatīpāta.
But by giving cows, land, gold, and clothing in this world, having cast off all evil, one attains the state of a god, the state of Indra, and freedom from disease.
A human being attains sovereignty over mortals.

‘Pañcānana’ means a lion; ‘samābhidhānā’ means having the same name as Pāraṇā; ‘tithiḥ’ means the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī); ‘karabheṇa’ means by the asterism Hasta. Thus is the meritorious Dvādaśī. [637]
Now, regarding the meritorious Trayodaśī: in the Skanda Purāṇa it is said, "The Trayodaśī at Kṣetra is meritorious; on those [other] days, the fruit is tenfold."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "The man who performs ritual bathing and charity on the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra obtains tenfold fruit for that deed."
Likewise: On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having fashioned an image of Madana out of *campaka* flowers and having worshipped it with diligence, one should join it with a fan.
Then desire was kindled, which bestows the prosperity of sons and grandsons.
In the Devīpurāṇa: On the thirteenth day, Kāmadeva, accompanied by his wife Rati and adorned with the qualities of the Aśoka tree, should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
One should draw [the deity] upon a water-pot or a white cloth with garments, fruits, and so forth;
by offering oblations of sugar-candy and sugar, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
And it should be noted that there is a worship of Damanaka in sequence.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"On the thirteenth day, Kāma should be worshipped by people according to their desire."
In the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra):
When the moon is in Maghā on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight and the sun is in Hasta,
then the Gajacchāyā occurs, which is attained through the merits of a Śrāddha.
Thus concludes the Puṇya-trayodaśī. [638] Now begins the Puṇya-caturdaśī.
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, there shall be the great festival of Kāma;
therein, by means of songs, instrumental music, and the like, as well as loathsome utterances, [the desires] of men [are fulfilled]."
The Blessed One creates desire, which bestows the abundance of sons and grandsons.
He who bathes on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra in the presence of Śiva,
and especially in the Gaṅgā, is not reborn as a preta.
If the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra falls on a Tuesday,
one shall not become a piśāca again by bathing and eating at the Gaṅgā.
In the Brahmapurāṇa:
Having worshipped Śiva on the fourteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, a person,
liberated from all sins, shall obtain every prosperity.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "When Mahendra has been propitiated and the flagstaffs have taken the form of banners,
then, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Hari as Ananta."
Having fashioned [an image] out of darbha grass and provided it with a water-vessel,
one shall obtain one's desired wish by means of incense, lamps, and other offerings to the deity.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vṛścika, which is known as Pāṣāṇacaturdaśī,
one should worship Gaurī at night by consuming stones."
The meaning is: with flour in the form of stones.
In the Brāhma [Purāṇa]: On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, under the Citrā asterism, on a Tuesday.
If Sthāṇu is propitiated there, he will certainly grant the city of Śiva.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada,
as well as that which falls in the dark fortnight of Māgha— these are indeed very powerful for the giving of gifts."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having reached any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one who goes there and remains self-restrained should offer libations to Yama."
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
Salutations to you, who hold the staff, the lord of the departed, the wielder of the noose,
the one made of udumbara wood, the terrible one, and Citragupta!
One should offer three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds for each individual;
the sin committed during a year perishes at that very moment.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Likewise, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight falling on a Tuesday (bhaumāha), one should perform the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
By the term "bhaumāha," it indicates an exceptional degree of excellence. On all fourteenth days, having bathed in river water and worshipped Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from sins.
Thus ends the fourteenth [day].
Now follows the meritorious full-moon day.
Saṃvarta says:
When the full moon day of the month of Māgha has arrived,
one who has fasted and given sesame seeds to the Brāhmaṇas is liberated from all sins.

In this context, the gift is prescribed for the full moon day because it is the primary element; consequently, by implication, the fast is observed on the fourteenth day. As stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"On all full moon days that are conjoined with the Maghā asterism..."
The fruit of gifts given here shall be tenfold.
The full moon day that is joined with Jupiter is a great Paurṇamāsī;
the full moons of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha yield especially great fruit.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O best of the twice-born, that day on which the soul of great power enters into conjunction with the full moon is to be known as the 'Great Full Moon' (Mahāpaurṇamāsī)."
Bathing, giving gifts, and likewise the recitation of prayers are recorded as yielding infinite fruit.
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): "That full-moon day on which the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky is declared to be 'Great' (mahatī) once every year."
In that [tithi], acts such as giving gifts and observing fasts are proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
When the moon and Jupiter are in the lunar mansion called Māsa, and the sun is fifteen degrees from that,
on a Thursday coinciding with the full moon— that lunar day is indeed called Mahatī.
At Harikṣetra, at the Gaṅgā, at the ocean, and likewise at Naimiṣa,
bathing, giving gifts, and performing śrāddha on Mahāśabda-tithi yield infinite merit.
When Jupiter and the Moon are in the constellation Aindra (Jyeṣṭhā) and the Sun is likewise in Prājāpatya (Uttarā Phalgunī),
the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha is celebrated as Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
‘Aindra’ is Jyeṣṭhā; ‘Prājāpatya’ is Rohiṇī.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "If the constellation Āgneya (Kṛttikā) should ever occur on the full moon day of Kārttika..."
That lunar day (tithi) should be known as great; it is supreme for rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts.
The asterism of Agni is Kṛttikā.
When the asterism of Yama occurs on that lunar day,
that lunar day is proclaimed by the sages to be exceedingly meritorious.
The lunar mansion of Yama is Bharaṇī.
O lord of men, when the lunar mansion of Prajāpati (Rohiṇī) falls on that same lunar day,
it is called Mahākārttikī, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The constellation of Prajāpati is Rohiṇī. On these three days— the Moon, the Sun, or Jupiter—
and on these three constellations, they were themselves proclaimed by Brahmā.
O King, for one who has bathed here, the merit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice accrues;
likewise, one's gifts become inexhaustible and the libations offered to the ancestors are likewise eternal.
That Kārttikī full moon which falls under the conjunction of the Kṛttikās, Rohiṇī, or the southern asterism (Śravaṇā) is especially auspicious.
That is called Mahākārttikī, which is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The Mahākārttikī is meritorious when the Moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikās; and when the Moon is in conjunction with both Maghā and Ārdrā, it is called Mahāmāghī."
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): when Saturn is on the back of Aries, Jupiter and the Moon are in Leo,
and the Sun is in the asterism Śravaṇa, that is known as Mahāmāghī.
The Mahājyaiṣṭhī performed at Śālagrāma yields great fruit for men;
likewise, the Vaiśākhī at the Gaṅgā and the Jyaiṣṭhī at Puruṣottama do so as well.
The full moon of Āṣāḍha is indeed at Kanakhala, likewise the Śrāvaṇī at Kedāra; the Mahābhādrī at Badarī, and the Āśvinī at Kubjā;
the Kārttikī at Puṣkara, and likewise the Mārgaśirī at Kānyakubja.
The Mahāpauṣī performed at Ayodhyā yields great fruit;
likewise, the Mahāmāghī at Prayāga and the Phālgunī at Naimiṣa do so as well.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"On the full moon day of Āśvina, when the constellations [are favorable], one should keep a vigil at night;
that is celebrated as Kaumudī, and it should be performed for the prosperity of the world."
On the Kaumudī day, one should worship Lakṣmī and Indra seated upon Airāvata;
with all fragrant and sharp-scented substances, as well as with the sense-objects (akṣas), there should be a vigil.
The full moon day of Phālguna is always the playful maiden Bālā;
she is to be known as Phālgunī, and she is to be known for the prosperity of the world.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
On the full moon day of Phālguna, she who sports upon the cloth [of the sky] is to be known as Phālgunī in the world; she should be worshipped for the prosperity of the world.
Thus ends the Puṇya-pūrṇimā.
Now follows the Puṇya-amāvāsyā.
Śātātapa says:
When the new moon day falls on a Saturday,
one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows merely by bathing in the Ganges.
In the Mahābhārata: When it falls on a New Moon, a Monday, or a Thursday,
that sacred site named Puṣkara is superior to a hundred solar eclipses.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"When the new moon day is conjoined with the asterisms of Anurādhā or Viśākhā,
the host of ancestors then attains satisfaction for eight years through the śrāddha."

In some places, however, the reading is "Viśākhā-Svāti-Yoginī. "Maitram" refers to Anurādhā. When the new moon occurs under Puṣya, Raudra (Ārdrā), or Punarvasu, then the ancestors, when honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.

*Raudrarkṣa* is Ārdrā. For one desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors, [this is auspicious] under the asterisms of Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā) and Ajaikapād (Pūrvabhādrapadā). Under the asterism of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) and Adhidevatya (Uttarabhādrapadā), it is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
‘Vāsava’ is Dhaniṣṭhā; ‘Ajaikapād’ is Pūrvabhādrapadā; ‘Vāruṇa’ is Śatabhiṣaj; and ‘Āpya’ is Pūrvābhādrapadā.
Sometimes the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha [falls under these].
If the time coincides with the constellation presided over by Varuṇa,
that is the supreme time for the ancestors;
indeed, O King, it is not obtained by those of little merit.
"The constellation of Varuṇa" refers to Śatatārakā (the Pleiades). Thus ends the section on the auspicious new moon days. Now, various other auspicious occasions:
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*: "The worship of the planet is prescribed even on the first lunar day (pratipad), as well as on the sixth. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
O Bhārata, having bathed on the third or fourth day of the bright fortnight,
or on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, why should one grieve?
In the Śāmbapurāṇa: Whether it be the sixth or the seventh lunar day, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight, that lunar day joined with Sunday is remembered as most meritorious.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "He who, fasting on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, constantly worships the Lord of the Gods— Śaṅkara is pleased with him."
He who, firm in his vows and desiring liberation, constantly worships Śiva on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, shall obtain his desired fruit.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
On the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], the propitiation of the Rākṣasas and others;
on the ninth, the sacrifice to the Mothers (mātṛ-yāga); and on the fifth, [the worship of] Janārdana.
The eighth day of the month of Pauṣa and Māgha is meritorious; the thirteenth day in the month of Caitra;
the full moon of Kārttika; and the twelfth day is proclaimed as Uttara.
"Uttarā" refers to the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa. In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The tenth and twelfth days of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha are likewise [auspicious]."
The fourth and the full moon day are always remembered as most meritorious.
Simply by fasting on the full moon day,
the new moon day, the eighth day, the *aṣṭakā* days,
and on the fourteenth day, a bath performed on the eighth day in the presence of Śiva [yields great merit].
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of beings, if it falls on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight under the Puṣya asterism,
or on the twelfth day, it is remembered as that which effects the destruction of all sins without exception.
Vyāsa says: Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, the fourth or the fourteenth lunar day is meritorious when it falls on a Tuesday, just as the new moon (kuhū) is on a Monday.
The new moon day (Amāvāsyā) on a Monday, the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) on a Sunday,
and the fourth lunar day (Caturthī) on a Tuesday yield fruit equal to that of the equinoxes (Viṣuvat).
Śaṅkha says: The new moon day [is auspicious] with the Moon, the seventh with the Sun,
the fourth with Mars, and the eighth with Mercury.
There are four meritorious lunar days (tithis) which become especially auspicious due to eclipses and other such events;
it is taught that here, all acts such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation of mantras become inexhaustible.
Śātātapa says:
[646] The new moon day on a Monday, the seventh lunar day on a Sunday,
when the second lunar day or the fourteenth falls on a Tuesday;
In that place, whoever performs an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
the doer experiences its fruit as its protector for sixty thousand years.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The ninth day of the Durgā festival, the twelfth day for the installation of Viṣṇu,
the sixth day for the installation of the sacred fire, and the great seventh day of Māgha."
Viṣṇu says: The fifteenth, the full moon day, the fifth, and the two twelfth days.
He who abstains from food for a year, remaining constantly self-controlled,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"The festival of fire should be performed at night on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha under the asterism Ārdrā;
or else, a great festival (*mahotsava*) should be held on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*)."
The Grandfather said: "The first lunar day is declared to belong to Wealth (Dhana); the second is remembered as belonging to Prosperity (Śrī);
the third belongs to Bhavānī; and the fourth belongs to her son."
The fifth is declared for the Nāgas; the sixth is declared for Guha;
the seventh is declared for Bhāskara; the eighth is remembered for Durgā;
the ninth is declared for the Mothers; and the tenth is remembered for Vāsuki.
The eleventh day belongs to the sages, while the twelfth belongs to the wielder of the discus;
the thirteenth is indeed for Anaṅga, and the fourteenth is said to belong to Śiva.
The full moon day is likewise remembered as the best of lunar dates for the [purification of] the bodily constituents;
the new moon day is declared suitable for all rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.

Thus ends the section on the auspicious lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) within the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time), in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri— the sovereign over all the offices of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya, and a master of all branches of knowledge.
[648] Now begins the fourteenth chapter. Next follows the determination of lunar days conjoined with asterisms.

In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, when conjoined with the lunar mansion Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī), even if it is obtained for only a single muhūrta, should be observed through fasting; it yields great fruit."
On the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī as well, it is exactly the same.
And it has been said:
"A Dvādaśī touched by the Śravaṇa asterism is remembered as entirely most meritorious."
"But it is not praised merely because it is conjoined with that [constellation].
However, in other cases, one must wait for as much time as it takes to complete the ritual action, observing the conjunction with the constellations and so forth. As it is said in the *Śāṅkara-gītā*:
"From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, or the days of the week ending with the Sun."
"These do not purify the entire lunar day merely by conjunction.
And it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"That portion of the lunar day which is conjoined with a [specific] asterism..."
That lunar day (tithi) is to be known as complete, even if it is not joined with the [specified] constellation at its end.
As long as that Brahmā remains, for that duration of time it is praised;
all acts such as giving and worship performed during that time will yield their fruit.
Thus concludes the determination of lunar days conjoined with asterisms.
Now follows the determination of the beginnings of the Yugas.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa* and the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, it is stated:
"On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kṛta Yuga emerged;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha (Rādha), the Tretā Yuga indeed came into being."
The Dvāpara Yuga commenced on the new moon day of the month of Māgha;
the Kali Yuga emerged on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya.
These are indeed remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas (Yugādis), which cause whatever is given to be inexhaustible.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "Now listen, O King of Kings, to the Yugādis, which are dear to the ancestors;
by the mere recitation of their names, even the accumulation of sins is destroyed."
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the third day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava,
the new moon day of Tapasya, and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya.
The rise of the Tretā, Kṛta, Kali, and Dvāpara ages occurs in succession;
yet, specifically regarding bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and especially the libations to the ancestors,
these [times] render performed deeds inexhaustible and yield great fruit for virtuous actions.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The third day of Vaiśākha, which is called *mādhava*; the bright fortnight (*sita*) of [the month] called *tapasya*, which is Māgha;
and the ninth day of Kārttika."
The fifteenth day of Māgha and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas; indeed, these cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
Devala says: The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha joined with Rohiṇī,
and the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya joined with Maghā.
For these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause what is given to become inexhaustible.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa:
"That which is the third day of the month of Vaiśākha is the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika."
On the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and on the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha.
These four days, which yield infinite merit, are declared in the Purāṇa to be the beginnings of the Yugas.
In the phrase "the fifteenth day of Māgha," the term "of the dark fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is to be supplied.

Therefore, it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "The wise know that there are two beginnings of the Yugas that are bright (śukla) and two that are dark (kṛṣṇa). The bright ones are to be observed in the forenoon, and the dark ones in the afternoon."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, it is stated that the full moon of Māgha is the beginning of the Yuga:
"The Kṛta Yuga began on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
while the Tretā Yuga began on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika."
Then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Dvāpara Yuga begins;
and likewise, on the full moon day of Māgha, the terrible Kali Yuga begins.
The lunar days (tithis) at the commencement of the yugas are therefore renowned as Yugādyas;
the fruit of gifts and oblations offered on them is proclaimed to be infinite.
Likewise:
these four lunar days beginning with the Full Moon (Ugādi) should be known as such that what is given and what is offered therein quickly becomes inexhaustible.
That which occurs over a hundred years in each age would occur in a single day at the beginning of a yuga.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The third day of Vaiśākha is equal to the Kṛta Yuga;
the ninth day of Kārttika is indeed equal to the Tretā Yuga."
The thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya is equal to the Dvāpara age;
O King, the fifteenth day of Māgha is equal to the Kali age.

In some places, however, the reading is "the beginning of the Kali age" (*kalikālādi*). O King of kings, these four auspicious beginnings of the ages (*yugādayaḥ*) are thus called by the ancient sages.
Fasting, austerity, charity, ancestral rites, burnt offerings, and recitation— at that time,
whatever is performed becomes ten million times more meritorious.

"Equal to the Kṛta Yuga" means that the merit which would be produced by performing rituals every single day throughout the entire Kṛta Yuga is obtained on this one lunar day alone. As stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"When the Moon, the Sun, [the constellation] Tiṣya, and Jupiter..."
When they shall come together in a single zodiacal sign, then the Kṛta age will enter.

On this point, some say: [652] It has been stated previously that words such as *vaiśākha* do not have their constituent meanings elided like the word *go* (cow) and others; rather, they denote both solar and lunar months. This being the case, since there are two Vaiśākhas and because the lunar dates (*tithi*) are doubled in both, there would be the contingency of two *yugādis* occurring therein. If that were so, the restriction to "four" would be untenable; it is only when there is oneness [of the month] that the distinction between solar and lunar months can be determined.

On this point, some say: the beginning of the yuga (*yugādi*), which is based on the lunar month, is fit for ritual performance because the beginnings of the yugas are primarily concerned with rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*); for even in ancestral rites, the lunar month is the starting point.
As it has been said:
"In annual rites and in rites for the ancestors, the lunar month is traditionally prescribed."
Thus, regarding the designation of the bright and dark fortnights, it is logical that they depend solely on the lunar month, because they consist of two fortnights. Furthermore:
"If the fifteenth day of the dark half of Māgha ever attains conjunction with the constellation Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj)..."
O King, that supreme time of the ancestors is reached by the constellation Ṛkṣa; indeed, it cannot be attained by those of little merit.
According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), that new moon day of Vaiśākha which coincided with the asterism Rohiṇī—

From this scriptural statement, it is understood that the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*) occur specifically within the lunar month; for indeed, when the sun is in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, the conjunction with Śatabhiṣā on the new moon day is not possible. If that were the case, because the moon would be situated within the solar disc and thus conjoined with the sun, the moon itself would also be in Capricorn; and if that were so, there could be no conjunction with Śatabhiṣā, since that [asterism] belongs to Aquarius. When the sun and moon are in the same zodiac sign while the sun is in Aquarius, the conjunction with Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣā) is to be recognized. Likewise, on the specific *yugādi* of the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following the full moon of Prauṣṭhapadī, [the recipient] is a worthy vessel...

He indicates a month; this being so, there is no possibility of postponement (*utkarṣa*) on the *yugādi* days, because since the focus is on the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), the lunar day (*tithi*) falling within the solar month would not be a *yugādi*, and thus there would be no occasion for postponement. Postponement occurs when there is an increase in time for rituals such as the *upākarma*;
however, there is no postponement on *yugādi* days even when there is an increase in [the number of] consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) and the like.

Because of this prohibition. Alternatively, even though there are two types of *yugādi* (beginnings of the yuga), since the lunar date (*tithi*) is an auxiliary element of the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), it is measured by the solar month; for there is the scriptural statement: "In the world, the lunar date is for divine rites like fire, while for ancestral rites it is considered lunar; 'they proceed with the after-offerings'—this is another time for the ancestors. Therefore, the postponement of ancestral rites connected to the time preceding that [solar date] is not untenable. Consequently, since the months of Māgha and others are obtained even during a solar month when the sun is in the sign of Aquarius and so forth, the status of being a *yugādi* belongs to the lunar dates such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). However, the statement regarding the four *yugādis* occurring within a solar month is intended to designate them as times for divine rites (*devakārya*).

Viṣṇu [states]: "Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha to be obligatory. In this context, the group of four beginning with the Yugādis (the beginnings of the Yugas), as well as the passage beginning with "that which is in the dark fortnight of Māgha under Varuṇa," etc., is to be explained as being intended to establish the Yugādis occurring within the lunar months. Thus it is said: "That very time is meritorious because of the exhaustion of the six flavors; it is more meritorious because it is a Yugādi; and it is most meritorious due to its conjunction with a lunar mansion."
Furthermore,
there is no postponement on the Daśaharā days, nor on the four Yugādis;
for this [rule] regarding the Upākarma and Mahāṣaṣṭhī is intended to apply starting from the month of Vṛṣa (Taurus).

As for the reading they cite, it should be disregarded because its source is unreliable and it is merely a figurative indication. Regarding this, the refutation stated by Paṇḍitaparitoṣakṛt—that only the lunar month possesses the designation of Vaiśākha and so forth, and that the application of the term there is secondary (gauṇī)—has already been rejected previously.

As for the claim that because the beginnings of the *yugas* (*yugādi*) are primarily occasions for rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*) is prescribed for ancestral rites, and therefore the *yugādis* occurring within that [lunar month] are what are intended—this is not so. For it has been stated that the rule regarding ancestral rites applies to both the solar and the lunar months. Furthermore, there is no primacy of ancestral rites during the *yugādis*, because they involve rites for both gods and ancestors. Thus it has been said: "The four lunar days are of infinite merit. Likewise, Vyāsa states:
"At the beginning of the *yugas*, all acts such as bathing and giving gifts become inexhaustible."
Moreover, the dark and light fortnights belong not only to the lunar month, for they are possible in the solar month as well.

As for the statement, "The fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha," this does not mean that the lunar date (tithi) such as the new moon occurring at the beginning of a lunar month is called the *yugādi* (the start of a Yuga); rather, it means that in the lunar month, the *sinīvālī* new moon conjoined with the asterism Maghā serves for the satisfaction of the ancestors. However, that specific time which is so dear to the ancestors is not the *yugādi*, because it is absent during the dark fortnights of Maghā and other months. If it is argued that the new moon of Māgha is the *yugādi*, and thus even in the lunar month that lunar date is the *yugādi*—[we reply: no.

It is not so. For there is no reason to determine whether these refer to solar or lunar months. Nor can both be considered the beginning of the Yuga (yugādi), because that would contradict the restrictive enumeration of "four. Nor is this statement intended to refer to the times for *śrāddha* rites; for from the statement, "The four *yugādis*, the *aṣṭakās*, the ripening of rice and barley," it is understood that the *yugādis* are four lunar dates (*tithis*). Nevertheless, it is stated which one among them is the *yugādi*: that which occurs within the solar month; otherwise, there would be a displacement [of the rite]. Nor should it be thought that the displacement of the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) follows from a scriptural injunction, as there is no such injunction. On the contrary, the rule "the displacement occurs on the *yugādis*" prohibits displacement in all cases regarding the lunar dates, since it designates the worship of the *tithis* such as the *daśaharā* based on the division of the sun's passage through the zodiacal signs beginning with Taurus.
According to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: "There is no postponement on the Daśaharās, nor on the four Yugādis;
for this [postponement] has been stated to apply from the month of Vṛṣa (Taurus) onwards, specifically regarding the Upākarma and the Mahāṣaṣṭhī."

And because of the prohibition against such an advancement [of the date], as in the statement, "The later time belongs to the ancestors," the word *para* signifies excellence (*śreṣṭhatā*) and does not establish an advancement of the ritual effect belonging to the earlier time. Nor is the statement "on the *daśaharā* days" without a source; for it has a basis, being accepted by those who know the entirety of the scriptures and being supported by the citation of its source. As for the explanation of Śāṅkhadhara—that this is not a Vedic statement such that we should accept it without reflection—[we reply: because it accords with what is well-known to all people and because there is respect for its performance, the beginning of the Yuga (*yugādi*) must be taken as occurring within the solar month, not the lunar month. For even though there is a rule stating that the tenth day of the bright fortnight when the sun is in Gemini (*mithuna*) is the *daśaharā*, and the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight (the new moon) when the sun is in Aquarius (*kumbha*) is the *amāvāsyā*, no one places their faith in that [interpretation]. Therefore, it is established that the beginning of the Yuga occurs within the solar month. We, however, say this: although it was determined in the discussion on months that words such as *vaiśākha* and so forth denote only the lunar month, nevertheless, for the sake of the aforementioned prohibition against advancing the Yuga and out of regard for established custom and performance, the beginning of the Yuga must be accepted as occurring within the solar month.
Thus concludes the determination of the beginnings of the Yugas. Now, the endings of the Yugas, according to the Brahma Purāṇa:
At the sun's entry into Leo, there is the end of the Kṛta Yuga;
then, at the entry into Scorpio, there is the end of the Tretā Yuga.
The Dvāpara age, however, is known by its name to end with the sun's entry into Taurus;
likewise, the end of the Kali Yuga occurs at the sun's entry into Aquarius.

In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Know that day on which the sun is in the constellation Revatī, when there is movement among the zodiacal signs, to be the day of the end of the Yuga; a gift given there is infinite."
If the sun is at the point of ingress (saṅkrānti), at the equinoxes, or at the solstices,
or on the seventh lunar day of either the bright or dark fortnight, they know that to be a Yugānta day.
"In the auspicious [period]" refers to the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*).
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "A *śrāddha* performed on the first days of the ages (*yugādya*) and at the ends of the ages (*yugānta*) is said to be inexhaustible."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Whatever bathing, giving of gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth is performed on the Yugādis and at the ends of the Yugas,
those Yugādis are the witnesses to the fruit thereof."
Manu says: A gift given on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas becomes a thousandfold;
likewise, rites such as the Śrāddha and others performed on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Manvantaras yield the same result.
Thus end the sections on the ends of the ages (*yugānta*). Now, the various characteristics of the ages (*yugadharma*).
Regarding this, Upakātyāyana says:
Revelation, purity, and conduct vary according to the time;
diverse dharmas prevail among human beings in age after age.
Manu says: "The dharma of men is one in the Kṛta age, another in the Tretā, and yet another in the Dvāpara;
it is different in the Kali age, in accordance with the decline of the ages."
Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge is best in the Tretā age;
they say sacrifice alone is paramount in the Dvāpara age, and charity alone in the Kali age.
"Austerity" (*tapas*) refers to practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to meditation (*dhyāna*).
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age; knowledge is best in the Tretā age."
In the Dvāpara age they say sacrifice alone is supreme; in the Kali age, charity alone.
Likewise: "In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā, knowledge is said [to be supreme];
in the Dvāpara, they say sacrifice alone [is supreme]; in the Kali age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are supreme]."
Bṛhaspati said: "In the Kṛta age, austerity is dharma; in the Tretā age, knowledge is traditionally taught;
in the Dvāpara age, sacrifice is proclaimed; and in the Tiṣya age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are the dharma]."
"Tiṣya" refers to the Kali age.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa it is said:
"Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age; in the Tretā age, knowledge is taught."
In the Dvāpara age, war prevails; in the Kali age, charity alone.
In the Śivapurāṇa it is said: "Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age, the act of offering oblations in the Tretā,
non-violence in the Dvāpara, and the festival of Śarva is prescribed for the Kali age."
Likewise: "Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age, the worship of the Liṅga in the Tretā,
study in the Dvāpara, and the chanting of the praises of Mahādeva in the Tiṣya."
Likewise: "Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age, as is sacrifice in the Tretā;
in the Dvāpara, worship of the Liṅga, and in the Kali, the chanting of the praises of Śaṅkara."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Knowledge is supreme in the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme in the Tretā,
likewise sacrifice in the Dvāpara, and ritual establishment in the Kali age."
Whatever merit would be gained from a year in the Kṛta age is obtained in the Tretā age in three seasons;
in the Dvāpara, it is gained in three fortnights; but in the Kali age, that same merit is gained in a single day.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The dharma that lasts for a year in the Tretā age is recorded as being monthly in the Dvāpara age;
by practicing it according to his ability even for a single day in the Kali age, a wise man shall obtain its fruit."
As stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"That which is accomplished in ten years during the Kṛta age is achieved in a single year during Tretā;
that same result is attained in a month during Dvāpara, and in a single day and night during Kali."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "In the Kṛta age, the god is Brahmā; in the Tretā, the Lord is Ravi (the Sun);
in the Dvāpara, the Lord is Viṣṇu; and in the Kali age, the god is Maheśvara."
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "In the Kṛta age, the pure Nārāyaṇa is worshipped in his subtle form;
in the Tretā age, in the form of sacrifice; and in the Dvāpara age, by means of the Pāñcarātra."
In the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam: "In these ages— the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— Keśava is worshipped according to various rites, with diverse colors, names, and forms."
In the Kṛta age, he is white, four-armed, with matted hair and clad in bark garments;
he bears a black antelope skin, a sacred thread, a rosary, a staff, and a water-pot.
But at that time, human beings were peaceful, free from enmity, friendly, and impartial;
they worshipped the God through austerity, equanimity, and self-restraint.
Vaikuṇṭha, who has the color of a swan, the excellent one, the Lord of Yoga, the stainless one, is celebrated as the Lord,
the Puruṣa, the Unmanifest, and the Supreme Self.
In the Tretā age, he is red in color, four-armed, and wears three girdles;
he has golden hair, embodies the Triple Veda, and is characterized by the sacrificial ladle (sruk), the dipping-spoon (sruva), and other such implements.
Then those most righteous men, exponents of the Veda, worship that Lord Hari— who embodies all the gods— with the threefold knowledge.
Viṣṇu, Yajña, Pṛśnigarbha, Sarvadeva, Urukrama,
Vṛṣākapi, Jayanta, and Uragāya— thus he is proclaimed.
In the Dvāpara age, the Blessed Lord Rāma appeared, clad in yellow garments, distinguished by his own weapons and marked with the Śrīvatsa and other auspicious signs.
O King, mortal men, desiring to know the Supreme, worship that Puruṣa— who is characterized as the Great King— through both the Vedas and the Tantras.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa as well;
salutations to you, the Blessed One, Pradyumna and Aniruddha.
Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, the seer, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul; to the Lord of the Universe, the Universe itself, whose self is all beings.
Thus, O Lord of the Earth, they praise the Lord of the Universe during the Dvāpara age; now hear how they do so even in the Kali age through various tantric rites.

The wise indeed worship Him who is dark-complexioned, black with splendor, together with His limbs, secondary limbs, and attendants, primarily through sacrifices consisting of congregational chanting.
In this way, O King, Hari, the Lord of all blessings, is worshipped by men living in the various ages according to the nature of each age, as the Blessed One.
In the *Aparājitapṛcchā*:
"One should carry the Moon with the left hand and the Sun with the right;
he who proclaims Vāsudeva carries the Fire within the center of his heart."
In the Kṛta Yuga, the primordial form, white in color, is to be worshipped by the twice-born;
thus Saṃkarṣaṇa carries both the plow and the pestle.
In the Tretā age, the red-colored [Kṛṣṇa] was worshipped by the Kṣatriya caste;
in the Dvāpara age, Pradyumna, the wielder of the bow Śārṅga, was to be worshipped by the Vaiśyas.
Yellow in color and clad in yellow garments, the bestower of knowledge in the arts—
known as Niruddha in the Kali age— he is worshipped by those of the Śūdra caste.
Dark in color, he indeed carries a shield and a sword in his two hands;
terrifying every obstacle, he shall destroy the multitude of sins.
In the *Aparājitapṛcchā*:
"Through the divisions of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, through the distinctions of the *Kṛta* and other ages,
and through the distinctions of the castes such as the Brahmins, [the Lord appears] with four faces and four arms."
Brahmā, Pitāmaha, Viriñci, and Kamalāsana—
these are declared to be the four forms of Parameṣṭhin.
A book, a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, and a water-pot—
this constitutes the form of Brahmā, which bestows happiness when fashioned in the Kṛta age.
He has a beautiful face and handsome arms, adorned with earrings;
he wears a garland, is richly endowed with splendor, possesses well-fleshed limbs, and has beautiful hair.
O you whose complexion is the color of molten gold, whose radiant luster is brightened by a necklace of jewels,
who are adorned with armlets and bracelets, and who are decorated with every kind of ornament!
The sages should be placed at the side of the deities;
and Brahmā, endowed with the four Vedas, should be present as the bestower of all peace.
The weapons are to be understood according to the sequence of the hands starting from the lower right:
the white mustard seed, the parasol, the book, the rosary, the sacrificial ladle, and the water-pot; thus Brahmā is fashioned with four faces.
And the one named Brahman, who has the Ṛgveda as his primary authority, is honored by the twice-born.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has lotus-like eyes, a sacrificial ladle, and a book;
in the Tretā age, he is the foremost of those who uphold the four Vedas and is honored by the Kṣatriyas.
In the *Aparājitapṛcchā*:
"The water-pot, the rosary, the sacrificial ladle, and likewise the book—
this shall be the form of the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the Tretā age, bestowing happiness."
In the *Siddhārthapṛcchā*:
"In the Dvāpara age, Viriñci, who bears the white Sāman chants, is to be worshipped by Vaiśyas;
he holds a rosary, a book, a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), and a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*)."
Holding a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, a book, and a water-pot, seated upon a lotus,
and preeminent among the Atharva-veda in his arts, he is worshipped by all social classes.
In the *Aparājitapṛcchā*:
"In his right hand is a rosary, and upon it rests a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*);
in his left hand is a book, and below that is a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)."
If he holds a lotus seat in his hand, he bestows happiness upon people of all castes.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Puṣkara should be resorted to in the Kṛta age, likewise Naimiṣa in the Tretā;
Kurukṣetra in the Dvāpara, but in the Kali age one should take refuge in the Gaṅgā."
Parāśara.
In the Kṛta age, the Dharma is that of Manu; in the Tretā, that of Gautama;
in the Dvāpara, that of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, that of Parāśara is remembered.
In the *Kālottarapavitrārohaṇaprakaraṇa*, the materials for the sacred thread (*pavitra*) are specified according to the divisions of the ages (*yuga*):
"In the Kṛta age, it should be made of jewels; in the Tretā, it should consist of gold;
in the Dvāpara, a thread made of silk; but in the Kali age, cotton thread is beneficial."
Ascetics should practice mental discipline, while those who give gifts should wear bark garments for their benefit.
Thus end the various dharmas of the yugas. Now, regarding things to be avoided according to the distinctions between the yugas, Śātātapa says:
One should abandon the country in the Kṛta age, leave the village in the Tretā age,
[abandon] a single family in the Dvāpara age, but [abandon] the perpetrator alone in the Kali age.
In the Kṛta age one falls by conversing [with such a person], in the Tretā by touching him,
in the Dvāpara by taking his food, but in the Kali age one falls through mere action.

In some places, however, there is a different reading: "But in the Dvāpara age, food is said [to be forbidden]. Thus are the things to be avoided according to the distinction of the ages. Now, the characteristics of the Kali age:
In the Mahābhārata:
"But whoever worships Śaṅkara even once at the proper time with this mantra, 'Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya,' is liberated from all sins."
Whether he has reached any state whatsoever or is joined with all manner of sins,
that man in the Kali age who [recites] "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" is liberated.
Even a salutation offered with deceit to the wielder of the trident (Śiva) is declared not to be fruitless in the Kali age, for it serves as a remedy against the defects of saṃsāra.
Likewise, O best of sages, he who always worships him with faith—
whether in a linga or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)— with curiosity and according to the prescribed rite, [attains the goal].
Having completely conquered the defects of the age, he rejoices in the world of Rudra.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "In the Kali age, Rudra, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita,
manifests in a deformed form for the sake of establishing Dharma."
Those wise ones who serve Śaṅkara by any means whatsoever,
having utterly conquered the defects of the Kali age, proceed to the supreme state.
Vyāsa says: What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one attains in the Kali age simply by chanting the praises of Keśava.
In the *Bhāgavata*: "In the Kali age, noble persons who recognize virtue and partake of its essence offer their worship [to this],
wherein the goal of all one's own purposes is attained through mere chanting (*saṃkīrtana*)."
"By means of *saṃkīrttana*"— the meaning is "by the chanting of Hari's names.
Indeed, there is no gain higher than this for embodied beings wandering here [in this world],
since through it one attains supreme peace and the cycle of worldly existence perishes.

In the Agni Purāṇa: "O Sage, in this terrible age of darkness (Tāmasa Yuga), which is devoid of sacrifices and the Vedas, there is nothing that brings greater welfare to men than the propitiation of Viṣṇu."

O King, one should perform worship of Vāsudeva in the Kali age; for that fruit which you obtained by worshipping Hari with devotion according to the prescribed rites for a hundred years, O monarch, is gained in the Kali age in a single day and night.
Likewise: Those men who constantly worship Hari, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age and the remover of all sins, they too are worthy of veneration just as Hari is.

Having transcended the excellence of dharma, a person attains it in the Kali age with very little effort; therefore, O knowers of dharma, I am pleased with the Kali age. O Brahmins, in the blessed Kali age, great fruit is obtained with little hardship.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"In the Kali age, cities must be constructed by kings desiring the heavenly world, preceded by temples for the deities."
Thus end the characteristics of the Kali Yuga.
Now, those things to be avoided in the Kali Yuga.
In the Ādityapurāṇa: "That dharma which belongs to the Kṛta age must not be performed in the Kali age.
"Kārta" means pertaining to the Kṛta age.
Likewise, it is stated in the context of *niyoga*:
"This dharma belongs to the *Kṛta* age; it is not to be performed in the *Kali* age, such as long-term celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the carrying of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)."

In the Kali age, the following must be avoided by the twice-born: marriage within the same lineage (gotra) or the maternal kinship group (mātṛpiṇḍa), the slaughter of cows, the human sacrifice and the horse sacrifice, and the consumption of intoxicants.
Likewise:

"In the Kali age, one should not perform these five things: the remarriage of a woman already married, the taking of the eldest brother's share, the killing of a cow, approaching a brother's wife, and [carrying] a water-pot."
In another Smṛti:

"One should avoid five things in the Kali age: obtaining a son through the husband's brother, the killing of a cow, the carrying of a water-pot, the [sacrifice of] unhusked grain, and the human sacrifice."
Likewise:
"Just as there is no slaughter even of a milch cow when it is for a righteous purpose according to the injunction,
so too the division of the 'extra share' (uddhāra) does not obtain in the present time."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: Oaths, omens, dreams, physiognomy, portents, vows,
and prophecies— these may occasionally occur in the Kali age.
Therefore, by obtaining only that much, one should not perform the five duties;
likewise, due to the penetration of dharma, other [duties] also [are suspended] in the Kali age.
