Things to be avoided: Even those actions prescribed by law have been abandoned by the wise in the Kali age due to the fear of violating dharma, because of the absence of witnesses and because of their own formal agreement.
The appointment of a brother-in-law for the procreation of offspring upon a widow,
and the formal marriage of a young girl whose virginity remains intact with another man.
The marriage of twice-born men with girls of a different caste, and the slaying of pre-eminent twice-born men who are assassins (ātatāyin) in a righteous war; these are [permissible].
The inclusion of a twice-born man who has traveled by boat upon the ocean, even after he has been purified;
the initiation for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) for all [castes]; and the carrying of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
The Great Departure, the instruction regarding the cow in the Gosava sacrifice,
and the inclusion of the taking of liquor in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
The licking of the Agnihotra ladle and the non-acceptance of gifts,
as well as entry into the forest-dweller’s stage of life, are enjoined by the sacred law.
Likewise, the contraction of sins dependent upon the study of the Vratas,
as well as the prescription of expiatory rites for Brahmins ending only with death.
Their fault lies in social association; their atonement for great sins consists of performing the rites of cooking and offering to gods, guests, and ancestors.
The adoption of others as sons, except for the *datta* and *aurasa* types; sexual intercourse with women of the same caste who are other than one's own wife, even if they have been purified;
and the abandonment of the wife of a guru when sexual intercourse occurs outside the vagina—[these are grounds for loss of caste]. [668]
The renunciation of one's own self for the sake of another, the avoidance even of what has been designated [for oneself],
and that which is consistent with the Dharma for the purpose of worshipping an image— this is the ritual manual (kalpa).
After the collection of the bones, touching the limbs [of the corpse],
the *saumitra* rite for Brahmins, likewise the selling of Soma,
stealing food from one who performs base acts, and eating while fasting for six meals— [these are forbidden].
At the beginning of the Kali age, these [practices] were set aside by great-souled, wise, and learned men for the sake of protecting the world, according to established rules; furthermore,
the agreement of the virtuous shall be authoritative, just like the Veda.
Āpastamba also states:
"The consensus of those who know all things and the Vedas are authoritative.

Now, one might object: that which is prohibited in the Kali age is for the purpose of supplying ellipses to Vedic sentences or has a visible purpose. However, it cannot have a visible purpose, because since such a prohibition would not be useful for performance, it is impossible for the comprehension of its meaning to serve as its purpose. Nor can it be otherwise, as that would result in an inconsistency.

It is replied: there is no fault, because even if the literal meaning of that sentence is not put into practice, it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by being useful for the knowledge of the distinctions and the original forms [of mantras], and so forth. Otherwise, even the study of sentences concerning the *Rājasūya* sacrifice and other rites would not be undertaken by a Brāhmaṇa. Or rather, the same course of reasoning that applies to the *Rājasūya* and similar rites applies here as well. Furthermore, by speaking thus, you are asserting the lack of authority for other Smṛtis that enjoin the avoidance of the Kali age. It cannot be considered unauthoritative merely because it lacks a visible purpose for the injunction to study, since—just as in the case of other Smṛtis—there is no difference here regarding its firm acceptance by the learned members of the three higher castes. If it is argued that it lacks a visible purpose for the injunction to study, then what does that matter in the present context?
Thus end the things to be avoided in the Kali Yuga. Now, the beginnings of the Manvantaras.
From the Matsya Purāṇa: The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada.
The new moon of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh day of Pauṣa;
the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of Māgha,
the full moon of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and likewise Jyeṣṭha—
these are the beginnings of the Manvantaras, which render whatever is given inexhaustible.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors— all these,
when performed on the first days of a Manvantara, are known to yield inexhaustible merit.

In this context, with the exception of the new moon day (amāvāsyā), all [the dates] are indeed the bright fortnight (śukla). In another Purāṇa, it is established that the new moon of Śrāvaṇa and the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada are the beginnings of the Yugas (yugādi).
For instance: "The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, as well as the [new moon] of Śrāvaṇa and likewise that of Kārttika..."
For these gifts, such as those to Manu, Anara, and others, cause what has been given to become inexhaustible.
Manu says: "A gift given on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas becomes multiplied a thousandfold;
likewise, rites such as the Śrāddha and others performed on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Manvantaras [yield the same result]."
Thus end the beginnings of the Manvantaras. Now follow the beginnings of the Kalpas.
In that section on the Nāgara [calendar]:
Now, O King, the auspicious lunar days (tithis) at the beginning of the kalpas and other periods are described,
by performing a śrāddha on which the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
In ancient times, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Śvetakalpa arose;
on the thirteenth day of that same bright fortnight, Udāna was born.
The Kalpa named Nārasiṃha began on the first day of the dark fortnight;
then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, the Gaurī-kalpa was also established.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Nīlalohita appeared;
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, however, the one named Gāruḍa set forth.
Samāna was born on the third day of the dark fortnight;
Māheśvara met with him on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
O King, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the manifestation of Mahādeva occurred;
and on the full moon of that same month, the Kūrma [Kalpa] commenced.
On the third day of the dark fortnight, Āgneya arrived;
on that very same day of the dark fortnight, Somakalpa also arrived.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, Raurava appeared;
on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of that same month, Mānava arrived.
Having reached the sixth [tithi] of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, he became the Lord of Breath (Prāṇādhipa);
but on the sixth [tithi] of the dark fortnight, his [form] was named Tatpuruṣa.
But on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, O lord of the people, Vaikuṇṭha entered the Vṛhatkalpa, and likewise on the dark fortnight.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kalpa named Kandarpa arose;
on the dark fortnight, however, the conception of the Lakṣmī-kalpa was born.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Kalpa was immediately attained;
and on the [ninth] of the dark fortnight, the Sāvitrī-kalpa began its commencement.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, Īśāna indeed appeared;
on the dark fortnight, the commencement of the Aghora Kalpa took place.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Vyāna was born;
on that very same dark night, Vārāha attained [his manifestation] for the welfare of beings.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, Sārasvata shone forth; and on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, the high-minded Vairāja likewise shone.
Thus, these thirty kalpas are the lunar days (tithis) of Parameṣṭhin.
At the commencement, the bright lunar days are desired and considered most meritorious;
when a śrāddha is performed on them, the merit lasts for the duration of a kalpa.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"The beginning of the Kalpa is proclaimed to be prior to the day of Brahmā,
on the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha and of Phālguna."
The fifth day of the month of Caitra, its final day, and another—
the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in Māgha, and the seventh day of Kārttika.
I remember these nine: the ninth [tithi] of Mārgaśīrṣa and these seven;
for they are the beginnings of the kalpas and cause what is given to be inexhaustible.

[672] Here, the "last" [days] are the new moon of Vaiśākha, the third of Phālguna, the third of Caitra, the fifth of Caitra, and the new moon of Caitra—these are the dark [fortnights]. The thirteenth of Māgha, the seventh of Kārttika, and the ninth of Mārgaśīrṣa—these are indeed the bright [fortnights].
These are the beginnings of the Kalpas. Now, the Vyatīpāta [yoga]:
In this regard, Yājñavalkya says:
"A gift of one hundred [cows] at the waning of the moon, but a thousand at the end of a day;
ten thousand at the equinox, and indeed an infinite amount at the Vyatīpāta [yoga]."

In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "A gift given on the new moon (darśa) yields a hundredfold merit; that same gift on the day of the sun's passage (dinakṣaya) yields a hundred times that; on the solstice (saṃkrānti) it yields a hundred times that, and likewise on the equinox (viṣuva) it yields a hundred times that."
At the beginning of a Yuga, a gift is a hundred times more meritorious; at the solstice, it is multiplied by a hundred;
during a lunar eclipse, it is multiplied by a hundred; and during a solar eclipse, it is multiplied by a hundred.
Those who know the Vedas declare that a gift given during the Vyatīpāta yoga is incalculable.
"Śataghna" means hundredfold. Here, "vyatīpāta" refers to the seventh yoga among the series of yogas beginning with viṣkumbha.
Gālava describes its origin:
"Its form is born from the gaze of the eyes of the Moon and the Sun."
A man resembling the radiance of the fire at the end of an aeon, exceedingly fierce, brandishing a weapon as he falls upon the earth while being watched,
and crying out, "I shall destroy!"— this is the *vyatipāta* yoga.

Furthermore, bathing, giving gifts, performing *śrāddha* rites, and so forth, when performed at the moments of its emergence, its circling, and its falling, as well as immediately after it has fallen, yield great fruit.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:
"At the moment of emergence, the merit is a hundred-thousandfold; during the hour of its circling, it is ten-millionfold."
If one falls from the practice of recitation, giving, and so forth, the merit is multiplied by a hundred million; if one has already fallen, it is even greater.
In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
"The fruit is said to be a hundred thousandfold at the moment of birth, ten millionfold during the flight;
ten billionfold at the fall, and what is given when he has fallen becomes inexhaustible."
And regarding the duration of birth and so forth, it is stated in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra):
"In the case of birth, it is twenty-two [nāḍīs]; in the case of wandering, twenty-one;
in falling, ten nāḍīs; and once fallen, seven nāḍikās."
Vyatīpāta is shown by Vriddha-Manu in another manner:
"If the new moon (amāvāsyā) falls on a Sunday when the moon is in Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, or the beginning of the Nāgadaivata (Āśleṣā), that is called Vyatīpāta."

"Nāgadaivata" refers to Aśleṣā; "mastaka" refers to the first quarter [of that asterism]. The term "mastaka" is connected individually with Śravaṇa and the others. Some, however, explain "mastaka" as Mṛgaśiras. "Amā" means the new moon day (amāvāsyā); when these asterisms are joined with Sunday, then this conjunction is known by the name Vyatīpāta. In another treatise: "When Jupiter and Mars are situated in Pañcānana..."
If the sun should be in Aries during the bright fortnight,
and the lunar day named Pāśā is conjoined with the Karabha [nakṣatra], this is the yoga known here as Vyatīpāta.
For by giving cows, land, gold, and clothing in this world, having completely abandoned all evil, one attains the state of a god, the state of Indra, and freedom from disease.
A human being attains sovereignty over mortals.
"Pañcānana" is the lion. "Guru and Bhūmiputra" are Jupiter and Mars. "Pāśābhidhānā" is the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). "Karabham" is the asterism Hasta.
This is Vyatīpāta. Now, Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta [are described].
In this regard, Bhṛgu says:
"The time of the equality of declination has been declared by the lords of sages to be similar to a solar eclipse."
Regarding that, Bhārgava has stated that offerings, oblations, recitations, and worship performed there yield millions upon millions of times the merit.

The meaning of this is as follows: when there is an equality of the longitudinal positions (*krānti*) of the sun and the moon at the time of *kutapa*, two things occur. During *vyatīpāta* there is *vaidhṛti*; therein, starting from the middle of the *gaṇḍa* interval of the *vyatīpāta* characterized by the equality of transits, its occurrence takes place sequentially over five and a half yogas. However, for *vaidhṛti*, starting from the *śukla-yoga*, its occurrence takes place sequentially over five and a half yogas.
Regarding this *vyatīpāta*, Pitāmaha (Brahmā) states that a *śrāddha* should be performed:
"On the new moon day, during *vyatīpāta*, on the full moon day, and on the *aṣṭakā* days..."

"A learned man who does not perform the *śrāddha* becomes liable for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). In this context, the statement "becomes liable for expiation" indicates the necessity of performing the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, the number of permissible times for that [rite] is possible from ten *ghaṭikās* up to one hundred and seventy-one.
Thus, it is stated in the *Jyotiṣa*, an auxiliary of the Vedas:

The conjunction arising from the *gaṇḍa* and the latter half of the *uttarārdha* occurs at the beginning of the bright fortnight and so forth; it is held by the Vaidikas to occur during another five and a half [periods].
Thus, this pair is the sole means for accomplishing that well-performed deed.
Viṣṇu:
"What is given during the Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta yoga becomes inexhaustible.
Bhāradvāja: [continues].
There is no end to what is given during the Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛta yogas;
indeed, the Vyatīpāta is especially distinguished, for it is proclaimed to be subtle.
In its broad sense, however, the twenty-seventh yoga is well known as Vaidhṛta. Thus end the sections on Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta. Now follows the miscellaneous auspicious times.
In this regard, Viṣṇu states: "The new moon day, the vyatīpāta yoga, eclipses of the moon and sun,
the beginnings of the manvantaras and yugas, the saṃkrānti (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign), and likewise the vaidhṛti yoga."
The loss of a day, the gap in a day, and likewise the omitted day (avama);
the two solstices, the equinox pair, and likewise the six openings of the Aśītimukha.
The four Viṣṇupadas, the birth of a son and other such events,
and the conjunctions of the planets beginning with the Sun with the lunar mansions.
This is to be recognized as a time of merit by discerning experts in the luminaries;
one should perform acts such as giving there for the increase of one's own merit.
The definition of *dinakṣaya* (the loss of a day) is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"That [lunar day] on which two *tithi*-ends fall on the same weekday is a *dinakṣaya*. Vasiṣṭha says:
When three lunar days (tithis) occur within a single solar day (sāvana), that is declared to be a "day of loss" (dinakṣaya); in such a case, the fruit [of an action] is said to be a thousandfold.
Bhṛgu states the definition of the "day-break" (dinacchidra):
"The half-tithi, the tithi, the yoga, the asterism, and the Vedas [four] at the beginning of the lunar fortnight—
these, Bhārgava says, are called the 'day-breaks' (divasacchidra), which are similar [in nature]."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Half of a lunar day" (*tithyarddha*) refers to a *karaṇa*. At the end or beginning of the *karaṇas*, lunar days, yogas, and asterisms—times equal to the [occurrence of] parvan or a lunar eclipse—that is designated as a "day-interruption" (*dinacchidra*). He also states the measurement of that time: "The time for the interruption and so forth at the junction of two lunar days is said to be two *ghaṭīs*."
Endowed with the palas of nāga and vahnipala, it is joined with the palas of that bhettṛ-tattva.
Two nāḍīs joined with sixteen palas at the conjunction is declared to be the time for cutting [the hair] and other rites; it bestows infinite fruit when used for giving.

‘Kṛti’ means five; ‘nāgas’ are eight; ‘vahnis’ are three; ‘bha’ is a lunar mansion (nakṣatra); ‘tattvas’ are twenty-five; and ‘yuti’ is conjunction (yoga). Thus, the meaning is as follows: at the beginning and end of a lunar day (tithi) and a karana, two ghaṭikās and thirty-eight palas constitute the auspicious time (puṇyakāla). For a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), it is two ghaṭikās joined with twenty-five palas. For a conjunction (yoga) as well, it is two ghaṭikās joined with sixteen palas. The definition of an intercalary day (avamadin) has been stated by Viṣṇu.
When a single weekday touches three lunar days (tithis), that is indeed an omitted day (avama). Where a lunar day touches three weekdays, it is said to span three days.

In this regard, there is this distinction between *dinakṣaya* (the loss of a day) and *avama* (an omitted lunar day): where the end of the weekday coincides with the end of two lunar days (*tithi*), that is *dinakṣaya*; where the weekday continues through both lunar days, that is *avama*. The equinoxes and other such occasions have also been shown in the determination of solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"On Saturday, Sunday, or Thursday—on these three weekdays..."
And these three constellations were proclaimed by Brahmā.
O King, the merit of bathing here shall indeed exceed that of the horse-sacrifice;
likewise, one's gifts become inexhaustible, as does the libation offered to the ancestors.
"The three constellations" refers to those of Agni, Yama, and Prajāpati. As stated in the *Mātsya*:
"When the moon, the sun, and Jupiter are in the constellation Mṛgaśiras..."
That lunar day remains meritorious and is proclaimed as inexhaustible.
As stated in the *Brahmaprokta*:
"The eleventh lunar day, the new moon, the full moon, the birth of a son, the *vaidhṛti* yoga, the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the *bhadrā* tithi, and the day of the waning moon."
The Yugas, Manvantaras, and so forth, as well as the conjunctions of the moon with the lunar phases,
the equality of declination, the gaps between days, eclipses, and the zodiacal signs— these are [to be calculated].
"Bhagama" refers to the transit through zodiac signs and lunar mansions.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Vyatīpāta, Viṣṇudina, and likewise Ṣaḍaśītimukha..."
[678] The equality of transits is the new moon (amāvāsyā), as well as an eclipse and the vaidhṛti conjunction.
The transit of the sun, the intercalary day, the increase of a lunar day, and the decrease of a day—
these and other such times are auspicious for rites such as fire-offerings and giving.

In the Skanda Purāṇa: "An eclipse of the moon or sun, the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), the equinox (viṣuva), the vyatīpāta yoga, and likewise the beginning of the sixtieth degree (ṣaḍaśītimukha) are supreme."
The gaps in the days, the transits (saṃkrānti), and likewise Viṣṇupada—
thus has the time been fully described, which increases the merit of men.
Gifts given here, as well as ritual baths, fire-offerings, and austerities,
shall yield infinite fruit and even bestow heaven and liberation.

Cyavana states: "The new moon day, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the solstices (*ayana*), the six *aśītimukha* periods, the *viṣuvat* and other such occasions, the *vaidhṛti* yoga, and lunar eclipses—these alone are the meritorious times. This is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*.
What is given during an eclipse, at the six-aśīti periods, likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, at the beginning of a yuga, and during the Vaidhṛti yoga, becomes inexhaustible.
Likewise, I shall declare the lunar days (tithis) on which what is given yields great fruit:
during an eclipse of a planet, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), and when moving through the zodiacal signs.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Mīṭhira, on the twelfth and seventh days, at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti, on festival days (parvan), and during the southern and northern solstices (ayana),
I always accept [the offerings] of my devotees; these are specifically proclaimed as such.
They say that a gift given on lunar days (tithis) is tenfold in merit; it is a hundredfold at the end of a solstice (ayana),
and tenfold during an eclipse of a planet.
And at the equinox, it is inexhaustible at the end of the Yuga.
Śātātapa says: That which is given during the solstices, at the beginnings of the six aśītis,
and during eclipses of the moon and sun, becomes inexhaustible.

In the *Śivarahasya*: "Whichever lunar day (tithi) is designated by the word 'great' (*maha*) or by a prefix, it should be known as equal to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) for the performance of acts such as giving gifts and Vedic study."
Śaṅkha says:
When Viṣṭi and Vyatīpāta coincide with Sunday, that is declared to be named Padmaka; it is four times more meritorious than an Ayanānta.
When the Vyatīpāta yoga occurs on the sixth lunar day and it is likewise a Sunday, that is declared to be named Padmaka; its merit is four times that of an Ayana.
When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; it is difficult to find even at Puṣkara.
Thus concludes the section on miscellaneous auspicious times.
Now follows the section on auspicious times that are always present in accordance with specific signs.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Every time has been prescribed, and every recipient has been described;
regarding the giving of what one has acquired, no deliberation need be made here."
That indeed is the time for giving when both [the recipient and the object] have appeared together.
Likewise:
"No fixed time is prescribed for the giving of shelter;
its gift is said to be at that very moment when a traveler arrives."
"One should not wait for the right time to give water to one who is thirsty;
food and water should always be given—thus said the Blessed Manu."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: One should give a cow that has half-delivered its calf, without considering the time or other such factors;
for that very moment is the proper time for the gift when the cow is indeed facing away from the birth.
Vyāsa says:
A cow with her calf should be given by one whose death is imminent, as previously described;
and in its absence, a cow alone is indeed for the sake of deliverance from hell.
If at that time he is unable to give the Vaitaraṇī cow,
then another capable person, having been requested, should give it for the benefit of the deceased.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "The Vyatīpāta yoga, the Saṃkrānti, as well as an eclipse of the sun—
all such auspicious times (puṇyakāla) are [ineffectual] when death has arrived."
Then, gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, shall become inexhaustible.

"A gift unseen and unheard of is not seen even after being enjoyed"—this specific statement from the *Vyāsa-smṛti* applies to a subject matter restricted by other scriptures. Regarding this, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: "They call that time equal to an eclipse of the sun."
O best of the twice-born, that which is given when the umbilical cord has not yet been severed upon the birth of a son,
as well as during the sacramental rites of the son, is proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Whenever wealth arises accompanied by a mind endowed with faith,
that very moment is the time for giving, for life is indeed transient."
Thus, according to the specific occasion, every moment is always a time for merit.
Now, that which is to be avoided on particular lunar days;
first, that which is to be avoided on the fourth day.
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says: "If the moon is seen on the fourth day of the dark fortnight when the sun is in Leo, it causes the fault of falsehood; therefore, one should not look at it then."
Thus, with the exception of the fourth [lunar day]. Now, the prohibitions regarding the seventh [lunar day] are stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
On the seventh lunar day, one should not touch oil, nor wear blue clothing;
a man should neither bathe with *āmalaka* fruits nor engage in quarrels.
On the seventh day, one must certainly not eat from a copper vessel.
On the seventh lunar day, a wise person should not consume neem, nor apply oil, sesame-seed offerings, or collyrium; furthermore, one should not eat from a copper vessel.
Thus end the prohibitions regarding the seventh lunar day. Now follows what is to be performed on the festival days (parvan).
Regarding this, Manu says:
One should constantly perform the *sāvitra* oblations and the *śānti* homas on the *parvan* days.
"Sāvitra" means those having the deity Savitṛ as their presiding divinity.
In this *homa*, the mantra is the *gāyatrī* and the ritual substance (*dravya*) is unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
As Śaṅkha says:
"One who desires peace, being pure, should offer oblations with unbroken grains while reciting the Gāyatrī;
and 'peace' (śānti) is the cessation of undesirable worldly results through righteousness."
The things to be avoided are shown in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, and the full moon— these, O King of kings, are the festival days (parvan), as is the transit of the sun."
"One who indulges in oil, women, or meat on these *parvan* days shall not [be so].
Because of the word "constantly" (*nityaśas*), this *homa* must necessarily be performed on *parvan* days; and the fruit of this *Sāvitra-homa* is peace (*śānti*).
— Viṣṇu.
On the festival days (parvan), one should certainly perform oblations of sesame seeds; being adorned, one should remain thus, practicing such conduct. Kātyāyana says:
"Sleeping on the ground is prescribed for the full moon and the new moon days."
This [rite] is also prescribed for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, after the fire has been established.
"One who has not established the [Śrauta] fires" refers to one who possesses the Smārta fire.
Āpastamba says:

"The sun protects living beings by day, and the moon by night; therefore, on the night of the new moon (amāvāsyā), one should desire the most excellent protection for oneself. During the period of ritual purity and celibacy, the Sun and the Moon dwell together with his wife on that night."
‘Sādhīyasī’ means exceedingly so. ‘Guptiḥ’ means protection.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* and the *Kātyāyana-smṛti*, it is stated:
“In the month of Nabhasya, on the new moon day, fresh *darbha* grass is prescribed to be taken.”
"Those Darbha grasses, being fresh, may be employed again and again. Thus [it is said].
And likewise, Kātyāyana, having prescribed the cutting of darbha grass on the new moon day, stated:
"One should take a garment for the purpose of recitation for the ancestors and the gods.
Likewise:
"They are to be appointed by the twice-born for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.
Therefore, *kuśa* grass must indeed be taken for the sake of rites for the ancestors and others.
However, Marīci has stated that the taking up of *darbha* grass occurs on the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the new moon day of the month of Nabhasya, the gathering of darbha grass is prescribed;
that darbha grass, being of undiminished potency, may be employed again and again.

[684] As for the prohibition against cutting *kuśa* grass on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), that refers to occasions other than those already mentioned. Thus concludes what is to be performed on the festival days (*parvan*). Now follows what is to be avoided on the festival days.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "On the festival days (parvan), one should not study, nor eat meat, nor approach a woman; for on the festival days, there are demons, piśācas, adulterers, and women with broad hips. Viṣṇu says:
On the *parvan* days, one should not cut even a blade of grass. Paiṭhīnasi says: On the *parvan* days, one should not use oil, a razor, engage in sexual intercourse, or eat meat.

‘Upeyāt’ means one should employ [it]. And in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, after enumerating the five festival days beginning with the fourteenth, it is said: “That man who indeed indulges in oil, women, and meat on these festival days...”
O King, one who eats excrement and urine goes to hell.
Manu says: On the fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, the full moon, and during the sun's passage into a new sign—
one should avoid oil, meat, and tooth-sticks.
On the fifteenth, fourteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, a wise man should avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.
Hārīta:
One should avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving on the days of the lunar festivals (parvan). Misfortune always dwells in these during the auspicious times.
Likewise, Alakṣmī always makes her abode in the Śleṣmātaka tree;
she constantly dwells in the female organ, in meat, in razors, in oil, and on the sacred festival days.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
Using a tooth-stick on the new moon day, sexual intercourse on the fourteenth day,
and taking oil on the eighth day destroys one's family for seven generations.
Yama says: By anointing the head on the fourteenth day, one destroys the family up to the seventh generation;
by eating meat on the fifteenth day, and likewise by indulging in sensual pleasure on the eighth day.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"He who cuts down plants while the moon is situated among the constellations of the plants,
or causes their leaves to fall, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin."
"Vīrutsaṃsthe" means when it has entered the forest trees. Paiṭhīnasi says: "On the new moon day, one should not cut kuśa grass nor sacrificial fuel."
If one causes injury while Soma is present everywhere, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.

In some places, the reading is: "One should not cause injury on the new moon day. It has been shown in the section concerning the performance of rites on festival days that *kuśa* grass must indeed be taken for the sake of rites for the ancestors and others.
Likewise:
"Evening twilight, the food of another, and likewise sesame flour..."
On the new moon day, one should not engage in sexual intercourse or eating at night.
From the *Smṛtisamuccaya*:
On the new moon day, one should avoid the evening twilight rites, food from others, eating at another's house, sexual intercourse, oil, meat, and flour-based foods.
If one should eat the food of another while the moon is situated in the asterism of the Sun (i.e.,
during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa), the merit he has accumulated throughout that month shall belong to the owner of that food.
On all new moon days, one should not wear new clothing.
Thus end the [impurities] to be avoided on specific lunar days (parvan). Now, various things to be avoided according to specific times, as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The skull, the entrails, nails, skin, and likewise sesame seeds—
one should always avoid these, respectively, on the eighth day and other such lunar days.
‘Head’ refers to coconut; ‘skull’ to gourd; ‘intestine’ to the fruit of the *paṭola*; ‘niṣpāva’ beans; ‘skin’ to lentils (*masūrī*); and ‘sesame’ to *vārttīka*—thus the elders explain.
However, in the *Caturviṃśatimata*, the latter half [of the verse] is read as follows:
“If one desires upward progression, one should avoid [these foods] on the eighth day and other such occasions.”
Vyāsa says: On the sixth, eighth, new moon, the fourteenth day of either fortnight,
sin is present in oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.
[687] Regarding this, some say: "In the sequence beginning with the sixth day, there is a prohibition of oil and the rest:
'On the sixth day, oil shortens life; likewise, meat on the eighth;
sensual enjoyment on the fourteenth; and shaving on the new moon.'"
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa), it follows that there is no fault in other substances such as oil and the like.
This is incorrect, because oil and the like are prohibited elsewhere as well.
Regarding this, Manu says:

The fifteenth day (Pañcadaśī) [is forbidden] for eating meat, the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) for anointing with oil, and the eighth day (Aṣṭamī) for sexual intercourse with a village woman; [on these days], one would cause even a blazing fire to fall.
"Village-dharma" means sexual intercourse.
Shaving and sexual intercourse [are forbidden] on the fourteenth day and the new moon day;
thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
On the day of a solar transit, on the fifteenth day, on the twelfth day, or on the day of a Śrāddha ceremony,
one should never wring out one's clothes, nor should one even be harmed by a razor.
The prohibition against sesame oil has already been shown in the context of other lunar days. Vyāsa also says:
"One should not touch oil, nor should one cut down trees such as the *dāma*."
And at the beginning of a lunar fortnight, on Sundays, on the sixth lunar day, and likewise on the *riktā* days.
The fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon—
these festival days (parvan), as well as the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), are to be avoided.
O King, he who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these sacred festival days goes to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana (the Eater of Excrement and Urine).
Bṛhaspati: [688] On the new moon day, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days,
a man shall be born from a Caṇḍāla womb by the consumption of oil, women, and meat.
From the *Purāṇa*: "On the new moon (*kuhū*), the full moon, the *saṃkrānti*, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days...

Here, the second half [of the verse] belongs to the preceding *śloka*. Therefore, since the prohibition of oil and other substances is already established here as well, the specific prohibition of oil and so forth in connection with particular lunar days is intended to indicate a specific gravity of the fault (*doṣa*). Furthermore, in this context, the prohibition of oil and other substances applies for as long as the time of the lunar day such as the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) lasts; it does not, however, extend to the entire day and night (*ahorātra*) by virtue of its connection to the sixth and other days, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a definition.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa: "One should perform an oil massage on the Nandā days, a haircut on the Riktā days, and eat meat on the Jayā days."
A woman should be avoided on full-moon days;
one should undertake all auspicious deeds.
One should not perform an oil massage on Sunday, nor a haircut on Tuesday; one should avoid meat on Friday and Tuesday, and one should not approach a woman on Wednesday.
In all remaining cases, one should always perform all [the rites].
Oil, shaving, and meat should be avoided under the asterisms Citrā, Hasta, Śravaṇa, Viśākhā, and Pratipad; likewise, meat should be avoided under Mūla, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and the Bhādrapadas.

One should avoid women during the Maghā, Kṛttikā, and the Uttarā constellations; on the fourteenth, eighth, new moon, and full moon days; and at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti). On these occasions, one should also avoid oil, meat, and the use of a tooth-stick.
Devala says: On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, and the eighth lunar days, O wise one,
one should completely avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.
Yama says: Just as on the eighth days of the bright fortnight, or on the fourteenth day and the new moon,
one should avoid oil massage, shaving, and sexual intercourse with women.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"On the fourteenth, the eighth, the fifteenth, and on other festival days (parvan),
one should avoid oil massage as well as sexual enjoyment with women."
A wise man should not take clay or water during the night, nor should he collect cow dung at dusk, nor cow urine at the same time.

The phrase "even at night with soft water" is also connected here. Furthermore, this prohibition against taking [water] at night is for the purpose of avoiding unseen karmic consequences. As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Bathing, great giving, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors..."
One should not perform [the rite] during the first year following the death of a great preceptor (mahāguru).
Māṇḍavya says:

The piercing of the ears, birth ceremonies, the first feeding of solid food, journeys, and the worship of images should be performed when Jupiter is situated in the house of the Sun; however, marriage should not be performed.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "When Viṣṇu is asleep, all auspicious and other rites cease—
marriage, the tying of the sacred thread, tonsure, purificatory ceremonies, and initiation."
Sacrifices, the entry into a new home, the consecration of gods and kings,
and whatever other meritorious deeds there may be— none of these would take place while the Lord of the World is asleep.
Thus, various things to be avoided [at specific times] have been stated according to particular periods of time.
Now follows the prohibited times for the act of shaving. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:

One should avoid shaving on the day of Saturn, the Sun, or Mars, as well as during their respective days and nights; likewise, one should avoid the first lunar day (pratipad) and the "empty" (riktā) lunar days.

In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): [One should not perform calculations] for those who have anointed themselves with oil, those who have eaten, those at the time of battle, those who are fasting, nor for those who have bathed, slept, departed, or are adorned with fine garments.

"Shaving is beneficial on the days of the twilight (sandhyā), night (niśā), Sun (arka), Mars (kuja), Saturn (sauri), and the Lord of the Day (dineśvara), but not during the Viṣṭi yoga. Thus it is said.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The eighth, the sixth, the ninth, and the fourteenth [lunar days],
as well as the junctions of the lunar phases (parvan-sandhi), are to be avoided for the rite of shaving.
Thus ends the prohibited times for the act of shaving.
Now follows the prohibited times for the act of shaving the beard. Marīci says:

One should avoid shaving when fasting, when asleep, or likewise while standing; also when one has eaten in the evening, when sitting at ease, when angry, or even when prepared for a journey or battle.
Thus ends the prohibited times for the practice of shaving the beard.
Now follows the time for abstaining from meat.
This is the statement of Īśvara in the Nandipurāṇa:
If indeed a man, intent on attaining heaven, should always avoid meat on the fourteenth day, he should especially avoid it during the principal solstice.
The fourth, the eighth, the twelfth, the fourteenth,
as well as the fifteenth, O noble ones, and the six *aśītimukhas*, are [the days of fasting].
Furthermore, on the sun’s transit, at the equinoxes, and during the rainy season,
a mortal who abstains from meat goes to heaven for three days.
Alternatively, a man should abstain from eating meat during the month of Āśvayuja;
by doing so, he shall obtain the merit accumulated over many months.
By renouncing the consumption of meat, a person becomes pure in mind;
that man who completely avoids meat during the month of Kārttika obtains the merit of abstaining from meat for an entire year.
Thus ends the time for abstaining from meat. Now follows the time for what is prescribed and forbidden regarding the bed.
Dakṣa says:
One should spend the first watch of the night and the last watch engaged in the study of the Vedas;
by sleeping for two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
[692] For the three castes, there is keeping vigil during the first part of the night. Pracetas:
Not during twilight, nor during the solstice;
so says Aṅgiras:
"One should not sleep with food remnants in the mouth, nor by day, nor during the two twilights, nor on ashes."
Vyāsa:
One should never sleep during the day, nor during the first or last watches of the night. Manu: [states the same].
At the end of the night, one who has studied the Veda while fatigued should not sleep again.
The meaning is that even if fatigued, he should not sleep again. Thus says Gautama.

Having studied during the latter part of the night, one should not sleep again. Hārīta says: "Having awakened during the Brāhma-muhūrta and having performed the recitation of the Veda, one should not go back to sleep."
Āpastamba: "Having engaged in sexual union, one should not sleep with her for the entire night. This refers to the prohibited time regarding sleeping.
Now follows the determination of the time for cleaning the teeth.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Having risen, having washed his eyes, and having become pure and composed..."
And having consecrated it with the mantra, one should chew the tooth-stick.
O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us long life, strength, fame, luster, offspring, cattle, and wealth; grant us sacred knowledge, wisdom, and mental acuity.
Thus is the mantra. Vyāsa says:
Having risen in the morning for the sake of purification, one should consume the tooth-stick.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey should not eat during the observances of a Śrāddha or a sacrifice.
Vyāsa says: On the occasion of a Śrāddha, on one's birthday, during a marriage, when the mouth is defiled,
and during a vow or a fast, one should avoid cleaning the teeth with a twig.
Saṃvarta states: On the first lunar day, on the ninth, during the waning of the moon,
on Sunday, and during a period of ritual impurity, one should avoid cleaning the teeth with a tooth-stick.
Kātyāyana says: On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth, and especially on the ninth,
the contact of a wooden stick with the teeth burns the family unto the seventh generation.

Vyāsa says: On the first day (pratipad), the new moon (darśa), the sixth day, and the ninth day, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with a leaf; however, the scraping of the tongue should always be done with a wooden twig.

The prohibition of using a tooth-stick on the *vyatīpāta* yoga, during the *saṃkrānti*, on the *nandā* days, and on festival days (*parvan*) has been shown in the section concerning various things to be avoided according to specific times.
In the absence of tooth-sticks, or when the day is otherwise prohibited,
one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
[694] However, in some places they read only the second half-verse as follows:
"One should cleanse the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water or with leaves. Likewise:
If one, out of delusion, should chew a tooth-stick at the time of bathing,
the deities and the ancestors depart from there disappointed.
One should carefully avoid a seat, a vehicle, a tooth-stick, or sandals made of *pālāśa* wood, as well as everything made of *aśvattha* wood.
This refers to the subject of the midday bath, since the procedure for the morning bath has already been prescribed.
As Parāśara says:
"First one should scrub the teeth below, and in the morning one should sprinkle the eyes."
It is traditionally taught that one should not brush the teeth when the mouth is full of water during the summer, nor in the cold season or autumn.
One should first rinse the mouth and then consume the tooth-stick, and having rinsed it again, one should discard it.
Thus concludes the determination of the proper time for brushing the teeth.
Now follows the determination of the time for the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*). Regarding this, Gautama says:
"One should stand during the morning prayer and sit during the evening prayer, remaining silent until the stars are visible."
The commencement [of the recitation] is at the time when the stars are still visible, and its cessation is upon the disappearance of those stars; this is the meaning.
Saṃvarta says:
"One should perform the morning twilight worship while the stars are still present, according to the prescribed rule."
Now, having described the duties pertaining to the Brāhmaṇas, Śātātapa said:
"He who [observes the fast] during the eastern [twilight] while the stars are still visible, and during the western [twilight] while the sun is still present..."
A twice-born man who does not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) is considered to have fallen from his status as a Brāhmaṇa.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
One should perform the evening *sandhyā* when the sun has set, but not while it is still visible, nor when it has already risen. Vyāsa says:
When the sun has set and darkness has arrived, having performed the rite of washing the feet,
one should perform the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) outside, holding kuśa grass in hand and with a concentrated mind.
In some places, however, the reading is "when the sun has reached the mountain of setting.
Manu says: "One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the appearance of the sun."
But when seated facing west, one attains perfection through the correct visualization of the constellations.
Yājñavalkya says:
One should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the stars rise;
likewise, one should stand during the morning twilight facing the east until the sun is visible.
That junction of day and night which is devoid of both the sun and the stars is what has been designated as "Sandhyā" by the seers who perceive the truth.

Having said this, it was stated: "One should perform the twilight worship there. That [injunction] is to be explained as follows, based on a careful consideration of the collection of statements previously shown: the morning twilight worship extends until the sun is seen, and the evening twilight worship extends until the stars are seen.
As the Śruti says: "Knowing thus, one performs the twilight worship in the evening and in the morning."
Here, by the word "sāyam" (evening), precisely the previously mentioned time of twilight is intended. As it is said:
"Twilight lasts until the appearance of the stars; that which follows it is the evening."
That night should be known as dedicated to that [purpose]; one should avoid performing religious duties during it.

Because of this statement, the time subsequent to the sighting of the stars is designated by the word "evening" (*sāyam*); therefore, upon considering the previous statement, it should be understood that the passing of the solar time (*sūryakāla*) occurs in some manner.
Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
"The decrease and increase of the days occur continuously in their respective order."
The twilight period lasts for exactly one muhūrta; it is traditionally held to be equal [in duration] during both waning and waxing.
From the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
Worship of the twilight (sandhyā) at all times is prescribed for kings,
except in cases of birth-impurity, ritual defilement, confusion, illness, or fear.
Pulastya said: One should perform the twilight prayers (sandhyā), the iṣṭi sacrifice, the caru oblation, and the fire-offering throughout one's entire life.
One must not abandon them even during a period of ritual impurity (sūtaka); by abandoning them, one goes to a low state of existence.
Such being the case, he states the established rule:
"During both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), a twice-born man should not perform the twilight rites;
he may mentally recite the mantras, except for the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma)."

And thus, those statements regarding the prohibition of twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like should be understood as intended to preclude the employment of sacred mantras (*mantra*); furthermore, the offering of the *añjali* (hand-clasp) must be performed while the *Sāvitrī* itself is being recited.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi:
"But during *sūtaka*, having offered the *añjali* with the *Sāvitrī*, having circumambulated [the sun], one should meditate upon the Sun."
One should pay obeisance.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
Now, regarding the things to be avoided during the twilight hours (*sandhyā*):
on this matter, Manu says:
"One should avoid these four actions during the twilight."
From food, disease arises; from sexual intercourse, a fierce embryo;
from sleep, misfortune arises; and from Vedic recitation, the exhaustion of life occurs.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
One should avoid food, sexual intercourse, sleep, ritual action, Vedic study, as well as giving and receiving gifts during the time of the twilights.
From eating food, disease arises; from sexual intercourse, a fierce fetus is conceived;
from sleeping, one becomes unfortunate; and in this state, ritual action is indeed fruitless.
The student goes to hell, and the giver does not obtain the fruit thereof;
the recipient becomes sinful—therefore, one should avoid [giving] during the twilight.
Indeed, the giver goes to hell, and the receiver sinks into the depths.
Thus end the things to be avoided during the twilight periods.
Now, the things to be avoided at night:
one should never, under any circumstances, perform a gift-giving ceremony at night.
Because Rākṣasas carry it away, it brings fear to the donor.
Especially at midnight, no auspicious ritual action for the sake of Dharma is appropriate;
therefore, a wise person should avoid the middle of the night for acts such as giving.
Devala says:

One should perform the giving of food and other such acts at night during an eclipse, a solar transit (saṃkrānti), a marriage, a time of calamity, or on occasions of prosperity, as well as during optional vows (kāmyavrata).
Vasiṣṭha says:

"Giving on occasions such as eclipses, weddings, the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), times of physical distress, and childbirth is to be known as occasional (naimittika) giving; that is desired even at night."
The reading is "yātrādau" (at the beginning of a journey,
etc.). These gifts are recommended at night during a sacrifice, a wedding, a pilgrimage, as well as when reciting a book, and likewise in a temple.
In the Mahābhārata: "They do not praise giving at night, except for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the solstice,
O best of the twice-born, as well as knowledge, a maiden, a lamp, food, and shelter."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The honoring of guests and likewise the honoring of travelers,
as well as the honoring of cows, should be understood as to be performed at night."
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"The 'great night' (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle watches;
one should not perform a bath there, except for those baths performed for specific desires or on specific occasions."
Viśvāmitra says:
"The 'great night' (mahāniśā) is to be understood as occurring during the two middle watches of the night;
at that time one should perform the occasional rites (naimittika), but not even slightly the obligatory rites (nitya)."
In some places, the reading is "but not even slightly [should one engage in] poetry. In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"One should not perform ritual bathing at night, and especially so with giving gifts."
[699] However, one should perform occasional rites and the giving of food during the nights.

"During eclipses, weddings, transits of the sun, times of distress, illness, and childbirth, as well as during the Śravaṇa festival, this Itihāsa is praised for being recited at night and for the giving of gifts.
[And: "At weddings, religious vows, solar transits, consecrations, and the birth of a child..."
Likewise, for the eclipse of the moon and other such occasions, as well as for bathing and giving gifts, the night is auspicious.

‘Ṛtu’ refers to the period favorable for conception; ‘pāta’ refers to the Vyatīpāta yoga. Bathing is recommended at the birth of a son, during a sacrifice, likewise at the sun’s transit (saṃkramaṇa), and upon the appearance of Rāhu [during an eclipse], but not otherwise, nor at night.
Likewise:
"That which is given on the birth of a son, during a journey, or at night is inexhaustible. Thus ends the section on what is to be avoided when performing rites at night.
In this regard,
[Vyāsa] states that the time for frequenting crossroads is always at midday, at dawn, and at midnight.
One should not frequent a crossroads, nor likewise either of the two twilights.
Manu says: At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
Now, regarding those things to be observed and those not to be observed at specific times,
Kātyāyana says: A Vedic scholar, a fortunate man, a cow, fire, and likewise one who has maintained the sacred fires.
Whoever rises in the morning and beholds this shall be liberated from calamities.
Vaiyāghrapāda said: He who,
with his breath controlled, beholds a learned Vedic scholar, a fortunate person, a cow, and likewise one who has maintained the sacred fire,
is liberated from calamities.
Kātyāyana says:
With a concentrated mind, one should look in the morning at rocanā, sandalwood, gold, a drum, a mirror, a gem, a guru, fire, and likewise the sun.

In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a brahmin, a cow, fire, gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise the king as the eighth. One should constantly look upon these and pay them homage with a concentrated mind.

Having seen those who perform sacrifices, those who give desired food, those who maintain perpetual sessions, those who live for a hundred years, the righteous, the pure, those perfected through knowledge, and those perfected through austerity, one is liberated from sin.

The builder of a fire-altar, a tawny cow, one who has performed a sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should look upon them constantly.
He who, having risen in the morning, sees one who is most wicked, unfortunate, intoxicated, naked, or whose nose has been cut off— that is a characteristic sign of the Kali age.
Thus, [the waters] are to be viewed or not viewed according to specific times. Now follows the determination of the period of turbidity (*rajaḥ*) for rivers.
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
For two months all rivers are indeed in their menses;
therefore, bathing at the beginning of the rains with fresh water is not recommended.
Kātyāyana says:
For two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not bathe in them, except for those that flow into the ocean.
Likewise:
"During the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not perform ritual bathing in them, nor the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors."
Those whose flow does not extend for eight thousand bow-lengths,
and which do not carry water with the sound of "nadī," are proclaimed by you as mere hollows (garta).
Between the signs of Leo and Cancer, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
a person should not perform ritual acts such as bathing in them.

Yogiyājñavalkya states: "Water that has just arrived from a river during its first surge, as well as water that has been agitated by anyone or has issued forth from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), is indeed unfit to be taken."
In some places, however, the reading is *agrimāḥ*. "Tīrtha" means a path for descending into water.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Goats, cows, female buffaloes, and Brāhmaṇa women who have recently given birth [should not cross]."
They become pure in ten nights, as do water that has reached the ground and newly fallen rainwater.
Yājñavalkya says:
As long as the Lord who adorns the southern quarter has not risen,
so long do rivers carrying semen remain impure, with the exception of the Jāhnavī.
O Goddess, during the first [fortnight] of Karkaṭaka, the Gaṅgā is menstruating for three days; all rivers carrying red water are proclaimed as being like the Karatoyā.
Kātyāyana says:
During the rainy season, the great rivers are constantly in their menstrual flow;
when the fourth day has arrived, the Gaṅgā becomes pure.
The Gaṅgā, daughter of the Sun, the Sarasvatī born from the Plakṣa tree,
and those others known as rivers, are not overcome by passion.
The Gaṅgā, daughter of the Sun, the Plakṣajā, and the Sarasvatī—
those who drink from these three rivers have their sins rendered stale.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī born from the Plakṣa tree,
and the great lake Śoṇa are not overwhelmed by passion (rajas).
The Kālindī, Gomatī, and Gaṅgā are pure and fashioned by the gods;
therefore, due to their commonality and their possession of virtuous qualities, passion does not overcome them.
The Gaṅgā, the Dharmadravī, the Puṇyā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī—
having internalized the cessation of passion, they remain stainless even during all the days of the waning moon.
A marketplace, contact with dust from against-the-current travel, and the settling of road-dust and water—
these do not defile one on the Gaṅgā, for it is itself a flow of dharma.
One should not bathe in those small streams on earth that dry up in the summer, until the appearance of clouds in the rainy season.
Kātyāyana says: One should not bathe during the rainy season in those small streams on earth that dry up in the summer until ten days have passed since they were last full.
From the beginning of Cancer, for three days, the Gautamī is defiled by menstrual flow;
so too are the Candrabhāgā, Satī, Bindhu, Śarayū, and Narmadā.
At the commencement and the conclusion of the Vedic term, those who discourse on Brahman go for the sake of ritual bathing;
yet embodied beings, being subject to thirst, proceed there as well, closely joined together.
All the Vedas, the Brahmins, and the celestial dwellers;
then the ancestors seeking water, as well as the sages beginning with Marīci.
But wherever these meet, there the stainless rising remains;
surely everything goes to destruction, how much more so a single grain of river-sand?
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, as well as at the ritual bath for the deceased,
and during lunar or solar eclipses, no impurity due to menstrual flow is found.
On the surface of the earth, all waters—even those situated in wells—become equal to the waters of the celestial river during a lunar or solar eclipse;
of this there is no doubt.

The *Svardhunī* is the Gaṅgā. It is established that fresh water situated on the ground is pure after three days have passed; however, on the earth, it remains eternally ancient by virtue of the force of its current.
Thus concludes the determination of the periods of turbidity for rivers.
Now follows the time for touching or not touching the Aśvattha tree and the ocean:
"The Aśvattha tree and the ocean are to be resorted to, but they must never be touched."
On the day of Kālavāra, one should touch the eastern [side], and on the full moon day (parvan), one should touch the northern [side].
In some places, however, the reading is "on a Monday.
Thus ends the section on the times for touching and not touching the Aśvattha tree and the ocean.
Now, the determination of the time for bathing. Kātyāyana says:
"Just as one bathes during the day, so should one bathe daily in the morning, remaining unwearied."
The body is utterly impure and endowed with nine apertures.
The morning bath, which is purifying, flows away [from impurity] indeed day and night;
for they praise the morning bath as it brings about both visible and invisible results.

Vaiyghrapāda says: "The morning bath is intended for the sake of purification; it is performed briefly. But at midday, it should be performed in detail according to the prescribed ritual with mantras."
One should always bathe in the morning and always bathe at midday;
by doing so for three years, one destroys the sins committed during seven lifetimes.
Bathing at every dawn, as well as during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
is equal for men to the Prājāpatya penance, provided it is done before the sun has risen.
In the Caturviṃśatimata: "Bathing at every dawn, during the twilight, and when the sun has risen,
is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and destroys even the most heinous sins."
Bathing at dawn and at midday is prescribed for forest-dwellers and householders;
for the ascetic, it is declared to be three times a day, while for the student, it is once.
Yogiyājñavalkya states: "Brahmins residing as householders must bathe during both twilights;
ascetics must bathe during all three twilights."
Vyāsa: On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who desires an auspicious lineage, or even those intent on wealth and grain, should by no means bathe.
The tenth lunar day leads to the loss of one's son, and the thirteenth to one's own destruction;
the second leads to the loss of fear—one should avoid these days for bathing.
In some places, the third quarter is recited differently as: "The third [lunar day] leads to the destruction of the husband.
Vasiṣṭha says:
"On the first [lunar day] one would be childless; on the third, one would have only daughters."
On the tenth day, bathing destroys everything; so does the thirteenth day. He himself says: "The tenth, the ninth, the third, and the thirteenth."
One should especially avoid those [days] during the ritual bath on the day of the moon's change.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"One should not perform a ritual bath on the new moon day while one's mother and father are still living,
nor on the ninth lunar day, unless there is the occurrence of another specific occasion."
Yama says: One should not perform a ritual bath on the new moon day while one's mother and father are living;
by performing it, a son casts away the life of his mother and father.
One should perform [the rite] when either [of these] has passed, or when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu. Garga and Jābāli state:
"On the thirteenth, the third, and the tenth day of the lunar fortnight, in every case."
Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas should never perform ritual bathing.
From another Smṛti:

"Any bath performed by men for the sake of enjoyment or out of mere whim is prohibited on the tenth day and other such occasions; however, this does not apply to obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) baths."
Garga and Jābāli state:
"That bathing which is performed either with or without the constraints of the scriptures,
and which results in the removal of impurity, is indeed 'voluntary' (yādṛcchika) bathing."
A wise man seeking eternal prosperity should not perform it on the third lunar day, nor likewise on the fourteenth, nor even on the tenth.
Likewise:
One should never neglect the daily bath, nor that which is performed for specific desires or on specific occasions;
it should be performed even on the tenth day, but never at random.
Baudhāyana says: "One should not bathe except during the daily obligatory bath, nor on the tenth lunar days. Vasiṣṭha and Paiṭhīnasi [state the same].

Upon the birth of a son, during the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), at a śrāddha ceremony, and likewise on one's birthday, one must always perform a ritual bath; in these cases, no defect regarding the lunar day (tithi) exists.
Regarding the continuation [of the rule] "one should avoid," Āpastamba states: "And bathing while the sacred fire has not been kindled. Parāśara states:
Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised;
bathing at night is not recommended, except during an eclipse of the moon (Rāhu) or in the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Just as bathing and giving gifts are prescribed during a solar eclipse by day, [so too are they prescribed during a lunar eclipse].
Likewise, for Soma as well, bathing at night is prescribed as purifying.
Bathing at night is not recommended, except during an eclipse of Rāhu;
likewise, one should never bathe in the water used by others, nor should one ever bathe without wearing a turban.
Vasiṣṭha says:
Bathing is recommended on the birth of a son, at a sacrifice, during the transit of the sun, and upon the sighting of Rāhu; it is not so [recommended] otherwise at night.
Vyāsa states: "Bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and performing ancestral rites yield infinite merit during an eclipse of Rāhu;
at other times, it is a demonic night, therefore one should avoid it."
Likewise: "One should not perform a ritual bath at night, nor especially a gift;
however, one may perform occasional (naimittika) baths and gifts even during the nights."
Parāśara says: "The supreme bath is prescribed at the time of an eclipse; for one who has died, it is declared to be on the day [of death].
However, 'mahāniśā' (the dead of night) should be understood as the two middle watches [of the night]."
One should perform one's ritual duties during the first and last watches of the night as if they were daytime;
and having mixed water collected during the day with gold, one should use it.
When bathing at night has arrived, one should bathe near a fire;
bathing on account of being defiled by food remnants and the like is known as occasional (naimittika) bathing.
The same applies during lunar and solar eclipses, as well as during the birth-impurity caused by a planetary event.
Manu [708]: One should not perform a ritual bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight,
nor repeatedly with one's clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water.

The phrase “having eaten” does not constitute a prohibition against daily bathing (*nityasnāna*), because that [daily bath] does not occur immediately after eating. Nor does it refer to bathing necessitated by contact with a *caṇḍāla*, for that would entail a contradiction with the scriptural injunction, “One should not remain impure even for a moment,” and because it was demonstrated in the determination of the time for oil massage (*tailābhyaṅga*) that a prohibition cannot apply to what is already established by a mandatory rule (*vidhi*). Therefore, this is a prohibition against occasional (*yādṛcchika*) bathing; however, for one who is ill, there is always a prohibition against bathing with water (*vāruṇasnāna*). “*Ajasram*” means continuously. One should not bathe when a festival has passed, nor once auspicious rites have been concluded.
Having followed his friends and kinsmen and having honored his chosen deity.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should know that the "great night" (mahāniśā) consists of the two middle watches of the night;
at that time, one may perform occasional rites (naimittika), but not even the slightest optional rite (kāmya).
In some places, however, the reading is "but never even for a moment.

From this statement, it is understood that the daily bath, even if its proper time has somehow been missed, must be performed during the night as well—excluding the *mahāniśā* (the dead of night)—and that there is no omission of the ritual act (*karman*).
The *mahāniśā*, moreover, should be known as the two middle watches of the night.
One should not perform a ritual bath there, except for those required by specific desires or occasional occasions.

In this context, by the word *kāmya*, bathing for the sake of a specific result is meant; however, there is no contradiction with the previous statement, where it was said to be "voluntary" (*yādṛcchika*). Viśvāmitra says:
"The 'great night' (*mahāniśā*) should be understood as the two middle watches of the night."
One should not perform a ritual bath or the act of sipping water for the sake of fulfilling specific desires in that [river].
In this context, "optional" (kāmya) is understood as that which is performed by chance or desire.
Even by means of sipping water (ācamana), there is no prohibition of the occasional (naimittika) rite. Therefore, he says:
A wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) after voiding urine or excrement during the middle of the night;
such a Brahmin becomes liable for expiation and deserves half of the prescribed penance.
Pulastya said:
Those men who perform ritual bathing on the days of the Sun, Mars,
or Saturn are not afflicted by diseases, just as lions are not troubled by deer.
Furthermore, it is heard:
"One may plunge into the ocean, but one does not plunge elsewhere," said Pulastya.
Bathing in a river during the Puṣya asterism, one’s birth star, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Vaidhṛti yoga, or on the new moon day, purifies one’s lineage up to the seventh generation.
On the eighth day, during the conjunction with Revatī, likewise in the waters of the Airāvata [ocean],
having reached Śrāvastī, or at any confluence whatsoever.
Every fourteenth day is meritorious, as is bathing in the waters of the Devikā;

Furthermore, by bathing at Saṃnihatyā on the new moon day and likewise at Prabhāsa,

Pulastya said:
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, on the tenth day conjoined with the asterism Hasta, the Gaṅgā destroys the sins of ten births; therefore, she is remembered as the remover of evil.
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha in conjunction with the Sarayū river, and likewise constantly on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.
Yama says: On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of both the month of Prauṣṭhapada and the month of Māgha,

having duly worshipped the gods and the ancestors, is liberated from all sins.
Whether child, youth, or old man; whether man, woman, or neuter—having bathed in the auspicious Māgha at a sacred ford, they obtain their desired fruit.

"Whom shall we purify as they descend—the slayer of a Brahmin or the drinker of liquor?"
Those who bathe in the month of Māgha at sunrise go there, where the palaces are made of gold and the women resemble celestial nymphs.
Restrained and observing silence on the road,
one should avoid backbiting if one desires vast, auspicious enjoyments comparable to the moon and the sun.
Between the months of Māgha and Phālguna, one should always perform the morning bath; indeed,
that man who performs the bath while his body is uncovered obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with his father, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, along with twenty-one generations of his lineage,
he goes to the world of Viṣṇu after bathing in the waters of the month of Māgha.
From the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
When the month of Māgha, which is beloved by those who practice austerities, has arrived,
all waters cry out as the sun enters the ocean.

even those belonging to a slayer of a Brahmin, and those committed through violent deeds.
The month of Māgha is indeed difficult to obtain and is proclaimed to be of great merit;
for in the waters of the month of Māgha, the gods have indeed infused their own splendor.
Therefore, water is indeed pure and the destroyer of the entire multitude of sins.
However, one should not bathe in waters within reed-thickets, nor in pond-water that has settled among lotuses;
for merit is not obtained easily, but merit is obtained through hardship.

And so Kātyāyana says: "Where there is a greater degree of hardship for even a wise person seeking the highest good, the wise declare that in such a case the higher good is attained through that very hardship."
Therefore:

Likewise, river water of great velocity contained in a new jar,

Viṣṇu says: One should perform the ritual bath beginning from either the new moon or the full moon day,

From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmātṛkā*:
"Water is pure by its very nature; it becomes especially so when heated by fire. For that reason, the virtuous praise bathing with warm water."
Yama said:
Water is always sacred, and fire is its purifier;

One should always perform [these] as they arise by chance, according to one's inclination.

"One should perform the ritual bath without [hot water], using either cold water or water from a river."
Likewise, for a twice-born man who has bathed here, there is no fruit whatsoever.
Regarding this, Yama states a specific rule: "The daily obligatory rites (nitya), occasional rites (naimittika), ritual acts, auspicious ceremonies,

But for one who is ill, there is indeed bathing with water that is entirely warm.
Regarding this, he himself says:

It is traditionally taught that boiled water is recommended for the ritual bathing of one who is ill.
One should bathe with cold water that has been consecrated by the application of mantras and heat;

Upon death, birth, the transit of the sun, an eclipse of the moon or sun, and upon touching those who are untouchable, one should not bathe with warm water.

On the occasion of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on a Sunday, on the seventh lunar day, and during an eclipse,

"Viṣṇu is pleased by *āmalaka* fruits, especially on the eleventh lunar day."

Furthermore, because of the prohibition of bathing with *āmalaka* on a Sunday, the injunction for bathing with *āmalaka* on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) does not apply to other days of the week; nor does the injunction for bathing with *āmalaka* on the eleventh lunar day necessarily imply that the prohibition of bathing with *āmalaka* on a Sunday applies to other lunar days. How, then, is the decision to be made? It is said: the prohibition concerns bathing undertaken out of worldly inclination (*rāga*), for if it applied to what is enjoined by scripture, it would result in a contradiction (*vikalpa*), which is improper. Therefore, it is established that on a Sunday falling on the eleventh lunar day, one should perform the *āmalaka* bath.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the *āmalaka* bath. [716]

He who always performs an oil massage, except on the days previously specified,

Baudhāyana says:
One should avoid anointing the head on the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially the ninth lunar days, and likewise on the day of the full or new moon (parvan).
Thus end the times prescribed and prohibited for oil massage;
herein concludes the determination of the proper time for oil massage and related practices.

Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "If one is anointed with oil on the first day of the lunar fortnight, on a Sunday, on the sixth lunar day, or likewise on a Riktā tithi, he is deprived of four things."

In this context, the oil produced from sesame seeds—and not that produced from safflower and the like—is intended; such is the rule of Pāṇini regarding its derivative form (*tasya vikāraḥ*). Consequently, the word *taila*, established by Pāṇini, cannot denote anything else.

As for the rule established by the author of the Vārttika, "oil is [used] in the sense of unctuousness" (*snehe tailam*), that refers to the word *taila* as denoting unctuousness in general, as in "linseed oil," "castor oil," and so forth. Any occasional use of the simple word *taila* to refer to other types of unctuous substances is justified on the basis of similarity.
Therefore, those learned in grammar say:
"In this context, the quality [of oil] is established; thus, even in other substances, the state of being oil (tailatva) occurs.
Consequently, oil is specifically a derivative of sesame seeds (*tila-vikāra*), and not merely any kind of unctuousness (*sneha*)."

On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, and the seventh lunar days, as well as during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti),
one should avoid contact with oil on the twelfth, seventh, and sixth lunar days.
One should not perform an oil massage on the thirteenth, the third, the first, or the ninth lunar days; however, one may do so on the other days, excluding the ninth.
In this regard, on which lunar days (tithis) is an oil massage prescribed and on which is it prohibited?
On this point, some say that the injunction concerns cooked oil, whereas the prohibition concerns uncooked oil.
This has been stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

On Sundays, Mondays, and other such days, as well as on prohibited lunar dates (*tithis*), whether one has bathed or not, refined oil (*pakvataila*) is not forbidden. That is incorrect, because the prohibition concerns oil massage obtained through natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*), whereas if it were to concern oil massage prescribed by rule (*vidhi-prāpta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of an option (*vikalpa*). Nor should it be argued that there is no option because the prohibition concerns a specific type of oil—unrefined oil—whereas the injunction from the scriptural rule (*vidhi-śāstra*) only establishes oil in general; for if that were so, then since the *ye yajāmahe* formula is established for all sacrifices by the statement, "And Prajāpati, seventeenfold, at every sacrifice," and there are likewise specific prohibitions regarding the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) and so forth, it would follow that there could be no option in those cases either. And whatever solution is offered there applies here as well, so there is no fault. Furthermore, if the prohibition concerned both what is obtained through inclination and what is obtained through rule, then a discrepancy in the injunctions (*vidhi-vaiṣamya*) would arise: in one case the prohibition would depend on the sublation of another scriptural rule, while in the other it would be independent. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition must concern only what is obtained through rule in order to avoid this discrepancy in injunctions; for when a prohibition is possible without the sublation of another scriptural rule, such sublation is logically untenable. Therefore, the prohibition concerns oil obtained through inclination; and since that would entail a prohibition of all oil, the statement "on Sundays, Fridays, and so forth" serves to specify that the prohibition does not apply to refined oil. Thus it is established that unrefined oil is to be used for the prescribed oil massage.

On the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on a Sunday, on the sixth lunar day, and likewise on a Tuesday,

Therefore, the meaning is that oil contained within another substance is never defiled during [specific occasions such as] the *saṃkrānti* and so forth.

Alternatively, remembering the boon granted to women, he may act according to his desire.

The "sixteen nights" beginning from the appearance of the menses constitute the "ṛtu," the period for conception, for women. During that time, he should "approach"—that is, have intercourse—on the "even" nights if he desires a son; however, if he desires a daughter, he should approach on the odd nights.
As Manu says:
"Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on odd nights."
Therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her fertile period on even nights.
Śaṅkha says:
"When a man approaches his wife during her season, sons are born on the even nights up to the sixteenth day, while daughters are born on the uneven nights."
Even among the even nights, each subsequent one is more highly recommended;
as Āpastamba says:
"From the fourth night onwards, among the sixteen, each successive even night [is preferred]."
Prajāpati teaches: "O, [this is] approaching [one's wife] during the proper season. Vyāsa [says].
If [conception occurs] at night on the fourth lunar day, there will be a son who is short-lived and destitute of wealth;
on the fifth, a woman will have daughters; and on the sixth, a son of middling quality.
On the seventh day, a woman bears no offspring; on the eighth, a man becomes a lord;
