on the ninth, a woman becomes fortunate; and on the tenth, an excellent son is born.
On the eleventh day, she is a woman of unrighteousness; on the twelfth, she is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
on the thirteenth, she is deceitful, sinful, and a cause of the intermixture of castes.
Such a woman, entirely wicked, is born as one who bestows suffering, grief, and fear.
One who possesses the banner of Dharma, is grateful, self-knowing, and firm in his vows,
is born on the fourteenth lunar day as a lord of the world through qualities and other virtues.
That highly fortunate princess, however, becomes subject to the king;
on the fifteenth day, she gives birth to many sons and remains devoted to her husband.
Complete in the characteristics of knowledge, truthful in speech, and with senses conquered,
such a man is born on the sixteenth day as a refuge for all living beings.
By the mention of "night," daytime is prohibited;
therefore, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated:
"One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day; those born by day are impotent, of little vigor, short-lived, and [of small stature]; therefore, one should avoid it."
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra):
"One born here [under such conditions] becomes short-lived, deficient in virility, or even impotent;
thus is the embryo corrupted when conception occurs during the daytime."
This is true even outside the fertile period;
as Āpastamba says:
"The vow for householders is not to sleep during the day, and they remain celibate during the fertile period and on the sacred festival days."

The five festival days (*parvan*)—the eighth, the fourteenth, the full moon, the new moon, and the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*)—have been shown in the context of what is to be practiced on those occasions. In that regard, the meaning is that one should remain celibate and not approach a woman. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"One should wait for the fertile period (*ṛtu*); even during that time, one should avoid the festival days and cause [the wife] to approach the man."
Manu:
He should approach his wife during her fertile period, being devoted to his own wife and pure;
he may go to her on other occasions except for the sacred festival days (parvan), but not during her fertile period out of a mere desire for sexual pleasure.
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"He should approach his wife during her fertile period, avoiding the forbidden days (parvan).
The mention of the forbidden days is intended to indicate other specific times as well."
Manu says:
A twice-born Snātaka should always remain celibate on the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon day, and the fourteenth, even during the period favorable for conception.

In this context, due to the association with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), [sexual intercourse] is forbidden on the eighth and fourteenth days of both lunar fortnights, as well as during the menstrual period. Viṣṇu states:
"One should not approach a woman on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth days; nor after eating at a *śrāddha*, nor after giving one; nor during the junctions of the seasons (*ṛtu-saṃdhi*)."
In the *Śivarahasya*: "One observing a vow should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day,
on his birthday, after having offered a *śrāddha*, after having eaten [at a funeral feast], or on the sacred festival days (*parvan*), if he seeks spiritual welfare."
In the Saura Purāṇa: "On the sixth, eighth, fifteenth, new moon, and fourteenth [lunar days],
one should always remain celibate, especially on one's birth asterism."
In the Vārāha Purāṇa, concerning the Vaiṣṇava, Varāha said:
"One should never engage in sexual intercourse on the sixth, the eighth, the new moon, the fourteenth day of both fortnights, or the twelfth day, which is dear to me."
Likewise, O King, he who does not engage in sexual intercourse on the eighth, the fourteenth, the sixth, the twelfth, the new moon day, or the fifteenth;
He shall not go to the womb of an animal; indeed, he goes to my world.
"The first four" means that one should avoid [sexual intercourse] for four nights starting from the appearance of the menses.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi:
"One should not summon [the husband] on the first, nor on the second, nor on the third, nor on the fourth."

Others, however, say: "One should avoid her for four nights starting from the bath," because by the very prohibition of touching her beforehand, her approach is also prohibited. That is incorrect; for there is a difference in the result, since from the prohibition of touching follows sin from touching, whereas from the prohibition of approaching follows sin even from that [touching]. For this very reason, distinct penances are prescribed for touching a woman in her menses and for approaching her. "The natural menstrual period of women is recorded as sixteen nights."
Together with the other four days, which are censured by the virtuous.
And because this contradicts the statement of Manu, since a "despised night" cannot occur after the ritual bath;
likewise, Kātyāyana says:
"A menstruating woman attains purity by bathing on the fourth day."

Furthermore, because of the hearing of censure in such statements as, "On the contrary, the remaining nights are censured; for women, he in whose month the appearance of the menses occurs does not become [a fit husband] for that long, and he is accused," therefore, four nights starting from the appearance of the menses are to be avoided.
However, Devala has stated that three nights are to be avoided:
"If one should approach her for sexual intercourse on these impure days..."
The lifespan, progeny, and merit of that man perish;
therefore, one should indeed avoid his wife when she has reached her menses for three nights.
According to some, conception occurs after three nights have passed;
Hārīta also states that the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) should take place on the fourth night.
On the fourth day, when she has bathed, or during the even-numbered nights thereafter, the Brahmin who has been initiated should approach her for the purpose of *garbhādhāna*.
She conceives a fetus.

From that arises conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and it is established [as follows]: on the fourth day, when the menstrual flow has ceased, there is permission; however, if there is a deviation from the prescribed rule, there is a prohibition.
For this very reason, Gobhila says:
When she has reached her menses and the menstrual blood has ceased, that is the time for conception.
And so Manu says:
"A virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by bathing once the flow has stopped."
A "virtuous woman" (*sādhvī*) is one who is fit for the rites of conception and so forth. Manu says:
"One should not approach a woman during her menstrual period, even if he is overcome by passion."
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, vitality, fame, sight, and lifespan are diminished.
For one who releases her when she is covered with dust,
wisdom, fortune, fame, vision, and lifespan increase.
Devala:
[727] If one should approach this woman for sexual intercourse while she is impure during her days,
that man’s lifespan, wisdom, and merit are diminished.
Therefore, for three nights, one should avoid a Caṇḍālī woman who has reached her menses.
The phrase "the first four" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), because [fasting] is also prohibited on the eleventh and thirteenth days. Thus says Manu:
"The first four [lunar days] are forbidden, as is the eleventh day."
The thirteenth day and the remaining ten nights are also praised.
In this context, the eleventh and thirteenth days are excluded from the fortnight;
likewise, one should avoid women on the first nights of the lunar phases and on other censurable nights.
He remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he may dwell in.

"In the censurable [nights] among the first"—meaning that among these six nights, namely the first four, the eleventh, and the thirteenth, as well as on any other nights that are not censured, one should avoid women; the sense is that one should approach women on only two nights. Devala says: "For a Brāhmaṇa woman, this period of menstruation is said to last for twelve days."
For the remaining [elements], ten, eight, and six [stages] are prescribed in successive order.
Even among these, having first avoided her during the three days of menstruation,
they should approach their wife when she is pure and has bathed for the sake of obtaining a son.

Furthermore, this statement regarding Brāhmaṇīs and others concerning the observance of twelve or more menstrual periods (*ṛtu*) intends to indicate their approachability (*gamyatva*), not to prescribe the specific time of the period itself; for that would contradict the statement of Manu: "The natural menstrual period of women is traditionally held to be sixteen nights. The meaning is that when the moon is auspicious according to the time, one who is healthy, avoiding the asterisms of Maghā and Mūla while the moon is strong, shall procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks.
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): having avoided the constellations of Pitṛ, Pūṣan, and Nirṛti, a man, being well-pleased, should approach his wife who is likewise well-disposed.
For one desiring a son who approaches a woman who is well-nourished or slender, endowed with auspicious marks, obtains a son possessed of excellent characteristics.
But a fetus conceived by a woman under the asterisms of Pitrya, Pauṣṇa, or Nairṛta does not arise safely, nor is it endowed with virtues.
If a man twenty years of age unites with a woman who is full sixteen years of age, even when her womb is pure and her menses have appeared.

And there should be ten children as the result of their effort; however, if those two [parents] have fewer years [of lifespan], the fetus will be diseased, short-lived, unfortunate, or it may not even come to be.
Regarding travel when multiple pilgrimage sites coincide during the same season, Devala states the following order:
"When pilgrimage sites coincide, one should proceed to them in order, beginning with the Brahmins;
or for the sake of protection, or according to the order of the sequence of invitations, even if a woman without sons is involved."

The "tīrtha" refers to the fertile period (ṛtu). When these periods coincide, she should approach [her husband] according to the order of her caste or the order of marriage; or, if she is childless, first—this is the meaning.
Kaśyapa says:
"But when the fertile periods coincide, she should approach him according to the order of marriage."
"Either for the sake of protection, or for one who is childless, or even according to the order of succession. Thus it is said.
In this context, the "sequence of taking" refers to the sequence of taking [the wife] according to the seasons; and this seasonal approach is mandatory.
Thus says Yama:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present nearby..."
He incurs the terrible sin of killing an embryo; of this there is no doubt.
Parāśara:
He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him goes to a terrible hell; likewise, he is called a "slayer of a Brahmin."
Baudhāyana says: "If a man does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him,
his ancestors lie for that month upon that [neglected] semen."
Likewise: "He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years undoubtedly incurs a fault equal to that of killing a Brahmin."
Devala says:
He who does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him incurs the sin of killing an embryo, for he destroys the attainment of conception.
There is no fault for one who is incapable even when [the wife] is present.
Likewise, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"He who, being healthy, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses..."
He incurs the sin of killing an embryo by destroying offspring that has been obtained.

On this point, some say: "This refers to one who has not yet fathered a son," because the following Vedic revelation—*When a Brāhmaṇa is born, he is born with three debts: through studentship to the sages, through sacrifice to the gods, and through progeny to the ancestors; he alone is free from debt who has a son, who is a sacrificer, or who is a student*—is fulfilled by the procreation of even a single son.
And it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"He should approach his wife during her fertile period until a son is born."
"Is there not also a Vedic injunction prescribing the procreation of other sons, namely, 'Place ten sons in her'?
True; however, if this were an injunction, it would be so, but it is actually intended as a praise of having many offspring.
Others, however, say that this does not refer to one who has no sons at all.
One should desire many sons, so that even one of them might go to Gayā,
or perform the horse sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull.

Because of such statements supporting the practice of having many sons, the meaning of this passage from the *Kūrma Purāṇa* is as follows: one should approach [the wife] only during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) until conception occurs; once conception has occurred, one should not approach her. The signs of conception are shown in the *Suśruta Saṃhitā*:
"In a woman who has just conceived, there is fatigue, lassitude, thirst, throbbing of the thighs, the retention of semen and blood, and a tingling sensation in the vagina."

Approaching women during their fertile period is also mandatory. If a woman who has bathed after her menses does not approach her husband, she shall be proclaimed throughout the village and banished as a destroyer of the embryo.
Likewise, by the phrase "acting according to her desire," it is prescribed that one should approach his wife even outside the fertile period (*ṛtu*), without overriding her wishes; so says Gautama:
"One should approach her during the fertile period, or at all times except for those occasions that are prohibited."
Devala said:
A man should diligently approach his wife during her fertile period;
indeed, that is always desired by women, except on the forbidden lunar days (parvan).
As for the statement of Baudhāyana:

"They say that the fault is equal for those two: he who does not approach his wife during her season, or he who approaches her outside the season, as well as he who discharges seed in a place other than the womb."
This should be understood to apply when women have no desire [for intercourse].

On this point, some say: the word *vā* (or) indicates an option regarding approaching [the wife] during her season; therefore, even one who approaches her, provided he has the capacity to protect his wife, should approach her only during her season. And thus the reason is stated: "Since women are declared to be protected."

That is incorrect; for if there were no approach even when women have the desire, then the rule "one may act according to one's wish" would be contradicted. The word *vā* (or) refers back to the previously mentioned non-approach during the non-season (*anṛtu*). In a case of conflict, the decision is made by the purpose and the force of the reason. This is also understood in this very way by reflecting on the statement, "remembering the boon granted to women. And so it is stated in the Taittirīyaka, concerning Indra and women: [The passage from the Taittirīyaka follows: "Indra said to the women... etc.

They said, "Let us choose a boon: let us obtain offspring in season, and let us unite according to our desire until the time of birth. Therefore, women obtain offspring in season and unite according to their desire until the time of birth, for this was the boon chosen by them.
And so says Vasiṣṭha;
moreover, it is known from the Kāṭhaka texts: "May we, even those about to give birth tomorrow, be united with our husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra.
The specific times for approaching [one's wife] according to the particular seasons are stated in the Āyurveda:
"In the spring, one may do so every two days; at its end, thereafter every fortnight during the onset of the clouds (the rainy season);
and one may indulge in desire as one pleases during both the late autumn and the winter."

In another text, the first half-verse is recited differently as: "In the fortnight, in spring and autumn, in the month, in summer and the rainy season. This arrangement is according to one's capacity (*śakti*).
Thus says Āpastamba.

One who is engaged in the study of the sacred teachings should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn; and this refers specifically to one who has returned home after completing his studies. For this very reason, Śaunaka says:

Having returned home from his studies, he should study according to the rule of a student (*brahmacārin*) in accordance with the law; others say that one who has married should do so, for that [act] is the procreative rite (*prājāpatya*) directed toward offspring.
The word "that" means the procreative rite known as the union with a wife.
This concludes the determination of the time for sexual intercourse.
Now follows the time for the *puṃsavana* rite. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"The *garbhādhāna* [conception] occurs during the fertile period; the *puṃsavana* [rite for ensuring a male child] takes place before the movement of the fetus."
The meaning is that the rite called *puṃsavana* should be performed before the movement of the fetus.
Yama states: "For a woman who has conceived, on the first, second, or third month, on whichever day the moon is joined with a male asterism."
The male asterisms are also shown in the *Ratnakośa*:
[733] "Hasta, Mūla, Śravaṇa, Punarvasu, Mṛgaśiras, and likewise Puṣya—
these lunar mansions are auspicious for undertakings designated as masculine."
The *dhiṣṇyas* are the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). Bṛhaspati.
"The male-making [seed] quivers within the embryo."
Thus ends the time for the *puṃsavana* rite.
Now follows the time for the *anavalobhana* rite. Śaṅkha says:
The consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is proclaimed [to occur] upon the knowledge of the manifestation of the embryo (*garbha*). Viṣṇu says:
"The consecration is the ritual action upon the knowledge of the manifestation of the embryo."
Soma [says]:
"The characteristics of pregnancy are described in the fourth [chapter] of the Āśvalāyana-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa."

In the fourth [month], the *anavalobhana* rite; according to the *Vaijavāpa-gṛhya*: "Then he performs the *puṃsavana* and *anavalobhana* in the second or third month, before the fetus begins to move, during the waxing fortnight, so that the moon may be joined with a male lunar mansion."
Thus ends the section on the time for the non-provocation [of the fetus].
Now follows the time for the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). Regarding this, Laugākṣi says:
In the third month of pregnancy, one should perform the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight, or on a festival day (*parvan*).
Thus says Āpastamba.
The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) takes place during the first pregnancy in the fourth month; according to Vaijavāpa:
"Now, the parting of the hair is performed in the fourth, fifth, or sixth month."
Soma.
The parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) takes place in the sixth [month].
According to the Sāṅkhyāyana Gṛhya-sūtra.
The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) takes place in the seventh month, during the first pregnancy;
Bṛhaspati says it may be in the sixth or eighth month.
Viṣṇu: The parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) takes place in the sixth or eighth month. Śaṅkha and Yājñavalkya [state the same].
The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) takes place in the sixth or eighth month.
Śaunaka says: "In the fourth month of pregnancy, or in the sixth or eighth, during the waxing fortnight, it should be performed when the moon is conjoined with a male lunar mansion."
The male lunar mansions (*puṃnakṣatra*) have been shown in the context of the discussion on the time for the *puṃsavana* rite. Gobhila states:
"Now, the parting of the hair (*sīmantakaraṇa*) takes place during the first pregnancy, in the fourth, sixth, or eighth month."
Śaṅkha: [The rite of] Sīmantonnayana [should be performed] from the time of the first movement of the fetus until the birth. According to the Jyotiḥśāstra:
One should perform the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) in the sixth or even the eighth month,
when the moon is situated in a constellation containing a masculine name and is observed by powerful planets.

In the sixth or eighth month, when Jupiter— the lord of that month— is strong, aspected by benefics, situated in a masculine asterism, and has entered the ninth-part (navāṃśa) of a masculine sign, the parturition-house (narabhavana), the rite of parting the hair (sīmantakarma) for women should be performed,
provided Jupiter, the preceptor of the gods, occupies a quadrant or the eleventh house.
Malefic planets cause strength through the quadrants, trines, the twelfth, the eighth, the outer houses, and the secondary divisions (bahirgarbha).

The meanings of terms such as "nourishing the embryo" (*garbhapuṣṭi*) and so forth have been demonstrated at the time of commencing the construction of a palace and similar works. Furthermore, this *sīmantonnayana* rite should be performed only once if it is regarded as a consecration of the field (*kṣetrasaṃskāra*).
As Hārīta says:
Twice-born women who have not undergone the sacraments should perform them once at each pregnancy by means of the parting of the hair;
whatever child they give birth to, that child shall be considered as having been consecrated.
However, according to the view that it is a rite for the embryo (*garbhasaṃskāra*), it must be repeated with each pregnancy. And so Viṣṇu says:
"The rite of parting the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is not intended as a sacrament for the woman."
Some, for the sake of purifying the womb, employ [the mantra] in every single conception.
Regarding the birth of a child from a woman who has not undergone the *sīmanta* ceremony, Satyavrata says:
"If a woman should somehow give birth while the *sīmanta* has not been performed, she,
having taken hold of her son, deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again according to the rule."
Thus ends the time for the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).
Now follows the time for the birth-rite (*jātakarma*).
And in that regard, Śaṅkha says:
"The birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed when [the child] is born.
Viṣṇu says:
When a son is born, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed; so says Viṣṇu:
"And when he is born, the birth-rite is performed."
Stokaviṣṇu:
"Then one should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman) for the son born, as prescribed. "As prescribed" means as stated in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra; "then" means immediately after the bath.
And likewise Saṃvarta says:
"Upon the birth of a son, a bath with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father. Manu says:
"The birth-rite (jātakarma) for a male child is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord. Here, "cutting of the umbilical cord" means the severing of the navel-string. Thus says Hārīta.
"Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, they perform the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) and acts for the sake of merit (*puṇyārtha*);
once it is cut, there is ritual impurity (*āśauca*). Here, "purificatory rite" refers to the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*), and "acts for the sake of merit" refers to gifts (*dāna*).
Vaijavāpa says:
"The birth-rite (jātakarma) must be performed according to the rules immediately after birth;
if, by chance, it has passed its time, it should be performed once the period of impurity (sūtaka) has elapsed."
And this [rite] should be performed even during a period of impurity (aśauca).
As Prajāpati said:
"When the birth of a son occurs while a period of impurity has arisen..."
The immediate purification of the performer is cleansed by the preceding period of impurity.
In the science of astrology:

during the three auspicious weekdays associated with the soft, fixed, movable, and swift nakṣatras, and when Jupiter or Venus is in a quadrant, the birth-rite (jātakarman) and the naming ceremony (nāma) should be performed.

The "fixed" (*mūḍha*) asterisms are Citrā, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, the three Uttarās, and Rohiṇī. The "movable" (*cara*) ones are Punarvasu, Svātī, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj. The "swift" (*kṣipra*) ones are Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya. "Bhāni" refers to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). The *kendras* have been shown [to be auspicious] at the time of commencing the construction of a temple and other such works.
Thus ends the section on the time for the birth-rite (*jātakarma*). Now follows the time for the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*).
On this point, Pārāśara states:
"Having raised [the child] on the tenth day and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, the father performs the naming ceremony.
[In the] Viṣṇupurāṇa:
Then, on the tenth day, the father himself bestows a name; [the names] Soma and so forth. On the tenth day, the naming ceremony is performed.
Viṣṇu:
[738] The naming ceremony should take place at the end of the period of impurity.
Śaṅkha:
When the period of impurity has passed, the naming ceremony (nāmakarma) is prescribed;
Yājñavalkya and Bṛhaspati state that the name should be given on the eleventh day.
Yama says: "One should perform the naming ceremony on the tenth or the twelfth day,
on an auspicious lunar date, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities."
And here, since the father may for some reason be unfit to perform the naming ceremony, it is ordained that "he should have [it] performed.
For this very reason, Śaṅkha states:
"The father, or another, should perform [the naming] in connection with the family deity and the lunar mansion."
Regarding the term "family elder" (*kulavṛddha*):

if the father is somehow unfit or absent, the family elder may perform [the rite]; however, this does not apply when a fit person is present, as that would entail a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Viṣṇu. On this point, some explain the verb *kārayet* (should cause to be done) as meaning *kuryāt* (should do).

That is incorrect, because there is no reason for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); furthermore, the contradiction with the statement "one should act like a father" is thereby fully resolved, and it is logical that a restriction [of the rule] should arise from metaphorical indication. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O King, some desire the naming ceremony on the tenth day."
On the tenth day, or during the latter part of the night, or when the month is complete,
or likewise on the eleventh day— thus some wise men declare.
In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"The naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) takes place when ten nights have passed from birth, or after a hundred nights, or after a year.

[739] In this matter, the determination is according to one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*; however, for those for whom no specific time is mentioned therein, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*). Among these, even if the earlier time is impossible, the subsequent one should be adopted.

In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): "Or during the rising of these [lunar mansions]— the soft (mṛdu), fixed (dhruva), movable (cara), and swift (kṣipra)— or when Jupiter or Venus is in a quadrant (kendram), the birth-rite (jātakarma) and the naming ceremony (nāma) should be performed."

The asterisms beginning with Mṛdu have been shown for the time of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). The meaning of the term "quadrant" (*kendram*) has been shown for the time of commencing the construction of a palace and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the time for the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Now follows the time for the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*).
In that regard, the Vārāha Purāṇa states:
"On the twelfth day, the child's first exit from the house (niṣkramaṇa) should be performed.
Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:
Thereafter, in the third month, the Niṣkramaṇa ceremony [is performed]; according to Yājñavalkya and Bṛhaspati:
"In the fourth month, the infant's departure from the house should be performed."
In response to the inquiry as to what should be done in that situation, Laugākṣi says:
"On the third half-month, however, there is the sight of the sun.
Yama [says]:
Then, in the third month, the viewing of the Sun should be performed; Viṣṇu says:
"In the fourth month, the viewing of the Āditya."
Śaṅkha:
"In the fourth month, the infant's first viewing of the sun should be performed. Yama: [same].

In the fourth month, the infant’s first viewing of the moon (candrasya darśana) should be performed. In this matter as well, the determination is according to one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. However, for those whose *Gṛhya* does not mention a specific time, any of these times may be adopted optionally. Even in that case, if the preceding time is impossible, the subsequent time is to be taken.
Thus concludes the time for the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*).
Now follows the time for the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*).
Regarding this, Viṣṇu, Soma, Śaṅkha, Bṛhaspati, and Yājñavalkya state:
"The first feeding of solid food should take place in the sixth month, or at whatever auspicious time is desired by the family."
Yama says: Then, in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) should be performed according to the prescribed rule;
or it may be performed in the eighth month, or whenever an auspicious occasion is desired by the family.
Laukāxi says: The first feeding with solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place in the sixth month, or when teeth have appeared, or when a full year has passed; some say in the half-year.
Here too, as in the case of the naming ceremony, the specific arrangement should be understood according to one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Thus end the times for the first feeding of solid food.
Now follows the time for piercing the ears.
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): "They commend the piercing of the ears in the months of Kārttika, Pauṣa, Caitra, or Phālguna, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day."
Under a male asterism, when the moon is auspicious, during a period of happiness, or even at the time of a head-ascendant;
avoiding the "day-defects" (dinacchidra), Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and Vaidhṛti;
for an infant whose teeth have not yet emerged, while crawling upon his mother’s lap.
"The piercer should pierce the ears with a needle and a double-thread. Thus [it is said].
And under the asterisms of Hasta, Aśvinī, Svātī, Punarvasu, Tiṣya, Indu, Citrā, Hari, and Revatī...
When the moon is favorable, on a Thursday or Friday,
the ears should be pierced during a lagna presided over by Indra or the Lord of the Immortals.
Bṛhaspati is "not to be reviled.
Likewise, [it is auspicious] under Puṣya, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and Maitra.
If the moon moves from the asterism Pauṣṇa (Revatī) during the month of Pauṣa, the year, the month, or on a Sunday,
the waters dry up due to drought; yet they become free from disease, and the child is never at all afflicted.
On a Sunday, there is rapid drying; on a Monday, moisture arises in the ears;
on a Saturday, there is separation from kinsmen; and on the sixth [tithi] of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the ear-lobes split.
Thus ends the time for ear-piercing.
Now follows the time for the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma). Regarding that, [the text says]: "The tonsure ceremony takes place in the first year."
Viṣṇu: The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is to be performed in the third year. Laugākṣi: [Thus it is stated].
When the greater part of the third year has passed, one should have the *cūḍā* ceremony performed.
Bṛhaspati says:
"The *cūḍākarma* [should take place] when he is three years old."
Vaijavāpa:
The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed in the third year. Pāraskara: [same].
The tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) takes place in the third year, or at any time other than the prohibited periods. Manu says: "The tonsure rite for all twice-born classes is prescribed by dharma."
It should be performed in the first or the third year, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
In the Sāṅkhyāyana Gṛhya-sūtra:
"The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) takes place after one year or in the third year. Yama states:
Then, when one year has passed, the rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma) is prescribed;
it should be performed in the second or third year, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
"The rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma) takes place in the third year, or even in the fifth.
Śaṅkha and Yājñavalkya: [same].
The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) is according to family custom; as stated in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra:
"In the third year, the tonsure is performed, or according to the family tradition."
Laukāxi: "The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight or on a festival day.
[Vaijavāpa-gṛhya]
The tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) takes place during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day;
according to the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya*:
"During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, [one performs] the tonsure ceremony."
Āpastamba says: "The *caula* ceremony, from birth until the third year, should take place under the asterism Punarvasu. Vyāsa says:

One should perform [the rite] under the asterisms of Āśvinī, Śravaṇā, Svātī, Citrā, Puṣya, Punarvasu, Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Hasta; likewise during auspicious conjunctions of weekdays and asterisms, and under favorable Karaṇas.
The three Hastas, Mṛgaśiras, the three Śravaṇas,
Puṣya, Aśvinī, Svātī,
and Punarvasu are auspicious for shaving and for the commencement of new undertakings.
And if the auspicious stars are conjoined with the lord of the lunar mansions (the Moon).
All specific details regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) remain as follows.
And so it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"By the command of the king and with the consent of the Brahmins..."
At the time of the release from a fast, at the initiation for a sacrifice,
at the time of marriage, and during the birth or death impurity— on all these occasions, the performance of shaving is recommended.
"In those" [is said] with reference to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Thus ends the time for the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*); now follows the forbidden times for the rite of tonsure.
Vyāsa says: One should not perform [the rite] under the lunar mansion in which a man was born;
nor should it be done under the two Proṣṭhapadas, nor under those belonging to Agni, O Bhārata.
And among all harsh things, one should avoid harshness toward those who are wicked.
One should avoid the days of Saturn, the Sun, and Mars, as well as the night; one should also avoid the first lunar day (pratipad), the "empty" days (riktās), and the Viṣṭi yoga.
Thus concludes the prohibited times for the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*).
Now follows the time for the commencement of learning (*vidyārambha*). On this point, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
When the fifth year has arrived while Janārdana is not asleep,
one should avoid the sixth and the first lunar days, as well as the eighth,
the empty (riktā) dates, the fifteenth, and likewise the days of Saturn and Mars.
When the time has been thus well determined, one should cause the commencement of learning to take place.
Having worshipped Hari, the goddess Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as the authors of the sūtras of one's own branch of knowledge and that very branch of knowledge itself in particular;
From that time forward, one should avoid those occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) that ought to be avoided:
both the eighth days of the lunar fortnights, as well as the three days at the end of each fortnight.
"In cases of impurity, during a festival of the senses, during an earthquake, upon seeing the king,
and likewise when a meteor falls, [the period of impurity lasts] for one day and night once that time has passed.
Thus ends the section on the time for beginning formal study.
Now follows the time for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
On this point, Laugākṣi says:
"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa is in the seventh year, [and] in the ninth..."
For a Kṣatriya it is in the eleventh year, and for a Vaiśya [in the twelfth].
Baudhāyana says: the years are counted from conception; one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from that, a Kṣatriya in the year after that, and a Vaiśya in the year after that.
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth. Paiṭhīnasi: [same as above].

One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the fifth year from conception, or in the eighth; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception, or in the twelfth; and a Vaiśya in the sixteenth year from conception, or in the twelfth. Devala states:
"First consecrated by his mother and father through the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, he becomes fit for initiation (*upanayana*) in the eighth year from conception."
Manu and Śaṅkha state:
"They perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya it is in the eleventh, and for a Vaiśya it is traditionally prescribed in the twelfth."
Viṣṇu: One should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
that of a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception; and that of a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception.
Viśvāmitra and Yājñavalkya:

"The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth]; for Kṣatriyas in the eleventh year plus one; for Vaiśyas, some say in the twelfth; or according to family custom."

The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be performed in the eighth year from conception, or from birth, with one added—that is, in the eleventh or twelfth [year]. However, some teachers hold the view that the initiation should be performed according to family custom;
others, however, explain it thus: some maintain that the arrangement regarding the eighth year from conception and so forth is determined by the established tradition of the family.
On this point, some say that by the word *upanāyana* here, the act of initiation (*upanayana*) itself is denoted.
That is incorrect, because the word *upanāyana* denotes the activity of the agent directed toward the object of initiation, and there is no reason for a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) [to be invoked].
For this very reason, the wise one said:

In the eighth year from conception, a Brāhmaṇa should have himself initiated in the spring; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year in the summer; and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year during the rainy season. From that initiation, the rite of *upanayana* is also prescribed. Bṛhaspati says:
"In the eighth year from conception for a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise in the eleventh for a Kṣatriya..."
For a Vaiśya, the investiture with the girdle of muñja grass should be performed in the twelfth year.
Regarding the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
For the twice-born, the seasons are spring, summer, and autumn;
these are the seasons in their respective order for the social classes.
— Āpastamba.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn;
likewise, the five months beginning with Māgha are to be accepted for initiation.
And so it is stated in the Jyotiḥśāstra:
"The *mauñjī* [initiation] is recommended during five months beginning with Māgha;
this applies equally to all three castes, which is not correct. Regarding that very point:
"Spring is the auspicious season for the first-born [castes]."
For kings, the summer season is auspicious; for vaiśyas, the autumn;
and for the initiation into all vows, the five months beginning with Māgha are prescribed.
And this refers to the period of the fertile season (*ṛtu*) for all castes (*varṇa*),
since it is stated in the *Ratnakośa*:
"O son, if [the union] is according to a specific month, for one who is the eldest of all..."
For a Brahmin who has been initiated, both dullness of intellect and death [result from such conduct].

It has been stated in the *Dharmabhāṣya* that for those belonging to the Yajurvedic schools, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) may take place at any time, yet the specific mention of "spring" is for the purpose of restriction;
namely, during the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, or the spring season.
And so says the Śruti:
"Madhu and Mādhava are the two spring seasons; when [the sun is] in Pisces and Aries, it is spring."

And so it is stated in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*): "From the Sun's transit through two zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn, there are six seasons: the cool season (*śiśira*), spring (*vasanta*)," and so forth.
Likewise, summer, the rainy season, and autumn;
here, the sixth is called by the name of winter.
‘Mṛga’ refers to the crocodile. Baudhāyana says:
the spring consists of Pisces and Aries, or alternatively, Aries and Taurus.
Gautama states the time for the optional initiation (*kāmyopanayana*):
"The optional [initiation] occurs in the ninth or fifth year, counting from conception;
this refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas."
As Aṅgiras said: "The tying of the Muñja-grass girdle should be performed in the fifth year for a twice-born man desiring spiritual luster, and in the ninth year for one desiring long life."
Manu states that for a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), the initiation should take place in the fifth year.
Regarding the optional time for the initiation of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, Aṅgiras says:
Likewise, for a king, [the increase of] power and lifespan occurs in the sixth and twelfth [houses];
for a Vaiśya, however, it occurs in the eighth and fourteenth [houses].
‘Īhā’ refers to exertion directed toward activities such as agriculture. Here, the sequence should be observed according to the first half-verse.
Thus Manu says:
“For a king seeking military power, [the tax is] one-sixth; for a Vaiśya seeking livelihood, it is one-eighth.”

Āpastamba: Now follow the optional rites: in the seventh year [one should initiate] one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); in the eighth, one desiring long life; in the ninth, one desiring splendor (*tejas*); in the tenth, one desiring food; in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power (*indriya*); and in the twelfth, one desiring cattle.
And this applies equally to the three social classes (*varṇa*), because it is stated in the commentary on that [text] that this rule is prescribed immediately after his initiation (*upanayana*).

That is incorrect, because it contradicts the statements of Atri and Aṅgiras previously cited, such as "for one desiring spiritual luster" (*brahmavarcasakāmasya*). Therefore, it should be understood that here the first two injunctions concern non-Brāhmaṇas, while the subsequent four injunctions apply to all three castes, as there is no sublation [of them].
In the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "In the three asterisms beginning with Hasta, and in Puṣya and Dhaniṣṭhā..."

The initiation into vows and the release from them for the twice-born should be performed under the asterisms of Puṣya, Aśvinī, Soma (Mṛgaśiras), Aditi (Punarvasu), and Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), on an auspicious lunar day endowed with the strength of the moon.
The son of Bhṛgu (Venus), the son of the Earth (Mars), and the son of the Moon (Mercury)—
these are, respectively, the presiding deities of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas.

If the lord of the branch (the planet ruling the *dvādaśāṃśa*) is strong and situated in a quadrant (*kendram*), the investiture with the sacred thread (*mauñjī-bandha*) should be performed on its day for the attainment of happiness; however,
if it is devoid of strength, [it should be done] on the day of the twice-born (the *tithi* ruled by that planet).
The wise declare that there would thus be a confusion of castes.
The term *kendra* has been explained in the determination of the commencement time for the construction of a temple.

At a distance of three cubits, on an auspicious lunar day, the investiture with the sacred thread (*mauñjībandha*) for the twice-born should take place by virtue of the strength of the zodiacal sign; however, if it occurs in the sign of Love (*smara*, i.e., the seventh house), the rite becomes fruitless.
If it occurs in signs presided over by malefic or dull planets, one becomes sinful and afflicted by the disease of pulmonary consumption (*pāṇḍuyakṣmā*).
The fool [suffers] during the periods of Venus and the other planets as they successively rise.
One who performs the six rites, possesses excellent intellect, and is honored by the king of the gods will be initiated and very happy and wealthy if Venus is [the lord] of the fifth house.
If Mercury is so, he will be a teacher; if Saturn, he will be a servant of the lowest castes.
When the moon, the source of light for those who live under the king, is situated in Cancer.
If the marriage ceremony of the son of the Earth is performed under Kaṇṭakasthāyin, one who lives by weapons and missiles becomes skilled in the livelihood of a Vaiśya.
When Jupiter is situated in a quadrant and Venus is in the ninth or fifth house,
and the Moon is in a Navamsha occupied by Venus, every man shall become a knower of all branches of knowledge.
If the Moon is in its own sign, one becomes ungrateful; if it is in the sixth house, one becomes a direct traitor to one's guru;
if it is in the eighth house, the seeker of knowledge, though endowed with good character, will be lifeless.
If Jupiter is with Saturn, one is devoid of virtues and destitute of wealth;
if with Mars, he is cruel; and if with Mercury, he is base. With the son of the Sun (Saturn), there will be no luster.
May Chukreṇḍu always be like Saumya to me.

In the *Ratnakośa*: "Even when the moon has waned, Venus has set, and the sun is without its digits, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) should be performed; it should not be avoided during periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*) or when the planets are in conjunction (*galagraha*)."
The Sun situated in the first portion of a zodiac sign is "without degrees" (niraṃśa).
The four Trayodaśīs, as well as the three beginning with the seventh [tithi],
and Kākinī in the fourth [tithi]— these eight are declared to be the *galagrahas* (throat-seizers).
Thus [conclude] the times for the initiation (*upanayana*) that are prescribed and prohibited.
Now, the secondary times (*gauṇakāla*) for initiation. Regarding this, Manu says:
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
The prefix *ā* here signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*).
Vyāsa says:
"The period for initiation (*upanayana*) extends up to the sixteenth year."
Another [series] has twenty-two [syllables] as its maximum; the next [series] has twenty-four as its maximum.
The *Avantimihira* also states:

"In the case of the *chandas*, just as with words and syllables, so too is the aggregate [the unit]; the initiation (*upanayana*) for a Brāhmaṇa is by means of the *gāyatrī*. Since there are eight syllables in one foot of that [meter], the initiation occurs when the aggregate of sixteen years is complete. And this is appropriate in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). Regarding the fall from caste (*pātitya*) that results from its transgression, Yama says:"
Those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī are outcasts (vrātyas) and must be avoided with great effort.
Yājñavalkya says: Up until the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth year [respectively for the three classes].
The time for the initiation ceremony for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is later than this.
From this point forward, these people, excluded from all religious duties,
fallen from the Sāvitrī, and become Vrātyas, may be purified in due order by means of the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"For a Brāhmaṇa, the time [for initiation] does not expire until the sixteenth year; for a Rājanya, until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth. Beyond these limits, they fall—so says the Śruti. By the successive transgression of these subsequent periods, they become fallen Vrātyas. Thus says Śaṅkha.
Sixteen years for a Brāhmaṇa, twenty-two for a Kṣatriya,
and twenty-four for a Vaiśya are proclaimed as the periods for the Sāvitrī; beyond this, she does not wait, for after this time she turns away.
All three of these should be understood as being, at the appropriate time, unrefined;
they have fallen from the Sāvitrī, are outcasts, and are excluded from all religious duties.
Gautama says: For a Brāhmaṇa, there is no lapse until the sixteenth year; for a Kṣatriya, until the twenty-second;
and for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth.
Baudhāyana says that there is no transgression [of the time for initiation] until the sixteenth, the twenty-second, or the twenty-fourth year. Paiṭhīnasi says the same.
Twenty-two, sixteen, and twenty-four—these are the past contradictory times.
The period of division for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas has been explained. Yama says:
Likewise, for a Brāhmaṇa who has not disciplined his self, the Sāvitrī does not expire until the sixteenth year; beyond that, it is forfeited.

The *triṣṭubh* metre of the Kṣatriya ceases at the twenty-second year. Beyond this, if these three [classes] remain uninitiated according to the proper time, they become fallen from the *sāvitrī*, known as *vrātyas*, and are censured by the Āryas.

Thus ends the secondary periods for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Now follows the determination of the occasions when study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*). Regarding that, Likhita states the fault incurred by studying on such forbidden days:
These days proclaimed as unfit for study are the vulnerabilities of Brahmins;
through these vulnerabilities, the sacred knowledge (brahman) that has been acquired by a Brahmin leaks away.
At that time, the Rākṣasas take away his prosperity, sacred knowledge, fame, and strength—
taking all of these— and depart, leaving behind only the fruit he desires.
Śaṅkha says:
Whatever beings, such as men and others, reside within the cavities,
they, remaining there, destroy that Brahman of a Brāhmaṇa of small intellect.
At that time, the Rākṣasas take away his prosperity, Vedic knowledge, fame, and strength— everything— from those who study during forbidden times.
Hārīta says:
These gaps of the Brahmins which are proclaimed as times unfit for study—Rākṣasas cause harm during them; therefore, one should avoid them.
Viṣṇu:

Because the mere study of the Veda on a day unfit for study does not yield its fruit, and because through such study on an unfit day there is a depletion of the lifespan of both teacher and pupil, one should therefore avoid days unfit for study. [Thus it is said] in the dialogue between Indra and Nārada.
O Śakra, why will you not slay those Asuras— those evil-minded ones who study on forbidden days, who are killers of Brahmins and defilers of the Veda?
Those who study during forbidden times do not attain their own Vedic merit;
when dead, they do not go to heaven—O Nārada, are they not destroyed?
Yama says: The wise declare that the days on which study is forbidden are the vulnerabilities of the twice-born;
through these vulnerabilities, the sacred knowledge (brahman) that has been acquired by a Brahmin flows away.
"Longevity, progeny, cattle, wisdom, and both the performed and the unperformed [merit]—
by practicing [study] during times unfit for study, one likewise destroys the Veda."
Likewise: "When one studies during forbidden times, Yama himself cuts short one's wisdom, lifespan, progeny, women, sacred knowledge, vigor, fortune, and splendor."
Out of fear that the power of his mantra might be exhausted, Indra strikes with his thunderbolt;
he then becomes a brahmarākṣasa and shall not attain human status again.
I cut short his life; I take away his progeny and his intelligence—those who speak while impure from remnants of food, or even those who recite their Vedic studies.
The eighth day destroys the teacher, the fourteenth destroys the pupil, and the fifteenth destroys intelligence; therefore, one should avoid these sacred festival days (parvan).
For all branches of knowledge reside in Prajāpati, who is present in the parvan days;
therefore, one should not recite these [Vedas] on the parvan days for the sake of dharma, artha, or kāma.
Manu says: "The new moon day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the eighth day and the full moon day destroy the Veda; therefore, one should avoid them."

Gautama says: On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), there is a suspension of study for a full day and night, or for two days; when there are two new moons [in a month], then there is a suspension of study for two days.
Hārīta says: On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the fourteenth, on the eighth, on the two festival days (the new and full moon),
during the periods of non-study, and on the night of the new moon, one should not study under any circumstances.
And in another *Smṛti*:

"If there is a non-study day tomorrow, then there is non-study during the night; however, when two non-study days occur together, there is no non-study in the latter part of the night. Some say that after a pair of non-study days, there is non-study on the night following the first day of that pair. Thus says Pāraskara.
Regarding the statement "on the new moon day during a windstorm," Yājñavalkya states that this applies to all periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*) for both day and night:
"On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, the eighth, and during the birth of Rāhu."
Or having eaten during the junctions of the seasons, or having accepted food offered at a Śrāddha ceremony.
‘During the Rāhusūta’ means during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
In this case, there is an option between a three-night period, the time before noon, or a single day and night. [756] Manu says:
Having accepted an invitation for an Ekoddiṣṭa rite,
a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, except during the period of impurity caused by Rāhu (an eclipse).
As long as the fragrance and the unguent remain on the body of a learned Brahmin at the conclusion of an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, so long one should not recite the Veda.

There is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for as long as the fragrance of incense, sandalwood, and the like persists. "Invitation" (*ketana*) means an invitation; "for one person" (*ekoddiṣṭa*) refers to a rite performed for a single deceased individual. [Regarding this] Śaṅkha says: Upon the death of a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), a king, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), or a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*); during an eclipse of the moon or sun by Rāhu; upon the falling of Indra’s banner; and upon the death of one's own teacher (*ācārya*), there is a three-night suspension of study.

Gautama says: In the case of untimely thunder, earthquakes, eclipses, and the falling of meteors, as well as during the junctions of the seasons, and for three days when the sun sets while being eclipsed, they declare that there shall be no study.
Regarding "junctions of the seasons," this refers to the first lunar days (*pratipad*) at the transitions between the seasons, such as spring and so forth.
And so, in the Rāmāyaṇa, Hanumān’s words to Rāma:
"She, slender-limbed by nature, is further emaciated by separation from you;
she has become thin like the knowledge of one who studies poorly on the first day of the lunar fortnight."
Ślokagautama says: One should not study during the evening twilight on the thirteenth day, nor on the first days of the lunar fortnights,
nor on the new moon day, nor on the Aṣṭakās, nor on the anniversary of a death, nor during either of the two twilights.
If [the rite is performed] on the new moon day or the first day of the lunar fortnight, the knowledge quickly perishes.
The junction of two years is called *ābdika*; having accepted food offered at that time, there is a suspension of study for a day and night—this is the meaning.
And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"Fruits, water, sesame seeds, edible foods, and whatever else may be part of a śrāddha..."
Even after accepting [food], there is no suspension of study; for Brahmins are said to have their hands as their mouths.
And this refers to cases other than the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, because in that case, a three-night period is prescribed by the previously cited statement of Anu. Gautama states:

"For those who perform the *śrāddha*, for those who eat it, and for those who receive it, [the impurity is] *akālika*; and when there is a connection with a *śrāddha* where cooked food has not been prepared, [it is likewise]. Therefore, there is an option between *akālika* and a full day and night (*ahorātra*).
In another Smṛti: "But upon eating at a *navaśrāddha*, [the impurity lasts] until the food has been digested. Manu says:
Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha, upon touching that there shall be no study; for the twice-born are said to have their hands as their mouths.
Ātāpa says: On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, on the Aṣṭakās, during a great festival,
at nightfall, on the thirteenth day, the eighth day, and also on the first day [of the lunar fortnight].
From the Purāṇa:
One desiring intelligence should never recollect or recite [the name] on the thirteenth, the fourth, or the seventh lunar day, nor during the evening twilight.
Prajāpati says:
One should not study during the sixth and twelfth lunar days, nor during the last few nāḍīs of midnight; nor during the evening twilight, nor for nine nāḍīs on the third lunar day.

The meaning is "not at the hour of midnight. It should be understood that [the time] is nine *nāḍikās* during the night. "At dusk" (*pradoṣe*) means during the first watch of the night. Gautama states:
"During the night, for four *muhūrtas*."
And this refers to the thirteenth lunar day; for thus says Uśanas: "One should not study the first four quarters on the thirteenth [lunar day]."
The skillful one should spend the last two watches of the night devoted to the study of the Vedas;
by sleeping for only two watches, he is fit for becoming Brahman.

Āpastamba states: "Having commenced the term of study on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the evening for one month. Also: "That which lasts for three muhūrtas at either sunrise or sunset..."
"Those who know the rules regarding the suspension of study (anadhyāya) understand that such a day and night is split.
This refers to the case of equality [of lunar days].
"Whether it be one muhūrta at the end of the day, or a lunar day that is subject to decrease..."
For that lunar day which increases by more than three muhūrtas, the asterism should be accepted in the same manner as the lunar day; however, it is the opposite at sunrise.
Because of this statement, some say: "In a certain region, as long as the pierced nāḍīs persist, for that long alone there is no study; it does not apply on the intervening days of the mixture."
They likewise declare the lunar days for the vows of fasting and other observances;
[specifically] when [the moon] is seen within nine nāḍīs before midnight on the fourth day.
One should not study during the first part of the night on the seventh or thirteenth lunar days;
however, if these days fall after midnight, one may study during the first part of the night.
Śaṅkha, following the phrase "one should not study," states:
"On the eighth day, at nightfall. Paiṭhīnasi says the same.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and on all eighth days, there is no study during the night, except for the *aṣṭakā* festivals. According to the *Purāṇa*:
"The *mahānavamī*, the twelfth day, and the seventh day of the month of Māgha..."
O Kṛṣṇa, by reciting it in that manner, one will certainly destroy ignorance.
From the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:
"On the Mahānavamī, on the twelfth lunar day, on the Bharaṇī asterism,
and likewise on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, a wise man should not teach his disciple."
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, known as Rathasaptamī, one should avoid [certain activities].
The *Mahānavamī* is [the ninth day] of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja; the *Mahādvādaśī* is [the twelfth day] of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika. In another Smṛti:

there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) during the asterisms Maghā and Bharaṇī in the month of Bhādrapada, as well as during Śravaṇā; on the eleventh and twelfth days [of the dark fortnights]; on the second days preceding the full moons of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Phālguna; at the end of the dark fortnight; and likewise on the second day [of the dark fortnight].
Gautama states that one should not study during the *anvṛtti* (the period following the full moon).
This refers to the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha;

the meaning is that the period begins from these full moons and lasts for three nights. By the word *aṣṭakā*, the three-night period beginning with the seventh lunar day—which constitutes the constituent part of the *aṣṭakā* rite—is indicated.
Regarding this, they say that the *aṣṭakā* ending with *maghā* is specifically a cause for the suspension of Vedic study. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"The three *aṣṭakās* occurring in the dark fortnights beginning with the month of Prauṣṭhapada [Bhādrapada], and those beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, according to some."
Śaunaka, however, says: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. Manu [says the same].
On the *aṣṭakā* days, on the nights at the end of the seasons, and according to the *Nāradīya*:
"At the solstices, at the equinoxes, and during the sleeping and waking of Hari."
However, one must observe a suspension of study on the anniversaries of Manu and other progenitors, as well as on the beginnings of the Yugas.

Manu and others, as well as the beginnings of the Yugas, have been shown in that determination. One should observe a suspension of study for two nights during the day [at the solstice], and two days during the night [at the equinox]; this applies until the lunar day (tithi) with its secondary name (sopapada) has passed.
Likewise: the second lunar day of Jyeṣṭha when it is bright (the waxing fortnight), the tenth of Āśvina when it is bright,
and the fourth and twelfth of Māgha— these are remembered as *sopapada* (with secondary designations).
Yājñavalkya, continuing from the phrase "for three days," states:
"At the Upākarma and at the Utsarga, and when a Śrotriya of one's own Vedic branch has died. Thus it is said in another Smṛti.

Upon the completion of the Veda, there is no study for that day and night during the first twilight, but during the second and subsequent twilights, [there is no study] for a full day and night. Upon the commencement of a *kāṇḍa* by one who has lost his mother, or upon the completion of a *kāṇḍa* by one who has lost his father, and in the case of deities of human nature, there is non-study for a single day due to the consumption of *yajus*—that is, with rice grains that have been kept overnight or until they have fully ripened—and likewise when one performs the commencement or completion of a *kāṇḍa* using the roots and fruits of herbs and trees, he shall not study on that day; so too at the commencement and completion of the formal opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*).
— Manu.

"Having thus performed the formal dismissal of the Vedic texts outside [the village] according to the scriptures, one should cease [recitation] for a night with its two flanking days (pakṣiṇī), or else for a single day and night.
Regarding both the Upākarma and the Utsarga, a three-night suspension is prescribed. Thus it is said.
A night that has dawn on both sides is called *pakṣiṇī*; the determination of these fortnights is according to one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Manu says:
"In the case of lightning, thunder, and rain, as well as when there is a downpour of great heat..."
Manu has declared that there is no interruption of study on these occasions; it is timeless.

The meaning is that for each of these, such as lightning and so forth, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) from the time the omen occurs until the same time on the following day. Among these three—lightning and the others—there is a suspension of study during the twilight hours, except during the rainy season.
As he himself says:
"One should know these [omens] to have occurred when the sacred fires have been made manifest."
Then one should consider it a time unfit for study, as well as during the non-seasonal appearance of clouds.
"Prāduṣkaraṇa" means making manifest; by this, it is not characterized by the time of twilight.
Gautama states that [the impurity lasts] until the same time [on the following day] when thunder, rain, lightning, and meteors appear while the fires have been made manifest.
The suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasts for the entire duration [of the event].
As Āpastamba says:
"In the case of a meteor and a fire-omen, the suspension of all branches of knowledge lasts for the entire duration."
Manu says:
When a village is harassed by thieves, during a panic caused by fire,
and during all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study for the duration of the event.
Regarding "in portents," such as rains of blood;
as Vasiṣṭha says:
"In the case of the burning, sweating, breaking, or collapsing of the quarters and mountains, and in the falling of stones, blood, and dust."
"It is immediate. This refers to cases of heavy dust. The statement of Yājñavalkya, which establishes the suspension of study for that specific time, refers to cases of light dust. In another Smṛti:
In the event of a fire-omen or untimely rain, there is a suspension of study for that entire day.

Śaṅkha states: In cases of a thunderclap, an earthquake, the fall of a meteor, a conflagration of the quarters, or the raining down of dust, blood, flesh, bones, raw meat, parched grain, or gold; and upon seeing an auspicious rite performed, or upon smelling anointed oil, hearing a cry of distress, vomiting, exhaustion, or witnessing a bad dream; and during the periods of impurity following an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a birth, or a death—one should perform the initial expiation, offer the *brāhmaṇa-gamana-iṣṭi* and other sacrifices, and having obtained permission, they may then resume their studies.
However, when there is the simultaneous occurrence of the triad beginning with lightning, there is a three-day suspension of study.
And likewise, Gautama states, following the recurring phrase "for three nights":
"In the case of the conjunction of rain, lightning, and thunder."

This applies except during the rainy season. As Āpastamba says: "When lightning, thunder, and rain occur together outside the rainy season, there is a suspension of study for three days; according to some, as long as the ground remains wet. For one or two of these occurring, the suspension lasts until the time [the next day].
On this point, Bharadvāja also says:
When there is a fire-omen or a rain of dust, there shall be a suspension of Vedic study in the village;
however, when there is lightning accompanied by thunder, the suspension lasts for three nights, even if it occurs during the rainy season.
Paiṭhīnasi:

Having eaten on the eleventh day [of the funeral rites], upon seeing a rainbow at night, from the falling of a thunderbolt, from the death of a teacher, from an eclipse of the sun or moon, and upon the appearance of a comet, a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an inundation—one must not study for three nights in each of these cases. Also when a Śrotriya has died, when the twilight has set, when hail falls, and when something blue or red appears [in the sky].
But when there is lightning and thunder during the twilight in the rainy season, then the suspension of study lasts as long as the light remains.

And so Manu says: "But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be a suspension of study for as long as the light remains; in other cases, it is as during the night [that it is forbidden] by day."

If an omen arises during the morning twilight (*prātaḥsandhyā*), there is no study as long as there is light—that is, until the sun appears; the meaning is that this applies only during the day. In the case of the evening twilight (*aparā*), however, it lasts only as long as the stars are visible. Regarding "the remainder," namely rain: the meaning is that just as there is no study during the day, so too at night. Hārīta states a specific rule regarding thunder: if there is thunder during the evening twilight, they should not study during the night; but if there is thunder during the morning twilight, they should not study for a full day and night.

Āpastamba says: At the junction [of day and night], when there is thunder with heavy clouds, until the end of sleep; during lightning at dawn, for as long as a black or red cloud moves within the range of a *śamyā*-throw; one should know that during this time, while lightning is flashing, the entire day including the evening is unfit for study (*anadhyāya*); or, according to some, from the latter part of the day until midnight due to thunder; and also when cattle are being penned.

"At the junction" (*saṃdhau*) means at the time characterized by the junction of day and night; "during the thundering of clouds" (*ghanastanite*) means during the roar of the rain-clouds. One should not study for the remainder of the night, "until the end of sleep" (*svapnaparyantam*), meaning until one wakes up on the following day. "At dawn" (*uṣasi*) means during the last watch of the night. "When lightning flashes" (*vidyotamānāyām vidyuti*): or rather, when a cow standing in a space measured by a *śamyā* (the distance of a throw of a spear) moves about, whether it be black or red, then that day, including the evening, is a period of non-study; the meaning is that the day, together with the evening, is a time of non-study due to the cause of thundering in the latter part of the day.

Regarding thunderclaps and similar phenomena during the rainy season, Manu has declared that the suspension of study is to last until the same time the next day; for he says: "In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries, one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study lasting until the same time [the following day], even during the proper season."
"Nirghāta" is a specific kind of atmospheric sound; "the eclipsing of the luminaries" refers to a halo around the sun and moon, or the conflict of planets and so forth. Yājñavalkya states:
"During the twilight, thundering, a nirghāta, an earthquake, or the falling of a meteor..."
Having completed the Veda and having studied the Āraṇyaka day and night, [he should perform the final bath].
‘Day and night’ (adyuniśam) means a full day and night. Consequently, there is an option here between the [one-day] period and the day-and-night period. As for the statement of Manu:
“And when the banner of Indra falls, and likewise when a meteor falls...”
"There is a three-night suspension of study during an earthquake, and likewise in such cases.

This should be understood to apply when a meteor and lightning occur together; there is a three-night suspension when a meteor and lightning coincide, [and also] when the wind is audible at night or when dust is stirred up by day.
Those who know the rules of study declare these two to be occasions when study must be suspended.
Since hearing is impossible without the ear, it is "excellence" (atiśaya) that is intended here; alternatively, there is the reading "divā vātasamūhane. [This is from] Yājñavalkya:
"There is a suspension of study for three days upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative."

In this context, "guru" refers to the teacher (ācārya) and not the primary [spiritual preceptor], because a ten-day period is prescribed for that [latter]. Regarding the statement, "They say the impurity lasts three nights when the teacher has passed away," the term "relatives" (bandhu) here should be understood as those who are non-sapiṇḍas, since a ten-day period is prescribed specifically for sapiṇḍas.
Vasiṣṭha has prescribed a period of one day and night for students, officiating priests, and others:

"For the son of a teacher, a student, and a wife, as well as for officiating priests and those not related by birth, the period is one day and night. "Not related by birth" refers to maternal uncles and the like.
Gobhila, continuing from the context of "day and night" (*ahorātra*), states:

"When a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) has died, or when a king has died. In another *Smṛti*, it is stated that there is impurity for a day and night following the carrying out of a corpse, attending to one, or upon seeing the corpse of a *cakora* bird.
Yama says: Not during thunder, nor when the sun has set, nor likewise during crackling sounds; not during an eclipse of the moon or sun, nor likewise during a royal calamity.
And likewise when one who shares the same sacred knowledge has died, as well as a fellow student of the Veda.
Gautama has stated that there shall be no study when dogs and other such animals enter among those who are studying.

Furthermore, if a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat enters between [the teacher and student], there must be a formal re-entry (*upasadana*); for a Brahmin, there is a three-day fast, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*), while for others, it is the same as for studying in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). Moreover, whenever anyone else enters between them, a formal re-entry (*upasadana*) must be performed.

The "approaching" (*upasādana*)—that which is prescribed daily by the rule beginning with "having clasped hand with hand"—must be performed again; furthermore, if a dog or similar animal enters between them, both the student and the teacher must observe a three-day fast, and even if they reside together, it is likewise for three nights.
Thus says Hārīta:

"In the case of the continuous presence of a dog, jackal, cat, snake, mongoose, or mouse, if these enter between those who are studying, there shall be a three-night fast and one should remain secluded for three days."
Because it has been stated thus, there is a three-day suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). Regarding the purpose of fasting for three days, Vasiṣṭha says:

"In the case of cats, mongooses, and tigers, however, there is a fast of one day and night. Here, "fasting" refers to the subject at hand; if one passes between cats, one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and fast for three days.
Āpastamba states that there is a suspension of study for six months in the event of sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste;
the rule "there is a suspension of study for six months" applies to the Caṇḍāla, the Śvapāka, and the Śaśa.
He further states that if an elephant or a tiger passes between [the teacher and student], there is a suspension of study for one year.
If an elephant, a year, or likewise a tiger [is encountered],
Yājñavalkya states that there is no study for a day and night due to the passing of such animals and others:
"By a cow, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a rat..."
During the Kṛta age, however, a day and night [of Brahmā] lasts as long as the fall and the rise of Śakra.
The time for the raising of the banner of Śakra has been shown previously as being in the month of Bhādrapada,
O King; it is the ancient tradition that the setting up of Śakra’s staff occurs in the month of Bhādrapada.
That which is known as "arousing" is called a non-study period.
Manu says:
"If one passes between [the teacher and pupil) with a domestic animal, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat, one should know that there is no study for a day and a night."
But others say:

If a crow, owl, cock, mouse, frog, or similar creature passes between [the teacher and pupil], there is a suspension of study for two days; if it occurs at the end of the day, it lasts until the end of the night, and if at night, until the end of the following night. In the case of a Śūdra, a mouse, a snake, a mongoose, and the like, the suspension lasts for one day and night, as does that for a dog or a cat. However, during the first lesson, if a dog, mongoose, snake, frog, or cat passes between them, there must be a three-day fast and a stay away from home for the Brāhmaṇa. For wild cats, snakes, mongooses, and the five types of animals beginning with the jackal, the suspension lasts for three nights. For donkeys, boars, camels, and the like, for Caṇḍālas and others, for women in childbirth or menstruating, and during festivals, the suspension lasts for a month. For elephants, gavayas, goats, and the like, for tigers, atheists, and so forth, the suspension lasts for three months. The sight of an elephant, a rhinoceros, a crane, a lion, a tiger, a great sinner, or an ungrateful person constitutes a suspension of study. Furthermore, while the recitation of the Veda is in progress, if someone passes between the teacher and the pupil, it brings mental anguish, disease, death, obstacles, and sin upon both.
In another Smṛti:
"In the presence of all foul odors, in a ditch, in assembly halls,
during anointing, at the time of bathing, on a great altar, and during a violent earthquake."
In all kingdoms, during the obstruction of cows or Brahmins, and within the rows of those performing ancestral rites (śrāddha),
as well as in the shade of the śālmali, madhūka, kovidāra, kapittha, and śleṣmātaka trees, these are known to cause immediate impurity.

Yājñavalkya: [One should not study] when there is the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, or the *sāman* chant, nor during cries of distress; nor near impure substances, a corpse, a Śūdra, an outcaste (*antyaja*), a cremation ground, or a fallen person.
In a place that is not pure, or when one is impure oneself; during lightning, thunder, or rain;
after eating while the hands are still wet; inside water; at midnight; or during a violent wind—one should not study.
During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mists,
while running, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at the house.
When there is the sound of asses, camels, vehicles, elephants, horses, or boats, or when trees are growing on barren ground—
these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interdictions for study.

When the sound of dogs and the like is heard, there is a suspension of study for that duration; "kroṣṭā" refers to a jackal. However, when the sound of the *Sāman* is heard, there is a suspension of study for the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* Vedas.
As Yama says:
"By the sound of the *Sāman*, the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* [are suspended], as well as when the wind blows strongly."
Manu also says:
"One should never recite the Ṛgveda or Yajurveda while the sound of the Sāmaveda is being heard.
He states the reason for this:
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
