Aṅgiras said: Since the constant worship of the deities of the cremation grounds is performed with the Sāmaveda, therefore its sound is impure.
This is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
As that very same [author] said:
"Because sound is formless, it does not exist here as a primary object."
Therefore, this has been stated as a mere introductory cause by way of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), serving only as a basis for the prohibition.
Thus, there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) when the sound of the *Ṛg* and other Vedas is heard;
and likewise says Āpastamba:
Furthermore, there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) when the sound of other Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*) or of *Sāman* chants is heard.
"Lute" (*vāṇa*) refers to a specific type of lute. "Afflicted" (*ārta*) means one who is suffering.
Manu also [states this].
"In mist and in the sound of arrows, and also during both twilights.
Regarding "in mist," it means in fog.
[This is from] Gautama.
In the sounds of arrows, kettledrums, clay drums, and *gardā* carts— *gardā* meaning a cart— there is a suspension of study.
Regarding the continuation of these occasions for non-study, Baudhāyana states:

[770] For as long as there is the sound of dancing, singing, instrumental music, or weeping, and likewise during distress, so says Gobhila: "Or rather, during those [sounds], for the duration of each respective [sound]."
Āpastamba:

During the sounds of dogs and donkeys, the cries of hyenas, crows, and owls, the sounds of loud musical instruments, and the sounds of weeping, singing, and Sāman chants—during these, there is a suspension of study for that duration.
"In the vicinity" (*antike*) means near impure things and the like; "the lowest castes" (*antyāḥ*) refers to those inferior to Śūdras.
Viṣṇu also says:

"Neither near a Śūdra nor a fallen person (patita), nor in a temple, a cremation ground, or at a crossroads; nor with feet struck by a seat, nor without having sipped water (ācamana), nor while lacking self-restraint, nor when food is undigested.
Pracetās says:
One should not study at crossroads, on highways, on bridges, or in gardens, nor in the presence of a deity.
Manu says: "One should not study near a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen."
Having stayed overnight, having engaged in sexual intercourse, and having accepted clothing offered by a person performing a funeral rite;
"Antaḥ" means near; "maithunaṃ vāsaḥ" means having put on that garment with which sexual intercourse was performed—this refers to the case of an unwashed garment.
For this very reason, Yama says:
"Whenever sexual intercourse has been performed while even the garment remains unwashed..."

Vasiṣṭha: When one has vomited in a bed free from sexual intercourse, using a garment free from sexual intercourse that has not been washed, there is a suspension of study for a day and a night in the interior of a village. For one day and night following the completion of the *vedasamāpti* (Vedic study) for all [the Vedas], as well as after a *śrāddha*, and during meals at a *manuṣyayajña* (a feast for guests).

"Agni-utpāta" refers to the consecrated fire (*upāhita*); a "human sacrifice" (*manuṣyayajña*) is a meal provided by a village for the sake of a journey or similar purpose. Some say that for one day and night following a meal where humans and others are fed, the period lasts until the end of sleep. Or, having consumed clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one may study; thus says Āpastamba.
Having vomited at the end of the dream, or having consumed clarified butter; "at the end of the dreams" means until their cessation— so says Manu.
For those who desire proficiency in Dharma, there should be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, and everywhere where there are foul odors.
Those who have already acquired knowledge desire proficiency in the Dharma, while others desire proficiency in the sciences; for them, even study in a village is prohibited.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"In a city, however, one may study at will, provided it has been sprinkled with cow dung or has been smeared [with clay]."
For this very reason, Manu said: "There is no study in a village where a corpse is present, nor in the proximity of a *vṛṣala*, nor while one is weeping, nor in a gathering of people."

The term *vṛṣala* here refers to one who is unrighteous (*adhārmika*), because the study [of the Veda] is prohibited by that very same [authority] in the presence of a Śūdra, as in the rule: "not in the vicinity of a Śūdra person. Vasiṣṭha also states: "[Vedic recitation is forbidden] during the twilights, in a state of impurity, and in the presence of a Divākīrti."
The meaning is that one should not study "divākīrtya" texts in a village of Caṇḍālas.
Gautama says: according to some, this applies constantly in a city.
Pracetas says: One should not study at crossroads, on great highways, in royal gardens, or in the presence of a deity. Gautama says: [the same].
Regarding the impurities of cremation grounds, villages, and highways, Āpastamba states a specific rule concerning cremation grounds:

"In a cremation ground, there is no study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from all sides; nor is there non-study in a field or area inhabited by a village, provided that [the cremation ground] itself is not known to be present. One should not study in that very place where it is known to exist. Some say that a *śūdra* and an outcast (*patita*) are like a cremation ground if they share the same house. However, in the case of a *śūdra* woman, there is non-study only during mutual gazing. Likewise, there is non-study when another woman of a different caste is engaged in sexual intercourse, or when there is a simultaneous occurrence of lightning, a pillar of light, and thunder."
One should never study while standing near a tree, nor at a sacred bathing place, nor in water, nor on boats, nor in assembly halls, nor in the midst of a great crowd.
Śaṅkha says: One should not study even when intent on it while riding in a vehicle, nor while mounted on a cow,
nor in the vicinity of a temple, an anthill, a cremation ground, or a forest.
Manu says: One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant;
nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor while using a girdle-band (avasakthikā);
nor after eating meat, nor after consuming food from a house where birth or death impurity (sūtaka) has occurred.
[773] Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor during a birth-impurity.
‘Īriṇa’ means saline soil. ‘Prauḍhapādaḥ’ refers to sitting with the knees bound by a cloth or similar object between the thighs. ‘Bhuktamātre’ means as long as the hands are still moist from eating.

Regarding water, however, the prohibition against reciting for the sake of dharma does not apply; rather, it applies to the acquisition of new knowledge. Some hold that these [rules] are for the sake of showing respect, and that mental recitation is permitted during other times of non-study (anadhyāya). Others, however, maintain that mental recitation is always intended. Thus says Baudhāyana:

And in other cases of miraculous portents or calamities, there is a suspension of study, except for that which is mental. "Mental" refers to the suspension of study during [the news of] a death in a secluded place. Manu says:
One should avoid voiding excrement or urine in water or at midnight; while impure from food remnants or after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony, one should not even contemplate such acts in one's mind.
Gautama: After eating at a festival, and after the commencement of study at a festival, there is a suspension of study for one day and night from the time of the initiation ceremony onwards;
"after eating" means for one who has begun his studies, there is a suspension as previously stated even when it is not a festival.
In another Smṛti:

there is no study in a beautiful house or on an auspicious day; nor is there study during marriages, the tying of the sacred girdle (*mauñjībandhana*), consecrations, or the concluding rites of festivals (*udyāpana*); nor is there study for those who have performed the purification (*mārjana*) or sweeping (*saṃmārṣṭi*) among sapindas and those of the same lineage (*sagotra*). Furthermore, during a sacrifice, there is no study for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the teachers (*ācārya*) as long as the ritual continues.

Manu says: A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a rain of dust, when there is a conflagration of the quarters, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, or camels are barking, nor while in a row.
Yama says:
Having heard the cry of a jackal at either twilight, the best of the twice-born should not [study] at afternoon,
nor at midday, nor ever at midnight.
Furthermore, when a learned person (śiṣṭa) has come to one's house, the suspension of study lasts until he grants permission.
Likewise, Yama says:
"Upon seeing a guest who has arrived, a wise man should certainly not study."
Once he has granted permission, one should study with diligent effort.
Manu says:
[The time for study is suspended] when one has not taken leave of a guest, while the wind blows violently,
when blood flows from the body, or when one is wounded by a weapon.

Upon the arrival of Brahmins, having offered the *arghya* and other honors and having obtained their permission, they may study. Āpastamba says: "One who is studying the Veda should not converse with one wearing soiled clothes; even if he meets him, he should continue his study."

One should converse with those worthy of conversation; having conversed, a Brahmin should not study until he has again conversed. Likewise, one desiring to learn from a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), whether already studying or wishing to begin, should study or teach only after having obtained permission. Or, in the presence of his teacher, when told "Recite, sir," he may recite or teach. In both cases, for one desiring to learn, there must be a formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) before studying, or while others are studying. Where another person passes by, one should continue reciting only after letting out that same sound.
Similarly, Gautama states that there is no study even at times other than the forbidden seasons (*anṛtu*) when clouds are visible.
Regarding the phrase "and when clouds are seen during the rainless season": "cloud" (*abhra*) refers to a water-bearing mass, a rain-cloud; [this is] Yama.
One should never study under the shade of the Śleṣmātaka, the Śālmali, the Madhuka, the Kovidāra, or the Kapittha trees.
As for that which was stated by Manu: "A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study: an impure place for Vedic recitation and himself when he is impure."
That refers to the subject of studying for the *brahmayajña*.
And so, with reference to the *brahmayajña*, the Taittirīyakas record:
"Of this very *brahmayajña*, there are two occasions when study is suspended: when one is personally impure, and when the place is [impure]."
For this very reason, Manu also says:
"Regarding the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, in the daily private recitation,
and indeed in the sacrificial formulas for the burnt oblation, there is no restriction concerning days unfit for study."

The "accessories of the Veda" are the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*); "constant private recitation" (*nityasvādhyāya*) refers to that which is connected with the *brahmayajña*. The mention of "sacrificial mantras" (*homamantra*) is also an elliptical indication for the mantras used in the *baliharaṇa* sacrifice and others. "In daily rites there is no suspension of study; that is remembered as the *brahmasatra*. It is a meritorious offering to Brahman, performed even during times when study is forbidden, consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call."
Or rather, the suspension of study is for the purpose of grasping what is not previously known, but it does not apply to the ritual act itself.
Prayogaśaunaka also says:

"In the case of obligatory recitation, optional recitation, a ritual sacrifice, or even the complete study of a Veda, there shall never be a suspension of study; this is the rule remembered regarding the occurrence of an eclipse."
From the Purāṇa:
A student performing his studies should avoid days unfit for study;
likewise, one who performs teaching should also avoid days unfit for study.
Manu says: One who is studying should always avoid these occasions of non-study,
as should one who is teaching students according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, one should always [recite] the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, and the Śiras during obligatory rites, occasional rites, vows, sacrifices, and ritual offerings.

Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that there are no days unfit for study when the performance of rites for one's desires is prepared; likewise, it is traditionally taught that there is no day unfit for study regarding the mantras used for the worship of deities.
Likewise: "On the fourteenth, the eighth, the festival days, and the first day of the lunar fortnight,
there is always a suspension of study for those of dull intellect, as well as during journeys."
In that regard, for those whose character is forgetful, even though they have recited many Vedic texts.
And on days other than the fourteenth, the eighth, the festival days, and the first day of the lunar fortnight,
one should study the Vedāṅgas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras.
Gautama:

As they prescribe for each specific branch of knowledge (*vidyā*), so too there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the *Chandoga*s at a crossroads after a meal; likewise, prior to eating, one should recite those texts to be studied in the forest (*araṇyageya*).
Āpastamba: [777]
As it has been stated even in other assemblies (*pariṣat*):

thus [ends the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign over all the faculties of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya, and is proficient in all branches of knowledge.
In the section on Supplements (*pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), within the determination of time (*kālanirṇaya*), is the determination of the times for non-study (*anadhyāyakālanirṇaya*).
[778] Now follows the time for the *keśānta* rite.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"And the Keśānta [ceremony] is in the sixteenth year.
"Keśānta" refers to the rite known as Godāna; and this pertains to the Brāhmaṇa class.
As Manu said: "The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, two years beyond that."

In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), those very lunar mansions (bhāni) which have been prescribed for the tonsure ceremony (kṣaura) are likewise recommended for the tonsure of the top-knot (cūḍākaraṇa), the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana), the parting of the hair (godāna), and the final shaving (keśānta).
Thus concludes the time for the ceremony of tonsure (*keśāntakarman*).
Now follows the rule regarding the duration of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
On this matter, Āpastamba says:

For one who has approached the teacher’s family, the residence as a *brahmacārin* lasts forty-eight years—whether reduced by a quarter, by a half, or by three [quarters]. Twelve years is the minimum; there is no reduction below twelve for a *brahmacārin*. "Reduced by three quarters" means twelve years minus a quarter, i.e., nine years; this refers to the case of one who is incapable [of the full term]. As Devala says:
Beyond this, one should observe the practice of Vedic vows for forty-eight years; if incapable, for thirty-six years, or twenty-four years. This applies to each individual Veda. As Yama says:
He should dwell for twelve years, or indeed twenty-four,
or thirty-six years, performing the vow for each Veda.

Baudhāyana also says: "One should practice Vedic studentship for forty-eight years; or twenty-four, twelve, or six years for each Veda; or even for half a year, because life is unstable from the moment of conception; or until one's hair turns black, according to the Śruti: 'One should establish the sacred fires while his hair is still black. Paiṭhīnasi says:
One should practice the student's life (brahmacarya) for twelve years for each Veda, or twelve years for all of them together, or until they have been mastered;
so say Śaṅkha and Likhita.
One should practice the life of a student (brahmacarya) for twelve years for each Veda, or until one has mastered it; thus says Manu.
The vow of the Traividya student consists of practicing the conduct toward the teacher for thirty-six years;
or half of that, or a quarter, or even until the time of initiation.

The meaning of this is as follows: "Traividyā" refers to the subject matter of the three Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman; it is stated that this [period of] thirty-six years must indeed be observed, meaning twelve years of *brahmacarya* for each Veda. According to the half-year option, there are six years per Veda; however, according to the quarter-year option, there are only three. Yājñavalkya states:
"The period of *brahmacarya* for each Veda is twelve years or five."
"Until the time of grasping," say some.
Thus ends the determination of the period of celibacy.
Now follows the time for the return home (*samāvartana*). Regarding this, Dakṣa says: "When he has mastered the Veda and undertaken the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*),"
One should be a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) after having performed the ritual bath (snāta), and thereafter one should become a householder (gṛhī).
The "acquisition of the Veda" (*vedasvīkaraṇa*) is also an elliptical expression for the investigation of the meaning of the Veda (*vedārthavicāra*).
Thus, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Having studied the Veda and having understood the meanings pertaining to the meters, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)."
And so Vyāsa says:
"One should not cause the teacher to be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Veda;
for one who rests content with the mere recitation sinks like a cow in the mud."
Just as a beast that carries a burden does not obtain its fruit,
so a twice-born man who does not understand its meaning does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda.
All study of the Veda and of the Dharmaśāstra that is undertaken by one who does not understand their meaning is like the threshing of husks.
That Brahmin who, having studied, does not reflect upon the meaning of the Veda,
is equal to a beast along with his lineage and does not attain the status of a worthy recipient.
Having studied even a little, one who is intent on comprehending the meaning of the Vedas attains the world of Brahman through the perfection of the practice of Brahman;
though he may lack wealth and be deficient in sacred learning, whatever merit he gains here shall also accrue to him in the hereafter.
Likewise: Knowledge and action, when joined with faith as they are conceived,
and study joined with what has been heard— these are superior, whereas that which is solitary is not.

A wise person should not honor— even with mere words— those twice-born who are constantly devoted only to the recitation of texts and devoid of the true meaning, treating them as if they were mere cattle.
Having studied even a single quarter-verse of the Rigveda and having understood its meaning through right reasoning within,
and having properly observed the vows, one is worthy of the return ceremony (samāvartana).
This refers to the case where one is capable [of performing both], because the rule for bathing is prescribed even upon the completion of each [vow] individually.
Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"There are three types of *snātaka*s: the *vidyā-snātaka* (one who has bathed after completing his studies) and the *vrata-snātaka* (one who has bathed after completing his vows)."
And the *vidyāvratasnātaka*.

He who, having completed the Veda but not having completed the vows, performs the return ceremony (*samāvartana*), is a *vidyāsnātaka*; he who, however, having completed the vows but not having completed the Veda, is a *vratasnātaka*; and he who has completed both is a *vidyāvratasnātaka*. — Yājñavalkya.
Having given a gift to the teacher, he should bathe with his permission;
or, having brought the Veda, the vows, or both to completion.

According to some, one should follow the *Āpastamba-dharma-sūtra*. Likewise, according to others, one should do so by means of the vow (*vrata*) consisting of forty-eight parts, as well as the vow of sacred knowledge (*vidyā-vrata*). Having understood that which follows the kindling of the fires (*ādhāna*), one should perform this vow for a year—consisting of bathing three times a day in water, not eating food cooked with fire, and remaining apart from women and those who have reached the stage of a forest-dweller (*yogastha*)—for they declare that this is commensurate with the forty-eight [parts]. Vyāsa says:
"Having duly obtained sacred knowledge through service to the teacher, the twice-born..."
Having given him a cow as a sacrificial fee, he should bathe with his permission.

Gautama says: "At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with a gift; for one who has received permission, there is the ceremonial bath. This means that at the end of his studies, the teacher is to be "invited" by means of a gift—that is, he should be asked, "What gift should be given to you? Having been thus questioned, whatever the teacher may say, that gift should be given to the preceptor, and then one should bathe; or, in the event of inability, one may do so with his permission—this is the meaning.
The wise one, too, should bathe when permitted by his teacher. Thus ends the section on the time for the return ceremony (samāvartana).

Now follows the determination of the sequence of the stages of life (*āśrama*). Regarding this, there is both a combination and an option among the four stages of life. With reference to their combination, Manu says:
"The student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and likewise the ascetic (*yati*)."
These four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these, when practiced in succession according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
"Dependent on householders" means those who subsist upon them. "In due order" implies that the reverse order is forbidden.
Thus Dakṣa says:
"For the three [higher castes], there is the natural order (ānulomya), but the reverse order (prātilomya) does not exist."
There is no greater evildoer than he who proceeds in the reverse order.
He who, having entered the householder stage of life, becomes again a celibate student—
neither an ascetic nor a forest-dweller, yet having abandoned all [other] stages of life.

Therefore, even though that man whose wife has died may lack the capacity for remarriage, he must not become a lifelong celibate (*brahmacārin*); in this context, the terms *brahmacārin* and *gṛhāśrama* are intended to demonstrate that those in each subsequent stage of life (*āśrama*) do not abandon the preceding stages. Otherwise, the inclusion of the rule "there is no [return] in the reverse order" would be meaningless. As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and likewise the ascetic (*yati*)."
The stages of life (āśramas) have been declared in their proper sequence; otherwise, it would be for a specific reason.
Having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), one should not enter a home again;
nor should a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) dwell in the forest, nor a seeker (sādhaka) [abandon] the life of celibate discipline (brahmacarya).
From the Purāṇa:
"O son, as a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant, remain vigilant; do not follow a wrong path as a twice-born man."
Āpastamba states:

"There are four stages of life (āśramas): the householder's life, residence in the teacher's family, renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and the forest-dweller's life. One who conducts oneself without distraction in all of these according to the instruction attains the [highest] stage of life.
By the phrase "conducting oneself in all of these," the practice of their combination (samuccaya) is indicated.

The Jābāla-śruti also states that there is a combination of four, three, or two [stages]: "Having completed the stage of the student (brahmacarya), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Or otherwise, one may renounce directly from the stage of the student, or from the home, or from the forest. Regarding the requirement for specific times in the case of such a combination, Manu says:
Having lived for the fourth part of his life under his own guru, the twice-born man,
having taken a wife, should dwell in his house during the second part of his life.
Having thus spent the third part of his life wandering in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.

"A man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years"—thus it is stated in the Śruti; a fourth part of that lifespan is twenty-five years. Gautama, however, states an alternative: "Some declare that there is an option regarding his [the student's] stage of life."
But this alternative applies to cases other than those concerning the stages of life (*āśrama*) and the practice of vows (*vrata*). Vasiṣṭha says:

"There are four stages of life: the student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Having studied the Veda—or the Vedas—without violating the vow of celibacy (*aviśīrṇabrahmacarya*), one may enter whichever of these one desires."

Intending that there may be an abundance of fruit, one should study either one Veda or two Vedas; having studied the Veda, one who has maintained his student-life (*brahmacarya*) without breaking its rules may "enter" whichever of those stages of life (*āśrama*) he desires—that is, he should take refuge in it and reach firm completion therein.
As stated in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "O King, if one desires the householder's state (*gārhasthya*), he should take a wife."
Or he should spend his time in celibacy (brahmacarya), preceded by a formal resolve.
Or he may become a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), or a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) according to his wish;
having given a boon to the guru and being permitted by the guru,
that best of the twice-born should bathe and then either dwell at home, in the forest, or go forth into homelessness.
Uśanas says:
Having been authorized by his teacher, he should duly observe one of the four stages of life until the liberation of the body.
And this alternative is to be understood as applying to those who do not practice the stages of life in combination.
Thus concludes the determination of the stages of life and their timing. Now follows the alternative regarding marriage.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
Having studied the Vedas according to the rule and returned home after completing his vows without bathing [in the river],
he should marry a wife of equal status who possesses fame, good character, youth, and virtues.
Having studied the Vedas— either all four, two, or even one— in the proper sequence,
and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.
Or, having obtained the permission of his teacher and having given him the teacher’s fee, he should,
remaining obedient to the will of his mother and father, take a wife suitable to himself.
Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas according to the prescribed rule,
and having remained firm in his vow of celibacy, he shall take a wife in accordance with the Dharma.
In this regard, Śaṅkha and Likhita state immediately after the section on lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika):

"Then, having been permitted [by his parents], he should perform the initiation (upanayana) with the muñja grass and so forth, and marry a woman of the same caste through a Brāhma or other form of marriage."
Dakṣa says:
When he accepts the Vedas and observes the Vedic vows, he is a *brahmacārī*; thereafter, having performed the ceremonial bath (*snāta*), he becomes a householder (*gṛhī*).

Having bathed and married in whatever manner, a twice-born man who has not studied the Vedas should study the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs in the house of his teacher through the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
When the year is even, he should bestow it [upon his wife], for it always provides knowledge, dharma, desire, and long life.
In an odd year, a daughter will undoubtedly become dear to her husband.
A maiden married in the month of Māgha shall be endowed with good fortune;
one married in Phālguna shall be a virtuous wife; and one married in Vaiśākha shall have sons.
In the month presided over by Jupiter (Mārgaśīrṣa), she shall be endowed with righteousness; in Kārttika, she shall become wealthy;
and in the month whose deity is the Moon (Māgha), she shall be constantly devoted to the worship of the gods.
If she should undergo marriage during any other months besides those previously mentioned,
that maiden would be devoid of sons, good character, and wealth.
In the bright fortnight, she illuminates her family with glory;
but if she is married off on the first day of the dark fortnight, it is a sign of total ruin.
Likewise,
Vasiṣṭha says: "They praise the bright fortnight, and especially the northern course [of the sun]."
The marriage of a Brāhmaṇa should take place during the waxing fortnight;
however, for the other castes, it is prescribed during the waning fortnight.
Vyāsa says:
On the Ugra, Asana, Ugra, and Riktā lunar days, she remains uncrushed; on the remaining days, she is unfortunate, whereas on the others she is endowed with sons and good fortune.
Likewise:
affection cultivated at dawn brings good fortune, yet the depletion of wealth;
happiness and its objects involve many obstacles, while the fame of virtuous conduct brings true bliss.
Grief and disease, joy and happiness, fortune, and even one's children and so forth—these are the afflictions; yet on the bright fortnight, the first lunar day and the others yield full results.
Likewise:
A maiden who is married on the days of Jupiter, Venus, the Moon,
or Mercury will always be compliant with the mind of her husband.
On the days of the Sun, its son (Saturn), and Mars, she is fond of quarreling;
on the day of the Moon, however, she experiences rivalry with a co-wife.
When a benefic planet has entered the eighth house division (aṣṭavarga) and reached an unfavorable position,
then on that day marriage is not recommended.
Whatever good or evil fruit has been declared for a planet on its [natal] day,
one should indicate all of that in its corresponding hour as well.
Some say that [the practice] is auspicious when performed under the birth stars; others say it yields results by avoiding the second star from one's birth asterism.
Whatever result is associated with the day of the Sun and other planets,
that same result occurs when they are situated in the ascendant, in their respective decans (vargas), and especially in their respective hours (horās).
The great seers declare that on days other than those beginning with Sunday, the planet [presiding over] the season and the solstice is its presiding deity.
Whatever fruit has been declared here regarding the seizing of these [planets] during the day,
that shall always be entirely complete for months, seasons, solstices, and years.
There are five lines extending horizontally and five extending upwards, with two lines each at the corners;
having laid out the lunar mansions there in a clockwise direction starting from the line of the Śaṅku, [one should proceed].
If, at that time, a planet situated in a single zodiac sign pierces with its rays a lunar mansion such as Kṛttikā and so forth,
it will be inauspicious for a marriage.
Likewise:
those belonging to Mitra, Pitṛs, Viśvedevas, Brahmā, Nirṛti, and the deities;
or also those of Ahirbudhnya, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, and the Moon.

Likewise: In the first quarter of Maghā, in the very first [quarter] of the Nakṣatra situated in the southwest (Nairṛta), and in the remaining six quarters of the other Nakṣatras, [the rite] is not recommended.
A marriage in the fourth quarter of the Revatī asterism leads to the destruction of life;
however, the taking of the hand (marriage) is always desired during the last three [asterisms] beginning with Svāti.
Likewise:
Hastottarā, Vāyavya, Maitra, Mūla, and Revatī; Rohiṇī, Saumya, and Maitra are always auspicious for taking the hand in marriage.

One should carefully avoid the equinoxes (viṣuvat), as well as the vyatīpāta yoga and the solstices (ayana); one should also avoid a lunar mansion defiled by portents, and especially the vaidhṛti yoga.
Vātsyāyana says: One should also specify the Muhūrtas conjoined with the wind [Muhūrta] of Sāvitrī;
one should predict the results as being equal to those of the constellations that share the same deity.
The astrologer [should determine] the auspicious day among the muhūrtas, excluding Abhijit;
for that moment of the eighth part of the day is designated as Abhijit.
That boon granted by Brahmā is eternal and auspicious at all times;
through its grasp and through compassion and other virtues, one is indeed not bound by those sins.
Likewise,
the taking of the hand of young maidens performed even during the asterisms, deities, and auspicious moments pertaining to marriage bestows the fruits of one's desired goals.
Widowhood from the Sun, the Lord of Day; loss of offspring from the Moon, the Son of the Earth;

loss of wealth from Jupiter, the Preceptor of the Gods; likewise, servitude and misery from Venus, the Delighter of the Bhṛgus; renunciation from Mercury; and even praise followed by abandonment from Saturn, O Purandara.
For women, the state of being a courtesan is the mark of darkness; for Ketu, it is death resulting from the stroke of fate.
In the *Sārāvalī*:
"Even if all [planets] are favorable, yet the Moon and Sun are not purified by their *gocara* positions,
then even if she is married to the husband of Śakra or of Kubera, she will be unchaste."
When Jupiter has entered the sign of the Sun, or when the Sun has entered the sign of Jupiter,
one should avoid all ritual acts, as well as vows and rites for prosperity.
One should not perform a marriage when Jupiter is in the eighth house from the birth sign,
nor likewise when Saturn is situated in the birth sign;
nor should one do so when the Moon is in the eighth house.
If the Sun is diligently placed in the eighth house from the Varā.
If two eclipses occur within a period of seven nights starting from the first eclipse,
a wise person should not even mentally contemplate the timing of a journey or a marriage.
One should never perform the initiation of vows for the twice-born, nor marriage with beautiful women,
when the preceptor has set, nor likewise when Venus has set.
[790] Even marriage, the sages such as Kāśyapa and others do not desire;
some wise men desire it in Caitra just as they do in Pauṣa,
and likewise Bādarāyaṇa [desires it] when Jupiter is situated in Leo during a marriage.
Vasiṣṭha says:
At a marriage, at the initiation of vows, on a journey, or during the performance of a vow,
one may marry a girl born when Jupiter (Guru) or Indra (Śakra) has set.
If Jupiter is combust, he destroys the husband; if Venus is combust, he destroys the bride.
If the Moon is combust, it destroys both; therefore, one should avoid those two [planets] during a marriage ceremony.
If the moon rises after sunset, it is unfavorable for ten days until the end of the day; however, if it rises before sunset, it is unfavorable for a fortnight.
If the moon is waxing, it is unfavorable for five days before the end of the day, and for five days after the end of the day if it is waning.
The mind goes to destruction during the northern course, while strength and majesty prevail during the southern course.
[Thus says] Varāha: first, the local customs of the region must be considered.
In every land, one should act according to the local custom;
for in the world, the wise avoid what is corrupt.
Therefore, an astrologer should proceed according to the ways of the world.
The Southerners indeed desire marriage when Jupiter is situated in a favorable transit;
the Gaudas, however, say it is so when the Sun is in a favorable position.
The measure [of the distance] to Mālavaka is not within range.
The Gaudas say that the strength of the Sun is essential; the Southerners, the strength of Jupiter;
the Maṇavas desire the Ascendant; and for the Lāṭhas, the "snānajambala" (the power of the bath).
The people of Magadha rely on the strength of Tārā; the Mādreyas perform rites by the power of Tārā and the Moon;
likewise, those closely associated with Aukula rely on the North Star.
In Māṇḍavya, Tittira, and Tuṣāraka.
The numerous auspicious and inauspicious conjunctions of planets and lunar mansions, as well as those of lunar days and weekdays, which have been described,
produce their stated results in Vaṅga.
They are not to be contemplated in other regions.
In the *Sārāvalī*: "If the Sun is in the sixth or eighth house from the ascendant, and the *muhūrta* is also favorable,"
The *godhūlikā* [time], when joined with the strength of the sun, moon, and stars, is the bestower of all fruits.
When there is no purity of the ascendant (lagna), yet youth is highly commended,
then for all castes, the time known as *godhūlika* is prescribed.
If neither the zodiacal sign is known nor is there certainty regarding the ascendant,
then whatever has the Sun as its strongest factor in the ascendant is praised in every respect.
The Sun is known to possess one power; Mars is remembered as having two powers;
Mercury is known to have three powers; and Jupiter has fourfold power.
Venus is to be known as possessing five strengths, and the Moon is said to possess six strengths;
likewise, the Sun is always equal to all the planets.
During journeys, at the time of marriage, and in various undertakings,
where there is no strength of the Sun, there is no strength at all from any other source.
The sun is remembered as the source of men, and the moon, whose radiance is like nectar, is the source of women;
therefore, the strength of both men and women is derived from the sun and the moon.
Where both the moon and the stars— these two most powerful bodies—
are present, there all defects dissolve, even if they should flow from every direction.
When Venus and the Moon have vanished and Jupiter has set,
one should perform neither marriage, nor journey, nor indeed any act of giving.
If Jupiter attains marriage in the twelfth, second, fourth, eleventh, sixth, eighth, or third house from birth,
she incurs widowhood.
If Jupiter is in Siṃha (Leo), which has Bhaga as its presiding deity, a woman will have sons;
she will be exceedingly fortunate, virtuous, and beloved by her husband, and possessed of wealth and grain.

Vātsyāyana says: In the marriage ceremony, those who know the reality of things should apply the eleven categories [of analysis] to the lunar day, the lunar mansion, the moment, the *karaṇa*, the ascendant, the moon, the sun, the ascendant, and the lunar asterism.
The great sages, such as Māṇḍavya and others, do not approve of the marriage ceremony when the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is asleep, nor when he has departed after his cry has been uttered.
When Jupiter is situated in Leo, during an intercalary month,
and likewise in the month of Jyeṣṭha— for the son as well as for the daughter—
one should not perform [the rite] when the Sun and Jupiter are in their signs of debilitation or when they occupy the ascendant.
And may all auspicious things pertaining to birth also be present.
If joined with the Sun and the Moon, a woman shall attain widowhood;
if with Mars, she is carried off by thieves; and during the bright fortnight, she may commit evil deeds.
O gentle one, when one is under the influence of Ketu's appearance, she becomes skilled in secrets, shameless, and fond of sexual pleasure; she will quickly go to another husband.
If Jupiter and the Moon should occupy the seventh house endowed with strength, one obtains wealth, good fortune, and sons; of this there is no doubt.
Adorned with jewels, pearls, corals, and beautiful golden ornaments,
she shines when permitted by her elders and looked upon by those who are disciplined.
But she who is always dear to her husband when Mercury or the Moon is in the seventh house from the Sun,
will experience widowhood and even great poverty through that Sun.
When the Moon and Mars are visible, one should not undertake a journey;
if they are aspected by Saturn, the woman will be barren or her children will die.
Vasiṣṭha says: Death, violent rashness, intense suffering, servitude, and even immorality—
these the planets may bring about during a lunar conjunction, provided the Sun and Venus are not detached [from their positions].
The planets joined with Mercury and Jupiter produce, respectively, for the native and for the maker [of the horoscope], skill, honor in one's family, unchastity, and indeed disease.
Furthermore, when conjoined with two, three, or four malefic planets,
it certainly brings about either poverty or death for the daughter.
A woman adorned with excellent red ochre goes to the edge of the earth,
or she may go to a foreign land, provided that the Moon is joined with the benefic planets.
Among the ascendants, Gemini is the best, followed by Virgo and then Libra;
likewise, Aries as an ascendant at the time of marriage is considered fruitless.
In other signs, such as Gemini, Taurus, and the rest, the wise should take two, four, and so forth, degrees;
however, in Gemini, Virgo, and Libra, there is neither one's own degree nor another's degree.
The six auspicious groups of planets are friends when aspected by benefics from the ascendant,
or when they are so situated at the time of marriage, entry [into a house], or other auspicious rites.
When Venus and Jupiter are in conjunction, she makes a Brahmin her paramour;
when Jupiter and the Sun are in conjunction, she makes one who has bathed after a vow her husband.
When there is a conjunction of Deveśa and Saumya, a maiden, having abandoned her kinsmen as well as her husband, becomes a thief and a paramour; of this there is no doubt.

If the degrees of the ascendant are not seen at the time of marriage due to their own disappearance, then there will be the destruction of the man; if it is likewise so for these degrees, then there will be the destruction of the woman.
In the tenth and third, the ninth and fifth, and the fourth and eighth houses, the wife [is situated];
and thus they yield their results by increasing in degrees.
Vyāsa says: Of those twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries which were previously mentioned by me, Virgo, Libra, and Gemini are observed [to be favorable].
In the ascendants of Virgo, Libra, and Aries, [the full result does not occur] in the final degree;
therefore, listen as I describe the complete result for each degree.
Among them, she whose mind is fixed on another youth while her own husband is still alive—
One born in the portion of Vṛṣabha is virtuous and endowed with good character.
In the portion of Cancer, she will be a courtesan; likewise, in the remainder of that period, she will be fierce. In the portion of Leo, she is praised for being devoted to her father's house.
A girl born in the portion of Kanyā will be endowed with beauty, virtue, and good qualities;
one born in the portion of Tulā will be burdened by debt, ill-behaved, and defiled by impurity.
If she is born in the final degree of Scorpio, she will be a courtesan and highly irascible;
in the fourth group (of signs), she will be unchaste in the degrees of Capricorn, Aquarius, or Aries.
Through great prosperity, she will become attached to another man; there is no doubt regarding this for a girl born under these conditions.
Garga said: [One should avoid] those defects arising from intercalary months, those produced by seasons, fortnights, and solstices,
as well as those occurring at specific auspicious moments (muhūrta), and those resulting from lunar days (tithi) and portents.
Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury, when properly situated in the ascendant, destroy the malefic planetary aspects arising from the decans, navāṃśas, and signs, which are otherwise difficult to overcome.
The Preceptor says:
Rāhu is to be avoided when conjoined with the ascendant or situated in the seventh house.
Indeed, if he is in the ascendant there is discord, and if he is in the seventh house there is the death of the bride.
When the [ascendant] is joined with a sign, those [signs] are not always to be avoided for the renunciant's life;
however, if it is situated in the eastern ascendant (the first house), there will be death, and if in the second house, there will be loss of wealth.
If Venus is in the third house, there will be an increase in wealth; if in the fourth, the destruction of kinsmen;
if situated in the fifth, the loss of children; likewise, O Aṅgiras, if in the seventh, there is an increase in the husband's prosperity; and if in the eighth, widowhood and an increase in lifespan.
If the Sun is in the ninth house, there will be loss of wealth; if in the tenth house, there will be lack of discipline.
If the Sun is in the eleventh house, there will be gain; if it is in the twelfth house, there will be expenditure.
If the Moon is in the seventh house from the ascendant, one has beloveds; if in the second house, one becomes wealthy.
In the third house, she becomes fortunate, virtuous, and dear to her kinsmen;
in the fifth house, she is a daughter whose mother meets death; and in the sixth house, she shall incur death herself.

If [the moon] is situated in the seventh house (jāyā), she will have a co-wife; if in the eighth house (mṛtyu), she will meet death. A daughter will be born who bears children, provided there is no deviation from dharma during the act of procreation.
When the Moon is situated in the eleventh house, there will be a woman devoted to her husband;
when it is in the twelfth house, she will belong to a noble family; and when Saturn is there, she will be a young girl who gives off a cold sensation.
Even if the Moon has entered an unfavorable sign, it bestows praiseworthy results if it is situated in a benefic Navāṃśa and is aspected by a powerful benefic.
If Mars is situated in the ascendant, the girl will suffer widowhood;
if the son of the Earth (Mars) is in the second house, she will be afflicted by fear of fire and thieves.

If Mars is situated in the third house, she will be endowed with wealth; if in the fourth, she will be seen by her kinsmen. If in the fifth, she will be childless; if in the sixth, she will possess sons. If Mars is situated in the seventh house, she will be unchaste and associated with wicked men.
If Mars is situated in the fifth house, the son will suffer from hemorrhaging, and the daughter will likewise obtain it.
In the ninth house, she is hated by her husband; in the tenth, she is fond of deceit; likewise, in the eleventh, she is endowed with wealth; and in the twelfth, she shall have lost her property.
If Mercury is situated in the ascendant, one will possess knowledge of the Dharma, have virtuous offspring, and be steadfast;
if Mercury is in the second house, there will be constant devotion to one's own family.
If the Moon is situated in the third house, there will be honor from one's mother-in-law and father-in-law;
if it is in the fourth house, there will be honor from kinsmen, and the woman will be fortunate and endowed with wealth.
If [Venus] is in the fifth house, O Aṅgiras, there will be many sons; likewise, one's enemies are destroyed.
However, if it is situated in the seventh or the eighth house, she encounters painful calamity and suffers the loss of her children, being afflicted by disease and partaking of misery.
One should be devoted to austerity in the abode of Dharma, yet practice deceit through one's actions.
If Mars is in the twelfth house, a girl will be endowed with learning, servants, and a husband;
however, if Mercury is there, she will always be joined with constant expenditure.
If Jupiter is situated in the ascendant, the daughter will be virtuous in character and bear many children;
she attains a very long life, and her death shall occur in the eighth house.
One should always live with great joy when [the Sun] is situated in Scorpio;
one should know that there will be prosperity for one's kinsmen, endowed with all desirable qualities.
If situated in the fourth house, she is of virtuous character; if in the fifth, she has many children;
if in the sixth, she is joined with a co-wife; and if in the seventh, she is firmly established in her own home.
When Jupiter is in the tenth house, one who was previously deformed, unfortunate, and self-interested manifests stainless fame and attains complete success in his undertakings.
In the eleventh house from Jupiter, there is a maiden accompanied by a son, adorned with various garlands and ornaments, and enriched with gold, jewels, and diamonds.
When Venus is situated in the twelfth house, she constantly and generously bestows wealth without weariness;
when the son of Bhrigu is situated in the ascendant, she is endowed with long life, virtue, and other such qualities.
If Venus is in the third house, she will be endowed with many virtues yet remain destitute despite relying on wealth; she will be unchaste and take pleasure in her brother-in-law.
Where Venus is always situated in the fourth house, that maiden will be adorned, beautiful, and endowed with wealth; when it is in the fifth house, she will have many offspring.
If Venus is in the sixth house, the husband's circle of kinsmen will be rich with elders;
if Venus is in the seventh house, she will be an unchaste woman, despised by the world.
If Venus is situated in the eighth house, she will be afflicted by disease;
if it is in the ninth house, she will be endowed with righteousness and be pleasant-spoken.
In the tenth house, Venus makes a woman devoted to virtuous deeds and dedicated to dharma;
in the eleventh house, she becomes a widow possessed of wealth, and thus [the former state] must be abandoned.
If Venus is situated in the twelfth house, the daughter born will be wasteful by nature;
if Saturn has gone to the ascendant, the daughter will be unchaste, unfortunate, and emaciated.
If the son of Dharmastha and Arka (Saturn) is present, she will be penniless, wretched, and miserable;
furthermore, she will be afflicted by the pain of poverty, suffering from heart disease, and tormented by distress.
If Saturn is situated in the fifth house, there will be excellent sons; if in the sixth house, she will be struck by weapons;
and if in the seventh house, she will be constantly afflicted by miscarriages.
If Saturn is situated in the eighth house, a girl will always be free from illness;
if the son of the Sun is situated in the ninth house, she will be one who has lost her religious duties and vows.
Situated in the fourth or seventh house, it causes death or physical imbalance;
however, when situated in the houses of Rāhu or other [malefics], it becomes fruitless if located in the twelfth house.
A discerning man should certainly avoid these five defects in taking a wife:
poverty, death, discord, unchastity, and childlessness.
For eight months and half-months at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or for the sake of water, [the results] are auspicious or inauspicious; however,
one should perform the marriage when the planets are situated in auspicious places from the fifth or the tenth house of the ascendant, because a faultless time is very difficult to find.
When Jupiter is situated in the third, tenth, eleventh, fourth, seventh, or ninth house from the ascendant,
and Venus is located in the ascendant, all defects are destroyed.

Having abandoned their expenditures and fuel, the benefic planets always bestow auspiciousness; and the Moon, worshipped by the Asuras, situated in Dhanus, Taurus, or the eleventh house, [brings fortune].
And when the malefic planets reach the abode of the Moon, they bring joy to the earth.
Once released, it would no longer be made of wick; yet, in the grasping of hands, it grants one's desires.
Whatever planet should be situated in the eighth house from the natal ascendant,
even if it is auspicious, it yields inauspicious results when positioned in the marriage ascendant.
Śaunaka said:
One should determine the desired, the adverse, the prosperous, the undesirable,
and the prediction by means of the four Yavanas, who are endowed with the strength of their respective positions and other factors.
When the Sun is favorable, when the one worshipped by the gods (Jupiter) has attained growth, and when the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is likewise,
women obtain the abundance of happiness from their children.
Possessors of good fortune, they have destroyed the factions of their enemies.

In a planetary conflict, during the crushing of the Sun and Moon, at a crossroads, when there is smoke on the ground, at a tree, or when a halo is formed around the sun; and when an eclipse occurs, or when the wheels of a chariot become stuck.
And when the Moon has reached a malefic sign.
The grasping of hands occurs between two stones, or between two surrounding mirrors with broken reflections,
or between the cold and hot rays of the sun and moon when their positions are reversed.
He was cast down by Kabandha and Kālāntika.
Parāśara states: A water-clock (*ghaṭikā*) is one that is filled with sixty *pala* of water when it has a white bowl of ten *pala*, is perfectly circular and even, six finger-breadths in height,
and twelve finger-breadths in circumference at its opening.
Vātsyāyana says: A copper vessel with three folds and measuring six finger-breadths [in height]—
such is the time for marriage.
Now follows the time for the marriage rites. Vātsya says:
All things such as the threshing, pounding, barley sprouts, the pavilion, the clay altar, the sacrificial mound, and the pigments [should be prepared].
One should perform the coming and going related to that [marriage] when the asterism is auspicious for marriage.
On the day of the wedding, or on an auspicious day or lunar date,
when the moon is in the sign of the bride's *jāmitra* (seventh house) and the ascendant is endowed with auspicious planets,
one should perform the *caturthikā* rite according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
Thus concludes the time for the marriage rite. Now follows the determination of the time for the wedding ceremony.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
If a maiden, on account of her father, sees her menses while still unconsecrated by marriage, she incurs the guilt of foeticide for her father; such a maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*.
If a Brāhmaṇa, deluded by pride, should marry such a maiden, he is unfit for company and excluded from the ritual row; that Brahmin is the husband of a Vṛśalī.
For that Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by intoxication, has consorted with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
there is a perpetual state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (brahmahatyā) day after day.
Āpastamba: When the twelfth year has arrived, the menses begin for women;
he who, out of delusion, marries her, should be known as the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
A man of thirty years may marry a girl of ten who has not yet reached puberty;
or one of twenty-one years may take a girl of seven.
Manu says: A thirty-year-old man should marry a pleasing twelve-year-old girl,
or a twenty-four-year-old man an eight-year-old girl, if he is in haste to fulfill his religious duty.
A man who is three times as old as his wife may marry a wife who is one-third his age.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for marriage. Now follows the determination of the age at which a girl should be given in marriage.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
An eight-year-old girl is called Gaurī, while a ten-year-old is called Kanyakā;
when she reaches her twelfth year, she is designated as Kumārī.
Saṃvarta says: In the eighth year she becomes Gaurī; in the ninth she becomes Nagnikā;
in the tenth she is called Kanyakā; and in the twelfth she is remembered as a Vṛṣalī.
In this context, "vṛṣalī" refers to a woman in her menses.
And so Devala says:
"A barren woman is to be known as a vṛṣalī, and a woman whose children have died is also a vṛṣalī."
Another is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*: either a maiden or one who has reached her menses.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"If an unmarried maiden sees her menses while in her father's house, her father incurs the sin of killing an embryo; that maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*."
Viṣṇu:
A maiden who sees her menses while still in her father’s house and remains unconsecrated by marriage is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; one who abducts her does not incur sin.
And this is general; for some, menstruation occurs even before [the ages mentioned].
For this very reason, Yama says:
"A girl of eight years is Gaurī, while one of nine years is Rohiṇī."
A girl becomes ten years old; beyond that age, she is a woman of menses.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Yama, Parāśara, and Āpastamba:
"When the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter—
month after month, her father drinks her menstrual blood."
A girl of eight years is Gaurī, while one of nine years is Rohiṇī;
when the twelfth year arrives, the menses appear in women.
This too is a general rule, since for some women even at that age the appearance of menses is impossible.
For this very reason Manu said:
"A man thirty years of age should marry a pleasing girl of twelve years."
Or else, at twenty-four years of age, he may swiftly settle into the Dharma.
And thus, it is stated that the marriage should take place before the appearance of the menses. To this effect, Gautama says:
"Before the giving away [of the girl], and before the first menses, he who does not give her away incurs guilt; [the guilt applies] even before the wearing of the garment."
Some say it is for the sake of practice;
this is the restraint (yama). Therefore, one should marry off a girl before she reaches puberty.
Vasiṣṭha says:
Out of fear of the onset of puberty, the father should give away his daughter while she is still a girl;
for if she remains until she has reached puberty, the fault falls upon the father.
In the *Saṃgraha*: As long as she does not take up a garment, as long as she plays with dust,
and as long as she does not recognize her own faults, so long does she remain naked.
Amarasiṃha says:
"A *nagnikā* is one who has not yet reached her menses.
Aṅgiras says:
A girl who has not reached puberty is called Gaurī; once she has reached puberty, she is Rohiṇī.
She who lacks secondary sexual characteristics is called Avyañjanā, while one devoid of breasts is termed Nagnikā.
When the secondary sexual characteristics have appeared, Soma enjoys the girl;
when the breasts have developed, Gandharva enjoys her; and when she has reached her menses, Agni enjoys her.
Therefore, one should marry off a maiden before she reaches puberty;
for marriage at the age of eight years is commended for a maiden by the wise.
Bṛhaspati says:

A girl destroys her family upon the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics; she destroys her ancestors when her breasts develop; and she destroys both her sacrificial merit and her charitable works once her menses have arrived.
Parāśara says:
The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother—
these three also go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses.

Paiṭhīnasi: As long as her breasts have not emerged, so long should she be given [in marriage]. If she becomes menstruating, both the giver and the receiver fall into hell, and the grandfather and great-grandfather are born in excrement; therefore, she should be given while still a girl (nagnikā). Yājñavalkya:
By not giving her away, he incurs the sin of killing an embryo for every single fertile season.
Nārada says:
"As many seasons as pass for her without a husband..."
So many instances of foeticide would there be for him who does not give her away.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
"A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house at will until death;
but he must never give her away to one who is devoid of good qualities."

This means that one should give [the daughter] to someone who possesses good qualities, but not to one devoid of qualities; it does not, however, intend to prohibit giving to one devoid of qualities altogether.
For Yama says:
"One should give a maiden while she is still prepubescent (*nagnikā*) to a man of merit, according to one's ability."
But one should never give [the sacred texts] to one devoid of virtue, nor should one have sexual intercourse with a woman in her menses.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for giving away a daughter in marriage.
Now follows the determination of the time for a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage).
Yama says: A maiden shall not remain in the house of her giver beyond the twelfth year;
her father incurs the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā), and that maiden shall choose a husband for herself.
Manu also says:
"A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may find a suitable husband."
If she should approach a husband of her own accord when not being given away,
she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he whom she approaches.
The meaning is that even he does not incur sin.
Baudhāyana says: "If a similar [teacher] is not available, one may resort to one who is deficient in qualities."
"In a suitable [husband]," meaning one who possesses good qualities.
Vasiṣṭha says:
"A maiden who has reached puberty shall wait for three years; after those three years have passed," [she may choose].
She should find a suitable husband;
as for that which was stated by Gautama:
"Having passed three seasons, she may unite herself [with a husband] of her own accord."
And as for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "A maiden, having waited until three menstrual periods have passed, may choose her own husband;
but once three periods have elapsed, she has the same authority over herself."

[806] That [rule] is intended as a prohibition for a period of less than three seasons; however, when one is unable to wait for three years, then one may choose [a bride] even after three seasons. Kātyāyana says:
"But when, having chosen [a bride], a certain man should perish..."
Having passed over three suitors who have come with gifts of red items and meat, she may choose another man as her husband.
"Raktāgamān" means the seasons.
Nārada says: "But if a groom, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country..."
Having passed three seasons, a maiden may choose another bridegroom.
"Having accepted" means having chosen [a husband].

Some, however, explain that after three menstrual periods have passed, there is no [longer] room for the procedure of self-choice (*svayaṃvara*), on the grounds that this is consistent in meaning with the previously cited statements of Viṣṇu, Gautama, Nārada, and Kātyāyana.

That is incorrect; for in that context, the non-giving by the father is the subject under discussion, not the departure to another country or the death of the suitor. Therefore, in accordance with the sequence [of the text], the previous explanation alone is superior. However, when no such person exists, the girl may approach the king; having obtained his permission, she may wait for a suitor and choose him herself. Or, one among those mentioned might be a giver. Yājñavalkya says: "In the absence of givers, however, the girl may perform a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice)."
"Suitable" means fit for approaching.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the *svayaṃvara*.
Now follows the determination of the time for undertaking the fourth stage of life: Having thus properly dwelt in the third stage of life,
one who has offered the oblations and conquered his senses should proceed to the fourth stage.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having spent the remainder of his life in the fourth stage, he should attain tranquility;
then, having shaved off his hair, body hair, and nails, he becomes a forest-dwelling sage (*vānaprastha*)."
By moving immediately from one stage of life to the next, he becomes purified by his actions;
his father likewise becomes such through that same sequence, being perfectly composed in mind.
Having entered the forest-dweller stage (vānaprastha), he proceeded to the fourth stage of life;
having spent the third part of his life wandering in the forest,
he should wander as a mendicant (parivrajet), free from attachment, during the fourth part of his life.

"The third part" refers to that duration of time during which the perfection of austerity is achieved and desire for sense-objects ceases; it does not mean the literal third part of life. Nor does it mean that one should renounce at whatever age one experiences an onset of intoxication. The meaning is:

having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered the senses, and having become weary from begging and making offerings, one should renounce; thus he prospers after death.

This refers to the position of cumulative practice (*samuccaya*): when one has completed both the householder stage and the forest-dweller stage, having conquered the senses through the necessary performance of duties in both, then by renouncing (*pravrajana*), one prospers; thus it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the duties of the preceding stages.
As stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Without having procreated sons, O gods, and likewise without having satisfied the ancestors..."
And how can one wish to go to heaven through the tonsure of the head for the sake of the elements and so forth?
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having discharged the three debts by performing sacrifices, one should renounce."
Having been permitted by his teacher and having bathed together with his wife, that best of the twice-born—
a Brāhmaṇa— should never go forth from his home as a renunciant without first having procreated a son.

In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "One who has not discharged the three debts, who has not mastered his senses through the lack of prescribed rules, and who desires liberation without having conquered passion and hatred, falls downward."
Manu says: Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Since liberation is the sole fruit, knowledge itself is here designated by the word "liberation"; for this very reason, there is the expression "practicing for liberation.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having performed sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should fix the mind on liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.

The statement that disparages the other alternative while relying on the position of combination (*samuccaya*) is not, however, an absolute prohibition, as in the case of the *udita* (after sunrise) and *anudita* (before sunrise) fire-sacrifices; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the direct Jābāla Śruti: "Or else, one may renounce even from the state of studentship itself. Furthermore, this statement from the Taittirīya Śruti—“A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born indeed burdened with three debts: by studentship to the sages, by sacrifice to the gods, and by progeny to the ancestors; he alone is debt-free who has a son, has performed sacrifice, or has lived as a student”—is also based solely upon the position of combination.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"After dwelling in the forest, for one who is peaceful and of mature age, wandering forth as a mendicant by his own will—having internalized the sacred fires, being free from fear, greed, delusion, anger, grief, malice, pride, and envy, and whose mind is established in appropriate contemplation—it becomes unrestricted by faith and other such qualities; therefore, on that very day he should attend to it, abandoning all undertakings and possessions, on the very day he renounces.
From the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
Having abandoned attachment to son, wealth, and wife, O lord of men,
he should go to the fourth stage of life, with all envy shaken off.
When he has become dispassionate toward divine and human enjoyments, toward the fivefold objects of the senses, and even toward those things seen and heard, he should renounce from the forest.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "O best of Brahmins, you who know all things, tell me which among these is most conducive to supreme welfare in this world: sacrifice, austerity, or renunciation?"
Having propitiated the Lord, the supreme master and yogin, through austerity,
one should first worship the foremost of gods with sacrifices according to the rules, and then go forth into the life of renunciation.
Exhausted by dwelling in the forest, one may go forth according to the prescribed rule—
whether impelled by disease and the like, or out of dispassion, or even when not ill or in pain.
For those who are afflicted by illness, there is no specific distinction, nor is there a formal ritual or hospitable treatment;
for the sick, renunciation is ordained as consisting merely of the utterance of the command.
When a terrible crisis had arisen, within the range of thieves, tigers, and other dangers,
the sage Aṅgiras, terrified by fear, spoke of renunciation.
A learned and excellent twice-born man, having become dispassionate, may renounce even without having performed sacrifices;
or else, having sacrificed with various kinds of sacrifices, he may then resort to the forest.
Having performed austerities and become dispassionate through the power of yoga, he should likewise renounce;
even if he is unable to perform the rites of offering oblations and sacrificing.
A twice-born man who is blind, lame, or poor, or who has become dispassionate, should renounce;
for when dispassion toward all things arises in everyone,
at that very moment the wise man should renounce, otherwise he becomes fallen.
Yama says: A Brāhmaṇa who has fulfilled the vows prescribed by the Vedas and possesses knowledge should resort to liberation;
being equal toward all beings and having accomplished his duty, he should wander as a mendicant.
Furthermore, in the absence of taking a wife, one whose wife has died may renounce the world;
or, having shaken off his sins, he may resort to the supreme path from the forest.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "One who has attained knowledge and realization and reached supreme detachment should desire that highest goal which is reached through celibacy and the other stages."

Having taken a wife according to the prescribed rule, he should duly worship with various sacrifices; remaining established in that state, he should procreate offspring, but if he becomes dispassionate, he should renounce.
Without having performed sacrifices according to the rules, nor having likewise procreated a son,
a wise twice-born man should not take up the life of a householder and then renounce it.
If, through the force of dispassion, one does not venture to go home even to bathe, then at that very moment the wise man should renounce; he should reflect without despondency.
[811] Or else, having become dispassionate toward the ocean of existence even from the first stage of life,
a Brahmin seeking liberation should abandon attachments and conquer them.
Then, having reached the third and most excellent stage of life, that of the householder,
one should either remain in it for the fourth part of one's lifespan or, while remaining therein, go forth as a wandering mendicant.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*).
Now follows the determination of the time for establishing the sacred fires (*agnihotra*), the consecration (*ādhāna*), and the taking of a wife.
On this point, Manu and Śātātapa state:

He who enters into the relationship of marriage and the sacred fire while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder), and the elder brother is a *parivitti*.

And that uterine brother is not one born of another [man], nor one born of another mother. This very point will become clear later on. Likewise, it should be understood that there is no fault regarding those who are outcasted, insane, eunuchs, blind, deaf, mute, dull-witted, humpbacked, afflicted with leprosy, vitiligo, or pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), those overcome by incurable major diseases such as abdominal dropsy, atheists, students of scripture, ascetics, or those who have been away abroad for a long time; for these individuals lack the qualification for marriage and so forth.
For this very reason, Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Those residing in another country, eunuchs, those with a single testicle, and those with a massive abdomen..."
And those who have made a profession of courtesans, those fallen, those equal to Śūdras, and those afflicted with disease.
Those who are eunuchs, mute, deaf, humpbacked, dwarfs, or one-eyed; those who are very old, those without wives, those devoted to agriculture, and those belonging to the king.
One does not incur blame by marrying a younger brother who is addicted to the increase of wealth, who acts out of lust, or who is unchaste, insane, or a thief.
Śātātapa says:
"If the elder brother is impotent, resides in another country, has become an outcast, is likewise insane,
or is devoted to the practice of Yoga, there is no fault in marrying before him."
Sumantu says:
"Whether the elder brother is one whose mind is addicted to vices, or an atheist,
the younger brother who desires to practice dharma may then perform the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires)."

There is no fault in superseding the sons of a paternal uncle, the sons of a co-wife, or the sons of another man's wife, provided one has already established a connection with a wife and the sacred fires.

The reading is: “Yama and Bāṣkala say there is no unrighteousness for one who marries again while his wife and the sacred fires are still present. [Regarding the phrase] “the sons of another’s wife,” this refers to brothers such as those adopted (*dattaka*), purchased (*krīta*), and so forth.
Vasiṣṭha says: He who, for eight, ten, or twelve years, does not wait for his brother who has not yet married becomes liable to penance.
[He was] not conceived in his mother’s womb. And there are verses on this matter:
"If he is heard from again and again, it is proper for a brother to wait for twelve years at most, in accordance with the pursuit of dharma and artha."
One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, outcast, or even impotent,
as well as one afflicted by consumption and other such diseases, would not be fit to wait upon [the preceptor].
There is no fault in superseding one who is a eunuch, a dwarf, a hunchback, blind, fallen, insane, a cripple,
diseased, deaf, or mute.
Sumantu:
When the eldest brother is present, one should not perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*);
however, having obtained his permission, one may do so, according to the words of Śaṅkha.
Likewise, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
"When the elder brother is without a sacred fire, how may the younger brother establish it?
With the permission of the elder, he may perform the Agnihotra according to the rule."

And this should be understood to apply when the brother who is entitled [to marry] does not do so; for if he is not entitled, there is no transgression, and thus it is not appropriate to seek his permission.
For this very reason, Hārīta says:
"How could one become a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder) among all uterine brothers?"
But wives are distinguished by their conduct, not by the Agnihotra sacrifice nor by other ritual worship.

The meaning of this is as follows: when a full brother who is the elder and the rightful authority has not yet married, but is desirous of marriage, one must wait while he remains in that position; having obtained his permission, the marriage should not be performed at all, just as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not.
As Uśanas says:
"For one whose father, paternal grandfather, or elder brother [remains unmarried], or for anyone else [in such a state]..."
There is no fault in marrying before one's elder brothers in the case of asceticism, the Agnihotra sacrifice, or Vedic mantras.
Sumantu: But how can the son of one whose father has not studied [the Veda] perform [the rites]?
He has the right to the Agnihotra, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says that [the sin of] "marrying before [the elder brother]" applies when permission has been granted or when [the elder] is present:
"The sacred fires marry before [their owner], or the younger brother marries before [his elder]; likewise, a maiden may be deformed.

And because of the previous statement that this refers to a brother who lacks the qualification [to marry], even an elder sister who is extremely ugly cannot be a cause for obstructing the marriage of the younger brother.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the Agnihotra, the establishment of the sacred fires (Ādhāna), and the taking of a wife.
Now follows the determination of the time for establishing the domestic fire (Āvasathya).
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

He who, disregarding the domestic fire (āvasathya), proceeds with the three sacred fires (tretā), becomes one who has not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) and is likewise called a "supplanter" (parivettṛ).

On this point, some say: because of the employment of the term "fault of the fire" (*agnidoṣa*) in the passage, "He who should enter into the union of wife and *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains," there is no such thing as "leaving home" (*parivedana*) even when taking up the *aupāsana* fire; for the application of a word has the result of excluding other [possibilities].
That is improper, because the exclusion of others is not expressed by the words [of the rule].
For this very reason Gārgya said: "While an elder uterine brother remains, one should not take a wife."
The establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya) is likewise; however, it would be otherwise for one who has already established the sacred fires.
Brahmagarbha also says:
"By officiating at sacrifices, by teaching, and by means of wealth from blameless persons,
one should undertake the service [of the teacher], announcing it at the proper time."
"At its own time" means at the time prescribed by rule.
And so says the Smṛti:
"The establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) according to the injunctions, even for one fallen from a Vaiśya family... [815]
