It is great either in the case of non-respect or in the case of the time for giving and inheritance.
Pāraskara:
The establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya) occurs at the time of marriage, or at the time of inheritance, according to some.
Gautama: [The same].
Having procreated a son and established the domestic fire (*āvasathya*), one should honor guests. Vyāsa says: "If a negligent man has not taken the nuptial fire..."
When the father has passed away, he should take possession of it with great care.
He who, having taken a wife, considers himself a householder [merely for that], his food must not be eaten; for he is remembered as one whose cooking is in vain.

This is to be understood as applying to the eldest brother who is entitled [to perform the rites]; and even if the younger brother has established the *agnihotra*, if the eldest brother is incapable of studying the Veda and so forth, he is not held liable for sin even if he does not undertake the maintenance of the sacred fires.
On this point, Garga says:
"Or one who lives on the father's cooking, or one who lives on the brother's cooking..."
Or one who is devoted to knowledge and study does not incur fault even without the sacred fire.
Satyavrata has shown that even for one who has not studied the Vedas, marriage after returning from studentship is permitted:
"If a twice-born man, having failed to study the Veda, bathes and marries in whatever manner,
he should [later] master the Veda with its auxiliary limbs in the house of his teacher, once his period of studenthood has passed."
Thus concludes the determination of the time for establishing the domestic fire (āvasathya).
[816] Now follows the time for the agnihotra.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Whether at sunrise, before sunrise, or likewise at the time of twilight, the sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation."
When the night has reached its sixteenth part, adorned by planets and constellations,
the wise man, knowing that the time has not yet dawned, should perform the fire-oblation.
Likewise, at the time of dawn, when the circle of stars has vanished but the sun is not yet visible— that interval is called *samayādhyuṣita*.
If even a mere line appears there, accompanied by a depression, one should recognize that as "udita"; one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) therein.
Śaṅkha: One should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice according to the rules both in the evening and in the morning.
Baudhāyana.
The morning oblation for the evening rite, and the evening oblation for the morning rite, should not be delayed;
nor should the full-moon offering be delayed beyond the next full-moon festival.
In the *Sautrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*:

"The Prājājakas, being seers, used to perform the Agnihotra; at the end of the fortnight, having omitted all the combined offerings (*samastahoma*), they performed the Agnihotra for two nights, six nights, six months, and half-months. Therefore, one who is traveling, or afflicted by disease, or suffering from illness, should perform the Agnihotra for half a month. On the day of service, he should offer fourteen portions of four ladlings each in the morning and fourteen in the evening.
The mention of "fourteen" is for the purpose of illustration; sometimes there are fifteen, sometimes four [drawings], and sometimes sixteen.
Marīci: Having offered the fortnightly oblations, why does one return after having gone?
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) once again, and one shall not be subject to that fault.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the Agnihotra.
Now, the time for commencing the construction of palaces and other buildings: having ascertained an auspicious time according to the season, one should always undertake the building.
The man who has a house built in Caitra incurs disease;
in Vaiśākha, he gains wealth and jewels; likewise, in Jyeṣṭha, there is death;
in Āṣāḍha, he obtains servants, jewels, and a herd of cattle.
In Śrāvaṇa there is the gain of servants, but in Bhādrapada there will be loss;
in Āśvina there will be the destruction of one's wife, while in Kārttika there will be wealth and grain.
Likewise, in Mārgaśīrṣa there will be food, and in Pauṣa there is danger from thieves.

"Bhakta" (food) is an indicative mark for all kinds of eatables. One should predict that in the month of Māgha there will be frequent gains of fire, and in Phālguna, gold and sons; thus is the power of time remembered.
According to the system of Viśvakarman:
In the month of Caitra, the husband is overwhelmed by grief; in Vaiśākha, he is endowed with wealth;
in Jyeṣṭha, the householder shall perish; and in Āṣāḍha (Śuci), his livestock are destroyed.
In Śrāvaṇa there shall be an increase of wealth; in Nabhasya the householder should not dwell at home;
in the month of Āśvina there will be quarrels; and in Kārttika servants perish.
In Mārgaśīrṣa there is the acquisition of wealth; in Sahasya (Pauṣa), the fulfillment of desires. In Māgha there may be fear of fire, and in Phālguna, unsurpassed prosperity.
Likewise, in the Saṅgraha: "In Caitra, there may be illness and grief; in Vaiśākha, one is endowed with wealth and jewels;
indeed, the householder is always possessed of cattle, buffaloes, and so forth."
In Jyeṣṭha one meets death; in Āṣāḍha there is the loss of cattle;
likewise, there is the gain of servants, excellent jewels, and the acquisition of wealth.
In Śrāvaṇa, there is the acquisition of servants and untroubled increase of wealth;
in the month of Bhādrapada, a house is certainly born to bring suffering.
In that case, there would be the loss of all one's possessions for the householder;
moreover, in the month of Āśvina, there would invariably be the destruction of his wife as well as strife.
In the month of Kārttika, there shall be wealth and grain, yet there will be the loss of servants day and night;
for this very reason, sons are pacified when the construction of a palace begins.
The commencement of a house in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa bestows wealth, gain, and happiness;
therein one obtains various kinds of food as well as excellent jewels such as elephants and horses.
In this [year], there is the acquisition of a dwelling and auspiciousness;
moreover, there will be great gain of progeny, as well as the supreme acquisition of friends, sons, and wives.
In the month of Pauṣa, a most terrible fear of thieves is to be recognized;
yet there shall be the acquisition of wealth, grain, and the like, as well as the prosperity of sons, friends, and others.
In Māgha, danger from fire is to be known; it always takes away everything and causes distress. In Phālguna, one should know that there will be auspicious gain arising from gold.
"In this [month], there is the gain of a son, accompanied by great happiness and affection.
Thus has the fruit of the month been declared; now I shall describe its threefold nature:
it is of three kinds—excellent, middling, and inferior.
Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Phālguna are declared to be the best; likewise, the middling ones are now described:
Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Puṣya are proclaimed to be the middling months.
I shall now describe those [months] that are youngest; listen to them in brief:
Caitra, Jyaiṣṭha, and Nabhasya are the youngest Īṣomāsas.
‘Īṣaḥ’ refers to the Āśvina [month]. The fruit of these has been clearly set forth in summary in the Aparājitapṛcchā.
When the Sun is situated in Virgo, Libra, or Scorpio, the head of the Vāstu is located in the east;
"Ali" refers to Scorpio.
When it is in Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, it is situated in the south.
On account of its conjunction with Sunday, that site moves due to its wandering.
Where the sun is located at the head, that direction should be identified according to the movement of the sun;
one should not construct a temple or a house facing directly toward the head.

There will be fears of death and disease; facing the south is recommended. If the Sun is situated in Libra, Scorpio, or Virgo, one should not then construct a house facing the east, for it becomes fruitless.
When the sun stands in Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius,
a house facing south brings fear of kings, thieves, and fire.
In the signs of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, one should face west; this brings about quarrels with women.
One should not face north in the signs of Gemini, Cancer, or Leo;
a house built in such a manner will bring about defects, sorrow, and fear.
Viśvakarman:
When the Sun is situated in Virgo, Libra, or Scorpio, one should not construct a house facing the direction of Varuṇa (the west);
for that house would become empty, O Lord, and there would be no prosperity.
When the sun is situated in the sign of Capricorn facing south,
one should not perform [the rite], for it would be fruitless and cause such things as royal punishment and death.
One should not perform [the rite] while facing east when the sun is situated in Pisces,
Taurus, or Leo, because that destroys wealth and brings about obstacles, hunger, kings, thieves, and so forth.
When the Sun is situated in Gemini or Leo, but not in Cancer, one should perform that rite facing north;
otherwise, it would bestow poverty and cause the fault of emaciation.
As proclaimed by Viśvakarman:
Now, the Kuṇḍalī-cakra, which is the weapon of the solar wheel, is fixed;
two lines must be drawn there, indeed from east to west.

Likewise, one line should run from south to north, another from fire (southeast) to wind (northwest), and a third from Ishana (northeast) to Nairrita (southwest); there, one should place the zodiac signs.
Successively, from the tip of the line toward the northeast, there shall be twelve lines;
therein, the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Virgo and ending with Leo are situated in order.
Wherever the sun may be, there the head of the site (vāstu) is situated;
at night, the gaze of the site falls sequentially upon the seventh position from its own location.
On whichever line the sun may be situated, joined with the head of the site (vāstu), it will corrupt the zodiac sign knotted to that line as well as the one facing it.
One should know that the sign situated in the aspect of the Sun is designated as "named" (abhidhāmita);
however, the sign actually occupied by the Sun is proclaimed to be "burned" (dagdha).
One must never, under any circumstances, construct a doorway when the sun is situated over the head [of the house];
if it is built out of ignorance, the householder will suffer ruin.
One should declare the location of the door of the house according to the zodiac sign situated in the *vāstu-dṛṣṭi*;
in that case, there will be loss of wealth and the decline of sons, friends, and cattle.
If the Sun is placed in the Lagna at the time of a solar eclipse, there will be great fear of disease,
as well as from thieves and the like, and from fire, kings, and royal families.
Indeed, in whichever zodiac sign the Sun's aspect reaches, that is the door of the house;
for one constantly residing there, there will be most terrible disease and suffering.
If the door is burnt due to [negligence regarding] knowledge, there will be loss of wealth for its master.
When the Sun is in Capricorn, Aquarius, Leo, or Cancer,
one should then have the house constructed facing either east or west.
This result has been declared for the castes regarding their dwelling-places; one who desires auspiciousness should never begin building a house during the period beginning with Kanyā.
He states the realized meaning of the Kuṇḍalī-cakra:
"I shall proclaim the enumeration of the fruits, clearly for each [cakra]:
the increase of happiness, as well as peace, and the destruction of all sins."
The loss of kinsmen and likewise the failure of one's enterprise—such is the fruit in the mouth of the crocodile;
yet it bestows abundant fortune upon the householder because of the dust [it brings].
All such results as these are to be known; indeed, everything was present in the water-pot (kumbha).
Sons and grandsons shall increase, and prosperity shall become unshakable.
The husband will be heroic, of good conduct, and endowed with happiness and good fortune;
in Leo, all such results as these will be obtained in their entirety.
Joyful, well-nourished, prosperous, with well-proportioned limbs and endowed with splendor—the husband indeed attains happiness; such is the fruit when [the Moon is] in Cancer.
When the sun is in Aries, Taurus, Libra, or Scorpio,
one should cause the cremation of the deceased to take place with the house facing north.
I shall now describe their results in due order:
an auspicious result of good fortune for the sake of the prosperity of sons and grandsons.
He shall be a speaker of the Brahman, endowed with all prosperity;
indeed, the husband obtains such fruits as these for a long time when [the moon is] in Aries.
Under Taurus, auspiciousness, long-lasting fortune, and undisturbed increase of cattle occur;
many sons and beautiful women are born to him.
Such results for the master have been proclaimed therein by the wise;
in the case of the balance (tulā), the most desirable result for men is correctly stated.
Wealth, grain, happiness, enjoyments, abundance of cattle, horses, and sons,
many friends as well as servants, and beautiful livestock in the home—
such is the fruit for the husband when [the wife] possesses a heap of merit.
There shall be the complete destruction of enemies and indeed the prosperity of one's own family.
The husband shall be illustrious, endowed with enjoyments, and accompanied by beloved ones;
such fruits as these certainly arise there in the case of Scorpio.
The crocodile and the pitcher are to be recognized as suitable for a temple intended for the fulfillment of desires;
the lion and the crab are to be known as appropriate for a house facing west.
‘Hari’ is the lion; the ram and the bull are likewise beneficial when commencing work in the northern quarter. Both Libra and Scorpio are beneficial in the southern quarter.
Now I shall describe the results for those situated in the corners, such as Virgo and the others, according to their effects;
for when the crow is situated in Virgo, the bow [of Sagittarius] becomes the locus of smoke.
A wise person should never undertake the construction of a house when the sun is in Scorpio, Pisces, or Aries; nor should one begin it when the sun has duly reached Virgo.
No prosperity shall arise there; there will be the loss of sons, grandsons, and cattle.
The husband, beset by every affliction, will dwell there—of this there is no doubt.
When the sun is situated in Sagittarius (Dhanus), one should never undertake the building of a house;
for there, one is struck down by enemies and no prosperity arises.
Alternatively, while living as a householder, one may be oppressed by royal punishment;
therefore, when the Sun is situated in Pisces, one should not have a house built.
If, however, it results in disease, grief, and great fear,
then his lack of fortitude will lead to exhaustion, with the fish as its fruit.
When the sun is situated in Gemini, one should not have a house built;
for that house will surely be consumed by fire and bring about suffering.

When the Sun is in Pisces, the commencement of a house for those who live by fire should take place in the southeast direction; however, when it is in Gemini, the commencement of a shelter is beneficial for renunciants in the northeast.
In the northwest, a maiden is to be known; the commencement of a house there always brings happiness, especially for those who live by their voices, such as courtesans and the like.
In the southwest, at the bow, there should be the commencement [of the house] in the home of a dog-cooker (outcaste).
Now I shall describe the conjunction of the houses, the zodiac signs, and the months.
One should not have a house built where Aries occurs in the month of Caitra;
if it is built there, a great disease arises for the householders.
But where Gemini occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha, there shall always be division.
"Dvaidha" means a duel or battle.
Cancer is unfavorable in Āṣāḍha; likewise, Virgo in Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa);
Libra is unfavorable in Āśvina; and likewise, Scorpio in Kārttika.
If the Sagittarius (Cāpa) ascendant occurs on the day of the journey, the path will be unfavorable; therefore, the journey is not auspicious.
If Aquarius (Kumbha) occurs during the month of Māgha, it is indeed unfavorable, and beginning [the journey] then is not auspicious.
The eighth month and the month of Māsa are indeed mutually defiled;
therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should not construct a temple during these months.
Likewise:
One should carefully avoid Jupiter when it is in Leo or Aries;
when Jupiter or Venus has set, the commencement of a house is not recommended.
In this world, the commencement of building a house should not take place when the lord of the night (the moon) is excessively diminished.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A wise person should not perform construction work during the rainy season.
Thus says Tapana.

In the final third of the dark fortnight, during the five days beginning from the eleventh day (ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight; and in the final third of the year of Venus, during the five days beginning from the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight—in this manner, a period of ten days beginning from the eleventh day of the dark fortnight becomes manifold.
Likewise:
One should avoid the fourth, the ninth, and the fourteenth lunar days; this is according to the Viśvakarmamata.
Those lunar days which are praised as auspicious for the work of building a dwelling—
In an auspicious month, during the bright fortnight, on the first or the second lunar day.
The third, fifth, sixth, seventh, tenth,
as well as the eleventh, thirteenth, and the full moon day are thus proclaimed [as auspicious].
These lunar days (tithis) are renowned by the name "Full" (pūrṇā);
on the fourth or the sixth [of these], one should avoid [the practice] situated in the south.
Since there would be the fear of a great disease for one living there,
therefore the days are praised as being those excluding Sunday and Tuesday.
That which is afflicted by existence due to portents from the heavens, the atmosphere, or the earth;
that which is seized by malevolent planets; and that which is struck by the *vyatīpāta* yoga—should all be abandoned.
"Afflicted by a planet" means corrupted by a malefic planet.

When the Moon and Mars are favorable to the asterism, one who understands the task of the agent should know that those fixed asterisms are auspicious, as are Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā) and likewise Nairṛta (Mūla).
"The fixed [asterisms] are Rohiṇī and the three Uttarās.
Also, according to the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Vāyavya, Vaiṣṇava, Puṇya, Pauṣṇa, and Sāvitra."
One should perform [the rite] during the Vajra, Vyāghāta, Śūla, Vyatīpāta, Atigaṇḍa,
Viṣkumbha, Gaṇḍa, Parigha, and Vajra yogas.
According to the opinion of Viśvakarman:
[826] Now I shall proclaim the *yogas* that have been avoided by the wise:
Atigaṇḍa, Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vajra.
Gaṇḍa, Śūla, Viṣkumbha, and Vyāghāta are extremely painful;
having avoided these conjunctions, [one should proceed] even in their absence.
In the Viṣkumbha yoga, a wise person should avoid three or five ghaṭikās;
in the Vajra yoga, however, one should avoid three or nine ghaṭikās.
In the *atigaṇḍa* yogas, six or nine [ghaṭikās] indeed bestow defects;
in *gaṇḍa*, six ghaṭikās; and in *vyāghāta*, nine or six.
In the Śūla yoga, five or seven ghaṭikās are considered to cause affliction by the humors;
likewise, in the Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta yogas, sixty ghaṭikās alone [are so considered].
In the Parigha yoga, thirty or thirty-six ghaṭikās are auspicious;
all the remaining ghaṭikās of these [yogas], as well as others, bring about auspiciousness.
Auspicious yogas should be employed in the rite of establishing a dwelling;
it is taught that the attainment of their results corresponds exactly to their names.
Likewise:
Now I shall describe the *karaṇas* for the auspicious commencement of a building site:
Taitila, Vaṇija, Nāga, and the other *karaṇa*, Vālava;
these bring about wealth, grain, prosperity, welfare, and happiness.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The day of Mars is called the *karaṇa* known as *viṣṭi*;
one should avoid it"—this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "One should begin the construction of a house during the Śveta, Maitra, Māhendra, Gandha, Virohaṇa, as well as the Vairāja and Sāvitra muhūrtas."

Having obtained the strength of the moon and sun, and when the ascendant is aspected by benefics, the raising of pillars and so forth should be performed; otherwise, one should avoid it. This same rule applies to temples, as well as to wells and tanks.
According to the system of Viśvakarman,
I shall describe the auspicious moments (muhūrtas) by which all prosperity is attained:
namely, Māhendra, Rauhiṇa, Sāvitra, and likewise Mitraka.
One should have houses constructed during the Gandharva, Abhijit, or Śveta muhūrtas;
now we shall describe the seven common muhūrtas.
Virāja, Vijaya, Śveta, Sāvitra, Maitrika, Abhijit, and Khala—
these are declared to be all bestowers of the accomplishment of every purpose.
Now, I shall tell you those [nakṣatras] to be avoided according to the specific days of the week:
for Sunday (Ādityavāra), Aryaman; for Monday (Somavāra), Vairāja and Candramas;
for Tuesday (Bhaumavāra), the Pitṛs; for Wednesday (Budhavāra), it is known that [the deities] are lost; and likewise, Abhijit [is lost] on Thursday (Jīva).
The two Bhaujaṅga muhūrttas should be avoided when Saturn is present.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"When the ascendant is fixed (*sthira*), and in a fixed degree (*aṃśa*), and endowed with the *upacaya* [houses] of the agent (*kartṛ*).

"Fixed ascendants" are Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius. "Of the agent" refers to the zodiac sign of the agent (*kartṛ-rāśi*). "Endowed with the *upacaya*" means situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh house.
And so it is stated in the *Jātaka*:
"The third, sixth, eleventh, and tenth houses are houses of increase (*upacaya*); the others are otherwise.
Whatever benefic planets are in a quadrant (*kendr*) or a trine (*trikoṇa*), as is Bhārgava (Venus)."
And when malefic planets are situated in a house of increase, one should undertake that undertaking.
Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon are "benefics" (*saumya*). The waning moon, the Sun, Mars, and Saturn are "malefics" (*pāpa*), as is Mercury when conjoined with them.
Thus it is said in the *Laghujātaka*: "The waning moon, the Sun, and Mars are malefics; a benefic is [also considered malefic] when conjoined with them."

‘Yama’ is Saturn (Śanaiścara); ‘Āra’ is Mars (Maṅgala); and ‘Saumya’ is Mercury (Budha). ‘Kendras’ are the angles, namely the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses from the ascendant (lagna). ‘Trikona’ refers to the fifth and ninth houses. Thus it is stated in the Jātaka: “The four Kendras and the Trikona are the five strong positions (kaṣṭhakas) starting from the ascendant; the seventh, tenth, and fourth are considered weak (saṅkṣaya).”
The ninth and fifth houses are the trines, as are the ninth and seventh houses;

one should avoid a malefic planet situated in a quadrant (kendrastha) in all types of rites according to every school of thought. However, a benefic planet occupying a quadrant is auspicious, and one should never leave it empty.
According to the Viśvakarmamata: Now I shall declare the auspicious *lagna* for the commencement of a house:
Taurus, Sagittarius, Libra, Virgo, Gemini, and Aquarius.
These ascendants are recommended for the construction of houses and palaces;
work performed under these ascendants will lead to complete success in this world.
Malefic planets in the eleventh, third, and sixth houses are auspicious;
however, if a malefic planet is in the eighth house, death is certainly attained.

All planets, beginning with the Moon and the Sun, bestow auspicious results when situated in their own signs or houses, provided they are not in their signs of debilitation, nor in a state of depression, nor afflicted by the Sun.

The respective domains (*kṣetra*) of the planets beginning with the Sun are as follows: Leo is the domain of the Sun; Cancer, of the Moon; Aries and Scorpio, of Mars; Gemini and Virgo, of Mercury; Sagittarius and Pisces, of Jupiter; Taurus and Libra, of Venus; and Capricorn and Aquarius, of Saturn. This is stated in the *Laghujātaka*:
"Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, and Saturn-Jupiter are the lords of the signs."
The meaning is that these are, in order, the lords of the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries:
‘Kuja’ is Mars, ‘Jña’ is Mercury, ‘Jīva’ is Jupiter, and ‘Sauri’ is Saturn; ‘Bhāni’ refers to the signs. Likewise, exaltation (ucca) and depression (nīca) are defined in the Jātaka.

The exaltations (ucca) of the planets beginning with the Sun are said to be the signs of the goat (Aries), the bull (Taurus), the deer-maiden (Virgo), the crab (Cancer), and the fish (Pisces); [the degrees] are ten, eighteen, twenty-eight, fifteen, five, and twenty-seven. The sign opposite the exaltation is the fall (nīca). Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: the first ten and thirty degrees of Aries are the exaltation of the Sun; the first thirty-three degrees of Taurus are the exaltation of the Moon; the first twenty-eight and thirty degrees of Capricorn are the exaltation of Mars. Likewise, the fifteen and thirty degrees of Virgo are the exaltation of Mercury; the five [degrees] of Cancer are the exaltation of Jupiter; the twenty-seven [degrees] of Pisces are the exaltation of Venus; and the twenty [degrees] of Libra are the exaltation of Saturn. Having thoroughly reflected upon and understood all of this, a wise person should diligently undertake the work of architecture (*vāstukarma*), which bestows complete success.

Thus ends the section on the site-plan (*vāstu*). Now follows the determination of the time for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). In this regard, first is the general determination of the time for consecration.
[830] In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*,
Vajra said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, at what time should the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) be performed?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen; I shall declare to you the proper time for performing the consecration, at which time, when it is performed, it becomes a bestower of the attainment of fruits.
When Jupiter is conjoined with the Lord of the Third Heaven (Jupiter), that [city] shall then become abundant with wealth and grain, prosperous, a granter of boons,
firm, and renowned.
When that [power], which is vast and capable of assuming a corporeal form, is kindled by the splendor of Indra,
being thus expanded, it brings about a burning sensation in the heart.
She is eternally endowed with wonders in the world of Tvāṣṭra, and likewise in Gamya;
she is eternally present in Ahirbudhnya, bestowing grace upon the worlds.
In the Pitrya direction, one meets with destruction, and it brings death to the performer;
in the Saumya direction, it is auspicious for the performer and likewise becomes a granter of boons;
in the Aindrāgna direction, by performing [the rite], one meets with destruction and ruin for the performer.
Having become illustrious during the month of Āśvina, she shall likewise obtain a son;
she shall become approachable by the world through good fortune, and she shall become fortunate for the sake of her husband.
O Best of Men, even when the time is inauspicious, a foundation must be established;
for in whichever age a particular protector or deity is proclaimed,
[the site] becomes abundant with wealth and grain, bringing prosperity and victory to the builder.
The twelve *yugas*, beginning with Viṣṇu, are mentioned in that very same place along with the five years starting with Prabhava.
In the years known as *saṃvatsara* and others, she is always endowed with command (*ājñāyutā*);
likewise, in those preceded by *pari*, she is the destroyer of beings (*bhūtaghnī*) and renowned throughout the world.
Likewise, Idāpūrvā is gentle, a bestower of boons, and beautiful to the world; Anupūrvā, moreover, is a bestower of boons and possesses wealth and grain.
Thus, in the former case, one meets with destruction; it brings about the destruction of the performer.
Even in that situation, at the time of Śambhu’s dance, she becomes Rohitā.

The five [years] beginning with *prabhava* are, in sequence, designated as *saṃvatsara*, *parivatsara*, *idāvatsara*, *anuvatsara*, and *vatsara*. Likewise, there is a fivefold designation for the group beginning with *Aṅgiras* in sequence; this applies similarly to what follows, as stated in that very same [text]. In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having reached the auspicious bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) when the sun has passed into its northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*)."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"During the northern transit (ayana), it is auspicious and brings about an increase in wealth;
yet even then, while the Lord of Gods is asleep, it increases all misfortunes."
O Lord of the Earth, she who is beloved by the world in the winter season shall be firm;
in the spring, she shall be flourishing, gentle, and likewise a bestower of boons.
In summer she is radiant and lovely, bringing about the subjugation of beings;
likewise, in the rainy season, she brings about destruction along with the agent.

Furthermore, the prohibition regarding the rainy season (*prāvṛṭkāla*) pertains to matters other than the installation of Śiva (*śivapratiṣṭhā*), because that [installation] is prescribed during the rainy season, as has been shown in the determination of the time for the installation of Śiva.
[It is said: "That which is performed in the autumn quickly meets with destruction;
whereas that which is done in the early winter (*hemanta*) is auspicious and brings about an increase in merit."
In Māgha, she leads to the destruction of the performer; in Phālguna, she becomes auspicious;
in Caitra, she brings joy to the world; and in Vaiśākha, she is endowed with excellence.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha she is always endowed with authority; in Āṣāḍha, she bestows the increase of Dharma;
in Śrāvaṇa, she would be destitute of wealth; and in Prauṣṭhapada, she perishes.
In Āśvina, one meets with destruction; likewise in Kārttika, by fire.
In Mārgaśīrṣa there is incomparable good fortune, and in Pauṣa, unsurpassed nourishment.
But in Māgha, it would bring harm to the performer himself.
Whether in Caitra, or Phālguna, or Jyeṣṭha, or Mādhava,
or likewise in Māgha, the installation of all the deities shall be auspicious.

Now, the prohibition regarding the month of Māgha concerns the installation of Viṣṇu, whereas the injunction concerns the installation of deities other than him; likewise, the injunction for the month of Mārgaśīrṣa concerns those other than the installation of Viṣṇu, since the prohibition of Mārgaśīrṣa has already been shown in the determination of the proper time for the installation of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the prohibition of the months of Śrāvaṇa and Āśvina concerns those other than the installation of Viṣṇu, because the injunction for these two months specifically applies to the installation of Viṣṇu, as demonstrated in that very same context.

Others, however, say: because of the statement, "In the month of Māgha [is the time] for all the gods," the installation of Viṣṇu should also be performed then. As for the prohibition regarding the month of Māgha and so forth, it applies specifically to those particular texts and to specific types of installations. In the second [year] it yields middling results, and in the third it bestows auspiciousness;
likewise, it becomes abundant with wealth and grain, prosperous, and a granter of boons.
It bestows auspicious results upon whichever side experiences growth.
On the second day she is endowed with wealth; on the third, she grants boons;
on the fourth, she meets her destruction; and for Yama, she brings happiness.
Likewise, there the goddess Vināyaka bestows welfare;
on the fifth day, she is endowed with splendor and likewise becomes a granter of boons to the performer.
On the sixth day she is always endowed with fortune; on the seventh, she destroys disease;
on the eighth, she possesses abundant grain; but on the ninth, she perishes.
The rite performed there for Bhadrakālī brings nourishment to the performer;
likewise, when performed on the tenth day, it should be known as increasing one's merit.
Likewise, when conjoined with the eleventh day, it grants all desires; on the twelfth day it is known to be so;
and on the thirteenth day, it perishes.
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, it brings about the destruction of the performer;
likewise, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, it fulfills all desires.
O King, one should know that it is "large-contacted" (bṛhatspṛśā) as well as "faulty" (doṣavatī),
when it is joined by portents in the heavens, in the atmosphere, and on the earth.
In that case, the installation should be performed by the agent who bestows the disease; however, the ritual action should take place there.
When there is a decrease in the lunar day (tithi), it should be known as a loss (kṣaya); when there is an increase, it is proclaimed as an increase (vṛddhi).
[Thus it is stated] in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The fifth, the second, the third, as well as the eighth, the tenth,
and the full moon day— if performed, they shall indeed be fruit-bearing.
In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"Among those [lunar days], on the bright fortnight, one should perform [the rite] on the second lunar day (*tithi*).
The second bestows longevity and intelligence; the third bestows abundance of sons."
The fifth [lunar day] always bestows prosperity, and the seventh destroys disease;
the tenth brings increase of land, and the thirteenth brings good fortune;
indeed, the full moon day (Paurṇamāsī) always grants various kinds of wealth.
Nandā is [formed] by twenty-one cubits, and Bhadrā by fifteen, seven, and twelve.
For when the *rāma*, *ahi*, and *kāma* [values] are subtracted from the *veda*, *graha*, and *indriya* [positions],
and the result is increased by the *vāṇa*, *dik*, and *tithi* [values], they are respectively deficient, equal, or beneficial.
These [planets] are favorable during the bright fortnight and unfavorable during the dark fortnight;
Jupiter bestows both longevity and wealth, while Mercury grants victory and riches.
Indeed, for the growth of peace, all [planets]—Arka (the Sun), Śubha (Mars), Śukra (Venus), and Candra (the Moon)—are auspicious;
as are Karka (Cancer), Vṛṣa (Taurus), Tulā (Libra), Ācārya (Jupiter), Śrī (Mercury), Siṃha (Leo), and the pair of Grāma (Pisces).
In Pisces, the predominance of the signs begins from Aquarius, Capricorn, and Aries;
however, this sequence of four signs proceeds from six, eight, four, and three [degrees] respectively.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, [it is said]: "On a Sunday it is radiant; on a Monday it brings security;
on a Tuesday one may be consumed by fire; and on a Wednesday it bestows wealth."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The Śitā [consecration] always brings joy to the world in a house that is large; the Pratiṣṭhā is declared for a *Saura* [temple], lasting as long as the moon and sun endure."
Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday—these three days bring auspicious results;
an ascendant and a lunar mansion aspected by these planets is highly commended.
In the [chapter on] the characteristics of the conjunctions: Prīti, Saubhāgya, Āyuṣmān, Sukarmā, Śobhana, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi,
Siddhi, Śubha, Sādhya, Varīyān, Śiva, and Śukla.
The yogas known as Brahma, Indra, and Śiva are likewise auspicious.
Vava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila,
Gara, Vaṇija, Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, and Kiṃstughna— these he declared to be the Viṣṭis devoid of [specific] days within the two fortnights.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "In the *śakuni* [yoga] it produces defects; in the *catuṣpada* it brings about existence;
in the *nāga* it is gentle; and in the *kintughna* it bestows auspiciousness."
In Kaulava, she is to be known as the Bestower of Boons; in Taitila, she is the Destroyer of Disease;
in the one called Gara, she is the Generator of Disease; likewise, in Vaṇij, she is the Giver of Nourishment;
in Viṣṭi, she brings death to the performer and is possessed of self-defects.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The two Āṣāḍhas, as well as Mūla, the three Uttarās,
Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Rohiṇī, and likewise Pūrvābhādrapadā."
Hasta, Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras,
Anurādhā, Svātī, and Rohiṇī are praised for consecrations.
In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"O twice-born one, when Puṣya is joined with Rohiṇī, it is the time for the *pragāḍha* [posture];
O King, [it is performed] under Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Citrā, and Jyeṣṭhā."
Dhaniṣṭhā and Śravaṇa belong to the Vaiśya caste; likewise, Bhādrapadā belongs to the Yuga;
Aśvinī and Revatī belong to the Bhadra; and both Svāti and Phālgunī belong to the same.
The four castes, women, and slaves [are assigned to] Mūla, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, and Maghā;
these same four, in reverse order, likewise belong to the outcaste (antyaja).
The three Rohiṇīs cause victory over disease, while [the third] increases fear; Hasta bestows success, and the pair of Āṣāḍhās grants longevity.
Punarvasu shall grant happiness, while Anurādhā grants prosperity;
Citrā grants constant wealth and happiness, and Jyeṣṭhā brings about the destruction of disease.
Dhaniṣṭhā bestows victory over enemies; Śravaṇa always grants knowledge;
Pūrvā- and Uttarā-Bhādrapadā bring prosperity; and Aśvinī brings many friends.
Revatī always bestows nourishment; Svātī shall bring much wealth;
the two Phālgunīs grant prosperity; and Bharaṇī effects the destruction of enemies.
Ārdrā brings the attainment of good fortune; in Mūla, there is honor from the king;
Mṛgaśiras always bestows peace; Śatabhiṣaj is auspicious, though one should avoid it [at certain times]; Aśleṣā, Kṛttikā, and Viśākhā likewise bestow auspiciousness.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The *Kṛttikā* [constellation] is radiant and brings about the subjugation of spirits;
having become somewhat so at that time, it is not [affected] by the fire associated with it."
That excellent woman [was born] from Agni, Sūrya, Soma, and Kumāra;
and Gaṅgā and others were created there, and they are not burned by fire.
In the Prājāpatya muhūrta, she is always the bestower of favor upon the worlds for the householder;
in the Saumya, she is declared to be the granter of boons, yet she is destroyed by mice.
Under Ārdrā, it brings about the death of the performer very quickly;
under Punarvasu, there is destruction, and one must undergo the funeral rites again.
In the Puṣya asterism, one attains nourishment through wealth and likewise through fame;
yet that [offering] may lead to the destruction of the performer and cause the ruin of the Nāgas.
It brings about the death of one's parents and likewise leads to the destruction of the performer;
it becomes accessible to the world through fortune, and likewise carries destruction for the performer.
There too, it brings happiness to its creator, the god of love;
likewise, for Aryaman, it is abundant through Sudṛśā and performs grace for the worlds.
Bestowing longevity when held in the hand, it meets its destruction under Citrā;
yet under Citrā, it grants benefit and eternal sovereignty in the world.
Under Svāti, she is the bestower of boons, gentle, and the performer of grace for the worlds;
under Indrāgnī, she brings about the destruction of the doer; and under Maitra, she serves for the increase of friends.
One born under Jyeṣṭhā will be endowed with splendor and possessed of wealth and grain;
likewise one born under Mūla will be of such a nature, yet she will be a refuge for living beings.
In the first [nakṣatra], she suffers distress; under Viśvedevas, she bestows happiness;
under Śravaṇa, she is rich in wealth and grain; and under Vāsava, she is endowed with riches.
O best of men, in the Vāruṇa [direction] it leads to swift destruction; likewise, in the Āpya [direction], it is firm and prosperous, bestowing happiness upon the builder.
In the Ahirbudhnya [direction], it is firm and flourishing, granting happiness to the maker.
In the asterism of Puṣya, it is endowed with wealth and grain; in Āśvinī, it destroys yoga;
in Yāmya (Bharaṇī), it brings death to the performer and likewise causes self-destruction.
With Saturn, she generates grief; with Saturn, she bestows death;
with Mars, she causes fear of speech; but with Rāhu, she is not stable.
When a constellation is fumigated by Ketu, one shall suffer from fire and burning;
by whatever [constellation] the rising of Ketu occurs, through that one shall experience famine.
By whichever [planet] there is an arising on a Tuesday, one shall be burned by that fire;
by whichever there is an arising on a Saturday, by that the doer perishes.
When a constellation is surrounded by a halo, there shall be fear of an enemy army;
when struck by a meteor, it portends destruction along with the dread of an earthquake.
Wherever a meteor fall occurs, there shall be the onset of disease; a lunar mansion (bha) associated with these three kinds of portents is proclaimed to be inauspicious.
It leads to the destruction of divine fame when occurring on a Tuesday, and to one's own destruction when occurring on a Saturday.
And she should be known as being in the intermediate space, likewise as the destroyer of the world.
One should avoid a single lunar mansion when it is joined with the *vaidhṛta* or *vyatīpāta* yoga; likewise, one should avoid those joined with the remaining defects until the return of the sun.
That [constellation] prescribed for the birth-star brings prosperity to the performer;
in the second, it brings wealth; in the third, it bestows fear from enemies.
In the fourth month it is auspicious; in the fifth, it increases disease;
in the sixth, it brings about the success of undertakings; and in the seventh, it bestows death.
In the eighth [month] she is the giver of boons and gentle; in the ninth, the increaser of prosperity;
she is declared to be the accomplisher of rites; and on the birthday, in the tenth, she is auspicious.
In the eleventh year she brings auspiciousness; in the twelfth, she bestows fear of enemies;
in the thirteenth, she should be known as secure; and in the fourteenth, she gives disease.
Nandā bestows intelligence in the fifteenth [day], grants final liberation in the sixteenth,
brings prosperity in the seventeenth, and shall likewise exist in the eighteenth.
In the nineteenth [year], it brings death to the doer;
likewise, in the second [year] it bestows wealth, and in the third, it grants fear from enemies.
In the fourth month she is the mother of security; in the fifth, she increases disease;
in the sixth, she should be known as the bringer of fortune, increasing wealth and grain.
In the second, fourth, fifth, as well as the eighth,
twelfth, and ninth lunar mansions, [a marriage] will be fraught with faults for the bridegroom.
When the third, sixth, eleventh,
tenth, and seventh houses from the Janma (ascendant) are pierced by planets;
One shall obtain results from sin progressively through the fifth, the ninth, the twelfth, and likewise the eighth, or the fourth and third houses respectively.
If the piercing is done in reverse order, even a malevolent [planet] is considered to produce auspicious results;
however, when the Sun is in the twelfth house from the Moon, or in the second, it bestows fear.
On the twelfth or the second Tuesday, one may suffer a burning fever;
on the twelfth or the second Saturday, it shall bring about death.
When the Moon is situated in the midst of malefic planets, it will certainly bring about death;
however, when the Moon is established in a single quadrant (kendram), [it brings prosperity].

Furthermore, if another triad of points is occupied by the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, then the consecration will lead to the destruction of the patron, O King. If the Moon is with the Sun, it leads to destruction; if Mars is there, one shall suffer from fire.
In the Sāsaura yoga, it should be known as bestowing death; in the Sarādau, it bestows destruction.
If the moon is eclipsed in the asterism of Āśleṣā, it brings death to the performer;
likewise, when the moon is in the final quarter of Jyeṣṭhā,
or when it is in the final quarter of Revatī, it causes the destruction of the performer.
In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
Jupiter is always auspicious in the nine, six, and eight houses, as well as in the seven positions.
Budha (Mercury) [is auspicious] when situated in the sixth, eighth, fourth, tenth, second, seventh, or ninth houses from the ascendant.

The Moon, situated in the third, seventh, sixth, or tenth house, bestows auspicious results; so does the Sun when placed in the tenth, third, or sixth house, and Rāhu when joined with the third or tenth house.
Mars, Saturn, and Ketu are auspicious when situated in the three and six houses;
likewise, all planets—whether benefic, malefic, or with malefics—are auspicious in the eleventh house.

The aspect of these [planets] upon the Moon is full; it is three-quarters for Mars and Jupiter; it is one-quarter when situated in the directions of Rāma (3) and the Vasus (8), being reduced by one quarter [respectively].
The second is called Sāpadā, while the fourth is designated Kṣema; the sixth is Sādhikā Tārā, the eighth is Śatrusāśikā,
and the ninth is Atimitrā— these five yield their respective fruits.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"If [the asterism] occurs at the rising of the natal sign (*janmarāśi*) of the performer, it will quickly bring about destruction.
In the second house, it leads to the loss of wealth; in the third, it bestows prosperity upon the performer."
In the fourth [house], it leads to the destruction of the home; in the fifth, it brings about disease;
in the sixth, it results in the destruction of enemies; and in the seventh, it is destructive of wealth.
In the eighth house, it should be known as bestowing death; in the ninth, it is the destroyer of dharma;
in the tenth, it leads to the increase of actions; and in the eleventh, it becomes the bringer of gain.

In the twelfth house, however, there would be expenditure; yet if the consecration is performed thus, it becomes excellent during the rising of the Gemini ascendant and shall be possessed of wealth and grain.
One should indicate the remaining results of the birth-ascendant for all positions.
O King, when Aries rises, an action performed quickly meets with destruction;
when Taurus rises, it is said to be stable and endowed with wealth and grain.
And she is beloved by the world, bringing much auspiciousness to the pair.
In Cancer there will be swift destruction; in Leo it shall become very firm;
in Virgo it will be beloved by sorrow; and in Libra it becomes stable.
In Scorpio, it is said to be stable; in Sagittarius, it leads to prosperity;
in Capricorn, there is swift destruction; and in Aquarius, it becomes firm when rising.
In Pisces, it bestows qualities upon the doer; at dawn, it likewise becomes void.
It is fierce when associated with the Sun, and gentle when associated with the Moon.
When conjoined with a malefic planet in a quadrant, it is said to lead to the destruction of the doer.

A gentle [planet] in the cloth [of the horoscope] brings great auspiciousness to the maker and bestows prosperity; O best of men, whatever result occurs in the ascendants and the ninth-parts (navāṃśas), that very same result is to be understood in the twelfth-parts (dvādaśāṃśas).
It should be known that when the Moon and Sun are at the thirtieth degree (triṃśāṃśa) for the destruction of the progenitor,
the progenitor shall live for a hundred years and it will bring prosperity to his great-grandsons.
O Great King, when the ascendant has a malefic aspect, a benefic portion is auspicious;
but when a highly auspicious ascendant is attained, a malefic portion is not purifying.
When the Sun is situated in the ascendant, it brings grief to the doer;
in the second house, there will be loss of wealth; in the third, there is union with riches;
in the fourth, there is a decline of life-span; and in the fifth, the destruction of children.
In the sixth [house], there is the destruction of enemies; however, in the seventh, poverty shall occur.
In the eighth house from the Sun, there is the death of the father; in the ninth, oppression of dharma;
in the tenth, the increase of sons; and in the eleventh, one becomes endowed with gain.
In the twelfth house, she will be joined with expenditure and likewise become destitute;
however, O best of men, when the Moon is situated in the ascendant, she should be known as very firm [in her character].
In the second [dasa], she is endowed with wealth; in the third, she is joined with gains;
in the fourth, she is beneficial to kinsmen; and in the fifth, she bestows the increase of sons.
In the sixth house, it leads to the destruction of enemies; in the seventh, it brings wealth;
in the eighth, it is said to cause death; and in the ninth, it results in the affliction of righteousness.
In the tenth house, O King, she is said to be a giver of Dharma; in the eleventh house, she becomes a bestower of gain;
in the twelfth house, she is spendthrift and likewise devoid of wealth.
When the moon is more than half-full, the fruit of the auspicious fortnight occurs;
now learn from me, in due order, what happens when it is more than half-waned.
If the Moon is situated in the ascendant, the destruction of kings should be known to occur swiftly;
if it is in the second house, there will be poverty; and in the third house, one will be endowed with wealth.
In the fourth house there will be abundant grain; in the fifth, it leads to the loss of sons;
in the sixth, to the destruction of enemies; and in the seventh, to the loss of one's wife.
In the eighth house she is said to lead to death; in the ninth, she is a destroyer of dharma;
in the tenth, she is endowed with wealth; and in the eleventh, she becomes possessed of gains.
If Mars is in the twelfth house, she will always be quarrelsome and likewise poor;
if it is in the ascendant, it brings death, and likewise, if in the second house, it bestows poverty.
Situated in the third house, it brings forth pure fame throughout the three worlds;
in the fourth, there shall be the loss of kinsmen, and likewise, in the fifth, the loss of sons.
Likewise, in the sixth [year] there is the destruction of enemies; in the seventh, one perishes by fire;
in the eighth, the death of the performer [of the rite]; and in the ninth, the falling out of teeth.
In the tenth house, there shall be success in action; in the eleventh house, one becomes possessed of gains;
and in the twelfth house, the wife, children, and others will always cause expenditure.
If Mercury is in the ascendant, she is endowed with wealth; likewise, if in the second house, it is so;
in the third house, she is said to be a bestower of boons; and in the fourth house, she is joined with riches.
Fame is to be known in the fifth [house], and in the sixth, the destruction of enemies;
it is to be known as bestowing happiness in the seventh, and likewise as bestowing joy in the eighth.

O King, she bestows happiness in the ninth house, and in the tenth house she grants the increase of one's actions; she should be known as yielding stable gains when situated in the fourth, and as being endowed with wealth when situated in the twelfth.
If Jupiter is situated in the ascendant, the native will be rich; likewise, it will be so if he is in the second house.
If he is in the third house, she will have a firm standing, and in the fourth house, she will be endowed with wealth.
In the fifth [position], it is said to bestow learning; in the sixth, it destroys enemies;
in the seventh, it grants kingship to the doer; and in the eighth, it bestows prosperity.
In the ninth house, it should be known as bestowing fame; in the tenth, it bestows abundance of food;
when situated in the eleventh, it should be known as bestowing gain; and in the twelfth, it is endowed with gain.
When Venus is situated in the ascendant, it becomes steady and bestows all desires;
in the second house, it grants wealth; in the third, it increases one's brothers;
in the fourth, it should be known as bringing good fortune; and in the fifth, it grants an increase in progeny.
In the sixth house, she is to be worshipped; likewise, in the fifth, she bestows an increase of wealth;
in the eighth, she is said to grant happiness; and in the ninth, she grants both happiness and wealth.
In the tenth house, she will be beloved by the world; likewise, in the ninth house, there will be the destruction of enemies.
Similarly, when situated in the twelfth house, she should be known as one who spends well; likewise, in the second house, she will possess wealth.
If Saturn is situated in the ascendant, it bestows death; if in the second house, one becomes impoverished;
if in the third, it leads to the gain of wealth; and if in the fourth, it brings death to the doer.
If a malefic planet occupies the fourth house, there will be loss of sons; likewise, if it is in the eighth house, there is destruction of enemies.
If it is situated in the seventh house, there is loss of the wife; and if a malefic planet has entered the eighth house, death occurs.
If [the Moon] is in the ninth house, there will be a loss of dharma; if in the tenth house, a loss of action (karma).
If it is in the eleventh house, there will be great gain; and if in the twelfth house, there will be expenditure.
One should avoid a void in the quadrant and instead place [the planet] right there;
having thus understood the auspicious time with effort, the expert knower of destiny should perform the consecration through sacrifice and undertake it with careful attention.
On an auspicious day, one should first place the image as it stood previously, together with its pedestal and mother-figures, into the pit;
one who is composed should perform this at that very time on the new moon day.
In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"In Pisces and Aries, the portion [of the day] from the fourth quarter shall consist of three and three-quarter nāḍīs;
and Taurus and Libra, while consuming [the day], consist of four nāḍīs less one quarter."
In Capricorn and Gemini, as well as in Sagittarius, Aries, Libra, and Cancer, the degrees are three-quarters of a sign; in Virgo, they are five and a half ghatis.
Leo, Taurus, and Aquarius are fixed signs; they grant success.
Sagittarius, Libra, Aries, Gemini, Pisces, and Virgo are movable signs; Cancer and Scorpio are dual signs. These [latter] should be avoided as they cause the destruction of one's undertakings.
A stable ascendant, aspected by benefic planets, is auspicious;
when the ascendant is occupied by benefics, it bestows wealth and long life, especially when joined by Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury.
Kingdom, happiness, strength, and many things such as the customs of the country belong to men [when these houses are strong].
The first, seventh, fourth, and tenth are called kendras (angular houses).
Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury situated therein are bestowers of all success.

Malign planets situated in the third, eleventh, and fourth houses from the ascendant, while auspicious planets occupy other positions; likewise, the lunar days and so forth should be employed by the wise for purposes other than those that are inauspicious.
In a good conjunction, the eternal dharmas are attained; in a stable [ascendant], there is nourishment and long life;
in a favorable lagna, O illustrious one, and during the equinoxes, the desired fruit is obtained.
On the auspicious occasion of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, during the [solar] transit (*ayana*), and on a great lunar day (*tithi*),
prosperity, health, and sovereignty shall arise from the consecration of a deity.
When the ascendant has reached the twilight hour and all malefic planets have set,
yet there remains a malefic planet in a malefic ascendant and a lunar mansion conjoined with inauspicious factors.
When ill omens, portents, or the eclipsing of the moon and sun occur,
the deities installed in such places bring about destruction, famine, and disease.
Therefore, one should first observe the day and then procure all the necessary materials.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having ascertained the strength of the planets and stars, having performed the worship of the planets,
and having obtained favorable omens and signs while avoiding hunger and other such impediments..."
During an auspicious time, in an auspicious place, free from malefic planets,
one should perform the installation and other such excellent rites when the ascendant and the lunar mansion are favorable.
Likewise, during the solstices, the equinoxes, and similarly at the commencement of the six-aśīti periods,
one should perform the installation according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O best of kings, whatever fruit is declared for a particular lunar mansion,
that very same fruit is said here [to apply] even for its corresponding muhūrta, O Yādava."
The Raudra, the Sārpa, the Maitra, the Paitra, and the Vāsava;
the Ādya, the Vaiśya, the Brāhma, the Keśvara, and the Śakradevata.
O Lord of the Earth, the Muhūrtas of the Sun are Aindrāgneya, Nairṛta, Vāruṇa, Aryaman, and Bhāgya.
Raudra, Ajapāda, Ahirbudhnya, Pauṣṇa, and Āśvina;
Yāmya, Agnidevata, Brāhma, and likewise Saumya.
Āditya, Jīvadaivatyaka, Vaiṣṇava, Sūryadevata, Tvāṣṭra, and Yāmya are the Muhūrtas that move during the night.
Likewise: when the sun has reached the middle of the day during the eighth muhūrta called Abhijit,
one shall have all desires fulfilled and be freed from all calamities.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The reclining [of the deity] should take place during the Prājāpatya muhūrta, and the awakening during the Brāhma;
the wise man should perform the installation during that Brāhma muhūrta."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "When Jupiter has set or is situated in its sign of debilitation, [the lunar day] is a slayer of the performer."
Therefore, when Jupiter is situated in its own strength, it brings about wealth and grain.
In the Brahma [mudrā] it is known as firm; in the Raudra, it brings happiness; in the Prajāpatya, it bestows the heavenly realm;
and in the Svarga, she is the one who sets the wheel in motion.
In the Vānaspatya [yoga], she is the bestower of boons; in the Antya, she increases the end;
in the Vāsa, she is richly clothed; and in the Kāla, she is the giver of death.
In the southeast (Āgneya) one undergoes burning; likewise, in the quarter of the water-god (Varuṇa), one becomes impotent.
In the quarter of Sūrya (the Sun) she becomes very prosperous, and in that of Candra (the Moon), she is likewise a bestower of boons.
In the month of Āśvina, it is for the gods; in the month of Kārttika, it brings prosperity. In Caitra, it is said to bestow nourishment when it is worshipped accordingly.
In the Kaumāra [yoga] one attains growth, and likewise destruction in the Pitrya;
the Vāruṇa is said to bestow disease, while that presided over by Ananta is auspicious.
In the quarter of the forest deities (Vanadevatya), it is fickle; in the southern quarter (Yāmya), it bestows death;
in the quarter of the goddess of speech (Vāgdevatya), one always becomes eloquent; and in the quarter of Śrī, one becomes endowed with prosperity.
In the house of wealth, one is endowed with riches, very firm, and has the mountain as its presiding deity.
When conjoined with Pṛthvīdeva, it is firm, gentle, and auspicious; when with Vedadaivata, it likewise increases manifold merit and brings happiness to the performer;
and when joined with Tvāṣṭra, it is likewise so.
Thus concludes the general consecration.
Now follows the consecration of Śiva.
Now, regarding the compendium of characteristics:
when the sun has reached the northern quarter, the installation of the linga is most excellent;
however, during the southern solstice, it should be avoided, for it brings fear after three years.
Installation during an eclipse is not desired, nor likewise during the southern transit of the sun;
when a *liṅga* is installed during an eclipse, the subjects are afflicted by disease.
The princes are greatly oppressed, and a destruction of desires arises;
then, a very great decline of weapons occurs among kings.
For the maker, there is always destruction and terrible grief in the home;
therefore, one should not install the deity during an eclipse or during the southern solstice.
The installation should indeed be performed during the three seasons beginning with winter;
installed during the rainy season, it leads to success and bestows the yoga of the boon-granters.
In the winter, the installation of the *liṅga* bestows knowledge; in the cool season (*śiśira*), it grants all prosperity;
in the spring, it bestows fortune; and in the summer, it grants victory and peace.
For ascetics (*yatis*), the installation of the *liṅga* is prescribed at all times.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: "During the five months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha,
in their bright fortnights, when they are free from malevolent planets."
The second, fifth, sixth, seventh, ninth,
as well as the twelfth, eleventh, full moon day, and the thirteenth should be observed.
Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon should choose a time that brings happiness;
likewise, the asterisms Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣā, Svātī, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, and the sign Taurus [are auspicious].
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, and Revatī; Citrā, Hastā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Anurādhā—these are the constellations that bestow success.
In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"In whatever constellation [it may be], at all times during both fortnights,
the installation of the Liṅga is certainly recommended for an ascetic who desires his goals."
In the *Ratnāvalī*: Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Ayujman, Siddha, Sādhya,
Śiva, Śubha, Vṛddhi, Prīti, Dhṛti, Siddhi, Dhruva, Śukla, and Suśobhana.
Vava, Bālava, Kaulava, the auspicious Taitila,
Maitra, and Paramamaitra— these are prosperity, security, and likewise auspiciousness.
Scorpio, Leo, Aries, Gemini, Cancer,
as well as Virgo, Libra, Aquarius, and Taurus are praised as favorable ascendants.
Success shall be attained when the sun is in Hasta; likewise with Mṛgaśiras on Monday;
Kṛttikā on Tuesday; and Anurādhā when it falls on Wednesday.
Revatī conjoined with Bhṛgu on a Friday, Punarvasu on a Friday,
and Śravaṇa on a Monday are considered auspicious Siddhi-yogas.
Furthermore, the first, sixth, seventh, eleventh, and second houses from the birth sign are auspicious;
Mars and Saturn should be in Taurus, and Jupiter should be at two, seven, nine, or five signs [from the ascendant].
The auspicious Mercury situated in the fourth, seventh, eighth, or tenth house from the ascendant,
and Venus situated diligently in the seventh, eleventh, or second house;
All planets situated in the middle of the field are determined to be "Yamakaṇṭha";
since they destroy all undertakings, one should not employ them in those [tasks].
The waning moon is likewise dull, as are Mars and the Sun; Mercury is conjoined with them.
Since these are malefic planets and possess a malevolent disposition, one should therefore avoid them.
When Jupiter and Venus are situated in the tenth house, and when no planets are present in the ascendant or the moon's position;
likewise, when the moon has vanished and Venus and Jupiter have set,
one should avoid auspicious undertakings such as consecrations and long-distance journeys.
Whatever else is more secret than that, an expert in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra),
having thoroughly examined it, should employ it and then perform all tasks to be accomplished.

In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*: On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, adorned by the sun’s day and its asterism, with a favorable conjunction of the moon and stars, in a good *lagna* accompanied by a favorable *karana*. [Broken letters]
In the dualistic [view], there is establishment in the divine; in the mixed [view], it is in the white fortnight;
and in the non-dualistic [view], it is even in the black [fortnight], according to the distinctions of the mantra and the form.
The Raudrī of the Dvaita Siddhānta remains for a hundred years;
the Miśrā of Hari’s Pañcarātra remains for five hundred years.
That Bhairavī is indeed non-dual, born from the mantras of the Left (Vāma) and the Right (Dakṣiṇa);
she who abides as half of half of a hundred [fifty] within the self-manifested Bāṇaliṅga.
Thus concludes the installation of Śiva.
Now follows the installation of Viṣṇu.
In the *Vaikhānasa-saṃhitā*:
"One should perform [the rite] during the northern course of the sun, or during the southern course with haste.
This is stated in the *Devī-purāṇa* and the *Vaikhānasa-saṃhitā*.
"In former times, the two months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Māgha were censured by Brahmā.
Among the months, Phālguna is the best, as are Caitra and Vaiśākha;
it may also take place in Taiṣa, or in the month of Aśvayuj, or in the month of Śrāvaṇa."
In the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*:
"The installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) which was proclaimed by the sages shall now be described in due order:
the first lunar day (*pratipad*), the second, the ninth, and the thirteenth."
The tenth, the twelfth, and the full moon day in the bright fortnight are endowed with auspiciousness.
In the Mahāpañcarātra:
on the full moon day, the thirteenth, the twelfth, or during the bright fortnight on the first,
second, fifth, or even the tenth.
These lunar days are thus established; now hear from me the conjunctions with the constellations.
In the *Vaikhānasa-saṃhitā*:
"On the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Hasta,
Punarvasu, the three Uttaras, Revatī, Śraviṣṭhā, and likewise Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj)..."
Under the asterisms of Saumya (Mṛgaśīrṣa), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Anurādhā, and especially Tiṣya (Puṣya),
or under any other highly auspicious asterism endowed with the qualities as previously described.
In the conjunctions of Aśvinī and Rohiṇī, in Punarvasu, and in Puṣya;
in Bharaṇī, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Revatī, and the three Uttarās—
in these three sets of lunar mansions, respectively, during the northern course of the sun.
In the *Sāgarasaṃhitā*:
"Soma, Bṛhaspati, Bhārgava, and likewise Budha—
these are declared to be the gentle planets (*saumya-graha*) for the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā-yoga*)."
"Planets" (grahāḥ) refers to the days of the week. "Auspicious" (saumyāḥ) means favorable. As stated in the Mahāpañcarātra:
"On an auspicious day with a favorable planet, on a Monday, a Thursday, or a Friday."
Such a planetary conjunction should occur for the rites of consecration and sacrifice.
In the *Vaikhānasa-saṃhitā* of the *Nṛsiṃha-purāṇa*: "During the bright fortnight, at an auspicious time, when the asterism is stable and facing upward,
and when the *lagna* is favorable, Hari should likewise be installed by men."
On an auspicious lunar mansion and lunar day that form a favorable pair, free from the *viṣṭi* yoga,
and joined with a propitious weekday of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, or the Moon.
Even if it is favorable for the village and the sacrificer,

one should nevertheless avoid a movable zodiac sign (*cararāśi*) there and instead adopt a fixed zodiac sign (*sthirarāśi*); then, at a truly auspicious moment, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Hari.

In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*: On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, adorned with a favorable weekday, asterism, and lunar mansion; in a conjunction of a favorable moon and stars, at an auspicious moment (*lagna*), and endowed with a favorable *karana*.
In the dualistic [view], there is establishment in the divine; in the mixed [view], in the bright fortnight;
and in the non-dualistic [view], in the dark [fortnight], according to the distinction between the mantra and the form.
The dualistic (dvaita) Raudrī of the Siddhānta remains for a hundred years;
the mixed (miśra) Pāñcarātrī of Hari remains for fifty years;
but that non-dualistic (advaita) Bhairavī arises from the mantras of both the Left (vāma) and the Right (dakṣiṇa).
The procedure for the consecration of an image made of Madhūka wood is described in the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, under the Revatī asterism,
one should perform the installation there as a means to achieve success on earth."
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the installation of Viṣṇu.
Now follows the time for the installation of the Goddess (Devī),
as stated in the Devīpurāṇa.
When Venus is situated in Aries, one should then install the Goddess;
in this very world he shall be fortunate, and upon death, he shall go to the supreme state.
Therefore, when Venus is situated in Aries, the ninth lunar day is declared to be most excellent;
likewise, the months of Māgha and Āśvina are proclaimed to be most excellent.
The Goddess, though always composed of semen and dust, is established there;
she bestows fruit upon men when [the Sun] is situated in Cancer and in Taurus.
Likewise, Siddhas, Gandharvas, or kings desiring sovereignty should always worship the Goddess after having installed her according to the prescribed ritual.
Neither the lunar day (tithi), nor the asterism (nakṣatra), nor fasting is a requirement here.
The Mother-goddesses, Bhairava, Vārāha, Narasiṃha, Trivikrama,
and the slayers of the demon Mahiṣāsura should indeed be installed during the southern transit of the sun (dakṣiṇāyana).
And likewise, in the *Catuḥṣaṣṭi-pratiṣṭhā*:
Brahmā said:
"I shall now proclaim the ritual of installation (*sthāpana*), which accomplishes all desires."
It should be performed at all times, especially during the dark fortnight.
Since the Goddess has the form of night and Maheśvara has the form of day,
the Supreme Goddess bestows accomplishment through worship at their respective times.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the consecration of a goddess. Now follows the time for the consecration of tanks, wells, and so forth, according to the Vahnipurāṇa.
At that time, the ritual for step-wells, wells, and tanks is prescribed;
it is taught that the consecration performed on an auspicious day and under a favorable lunar mansion bestows blessings.
In Cancer there is the gain of a son; in Capricorn there will be happiness;
in Pisces there is fame and the gain of wealth; and in Aquarius there is an abundance of water.
In Taurus and Gemini there is prosperity; in Scorpio there shall be auspicious signs. In Virgo there is satisfaction for the ancestors, while in Libra there is eternal progress.
In Leo and Aries there is loss of wealth, yet O twice-born one, Lakṣmī bestows her grace.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"In that month of Kārttika, when it is especially full of water,
the rite for a pond should be performed during the conjunction with a fixed (*sthira*) lunar mansion."
Some sages maintain that [the rite may be performed] even after the northern course of the sun has passed;
there is no restriction regarding time in that case, for water itself is the essential cause.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the consecration of ponds and other waterworks.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Time for Consecration," within the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time) in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri—the illustrious Hemādri, the sovereign over all the faculties of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādevīya, and a master of all branches of knowledge.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Now, regarding the time for initiation (*dīkṣākāla*):
therein, the time for initiation for various deities is described in the *Kālottara*.
The conjunction of autumn and spring is the most excellent for the performance of the rite of initiation;
in their absence, the rainy season is recommended, but no other time is praised.
During initiation and consecration, as well as during the formal reception of mantras, at the commencement and conclusion of vows, in rituals involving the handling of ritual substances,
on the full moon days of Kārttika and Vaiśākha, and during an eclipse of the sun—
In that very same [text]:
"During lunar and solar eclipses, at the beginnings of the six-aśīti periods,
during the conjunctions of planets and constellations, and on the days of the equinoxes."
And in all the solstices, yoga bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
In the month of Pūrvāṣāḍha, in the month of Āṣāḍha, and in the month of Mṛgaśīrṣa,
the wise one should not perform initiation; he should perform it in other months.
In the bright fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, and joined with an excellent day and lunar date.
In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*:
"Initiation does not take place except on a festival day during the months of Vaiśākha and Pauṣa in the rainy season;
however, at other times, it may always be performed for the purification of both teacher and disciple."
At the beginning of the year, however, one should observe the auspicious omens.
The meaning is that even during times such as the rainy season when [initiation] is prohibited, initiation should nevertheless be performed whenever auspicious omens and the like are perceived.
The well-known lunar days, the sighting of Rāhu, the festival of the Guru,
and the Pavitraka day are also excellent for the performance of the rite of initiation.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: "The fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, and fourteenth—
excluding the full moon— are beneficial for those seeking liberation on the path to freedom."
For the sake of prosperity, one should avoid the days of Āditya (Sunday), Maṅgala (Tuesday), and Sauri (Saturday).
In the *Suprabheda*:
"On the seventh or the ninth, or else on the eleventh,
or on the tenth and the thirteenth, the rite of initiation is recommended."
In some places, however, the reading is "on the thirteenth day" or "on the new moon. One should examine the white, the moon, and the planet Jupiter according to their merits and demerits;
those endowed with merits should be accepted, while those devoid of merits should be rejected.
In the Kālottara:
"Furthermore, on the fourth, the eighth, and likewise the fourteenth,
as well as on the full moon day during the bright fortnight, [the rite] should be performed by those desiring prosperity."
Those who desire liberation should perform whatever rite they may during the dark fortnight,
with the exception of the days of the moon's change and those other lunar days that are traditionally prohibited.
In the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
[858] "Having first observed each respective lunar day (tithi) as prescribed therein, one should initiate [the disciple] on that occasion.
Indra said:
O Nārada, tell me specifically which lunar day (tithi) is prescribed for whom;
likewise, explain briefly the specific occasion for initiation (dīkṣā).
Nārada said:
The full moon day (pūrṇamāsī) is declared for Brahmā; the twelfth day (dvādaśī) for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu);
the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) is declared for Śiva; and the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) is proclaimed for Vāc.
The second is declared to belong to Śrī, and the third to Pārvatī;
in the Nitya paths, the eighth and fourteenth [tithis] belong to Pārvatī.
The eighth day is prescribed for Gaṇanātha, while the seventh is said to belong to Bhānu (the Sun).
Thus, the lunar days have been briefly defined by their primary designations;
however, in detail, all lunar days are remembered as suitable for the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*).
In the case of the cause [of the eclipse]: the asterism of Puṣya, Rohiṇī, Āditya (Punarvasu), Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Sāvitra (Hasta),
Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Vāyavya (Svātī), Nairṛta (Mūla), and Maitra (Anurādhā).
O observer of noble vows, the lunar days, the three Uttarā-phalgunīs, Ārdrā, and Śraviṣṭhā— the three birth asterisms— are the auspicious constellations for the rite of initiation.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: the three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Maghā, Mūla, and Revatī.
Abhijit and Śravaṇa, as well as the fourteenth lunar day in conjunction with Śiva-yoga;
and the yogas are remembered as Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and Śobhana.
Sukarmā, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, Harṣaṇa, Varīyān,
Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Aindra are the sixteen [Muḥūrtas].
All those [actions] are censurable, yet they are praised for the sake of liberation;
however, regarding the initiation by a teacher and so forth, they are auspicious here as well, just as before.
The first lunar day with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, likewise the fifth with Kṛttikā;
the tenth with Pūrvabhādrapadā, and likewise Rohiṇī with Jyeṣṭhā.
The twelfth lunar day with the constellation of the Serpents (Āśleṣā), and the thirteenth with Āryaman (Pūrvaphalgunī)—
these are known as the "Lamba" constellations, and they bring destruction even to the gods.
Regarding the cause:
both the movable and fixed signs are recorded as being either excellent or middling;
however, all planets are to be avoided when situated in the eighth house (the house of death).
The mutual compatibility between the teacher and the disciple will bring about auspiciousness.

In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*, the purification of the divisions such as the zodiac signs, as well as the strength of the ascendant, the Moon, and the Sun, and the purity of their transits (*gocara*), should be understood from the treatises on astrology (*yogaśāstra*).
O auspicious lady, all defects of the ascendant and all defects of the planets are destroyed when Venus is mature and situated in the ascendant,
and Jupiter is situated in a quadrant.
Having thus skillfully examined [the matter], regarding initiation for those seeking liberation,
no restriction of time or other such factors is prescribed for those seeking liberation.
The wise one should indeed combine those who are Siddhas and Susiddhas among the syllables of the mantra;
he should count those who are Vaivarṇas and Udāsīnas separately by tens.
One should divide the heap of Siddhas by eight, twelve, and six;
whatever remains as the pure heap is indeed declared to be the number for the watch (yāma).
The remaining month, situated in the enemy zodiac sign, is thus proclaimed;
one should divide it by fifteen parts for the sake of knowing the lunar days (tithis) pertaining to the mantra.
In that month and at such a watch, one should perform the initiation into the *mantra*;
or, having determined the auspicious moment (*lagna*) with certainty from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), one should become initiated.
Having established here the auspicious lunar days (tithis) for the purpose of initiation (dīkṣā), it is indeed stated in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"Listen now to the special occasion for initiation even without regard for the lunar day:
when a rare and singular opportunity to meet a true guru has arisen."
When permission for that has been obtained, it shall be the occasion for initiation.
Whether in a village or in a forest, in a field or by day or by night,
whenever the Guru arrives by chance, then the initiation shall take place.
Then initiation should be known as attained when the Guru is present;
whenever there is the desire [for it], then initiation occurs in accordance with the Guru's command.
Thus ends the time for initiation into various deities.
Now follows the time for initiation into Viṣṇu,
according to the Kratupañcarātra.
Having recognized that his disciple was inclined toward statesmanship,
at a time when the moon was waxing and joined with an auspicious conjunction during the period of the hot-rayed sun, he [instructed him].
The guru, indeed, should initiate [the disciple] out of compassion.
In the *Mahāpañcarātra*:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, likewise at the sun's transit (*saṃkramaṇa*),
