on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, or on the full moon day, O Sage."
On the new moon day, or else having designated a specific time,
the preceptor should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) one, two, or three days prior to that.
In the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"The full moon day is declared for Brahmā; the twelfth day for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu);
the fourteenth day is prescribed for Śiva; and the fourteenth day is likewise prescribed for Vāc."
In the *Aurva-pañcarātra*, regarding the matter of the ninefold initiation (*navaka-dīkṣā*),
it is stated that within the ritual procedure for initiation,
the lunar days (*tithi*) of the twelfth and the fifteenth should occur during the ninefold period.
Whether it be the eleventh, the fifteenth lunar day, the fourteenth, or the eighth,
these are praised for rituals involving conjunctions, such as journeys and the like.
For the deities, the ninth and the fourth [syllables] may be [the long ones].

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Time for Initiation," in the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time) within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the lord of all the faculties of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
[862] Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Next is the time for the worship of the deities beginning with Naimittika, as well as its constituent parts.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Time should be known as twofold, characterized as gross and subtle;
the gross is to be known as worldly, and likewise the subtle as pertaining to the self (*adhyātmika*)."
Everything should be performed in its gross form; now hear the gross rules for time.
A *truṭi* is said to consist of one-fourth of the blink of an eye at rest.
Two of those [lava-s] are said to be a lava; two of those would be a nimeṣa.
Fifteen nimeṣas are a kāṣṭhā, and thirty kāṣṭhās are recorded as a kalā.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, which is the same as two *ghaṭikās*.
Seven and a half *nāḍikās* are called a *yāma*;
these junctions (*sandhi*) are declared by the wise to be eight in number within a day and night.
But the sacrifice of the image is proclaimed as the most excellent;
it should be performed at sunrise, at midday, at dusk, and during the half-watch of night.
Sacrifice is middling when the [sun] rises or sets at midday;
however, one should especially worship during these times, which constitute the supreme limit.
One should perform worship for one's own sake twice or thrice a day;
for the commencement of worship, perform the entire ritual of the junctions (saṃdhyā), beginning with the offering of oblations (bali) and ending with the final rites.
If faults arise from transgressing the sequence of the twilight rites and so forth, there is no fault when it has been performed;
one should offer the bali-oblation in the forenoon, at midday, and at nightfall.
One should not perform the sequence of offerings at any other junctions of time;
however, one who desires specific results should especially offer the bali during the half-watch of the night.
One should especially perform [the rite] during daily festivals, during worship, and likewise during annual festivals; otherwise, one should not perform it.
Beginning from sunrise until ten nāḍikās have passed,
this is declared to be the morning time for rites such as installation and consecration.
Starting from the forenoon until ten *nāḍikās* have passed,
it should be understood as "midday" for rites such as the installation and consecration.
The period beginning from midday until ten nāḍikās [has] been called evening; now hear about *pradoṣa*.
Starting from sunset, seven and a half nāḍikās are known as *pradoṣa*; now hear about the *ardhayāma* that follows.
Beginning from the end of *pradoṣa*, three *nāḍikās* consisting of three quarters [of a *yāma*] are declared to be half a *yāma*; now, *ardharātra* (midnight) is described.
Starting from the end of the half-watch (ardhayāma) until ten nāḍikās [have passed], it is called "midnight" (ardharātra); thereafter, the night is called "nakta."
Three *nāḍikās* consisting of three quarters prior to the rising of the sun are declared to be "night" (*nakta*); knowing this, one should perform everything accordingly.
The collection of water, the gathering of flowers, and likewise the sacrifice should be performed at sunrise,
or the taking of water may be done at the end of the night;
one should perform the installation of the deities and the pilgrimage to the sacred ford during the morning hours.
O Prajāpati, the rites for the sacred ford (tīrtha) should be performed starting from the time of dawn until ten nāḍikās have passed.
In the rite of depositing the sprouts, however, there is the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the festival.
In the evening, the wise one should begin both the protection and the binding.
One should perform all the preliminary consecrations (adhivāsana) at midnight, including the installation, the sprinkling, and likewise the deposition of the embryo.
Especially at the end of the night, for the sake of performing all divine rites,
one should raise a great sound to bring about the cessation of inauspiciousness.

Thus concludes the section on the timing for the subsidiary rites of worship to the deities of the daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) types. Now follows the time for the worship of Viṣṇu; regarding this, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
One should worship the Dharma once, twice, or thrice a day;
a person who eats without having worshipped it shall go to the hells.
In the *Nāradīya*: "One should commence the worship of Viṣṇu in the morning, at midday, and in the evening;
like the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), the daily worship of the deity is so ordained by the wise."
If one is unable to perform it in detail, having worshipped Keśava in the morning,
one should also offer a handful of flowers at midday and at evening.
At midday, having worshipped Hari either elaborately or briefly, one should take food; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
On all auspicious occasions, and especially at that specific time,
one should worship the Lord of the Gods after having diligently procured the necessary materials.
Thus concludes the time for the worship of Viṣṇu.
Now follow the specific lunar days (tithis) for the worship of particular deities,
as stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa.
The first is said to belong to Agni, the second to Śamana,
the third to the Daughter of the Mountain, and the fourth to the Dispeller of Obstacles.
The fifth lunar day is remembered as belonging to the Nāga kings, and the sixth is known as Skāndī.
The seventh belongs to the Sun (Saptasapti), and likewise the eighth to the Eight-formed One (Aṣṭamūrti).
The ninth belongs to the Yoginīs, and the tenth likewise to Yama.
The eleventh [tithi] belongs to the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada), and likewise, the twelfth belongs to the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrin).
The thirteenth day belongs to Anaṅga, the fourteenth to Bhūteśa,
the full moon to Prajeśa, and the new moon is said to belong to the Pitṛs.
Thus are the specific lunar days for the worship of specific deities.
Now follows the worship of specific deities on specific lunar days and so forth, according to specific desires, as stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Having worshipped and offered oblations to Agni, one obtains ambrosial ghee on the first day of the lunar fortnight;
by offering oblations of all kinds of grain, one shall attain immeasurable wealth.
And having worshipped Brahmā on the second lunar day and fed those who observe the vow of celibacy, one shall become a master of all branches of knowledge.
On the third lunar day, by worshipping the Lord of Wealth (Vitteśa), one certainly becomes a lord of wealth;
in transactions such as buying and selling, there shall be manifold profit.
O Brahmin, when Gaṇeśa is worshipped on the fourth lunar day for all undertakings, he ensures that there is no obstacle for the wise; indeed, he never causes the destruction of their work.
Having worshipped the Nāgas on the fifth lunar day, one is not overcome by poisons;
one obtains a wife or sons, and shall attain supreme prosperity.
By worshipping Kārttikeya on the sixth lunar day,
a twice-born man becomes a master of illusion, endowed with beauty, long-lived, and an increaser of his fame.
On the seventh day, one should worship the god Citrabhānu, the maker of day;
on the eighth day, the god Hara, adorned with cow-horn crests, is worshipped.
He bestows vast knowledge and grants the qualities born of desire.
The destroyer of death, the giver of wealth, and the remover of sin, when duly worshipped;
having fully worshipped Durgā on the ninth lunar day for the sake of crossing over difficulties,
one shall always be ordained victory in battle and in legal disputes.
On the tenth day, Dharmarāja certainly removes all diseases and delivers the human being from hell and untimely death.
When the Viśvedevas are worshipped on the eleventh lunar day as prescribed,
they bestow progeny, intelligence, grain, and likewise land.
When the God, endowed with all sovereign powers, is worshipped on the twelfth lunar day, one shall possess many sons and much wealth; of this there is no doubt.
And on the thirteenth day, having fully worshipped the mighty Kāmadeva, he—
being honored with supreme devotion— shall cause wealth and sons to be bestowed.
On the fourteenth day, O Mahādeva, that Umākānta, the teacher of the world,
when worshipped with great devotion, grants all desires.
And for that devoted man who worships Soma on the full moon day, there shall be great attainment; this is my settled conviction.
On the new moon day, having always worshipped the ancestors with funeral cakes (piṇḍas),
they perform worship, prosperity, the acquisition of wealth, protection, longevity, and indeed strength.

Even without fasting, these [mantras], when always worshipped with recitations (japa) and fire-oblations (homa), and gratified with devotion, bestow the aforementioned fruits. The root-mantras (mūlamantra) are designated by their names, while the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) are proclaimed by their titles.
And previously, the Lords of the Lunar Days (tithīśvaras) were to be made situated upon lotus petals.
The forms of these [deities] are to be observed in the Devatākāṇḍa.
Worship with offerings of perfumes and flowers should be performed according to one's capacity; it must not be performed on the Śādya day, for even if performed, it yields no fruit.
An oblation performed with streams of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, food, and honey, when offered with a peaceful mind, bestows the fruits as described; likewise for recitation (japa).
Having performed the sacrifice for ten years with devotion, one shall obtain here these aforementioned fruits exactly as described, and even more besides.
In this life and in another as well, the knower of mantras shall always dwell happily in those worlds,
for as many lunar days as are remembered here.
Therefore, one who has fallen from this state is born as a man devoted to that [deity].
Handsome, endowed with wealth, and having conquered his enemies, he becomes a lord of the earth;
whether female, male, or neuter, such a person is born as a supreme being.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"The worship of the deities destroys the entire multitude of sins for men;
he who, having reached the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), propitiates Bhava [Śiva],"
Having worshipped Brahmā, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
By worshipping Mahādeva on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and likewise on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa, one is liberated from all sins.
Likewise, on the night of the thirteenth day,
having worshipped the three-eyed Lord with offerings during the first watch of the night, one is liberated from all sins.
Furthermore, having reached the new moon day and honoring three Brahmins with the ancestors in mind, one is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the sixth day during the bright fortnight and being composed in mind,
one who worships the Sun on the seventh day is liberated from all sins.
On the day of Bharaṇī, on the fourth lunar day, and on a Saturday, one should worship Yama;
by doing so, a person is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes.
By fasting on the eleventh day and worshipping Janārdana,
one is liberated from great sins on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*,
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I shall describe to you the specific rites for the worship of each individual deity."
For a year, being always observant of fasts, one who seeks omniscience should constantly worship the god Brahmā on the first day;
O fortunate one, having fasted on the fifteenth day of both fortnights.
O knower of dharma, after one year, he attains the world of Brahmā by means of a vehicle yoked with swans, possessing great splendor and abundant gold.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra,
having performed the worship of Brahmā while observing a fast on that day,
one obtains happiness for a year, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
O knower of dharma, all the divisions of time on that day, as well as the lunar mansions and planets when honored, bestow unsurpassed happiness.
On that day, one should worship the Naga who is the lord of the year;
thereby one obtains happiness from the planets as well as supreme health.
There, O twice-born one, one should always worship Agni, who was first created by Brahmā in the three worlds, and then Dakṣa Prajāpati on the second day;
O knower of dharma, he obtains the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice, of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, O Bhārgava, by performing worship on that day for the two Aśvins,
one constantly attains health as well as beauty.
On the second day of the bright fortnight, having performed the worship of the young moon and offered salt before nightfall, one shall become fortunate.
O highly fortunate one, by performing the worship of those twelve who have been declared as the *sādhya*s on the third lunar day, the fruit of twelve days shall be obtained.
Then, having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara individually on the third [lunar day],
O illustrious one, one shall partake in the fruits of the three goals of life.
[870] Then, having properly and diligently worshipped the three worlds by name,
one attains great sovereignty and finds the highest state.
The third lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa which is conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa—
by worshipping Govinda on that day, one shall obtain prosperity.
Having fasted on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
one obtains inexhaustible fruit for every meritorious deed performed.
Therefore, that [lunar day] conjoined with Kṛttikā is especially well-honored;
whatever is given, offered as an oblation, or recited there is said to be entirely inexhaustible.
Therefore, that lunar day is inexhaustible; whatever merit is performed on it becomes inexhaustible.
Because Viṣṇu was worshipped with unbroken grains (akṣata), that day is likewise considered "Inexhaustible" (Akṣaya).
A man who has bathed with unbroken grains (akṣata), having likewise offered unbroken grains to Viṣṇu,
and having also offered well-prepared oblations and likewise unbroken grains into the fire;
O highly fortunate one, by giving those same well-prepared barley-meals to Brahmins,
one enjoys imperishable fruit.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, by performing even one of these after having spoken thus, and likewise a second,
on the third day of the month, one shall obtain the fruit of all of them.
O Blessed One, regarding those twelve gods who were proclaimed of old by name:
having performed their worship on the fourth lunar day, one shall attain heaven.
Having performed the worship of Yamarāja on the fourth lunar day itself,
a righteous man does not experience the suffering of hell when the Son of the Sun is pleased.
Then, O delighter of the Yadus, by worshipping Vināyaka on the fourth lunar day,
one shall be liberated from all obstacles and attain the fulfillment of one's purpose.
On that very day, one should worship Nidrā, Rati, Śraddhā, Kīrti, Medhā, Sarasvatī, Prajñā, Puṣṭi, and likewise Kānti.
O best of men, through his grace one obtains whatever one desires;
especially one who longs for knowledge should worship Sarasvatī.
All the mothers of the gods, when worshipped on various days,
should be known as the granters of all desires for a wise man.
Having performed worship on the fifth [lunar day] with both mind and body,
a person attains great good fortune and acquires preeminent fame.

By worshipping the goddess Pṛthivī on the fifth [day], a person attains her with effort; there is no need for deliberation on this point. As for the ten Viśvedevas who were previously mentioned by me—
Having performed their worship on the fifth lunar day, one shall attain heaven.
By worshipping the Gandharva Iṣṭa on the fifth lunar day, one becomes fortunate;
likewise, by especially worshipping Citraratha, the king of them.
Likewise, by worshipping all the wives of the gods, one becomes fortunate;
and by sacrificing to an Apsaras, one shall obtain beauty such as hers.
Having likewise worshipped the beloved Nāga, one attains unsurpassed prosperity;
on the fifth lunar day, one should properly begin the worship at Puṣkara in Vārāṇasī.
O King, just as a sacrifice that fulfills all desires yields a good fruit,
so too should one worship Nalakūvara.
Having performed the worship of Śrī on the fifth lunar day while always remaining self-restrained,
one obtains abundant prosperity as proclaimed for the year.
[872] O King, on every fifth lunar day, one should worship Sarasvatī, Umā, Medhā, Bhadrakālī, and also Kātyāyanī, with delight and affection.
Dhṛti, Svāhā, Svadhā, Ṛddhi, Anasūyā, as well as Kṣamā,
Surabhi, Devasenā, Velā, Jyotsnā, and Śacī.
Gaurī, the wife of Varuṇa, and likewise the wife of Yama,
the highly fortunate one named Dhūmra, and similarly Mṛtyucchāyā.
One should likewise worship the mother of one's chosen deity and the daughter of a god; by doing so, one undoubtedly attains one's desire from her alone.
O King, by likewise worshipping Airāvata, Garuḍa, Uccaiḥśravas,
and the bull of Hara, as well as all weapons and missiles,
one attains victory.
Likewise, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
by performing the worship of the Nāgas, a man shall become a possessor of wealth.
And likewise Kumāra, Skanda, Vibhāvasu,
and Guha— the Blessed One, the destroyer of Krauñca, was designated by the Four-faced One.
By worshipping him on the sixth lunar day, a man obtains his desired sons;
by honoring the children, a man undoubtedly attains spiritual welfare.
Having performed the worship of the seasons there, O King, one shall obtain happiness; likewise, by worshipping those who attend upon Skanda, those who attend upon Rudra,
and those who attend upon Yama, one shall attain liberation from disease.
Having likewise worshipped Kālapāśa and the highly resplendent Sūryapatnī, one obtains all desired objects; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
[873] Thus the forty-nine Maruts have been proclaimed; by performing their worship on the seventh lunar day, one shall attain heaven.
By then performing worship of the beloved mountain, one shall become happy;
likewise, by worshipping the desired river, one shall partake in merit.
Having performed the worship of Agni, one attains the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice;
having performed the worship of Vāyu, one reaches the supreme goal.
Having honored the seven sages who are remembered as the Soma sacrifices,
one always attains those very fruits and finds the highest goal.
On the seventh [lunar day], O tiger among the Yadus, one should worship the sage with offerings;
one obtains the fruit of Vedic study and likewise enjoys that very fruit.
O highly fortunate one, having then worshipped the oceans within the island,
a man attains his desired world, even if it be situated in the subterranean realm (pātāla).
Having likewise worshipped the seven worlds there, one shall become happy;
and one shall obtain foremost wisdom, as well as immeasurable intelligence.
By worshipping the Gaṅgā in her sevenfold form as well as the goddess Sarasvatī,
a man certainly attains the merit of the seven sacrifices.
Having worshipped Āditya, O best of the Yādavas, one is quickly liberated from diseases; on the seventh lunar day, one also attains the highest intelligence.
A man who then worships the goddess Ekānaṃśā in this manner obtains the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
Having performed worship to Narendrapūjana, one shall likewise obtain supreme intelligence;
having worshipped Jayanta, the son of Śakra, one shall become happy.
Having performed worship on the eighth lunar day to the Vasus, one who is most excellent in dharma and wealth attains the celestial realm and whatever fire is desired by the mind.
At crossroads, on the streets, and likewise upon the threshing floors.
One should offer the oblation to the Piśācas on mountain peaks, in streets, on riverbanks, and also in the caves where cattle roam.
Then, having performed worship of the gods beginning with Śakra,
and having offered them a bali-oblation, a human being attains security;
and by worshipping his weapon, he shall then obtain victory.
Having indeed worshipped the Vaiśvadevas on the tenth day, as well as ten others,
one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
In that same way, O King, one should worship the ten directions;
wherever one is born, one obtains the fruit of one's actions.
Having fully honored Dharma, the Lord of Gods who brings happiness to all sentient beings,
one attains the state of Dharma as well as the very fruit of Dharma.
O Lord, by worshipping the eleven Rudras on the eleventh day,
one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
Likewise, one should joyfully worship the all-pervading Rudras everywhere;
thus one attains all desires that are omnipresent and unconquered.
Likewise, a person should worship the twelve Ādityas on the twelfth lunar day;
by doing so on the twelfth day, one attains everything and finds the highest state.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, the sovereign of the waters, Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, on the twelfth lunar day, one obtains the merit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Having likewise worshipped Śakra, the lord of all gods,
a person attains all desires and goes to the heavenly world.
Having performed the complete worship of Viṣṇu, one obtains all desired objects;
having attained the most excellent and cherished fruit, one finds the highest state.
Then, by worshipping Kāmadeva, the Lord of the World, on the thirteenth day,
one attains great good fortune and finds the highest state.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should then worship Kāmadeva;
through this worship, one obtains the entire fruit proclaimed for the year.
By performing worship of the yakṣas and rākṣasas on the fourteenth day,
one attains security as well as the successful fruition of one's undertakings.
Having worshipped the Lord Vaiśravaṇa, the presiding deity of wealth,
one obtains abundant riches and the fruit proclaimed for the year.
Having likewise worshipped Śaṅkha and Padma, the two treasures honored by yakṣas,
and having likewise worshipped Maṇibhadra, one obtains wealth without a doubt.
Having worshipped Mahādeva, especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, one shall attain all desires.
Likewise, O King, one should worship the hosts of ancestors when the moon has waned;
he partakes of the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
Having performed the śrāddha ceremony, O King, one shall obtain all desires;
likewise, by worshipping the golden moon, one shall attain great good fortune.
Or else, O King, descendant of Yadu, by worshipping the malefic planet or the lunar mansion,
one obtains safety and the fulfillment of desires.
O King, by likewise honoring the name of the month, the lunar mansion, the karaṇa, and the yoga, one shall obtain great good fortune.
Having fasted, one should worship the lunar mansion and its presiding deity;
by doing so on the left side of the lunar mansion, one shall obtain one's desire.
A man should worship the highly fortunate Kārttikeya during the Kṛttikās;
he obtains the merit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice and uplifts his entire lineage.
Likewise, by worshipping during the Kṛttikās, one obtains a victorious moment;
and by worshipping the serpent Bhogin, one attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By worshipping Kāmadeva, one shall obtain fortune and good luck;
likewise, by reciting [the mantra] over the Sāvitra and Hasta [nakṣatras], one shall attain success.
By worshipping the deity, nāga, yakṣa,
gandharva, or even the graha that one desires, one shall obtain one's wishes from them.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should then worship Mahākāla;
one attains all desires as well as [the state of] Īśa—of this there is no doubt.
One should worship Maheśvara, the host of Mothers, and likewise Vahni;
or, O King, by worshipping even a single Mother, one obtains the desired object of one's wish.
Likewise, a person should worship the five Gandharvas beginning with Tumburu;
he attains victory everywhere—of this there is no doubt.
By worshipping those who attend upon Skanda under the constellation Kṛttikā,
a person likewise attains great health or whatever is always desired by the mind.
O King, a man should worship an image of Nṛsiṃha, the full moon,
and the host of Mothers who are delightful in the fulfillment of all desires.
Or, O King, by honoring a single mother, one obtains all desired objects;
and by honoring trees, one attains the state of a tree-deity.
Having performed worship of the gods, of human beings, and others who belong to their factions, one shall become happy on the fourteenth day.
Whether at the time of the ritual or at the auspicious moment (muhūrta), one should worship the deity according to the rules;
thereby one attains one's desire and finds the highest state.
Starting from the month of Caitra, on the day as previously described, a person who always worships his chosen deity attains the fruit as stated.
O knower of dharma, O knower of all duties, if for a year— whether on a particular lunar mansion, a lunar day, or during the presence of the planets— one remains composed and observes a fast;
Whether for a year, a solstice, a season, a month, or its half, one who eats only at night and remains self-controlled, having always performed worship of its presiding deity,
shall obtain his desire from that [deity] for that duration of time, O highly fortunate one.
O Great-souled One, whichever [deity] may please you, beginning from Caitra, by worshipping that god,
he shall obtain his supreme desire through that deity's satisfaction in this world.
O moon of the Yadu dynasty, you have attained this through great effort.
Thus, according to specific desires, there is the worship of specific deities on specific lunar days and so forth.
[878] Now, according to specific desires, there is the worship of specific deities under specific constellations.
In the Devīpurāṇa,
Brahmā said:
"When a deity is situated in the aspect of a particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra), at that time..."
But Yajñadeva, staying on his thighs, shall then be the partaker of the fruit.
I shall declare the deities of the lunar mansions in their proper order,
as well as all the lunar mansions and the sacrifices individually.
A man born under Aśvinī, having been pierced by the two Aśvins, becomes long-lived;
even one greatly afflicted by diseases is quickly freed from them.
Having worshipped Yama under the asterism Bharaṇī with auspicious black flowers,
as well as with pure perfumes and other offerings, one is liberated from untimely death.
Anala, when fully worshipped on the day of Kṛttikā with red garlands and other offerings, as well as by oblations of ghee, will certainly bestow supreme prosperity.
Prajāpati, who is beloved and worthy of worship, likewise bestows desired cattle;
and under Rohiṇī, O tiger among gods, one should give horses and elephants.
Likewise, by worshipping Soma under Mṛgaśīrṣa, one attains victory and health;
and by worshipping Śiva under Ārdrā, one enjoys cattle and victory.
One attains divinity through white substances such as animals and by means of milk;
and one always attains Aditi through worship and other rites under the asterism Punarvasu.
Satisfied by the Caru offering, he indeed protects them;
when Jupiter is in conjunction with the asterism Tiṣya, he bestows abundant wealth and prosperity.
In Aśleṣā, the Nāgas are worshipped with perfumes, drinks, and other offerings;
and the host of ancestors is gratified with sweet and auspicious foods and the like.
In Maghā one should grant victory, and likewise Bhaga in Pūrvaphalgunī;
he shall fulfill the desired husband for both the maiden and the man.
In this [month of] Jyeṣṭha, there is longevity; likewise, Āryamā is honored in Āṣāḍha, and Savitṛ, the eternal treasury of universal splendor, is always worshipped in Haste.
By offering all auspicious flowers and other articles, one bestows abundant wealth;
and on Citrā, Tvaṣṭṛ grants a kingdom free from rivals.
When Vāyu is fully gratified under Svātī, he shall grant longevity and supreme strength;
and one should worship Indra and Agni under Viśākhā with yellow and red offerings.
Having reached Anurādhā and having honored a friend with devotion, one shall always dwell in wealth, sovereignty, strength, affection, and splendors.
He becomes beloved by all and shall attain a stainless mind;
having worshipped Śakra as before during the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, he shall obtain prosperity.
Having honored him with all virtues, with ritual action, and with wealth,
one should properly worship Nirṛti at the base with devotion, as before.
Thus, according to specific desires, there is the worship of specific deities under specific lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
[880] Now, regarding specific conjunctions of causal signs, lunar mansions, and so forth, there is the worship of specific deities.
In the Devīpurāṇa, Brahmā said:
"Listen, my child; I shall explain to you according to what you have asked."
It involves little affliction and great merit, being determined by the conjunction of planets, constellations, and lunar days.
Listen to the conjunction of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, the most excellent among the auspicious yogas,
when the group of soft letters (mṛduvarga) and the Bhāgya yoga coincide with Umā on a Saturday.
When, by the conjunction of fate, the sixth lunar day falls on a Sunday under the Puṣya asterism, then the Skanda sacrifice should be performed; it accomplishes all desires.
But when the seventh lunar day (saptamī) falls on a Sunday, that is indeed Vijayā;
on that occasion, a sacrifice to the Sun (Bhānu) brings about all auspicious qualities.

O Sage, when the moon is in conjunction with the Śaśirikta yoga and the Ārdrā nakṣatra, one should perform the worship of the Mothers; the Māghā goddesses and the Kālikā goddesses should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite. One obtains the full fruit [of the ritual] and becomes a lord in one’s own place.
Having worshipped with white flowers and offered water in the eastern direction during the month of Caitra, as previously described,
one is swiftly liberated from both physical and mental sin.
Likewise, during the month of Āṣāḍha, a wise man who, through the conjunction with Uttarāṣāḍhā,
worships the Viśvedevas with flowers and other offerings, attains heaven for himself.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, by devoutly gratifying Viṣṇu with flowers and incense,
one obtains prosperity, wealth, and victory.
Having worshipped the Vasus under Dhaniṣṭhā, one finds no fear anywhere;
likewise, even great dangers [are averted] for them with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Furthermore, by duly honoring Varuṇa, one is completely freed from diseases.
The afflicted person attains nourishment, health, and even sovereignty.
By worshipping the Unborn One, who resembles pure crystal, on the day of Bhādrapadā, one attains liberation; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Under Uttarā, one attains the supreme goal, Ahirbudhnya;
under Revatī, Pūṣan, being worshipped, constantly bestows cattle.
Through white [oblations], one attains nourishment, stability, fortitude, and victory;
these sacrifices have been described by me here in brief.
Indeed, for the benefit of practitioners of the lunar mansions' deities,
these [deities] certainly bestow fruits when worshipped with devotion according to one's means.
And whenever one intends to go to a village, especially on a journey,
one should certainly perform a sacrifice to the deity of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and carry out all those rites.
For when this is done, one obtains the full fruit of the journey.
And the fruit of the ritual action is complete; thus it was declared by Bhānu himself:
"In the absence of a sacrifice, one should perform recitation (japa) and one should perform fire-offerings (homa) as desired."
Thus ends the worship of specific deities according to the particular conjunctions of lunar days (*tithi*), asterisms (*nakṣatra*), and so forth.
Now follows the time for the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*). Among these, first is the time for the offering of the sacred thread to Śiva.
In the Śivadharma and Bhaviṣyat Purāṇas:
"Having diligently worshipped Śiva on the full moon day as well as on the sixth lunar day,
one should offer a sacred thread to Śiva and feed those who are devotees of Śiva."

Furthermore, having thus worshipped Śambhu on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should ask for his forgiveness and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the ascetics, beginning with threads and garments.
Whoever performs this *pavitraka* ceremony even once during the four-month period shall be honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred divine *koṭis* of *kalpas*.
Having fallen from his state due to the exhaustion of merit, he who was a knower of the four Vedas is born again;
having returned to this world, he becomes a king endowed with the form of a preceptor.

In the *Śivarahasya*: "One should perform the *pavitrāropaṇa* for Śambhu in the months of Nabhas or Śuci, on the fourteenth or the eighth lunar day, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) according to the prescribed rule."

Whoever performs the Pavitrāropaṇa rite in the month of Śrāvaṇa or on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada shall remain undefiled throughout the remainder of the year. By offering the pavitra to Śambhu, one who is empty attains fullness.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, by means of that which is more purifying than the purifier itself, one should bring peace;
for through it, all the bodily actions of men, though impure, become pure.
In the Kālottara: "Having performed worship, one should always perform the Pavitraka rite;
or else, one may perform it according to a fixed rule once every three months."
At the end of Āṣāḍha, on the fourteenth day of the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya,
as well as on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed; it is not established for any other time.
[883] When time has thus elapsed, one should perform the penance;
this rule applies especially to material beings during the bright fortnight.

Regarding the phrase "on the fourteenth day at the end of Āṣāḍha," the meaning is "on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha," intended as a lunar month ending with the full moon. And so it is stated in the *Mohacaurasūrottara*: "Likewise, [the time] prescribed for Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa is both the bright and the dark [fortnights]."
And on the seventh and the thirteenth [lunar days], there [should be] fragrant offerings and sacred threads.

On the thirteenth day, the rite known as the "Fragrant Purifier" (gandhapavitra) should be performed; furthermore, the "Purifier" (pavitra) is prescribed on the fourteenth day, and the observance for the month of Āṣāḍha is traditionally taught.
Even if this were the case, [the rite] should not be performed in the absence of Viṣṇu’s sleep; rather, it must be performed only after Viṣṇu’s sleep.
And it has been said:
"It should not be performed even in Āṣāḍha if Madhusūdana has not yet slept."
The time for this is also not fixed; hear now the determination of the rule.
One should perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha,
and on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.

[Objection: But surely the time immediately following Viṣṇu’s sleep is obtained by the phrase "on the fourteenth day of Āṣāḍha" itself; why then say "while Madhusūdana is asleep"? [Response: True. However, Āṣāḍha is of two kinds: lunar (*cāndra*) and solar (*saura*). Among these, Viṣṇu sleeps at all times according to the lunar month; furthermore, it is stated that Viṣṇu sleeps specifically upon the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) into Cancer during the solar month, even when there is an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*). Thus, there is no fault. [884]
And it is said in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "When the sun, situated in Gemini, touches two new moons, that is to be known as 'Double Āṣāḍha'; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer."
Likewise: When the sun passes beyond two new moons, that should be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa), excluded from all ritual acts.

And because of this statement, the intention is that one should not perform the *pavitra* rite during *Pūrvāṣāḍhā*. However, when there is an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) among the six months beginning with Caitra, resulting in a "double Āṣāḍha" (*dvirāṣāḍha*), then Viṣṇu’s sleep occurs in Śrāvaṇa.
Regarding this, it is said in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:

"If there are two new moons (*darśa*) in a single month among the six beginning with Mādhava, then it is a double Āṣāḍha; even then, the [sleep] is displaced to Caitra and Śrāvaṇa. Therefore, in such a case, the offering of the *pavitra* should be performed at the beginning of Śrāvaṇa at the very latest.
And it is said in the *Mohacaurauttara*:
"From initiation (*dīkṣā*) up to the installation (*sthāpanā*), and [the rites] such as the *pavitra* for Indra—
[one] should not perform the *pavitra* and so forth if one desires one's own welfare."
Where two new moons occur without the sun’s transit [into a zodiacal sign], that is to be known as an intercalary month; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
The Pavitraka rite must be performed during the month of Tulā or the intercalary month;
otherwise, while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, one would become a partaker of fault.

[Objection: But why should the solar month alone be accepted instead of the lunar month? For in that case, there is the suspicion of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*). [Response: It is not so. Generally, in the rite of the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), the lunar month alone is intended, and not the solar, because an expiation is prescribed when the sun has entered Virgo (*kanyā*). While Janārdana is asleep during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha...
It is praised whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, provided it is easy to ascend.
One who is afflicted by the increase of disease, living abroad, or oppressed by the king—
if such a person does not perform the "sūtrarohaṇa" (the fixing of the thread) during the three months mentioned,
he is like one joined with Dakṣānu when the sun has entered Virgo.

One should perform the *pavitraka* rite for Śambhu with the *aghora* mantra using *dakṣāṇu*; one must never do so while on a scale (*tulā*). One should avoid the intercalary month (*malimluca*), which is censured in all ritual acts.
Regarding the cause: one should avoid other times than the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha;
it should be performed during both fortnights, the bright and the dark.
One should install the sacred thread (pavitraka) on the fourteenth or the eighth lunar day.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: "When one desires to perform the *pavitraka* and other rites for Śambhu on a single day, having performed the daily [rituals],
one should then perform the occasional (*naimittikī*) twilight worship (*sandhyā*) once."
Having properly prepared it with abundant fragrance, a person should worship the sacred thread (pavitra).
When there is a split lunar day (khaṇḍatithi) therein, then [the rite should be performed] during the portions of those two lunar days.
When the fourteenth day is mixed with half of the full moon day, then it has been stated regarding another time:
"If, due to being otherwise occupied, [the rite] must be performed on that very [fourteenth day],
then one should perform the purification (*pavitraka*) along with its consecration (*sādhivāsa*), having interposed it by the duration of milking a cow."
One should perform [the rite] during the fourteenth lunar day; the remainder should be carried out on the remaining lunar day.
Having prepared the fragrant *pavitraka* on the seventh or the thirteenth day,
one should likewise perform the *pavitraka* rite on the eighth or the fourteenth day.
It is the established rule that the excellent *pavitraka* must be performed on the following day.
Then others have declared that it should be performed by two [days] or by one day.
On the thirteenth day of the intercalary month, on the following day, if one's mind should become distracted, one should perform the two rites separated by the time of milking the cows.
On the fourteenth lunar day, one should perform the consecration (*sādhivāsa*) of the sacred thread (*pavitraka*).
On the full moon day, it becomes a most excellent purification; however, this procedure applies even when there is a variation in the lunar date.
This same sequence for the installation of the thread (*sūtraropaṇa*) should also be understood to apply on the eighth day.
Thus concludes the time for the Śaiva Pavitrāropaṇa.
Now follows the time for the Vaiṣṇava Pavitrāropaṇa.
In that regard, the Pavitrāropaṇa is both optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya).
In that regard, the *Viṣṇurahasya* states:
"The offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to Viṣṇu bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is meritorious, granting fame to both women and men, and bringing about happiness, prosperity, and wealth."
Indeed, among merits, this merit is such that it removes all sins;
therefore, the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is remembered as the supreme purifier.
Whatever fruit a person obtains by worshipping Janārdana with devotion throughout the entire year, that same fruit is obtained through the rite of the Pavitrāropaṇa.
O best of sages, for him who does not perform the Pavitrāropaṇa according to the prescribed rule, his worship throughout the entire year becomes fruitless.
Therefore, every year, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Hari should be performed by men who are devoted to Viṣṇu and endowed with faith.
In the *Mantraprakāśa*, however, it is said:
"I shall describe the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), which bestows the fruit of all worship.
Rākṣasas carry off the fruit of his year-long worship and other rites."
He who does not perform the *pavitraka* rite according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, [incurs sin].
Year after year, one should perform the Pavitraka rite with supreme devotion for the pleasure of Hari, following the path prescribed by the sacred rules.

Therefore, it should be understood that once the rite of *pavitrāropaṇa* has been performed, results such as longevity and other benefits also accrue according to one's specific desires. As stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"In the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun is situated in Cancer..."
On the twelfth day, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Vāsudeva is prescribed.
The rite should be performed when the sun is situated in Leo, or when it has entered Virgo;
it should be done correctly on that very lunar day even when the sun is in Libra, but never otherwise.
Likewise:
"O twice-born one, one should perform the auspicious Pavitrāropaṇa during autumn or the rainy season,
on the twelfth day, or under the Śravaṇa asterism, or on the fifth day."
And even for those rites not specifically mentioned, they should be performed on the fourteenth day.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"When the sun has entered Karkoṭaka [Cancer] or likewise when it has entered Siṃha [Leo],
one should offer the purifying thread (*pavitraka*) to Hari on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight."
If, however, due to the occurrence of obstacles the primary time cannot be obtained,
one may even perform it during the period of Kanyā, as long as Hari does not rise [from his sleep].
In the *Sātvata-saṃhitā*:
"In the midst of those four months, on an auspicious day,
one should perform [the rite] from the fifteenth day of Āṣāḍha until that of Kārttika."
Regarding the phrase "the day of the full moon":
from the transit [of the sun] into Karkoṭaka until the end of the consumption of Libra,
the solar duration of this fortnight is designated as "mean."
Know that the end of the Ekādaśī is the Vaiṣṇava period characterized by the Cāturmāsya; it is the supreme time-limit that bestows all perfections.
Until this period is reached,

however, another period— such as that of the moon and so forth— must be completed by some means of interruption; one should accomplish it according to rule within the four-month interval, preceded by yoga.
Thus concludes the time for the *pavitrāropaṇa* of Viṣṇu. Now follows the time for the *pavitrāropaṇa* of various other deities.
In that regard, the months are exactly as stated for Viṣṇu; the distinction lies in the lunar days (*tithis*).
In the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*: "The first lunar day is said to belong to the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), the second is considered to belong to Śrī,
the third to the Goddess Pārvatī, and the fourth to the Remover of Obstacles (Vighnahārin)."
The fifth is declared to belong to Śaśin, while the sixth is declared to belong to Guha;
the seventh is said to belong to Bhāskara, and the eighth is considered to belong to Durgā.
The ninth is said to belong to the Mothers; the tenth is remembered as belonging to Vāsava;
the eleventh belongs to the Sages; the twelfth to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu);
the thirteenth to Anaṅga; and the fourteenth is said to belong to Śiva.
O best of gods, the full-moon day was mentioned to me by my father.

The fourth lunar day has been declared for the Goddess Tripurabhairavī; for the other Nityās as well, the eighth and ninth are prescribed. These lunar days have been fully described as auspicious for the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
One should worship many sacrificial animals with oblations for Indra as one's own constant duty.
The Pavitrāropaṇa (the rite of offering the sacred thread) for that [deity] is proclaimed as a primary act distinct [from others];
it serves for the attainment of material wealth and likewise for the prosperity of the country.
"And that which is declared by the Lord as primary shall occur on its respective lunar day.
Thus has the time been fully explained; now hear the Sūtra, O Lord of the Gods, [as stated] in the Viṣṇurahasya:
O ascetics, the lunar days (tithis) renowned in the Sūtras have been described separately;
the first lunar day (pratipad) is declared to be the auspicious day for the rite of consecrating the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
The second lunar day is the most excellent of all lunar days, belonging to the goddess Śrī; the third belongs to Bhavānī, and the fourth to her son.
The fifth is said to belong to Somarāja, while the sixth is declared to be that of Guha;
the seventh is said to belong to Bhāskara, and the eighth is remembered as belonging to Durgā.
The ninth is declared to belong to the Mothers, the tenth is remembered as belonging to Vāsuki,
the eleventh to the Sages, and the twelfth to the Discus-bearer.

The thirteenth day is said to belong to Anaṅga, while the fourteenth belongs to Śiva; O Lord, best of sages, the new moon (Amāvāsyā) is remembered as the lunar day (tithi) belonging to the Full Moon (Paurṇamāsī).
On the lunar days of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa as previously described,
the rites for all the gods must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
And so it is stated in the Kālottara: "O child, it is specifically taught according to the sequence beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad):
for Agni, Brahmā, Gaurī, and Gaṇeśa and the others, [the worship] is on the fifth."
The new moon day (amāvāsī) is beneficial for Ṣaṇmukha, Sūrya, Śiva,
Ambikā, Kṛtānta, Rudra, and Cakrapāṇi.
One should perform the conjunction with Jupiter on the thirteenth lunar day for Kāma, on the fourteenth for Śiva,
and on the full moon for the ancestors.
Furthermore, the fourteenth and eighth days are common auspicious festivals that bring benefit.
In the Devīpurāṇa, concerning the Goddess:
"Alternatively, O Lord of the Gods, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) on the seventh or the thirteenth day of either the month of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa."
Thus ends the time for the offering of the *pavitra* to various deities.
Now follows the time for the offering of the *damanaka*. According to the *Devīpurāṇa*:
Brahmā said: "O child, one should perform my worship at the beginning of Caitra according to the prescribed rites,
with offerings of perfumes, incense, and flowers, and with garlands made of *damanaka* blossoms."
One should worship the God with oblations; one shall attain all desires.
A human being obtains the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas).
On the second day, one should worship Umā, Śiva, and Hutāśa;
sacrificial food (haviṣya) should be offered as the oblation, followed again by the offering of perfumes and worship.
O best of Brahmins, one obtains the fruit that was proclaimed by Umā.
On the fifth day, one should worship the Nāgas and Mahoragas, such as Ananta and others;
milk and ghee should be offered as the food-offering (naivedya), which removes all poisons.
On the sixth day, worship of Skanda should be performed with all kinds of offerings;
by this, one attains happiness and good fortune in this very life, and at the end, shall go to the abode of Skanda.
On the tenth day, a worship with exquisite perfumes should be performed for the King of Dharma;
thus, one becomes free from enemies and devoid of fear in this world, and attains the supreme state at the end.
On the eleventh day, worship of the Sage should be performed with all types of offerings;
such a person becomes wealthy, possessed of sons, and beloved, and is glorified in the world of the Sage.
On the thirteenth day, Kāmadeva should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite,
accompanied by Rati and Prīti, and adorned with Aśoka flowers and jewels.
Either in a jar, or on white cloth, or in a writing vessel, [one should draw] with the plow and other implements.
Likewise, it should be performed on the full moon day for the fulfillment of all desires.
One who offers a piece of sugar to Indra, who dwells with Sahasrākṣa, obtains physical rewards;
he who offers the desired portion shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
Thus concludes the time for the planting of the *damanaka* plant.
Now follow the specific merits according to particular months.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one obtains the desired fruit by worshipping with bilva and kalhāra flowers; worship with the *navamallikā* in the month of Nabhas yields great fruit.
Likewise, with *kadamba* and *campaka* flowers in the month of Nabhasya, one grants all desires;
in Āśvina, the worship of Śambhu with lotuses and *mālatī* is auspicious.

One obtains everything desired, for this worship bestows the fruit of all desires. Through the merits of the months of Māgha and Phālguna, one should perform worship with *kunda* and *mudgara* flowers;
and in Caitra, worship should be performed with *damanaka* and *śatapatraka* flowers.
By offering sandalwood or even flowers to the Teacher of the World according to the previous rule,
a mortal shall attain equality with the gods when a full year has passed.
In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Worship with *campaka* and *mālatī* flowers in the month of *Iṣa* bestows prosperity. "In *Iṣa*" means in the month of Āśvina.
In the month of Kārttika, worship with the hundred-petaled lotus fulfills all desires;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, worship with blue lotuses or with kubjaka flowers is auspicious.
O best of gods, he who performs [this rite] with *kunda* flowers in Māgha, with *uśīra* in Phālguna,
and likewise with *śatapatra* lotuses in Caitra,
obtains the fruit of all sacrifices as well as the fruit of all gifts.
Thus are the specific flowers according to the specific months.
Now, the distinctions of flowers according to the divisions of night and so forth:
*kanakāṇi* and *kadambāni* should be offered to Śaṅkara at night.

All [other flowers] should be offered during the day, while *mallikā* flowers may be offered both by day and by night; the *jātī* flower remains fresh for one watch (*prahara*), and the *karavīra* lasts throughout the day and night.
The meaning is that after the installation, [the mantra] should be recited for one watch of the day and night, or throughout the day and night, during worship;
this is stated in the *Kāmika* and *Kāraṇa* [Tantras].
[The flowers are]: *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, white *arka*, and white flowers.
One should place the *punnāga*, the *paṭṭikā*, the *ṣoḍha*, and the *mālatī* at the rising [of the altar].
One should cause the *paṅkaja*, *vṛhatī*, *vyāghrī*, *vyāghāta*, *karavīraka*,
*utpala*, *pāṭalī*, and *droṇa* to be offered at midday.
One should cause the Campaka, Vedaka, Bhadrā, Dhūstūra, Varakarṇikā, Mālatī, and Mallikā to be offered at the time of dusk.
One should cause the *jātī*, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), the *kunda* flower, the *kadambaka*, the *dvivarṇa*, and the *bhadra* to be offered during the half-watch of the night.
A flower equal to the blue lotus has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
the *kadamba*, *janaka*, and *jātī* flowers should be offered at midnight,
while all other flowers should be offered during the other watches of the day.
Thus are the varieties of flowers according to the distinctions of night and so forth. Now, the flowers suitable for all times:
the *bilva* flower, the *śamī* flower, the *karavīra*, and the *mālatī*.
The *unmattaka* and the *campaka* bring me immediate delight.
O tiger among the twice-born, when the campaka, aśoka, punnāga, and kalhāra flowers,
as well as others that are highly fragrant, bring me joy,
I am constantly worshipped by them and quickly attain delight.
Having worshipped Śiva with whatever flowers, whether grown in water or on land, one who departs after offering them with devotion is honored in the world of Śiva.

Thus, the specific worship with *śivapuṣpa* flowers according to particular times has been described. Now, it is established that in the absence of flowers and such, worship may be performed with leaves and other materials; as stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
In the absence of flowers and leaves, one should worship even with food and drink;
one should perform the worship with rice, wheat, or barley.
One attains the state of Gaṇapati and shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Indeed, in the absence of flowers, one should offer even leaves;
and in the absence of leaves, one should offer even fruits."
But even in the absence of fruits, he is then honored through grass, shrubs, and herbs;
and in the absence of herbs, he is honored through devotion.
Thus, the use of leaves and other materials as means for worship in the absence of flowers and such has been established.
[895] Now follows the general time for minor rites (kṣudrakarma).
In the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Elder Kulika, Yoga, Tārā, Vaināśika, Kuja, and the eighth sign—these and others are the times for minor rites. Thus it is said.

The *kulikas* are the eight [planets] beginning with Saturn; when they rise as the lords of the day and so forth, whether by day or evening, for the latter half [of the period], it is called the "rise of the *kulika*. This has been explained in detail in the section on the removal of poison (*viṣahara*). As for the one named "the Elder" (*sthavira*): if the day belongs to those very two [planets] while Jupiter is in its own *navāṃśaka* or sign.
On that day, if one's own Navāṃśa is empty (Rikta), there is the counteraction of diseases, debts, and the like.
The stars Tārā,
the three Pūrvas, Bharaṇī, and Maghā—
those who know them declare these five to be of fierce power.
In the signs of Raudra (Aries), Indra (Pisces), Mūla, and Uraga (Sarpa),
which are cruel, there should be fierce possession by those spirits.
The twenty-third [year] is called Vaināśika, as stated by Varāhamihira;
the twenty-second is known as Mandādya, lasting eighty-eight years and one month.

‘Kuja’ refers to Tuesday; ‘the eighth house’ refers to the time when the moon is in the eighth sign from the sign in which it was situated at the time of birth. By the word ‘etcetera,’ the lunar digits (kalā), lunar days (tithi), and time-measures (velā) are included. Among these, ‘lunar digits’ (kalā) refers to the fact that in the bright fortnight the lunar digits increase and in the dark fortnight they decrease; therein, during the period of waning, one should perform [the rite] starting from the eighth day until the new moon. ‘Lunar days’ (tithi) refers to the fourth day and so forth; starting from the rising of the moon, for fifteen ghaṭikās there occurs an agitation of the ocean, which is called the ‘moon-velocity’ (candravelā); at that time, one should not perform rites such as the planting of pillars. Starting from that point again, for another fifteen ghaṭikās there is no such velocity; at that time, one may plant the pillar.
Thus ends the general time for minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*).
Now, the specific times for particular rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth are described in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
The knowledge of the seasons beginning with winter is an auxiliary to ritual action, and that is now being described;
it was taught by the ancient teachers as the cause for the successful accomplishment of rites.
At the beginning of the day and at the end of the night, the six seasons—
beginning with Śiśira— are established, each occupying ten nāḍīs in succession.
A pale-red arrow is cool and used for the rite of subjugation;
for the rite of eradication, it should be known as the youthful spring, which is red.
Summer has a smoky body and is employed for killing;
the rainy season, however, has a smoky body and is employed for paralyzing.
Autumn is black and is drawn for the purpose of attracting by those who know mantras and worship their gurus;
winter is white and aged, and is employed for rites of pacification, subjugation, and so forth.
In the Mantra-tantras, one desiring prosperity should recite the mantra at the time of the morning session; likewise,
the recitation of the *brahmasārasvata* [mantra] should be performed at the time of the morning session.
Likewise, one seeking subjugation (vaśya) should recite the mantra during the forenoon;
for attraction (ākarṣaṇa), it is declared by the twice-born that it should be done at night, prior to the first watch.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, it is taught that in the forenoon, or during the *brāhma* period, one should perform auspicious rites:
namely, those for Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, as well as rites of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) and pacification (*śāntika*).
And the increase of lifespan—these six are declared to be auspicious.

In the Mantra-tantras: reciting a mantra at twilight leads to the destruction of the intellect; reciting it in the afternoon results in paralysis; one should recite it at midday for the purpose of inciting enmity, and for the sake of inducing fever as well.
For the purpose of eradication, one should recite the mantra after midday;
however, the rite of killing should be performed after the third watch.
Thus ends the specific determination of time according to the particular rites, such as those for subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like.
Now follows the determination of the time for Viṣṇu’s sleep (*viṣṇuśayana*) and so forth. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
In the months of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika, during the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Śravaṇa, and Revatī—
at their beginning, middle, and end— the festivals of the laying down and the turning over [of the image] are held.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "Viṣṇu sleeps here during the first quarter of Maitra (the month of Mārgaśīrṣa),
and according to the Śruti, he turns over in the middle."
The destroyer of Surā and the others awakens after four months, ending with the constellation Pauṣṇa.
In the month of Mādhava, during the early part of the year,
on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight, there is the festival of the awakening from sleep (prasvāpāvartana) in Mathurā.

One should not perform the rising or the lying down of Hari on the twelfth lunar day if it falls during the month of Pauṣa under the asterism of Puṣya, nor during the day under the asterism of Anurādhā and so forth, nor even at night.
Having recited, "One should likewise perform [the ritual] on the twelfth day," [it is said]:
sleeping at night, rising during the day, and changing position during the twilight—
these one should perform on the twelfth day itself, even if it falls under another [astrological] yoga.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Viṣṇu does not sleep by day, nor does he awaken at night;
when the twelfth lunar day is conjoined with [the appropriate] asterism, the conjunction of the lunar mansion's quarter is not the cause."
From the Purāṇa:
"In rising, in lying down, and likewise in turning over on one's side,
when the conjunction with the lunar mansion occurs on the twelfth day, the conjunction with the zodiacal sign (pādayoga) is not a cause [for concern]."
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "There is no restriction regarding the feet while sleeping or turning over;
even the conjunction of his feet with an asterism (nakṣatra) at that time [is of no consequence]."
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "When the moon is observed in Aries, up until the constellation Revatī,
Hṛṣīkeśa, who was rising, abandons his yogic sleep."
When the night is joined with the twelfth lunar day and ends with Revatī,
Viṣṇu awakens upon reaching Revatī at the end of the day.
Or it may occur on the twelfth lunar day, beginning with the asterism Revatī and ending with Rathānta;
if it is absent on both, then the great festival shall take place at twilight.
From the Purāṇa:
When the night has arrived during the festival of Nārāyaṇa, if it ends with the asterism Revatī,
the conjunction of the lunar day (tithi) is disregarded and the asterism alone prevails.
When the night has passed into the end of Revatī, even at the next quarter of the moon,
then Viṣṇu dispels his yogic sleep during the afternoon.
When the night ends with Revatī and is devoid of the twelfth lunar day, there shall be an absence of both; however, if it occurs at the twilight, it is a great festival.
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"At the time of the junction on the twelfth lunar day, even when the [required] asterisms are not present,
the rites of lying down, turning over, and so forth are to be performed during the bright fortnights of the months of Āṣāḍha and Bhādrapada."
This is the meaning.

For the festival of Hari’s sleep and other such occasions, the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) of the bright fortnight in the months of Āṣāḍha, Bhādrapada, and Kārttika is auspicious when it is joined with the first, middle, or last quarter (*pāda*) of the asterisms Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, or Revatī, as well as when it is joined with the night, the twilight, or the daytime. However, if the conjunction with the [specific] quarters cannot be obtained at the time specified above, then the conjunction of the twelfth day with the asterism itself should be observed. This distinction applies to both quarters; however, there is this specific rule: when the twelfth day is joined with Revatī during the day and the asterism extends into the night, Viṣṇu’s awakening occurs at the end of the remaining day; but when the twelfth day is without Revatī, the awakening and other rites take place at the twilight of the twelfth day.
Thus it has been said: "On the twelfth lunar day, at the time of the junction [of day and night], when the [required] constellations are not present,
the acts of lying down, turning over, and so forth are performed during the bright fortnights of the months of Āṣāḍha and Bhādrapada."

[900] Regarding this, some say: if the asterisms beginning with Maitra (Anurādhā) occur on the thirteenth lunar day, bypassing the twelfth, then on the fourteenth the subsequent ones beginning with Jyeṣṭhā (Jyeṣṭhā) follow; thereafter, on the full moon day, the subsequent ones beginning with Mūla occur. If that were the case, it would contradict the designation of the month as Āṣāḍha, because the full moon conjoined with an asterism occurs during the junction of the power of Jyeṣṭhā and so forth, and thus the month of Bhādrapada would somehow be attained. [However, the rule is: "The first and the penultimate months are to be known as having three lunar days [of the full moon], and Phālguna is also considered to have three."
The remaining months should be known as having two parts.
Because of this statement, the sleeping of Hari and other rites will not take place when Dhaniṣṭhā occurs at the beginning of Jyeṣṭha.
As it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Sleeping at night, rising during the day, and turning over during the twilight."
Through the conjunction of the feet on the twelfth lunar day of the final fortnight, there is the conjunction of debts.

Thus, in the *Ācārasāra*, however, it is read as "due to the conjunction with the asterism on the twelfth day. Therefore, when there is a connection with a lunar mansion such as Anurādhā occurring on another lunar day, the acts of lying down and so forth are to be performed at the time of the junction (saṃdhi) on the Kaṭa-dvādaśī.

On this point, Śrīkara says: When two new moon days (*amāvasyā*) occur within the same period, then—because of the state of Āṣāḍhī following the [end of the] Gemini sign—the moon and sun are asleep; if on that day the weekday of the Lord’s sleep (*grahavāraśayana*), Revatī, and so forth occur, or even if they fall on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), then because of the well-known tradition regarding the simultaneous rising and viewing of the two deities (Hari and Hara), it is difficult to bypass that [time]. At that time, if the festival were performed upon the arrival of the asterism (*nakṣatra*) in Scorpio, then since the fifth month would have arrived, the statement “He awakens after four months” would be untenable. Therefore, because of the connection with the quarters (*pādayoga*), one must instead assume a different transposition [of the dates], and thus [Śrīkara’s view] is not to be respected. As for the statement “The junction occurs on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) at Mathurā,” this was said by resorting to the *Māthura-kalpa*. For the ritual practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) of the Vaiṣṇavas is the *kalpa*; the *Māthura* is one such, and there are others besides it. The *Māthura* [tradition] prioritizes the twelfth day and observes the connection with the asterism, whereas [the other tradition] prioritizes the connection with the quarters of the asterism and depends on the twelfth day; thus, the conjunction of lunar day (*tithi*) and asterism is valid in both cases. Consequently, the ritual option is determined by the lunar day and the asterism. How then is it that there is no other lunar day for the “simultaneous rising” of Hari and Śaṅkara? Therefore, everything is consistent. Regarding this, the refutation stated by Paṇḍitaparitoṣakṛt is as follows: This is untenable. To explain: what is the meaning of the phrase “on another lunar day than the one connected to the quarters, there is a conjunction with the asterism on the twelfth”? Is it the eleventh or the thirteenth? Nor can the eleventh and twelfth be considered equal [in status]. There is no regard for the conjunction with the asterism or the connection with the quarters on that [specific] day.
Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Hari is eternally present on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days;
in that regard, when there is a conjunction with a lunar mansion, the conjunction with a specific quarter of the day is not a cause [for the efficacy of the fast]."

Now, if it were to be stated that [the awakening occurs] on the thirteenth day, that would contradict the term *ābhākā*. Nor can the word *kārttika* be considered merely conventional (*prāyika*) in accordance with the rule for awakening after four months; for the term *ābhākā* is fixed by its well-established etymological derivation involving great effort. Thus, it is more appropriate to regard the phrase "by four months" itself as a conventional restatement. Furthermore, when two full-moon days (*paurṇamāsī*) occur in the month of Kārttika, if Viṣṇu’s awakening takes place in that very Kārttika by resorting to the later month, yet his sleep occurs while the sun is in Gemini (*mithuna*), and there is an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), then the awakening occurring even after five months is not contradictory. As for the number "four," it is established by the rule that a month consists of sixty days; we shall demonstrate the distinction regarding the double Āṣāḍha later. Moreover, popular tradition—that Hari and Śaṅkara awaken together—is not a restrictive authority, because it is weaker than scriptural authority. Furthermore, what could such an arguer say regarding the sleep [of Viṣṇu], in accordance with which the duration of time would occur when the sun is in Taurus? In that case, would Hari’s sleep occur in that same month, or must Āṣāḍha be awaited? Even so, if the constellation [Anurādhā] falls on the fourteenth day, popular tradition—that Hari and Śaṅkara awaken together—is the restrictive authority. Does the world not speak of scripture [in this way]? Or rather, when Anurādhā falls on the fourteenth day while the sun is in Gemini, then [the awakening] depends on the month characterized by the full moon of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha.

Likewise, by what logic could the ritual of rising [from sleep] be performed based on that [specific] bed and so forth, given the fixed rule for Āṣāḍha? Even if a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is obtained in Jyeṣṭha and other months, the performance of the rite caused by the "bed" and so forth is impossible because of the inevitable occurrence of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), which necessitates the assumption of two Āṣāḍhas; for apart from the performance immediately following that [assumption], such predominance of a lunar mansion is untenable. Even if it were possible, the term *ābhākā* must necessarily be respected. Furthermore, one who speaks thus and asserts the raising of the deity in Āśvina while prioritizing popular tradition has forgotten even what he himself wrote: that "a month consists of sixty days. Therefore, it must be explained otherwise.
In this regard, it has been said: "Sleeping at night, rising during the day, and turning over during the twilight;
[this occurs] on another lunar day due to the conjunction of the lunar mansion (pādayoga), or on the twelfth day due to the conjunction of the asterism."

Thus, this is its meaning: even on another thirteenth day, if there is a conjunction with the *pāda* (quarter) of the asterism, the transition (*parivartana*) occurs during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). When there is a conjunction with the asterism on the twelfth day, sleeping at night and waking during the day takes place. However, festivals and other such rites do not occur on another lunar day merely because of a conjunction with the *pāda* of an asterism. This being the case, both [the rules]—"the *ābhākā* [months]" and "by means of four months"—are justified. Furthermore, even on the eleventh day, if there is a conjunction with the asterism, the practice of sleeping and so forth should be performed by the force of another scriptural statement. As for the rule, "One should perform that only on the twelfth," that is based on the *Māthurakalpa*; if the asterism is obtained on the eleventh day, bypassing the twelfth, nevertheless, the sleeping and other rites must be performed precisely at the moment of the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the twelfth. Whether there is a conjunction with the asterism on the eleventh or on the thirteenth, when the *ābhākā* period is reached everywhere, sleeping and so forth occur at the moment of the junction on the twelfth; and since twilight consists of both night and day, the rule "sleeping at night and waking during the day" is not entirely contradictory. Thus, let that very result of the asterism apply according to the *Mathuramādhavakalpa*. Or, if the asterism is obtained on the eleventh, one may perform either [rite] as being most excellent; or even on the thirteenth, provided it does not conflict with the month of Kārttika—so it has been stated.

This is improper. For if one accepts the meaning stated by you regarding the sentence "sleeping at night and rising during the day," it would entail a remote (vyavahita) connection, since that meaning is not understood from the words themselves; and because a statement will be cited later prescribing the option of rising during the day for the months of Libra and Scorpio when an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) falls between them. Since this statement is consistent with that intention in its straightforward sense, there is no reason to accept the meaning asserted by you. Therefore, the opinion of the Śrīkaras alone is correct. Furthermore, the word *Kārttika* is used in its primary sense, which is appropriate given the absence of an alternative. As for the claim that if Kārttika is an intercalary month, the awakening of Viṣṇu occurs specifically in the pure (*śuddha*) Kārttika—that too is incorrect, because an option will be stated later. Consequently, what has been stated [by us] is indeed superior.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "When the auspicious eleventh day of the month of Bhādrapada has arrived,
the gift of a mat to Viṣṇu shall be the destroyer of great sins."
"Kaṭadāna" is the turning over of the limbs of Viṣṇu as he lies down. Likewise:
"On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, being composed..."
And with a mantra, O Indra among kings, the twice-born should cause the deity to rise.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "O Lord, this twelfth day was indeed ordained by you, who lie upon Śeṣa, for the purpose of awakening,
for the benefit of all the worlds."
Thus, even for these gods, the practice of sleeping and so forth must be performed according to their respective lunar days (*tithi*) and asterisms (*nakṣatra*).
This is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Whichever asterism and whichever lunar day belong to whichever deity..."
"But for that deity, there is the turning over on the bed and so forth. Thus [it is said].

Some perform the sleeping and other rites for all [deities] according to the lunar day (*tithi*), while others do so according to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The fifteen lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*) belong to the deities beginning with Dhanada (Kubera). Among them, a single lunar day may belong to multiple deities; for example, the first lunar day belongs to Agni, Brahmā, and Dhanada. In that case, an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the performance of the rite would be improper. Furthermore, the twenty-seven lunar mansions are always pervasive; thus, the sleeping and other rites for the Gaṇapatyas and others should be performed according to the lunar mansion. Regarding the conjunction of lunar mansion and lunar day for Rudra and others during their sleep and so forth in Āṣāḍha and other months, there is no festival [based on such a conjunction], for it never happens that the *Raudra* lunar mansion (*Ārdrā*) occurs on the fourteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. Therefore, for those [deities], the sleeping and other rites are based solely on the lunar day, whereas in foreign lands they may also be based on the lunar mansion.
If one sleeps or wakes during the forenoon on the previous day, the fast should take place on that day;
however, if those two events occur during the afternoon, they know the observance to belong to the following day.

Starting from the forenoon, it is said that "the very forenoon" refers specifically to the night, because daytime sleep is prohibited. In this same way, it should be understood that when the Garuḍa-bannered Lord (Viṣṇu) rises at night, the fast should be observed on the previous day, and one should perform the religious duty on the following day. As stated in the *Kāśyapa-pañcarātra*:
"At my rising and my sleeping, and when I turn upon my side."
Now, whoever is an initiated Vaiṣṇava devoted to bhakti, [he should...]
Whether he should eat cooked food or even fruits and roots,
I shall never forgive his offense;
I cast him into a terrible hell, where he is born as a leech for many years.

Indeed, the time for the Lord Vāsudeva’s sleep and so forth has not been determined; however, when an intercalary month occurs, meritorious acts and the like should be performed during the signs of Cancer and Scorpio. Therefore, the procedure for that [intercalary period], including its abridgment and so on, is prescribed. Jyotiḥparāśara says:
"When two [months] have passed, along with five fortnights and two days and a half..."
In the eighth part of a day, one intercalary month falls.
Of the sixty parts of a day that the sun takes away during a season,
the moon likewise causes the loss of one day and one [part].

In this way, after the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), the sun and moon produce an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) by virtue of their specific motion at the beginning of Vaiśākha or other times prior to the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*); [they may also do so] occasionally after the southern course. Marīci said: "An intercalary month occurs in that [year] when there is a double Āṣāḍha."
Having observed two new moon days, one should designate it as a double Āṣāḍha.
Atri said:
When the sun, situated in Gemini, touches two new moons, that is to be known as a double Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
When the sun enters Aries on the tenth day or later of the dark fortnight, that should be known as the "double Āṣāḍha"; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
"From the tenth onwards, on the ninth"— likewise:
"When there are two new-moon days (darśa) during the six months beginning with Mādhava."
That should be known as a double Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in the sign of Cancer.
Viṣṇu: When the sun, having passed the new moon day, enters [the zodiacal sign], that is to be known as the double Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
When the sun enters Aries on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, that should be known as the second Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
