Here is the summary of the meaning: When an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) falls within the triad beginning with Aries (*meṣa*) prior to the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), then the "double Āṣāḍha" (*dvirāṣāḍha*) occurs in the very first year; at that time, Viṣṇu sleeps immediately after the southern solstice. When the intercalary month falls within the triad beginning with Cancer (*karkaṭa*), then in the following year, the full moon of Āṣāḍha necessarily occurs when the sun is in the remainder of Cancer, because that [month] is indeed Āṣāḍha; it is precisely there that Viṣṇu sleeps. Regarding both types of falling months, the two new moons (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth are recorded. This being so, when there are two new moons within the triad beginning with Cancer, then the solar ingress (*saṃkrānti*) into Virgo or Libra occurs on the first or second lunar day of the bright fortnight; the ingress into Aries in the following year likewise occurs in the same manner. And when, due to the increase of two days per month, the ingress into Gemini (*mithuna*) as the *ṣaḍaśīti* occurs on the fifth day, then one should designate it as "double Āṣāḍha," and the sleeping [of Viṣṇu] takes place in Cancer on that day—but not because there is actually a "double Āṣāḍha. Thus, even when the calculation of those skilled in mathematics shows the sun has passed through the portion of Gemini, if the sun is calculated to be still in the portion of Gemini, it is called Āṣāḍha; therefore, a "double Āṣāḍha" is not understood from the actual calculation of the new moon day and so forth.
Regarding this, Satya says:
"When the sixty-fourth [tithi] occurs on the white fortnight after the Vṛṣa [Taurus] has been left behind,
then the calculation of the double Āṣāḍha must be considered by the astrologer."
And so it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"When the Sun enters [its next sign] after passing the fourth day of the bright fortnight, one should designate it as the 'double Āṣāḍha'; then Hari shall sleep at the beginning of Cancer."
The sun enters Aries in either the first or the second bright fortnight;
the ritual of the two Āṣāḍhas continues until the awakening of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu shall sleep during the latter *karkaṭaka* [month]. The remaining rites, such as the festival of Indra (*śakrotsava*) and others, should be performed at their proper times.
For it is said:
"This option regarding two Āṣāḍhas applies with respect to the sleeping of Viṣṇu."
The banner is indeed Śatayajña, and it is thus ordained as Siṃha.
And Baudhāyana says:
"The ritual of the two Āṣāḍhas should be performed until the awakening of Viṣṇu;
once Hari is awakened, that ritual should be performed according to the course of the sun alone."

But when, in the first year of a leap-year (*dvirāṣāḍha*), Hari’s sleep occurs in Cancer, then his turning over (*parivartana*) and the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the Śaka festival take place in Virgo; the Durgā festival occurs in Libra; and the awakening of Vāsudeva takes place in Scorpio.
As Viriñci stated:
"If Hari should sleep while the sun faces the southern quarter..."
[The functions of] turning back and awakening belong only to Virgo and Scorpio.
Likewise:
"When the Moon is in Cancer and Hari is asleep, the raising of Indra’s banner is performed in Āśvina;
one should awaken the Goddess in Tula, and Janārdana in Vṛścika."
When, however, a second Āṣāḍha is calculated, and when it occurs according to its own nature, then, provided there are two Śravaṇas in the bright fortnight,
Satya stated how it should be performed:
"But when a second Āṣāḍha has arrived, if Hari should sleep in Leo..."
One should place the discus in the other [hand], but one should release it in the maiden [hand].

Now, if both *śravaṇa* constellations occur while the moon is in Virgo (*kanyā*), then during the first *śravaṇa* one performs the rite for raising Indra (*śakrotthāpana*), and in the other, the rite for raising Durgā (*durgotthāpana*). Regarding this, it is said:
"In the bright fortnight (*pakṣa*) when the moon is in Leo (*siṃha*) or Virgo (*kanyā*), and joined with the [first] fortnight, one worships Śakra on the day in Leo;
in Virgo, one worships both Siṃha and Durgā."
This other ritual for worship during the two white fortnights is prescribed by the wise; and the completion of the two Āṣāḍhas likewise occurs at that time.
In response to the question "Why?", he says:
"The raising of Śakra’s banner and the turning over of Viṣṇu are prescribed by the learned to occur every two months; [the same applies to] the period beginning with his lying down."
And from Durgā, after three months— excluding that month which has already passed—
one should certainly cause the forms of Indra and the other gods to arise in due order during the months of Kanyā, Tulā, and Vṛścika, even when an intercalary month occurs.

This is another meaning of the term *adhimāsa-nipāta*: when two full-moon days (*paurṇamāsī*) occur within the signs beginning with Cancer, then, upon the occurrence of an intercalary month, one should [offer] to Indra and the other gods in due order.
For it is thus:
"When there are two full-moon days associated with the two Āṣāḍhas, that is to be known as *dvirāṣāḍha*; Viṣṇu sleeps in the month of Karkaṭaka.
Thus it has been said.
If two full-moon days should occur from Vaiśākha until the end of Tulā,
that is to be known as a double Āṣāḍha, [relevant] for the rites of the Lord’s sleep, his return, and so forth.

The phrase "beginning with Vaiśākha" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes both Phālgunas as well, since a month can consist of three lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). In that regard, if an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs at the beginning of Phālguna and Hari lies asleep in Karkaṭaka, his awakening occurs after four months. However, if an intercalary month falls within the four-month period beginning with Karkaṭaka, Hari’s sleep occurs in Mithuna or Āṣāḍha; and since there are two possibilities for the months beginning with Śrāvaṇī in other cases, the month of Kārttika occurs specifically in Vṛścika. Therefore, his awakening takes place there even after five months. Because the rule "in the dark fortnights of the months beginning with Ābhākā" is widely accepted, it is considered superior; whereas the statement "he awakens after four months" is merely a restatement based on a general or common intention. Thus, this [awakening] constitutes a single month.
As Bādarāyaṇa said:
"If an intercalary month should occur while the sun remains in a single sign for sixty days,
that is considered to be indeed a single month."

Thus, when the fruit of two Āṣāḍhas is obtained, it is called "double Āṣāḍha," but it is not double Āṣāḍha by its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). The same should be understood regarding the festivals of Parivartanā and Durgā. For example, when there are two Śrāvaṇas and two Bhādrapadas, then the Lord’s sleep (*devaśayana*) occurs for three months [in Leo], the awakening of Śakra (*śakrotthāpana*) occurs in Virgo, and thereafter, the awakening of Durgā occurs after one month from that [awakening of Śakra] and the awakening of Viṣṇu after two months. However, when there are two Āśvina months, then the awakening of Śakra occurs in Leo itself, and the awakening of Durgā occurs after two months from that, while the awakening of Viṣṇu occurs after three months [from the awakening of Śakra]. But when there are two Kārttika months, then too, the designation of "double Āṣāḍha" applies; Hari sleeps in Cancer, while the festival of Śakra and so forth occur according to their proper time—this has been stated. Even in the *Bhaviṣyottara*, it is declared that upon the occurrence of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), the awakening of Kṛṣṇa takes place in Libra alone.
O Great King, when the sun is situated in Gemini, one should install Madhusūdana;
and in Libra, one should again raise him up.
When an intercalary month occurs, this very sequence of ritual procedure applies;
one should not establish the dark fortnight otherwise, nor likewise should one conclude it otherwise.
Thus, enough with excessive detail.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Prauṣṭhapada likewise..."
The king should cause Śakra to rise up in Viśvaśravaṇa and Vāsava.
"Viśva" is Uttarāṣāḍhā; "Vāsava" is Dhaniṣṭhā. The conjunction with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) during the first quarter of the Śravaṇa nakṣatra is most highly auspicious.
As it has been said:
"When the moon has entered the asterism of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa) and so forth, the king should raise up Indra (the banner)."
And at night, while one is asleep, one should release [the offering] during the final quarter of the lunar mansion Bharaṇī.
During the first quarter of Śravaṇā and during Bharaṇī, as well as in the seventh lunar mansion from them,
one should propitiate the god Śakra so that the king does not see [the offender].
On a Saturday or a Tuesday, during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity,
or when portents such as earthquakes occur, one should never praise Śakra.
However, when specific omens occur, it should be understood that one should begin from the verses ending with "bharaṇyanta-pādān.
Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha said:
"When Keśava sleeps while the sun has entered the lunar mansions..."
When the sun is in the house of the Moon’s son, Purandara should not be raised;
"the house of the Moon" is Cancer, and "the house of the Moon’s son" is Virgo. Or, it says:
If one does not awaken Śakra during the second Āṣāḍha while the moon is in Virgo,
the kingdom of the king will perish and the subjects will be oppressed.
"But when Śakra is established at the proper time, the king lives long; through this very festival for the subjects, the earth becomes possessed of stars (Ṛkṣavatī). Thus [it is said].
The remainder should be understood as shown in the *Dvirāṣāḍha-viveka*.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should erect [the image] on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada under an auspicious asterism,
or during the bright fortnight of Āśvina, or of Śrāvaṇa."
Garga says:
When the sun has entered Leo during the bright fortnight, and the moon enters the first quarter of the asterism of Mṛgaśiras;
"Then, at night, Vajrapāṇi rises, forming a multitude of various palaces, and subsequently settles in the southern quarter.
Furthermore, by the word *hari*, the asterism Śravaṇa, which has Hari as its deity, is understood.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "The great festival of the raising of Indra’s banner, accompanied by great gifts, should be performed every year by the king or even by another."
Then, however, it should be performed in the twelfth year, and not again in the interval.

In the *Devīpurāṇa*, after stating that if the procession of the Sun’s chariot (*sūryarathayātrā*) cannot be performed for some reason, the banner of Indra (*śakradhvaja*) must be erected in the twelfth year, it is further said:
"If the raising of the banner of Indra is likewise not performed,
then it must be done in the twelfth year, but not in the interim."
The festival of Indra should be celebrated in the month of Nabhasya when the sun is situated in Leo,
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight under the lunar mansion presided over by Viṣṇu.
And its conjunction with Bharaṇī occurs on the ninth day of the month of Āśvina;
having worshipped the Goddess, one should then immediately dismiss her.
In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "Having worshipped during the dark fortnight of the month of Kanyā, one should sleep during the day;
on the ninth day, one should awaken the Goddess with the sounds of songs and musical instruments."
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight, the untying of the Goddess’s hair is performed;
then, on the morning of the fifth day, one should bathe her with auspicious waters.
On the seventh day there is the worship of Ambikā; on the eighth, the Supoṣaṇa rite;
and on the ninth, for the sake of the vow, there is a vigil and an offering according to the rules.
On the tenth day, there should be a formal viewing accompanied by play, festivities, and auspicious rites;
and on the tenth day, the great lustration ceremony (nīrājana) is performed, which greatly increases strength.
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]: "One should awaken the Goddess under Ārdrā, worship her under Mūla,
perform the ritual worship under Uttarā, and dismiss her under Śravaṇa."
Having brought the entire branch of a bilva tree together with its root-mantra, one should worship it.
When the final quarter of the night coincides with the asterism Śravaṇā,
then on the ninth day, at the commencement of the daytime portion, the Goddess shall arise.
O King, on the tenth day, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the sake of increasing strength.
When the third lunar day falls on a Sunday during the asterism of Svāti in the month of Āśvina, one should perform a protective rite for seven days;
then, on the tenth day, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to one's capacity.
The meaning is that one should perform the propitiatory rite known as *nīrājana*.
Vyāsa says:
"One should awaken the Goddess under the constellation Ārdrā and worship her under Mūla."
Then the rising of the Goddess occurs on the ninth day, and not during the daytime.
When the final quarter of the asterism Śravaṇā occurs during the daytime,
then on the tenth day, one should behold the Goddess amidst the festivals of ritual practice.
During the three asterisms beginning with Mūla, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina,
one should worship Caṇḍikā with offerings for the prosperity of the kingdom.
"If one causes a new bride to rise [from her bed] during the asterism of Pūrvāṣāḍhā while the moon is in Virgo,
the kingdom shall perish and the subjects shall become impaired. Thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.

He who, during the evening twilight on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, offers a sky-lamp with sesame oil continuously for one month to the Lord of Śrī, who is accompanied by Śrī, shall never be deprived of prosperity.
To Dāmodara, in the sky under the sign of Libra together with Lolā, I offer lamps; salutations to Ananta, the Creator.
Thus is the mantra for the offering of lamps.
On the new moon day, when the sun is in Libra, Lakṣmī relinquishes her sleep;
she, being the very embodiment of the auspicious night, indeed manifests for the kindling of lamps.
With safflower blossoms, perfumes, lamps, yellow orpiment, and fruits,
the husband should inquire after the welfare of his wife and daughter-in-law with auspicious words.
One should always worship Lakṣmī, who destroys impurity and misfortune;
when the five banners have perished, one should place a single flagstaff in the house.
In the *Vārāha-purāṇa*: "On the new moon day when the sun is in Libra, Lakṣmī relinquishes her sleep;
at that time, Viṣṇu [awakens] in the bright fortnight while the sun is in Libra or Scorpio."
The awakening of Lakṣmī is known in the world as Dīpālikā;
likewise, Kaumudī, Yakṣarātri, Kausamī, Phālgunī,
and Vāsantī are to be understood [as festivals] based on the greatness of the region.
On the full moon day of Āśvina, the night-festival is prescribed;
it is celebrated as Kaumudī and should be performed for the prosperity of the world.
On the first lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the worship of the Yakṣas— known as Yakṣarātri— should be performed with flowers and garments for the sake of one's desired happiness.
Having propitiated Śrī with a boon on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
the worship performed on the fifth day with *kunda* flowers is known as the Kausumī.
When the Vāsavilāsaka occurs on the full moon day of Phālguna, that is to be known as Phālgunī in the world; it should be observed for the prosperity of the world.
On the eighth day of Caitra, one should worship Śiva with *aśoka* flowers, and on the thirteenth day, one should worship Smara;
that [worship] is performed for the sake of the *aśoka*, while the remainder is the Vāsantī rite.
Now, according to the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): on the new moon day when the sun is in Libra, Lakṣmī relinquishes her sleep;
when Viṣṇu enters Libra during that bright fortnight, [she likewise awakens].
Viṣṇu rises on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa, appearing first and [disappearing] afterwards.
Now, in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa: "Bathing and giving gifts on whichever lunar day occurs in the month of Kārttika yield a hundredfold merit;
and on the first day (pratipad) of Brahmā as well, [one should worship] with lamps mixed with jaggery."
And wearing unwashed, new garments, one shall go to that abode of Brahman.
On that first lunar day (pratipadā), the wise man should worship himself with flowers, perfumes, and new garments;
he shall go to the abode of Brahmā.

Thus ends the determination of the time for Viṣṇu’s sleep and other observances, titled "The Determination of Time," within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* (Supplementary Section) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious sovereign of great kings, the supreme lord of all the queens of the illustrious Mahādevī, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
The seventeenth chapter.
[916] Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Now, regarding the specific times for the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names,
the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: Vajra said:
At what time should which particular name of the Lord be proclaimed?
Cut through this doubt of mine, for you are said to be all-knowing.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should proclaim Puruṣa, Vāmadeva, Vyāsa, the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha in sequence among these.
One should likewise glorify Balabhadra and Kṛṣṇa during the two days.
Mādhava, the lotus-eyed one, as well as the one who reclines upon the serpent's coils,
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, and likewise the god Trivikrama.
O tiger among kings, one should recite [the names] in order during the seasons beginning with spring:
Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, and likewise the god Trivikrama.
Vāmana, Śrīdhara, and likewise Hṛṣīkeśa;
Dāmodara, Padmanābha, Keśava, and Yadūttama.

One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, and Govinda, the God of gods, in succession during the months beginning with Caitra; and one should contemplate Aniruddha during the bright and dark fortnights of both [the months].
One should thus recollect Śarva, Sarva, Śiva, Sthāṇu, Bhūtādi, Nidhi, and Avyaya, respectively,
on the days of the week beginning with Sunday.

Viṣṇu is the universe, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, and the lord of the past, the future, and the present; he is the creator of beings, the sustainer of beings, existence itself, the self of all beings, and the source of all beings.
The Unmanifest, the Lotus-eyed, the Architect of the Universe, the One of Pure Renown;
the Source, the Creator, the Sustainer, the Origin, the Lord, the Sovereign.
Immeasurable, Lord of the Senses, Navel of the Lotus, Lord of the Immortals, Ungraspable, Eternal, Sustainer— recollecting these names of Kṛṣṇa,
O Yādava, the names of the God of Gods have been declared.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu the Lord of Śrī, Kapila, the Lord who is the Master of Śrī,
Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Govinda, and Madhusūdana.
O Great King, O Yādava, one should always remember the God of gods among all the gods as bearing the earth, the mace, the conch, the lotus, and likewise the discus, starting from the first [mudrā].
O hero among men, all names belong to Janārdana, and all time belongs to him;
therefore, he is always the name of the omnipresent one.
O King, you may choose whatever boon you desire from the Giver of Boons.
Vajra said:
"At the commencement of an undertaking, how, where, and what indeed should one proclaim?
Cut through this doubt of mine, for you are said to be all-knowing."

Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, one who has gone forth for the sake of liberation should, while wandering, remember the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the plow, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the wielder of the sword, in the eastern and other directions.
One should always remember with devotion, during all worldly activities, the Imperishable One, who is supreme, the Lord of All, the vast Puruṣa.
When crossing water, one should meditate on the Tortoise, the Boar, or the Fish;
when kindling fire, one should recite the Name without weariness.
Going forth to face the battle, he should call to mind Aparājita;
he should likewise mutter the names Keśava, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and Puṣkarākṣa.
In all afflictions of the eyes, as well as in the preparation of medicinal herbs, one should likewise recite the names Hṛṣīkeśa, Acyuta, and Amṛta.
By recollecting the one whose banner is Garuḍa, a person is released from calamities;
fever, diseases of the head, and the potency of poisons are pacified.
During afflictions caused by planets and stars, in the face of divine obstacles or forest dangers, when obstructed by bandits or enemies, in peril from tigers, lions, and the like,
and likewise in intense darkness, one should chant "Narasiṃha."
In bad dreams, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the bearer of Śrī, the liberator of the elephant, Vāmana, and Khaḍgin.
When a fire has broken out, one should remember the One who reclines upon the waters;

one seeking victory in battle should remember Balabhadra; at the commencement of agriculture, one should remember Halāyudha; for crossing over [difficulties], one seeking success in trade should remember the Lord of Śrī; and for prosperity, O King, one should remember Him.
One should praise Viṣṇu, the auspiciousness of the world, during auspicious occasions;
likewise, one should recite [his name] during all fires and in times of sorrow.
Upon rising, a man should glorify Viṣṇu; during sleep, Mādhava;
at the time of eating, Govinda; and everywhere, Madhusūdana.
One should always utter "Nārāyaṇa" in cases of injury or stumbling,
during bathing, worship of the gods, burnt offerings (homa), prostration, and circumambulation.
One should invoke Vāsudeva, and among the Yādavas even those not specifically mentioned;
likewise, O King, at the commencement of any undertaking, one may invoke whichever name one desires.
For all names indeed belong to that man, O King, when he has accomplished all his goals;
therefore, let the name of the god be chosen according to your wish.
In all undertakings, one should recite [the mantra] with devotion.

Thus concludes the specific times for the chanting of the names of Viṣṇu. Now follow the times [for rites] when the primary time has elapsed. These are of two kinds: secondary (gauṇa) and scripturally enjoined (vācanika). Thus it is deliberated: when the primary time is impossible, should one adopt the secondary time or not? Now, what is the primary and what is the secondary? That which is prescribed is the primary, such as the morning and so forth in the case of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other rites. That which is not prescribed, but occurs in proximity to them and is brought into the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) within those very rites—such as the *saṅgava* period and so forth—is the secondary. Regarding this, Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana says:
"A secondary time for every ritual action is that which follows its own primary time;
or rather, some maintain that even the interval between the primary time of a future action and the present constitutes a secondary time for a preceding ritual. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: it refers to the intermediate period between the preceding and the succeeding [actions], namely, that which occurs after the own-time of the preceding action and before the time of the subsequent action.

In the preceding ritual act, it is secondary (*gauṇa*). Or rather, they consider that just as in the aforementioned interval, the time of the future action—which is the primary time—also possesses a secondary temporal status in relation to the preceding ritual act. But how can there be any suspicion of taking the time of the subsequent ritual act for the performance of the preceding one, given that the preceding act, having fallen from its own time, is as good as destroyed, while the subsequent act, not having fallen from its own time, remains in its undestroyed form? For if the preceding act were performed at the time of the subsequent act, it would result in the destruction of what is not yet destroyed for the sake of restoring what is already destroyed. That would be like seeking life for one who is already dead by killing one who is still alive.
To this we reply: this is said because there is room for both [the primary and secondary meanings] at the time of performing the subsequent rite, and not because that [primary meaning] is absent.

Now, one might argue that since a time occurring near the primary time is obtained through its inseparable connection with the primary meaning, it is more appropriate to regard it as being used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).

True, this is so; nevertheless, because that time is indicated by the qualities of softness and so forth, and because the worldly usage of words such as "morning" (*prātaḥ*) occurs based on those qualities, it also possesses a figurative character (*gauṇatva*). Thus, the statement regarding its figurative nature is not contradictory.
But surely, since that has not been taught, how can its status as an object of apprehension be suspected?
We reply: by way of the principle of the substitute (pratinidhi).

[Objection: "In that case, by some kind of similarity, might the morning rites and so forth ever apply even at midday and other times? What undesirable consequence is there in this? [Response: Indeed, this would be undesirable because, at such times, one might fail to obtain the *saṅgava* period and others which possess extreme similarity and are associated with frequent figurative usage. Thus, regarding this doubt, someone—considering that in sentences connected with specific times, such as "the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) for the gods should be performed in the forenoon," the action is enjoined as subordinate (*guṇa*) to the time, and concluding that one should not perform the rite at another time for the sake of favoring the subordinate action by transgressing the enjoined time which is the primary factor—has set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, the author of the Siddhānta has replied: "For the action is enjoined with respect to the time, not the time with respect to the action."

Therefore, time is subordinate to the ritual actions themselves, because the action is enjoined with reference to the time. Consequently, when there is a lapse of the time that has been prescribed as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) relative to the action, one must perform the rite even at a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) in order to favor the principal action (*pradhāna*). For it is improper to abandon the action simply because the time has passed; indeed, one does not discard the remainder of a meal merely for the lack of a single condiment.

That is incorrect. First of all, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that the action (*karman*) is subordinate here is not tenable, because the action is connected with a fruit; according to the maxim "that which lacks a fruit when in proximity to something possessing a fruit is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it," it is time alone that is the subsidiary. Nor should it be argued that the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), since the action is for the sake of another—namely, time—because time is understood to be for the sake of the action that possesses the fruit. Furthermore, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) stating that desire is subordinate is also untenable, because it presents a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); for in this case, the action is not enjoined by way of restating time, as there is no other source from which the time is already established.

[Objection: "But surely, even if time is not established by another scriptural statement, it will be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known through worldly usage in the form of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth.

[Reply: Not so. For if there were an injunction of a ritual act (*karma-vidhi*) based on a restatement of the nature of time as established in the world, that injunction would be purposeless; this is because the injunction itself lacks fruit and, consequently, cannot serve as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of a fruitful ritual act. Furthermore, the time prescribed for this particular ritual act cannot be connected to any other ritual act, since that [other] act has been performed immediately after the performance of this very act.

But if that is so, then even in the case of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," since the injunction regarding the sacrifice is determined by restating the person desiring heaven as already understood from common worldly experience, how is it not the case that the injunction is purposeless?

It is said: although the connection of the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) with the sentence is perceived as being in the capacity of the objective (*uddeśyatayā*), nevertheless, because the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) first requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), and because the person is already established in existence and thus incapable of being such an object, it is heaven itself—the object of the desire—denoted by the term *svargakāma* that is presented as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The person desiring heaven, however, is merely restated (*anūdyate*) as something already established, just as in the case of "the priests proceed wearing red turbans," where since the priests (the subjects) are already established, the statement must be understood as referring solely to the previously unestablished attribute; so it is here as well. This has been stated by Maṇḍana Miśra:
"Because that which is to be brought about (bhāvya) is expected, words such as 'kāma' are intent upon that;

the predominance of the qualifier in cases such as 'daṇḍin' has been demonstrated. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that there is an injunction of an action (*karma-vidhi*) therein by way of restating the time. Thus, the aforementioned prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions are both untenable. What, then, are the correct ones?

It is said: First, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): when an obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rite has become incumbent by necessity, and since it must be accomplished in its proper form according to the injunction "one should act as far as one is able," it is established that if the prescribed materials cannot be obtained, one must take a substitute (*pratinidhi*) similar to them. By extension, when one's own time for performance is not attained, one should adopt a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*). As the author of the *Trikālaṇḍamaṇḍana* says: "When it is impossible to perform the rite at the primary time..."
"It should be performed even during the secondary time; for here, the secondary [time] is also of such a nature."
‘Such’ means similar to the primary time; by this, its fitness as a substitute is shown. They also demonstrate the acceptance of secondary time even on the day of death:
“A person who understands that obligatory rites must be performed somehow or other should not omit what has been reached, especially those pertaining to the ancestors. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"If rites prescribed for the day have indeed been omitted through negligence,
one should perform them all during the first watch of the night."
Indeed, one should not perform a Śrāddha at twilight or at night; this is the settled rule.
Regarding the phrase "atyādi" and so forth:

the prohibition of specific times such as the twilight (saṃdhyā) and others is only possible when there is a possibility of adopting those times in a secondary (gauṇa) sense. Furthermore, because of the force of the injunction "one should perform the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites in such a way as one is able," these [times] are treated as obligatory; therefore, other ancillaries (aṅga) besides these are non-obligatory (anitya).
And thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
The subordinate ministers may or may not exist.

Now, if it is not contradictory to adopt a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) when the primary time has passed, then it would follow that rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *pārvaṇaśrāddha*, which are prescribed for times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), ought to be performed on the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) and so forth in the absence of their prescribed times. What kind of consequence is this? For indeed, the proponent of adopting secondary time would simply accept that performance at those times. Furthermore, this adoption of secondary time does not apply to optional (*kāmya*) rites, because in those cases, it is established that only one capable of performing all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*). However, regarding any specific distinction in the performance of a rite when adopting secondary time, it is stated here following the discussion of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) mentioned by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana.
During these secondary periods of time, one should perform the ritual action enjoined;
one should perform the expiation prescribed in the section on penances.
One should perform a rite prescribed for a later time during these aforementioned secondary times (*gauṇakāla*).
An alternative view has also been stated by that same author:
"Or, one may perform it during the secondary time even without having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*)."

In this context, the perception of priority [of time] expressed by the word *akṛtvā* (without having done) is not intended to be significant. Thus, when it might follow that a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) is to be accepted, it is stated in reply: since in all cases that which is indicated by a locative case ending is, being non-prescriptive (*anupādeya*), denoted as a causal condition (*nimitta*) whose sole nature is that of a subject of reference (*uddeśya*), and since there can be no entitlement (*adhikāra*) without the prescribed time when it serves as a qualification of the entitled person, an act performed at another time would be as if unperformed; therefore, one should not accept a secondary time. Furthermore, the absence of entitlement in the absence of the prescribed time was established in the section concerning the *Sāntapanīyā* sacrifice, under the sūtra: "And because the cause is brought forward."
For this very reason, Laugākṣi says:
"Time is known through calculation; the deities abide in time.
An offering made at the proper time, even if it is but one, is superior to millions or tens of millions made at the wrong time."

As for the mention of the acceptance of secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana, that was stated by him while mistakenly regarding a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), and thus it should be disregarded. As for the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) beginning with "in whatever way possible" (*yathā kathaṃcit*), secondary time is not being propounded there; rather, non-acceptance [of secondary time] is what is intended. For this is the meaning understood from it: one must not effect the omission or non-performance of a rite that has arrived at its own proper time simply because of the lack of primary materials and the like; rather, at that very same time, the rite must be performed even if it is somewhat deficient by employing something similar to the primary material, however it may be. Furthermore, as for the statement "rites prescribed for the day," etc., by that it is not said that for all rites and all secondary times, there is an acceptance of secondary times through the logic of secondary time; rather, for only certain rites, some other time is enjoined as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), which—according to the logic [of the primary time]—was not otherwise obtained. Therefore, on the strength of this statement, rites enjoined for specific times such as the year, season, month, or lunar day (*tithi*) cannot properly be performed at another time when those respective times have passed. As for the prohibition of *śrāddha* during twilight and at night, that too is applicable only to what is obtained through delusion produced by a lack of reasoning, just as eating [forbidden food] might be obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*). Or else:
These two are the perfection of a Brahmin regarding the Śrāddha:
a desire for it whether at the improper time or the proper time; thus, the Tīrtha-Śrāddha should always be performed by men.

This prohibition against performing the *śrāddha* during times such as the twilights (*saṃdhyā*) applies specifically to those instances where the *śrāddha* would otherwise fall outside the afternoon and other prescribed periods, as indicated by such statements as "for [the rite] must be performed precisely at the time of attainment. As for the observed performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites during secondary (*gauṇa*) times when the primary time has lapsed: in some cases this is for the sake of avoiding the reproach of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) or for mental satisfaction; in other cases, it is an injunction for an alternative method (*anukalpa*) as a different course of action. Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, since one lacks the qualification (*adhikāra*) to perform the rite once the prescribed time has passed, one should not intentionally let the primary time lapse out of greed for the principal materials. This very point was raised with due deliberation and resolved by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana.
If the primary means of accomplishment is not available at the primary time,
then between that time and the substance, which one is primary and which is secondary?
Relying upon the primary time, one should employ the secondary as a means for the primary;
one should not wait for the secondary time out of greed for the primary substance.

Thus, this is established: in the absence of an explicit statement, there should be no acceptance of a secondary time; however, when such a statement exists, a secondary [time] is accepted. Therefore, even the subsequent [time] must be accepted.

Thus ends the *Kālanirṇaya* (Determination of Time) in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, who was the sovereign over all the faculties of the illustrious Mahādevī, the supreme king of kings, and a master of all branches of knowledge.
May there be auspiciousness.
